Gellius, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMEN">flamen</a> Dialis might not on any account enter a place where there was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, to prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> from being corrupted by the stench of putrefied bodies, and the buildings from being endangered by the frequency of funeral fires. Burying in churches was not allowed for the first 300 years after Christ; and the same was severely prohibited by the Christian emperors for many ages afterwards. The first step towards it appears to have been the practice of erecting churches over the graves of some martyrs in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and translating the relics of others into churches in the city; the next was, allowing kings and emperors to be buried in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATRIUM">atrium</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-porch. In the 6th century, the people began to be admitted into the church-yards; and some princes, founders, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, into the church. From that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> seems to have been left to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the bishop.

BUSBECK

Pages 32-32

AUGER GISLEN, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">LORD</a> OF, a person illustrious on account of his embassies, was born at Comines in the year 1522; and educated at the most famous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>. He was engaged in several important employments and negotiations, and particularly was twice sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Soliman. He collected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>; bought <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>; searched after rare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; inquired into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of animals; and in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> journey to Constantinople, carried with him a painter, that he might be able to communicate to the curious the figures, at least, of the plants and animals that were not well known in the west. He wrote a Discourse of the state of the Ottoman empire, and a Relation of his two Journeys to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, which are much esteemed. He died in 1592.

BUSBY

Pages 32-33

DR RICHARD, son of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in Westminster, was born at Lutton in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> in 1656. He passed through the classes in Westminster school, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s scholar; and completed his studies at Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. In 1640 he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Westminster school; and by his skill and diligence in the discharge of this important and laborious office, for the space of 55 years, bred up the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of eminent men, in church and state, that ever at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> adorned any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. He was extremely severe in his school; though he applauded <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> in his scholars, even when it reflected on himself. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and healthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> purchased by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, died in 1605, aged 89; and was buried in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, where there is a fine monument erected for him, with a Latin inscription. He composed several books for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his school.

BUSH

Pages 33-33

Paul, the first bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, became a student in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> about the year 1513, and in 1518 took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of arts. He afterwards became a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the order called bonhommes; of which, after studying some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> among the friars of St Austin (now Wadham <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>), he was elected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a>. In that station he lived many years; till at length <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII, being informed of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> knowledge in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and physic, made him his chaplain, and in 1542 appointed him to the new episcopal see of Bristol: but having in the reign of Edward VI, taken a wife, he was, on the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, deprived of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and spent the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in a private station at Bristol, where he died in the year 1558, aged 68, and was buried on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the choir of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. Wood says, that while he was a student at Oxford, he was numbered among the celebrated poets of that university; and Pits gives him the character of a faithful Catholic in his want of chastity notwithstanding. He wrote, 1. An exhortation to Margaret <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">Burgess</a>, wife to John Burgess, clothier of King's wood, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Wilts. Lond. printed in the reign of Edward VI. 8vo. 2. Notes on the Psalms. 3. Treatise in praise of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. 4. Answer to certain queries concerning the abuse of the mails. Records, No. 25. 5. Dialogues between Christ and the Virgin Mary. 6. Treatise of salves and curing remedies. 7. A little treatise in English, called The extirpation of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, &c. in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, Lond. by Pinson, 4to. 8. Carmina diversa. Bush, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> of the same kind growing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together: thus we say, a furze-bush, bramble-bush, &c. Bush is sometimes used, in a more general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, for any assemblage of thick branches interwoven and mixed together.

BUSH ALSO

Pages 33-33

h also denotes a coronated frame of wood hung out as a sign of taverns. It takes the denomination from hence, that, evidently, signs where wine was sold were bushes chiefly of ivy, cypresses, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like plant, which keeps its verdure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. And hence the English proverb, "Good wine needs no bush." <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">Burning</a>-Bush, that bush wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> appeared to Moles at the foot of Mount Horeb, as he was feeding his father-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>'s flocks. As to the person that appeared in the bush, the text says, "That the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of fire, out of the middle of the bush;" but whether it was a created angel, speaking in the person of God, or God himself, or (as the most received <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is) Christ the Son of God, has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of some controversy among the learned. Those who suppose it no more than an angel, seem to imply that it would be a diminution of the majesty of God, to appear upon every occasion, especially when he has such a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of celestial ministers, who may do the business as well. But considering that God is present everywhere, the notification of his presence by some outward sign in one determinate <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> (which is all we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> by his appearance), is in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> less laborious (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> anything laborious could be conceived of God) than a delegation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> upon every turn from heaven, and seems in the main to illustrate rather than debase the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and existence. But however this be, it is plain that the angel here spoken of was no created being, from the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEXT">context</a>, and especially from his saying, "I am the Lord God, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEHOVAH">Jehovah</a>," &c. since this is not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of angels, who are always known to express themselves in such humble terms as these, "I am sent from God; I am thy fellow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>," &c. It is a vain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> to say, that an angel, as God's <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, may speak in God's name and person; for what ambassador of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> ever yet said, "I am the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>?" Since therefore no angel, without the guilt of blasphemy, could assume these titles; and since neither God the Father nor the Holy Ghost, are ever called by the name of angel, i.e. "messenger, or person sent," whereas God the Son is called by the prophet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACHI">Malachi</a> (chap. iii. 1.), "The angel of the covenant;" it hence seems to follow, that this angel of the Lord was God the Son, who might very properly be called an angel, because in the fulness of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was sent into the world in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, as a messenger from God, and might therefore make these his temporary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a> prefigures and forerunners, as it were, of his more solemn mission. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of the burning-bush is used as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Scotland, with this motto: Nec tamen confumebatur; i.e. "Though burning, is never consumed."

BUSHEL

Pages 33-33

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of capacity for things dry; as grains, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, &c. containing four pecks, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> eight gallons, or one eighth of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. Du Cange derives the word from buffellus, buffellus, or biffellus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of bus, or busa, used in the corrupt Latin for the same thing; others derive it from buffulus, an urn, wherein lots were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>; which seems to be a corruption from buxulus. Buffellus appears to have been first used for a liquid measure of wine, equal to eight gallons. Osto librae faciunt galonem vini, et octo galones vini faciunt buffellum <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, qua est octava pars quarterii. It was soon after transferred to the dry measure of corn of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>.—Pondus octo librorum fragmenti facit buffellum, de quibus octo confugit quarterium. By 12 Henry VII. c. 5, a bushel is to contain 8 gallons of wheat; the gallon 8 pounds of wheat <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">troy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> 12 ounces troy-weight; the ounce 20 shillings; and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> 32 grains, or corn of wheat, growing in the midst of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. This standard bushel is kept in the Exchequer; when being filled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and the water measured before the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons in 1696, in a regular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLELOPIPED">parallelopiped</a>, it was found to contain 2145.6 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> inches; and the said water being weighed, amounting to 1131 ounces and 14 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>-weights troy. Besides the standard or legal bushel, we have several local bushels, of different dimensions in different places. At Abington and Andover, a bushel contains <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> gallons: at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPLEBY">Appleby</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENRITH">Penrith</a>, a bushel of peas, rye, and wheat, contains 16 gallons: of barley, big malt, mixt malt, and oats, 20 gallons. A bushel contains, at Carlisle, 24 gallons; at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, a bushel of wheat, rye, &c. contains 32 gallons, and of oats 40: at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORCHESTER">Dorchester</a>, a bushel of malt and oats contains

BUSIRIS

Pages 33-34

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, to the south of Leontopolis, on that branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> called Bafriticus: Built by Busiris, noted for his cruelty, and slain by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, (Ovid, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Diodorus Siculus). Strabo denies such a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> ever existed; Ifocrates has written his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>. In this city there stood a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> temple of Isis, which gave it the appellation of the city of Isis. It was destroyed on a revolt by Diocletian.

BUSIRITICUS FLUVIUS

Pages 34-34

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, that branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> which empties itself at the mouth called Oftium Pathmeicum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Phatniticum, (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, according to an ancient map at the Oftium Mindeium; this river, or branch, dividing itself at Diospolis into two branches; called Bafriticus, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Bafiris, which stood on its left, or west branch. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> branch of the Nile, reckoning from the east. Buriaticus Nomos, in Ancient Geography, a prefecture, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; so called from the city Bafiris, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Pliny, Ptolemy.)

BUSITIS

Pages 34-34

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a district of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Deserta; so called from Bus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Buz, Nahor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Elihu, the fourth interlocutor in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>; called Buzetos, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>.

BUSKIN

Pages 34-34

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>, somewhat in manner of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOOT">boot</a>, and adapted to either foot, and worn by either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of dress, covering both the foot and mid-leg, was tied underneath the knee; it was very rich and fine, and principally used on the stage by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> in tragedy. It was of a quadrangular form; and the sole was so thick, as that, by means thereof, men of the ordinary stature might be raised to the pitch and elevation of the heroes they personated. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> was generally purple on the stage; herein it was distinguished from the sock worn in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, that being only a low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> shoe. The buskin seems to have been worn not only by actors but by girls, to raise their height; travellers and hunters also made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it, to defend themselves from the mire. In classic authors, we frequently find the buskin used to signify tragedy itself, in regard it was a mark of tragedy on the stage. It was also to be understood for a lofty strain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> style.

BUSS

Pages 34-34

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs, a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> vessel, used by us and the Dutch in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>-fishery, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> from 48 to 60 tons burden, and sometimes more: a bus has two small sheds <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cabins, one at the prow and the other at the stern; that at the prow serves for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>. Every bus has a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, an assistant, a mate, and seamen in proportion to the vessel's size; the master commands in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, and without his express orders the nets cannot be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> or taken up; the assistant has the command after him; and the mate next, whose business is to see the seamen manage their rigging in a proper manner, to mind those who draw in their nets, and those who kill, gut, and cure the herrings as they are taken out of the sea: the seamen generally engage for a whole voyage in the lump. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> which they take on board the buses, consist commonly in biscuit, oat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, and dried or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> fish; the crew being content for the rest with what fresh fish they catch. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">Fisheries</a>.

BUSTUARI

Pages 34-35

in Roman antiquity, gladiators who fought about the bustum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> funeral pile of a person of distinction, that the blood which was spilt might serve as a sacrifice to the infernal gods, and render them more propitious to the manes of the deceased. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was introduced in the room of the more inhuman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> one of sacrificing captives at the bustum, or on the tombs of warriors.

BUSTUARIAE MORS

Pages 34-34

according to some, women that were hired to accompany the funeral and lament the loss of the deceased: but others are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that they were rather the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> prostitutes, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> among the tombs, graves, and other such lonely places.

BUSTUM

Pages 35-35

in antiquity, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pile of wood, whereon were anciently placed the bodies of the deceased, in order to be burnt. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> borrowed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> their dead from the Greeks. The deceased, crowned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and drested in his richest habits, was laid on the bustum. Some authors say, it was only called bustum, after the burning, quae bene ubicum: before the burning it was more properly called pyra; during it, rogus; and afterwards, bustum. When the body was only burnt there, and buried elsewhere, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was not properly called bustum, but ufrina, or ufrinum. Bustum, in the Campus Martius, was a structure whereon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Augustus first, and after him the bodies of his successors, were burnt. It was built of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, surrounded with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> pallisade, and planted within side with alder trees. Bustum was also figuratively applied to denote any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>. Whence those phrases, facere bustum, violare bustum, &c. Bustum of an Altar, was the hearth or place where the fire was kindled.

BUTCHER

Pages 35-35

a person who slaughters cattle for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> who cuts up and retails the same. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, there were three kinds of established butchers, whose office it was to furnish the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> with the necessary cattle, and to take care of preparing and vending their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. The first provided hogs; the pecuarii or boarii, other cattle, especially oxen; and under these was a subordinate class, whose office was to kill, called lanii, and carniciers. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the office of butcher among the Jews with dexterity, was of more reputation than to under- stand the liberal arts and sciences. They have a book concerning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHAMBLES">shambles</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of any difficulty, they apply to some learned rabbi for advice; nor was any allowed to practise this art, without a li- cense in form; which gave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of his abilities, a power to kill meat, and others to eat what he killed; provided he carefully read every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> for one year, and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> the next year, and once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> during his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, the constitution above- mentioned. We have some very good laws for the better regula- tion and preventing the abuses committed by butchers. A butcher that sells swine's flesh mealed, or dead of the murrain, for the first offence shall be amerced; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, have the pillory; for the third, be impris- oned, and make fine; and for the fourth, abjure the town. Butchers not selling meat at reasonable prices shall forfeit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the value, leviable by warrant of two justices of the peace. No butcher shall kill any flesh in his scalding-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, or within the walls of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, on pain to forfeit for every ox so killed 12d. and for every other beast, 8d. to be divided betwixt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and the prosecutor. Butcher-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>. See Lanius, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Butcher-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">Broom</a>. See Ruscus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Butcher-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, in the East Indies, a small island about two miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and scarce one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. It has its name from cattle being kept there for the use of Bom- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, from which it is about three miles distant. It has a small fort, but of very little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. Bute, an island lying to the west of Scotland, being separated from Cowal, a district of Argyllshire, only by a narrow channel. In length it is about 18 miles; the broadest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> from east to west is about five. Part of it is rocky and barren; but from the middle south- wards, the ground is cultivated, and produces peas, oats, and barley. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which the natives have used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a fort and chapel in the neighbourhood of Rothay, which is a very ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough, head town of the shire of Bute and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAN">Arran</a>; but very thinly peopled, and maintained chiefly by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> fishery, with the profits of which all the rents of this island are chiefly paid. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of Rothay, are the ruins of an ancient fort, with its drawbridge, chapel, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>. Here are likewise the remains of some Danish towers. The natives are healthy and industrious, speak the Erse and the dia- lect of the Lowlands indifferently, and profess the Pro- testant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The island is divided into two parishes, accommodated with four churches; and belongs chiefly to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Bute, who possesses an elegant seat on the east side of the island. The name of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> has been variously written, as Bote, Both, Bothe, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOOT">Boot</a>, but now generally Bute. Our ancient writers suppose that it derived its name from a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> erected therein by St. Brendan, an Irish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> who flourished in the 6th century, because in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> such a cell was called Both. It is, however, probable, that this name was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, since we find it denominated Botis by the anonymous geographer of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>. It was from very early times part of the patrimony of the Stuarts: <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> possessions in it were granted to Sir John Stuart, son of Robert II. by his beloved mistress <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> More; and it has <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in that line to the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUTESHIRE">Buteshire</a>, comprehends the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Bute, Arran, the greater and lesser Cumbrae, and Ince-mar- noc. This shire and that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAITHNESS">Caithness</a> send a member to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> alternately. The earl of Bute is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> from his majesty; but no way dependent on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> admiral of Scot- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>: so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> case occurs within this jurisdiction, (even crimes of as high a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as mur- der or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRACY">piracy</a>), his lordship, by virtue of his powers as admiral, is sufficient judge, or he may delegate his au- thority to any deputies. The following is a view of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of this county at two different periods, taken from the Statisti- cal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Scotland. | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">Parish</a> | Population in 1755 | Population in 1790–1798 | |--------|------------------|----------------------| | Bute | | | | Rothay | 2222 | 4032 | | Kingarth | 998 | 727 | | Kilbride | 1369 | 2545 | | Arran | | | | Kilmorie | 2127 | 329 | | Total | 6866 | 10,563 | Increase, 3697 Buteo,

BUTLER

Pages 36-37
Charles, a native of Wycomb in the county of Bucks, and a master of arts in Magdalen college, Oxford, published a book with this title, "The principles of music in singing and setting; with the twofold use thereof, ecclesiastical and civil." Quarto, London 1636. The author of this book was a person of singular learning and ingenuity, which he manifested in sundry other works enumerated by Wood in the Athen. Oxon. Among the rest is an English grammar, published in 1633, in which he proposes a scheme of regular orthography, and makes use of characters, some borrowed from the Saxon, and others of his own invention, so singular, that we want types to exhibit them; and of this imagined improvement he appears to have been so fond, that all his tracts are printed in like manner with his grammar; the consequence whereof has been an almost general disgust to all that he has written. His "Principles of Music" is, however, a very learned, curious, and entertaining book; and, by the help of the advertisement from the printer to the reader, prefixed to it, explaining the powers of the several characters made use of by him, may be read to great advantage, and may be considered a judicious supplement to Morley's introduction. Butler, Samuel, a celebrated poet, was the son of a reputable Worcestershire farmer, and was born in 1612. He passed some time at Cambridge, but was never matriculated in that university. Returning to his native country, he lived some years as clerk to a justice of peace; where he found sufficient time to apply himself to history, poetry, and painting. Being recommended to Elizabeth countess of Kent, he enjoyed in her house, not only the use of all kinds of books, but the conversation of the great Mr Selden, who often employed Butler to write letters, and translate for him. He lived also some time with Sir Samuel Luke, a gentleman of an ancient family in Bedfordshire, and a famous commander under Oliver Cromwell; and he is supposed at this time to have wrote, or at least to have planned, his celebrated Hudibras; and under that character to have ridiculed the knight. The poem itself furnishes this key; where, in the first canto, Hudibras says, "Tis sung, there is a valiant mamaluke "In foreign land yclep'd — — — "To whom we oft have been compar'd "For person, parts, address, and beard." After the Restoration, Mr Butler was made secretary to the earl of Carbury, lord president of Wales, who appointed him steward of Ludlow castle, when the court was revived there. No one was a more generous friend to him than the earl of Dorset and Middlesex, to whom it was owing that the court raised his Hudibras. He had promises of a good place from the earl of Clarendon, but they were never accomplished; though the king was so much pleased with the poem, as often to quote it pleasantly in conversation. It is indeed said, that Charles ordered him the sum of 300l.; but the sum being expressed in figures, somebody through whose hands the order passed, by cutting off a cypher reduced it to 30l., which, though it passed the offices without fees, proved not sufficient to pay what he then owed; so that Butler was not a chilling Butler, the better for the king's bounty. He died in 1680; and though he met with many disappointments, was never reduced to anything like want, nor did he die in debt. Mr Granger observes, that Butler "stands without rival in burlesque poetry. His Hudibras (says he) is in its kind, almost as great an effort of genius, as the Paradise Lost itself. It abounds with uncommon learning, new rhimes, and original thoughts. Its images are truly and naturally ridiculous. There are many strokes of temporary satire, and some characters and allusions which cannot be discovered at this distance of time." Butler, Joepb, late bishop of Durham, a prelate distinguished by his piety and learning, was the youngest son of Mr Thomas Butler, a reputable shopkeeper at Wantage in Berkshire, where he was born in the year 1692. His father, who was a Presbyterian, observing that he had a strong inclination to learning, after his being at a grammar-school, sent him to an academy in Gloucestershire, in order to qualify him for a dissenting minister; and while there, he wrote some remarks on Dr Clarke's first sermon at Boyle's lecture. Afterwards, resolving to conform to the established church, he studied at Oriel college, where he contracted an intimate friendship with Mr Edward Talbot, son of the bishop of Durham, and brother to the lord chancellor, who laid the foundation of his subsequent advancement. He was first appointed preacher at the Rolls, and rector of Haughton and Stanhope, two rich benefices in the bishopric of Durham. He quitted the Rolls in 1726; and published in 8vo, a volume of sermons, preached at that chapel. After this he constantly resided at Stanhope, in the regular discharge of all the duties of his office, till the year 1733, when he was called to attend the lord chancellor Talbot as his chaplain, who gave him a prebend in the church of Rochester. In the year 1736, he was appointed clerk of the closet to Queen Caroline, whom he attended every day, by her majesty's special command, from seven to nine in the evening. In 1738 he was appointed to the bishopric of Bristol; and not long afterwards to the deanery of St Paul's, London. He now resigned his living of Stanhope. In the year 1746, he was made clerk of the closet to the king; and in 1752, was translated to Durham. This rich preferment he enjoyed but a short time; for he died at Bath June 16, 1752. His corpse was interred in the cathedral at Bristol; where there is a monument, with an inscription, erected to his memory. He died a bachelor. His deep learning and comprehensive mind appear sufficiently in his writings, particularly in that excellent treatise entitled, The Analogy of Religion, natural and revealed, to the Constitution and Course of Nature, published in 8vo, 1736. Butler, the name anciently given to an officer in the court of France, being the same as the grand echevin, or great cupbearer of the present times. Butler, in the common acceptation of the word, is an officer in the houses of princes and great men, whose principal business is to look after the wine, plate, &c. Butlerage of wine, is a duty of 2s. for every ton of wine imported by merchant strangers; being a composition in lieu of the liberties and freedoms grant- Butlerage was originally the only custom that was payable upon the importation of wines, and was taken and received by virtue of the regal prerogative, for the proper use of the crown. But for many years past, there having been granted by parliament subsidies to the kings of England, and the duty of butlerage not repealed, but confirmed, they have been pleased to grant the same way to some noblemen, who by virtue of such grant, is to enjoy the full benefit and advantage thereof, and may cause the same to be collected in the same manner that the kings themselves were formerly wont to do. BUTMENT. Butments of arches are the same with buttresses. They answer to what the Romans call ful-licas, the French culées and butées. Butments, or Abutments, of a bridge, denote the two masses at the end of a bridge, whereby the two extreme arches are sustained and joined with the shore on either side.

BUTRINTO

Pages 37-37

a port-town of Epirus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Canina, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, situated opposite to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Corfu, at the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 20. 40. N. Lat. 39. 45. BUTT is used for a vessel, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of wine, containing two hogsheads, or 126 gallons; otherwise called pipe. A butt of currants is from 1500 to 2000 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Butts, or Butt-ends, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, are the fore ends of all planks under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, as they rise, and are joined one end to another.—Butt-ends in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ships are most carefully bolted; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any one of them should <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> or give way, the leak would be very dangerous and difficult to stop. Butts, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where archers meet with their bows and arrows to shoot at a mark, which is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> at the butts: (See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">Archery</a>.)—Also butts are the short pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> in arable ridges and furrows.

BUTTER

Pages 37-38

a fat unctuous substance, prepared from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> churning. It was late ere the Greeks appear to have had any notion of butter; their poets make no mention of it, and are yet frequently speaking of milk and cheese. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> used butter no otherwise than as a medicine, never as a food. According to Beckman, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of butter belongs neither to the Greeks nor the Romans. The former, he thinks, derived their knowledge of butter from the Scythians, the Thracians and Phrygians; and the latter from the people of Germany. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> burnt butter in their lamps instead of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; and in the Roman churches, it was anciently allowed, during Christmas <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, to burn butter instead of oil, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> consumption of it otherwise. Butter is the fat, oily, and inflammable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the milk. This kind of oil is naturally distributed through all the substance of the milk in very small particles, which are interposed between the calcareous and ferrous parts, amongst which it is suspended by a slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a>, but without being dissolved. It is in the same state in which oil is in emulsions: hence the same whitening of milk and emulsions; and hence, by rest, the oily parts separate from both these liquors to the surface, and form a cream. See Emulsion. When butter is in the state of cream, its proper oily parts are not yet sufficiently united together to form a homogeneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. They are still half separated by the interposition of a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ferrous and calcareous particles. The butter is completely formed by pressing out these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> parts by means of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> percussion. It then becomes an uniform soft mass. Fresh butter which has undergone no change, has scarce any smell; its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is mild and agreeable; it melts with a weak <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and none of its principles are disengaged by the heat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. These properties prove, that the oily part of butter is of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the fat, fixed, and mild oils obtained from many vegetable substances by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. See Oils.—The half fluid consistence of butter, as of most other concrete oily matters, is thought to be owing to a considerable quantity of acid united with the oily part; which acid is so well combined, that it is not perceptible while the butter is fresh and has undergone no change; but when it grows old, and undergoes some kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, then the acid is disengaged more and more; and this is the cause that butter, like oils of the same kind, becomes rancid by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Butter is constantly used in food, from its agreeable taste; but to be wholesome, it must be very fresh and free from rancidity, and also not fried or burnt; otherwise its acrid and even caustic acid, being disengaged, disorders digestion, renders it difficult and painful, excites acid empyreumatic belchings, and introduces much acrimony into the blood. Some persons have stomachs so delicate, that they are even affected with these inconveniences by fresh butter and milk. This observation is also applicable to oil, fat, chocolate, and in general to all oleaginous matters. For the making of butter see <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The trade in butter is very considerable. Some compute 50,000 tons annually consumed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is chiefly made within 40 miles round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Fifty thousand firkins are said to be sent yearly from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> alone: each <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIRKIN">firkin</a> containing 56lbs. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UTTOXETER">Uttoxeter</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a> is a market famous for good butter, insomuch that the London <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> have established a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> there for that article. It is bought by the pot, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> cylindrical form, weighing 14lb. Shower of Butter. Naturalists speak of showers and dews of a butyric acid substance. In 1695, there fell in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, during the winter and ensuing <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, a thick <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>, which had the medicinal properties of butter. Butter, among chemists, a name given to several preparations, on account of their consistence resembling that of butter; as butter of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index. Butter-Bur. See Tussilago, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Butter-Milk, the milk which remains after the butter is produced by churning. Butter milk is esteemed an excellent food, in the spring especially, and is particularly Butterwort <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTON">Button</a>. Butter-Worm. See Pinguicula, Botany Index.

BUTTERFLY

Pages 38-38

the English name of a numerous genus of insects. See Papilio, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. BUTTERFLY-Shell. See Voluta, <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> Index. Method of preserving Butterflies. See Insects. Method of making Pictures of Butterflies. "Take butterflies <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> field moths, either those caught abroad, or such as are taken in caterpillars and nurled in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> till they be flies; clip off their wings very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to their bodies, and lay them on clean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, in the form of a butterfly when <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>; then have ready prepared <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> arabic that hath been some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> dissolved in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and is pretty thick; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you put a drop of ox-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALL">gall</a> into a spoonful of this, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be better for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; temper them well with your finger, and spread a little of it on a piece of thin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> paper, big enough to take both sides of your fly; when it begins to be clammy under your finger, the paper is in proper order to take the feathers from the wings of the fly; then lay the gummed side on the wings, and it will take them up: then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> your paper so as to have all the wings between the paper; then lay it on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, pressing it close with your fingers; and you may rub it gently with some smooth hard thing; then open the paper and take out the wings, which will come forth transparent: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> of the upper and under side of the wings, sticking to the gummed paper, form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> likeness of both sides of the wings in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> shapes and colours. The nicety of taking off flies depends on a just <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of moisture of the gummed paper: for if it be too wet, all will be blotted and confused; and if too dry, your paper will stick too fast together, that it will be torn in separation. When you have opened your gummed papers, and they are dry, you must draw the bodies from the natural ones, and paint them in water colours: you must take paper that will bear <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> very well for this use; for sticking paper will separate with the rest, and spoil all."

BUTTERIS

Pages 38-38

in the manage, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, fitted to a wooden handle, wherewith they pare the foot, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cut off the hoof, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. BUTTOCK of a Ship, is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of her which is her breadth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> aft, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TACK">tack</a> upwards; and a ship is said to have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> or narrow buttock, according as she is built broad or narrow at the transom.

BUTTON

Pages 38-39

an article in drefs, whose form and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> are too well known to need <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. They are made of various materials, as mohair, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, metal, &c. Method of making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> Buttons. Common buttons are generally made of mohair; some indeed are made of silk, and others of thread; but the latter are of a very inferior sort. In order to make a button, the mohair must be previously wound on a bobbin; and the mould fixed to a board by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BODKIN">bodkin</a> thrust through the hole in the middle of it. This being done, the workman wraps the mohair round the mould in three, four, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five columns, according to the button. Horse-hair Buttons. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> of these buttons are covered with a kind of stuff composed of silk and hair; the warp being belladine silk, and the shott horse hair. This stuff is wove with two selvages, in the same manner and in the same loom as ribbands. It is then cut into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> pieces <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the size of the button, wrapped round the moulds, and the selvages stitched together, which form the under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the button. Cleaning of Buttons. A button is not finished when it comes from the maker's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; the superfluous hair and hubs of silk must be taken off, and the button rendered glossy and beautiful before it can be sold. This is done in the following manner: A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of buttons are put into a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> sieve, called by workmen a fingeing box. Then a little spirit of wine being poured into a kind of shallow iron <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a>, and set on fire, the workman moves and shakes the fingeing box, containing the buttons, briskly over the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of the spirit, by which the superfluous hairs, hubs of silk, &c. are burnt off, without damaging the buttons. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> care, however, must be taken that the buttons in the fingeing box be kept continually in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are suffered to rest over the flame, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> immediately burn. When all these loose hairs, &c. are burnt off by the flame of the spirit, the buttons are taken out of the fingeing box, and put, with a proper quantity of the crumbs of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> bag, about three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and of a conical shape; the mouth or smaller end of which being tied up, the workman takes one of the ends in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and the other in the other, and shakes the hand briskly with a particular jerk. This operation cleanses the buttons, renders them very glossy, and fit for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>-twist Buttons. The mould of these buttons is first covered in the same manner with that of common buttons. This being done, the whole is covered with a thin plate of gold or silver, and then wrought over of different forms, with purple and gimp. The former is a kind of thread composed of silk and gold wire twisted together; and the latter, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CAPILLARY">capillary</a> tubes of gold or silver, about the tenth of an inch long. These are joined together by means of a fine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, filled with silk, thrust through their apertures, in the same manner as beads or bugles. The manner of making Metal Buttons. The metal with which the moulds are intended to be covered is first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into small ingots, and then flattened into thin plates or leaves, of the thickness intended, at the flattening <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>; after which it is cut into small round pieces proportionable to the size of the mould they are intended to cover, by means of proper punches on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of wood covered with a thick plate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. Each piece of metal thus cut out of the plate is reduced into the form of a button, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> it successively in several cavities, or concave moulds, of a spherical form, with a convex punchon of iron, always beginning with the shallowest cavity of the mould, and proceeding to the deeper, till the plate has acquired the intended form: and the better to manage to thin a plate, they form ten, twelve, and sometimes even twenty-four, to the cavities, or concave moulds, at once; often nealing the metal during the operation, to make it more ductile. This plate is generally called by workmen the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> of the button. The form being thus given to the plates or caps, they they strike the intended <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the convex side by means of a similar iron punchen, in a kind of mould engraven en creux, either by the hammer or the press used in coining. The cavity or mould, wherein the impression is to be made, is of a diameter and depth suitable to the sort of button intended to be struck in it; each kind requiring a particular mould. Between the punchen and the plate is placed a thin piece of lead, called by workmen a bob, which greatly contributes to the taking off all the strokes of the engraving; the lead, by reason of its softness, easily giving way to the parts that have relievo, and as easily infusing itself into the traces or indentures. The plate thus prepared makes the cap or shell of the button. The lower part is formed of another plate, in the same manner, but much flatter, and without any impression. To the last or under plate is soldered a small eye made of wire, by which the button is to be fastened. The two plates being thus finished, they are soldered together with soft folder, and then turned in a lathe. Generally indeed they use a wooden mould, instead of the under plate; and in order to fasten it, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> a thread or gut across, through the middle of the mould, and fill the cavity between the mould and the cap with cement, in order to render the button firm and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>; for the cement entering all the cavities formed by the relievo of the other side, sustains it, prevents its flattening, and preserves its bossie or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. Button, in the manage. Button of the reins of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of leather, with the reins passed through it, which runs all along the length of the reins. To put a horse under the button, is when a horse is stopped without a rider upon his back, the reins being laid on his neck, and the button lowered so far <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> that the reins bring in the horse's head, and fix it to the true posture or carriage. It is not only the horses which are managed in the hand that must be put under the button; for the same method must be taken with such horses as are bred between two pillars, before they are backed. Button-Wood. See Cephalanthus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Button's-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>, the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> part of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's bay</a>, in North <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, by which Sir Thomas Button attempted to find out a north-west passage to the East Indies. It lies between 80° and 100° west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between 60° and 65° north latitude. Button-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a kind of figured stone, so denominated from its resembling the button of a garment. Dr Hook gives the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of three sorts of button-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which seem to have been nothing else but the filling up of three several sorts of shells. They are all of them very hard flints; and have this in common, that they consist of two bodies, which seem to have been the filling up of two holes or vents in the shell. Dr Plot describes a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> finely iridated from the top, after the manner of some hair buttons. This name is also given to a peculiar species of flate found in the marquisate of Baireith, in a mountain called Fichtelberg; which is extremely different from the common sorts of flate, in that it runs with great ease into glass in five or six hours <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, without the addition of any <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> or other foreign substance, to promote its vitrification, as other stones require. It contains in itself all the principles of glass, and really has mixed in its substance the things necessary to be added to promote the fusion of other stony bodies. The Swedes and Germans make buttons of the glass produced from it, which is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and shining, and it has hence its name button-glass. They make several other things also of this glass, as the handles of knives and the like, and send a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of it unwrought in round cakes, as it cools from the fusion, into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUTTRESS">Buttress</a>, a kind of buttment built archwise, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of stone or brick, serving to prop or support the sides of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, wall, &c., on the outside, where it is either very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, or has any considerable load to sustain on the other side, as a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, &c.—Buttresses, are used against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of steeples and other buildings of stone, &c., on the outside, and along the walls of such buildings as have great and heavy roofs, which would be subject to thrust the walls out, unless very thick, if no buttresses were placed against them. They are also placed for a support and buttment against the feet of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, that are turned across great halls in old palaces, abbeys, &c.

BUTUS

Pages 39-39

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, on the west side of the branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, called Thermuthiacus; towards the mouth called Ophium Sebennyticum: in this town stood an oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LATONA">Latona</a>, (Strabo, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>). <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> places Butus in the Nomos Phthemonotes; it is also called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUTO">Buto</a>, -us, (Herodotus, Stephanus). It had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, but the largest was that of Latona, where the oracle stood.

BUTZAW

Pages 39-39

a town of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, in Germany; it stands upon the river Varnow, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Schwerin to Rostock, lying in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 12. N. Lat. 54. 50.

BUVETTE

Pages 39-39
or Beuvette, in the French laws, an established place in every court, where the lawyers and counsellors may retire, warm themselves, and take a glass of wine by way of refreshment, at the king's charge. There is one for each court of parliament, but there are only for persons belonging to that body; there are others in the palais, whither other persons also resort.

BUXENTUM

Pages 39-39

(Livy, Velleius, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Mela, Pliny); Pyxus, (Strabo, Pliny); a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>, first built by the people of Meliana, but afterwards deserted, (Strabo). A Roman colony was sent thither, (Livy, Velleius): and when found still thin of inhabitants, a new colony was sent by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. Its name is from baxus, the box-tree, growing plentifully there. Strabo says, the name Pyxus includes a promontory, port, and river, under one. Now Pulica/bro, in the Hither Principato of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 40. N. Lat. 40. 20.

BUXTON

Pages 39-41

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the peak of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, celebrated for its medicinal waters, and lying in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 20. N. Lat. 53. 20. It has been always believed by our antiquaries, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were acquainted with these <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, and had frequented them much, as there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> way still visible, called the Bath-gate, from Burgh to this place. This was verified about 50 years ago, when Sir Thomas Delves, of Cheshire, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of a cure he received here, caused an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> to be erected; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> the foundation for which, they came to the remains of a fold <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and magnificent structure of Roman workmanship; and in other places of the neighbourhood, very capacious leaden vessels, and other utensils of Roman workmanship, have been discovered. These waters have always been reckoned inferior to those in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>; but seem never to have been totally disused. They are mentioned by Leland, as well known 200 years ago; but it is certain they were brought into greater <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> by Dr Jones in 1572, and by George <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Shrewsbury, who erected a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> over the bath, then composed of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. This building was afterwards pulled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and a more commodious one erected at the expense of the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. In doing this, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of cures drawn up by the bath-warden, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> physician attending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, and subscribed by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the patients, was lost. The warm waters of Buxton are, the bath, consisting of nine springs, as already mentioned, St Ann's well, and St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s or Bingham well. St Ann's well rises at the distance of somewhat more than 32 yards <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east from the bath. It is chiefly supplied from a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> on the north side, out of a rock of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> marble. It formerly rose into a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> basin, shut up within an ancient Roman brick wall, a yard <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> within, a yard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> on three sides, and open on the fourth. But, in 1799, Sir Thomas Delves, as already mentioned, erected an arch over it which still continues. It is 12 feet long, and as many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, set round with stone steps on the inside. In the midst of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> now springs up into a stone basin two feet square. St Peter's or Bingham well rises about 20 yards south-east of St Ann's. It is also called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEIGH">Leigh</a>'s well, from a memorable cure received from it by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of that name. It rises out of a black limestone, in a very dry ground; and is not so warm as St Ann's well. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> to the waters, this place has grown into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> straggling town, which is daily increasing. The houses are chiefly, or rather solely, built for the reception of invalids; and many of them are not only commodious, but elegant. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Devonshire has lately erected a most magnificent building in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, with piazzas, under which the company walk in wet or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. It is divided into different hotels, shops, &c., with a public coffee-room, and a very elegant room for assemblies and concerts. The hot water resembles that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>. It has a sweet and pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. It contains the calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, together with a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and an inconsiderable portion of a purging salt, but no <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> can be discovered in it. This water taken inwardly is esteemed good in the diabetes; in bloody urine; in the bilious cholick; in loss of appetite, and coldness of the stomach; in inward bleedings; in atrophy; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the vessels and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, especially from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; in cramps and convulsions; in the dry asthma without a fever; and also in barrennesses. Inwardly and outwardly, it is said to be good in rheumatic and scorbutic complaints; in the gout; in inflammation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> and kidneys, and in consumptions of the lungs; also in old strains; in hard callous tumours; in withered and contracted limbs; in the itch, scabs, nodes, chalky swellings, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, and other similar complaints.—Besides the hot water, there is also a cold chalybeate water, with a rough iron taste: it resembles the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a> water in virtues. For the methods of composing <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> Buxton water, or of impregnating the original water with a greater quantity of its own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">gas</a> or with other gases, see Waters, Medicinal. Buxton, Jedediah, a prodigy with respect to skill in numbers. His father, William Buxton, was school-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> where he was born in 1754: yet Jedediah's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was so much neglected, that he was never taught to write; and with respect to any other knowledge but that of numbers, seemed always as ignorant as a boy of ten years of age. How he came first to know the relative proportions of numbers, and their progressive denominations, he did not remember; but to this he applied the whole force of his mind, and upon this his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was constantly fixed, so that he frequently took no cognizance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects, and when he did, it was only with respect to their numbers. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was mentioned, he would soon after say it was so many minutes; and if any distance of way, he would assign the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-breadths, without any question being asked, or any calculation expected by the company. When he once undertook a question, he began to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> with amazing facility, after his own method, without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, or chalk, or even understanding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rules of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> as taught in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. He would stride over a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> or a field, and tell you the contents of it almost as exact as if you had measured it by the chain. In this manner he measured the whole lordship of Elmton, of some thousand acres, belonging to Sir John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, and brought him the contents, not only in acres, roods, and perches, but even in square inches. After this, for his own amusement, he reduced them into square hair-breadths, computing 48 to each side of the inch. His memory was so great, that while revolving a question, he could leave off, and resume the operation again where he left off the next morning, or at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, or at several months, and proceed regularly till it was completed. His memory would doubtless have been equally retentive with respect to other objects, if he had attended to other objects with equal diligence; but his perpetual application to figures prevented the smallest acquisition of any other knowledge. He was sometimes asked, on his return from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, whether he remembered the text, or any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sermon; but it never appeared that he brought away one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, his mind, upon a closer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, being found to have been busied, even during divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, in his favourite operation, either dividing some time, or some space, into the smallest known parts, or revolving some question that had been given him as a test of his abilities. This extraordinary person living in laborious poverty, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was uniform and obscure. Time, with respect to him, changed nothing but his age; nor did the seasons vary his employment, except that in winter he used a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAIL">flail</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> a ling-hook.
