In the year 1754, he came to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he was introduced to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, who, in order to prove his abilities, asked him several questions in arithmetic, and he gave them such satisfaction, that they dismissed him with a handsome gratuity. In this visit to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, polis, the only object of his curiosity, except figures, was his desire to see the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and royal family; but they being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENSINGTON">Kensington</a>, Jedediah was disappointed. During his residence in London, he was taken to see King Richard III. performed at Drury-lane <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">playhouse</a>; and it was expected, either that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> and the splendour of the show would have fixed him in astonishment, or kept his imagination in a continual hurry; or that his passions would, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, have been touched by the power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, if he had not perfectly understood the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>. But Jedediah's mind was employed in the playhouse just as it was employed in every other place. During the dance, he fixed his attention upon the number of steps; he declared, after a fine piece of music, that the innumerable sounds produced by the instruments had perplexed him beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>; and he attended even to Mr Garrick, only to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> the words that he uttered, in which he said he perfectly succeeded. Jedediah returned to the place of his birth, where, if his enjoyments were few, his wishes did not seem to be more. He applied to his labour, by which he subsisted, with cheerfulness; he regretted nothing that he left behind him in London; and it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that a slice of rusty <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">bacon</a> afforded the most delicious repast.

BUXTORF

Pages 41-41

John, a learned professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, who, in the 17th century, acquired the highest reputation, for his knowledge of the Hebrew and Chaldee languages. He died of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> at Basil in 1629, aged 65. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. A small but excellent Hebrew <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>; the best edition of which is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1721, revised by Leuven, 2. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of the Hebrew grammar, 3. A Hebrew concordance, and several Hebrew lexicons, 4. Inflatus epistolarius Hebraicus, 5. De abbreviaturis Hebræorum, &c. Buxtorf, John, the son of the former, and a learned professor of the oriental languages at Basil, distinguished himself, like his father, by his knowledge of the Hebrew <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and his rabbinical learning. He died at Basil in 1664, aged 65 years. His principal works are, 1. His translation of the More Nevechim, and the Cozri. 2. A Chaldee and Syriac lexicon. 3. An anticritie against Cappel. 4. A treatise on the Hebrew <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> and accents against the same Cappel.

BUYING

Pages 41-41

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of making a purchase, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of acquiring the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of a thing for a certain price. Buying stands opposed to selling, and differs from borrowing or hiring, as in the former the property of the thing is alienated for perpetuity, which in the latter it is not. By the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, persons are allowed to buy hope, spero precio emere, that is, to purchase the event or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of any thing; e.g. the fish or birds a person shall catch, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> he shall win in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>. There are different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of buying in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among traders: as, buying on one's own account, opposed to buying on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>; buying for ready money, which is when the purchaser pays in actual specie on the spot; buying on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, or for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> certain, is when the payment is not to be presently made, but in lieu thereof, an obligation given by the buyer for payment at a time future; buying on delivery, is when the goods purchased are only to be delivered at a certain time future. Buying the Refulah, is giving money for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of purchasing a thing at a fixed price in a certain time to come; chiefly used in dealing for shares in stock. This is sometimes also called by a cant name, buying the bear. Buying the Small-Pox, is an appellation given to a method of procuring that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> by an operation similar to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INOCULATION">inoculation</a>; frequent in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, where it has obtained time out of mind. It is performed either by rubbing some of the pus taken out of a pustule of a variolous person on the skin, or by making a puncture in the skin with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> dipped in such pus.

BUZANCOIS

Pages 41-41

a small town of Berry in France, situated on the borders of Touraine, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 29'. N. Lat. 46° 38'.

BUZBACH

Pages 41-41

a town of Germany, in Westeravia, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Holmes, on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANAU">Hanau</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 1'. N. Lat. 50° 22'.

BUZET

Pages 41-41

a small town of France, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, seated on the river Torne, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 45'. N. Lat. 43° 47'.

BUZZARD

Pages 41-41

the name of several <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the hawk kind. See Falco, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BY-LAWS

Pages 41-41

are laws made obiter, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by the by; such as orders and constitutions of corporations for the governing of their members, of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-leets, and courts baron, commoners, or inhabitants in vills, &c. made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> assent, for the good of those that make them, in particular <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> whereunto the public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> doth not extend; so that they bind farther than the common or statute law: guilds and fraternities of trades by letters patent of incorporation, may likewise make by-laws for the better regulation of trade among themselves or with others. In Scotland these laws are called laws of birlaw or burlaw; which are made by neighbours elected by common consent in the birlaw-court, wherein knowledge is taken of complaints betwixt neighbour and neighbour; which men so chosen are judges and arbitrators, and styled birlaw-men. And birlaws, according to Skene, are leges rusticorum, laws made by husbandmen, or townships, concerning neighbourhood among them. All by-laws are to be reasonable, and for the common benefit, not private advantage of particular persons, and must be agreeable to the public laws in being.

BYBLUS

Pages 41-41

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Phoenicia, situated between Berytus and Batrys; it was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of Cinyras; sacred to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADONIS">Adonis</a>. Pompey delivered it from a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, whom he caused to be beheaded. It stood at no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on an eminence (Strabo): near it ran the Adonis into the Mediterranean. Now in ruins.

BYCHOW

Pages 41-41

a small town of Lithuania in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, situated on the river Nieper, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 30° 2'. N. Lat. 53° 57'.

BYNG

Pages 41-42

GEORGE, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Viscount Torrington, was the son of John Byng, Esq. and was born in 1663. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 15, he went volunteer to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s warrant. His early engagement in this course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> gave him little opportunity of acquiring learn- ing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cultivating the polite arts; but by his abilities and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> as a naval commander he furnished abundant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for the pens of others. After being several times advanced, he was in 1702 raised to the command of the Naflau, a third rate, and was at the taking and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the French fleet at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIGO">Vigo</a>; and the next year he was made rear-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. In 1704, he served in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> fleet sent to the Mediterranean under Sir Cloudely Shovel, as rear-admiral of the red; and it was he who commanded the squadron that attacked, cannonaded, and reduced Gibraltar. He was in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALAGA">Malaga</a>, which followed soon after; and for his behaviour in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> conferred on him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. In 1705, in about two months <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he took 12 of the enemies largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a>, with the Thetis, a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of 44 guns; and also several merchant ships, most of them richly laden. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men taken on board was 2070, and of guns 334. In 1718 he was made admiral and commander in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the fleet; and was sent with a squadron into the Mediterranean for the protection of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, according to the obligation England was under by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, against the invasion of the Spaniards; who had the year before surprized <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, and had this year landed an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. In this expedition he despatched <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Walton in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> with five more ships, in pursuit of six Spanish men of war, with galleys, fire-ships, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>-vessels, and storeships, who separated from the main fleet, and stood in for the Sicilian shore. The captain's laconic epistle on this occasion is worthy of notice; which showed that fighting was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> as well as his admiral's, and not <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. "Sir, "We have taken and destroyed all the Spanish ships and vessels which were upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, as per margin. Canterbury, off <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, I am, &c. August 16. 1718. G. Walton." From the account referred to, it appeared that he had taken four Spanish men of war, with a bomb-veffel and a ship laden with arms; and burned four, with a fire-ship and bomb-veffel. The king made the admiral a handsome present, and sent him plenipotentiary powers to negotiate with the princes and states of Italy as there should be occasion. He procured the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s troops free access into the fortresses that still held out in Sicily; failed afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, and brought out the Sicilian galleys, and a ship belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. Soon after he received a gracious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VI. written with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, accompanied with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of his imperial majesty, set round with very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> diamonds, as a mark of the grateful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> he had of his services. It was entirely owing to his advice and assistance that the Germans retook the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Melina in 1719, and destroyed the ships that lay in the haven; which completed the ruin of the naval power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. The Spaniards being much distressed, offered to quit Sicily; but the admiral declared, that the troops should never be suffered to quit the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> till the king of Spain had acceded to the quadruple <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>. And to his conduct it was entirely owing that Sicily was subdued, and his Catholic majesty forced to accept the terms prescribed him by the quadruple alliance. After performing so many signal services, the king received him with the most gracious expressions of favour and satisfaction; made him rear-admiral of England and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, one of his most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> privy-councils, Baron Byng of Southill in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>, Viscount Torrington in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, and one of the knights companions of the Bath upon the revival of that order. In 1727, George II. on his accession to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, placed him at the head of his naval affairs, as first lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> station he died <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 15, 1733, in the 70th year of his age, and was buried at Southill in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>. Byng, the honourable George, Esq., the unhappy son of the former, was bred to sea, and rose to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of admiral of the blue. He gave many proofs of courage; but was at last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, upon a dubious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> for neglect of duty, in 1757. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. BYRLAW or BURLAW Laws in Scotland. See BY-LAWS.

BYROM

Pages 42-43

JOHN, an ingenious poet of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, born in 1691. His first poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> appeared in the Spectator, No. 603, beginning, "My <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, O ye <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, was happily spent?" which, with two humorous letters on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>, are to be found in the eighth volume. He was admitted a member of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> in 1724; and having originally entertained thoughts of practising physic, to which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> is incident, that was the appellation by which he was always known: but reducing himself to narrow circumstances by a precipitate <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, he supported himself by teaching a new method of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> shorthand, of his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>; until an estate devolved to him by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of an elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of lively <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>; of which, whenever a favourable opportunity tempted him to indulge it, he gave many humorous specimens. He died in 1763; and a collection of his miscellaneous poems was printed at Manchester, in 2 vols. 8vo, 1773. BYRRHUS. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BYSSUS">BYSSUS</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Byssus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Byllum, a fine thready <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> produced in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a> in Achaia, of which the richest apparel was anciently made, especially that worn by the priests both Jewish and Egyptian. Some interpreters render the Greek Βύσσος, which occurs both in the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, by fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. But other versions, as Calvin's, and the Spanish printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1556, explain the word by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; and yet byssus must have been different from our silk, as appears from a multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, and particularly from Jul. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>. M. Simon, who renders the word by fine linen, adds a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> to explain it; viz. that there was a fine kind of linen very dear, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lords alone wore in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> as well as in Egypt." This account agrees perfectly well with that given by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HESYCHIUS">Hesychius</a>, as well as what is observed by Bochart, that the byssus was a finer kind of linen, which was frequently dyed of a purple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Some authors <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the byssus to be the same with our cotton; others take it for the linum aegaeum; and others for the lock or bunch of silky <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> found adhering to the pinna marina, by which it fastens itself to the neighbouring bodies. Authors usually distinguish two sorts of byssus; that of Elis; and that of Judea, which which was the finest. Of this latter were the priestly ornaments made. Bonferrius notes, that there must have been two sorts of byssus, one finer than ordinary, by reason there are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> words used in Scripture to denote byssus; one of which is always used in speaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of the priests, and the other of that of the Levites. Byssus Albellinus, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of asbestos or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INCOMBUSTIBLE">incombustible</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, composed of fine <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> fibres <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to one another. It is found plentifully in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or of different shades of green. At a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> mine in Westmanland it forms the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the vein out of which the ore is dug; and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> which melts the metal, is changed into a pure semitransparent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> or glaas.

BYZANTIUM

Pages 43-43

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Thrace, situated on the Bosphorus. It was founded, according to Eusebius, about the 36th Olympiad, while Tullus Hostilius reigned in Rome. But, according to Diodorus Siculus, the foundations of this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> were laid in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Argonauts, by one Byzas, who then reigned in the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and from whom the city was called Byzantium. This Byzas, according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUSTATHIUS">Eustathius</a>, arrived in Thrace a little before the Argonauts came into those seas, and settled there with a colony of Megarenese. Velleius Paterculus ascribes the founding of Byzantium to the Milesians, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMIANUS_MARCELLINUS">Ammianus Marcellinus</a> to the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>. Some ancient medals of Byzantium, which have reached our times, bear the name and head of Byzas, with the prow of a ship on the reverse. The year after the destruction of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> by Titus, Byzantium was reduced to the form of a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. In the year 193 this city took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a> against Severus. It was strongly garrisoned by Niger, as being a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the utmost importance. It was soon after invested by Severus; and as he was universally hated on account of his cruelty, the inhabitants defended themselves with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. They had been supplied with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of warlike <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, most of them invented and built by Pericus a native of Nicaea, and the greatest engineer of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. For a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time they baffled all the attempts of the assailants, killed great numbers of them, crushed such as approached the walls with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; and when stones began to fail, they used the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of their gods and heroes. At last they were obliged to submit, through famine, after having been reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of devouring one another. The conqueror put all the magistrates and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; but spared the engineer Pericus. Before this siege, Byzantium was the greatest, most populous, and wealthiest city of Thrace. It was surrounded by walls of an extraordinary height and breadth: and defended by a great number of towers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of which were built with such art, that the least noise heard in one of them was immediately conveyed to all the rest. Severus, however, no sooner became <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it, than he commanded it to be laid in ashes. The inhabitants were stripped of all their effects, publicly sold for slaves and the walls levelled with the ground. But by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> we are informed, that soon after this terrible catastrophe, Severus himself caused a great part of the city to be rebuilt, calling it Antonia from his son <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARACALLA">Caracalla</a>, who assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Byzantium. Antoninus. In 262, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> Galienus wreaked his fury on the inhabitants of Byzantium. He intended to besiege it; but on his arrival despaired of being able to make himself master of such a strong place. He was admitted the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, however, into the city; and without any regard to the terms he had agreed to, caused the soldiers and all the inhabitants to be put to the sword. Trebellius Pollio says, that not a single person was left alive. What the reason was for such an extraordinary massacre, we are nowhere informed. In the wars between the emperors Licinius and Maximin the city of Byzantium was obliged to submit to the latter, but was soon after recovered by Licinius. In the year 323, it was taken from Licinius by Constantine the Great, who in 330 enlarged and beautified it, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to make it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the first, city in the Roman empire. He began with extending the walls of the ancient city from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to sea; and while some of the workmen were buried in raising them, others were employed in raising within them a great number of stately buildings, and among others a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> no way inferior in magnificence and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> to that of Rome. He built a capitol and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> maximus, several forums, porticoes, and public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. He divided the whole city into 14 regions, and granted the inhabitants many privileges and immunities. By this means Byzantium became one of the most flourishing and populous cities of the empire. Vast numbers of people flocked thither from Pontus, Thrace, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Constantine having, by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, enacted this year (335), decreed, that such as had lands in those countries should not be at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to dispose of them, nor even leave them to their proper heirs at their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, unless they had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in this new city. But however furious the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> was that his city should be filled with people, he did not care that it should be inhabited by any but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. He therefore caused all the idols to be pulled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and all their churches consecrated to the true God. He built besides an incredible number of churches, and caused crosses to be erected in all the squares and public places. Most of the buildings being finished, it was solemnly dedicated to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, according to Cedrenus, but, according to Eusebius, to the God of Martyrs. At the same time Byzantium was equalled to Rome. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, immunities, and privileges, were granted to its inhabitants as to those of the metropolis. He established a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and other magistrates, with a power and authority equal to those of old Rome. He took up his residence in the new city; and changed its name to Constantinople.

BZOVIVS

Pages 43-45
ABRAHAM, one of the most celebrated writers in the 17th century, with respect to the astonishing number of pieces composed by him. His chief work is the continuation of Baronius's annals. He was a native of Poland, and a Dominican friar. Upon his coming to Rome, he was received with open arms by the Pope, and had an apartment assigned him in the Vatican. He merited that reception, for he has imitated Baronius to admiration in his design of making all things conspire to the despotic power and glory of the papal see. He died in 1630, aged 70. C, THE third letter, and second consonant, of the alphabet, is pronounced like k before the vowels a, o, and u; and like c before e, i, and y. C is formed, according to Scaliger, from the z of the Greeks, by retrenching the stem or upright line; though others derive it from the z of the Hebrews, which has in effect the same form; allowing only for this, that the Hebrews reading backwards, and the Latins, &c. forwards, each have turned the letter their own way. However the C not being the same as to found with the Hebrew caph, and it being certain the Romans did not borrow their letters immediately from the Hebrews or other orientals, but from the Greeks, the derivation from the Greek z, is the more probable. Add, that F. Montfaucon, in his Palæographia, gives us some forms of the Greek z which come very near to that of our C; thus, for instance, ζ; and Suidas calls the C the Roman kappa. The second found of C resembles that of the Greek Ξ; and many instances occur of ancient inscriptions, in which Ξ has the same form with our C. All grammarians agree, that the Romans pronounced their Q like our C, and their C like our K. F. Mabillon adds, that Charles the Great was the first who wrote his name with a C; whereas all his predecessors of the same name wrote it with a K; and the same difference is observed in their coins. As an abbreviation, C stands for Caius, Carolus, Caesar, condemnno, &c. and CC for confutibus. As a numeral, C signifies 100, CC 200, &c. C, in Music, placed after the clef, intimates that the music is in common time, which is either quick or slow, as it is joined with allegro, or adagio: if alone, it is usually adagio. If the C be crossed or turned, the first requires the air to be played quick, and the last very quick. CAABA; or CAABAH, properly signifies a square stone building: but is particularly applied by the Mahometans to the temple at Mecca, built as they pretend, by Abraham and Ishmael his son. Before the time of Mahomet, this temple was a place of worship for the idolatrous Arabs, and is said to have contained no less than 360 different images, equalling in number the days of the Arabian year. They were all destroyed by Mahomet, who sanctified the Caaba, and appointed it to be the chief place of worship for all true believers. The temple is in length from north to south about 24 cubits; its breadth from east to west is 23, and its height 27. The door, which is on the east side, stands about four cubits from the ground; the floor being level with the bottom of the door. In the corner next this door is the black stone, so much celebrated among the Mahometans. On the north side of the Caaba, within a semicircular enclosure 50 cubits long, lies the white stone, said to be the sepulchre of Ishmael, which receives the rain water from the Caaba by a spout formerly of wood, but now of gold. The black stone, according to the Mahometans, was brought down from heaven by Gabriel at the creation of the world, and was originally of a white colour; but contracted the blackness that now appears on it from the guilt of those sins committed by the sons of men. It is set in silver, and fixed in the south-east corner of the Caaba, looking towards Bafra, about seven spans from the ground. This stone, upon which there is the figure of a human head, is held in the highest estimation among the Arabs; all the pilgrims killing it with great devotion, and some even calling it the right hand of God. Its blackness, which is only superficial, is probably owing to the kisses and touches of so many people. After the Karmatians had taken Mecca, they carried away this precious stone, and could by no means be prevailed upon to restore it; but finding at last that they were unable to prevent the concourse of pilgrims to Mecca, they sent it back of their own accord, after having kept it 22 years. The double roof of the Caaba is supported within by three octagonal pillars of aloes wood; between which, on a bar of iron, hang some silver lamps. The outside is covered with rich black damask, adorned with an embroidered band of gold, which is changed every year, and was formerly sent by the caliphs, afterwards by the sultans of Egypt, and is now provided by the Turkish emperors. The Caaba, at some distance, is almost surrounded by a circular enclosure of pillars, joined towards the bottom by a low balustrade, and towards the top by bars of silver. Just without this inner enclosure, on the south, north, and west sides of the Caaba, are three buildings, which are the oratories or places where three of the orthodox sects assembled to perform their devotions. Towards the south-east stands an edifice which covers the well Zamzem, the treasury, and the cupola of Al Abbas. Formerly there was another cupola, that went under the name of the hemicycle or cupola of Judea; but whether or not any remains of that are now to be seen is unknown; nor is it easy to obtain information in this respect, all Christians being denied access to this holy place. At a small distance from the Caaba, on the east side, is the flat or place of Abraham; where is another stone much respected by the Mahometans; and where they pretend to show the footsteps of the patriarch, telling us he stood on it when he built the Caaba. Here the fourth feet of Arabs, viz. that of Al Shafei, assemble for religious purposes. The square colonnade, or great piazza, which at a considerable distance encloses these buildings, consists, according to Al Jannabi, of 488 pillars, and has no less than 38 gates. Mr Sale compares this piazza to that of the Royal Exchange at London, but allows it to be much larger. It is covered with small domes or cupolas, from the four corners of which rise as many minarets or steeples, with double galleries, and adorned with gilded spires and crescents after the Turkish manner, as are also the cupolas which cover the piazza and other buildings. Between the columns of both enclosures hang a great number of lamps, which are constantly constantly lighted at night. The first foundation of this second enclosure was laid by Omar the second caliph, who built no more than a low wall, to prevent the court of the Caaba from being encroached upon by private buildings; but by the liberality of succeeding princes, the whole has been raised to that state of magnificence in which it appears at present. This temple enjoys the privilege of an asylum for all sorts of criminals: but it is most remarkable for the pilgrimages made to it by the devout Mussulmans, who pay so great a veneration to it, that they believe a single sight of its sacred walls, without any particular act of devotion, is as meritorious in the sight of God, as the most careful discharge of one's duty, for the space of a whole year, in any other temple.

CAAMINI

Pages 45-45

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a name given by the Spaniards and others to the finest sort of Paraguayan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of a shrub which grows on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Maracaya, and is used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> as the tea is with us. The mountains where this shrub grows naturally are far from the inhabited parts of Paraguay: but the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> know so well the value and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it, that they constantly furnish themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of it from the spot. They used to go out on these expeditions many thousands together; leaving their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> exposed to the insults of their enemies, and many of themselves perishing by fatigue. To avoid these inconveniences, they have of late planted these trees about their habitations; but the leaves of these cultivated ones have not the fine flavour of those that grow wild. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> has permitted the Indians of Paraguay to bring to the town of Saint-foy 12,000 arbors of the leaves of this tree every year, but they are not able to procure so much of the wild leaves annually: about half the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is the utmost they bring of this: the other half is made up of the leaves of the trees in their own plantations; and this sells at a lower price, and is called paboa. The arbor is about 25 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; the general price is four piastres; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is always divided equally among the people of the colony.

CABAL

Pages 45-45

an apt name currently given to the infamous ministry of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. composed of five persons, Clifford, Ashley, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>, Arlington, and Lauderdale; the first letters of whose names, in this order, furnished the appellation by which they were distinguished.

CABALIST

Pages 45-45

in French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> person who is concerned in managing the trade of another.

CABALLARIA

Pages 45-45

in middle-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, lands held by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> of furnishing a horseman, with suitable Caballeros' equipage in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> had occasion for him.

CABALLEROS

Pages 45-45
or Cavalleros, are Spanish wools, of which there is a pretty considerable trade at Bayonne in France.

CABALLINE

Pages 45-45

denotes something belonging to horses; thus caballine aloes is so called, from its being chiefly used for purging horses; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> brimstone is called sulphur caballicum for a like reason. CABALLINUM in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Ædui in Gallia Celtica; now Chalon sur Saone, which see. CABALLINUS in Ancient Geography, a very clear fountain of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELICON">Helicon</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>; called Hippocrene by the Greeks, because opened by Pegasus on striking the rock with his hoof, and hence called Pegasus.

CABALLIO

Pages 45-45
or Cabellio, in Ancient Geography, a town of the Cavares in Gallia Narbonensis, situated on the Druentia. One of the Latin colonies, in the Notitia called Civitas Cabelliorum. Now Cavaillon in Provence.

CABBAGE

Pages 45-45

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. See Brassica; and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cabbage-Tree <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> True Cabbage-Palm. See Areca, Botany Index. Cabbage-bark Tree. See Geoffrea, Botany Index.

CABBALA

Pages 45-46

according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> style, has a very distinct signification from that wherein we understand it in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The Hebrew cabbala signifies <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>; and the rabbins, who are called cabalists, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> principally the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of particular words, letters, and numbers, and by this means pretend to discover what is to come, and to see clearly into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of many difficult <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Scripture. There are no sure principles of this knowledge, but it depends upon some particular traditions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; for which reason it is termed cabbala. The cabalists have abundance of names which they call sacred; these they make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in invoking of spirits, and imagine they receive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from them. They tell us, that the secrets of the Cabbala were discovered to Moses on Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>; and that these have been delivered to them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from father to son, without interruption, and without any use of letters; for to write them down, is what they are by no means permitted to do. This is likewise termed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORAL">oral</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, because it passed from father to son, in order to distinguish it from the written laws. There is another cabbala, called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, which consists in searching for arbitrary and mysterious significations of a word in Scripture, from whence they borrow certain explanations, by combining the letters which compose it; this cabbala is divided into three kinds, the gematria, the notaricon, and the temura <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> themura. The first whereof consists in taking the letters of a Hebrew word for ciphers or arithmetical numbers, and explaining every word by the arithmetical value of the letters whereof it is composed. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort of cabbala, called notaricon, consists in taking every particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of a word for an entire <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>; and the third, called themura, i.e. change, consists in making different transpositions or changes. CABALISTS of letters, placing one for the other, or one before the other. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, likewise, a certain sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> is, by mistake, called cabbala; which consists in using improperly certain passages of Scripture for magic operations, or in forming magic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> or figures with flares and talismans. Some visionaries among the Jews believe, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ wrought his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> by virtue of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the cabbala.

CABBALISTS

Pages 46-46

the Jewish doctors who profess the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the cabbala. In the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of these men, there is not a word, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, without some mystery in it. The Jews are divided into two general sects; the Karaites, who refuse to receive either <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALMUD">talmud</a>, or any thing but the pure texts of Scripture; and the rabbinites, or talmudists, who, besides this, receive the traditions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and follow the talmud. The latter are again divided into two other sects; pure rabbinites, who explain the Scripture in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and tradition; and cabbalists, who, to discover hidden mystical senses, which they suppose God to have couched therein, make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the cabbala, and the mystical methods above mentioned.

CABECA

Pages 46-46
or CABESS, a name given to the finest silks in the East Indies, as those from 15 to 20 per cent, inferior to them are called barina. The Indian workmen endeavour to pass them off one with the other; for which reason, the more experienced European merchants take care to open the bales, and to examine all the skeins one after another. The Dutch distinguish two sorts of cabecas; namely, the moor cabeca, and the common cabeca. The former is sold at Amsterdam for about 21½ schellinghen Flemish, and the other for about 18½. CABECA de Vide, a small sea port town of Alentejo, in Portugal, with good walls, and a strong castle. W. Long. 6. 43. N. Lat. 39. o.

CABENDA

Pages 46-46

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 2. S. Lat. 4. 5.

CABES

Pages 46-46
or GABES, a town of Africa in the kingdom of Tunis, seated on a river near the gulf of the same name. E. Long. 10. 35. N. Lat. 33. 40.

CABEZZO

Pages 46-46

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; having Oacco on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, Lubolo on the south, the Coanzo on the north-east, and the Reimba on the south-west. It is populous, and well stored with cattle, &c. and hath a mine of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> on a mountain from thence called the iron mountain, which yields <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of that metal; and this the Portuguese have taught the natives to manufacture. This province is watered by a river called Rio Longo, and other small rivulets, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, &c. The trees here are vastly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; and they have one sort not unlike our apple trees, the bark of which being flatted with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, yields an odoriferous resin of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and consistency of wax, and very medicinal in its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, only a little too hot for Europeans, unless qualified by some cooling drug.

CABIDOS

Pages 46-46
or CAVINOS, a long measure used at Goa, and other places of the East Indies belonging to the Portuguese, to measure stuffs, linens, &c. and equal to 4ths of the Paris ell.

CABIN

Pages 46-46

a room <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apartment in a ship where any of the officers usually reside. There are many of these in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ship; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which is designed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> or commander. In ships of the line this chamber is furnished with an open gallery in the ship's stern, as also a little gallery on each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. The apartments where the inferior officers or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sailors <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> and meals are usually called BIRTHS; which see. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> places built up for the sailors at the ship's side in merchantmen are also called cabins.

CABINDA

Pages 46-46

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> port of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a> in Loango in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It is situated at the mouth of a river of the same name about five leagues <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Palmerino, on the north side of the mouth of the river Zaire. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> is very commodious for trade, wooding, and watering.

CABINET

Pages 46-47

the most retired <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the finest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, set apart for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, studying, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> preserving anything that is precious. A complete apartment consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, antechamber, chamber, and cabinet, with a gallery on one side. Hence we say, a cabinet of paintings, curiosities, &c. Cabinet, also denotes a piece of joiners' workmanship, being a kind of press or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, with several doors and drawers. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> cabinets of oak or of chestnut varnished, cabinets of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, cabinets of inlaid-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and some of ebony, or the like scarce and precious woods. Formerly the Dutch and German cabinets were much esteemed in France; but are now quite out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>, as well as the cabinets of ebony which came from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. Cabinet is also used in speaking of the more select and secret councils of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or administration. Thus we say, the secrets, the intrigues of the cabinet. To avoid the inconveniences of a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, the policy of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and practice of France first introduced cabinet councils. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with first establishing this usage in England. Besides his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy council</a>, that prince erected a kind of cabinet council, or junto, under the denomination of a council of state; composed of Archbishop Laud, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Strafford, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Collington, with the secretaries of state. Yet some pretend to find the subsistence of a cabinet council of much greater antiquity, and even allowed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, which anciently settled a quorum of persons most confided in, without whose presence no arduous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> was to be determined; giving them power to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> without consulting the rest of the council. As <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> since as the 28th of Henry III., a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> passed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFIRMATION">affirmation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; which provided, that four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men, chosen by common consent, who were to be conservators of the kingdom, among other things, should see to the disposing of moneys given by parliament, and appropriated to particular uses; and parliaments were to be summoned as they should advise. But even of these four, any two made a quorum; and generally the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of England and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> were of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the conservators. Matth. Par. 28. Henry III. In the first of Henry VI. the parliament provides, that the quorum for the privy council be six, or four at least; and that in all weighty considerations, the dukes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, the king's uncles, should be present; which seems to be erecting a cabinet by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>.

CABIRI

Pages 47-47

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Pagans, signifying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and powerful gods; being a name given to the gods of Samothrace. They were also worshipped in other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEMNOS">Lemnos</a> and Thebes, where the cabiri were celebrated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of them; these gods are said to be in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> four, viz. Axieros, Axioercfa, Axioercfus, and Caflmus.

CABIRIA

Pages 47-47

festivals in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Cabiri, celebrated in Thebes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEMNOS">Lemnos</a>, but especially in Samothrace, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> consecrated to the Cabiri. All who were initiated into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of these gods were thought to be secured thereby from storms at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and all other dangers. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of initiation was performed by placing the candidate, crowned with olive branches, and girded about the loins with a purple ribband, on a kind of throne, about which the priests and persons before initiated danced.

CABLE

Pages 47-47

a thick, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, strong rope, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, which serves to keep a ship at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>. There is no merchant ship, however weak, but has at least three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>; namely, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cable, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cable of the sheet anchor, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> cable, and a smaller one. Cable is also said of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, which serve to raise heavy loads, by the help of cranes, pulleys, and other engines. The name of cable is usually given to such as are, at least, three inches in circumference; those that are less are only called ropes, of different names, according to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Every cable, of whatsoever thickness it be, is composed of three strands; every strand of three ropes; and every rope of three twits: the twist is made of more or less threads, according as the cable is to be thicker or thinner. In the manufacture of cables, after the ropes are made, they use sticks, which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> first between the ropes of which they make the strands, and afterwards between the strands of which they make the cable, to the end that they may all twist the better, and be more regularly wound together; and also, to prevent them from entwining or entangling, they hang, at the end of each strand and of each rope, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> or of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of threads each cable is composed of is always proportioned to its length and thickness; and it is by this number of threads that its weight and value are ascertained: thus, a cable of three inches circumference, or one inch diameter, ought to consist of 48 ordinary threads, and to weigh 192 pounds; and on this foundation is calculated the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, very useful for all people engaged in marine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; who fit out merchantmen for their own account, or freight them for the account of others. A table of the number of threads and weight of cables of different circumferences. | Circumf. | Threads | Weight | |----------|---------|--------| | 3 inches | 48 | 192 pounds | | 4 | 77 | 368 | Sheet-Anchor CABLE, is the greatest cable belonging to a ship. Stream CABLE, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAWSER">hawser</a> or rope, something smaller than the bowers, and used to moor the ship in a river or haven, sheltered from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, &c. Serve or Plate the CABLE, is to bind it about with ropes, clouts, &c., to keep it from galling in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAWSE">hawse</a>. To Splice a CABLE, is to make two pieces fast together, by working the several threads of the rope the one into the other. Pay more CABLE, is to let more out of the ship. Pay cheap the Cable, is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> it out apace. Veer more Cable, is to let more out, &c. CABLE'S Length, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of 120 fathoms, or of the usual length of the cable.

CABLED

Pages 47-47

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> formed of the two ends of a ship's cable; sometimes also to a cross covered over with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a> of rope; more properly called a cross carded. CABLED <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">Flute</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, such flutes as are filled up with pieces in the form of a cable.

CABO DE ISTRIA

Pages 47-47

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Istria, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; and the see of a bishop. It is seated on a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Venice, and is joined to the main <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> by draw-bridges. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 22. N. Lat. 45. 49.

CABOCHED

Pages 47-47

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is when the heads of beasts are borne without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the neck, full faced.

CABOLETO

Pages 47-47

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, worth about 3d. of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>.

CABOT

Pages 47-48

Sebastian, the first discoverer of the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, was the son of John Cabot, a Venetian. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> in 1477; and was taught by his father, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, and cosmography. Before he was 20 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> he made several voyages. The first of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> seems to have been made with his father, who had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> from Henry VII. for the discovery of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west passage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. They sailed in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1497; and proceeding to the north-west they discovered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, which for that reason they called Primavista, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Newfoundland. Another smaller <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> they called St John, from its being discovered on the feast of St John Baptist; after which, they sailed along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of America as far as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>, and then returned to England. land with a good cargo, and three Indians aboard. Stowe and Speed ascribe these discoveries wholly to Sebastian, without mentioning his father. It is probable that Sebastian, after his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, made several voyages to these parts, as a map of his discoveries, drawn by himself, was hung up in the privy garden at Whitehall. However, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> gives but little account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for near 20 years: when he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, where he was made pilot-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, and intrusted with reviewing all projects for discoveries, which were then very numerous. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> capacity and approved integrity induced many eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> to treat with him about a voyage by the new found straits of Magellan to the Moluccas. He therefore sailed in 1523, first to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a>; then to the Cape de Verd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; thence to St Augustine and the island of Patos; when some of his people beginning to be mutinous, and refusing to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the straits, he laid aside the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of sailing to the Moluccas; left some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> mutineers upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> island; and, failing up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of Plate and Paraguay, discovered, and built forts in, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tract of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, that produced <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and other rich commodities. He hence despatched messengers to Spain for a supply of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, ammunition, goods for trade, and a recruit of men: but his request not being readily complied with, after staying five years in America, he returned home; where he met with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> reception, the merchants being displeased at his not having pursued his voyage to the Moluccas, while his treatment of the mutineers had given umbrage at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Hence he returned to England; and being introduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Somerset, then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> protector, a new office was erected for him: he was made governor of the mystery and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of the merchant-adventurers for the discovery of regions, dominions, islands, and places unknown; a pension was granted him, by letters patent, of 166l. 13s. 4d. per annum; and he was consulted in all affairs relative to trade. In 1522, by his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, the court fitted out some ships for the discovery of the northern parts of the world. This produced the first voyage the English made to Russia, and the beginning of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> which has ever since been carried on between the two nations. The Russia company was now founded by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> granted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; and of this company Sebastian was appointed governor for life. He is said to be the first who took notice of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, and who published a map of the world. The exact <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his death is not known, but he lived to be above 70 years of age. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABRA">Cabra</a>, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Tombut in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It is a large town, but without walls; and is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a>, about 12 miles from Tombut. The houses are built in the shape of bells; and the walls are made with stakes or hurdles, plastered with clay, and covered with reeds after the manner of thatch. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is very much frequented by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> who come here by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to trade. The town is very unhealthy, which is probably owing to its low situation. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the inhabitants is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> a sort of Mahometanism. They have plenty of corn, cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> is very scarce. The judge who decides controversies is appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Tombut. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 50. N. Lat. 14.

CABUL

Pages 48-48
or CABOUL, a city of Asia, and capital of the province of Cabulistan. It lies in E. Long. 68° 15'. N. Lat. 33° 30' on the frontiers of Great Bukharia, on the south side of the mountains which divide the territories of the Mogul from that part of Great Tartary. It is one of the finest places in that part of the world; large, rich, and very populous. As it is considered as the key of the Great Mogul's dominions on that side, great care is taken to keep its fortifications in repair, and a numerous garrison is maintained for its security. It lies on the road between Samarcan and Lahore; and is much frequented by the Tartars, Persians, and Indians. The Uzbeg Tartars drive there a great trade in slaves and horses, of which it is said that no fewer are sold than 60,000 annually. The Persians bring black cattle and sheep, which renders provisions very cheap. They have also wine, and plenty of all sorts of eatables. The city stands on a little river which falls into the Indus, and thereby affords a short and speedy passage for all the rich commodities in the country beyond it, which when brought to Cabul, are there exchanged for slaves and horses, and then conveyed by merchants of different countries to all parts of the world. The inhabitants are most of them Indian pagans, though the officers of the Mogul and most of the garrison are Mahometans.

CABULISTAN

Pages 48-48

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, formerly belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul; but ceded in 1739 to Kouli Khan, who at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> governed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Bukharia, on the east by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASHMERE">Cashmere</a>, on the west by Zabulistan and Candahar, and on the south by Moultan. It is 250 miles in length 240 in breadth, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CABUL">Cabul</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in general is not very fruitful; but in the vales they have good pasture lands. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> are much infested with banditti; which obliges the natives to have guards for the security of travellers. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Cabulistanis is pagan; and their extraordinary time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> is the full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> in February, and continues for two days. At this time they are clothed in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, make their offerings, dance to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, and make visits to their friends in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASQUERADE">masquerade</a> dresses. They say, their god Cruifman killed a giant who was his enemy, and that he appeared like a little child; in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of which, they cause a child to shoot at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a giant. Those of the same tribe make bonfires, and feast together in a jovial manner. The moral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their religion consists in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>; for which reason, they dig <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> and build houses for the accommodation of travellers. They have plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYROBALANS">myrobalans</a>, aromatic woods, and drugs of many kinds. They carry on a great trade with the neighbouring countries; by which means they are very rich, and are supplied with plenty of all things.

CABURNS

Pages 48-48

on ship board, are small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> made of spun yarn, to bind <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> tackles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like. CACALIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CACTUS. See THEOBROMA, Botany Index. CACCOONS. See FLEVILLEA, Botany Index.

CACERES

Pages 48-49

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Extremadura, is seated on the river Saler, and noted for the exceeding fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> which the sheep bear in the neighbourhood. Between this town and Brocos, there is a wood, where the allies defeated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REAR_GUARD">rear-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of the CACHALOT. See Physeter, Cetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CACHAN

Pages 49-49
or CASHAN, a considerable town of Persia, in Irac Agemi, where they carry on an extensive trade in silks, silver and gold brocades, and fine earthenware. It is situated in a vast plain, 55 miles from Ispahan. E. Long. 5°. 2. N. Lat. 34°. 10.

CACHAO

Pages 49-49

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of that name, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TONQUIN">Tonquin</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 105°. 31. N. Lat. 22°. 10. at about 80 leagues distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is prodigiously crowded with people, insomuch that the streets are hardly passable, especially on market days. These vast crowds, however, come mostly from the neighbouring villages; upon which account these villages have been allowed their halls in particular parts of the city, where they bring and dispose of their wares. The town itself, though the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the whole Tonquinese kingdom, hath neither walls nor fortifications.
