The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> streets are wide and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a>, but the rest of them narrow and ill paved; and except the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> and arsenal, the town has little else worth notice. The houses are low and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, mostly built of wood and clay, and not above one story <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The magazines and warehouses belonging to foreigners are the only edifices built of brick; and these, though plain, yet, by reason of their height and more elegant structure, make a considerable show among those rows of wooden huts. From the combustibility of its edifices, this city suffers frequent and dreadful conflagrations. These spread with such surprising velocity, that some thousands of houses are often laid in ashes before the fire can be extinguished. To prevent these sad consequences, every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> hath, either in its yard <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even in its centre, some low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of brick, in form of an oven, into which the inhabitants on the first alarm convey their most valuable goods. Besides this precaution, which every family takes to secure their goods, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> obliges them to keep a cistern, or some other capacious vessel, always full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> on the top of their house, to be ready on all occasions of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: as likewise a long pole and bucket, to throw water from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENNEL">kennel</a> upon the houses. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> these two expedients fail of suppressing the flames, they immediately cut the straws which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the thatch to the walls, and let it fall in and waste itself on the ground. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s palace stands in the centre of the city; and is surrounded with a stout wall, within whose circuiture are seen a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of apartments two stories high, whose fronts and portals have something of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Those of the king and his wives are embellished with variety of carvings and gildings after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> manner, and all finely varnished. In the outer <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> are a vast number of sumptuous stables for the king's horses and elephants. The appearance of the inner courts can only be conjectured; for the avenues are not only shut to all strangers, but even to the king's subjects, except those of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ministers of state; yet we are told, that there are staircases by which people may mount up to the top of the walls, which are about 18 or 20 feet high; from whence they may have a distant view of the royal apartments, and of the fine parterres and fish ponds that are between the circuiture and them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> wall hath a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> gate well ornamented, which is never opened but when the king goes in and out; but at some distance from it on each side there are two posterns, at which the courtiers and servants may go in and out. This circuiture, which is of a vast circumference, is faced with brick within and without, and the whole structure is terminated by wide spacious gardens; which, though stored with great variety of proper ornaments, are destitute of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and elegance observed in the palaces of European princes. Besides this palace, the ruins of one still more magnificent are to be observed, and are called Libarina. The circumference is said to have been between six and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles; some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, porticoes, and other ornaments are still remaining; from which, and some of its courts paved with marble, it may be concluded to have been as magnificent a structure as any of the eastern parts can show. The arsenal is likewise a large and noble building, well stored with ammunition and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. The English <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> is situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the city, fronting the river Song-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>. It is a handsome low-built house, with a spacious dining room in the centre; and on each side are the apartments of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, factors, and servants. At each end of the building are smaller houses for other uses, as storehouses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, &c., which form two wings with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> in the middle, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with the river, near the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of which stands a long <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, on which they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> display the English colours on Sundays and all remarkable days. Adjoining to it, on the south side, is the Danish factory, which is neither so large nor so handsome. On the same side of the river runs a long dike, whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are so firmly fastened together, that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it can be stirred without moving the whole. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was raised on those banks to prevent the river, during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their vast rains, from overflowing the city; and it has hitherto answered its end; for though the town stands high enough to be in no danger from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> floods, it might yet have been otherwise frequently damaged, if not totally laid under water, by the overflowing of that river. Some curious observations have been communicated to the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> concerning differences between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> of those seas and those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, viz. that on the Tonquinese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> ebbs and flows but once in 24 hours; that is, that the tide is rising during the space of 12 hours, and can be easily perceived during two of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, but can hardly be observed during the other two. In the rising tides, which last 14 days, the waters begin to rise at the rising of the moon; whereas in the low tides, which continue the same number of days, the tide begins not till that planet has got below the horizon. Whilst it is passing through the six northern signs, the tides are observed to vary greatly, to rise sometimes very high, and sometimes

CACHECTIC

Pages 49-50

something partaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> belonging to, a cachexy. CACHÉO, a town of Negroland in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, seated on the river St Domingo. It is subject to the Portuguese, who have three forts there, and carry on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in wax and slaves. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 55'. N. Lat. 12° 0'.

CACHEXY

Pages 50-50

in Medicine, a vicious state of the humours and whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CACHRYS. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index.

CACHUNDE

Pages 50-50

the name of a medicine, highly celebrated among the Chinese and Indians, and made of several aromatic ingredients, the perfumes, medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>: they make the whole into a stiff paste, and form out of it several figures according to their fancy, which are dried for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; these are principally used in the East Indies, but are sometimes brought over to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> persons usually carry a small piece in their mouths, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> cordial, and gives their breath a very sweet smell. It is a highly valuable medicine, also, in all nervous complaints; and is esteemed a prolonger of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and a provocative to venery, the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> intentions of most of the medicines in use in the East.

CACOCHYLIA

Pages 50-50
or CACOCHYMIA, a vicious state of the vital humours, especially of the maws of blood; arising either from a disorder of the secretions or excretions, or from external contagion. The word is Greek, compounded of ξακος ill, and χυμος juice.

CACOPHONIA

Pages 50-50

in Medicine, denotes a vice <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> depravation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> or speech; of which there are two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, aphonia and dyphonia. CACTUS. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The cacti are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of a singular structure, but especially the larger kinds of them; which appear like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, fleshy, green melon, with deep ribs, set all over with strong sharp thorns, and, when the plants are cut through the middle, their inside is a soft, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>-green, fleshy substance, very full of moisture. The fruit of all the species is frequently eaten by the inhabitants of the West Indies. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> are about three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an inch in length, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> form, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> to a point at the bottom toward the plant, but blunt at the top where the empalement of the flower was situated. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is agreeably acid, which in a hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> must render the fruit more grateful. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a> animals are supported on a species called cacus cochinchinensis. The flower of the cacus grandiflora (one of the creeping cereuses) is said to be as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and beautiful as any in the vegetable system: It begins to open in the evening about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> o'clock, is in perfection about eleven, and fades about four in the morning; so that the same flower only continues in perfection about six hours. The calyx when expanded is about a foot in diameter, of a splendid <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> within, and a dark <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> without; the petals are many, and of a pure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of recurved stamina, surrounding the style in the centre of the flower, make a grand appearance, to which may be added the fine scent, which perfumes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> to a considerable distance. It <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>.

CACUS

Pages 50-50

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an Italian shepherd upon Mount Aventine. As <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> was driving home the herd of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Geryon whom he had slain, Cacus robbed him of some of his oxen, which he drew backward into his den lest they should be discovered. Hercules at last finding them out by their lowing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the robbery being discovered to him, killed Cacus with his club. He was Vulcan's son, of prodigious bulk, and half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> half satyr.

CADAN

Pages 50-50

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, in the circle of Zatec, seated on the northern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river Egera, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° 34'. N. Lat. 50° 20'.

CADARI

Pages 50-50
or Kadari, a sect of Mahometans, who assert free will; attribute the actions of men to men alone, not to any secret power determining the will; and deny all absolute decrees, and predestination. The author of this sect was Mabeb ben Kaled al Gihoni, who suffered martyrdom for it. The word comes from the Arabic, cadara, "power." Ben Aun calls the Cadarians the Magi or Manichees of the Muffelians.

CADE

Pages 50-50

a cag, caulk <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>. A cade of herrings is a vessel containing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of 500 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> herrings, or 1000 sprats. CADE Lamb, a young lamb weaned, and brought up by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; called, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>, pet lamb. CADE <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">Oil</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, a name given to an oil much in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in some parts of France and Germany. The physicians call it oleum cadea, or oleum de cadea. This is supposed by some to be the pissevum of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, but improperly; it is made of the fruit of the oxycedrus, which is called by the people of these places cadea. CADE Worm, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGGOT">maggot</a> or worm of a fly called phryganea. It is used as a bait in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANGLING">angling</a>. See Phryganea, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CADEA

Pages 50-50

OF THE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">LEAGUE</a> OF THE <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">HOUSE</a> OF GOD, is one of those that compose the republic of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRISONS">Grisons</a>, and the most powerful and extensive of them all. It contains the bishopric of Coire, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> valley of Engadine, and that of Bragail <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Pregal. Of the 11 great, or 21 small communities, there are but two that speak the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; that of the rest is called the Rhetic, and is a dialect of the Italian. The Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is most prevalent in this league, which has been allied to the Swiss cantons ever since the year 1498. Coire is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

CADENAC

Pages 50-50

a town of France, in Quercy, on the confines of Rouergue, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 12'. N. Lat. 44° 36'.

CADENCE

Pages 50-51

in the manege, an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> proportion, observed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> in all his motions; so that his times have an equal regard to one another, the one does not embrace or take in more ground than the other, and the horse observes his ground regularly.

CADENE

Pages 51-51

one of the sorts of carpets which the Europeans import from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. They are the worst sort of all, and are sold by the piece, from one to two piastres per carpet.

CADENET

Pages 51-51

a town of France in Provence, and in the vigurie of Apt. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 30'. Lat. 43° 40'.

CADES

Pages 51-51
or KADES, in Ancient Geography, a town in the wilderness of Zin, in Arabia Petraea; the first encampment of the Israelites, after their departure from Eziongeber; and from which the wilderness of Zin was called Cades; the burial place of Miriam, with the rock and water of Meribah in it. Another Cader, a town of the tribe of Judah, Joshua xv. 23. Cade/barnae, called also Gades.

CADESBARNEA

Pages 51-51

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the wilderness of Paran, on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, from which the spies were sent out; sometimes simply called Cader, but distinct from the Cades in the wilderness of Zin.

CADET

Pages 51-51

the younger son of a family, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> naturalized in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> from the French. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, among the citizens, the cadets have an equal patrimony with the rest. At Caux, in Normandy, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, as with us, is to leave all to the eldest, except a small portion to the cadets. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, it is usual for one of the cadets in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> families to take the mother's name. Cadet is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> term, denoting a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who chooses to carry arms in a marching regiment as a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. His views are, to acquire some knowledge in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and to obtain a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Cadet differs from volunteer, as the former takes pay, whereas the latter serves without pay.

CADI

Pages 51-51
or CADHI, a judge of civil affairs in the Turkish empire. It is generally taken for the judge of a town; judges of provinces being distinguished by the appellation of mollas. We find numerous complaints of the avarice, injustice, and extortion, of the Turkish cadis; all justice is here venal; the people bribe the cadis, the cadis bribe the moulas, the moulas the cadilechers, and the cadilechers the mufti. Each cadi has his ferjeants, who are to summon persons to appear and answer complaints. If the party summoned fails to appear at the hour appointed, sentence is passed in favour of his adversary. It is usually vain to appeal from the sentences of the cadi, since the affair is never heard anew, but judgment is passed on the case as stated by the cadi. But the cadis are often cashiered and punished for crying injustice with the bastinado and mulcts; the law, however, does not allow them to be put to death. Constantinople has had cadis ever since the year 1392, when Bayazet I. obliged John Paleologus, emperor of the Greeks, to receive cadis into the city to judge all controversies happening between the Greeks and the Turks settled there. In some countries of Africa, the cadis are also judges of religious matters. Among the Moors cadis is the denomination of their higher order of priests or doctors, answering to the rabbins among the Jews.

CADILESCHER

Pages 51-51

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> officer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> among the Turks, answering to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> justice among us. It is said, that this authority was originally confined to the soldiery; but that, at present, it extends itself to the determination of all kinds of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>-suits; yet is nevertheless subject to appeals. There are but three cadilechers in all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior's territories; the first is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>; and the third resides at Grand <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>. This last is the most considerable: they have their seats in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVAN">divan</a> next to the grand vizir.

CADILLAC

Pages 51-51

a town of France in Guienne, and in Bazadois, near the river Garonne, with a handsome castle, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 15'. N. Lat. 44° 37'.

CADIZ

Pages 51-52

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Leon, opposite to Port St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> on the continent, about 60 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>, and 40 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Gibraltar. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 40'. N. Lat. 36° 30'. It occupies the whole surface of the western extremity of the island, which is composed of two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> circular parts, joined together by a very narrow <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of sand, forming altogether the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a chain-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. At the south-east end, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of Suaco, thrown over a deep channel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> river, affords a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the island and the continent; a strong line of works defends the city from all approaches along the isthmus; and, to render them still more difficult, all the gardens and little villas on the beach were in 1762 cleared away, and a dreary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> glade left in their room, so that now there is scarce a tree on the whole island. Except the Calle Ancha, all the streets are narrow, ill paved, and infusible stinking. They are all drawn in straight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and most of them intersect each other at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>. The swarms of rats that in the nights run about the streets are innumerable; whole droves of them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> and repass continually, and these their midnight revels are extremely troublesome to such as walk late. The houses are lofty, with each a vestibule, which being left open till night, serves passengers to retire to; this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, which prevails throughout Spain, renders these places exceedingly offensive. In the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> like a deep well, under which is generally a cistern, the breeding <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of gnats and moquitoes; the ground floors are warehouses, the first stories counting-house or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> apartment up two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of stairs. The roofs are flat, covered with an impenetrable cement, and few are without a mirador or turret for the purpose of commanding a view of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>-wall at top are placed rows of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> pillars, meant either for ornament according to some traditional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a>, or to fix awnings to, that such as sit there for the benefit of the sea breeze may be sheltered from the rays of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; but the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> made of them, is to fasten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> for drying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> upon. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> above all these pinnacles, which give Cadiz a most singular appearance, stands the tower of signals. Here flags are hung out on the first sight of a sail, marking the size of the ship, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> it belongs to, and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a Spanish Indianman, the port of the Indies it comes from. The ships are acquainted with the proper signals to be made, and these are repeated by the watchmen of the tower: as painted lists are in every house, persons concerned in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> soon learn the marks. The city is divided into 24 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, under the inspection of as many commissioners of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>; and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is reckoned at 140,000 inhabitants, of which 12,000 are French, and at least as many more Italians. The square of Saint Antonia is large, and tolerably handsome, and there are a few smaller openings of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. The public walk, or Alameda, is pleasant in the evening: it is fenced off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">coach</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> by a marble rail. The sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> prevents the trees from thriving, and destroys all hopes of future <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. From the Alameda, continuing your walk westwards, you come to the Campolanto, a large esplanade, the only airing-place for coaches; it turns round most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the west and south sides of the island, but the buildings are straggling and ugly; the only edifice of any show is the new orphan house; opposite to it is the fortress of St Sebastian, built on a neck of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> running out into the sea. The round tower at the extremity is supposed to have saved the city, in the great earthquake of 1755, from being swept away by the fury of the waves. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> proved sufficiently <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> to withstand the shock, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the immense volume of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> that threatened destruction to the whole island. In the narrow part of the isthmus the surge <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> over with amazing impetuosity, and bore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> all before it; among the rest, the grandson of the famous tragic poet Racine, who strove in vain to escape, by urging his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> to the utmost of his speed. On St Sebastian's feast, a kind of wake or fair is held in the fort; an astonishing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people then passing and repassing, on a string of wooden bridges laid from rock to rock, makes a very lively moving <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>. From hence to the wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> where they exhibit the bull feasts, you keep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> to the left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> above the sea, which on all this side dashes over large ledges of rock: the shore seems here absolutely inaccessible. On this shore stands the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of great expense, but carried on with so little vigour, that it is difficult to guess at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of years it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> require to bring it to perfection. The vaults are executed with great solidity. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> from the cluttered pilasters to support the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, are very bold; the minute <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> bestowed upon them seems superfluous, as all the effect will be lost from their great height, and from the shade that will be thrown upon them by the filling up of the interstices. From the sea, the present top of the church resembles the carcase of some huge monster <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon its side, rearing its gigantic blanched ribs high above the buildings of the city. The outward casings are to be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, the bars of the windows of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>. Next, crossing before the land gate and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, a superb edifice for strength, convenience, and cleanliness, you come down to the ramparts that defend the city on the side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>. If the prospect to the ocean is solemn, that towards the main land is animated in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; the men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> ride in the eastern booms of the bay; lower down the merchantmen are spread far and near; and close to the town an incredible number of barks, of various shapes and sizes, cover the surface of the water, some moored and some in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, carrying goods to and fro. The opposite shore of Spain is studded with white houses, and enlivened by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of St Mary's, Port-real, and others, behind which, half-way, on a ridge of hills, stands <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-MEDINA_SIDONIA">Medina Sidonia</a>, and further back rise the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>. Westward, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTA">Rota</a> closes the horizon, near which was anciently the island and city of Tartessos, now covered by the sea, but at low water some part of the ruins are still to be discerned. In a large baillon, jutting out into the bay, they have built the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE">custom-house</a>, the first story of which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the walk upon the walls. When it was resolved to erect a building so necessary to this great emporium of trade, the marquis di Squillace gave orders that no expense should be spared, and the most intelligent architects employed, in order to erect a monument, which by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and magnificence might excite the admiration of posterity: the result of these precautions proved a piece of vile <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, composed of the worst of materials. The fire here is prodigious during the last months of the stay of the flota. The packers polish the art of pressing goods to great perfection; but, as they pay the freight according to the cubic palms of each <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">bale</a>, they are apt to squeeze down the cloths and linens so very close and hard, as sometimes to render them unfit for use. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of French luxuries in drapery is enormous; Lyons furnishes most of them; England sends out bale goods; Brittany and the north linens. Every commercial nation has a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> resident at Cadiz; those of England and France are the only ones not allowed to have any concern in trade. In 1596, Cadiz was taken, pillaged, and burnt by the English; but in 1702 it was attempted in conjunction with the Dutch, without success.

CADIZADELITES

Pages 52-52

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Mahometans very like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Stoics. They shun feasts and diversions, and affect an extraordinary gravity in all their actions; they are continually talking of God, and some of them make a jumble of Christianity and Mahometaanism; they drink wine, even in the fast of the Ramazan; they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and protect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; they believe that Mahomet is the Holy Ghost, practise circumcision, and justify it by the example of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ.

CADMEAN LETTERS

Pages 52-52

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ionic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, such as they were first brought by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a> from Phoenicia; whence <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> also calls them Phoenician letters. According to some writers, Cadmus was not the inventor, nor even importer of the Greek letters, but only the modeller and reformer thereof; and it was hence they acquired the appellation Cadmean or Phoenician letters; whereas before that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they had been called Pelagian letters. CADMIA. See CALAMINE.

CADMUS

Pages 52-53

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thebes, the son of Agenor king of Phoenicia, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Phoenix, Cilix, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPA">Europa</a>. He carried into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> the 16 simple letters of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>; and there built Thebes, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>. The poets say, that that he left his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in search of his sister Europa, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> had carried away in the form of a bull; and that, inquiring of the Delphic oracle for a settlement, he was answered, that he should follow the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a cow, and build a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> where she lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. Having arrived among the Phoenicians, he was met by a cow, who conducted him through Boeotia to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where Thebes was afterwards built: but as he was about to sacrifice his guide to Pallas, he sent two of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> to the fountain Dirce for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; when they being devoured by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dragon, he flew the monster, and afterwards, by the advice of Pallas, showed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, when there sprung up a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of armed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, who prepared to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the serpent; but on his casting a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> among these upright warriors, they turned their weapons against each other with such animosity, that only five survived the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, and these assisted Cadmus in founding his new city. Afterwards, to recompense his labours, the gods gave him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONIA">Harmonia</a>, or Harmonie, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> and Venus; and honoured his nuptials with presents and peculiar marks of favour. But at length resigning Thebes to Pentheus, Cadmus and Harmonie went to govern the Echellenes: when grown old, they were transformed into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>; or, as others say, sent to the Elysian fields, in a chariot drawn by serpents. See THEBES. CADMUS of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>, a celebrated Greek historian, was, according to Pliny, the first of the Greeks who wrote history in prose. He flourished about 550 before Christ.

CADORE

Pages 53-53
or PIEVE DE CADORE, a town of Italy, in the territory of Venice, and capital of a district called Cadoreino; famous for the birth of Titian the painter. E. Long. 13° 45'. N. Lat. 46° 25'.

CADORINO

Pages 53-53

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; bounded on the east by Friuli Proper, on the south and west by the Bellunese, and by the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIXEN">Brixen</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. It is a very mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but pretty populous. The only town is Pieve de Cadore.

CADRITES

Pages 53-53

a sort of Mahometan friars, who once a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> spend a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the night in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round, holding each other's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and repeating incessantly the word hai, which signifies living, and is one of the attributes of God; during which one of them plays on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>. They never cut their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, nor cover their heads; and always go bare-footed: they have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to quit their convent when they please, and to marry.

CADSAND

Pages 53-53

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, situated at the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHELDT">Scheldt</a>, whereby the Dutch command the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of that river.

CADUCEUS

Pages 53-53

in antiquity, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>'s rod <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sceptre, being a wand entwined by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, borne by that deity as the ensign of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and office, given him, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>-stringed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>. Wonderful properties are ascribed to this rod by the poets; as laying men asleep, raising the dead, &c. It was also used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> as a symbol of peace and concord: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> sent the Carthaginians a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a> and a caduceus, offering them their choice either of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> or peace. Among that people, those who denounced war were called feciales; and those who went to demand peace, caduceatores, because they bore a caduceus in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The caduceus found on medals is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> symbol, signifying good conduct, peace and prosperity. The rod expresses power, the two serpents <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, and the two wings diligence.

CADUCI

Pages 53-53

from cadu "to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>"; the name of a clas in Linnaeus's calycina, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> whose calyx is a simple perianthium, supporting a single-flower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fructification, and falling off either before or with the petals. It stands opposed to the clas pedicellata in the same method, and is exemplified in mustard and ranunculus.

CADURCI

Pages 53-53

CADURCUM, Cadurcus, and Cadurs, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Cadurci, a people of Aquitania; situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Oldus, running from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and the Tarnis from the south, and falling into the Garumna; Now <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAHORS">Cahors</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the territory of the Querci, in Guienne. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Cadurci, to the south next the Tarnis, were called Eleutheri.

CADUS

Pages 53-53

in antiquity, a wine vessel of a certain capacity, containing 80 amphorae <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> firkins; each of which, according to the best accounts, held <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> gallons.

CADUSII

Pages 53-53

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a people of Media Atropatene, situated to the west in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and reaching to the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; between whom and the Medes perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and enmity <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>.

CAECILIA

Pages 53-53

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> belonging to the amphibious clas. The caecilia has no scales; it is smooth, and moves by means of lateral rugae <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prickles. The upper lip is prominent, and furnished with two tentacula. It has no tail. There are but two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, viz. 1. The tentaculata, has 135 rugae. It is about a foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and an inch in circumference, preserving an uniform cylindrical shape from the one end to the other. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are very small. It has such a resemblance to an eel, that it may easily be mistaken for one; but as it has neither fins nor gills, it cannot be clasped with the fishes. It is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and its bite is not poisonous. 2. The glutinosa, has 340 rugae or prickles above, and 10 below, the anus. It is of a brownish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> line on the side, and is a native of the Indies.

CAELIUM

Pages 53-53

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an inland town of Peucetia, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Apulia; a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five miles above Barium or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, and which still retains that name.

CAELIUS

Pages 53-53

Aurelianus, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> physician, and the only one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a> of whom we have any remains. He was of Sicca, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>; but in what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> he lived, cannot be determined: it is probable, however, that he lived before Galen: since, though he carefully mentions all the physicians before him, he takes no notice of Galen. He had read over very diligently the ancient physi-

CAELIUS MONS

Pages 53-53

(Itinerary); a town of Vindelicia, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> west side of the Ilargus. Now Kelmuntz, a small town of Suabia, on the Iller. CAELIUS MONS at Rome. See COELIUS.

CAEN

Pages 53-54

a handsome and considerable town of France, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Lower Normandy, with a celebrated university, and an academy of literature. It contains 60 streets, and 12 parishes. It has a castle with four towers, which were built by the English. The town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> with four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> towers. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> is the handsomest in all Normandy, and has fine houses on three sides of it; and in the middle is the statue of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, standing on a marble pedestal, and surrounded with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> ballustrade. It is seated in a pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORNE">Orne</a>, about eight miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. William the Conqueror was buried here, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Stephen, which he founded. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 27. N. Lat. 49. 11.

CAERE

Pages 54-54

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Etruria, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of Mezentius. Its ancient name was Argylla. In Strabo's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> not the least vestige of it remained, except the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> called ceretana. From this town the Roman censor's tables were called cerites tabulae. In these were entered the names of such as for some misdemeanor forfeited their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of suffrage, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> were degraded from a higher to a less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> tribe. For the people of Caere hospitably receiving those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> who, after the taking of Rome by the Gauls, fled with their gods and the sacred fire of Vesta, were, on the Romans recovering themselves from this disaster, honoured with the privilege of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, but without a right of voting. CAERITESTABULAE. See the preceding article.

CAERFILLY

Pages 54-54

a town of Glamorganshire in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, seated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Taff and Towy, in a moorish ground among the hills. It is thought the walls, now in ruins, were built by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; there being often Roman coins dug up there. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 12. N. Lat. 51. 25.

CAERLEON

Pages 54-54

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a> in England, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. It was a Roman town, as is evident from the many Roman antiquities found here. It is commodiously situated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USK">Usk</a>, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. The houses are generally built of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and there are the ruins of a castle still to be seen. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. o. N. Lat. 51. 40.

CAERMARTHEN-SHIRE

Pages 54-54

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> St George's channel, Cardiganshire on the south, the shires of Brecknock and Glamorgan on the east, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>-shire on the west. Its greatest length is between 30 and 40 miles, and its breadth upwards of 20. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is wholesome, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> less rocky and mountainous than most other parts of Wales, and consequently is proportionally more fertile both in corn and pasture. It has also plenty of wood, and is well supplied with coal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>. The most considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Towy, the Cothi, and the Tawe; of which, the first abounds with excellent salmon. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Caerphilly the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, Kidwelly, Llanidloes, &c. This county abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> forts, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>, and tumuli or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROWS">barrows</a>. Near to Caerphilly, towards the east, may be seen the ruins of Castell Carreg, which was situated on a steep and inaccessible rock; and also several vast caverns, supposed to have been <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Near this spot is a fountain which ebbs and flows twice in 24 hours like the sea.

CAERNARVON

Pages 54-55

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of that name. It was built by Edward I. near the site of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Segontium, after his conquest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in 1282, the situation being well adapted to overawe his new subjects. It had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> requisites for strength; being bounded on one side by the arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> called the Menai; by the estuary of the Sciont Caernarvon Sciont on another, exactly where it receives the tide from the former; on a third side, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the fourth, by a creek of the Menai; and the remainder has the appearance of having the infestation completed by art. Edward undertook this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> immediately after his conquest of the country in 1282, and completed the fortifications and castle before 1284; for his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, on April 23rd in that year, brought forth within its walls Edward, first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Wales of the English line. It was built within the space of one year, by the labour of the peasants, and at the cost of the chieftains of the country, on whom the conqueror imposed the hateful task. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> state of the walls and castle, Mr Pennant informs us, are at present exactly as they were in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Edward. The walls are defended by numbers of round towers, and have two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> gates: the east, facing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; the west, upon the Menai. The entrance into the castle is very august, beneath a great tower, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of which appears the statue of the founder, with a dagger in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> menacing his new acquired unwilling subjects. The gate had four portcullises, and every requisite of strength. The towers are very beautiful. The eagle tower is remarkably fine, and has the addition of three slender angular turrets rising from the top. Edward II. was born in a little dark room in this tower, not twelve feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> nor eight in breadth: so little did, in those days, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> comfort consult either pomp <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> convenience. The gate through which the affectionate Eleanor entered, to give the Welsh a prince of their own, who could not speak a word of English, is at the farthest end, at a vast height above the outside ground; so could only be approached by a drawbridge. The quay is a most beautiful walk along the side of the Menai, and commands a most agreeable view. Caernarvon is destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, but has a brisk trade with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, for the several necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. It is the residence of numbers of genteel families, and contains several very good houses. Edward I. bestowed on this town its first royal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, and made it a free borough. Among other privileges, none of the burgesses could be convicted of any crime committed between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Conway and Dyfi, unless by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> of their own townsmen. It is governed by a mayor, who, by patent, is created governor of the castle. It has one <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>, two bailiffs, a town clerk, and two sergeants at mace. The representative of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is elected by its burgesses, and those of Conway, Pwllheli, Nefyn, and Crickaeth. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of voting is in every one, resident or non-resident, admitted to their freedom. The town gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> and marquis to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Chandos, and has a good tide harbour.

CAERNARVON-SHIRE

Pages 54-54

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and west by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the south by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERIONETHSHIRE">Merionethshire</a>, and on the east divided from Denbighshire by the river Conway. It is about 40 miles in length, and 20 in breadth; and sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for the shire, and another for the borough of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAERNARVON">Caernarvon</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very piercing; owing partly to the snow, that lies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> eight months of the year upon some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which are so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> that they are called the British <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>; and partly to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, which are said not to be fewer than 50 or 60. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in the valleys on the side next <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> is pretty fertile, especially in barley; great numbers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, sheep, and goats, are fed on the mountains; and the sea, lakes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, abound with variety of fish. The highest mountains in the county are those called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SNOWDON">Snowdon</a> hills, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">Pen</a>-maen-mawr, which last hangs over the sea. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> cut out of the rock on the side next the sea, guarded by a wall running along the edge of it on that side; but the traveller is sometimes in danger of being crushed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of pieces of the rock from the precipices above. The river Conway, though its course from the lake out of which it issues to its mouth is only 12 miles, yet is so deep, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the many brooks it receives, that it is navigable by ships of good burden for eight miles. Pearls are found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> black mussels taken in this river. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a>, Caernarvon the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and Conway. In this county is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> road said to have been made by Helena the mother of Constantine the Great; and Matthew of Westminster asserts, that the body of Constantius the father of the same Constantine was found at Caernarvon in the year 1283, and interred in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> there by order of Edward I.

CAERWIS

Pages 55-58

a market town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLINTSHIRE">Flintshire</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 25', N. Lat. 53° 20'. CÆSALPINIA BRASILETTO, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> wood. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Of this there are three <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, the most remarkable of which is the brasiliensis, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Brazilletto. It grows naturally in the warmest parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, from whence the wood is imported for the dyers, who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it much. The demand has been so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that none of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trees are left in any of the British plantations; so that Mr Catesby owns himself ignorant of the dimensions to which they grow. The largest remaining are not above two inches in Caesalpinus, thickness, and eight or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet in height. The branches are slender and full of small prickles; the leaves are pinnated; the lobes growing opposite to one another, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> at their ends, with one notch. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, papilionaceous, with many stamens and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> spicules, growing in a pyramidal spike, at the end of a long slender stalk: the pods enclose several small round seeds. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> produced from this wood is greatly improved by solution of tin in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> regia.* See Co. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort is a native of the same countries with the first, but is of a larger size. It sends out many weak <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> branches, armed with short, strong, upright thorns. The leaves branch out in the same manner as the first; but the lobes, or small leaves, are oval and entire. The flowers are produced in long spikes like those of the former, but are variegated with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> may be propagated from seeds, which should be sown in small pots filled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> rich <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> early in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and plunged in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of tanner's bark. Being tender, they require to be always kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, and to be treated in the same manner as other exotics of that kind. CÆSALPINUS, of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AREZZO">Arezzo</a>, professor at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, and afterwards physician to Pope Clement VIII., one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> writers in botany. See Botany Index. CÆSAR, Julius, the illustrious Roman general and historian, was of the family of the Julii, who pretended they were descended from Venus by Aeneas. The descendants of Alcanius, son of Aeneas and Creusa, and surnamed Julius, lived in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a> till that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> was ruined by Tullus Hostilius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Rome, who carried them to Rome, where they flourished. We do not find that they produced more than two branches. The first bore the name of Tullus, the other that of Caesar. The most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> of the Caesars were those who were in public employments in the 7th year of the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. After that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> we find there was always some of that family who enjoyed public offices in the commonwealth, till the time of Gaius Julius Caesar, the subject of this article. He was born at Rome the 12th of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> Quintilis, year of the city 653, and lost his father an. 669. By his valour and eloquence he soon acquired the highest reputation in the field and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. Beloved and respected by his fellow citizens, he enjoyed successively every magisterial and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> the public could bestow consistent with its own free <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. But at length having subdued Pompey the great rival of his growing power, his boundless ambition effaced the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of his former actions: for, pursuing his favourite maxim, "that he had rather be the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in a village than the second in Rome," he procured himself to be chosen perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>; and, not content with this unconstitutional power, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> had resolved to raise him to the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; when the friends of the civil liberties of the republic rally affianced him in the senate-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where they should only have seized him and brought him to a legal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> for usurpation. By this impolitic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> they defeated their own purpose, involving the city in consternation and terror, which produced general anarchy, and paved the way to the revolution they wanted to prevent; the monarchial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> being absolutely founded on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of Julius Caesar. He fell in the 56th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, 43 years before before the Christian era. His commentaries contain a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> voyages, battles, and victories. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> edition in 1712, in folio, is preferred. The detail of Cæsar's transactions (so far as is consistent with the limits of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>) being given under the article Rome, we shall here only add a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of him as drawn by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>.* * From the Melanges Philosophiques of M. Opheliot. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> of 18 centuries, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> may be published without offence, a philosopher might, in the following terms, censure Cæsar without calumniating him, and applaud him without exciting his blushes. "Cæsar had one predominant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>: it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of glory; and he passed 40 years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in seeking opportunities to foster and encourage it. His <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, entirely absorbed in ambition, did not open itself to other impulses. He cultivated letters; but he did not love them with enthusiasm, because he had not leisure to become the first orator of Rome. He corrupted the one half of the Roman ladies, but his heart had no concern in the fiery ardours of his senses. In the arms of Cleopatra, he thought of Pompey; and this singular man, who disdained to have a partner in the empire of the world, would have blushed to have been for one instant the slave of a woman. "We must not imagine, that Cæsar was born a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, as Sophocles and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> were born poets. For, if <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> had made him a citizen of Sybaris, he would have been the most voluptuous of men. If in our days he had been born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>, he would have been the most inoffensive of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, and would not have disturbed the tranquillity of the new world. "The moderation with which he conducted himself after his victories, has been highly extolled; but in this he showed his penetration, not the goodness of his heart. Is it not obvious, that the display of certain virtues is necessary to put in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> machine? It was requisite that he should have the appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>, if he inclined that Rome should forgive him his victories. But what greatness of mind is there in a generosity which follows on the usurpation of the supreme power? "Nature, while it marked Cæsar with a sublime character, gave him also that spirit of perseverance which renders it useful. He had no sooner begun to reflect, than he admired Sylla; hated him, and yet wished to imitate him. At the age of 15, he formed the project of being dictator. It was thus that the prescient Montesquieu conceived, in his early youth, the idea of the Spirit of Laws. "Physical qualities, as well as moral causes, contributed to give strength to his character. Nature, which had made him for command, had given him an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of dignity. He had acquired that loft and infusing eloquence, which is perfectly suited to seduce vulgar minds, and has a powerful influence on the most cultivated. His love of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> was a merit with the fair <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; and women, who even in a republic can draw to them the suffrages and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of men, have the highest importance in degenerate times. The ladies of his age were charmed with the prospect of having a dictator whom they might subdue by their attractions. "In vain did the genius of Cato watch for some time to sustain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. It was unequal to contend with that of Cæsar. Of what avail were the eloquence, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and the virtue of this republican, when opposed by a man who had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to debauch the wife of every citizen whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> he meant to engage; who, possessing an enthusiasm for glory, wept, because, at the age of 30, he had not conquered the world like Alexander; and who, with the haughty temper of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a>, was more desirous to be the first man in a village than the second in Rome. "Cæsar had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to exist in times of trouble and civil commotions, when the minds of men are put into a ferment; when opportunities of great actions are frequent; when talents are everything, and those who can only boast of their virtues are nothing. If he had lived an hundred years sooner, he would have been no more than an obscure villain; and, instead of giving laws to the world, would not have been able to produce any confusion in it. "I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> here be bold enough to advance an idea, which may appear paradoxical to those who weakly judge of men from what they achieve, and not from the principle which leads them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>. Nature formed in the same mould Cæsar, Mahomet, Cromwell, and Kouli Khan. They all of them united to genius that profound policy which renders it so powerful. They all of them had an evident superiority over those with whom they were surrounded; they were conscious of this superiority, and they made others conscious of it. They were all of them born subjects, and became fortunate usurpers. Had Cæsar been placed in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, he would have made the conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, he would have been the founder of a new <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; in London, he would have stabbed his sovereign, or have procured his assassination under the sanction of the laws. He reigned with glory over men whom he had reduced to be slaves; and, under one aspect, he is to be considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>; under another, as a monster. But it would be unfortunate, indeed, for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, if the possession of superior talents gave individuals a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to trouble its repose. Usurpers accordingly have flatterers, but no friends; strangers respect them; their subjects complain and submit; it is in their own families that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> finds her avengers. Cæsar was assassinated by his son, Mahomet was poisoned by his wife, Kouli Khan was massacred by his nephew, and Cromwell only died in his bed because his son Richard was a philosopher. "Cæsar, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of his country; Cæsar, who destroyed the agents of his crimes, if they failed in address; Cæsar, in fine, the husband of every wife, and the wife of every husband, has been accounted a great man by the mob of writers.
