in the manege, the decent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flopping declivity of a rising manege ground, being a small eminence upon which we ride <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> several times, putting him to a short gallop, with his fore hams in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, to learn him to ply or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> his haunches, and form his stop upon the aides of the calves of the legs, the stay of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a>, and the cavelon fealona- bly given.

CALAGORINA

Pages 66-66
or Calaguris, distinguished by the surname Nafica, in Ancient Geography, a city of the Valcenes in the Hither Spain: now Calahorra.

CALAHORRA

Pages 66-66

an episcopal town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Old Castile, seated on a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, on the side of a hill which extends to the banks of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EBRO">Ebro</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 7. N. Lat. 42. 12.

CALAIS

Pages 66-67

a strong town of France, in Lower Picardy, now called the department of the straits of Calais, which has a citadel and a fortified harbour. It is built in the form of a triangle, one side of which is towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The citadel is as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as the town, and has but one entrance. It is a trading <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with handsome streets, and several churches and monasteries; the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants is reckoned to be 4000. Calais was taken by Edward III. in 1347. Hither he marched his victorious <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> from Creully, and invested the town on the 8th of September. But finding that it could not be taken by force without the destruction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> multitudes of his men, he turned the siege into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a>; and having made strong intrenchments to secure his army from the enemy, huts Calais, to protect them from the inclemency of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and stationed a fleet before the harbour to prevent the introduction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, he resolved to wait with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> till the place fell into his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> by famine. The besieged, discovering his intention, turned seventeen hundred women, children, and old people, out of the town, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> their provisions; and Edward had the goodness, after entertaining them with a dinner, and giving them two-pence a piece, to suffer them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. The garrison and inhabitants of Calais having at length consumed all their provisions, and even eaten all the horses, dogs, cats, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> in the place, the governor John de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a> appeared upon the walls, and offered to capitulate. Edward greatly incensed at their obstinate resistance, which had detained him eleven months under their walls, at an immense expense both of men and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, sent Sir Walter Mauny, an illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, to acquaint the governor that he would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them no terms; but that they must surrender at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. At length, however, at the spirited remonstrances of the governor, and the persuasions of Sir Walter Mauny, Edward consented to grant their lives to all the garrison and inhabitants, except six of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> burgesses, who should deliver to him the keys of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> about their necks. When these terms were made known to the people of Calais, they were plunged into the deepest distress; and after all the miseries they had suffered, they could not think without horror of giving up six of their fellow citizens to certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. In this extremity, when the whole people were drowned in tears, and uncertain what to do, Euiface de St Pierre, one of the richest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> in the place, stepped forth, and voluntarily offered himself to be one of these six devoted victims. His noble example was soon imitated by other five of the most wealthy citizens. These true patriots, barefooted, and bareheaded, with ropes about their necks, were attended to the gates by the whole inhabitants, with tears, bleatings, and prayers for their safety. When they were brought into Edward's presence, they laid the keys of the city at his feet, and falling on their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> implored his mercy in such moving strains, that all the noble spectators melted into tears. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s resentment was so strong for the many toils and losses he had suffered in this tedious siege, that he was in some danger of forgetting his usual <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>; when the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, falling upon her knees before him, earnestly begged and obtained their lives. This great and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> conducted these virtuous citizens, whose lives she had saved, to her own apartment, entertained them honourably, and dismissed them with presents. Edward took possession of Calais August 4th; and in order to secure a conquest of so great importance, and which had cost him so dear, he found it necessary to turn out all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants, who had discovered so strong an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to their native prince, and to people it with English. Calais remained in subjection to England till the reign of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, when it was retaken by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Guise. This general began the enterprise by ordering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a> of Normandy and Bretagne to cruise in the Channel, more especially in the very straits of Calais: he then detached the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVERS">Nevers</a> with a considerable army towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Luxembourg; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> which drew the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the Spaniards that way: when all things were ready, he procured an application from the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOULOGNE">Boulogne</a>, for a body of troops to secure them against the incursions of the Spaniards; he sent a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> at their request, which was followed by another, under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of supporting them; then repaired thither in person, secure that his officers would follow his instructions: and thus, on the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the new year, 1557, Calais was invested. He immediately attacked Fort St Agatha, which the garrison quitted, and retired into the fort of Nicolaï, which, together with the Ribank, the besiegers attacked at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, granted good terms to the officer who commanded in the former, but obliged the garrison of the latter to surrender prisoners of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. By these means he opened a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the sea; and having received from on board the ships an immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of hurdles, his infantry, by the help of them, paved the morasses that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> round the town. He then made a false attack at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-gate, which drew the attention of the garrison, who fatigued themselves exceedingly in making intrenchments behind the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a>; but when they had finished their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, he began to fire upon the castle, where the walls were very old, and had been neglected on account of the breadth of the ditch, which was also very deep when the tide was in; but a great breach being made, the duke caused it to be attacked in the night, and during the ebb, the foldiers passing almost up to the shoulders. The place was easily carried, though the governor made three vigorous attacks before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> of day, in order to dislodge them; but the French, though they lost a considerable number of men, kept their posts. The governor then <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that it was impracticable to defend the place any longer, and therefore made the best terms for himself that he could obtain, which, however, were not very good: and thus in eight days the duke of Guise recovered a fortress which cost the victorious Edward III. a whole year's siege, and which had been now 210 years in the possession of the English, without so much as a single attempt to retake it. There are very different accounts given of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Some English historians say, that King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> penetrated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the French upon this fortress, gave notice of it in England, and offered to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of it upon himself; but that this, out of jealousy, was refused, it being believed to be only an artifice to get a place of such <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> into his own hands. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the matter seems to be this: The strength of Calais consisted in its situation and outworks, which required a very numerous garrison; but this being attended with a very large expense, the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the troops had been sent to join Philip's army, so that the governor had not above 500 men, and there were no more than 250 of the townsmen able to bear arms. As to ammunition, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, and provisions, the French found there abundance; but with so slender a garrison, it was impossible to make a better defence; and therefore when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Wentworth, who was governor, and whom the French call Lord Dumfort, was tried by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> for the loss of this place, he was acquitted. The duke obliged all the English inhabitants to quit Calais; and befellowed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of it upon Des Termes, who was soon after made a marshal of France. The fortifications of Calais are good; but its greatest strength is its situation among the marshes, which may be overflowed at the approach of an enemy. The harbour is not so good as formerly, nor <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> it admit vessels of any great burden. In times of peace, there are packet boats going backward and forward twice a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> to Calais, which is 21 miles distant. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 6. N. Lat. 50° 58'. Calais and Zetes, in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, sons of Boreas and Orynthia, to whom the poets attributed wings: they went on the voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a> with the Argonauts; delivered Phineus from the harpies; and were slain by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>.

CALAMANCO

Pages 67-67

a sort of woollen stuff manufactured in England and Brabant. It has a fine glofs; and is checkered in the warp, whence the checks appear only on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side. Some calamances are quite plain, others have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> stripes adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, some with plain broad stripes, some with narrow stripes, and others watered. CALAMARIÆ, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> in the Fragments methodi naturalis of Linnaeus; in which he has the following genera, viz. behartia, cirpus, cyperus, eriophorum, carex, schœnus, flagellaria, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCUS">juncus</a>. See Botany.

CALAMATA

Pages 67-67

a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in the Morea, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Belvedera. It was taken by the Venetians in 1685; but the Turks retook it afterwards with all the Morea. It stands on the river Spinarza, eight miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> 22. 15. N. Lat. 37° 8'.

CALAMINE

Pages 67-68

CALAMY, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">LAPIS</a> GALAMINARIS, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> CADMIUM FOSSILIS, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or mineral containing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and sometimes other substances. It is considerably heavy; moderately hard and brittle, or of a concretion between stone and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> sometimes whitish or gray; sometimes yellowish, or of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>; sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> or blackish. It is plentiful in several places of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, Transylvania, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, Gollard, France, and England, particularly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, as also in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. The calamine of England, however, is by the best judges allowed to be superior in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to that of most other countries. It seldom lies very deep, being chiefly found in clayey grounds near the surface. In some places it is mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> ores. It is a true ore of zinc, and is used as an ingredient in making of bras.—Newman relates various experiments with this mineral, the only result of which was to show that it contained iron as well as zinc. The most remarkable are the following: A saturated solution of calamine in the marine acid, concentrated by evaporating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the liquor, exhibits in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> an appearance of fine crystals, which on the application of warmth dissolve and disappear. A little of this concentrated solution tinges a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of a bright yellow colour; and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> deposits by degrees a fine, spongy, brownish precipitate. Blue dissolved in this solution, and afterwards inspissated, forms an extremely slippery tenacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, which does not become dry, and, were it not too expensive, might be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for entangling flies, caterpillars, &c. Sulphur boiled in this solution, seems to acquire some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of transparency. transparency.—This mineral is an article in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>; but, before it comes to the shops is usually roasted or calcined, in order to separate some arsenical or sulphurous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which is in its crude state it is supposed to contain, and to render it more easily reducible into a fine powder. In this state it is employed in collyria against defluxions of thin acrid humours upon the eyes, for drying up moist running ulcers, and healing excoriations. It is the basis of an official epulotic Cerate. There is another substance from which this semi-metal is also obtained. This is called cadmia furnacum, or cadmia of the furnaces, to distinguish it from the other. This is a matter sublimed when ores containing zinc, like those of Rammelberg, are melted. This cadmia consists of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of the semi-metal sublimed during the fusion, and adhering to the inner surfaces of the walls of furnaces, where they suffer a semi-fusion, and therefore acquire some solidity. So <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a quantity of these is collected, that they form very thick incrustations, which must be frequently taken off. CALAMINT. See Melissa and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTHA">Mentha</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALAMUS">CALAMUS</a>. See Botany Index. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, the rotang. The stem is without branches, has a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> at top, and is everywhere beset with straight spines. This is the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, which is not visible on the outside; but the bark being taken off discovers the smooth stick, which has no marks of spine on the bark, and is exactly like those which the Dutch sell to us; keeping this matter very secret, left travellers going by should take as many canes out of the woods as they please. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a> is said to be the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where most of these sticks grow. Such are to be chosen as are of proper growth between two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, suitable to the fashionable length of canes as they are then worn; but such are scarce. The calamus rotang is one of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> from which the drug called dragons blood is obtained. Calamus, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets, denotes a simple kind of pipe or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISTULA">fistula</a>, the musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of the shepherds and herdsmen; usually made either of an oaten stalk or a reed. Calamus Aromaticus, or Sweet-scented <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">Flag</a>, in the materia medica, a species of flag called acorus by Linnaeus. See Acorus. Botany Index. Calamus Scripserint, in antiquity, a reed or rush to write with. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> made use of styles to write on tables covered with wax; and of reed, or rush, to write on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, or Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>.

CALAMY

Pages 68-69

EDMUND, grandson to the preceding, (by his eldest son, Mr Edmund Calamy, who was ejected from the living of Moxton in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> on St Bartholomew's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> 1662) was born in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, April 5, 1671. After having learned the languages, and gone through a course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and logic at a private academy in England, he studied philosophy and civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, and attended the lectures of the learned Graevius. Whilst he resided here, an offer of a professor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> was made him by Mr Carstairs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of that university, sent over on purpose to find a person properly qualified for such an office. This he declined; and returned to England in 1691, bringing with him letters from Graevius to Dr Pococke canon of Christchurch and regius professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, and to Dr Bernard, Savilian professor of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, who obtained leave for him to prosecute his studies in the Bodleian library. Having resolved to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> his principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, he entered into an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the controversy between the conformists and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NONCONFORMISTS">nonconformists</a>; which determined him to join the latter; and coming to London in 1692, he was unanimously chosen assistant to Mr Matthew Sylvester at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACKFRIARS">Blackfriars</a>; and in 1694, he was ordained at Mr Annelly's meeting-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Little St Helena, and soon after was invited to become assistant to Mr Daniel Williams in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">Hand</a>-Alley. In 1702, he was chosen to be one of the lecturers in Salters-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; and in 1703, succeeded Mr Vincent Allop as pastor of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> in Westminster. He drew up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of contents to Mr Baxter's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and times, which was sent to the press in 1666; made some remarks on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> itself, and added to it an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a>; and, reflecting on the usefulness of the book, he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the expediency of continuing it, for Mr Baxter's history came no lower than the year 1684. Accordingly he composed an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of it, with an account of many other ministers who were ejected after the restoration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II.; their apology, containing the grounds of their non-conformity and practice as to stated and occasional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England; and a continuation of their history till the year 1691. This work was published in 1702. He afterwards published a moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of nonconformity, in three tracts, in answer to some tracts of Dr Hoadley. In 1709, Mr Calamy made a tour to Scotland; and had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of divinity conferred on him by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Edinburgh, Aberdeen, and Glasgow. In 1713, he published a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of his Abridgement of Mr Baxter's history of his life and times; in which, among other additions, there is a continuation of the history through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William's reign, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the passing of the occasional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> is subjoined the reformed liturgy, which was drawn drawn up and presented to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> in 1661, "that the world may judge (he says in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>) how fairly the ejected ministers have been often represented as irreconcilable enemies to all liturgies." In 1718, he wrote a vindication of his grandfather, and several other persons, against certain reflections <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon them by Mr Archdeacon Echard in his History of England; and in 1728 appeared his Continuation of the account of the ministers, lecturers, matters, and fellows of colleges, and schoolmasters, who were ejected, after the restoration in 1660, by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of uniformity. He died <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 3, 1732, greatly regretted not only by the dissenters, but also by the moderate members of the established church, both clergy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>, with many of whom he lived in great intimacy. Besides the pieces already mentioned, he published a great many sermons on several subjects and occasions. He was twice married, and had 13 children.

CALANDRE

Pages 69-69

a name given by the French writers to an insect that does vast mischief in granaries. It is properly of the scarab <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> beetle class; it has two antennae or horns formed of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of round <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, and covered with a soft and short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; from the anterior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the head there thrusts out a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, which is so formed at the end, that the creature easily makes way with it through the coat or skin that covers the grain, and gets at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> or farina on which it feeds; the inside of the grains is also the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> deposits her eggs, that the young progeny may be born with provision about them. When the female has pierced a grain of corn for this purpose, she deposits in it one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, or at the utmost two, but the most frequently lays them single; these eggs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCH">hatch</a> into small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, which are usually found with their bodies rolled up in a spiral form, and after eating till they arrive at their full growth, they are changed into chrysalises, and from these in about a fortnight comes out the perfect calandre. The female lays a considerable number of eggs; and the increase of these creatures would be very great, but <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has so ordered it, that while in the egg state, and even while in that of the worm, they are subject to be eaten by mites; these little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> are always very plentiful in granaries, and they destroy the far greater number of these larger animals.

CALAS

Pages 69-69

JOHN; the name of a most unfortunate Protestant merchant at Thoulouse, inhumanly butchered under forms of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> cruelly prostituted to shelter the sanguinary dictates of ignorant Popish zeal. He had lived 40 years at Thoulouse. His wife was an English woman of French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>; and they had five sons; one of whom, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, had turned Catholic through the persuasions of a Catholic maid who had lived 30 years in the family. In October 1761, the family consisted of Calas, his wife, Mark Anthony their son, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son, and this maid. Anthony was educated for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>; but being of a melancholy turn of mind, was continually dwelling on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> from authors on the subject of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUICIDE">suicide</a>, and one night in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> hanged himself on a bar laid across two folding doors in their shop. The crowd collected by the confusion of the family on so shocking a discovery, took it into their heads that he had been strangled by the family to prevent his changing his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and that this was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> practice among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. The officers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> adopted the popular tale, and were supplied by the mob with what they accepted as evidences of the fact. The fraternity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Penitents got the body, buried it with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, and performed a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> for him as a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>; the Franciscans did the same; and after these formalities no one doubted the guilt of the devoted heretical family. They were all condemned to the torture, to bring them to confession: they appealed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; who, as weak and as wicked as the subordinate magistrates, sentenced the father to the torture, ordinary and extraordinary, to be broken alive upon the wheel, and then to be burnt to ashes. A diabolical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>! which, to the shame of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, was actually carried into execution. Peter Calas, the other son, was banished for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and the rest were acquitted. The distracted widow found some friends, and among the rest M. Voltaire, who laid her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of state at Verailles, and the parliament of Thoulouse was ordered to transmit the proceedings. These the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and council unanimously agreed to annul; the capitoul <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of Thoulouse was degraded and fined; old Calas was declared to have been innocent; and every imputation of guilt was removed from the family, who also received from the king and clergy considerable gratuities.

CALASH

Pages 69-69
or CALES, a small light kind of chariot or chair, with very low wheels, used chiefly for taking the air in parks and gardens. The calash is for the most part richly decorated, and open on all sides for the convenience of the air and prospect, or at most enclosed with light mantlets of wax-cloth to be opened and shut at pleasure. In the Philosophical Transactions we have a description of a new sort of calash going on two wheels, not hung on traces, yet easier than the common coaches, over which it has this further advantage, that whereas a common coach will overturn if one wheel go on a surface a foot and a half higher than the other, this will admit of a difference of 3½ feet without danger of overturning. Add, that it would turn over and over; that is, after the spokes being so turned as that they are parallel to the horizon, and one wheel flat over the head of him that rides in it, and the other flat under him, it will turn once more, by which the wheels are placed in statu quo, without any disorder to the horse or rider.

CALASIO

Pages 69-69

MARIUS, a Franciscan, and professor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> at Rome, of whom there is very little to be said, but that he published there, in the year 1621, a Concordance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, which consisted of four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> volumes in folio. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> has been highly approved and commended both by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and Papists, and is indeed a most admirable work. For besides the Hebrew words in the Bible, which are in the body of the book, with the Latin version over against them; there are, in the margin, the differences between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> version and the Vulgate; so that at one view may be seen wherein the three Bibles agree, and wherein they differ. Moreover, at the beginning of every article there is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, which gives the signification of each Hebrew word; affords an opportunity of comparing it with other oriental languages, viz. with the Syriac, Arabic, and Chaldee; and is extremely useful.

CALASIRIS

Pages 69-70

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> tunic fringed at the bottom, and worn by the Egyptians under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> woollen garment; but this last they were obliged to pull off when they entered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, being only allowed to appear there in linen garments.

CALATAJUD

Pages 70-70

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Arragon; situated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Xalon and Xiloa, at the end of a very fertile valley, with a good castle on a rock. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 9. N. Lat. 41. 22.

CALATHUS

Pages 70-70

in antiquity, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> wood <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rushes; used by the women sometimes to gather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, but chiefly after the example of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> to put their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the calathus, as represented on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments, is narrow at the bottom, and widening upwards like that of a top. Pliny compares it to that of a lily. The calathus or work basket of Minerva is no less celebrated among the poets than her distaff. CALATHUS was also the name of a cup for wine used in sacrifices.

CALATOR

Pages 70-70

in antiquity, a crier, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> officer appointed to publish some thing aloud, or call the people together. The word is formed from καλῶν, voco, I call. Such ministers the pontifices had, whom they used to send before them when they went to sacrifice on feriae or holidays, to advertise the people to leave off <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The magistrates also used calatores, to call the people to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a>, both curiata and centuriata. The officers in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> also had calatores; as had likewise many private families, to invite their guests to entertainments.

CALATRAVA

Pages 70-70

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of New Castile, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, situated on the river Guadiana, 45 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 20. N. Lat. 39. 0. Knights of Calatrava, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> order in Spain, instituted by Sancho III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Castile, upon the following occasion: When that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> took the strong fort of Calatrava from the Moors of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, he gave it to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPLARS">Templars</a>, who, wanting courage to defend it, returned it him again. Then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Raymond of the order of the Cistercians, accompanied with several persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, made an offer to defend the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which the king thereupon delivered up to them, and instituted that order. It increased so much under the reign of Alphonso, that the knights desired they might have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, which was granted. Ferdinand and Isabella afterwards, with the consent of Pope Innocent VIII. re-united the grand mastership of Calatrava to the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; so that the kings of Spain are now become perpetual administrators thereof. The knights of Calatrava bear a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULES">gules</a>, fleurdelished with green, &c. Their rule and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> was originally that of the Cistercians.

CALAURIA

Pages 70-70

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> in the Saronic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, over against the port of Troezen, at the distance of 40 stadia. Hither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a> went twice into banishment; and here he died. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> was said to have accepted this island from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for Delos. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> stood on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> ridge nearly in the middle of the island, commanding an extensive view of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> and its coasts. There was his holy temple. The priestess was a virgin, who was dismissed when marriageable. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> of the cities near the island held a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> at it, and sacrificed jointly to the deity. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, Aegina, and Epidaurus, were of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, with Nauplia, for which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> contributed. The Macedonians, when they had reduced Greece, were afraid to violate the sanctuary, by forcing from it the fugitives, his suppliants. Antipater commanded his general to bring away the orators, who had offended him, alive; but Demosthenes could not be prevailed on to surrender. His monument remained in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, within the enclosure of the temple. The city of Calauria has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> abandoned. Traces of buildings and of ancient walls appear nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the ground; and some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, in their places, each with a seat and back forming a little circle, once perhaps a bath. The temple, which was of the Doric order, and not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, as may be inferred from the fragments, is reduced to an inconsiderable heap of ruins. The island is now called Poro. It stretches along before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Morea in a lower ridge, and is separated from it by a canal only four stadia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> wide. This which is called Poro or the Ferry, in still <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> may be passed on foot, as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is not deep. It has given its name to the island; and also to the town, which consists of about 200 houses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> and low, with flat roofs; rising on the slope of a bare disagreeable rock.

CALCADA

Pages 70-70
or St Domingo Calcada, a town of Spain, situated in W. Long. 3. 5. N. Lat. 42. 36.

CALCAR

Pages 70-70

a very strong town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>. It belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, and is seated near the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 41. N. Lat. 51. 45. Calcar, in glas-making, the name of a small oven <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> reverberatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, in which the first calcination of sand and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a> is made for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> them into what is called frit. This furnace is made in the fashion of an oven, ten feet long, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> in the widest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, and two feet deep. On one side of it is a trench five inches <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, the upper part of which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the calcar, and separated only from it at the mouth by bricks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches wide. Into this trench they put <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coal, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of which is carried into every part of the furnace, and is reverberated from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> upon the frit, over the surface of which the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> flies very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and goes out at the mouth of the calcar; the coals burn on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a>, and the ashes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> through. Calcar, John de, a celebrated painter, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Titian, and perfected himself by studying Raphael. Among other pieces he drew a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a>, representing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> around the infant Christ; and so ordered the disposition of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> all proceeds from the Child. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in 1746, in the flower of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. It was he who designed the anatomical figures of Vesali, and the portraits of the painters of Vesali.

CALCAREOUS

Pages 70-70

something that partakes of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and qualities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lime. We say, a calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CALCEARIUM

Pages 70-71

in antiquity, a donative <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> larg- CALCEOLARIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CALCHAS

Pages 71-71

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a famous diviner, followed the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. He foretold that the siege would last ten years; and that the fleet, which was detained in the port of Aulis by contrary winds, would not fail till Agamemnon's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> had been sacrificed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>. After the taking of Troy, he retired to Colophon; where, it is said, he died of grief, because he could not divine what another of his profession, called Mopshis, had discovered.

CALCINATION

Pages 71-71

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, the reducing of substances to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> powder, by fire. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">Limestone</a> is said to be calcined or burned by being deprived of its carbonic acid, and thus brought to the caustic state. But when a metallic substance is calcined by being exposed to strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, it assumes the form of powder or calx, by combining with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a>. See Chemistry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CALCINATO

Pages 71-71

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, remarkable for a victory gained over the Imperialists by the French in 1706. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 55'. N. Lat. 45° 25'. CALCULARY of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">Pear</a>, a congeries of little strong knots dispersed through the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENCHYMA">parenchyma</a> of the fruit. The calculary is most observed in rough-tailed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> choke pears. The knots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> more continuous and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> together towards the pear where they surround the ACETARY. About the stalk they stand more distant; but towards the cork, or stool of the flower, they still grow closer, and there at last gather into the firmness of a plum <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The calculary is no vital or essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the fruit; the several knots whereof it consists being only so many concretions or precipitations out of the sap, as we see in urines, wines, and other liquors.

CALCULATION

Pages 71-71

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of computing several sums, by adding, subtracting, multiplying, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dividing. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>. Calculation is more particularly used to signify the computations in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, for making tables of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a>, ephemerides, finding the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of eclipses, &c. See Astronomy, Geometry, and Logarithms.

CALCULUS

Pages 71-75

primarily denotes a little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pebble, anciently used in making computations, taking of suffrages, playing at tables, and the like. In after times, pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, and counters struck of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and other matters, were used in lieu thereof, but still retaining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> names. Computists were by the lawyers called calculones, when they were either slaves, or newly freed men; those of a better condition were named calculatores; or numerarii: ordinarily there was one of these in each family of distinction. The Roman judges anciently gave their opinions by calculi, which were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> for abolition, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a>. Hence calculus albus, in ancient writers, denotes a favourable vote, either in a person to be absolved and acquitted of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, or elected to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>; as calculus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">niger</a> did the contrary. This usage is said to have been borrowed from the Thracians, who marked their happy or prosperous days by white, and their unhappy by black, pebbles, put each night into an urn. Besides the diversity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, there were some calculi also which had figures or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> engraven on them, as those which were in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in taking the suffrages both in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and at assemblies of the people. These calculi were made of thin wood, polished and covered over with wax. Their form is still seen in some medals of the Caecilian family; and the manner of casting them into the urns, in the medals of the Licinian family. The letters marked upon these calculi were U. R. for uti rogas, and A. for antiquo; the first of which expressed an approbation of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the latter a rejection of it. Afterwards the judges who sat in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> causes used calculi marked with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> A. for absolutio; C. for condemnatio; and N. L. for non luet, signifying that a more full information was required. Calculus is also used in ancient geometric writers for a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> equal to two grains of cicer. Some make it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the siliqua, which is equal to three grains of barley. Two calculi made the centarium. Calculus, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>, is a certain method of performing investigations and resolutions, particularly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. Thus there is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIFFERENTIAL">Differential</a> calculus, the Exponential, the Integral, the Literal, and the Antecedential. Calculus Differentialis, is a method of differencing quantities, or of finding an infinitely small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, which being taken infinite times, shall be equal to a given quantity; or, it is the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> of the infinitely small differences of variable quantities. The foundation of this calculus is an infinitely small quantity, or an infinitesimal, which is a portion of a quantity incomparable to that quantity, or that is less than any assignable one, and therefore accounted as nothing; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> accruing by omitting it being less than any assignable one. Hence two quantities, only differing by an infinitesimal, are reputed equal. Thus, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, the diameter of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is an infinitesimal, in respect of the distance of the fixed stars; and the same holds in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> quantities. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, infinitesimal, therefore, is merely relative, and involves a relation to another quantity; and does not denote any real ens or being. Now infinitesimals are called differentials, or differential quantities, when they are considered as the differences of two quantities. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton calls them moments; considering them as the momentary increments of quantities, e.g., of a line <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> of a point, or of a surface by the flux of a line. The differential calculus, therefore, and the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">fluxions</a>, are the same thing under different names; the former given by M. Leibnitz, and the latter by Sir Isaac Newton: each of whom lays claim to the discovery. There is, indeed, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of expressing the quantities resulting from the different views wherein the two authors consider the infinitesimals: the one as moments, the other as differences. Leibnitz, and most foreigners, express the differentials of quantities by the same letters as variable ones, only prefixing the letter \(d\): thus the differential of \(x\) is called \(dx\); and that of \(y\), \(dy\); now \(dx\) is a positive quantity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> \(x\) continually increase; <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, if it decrease. The English, with Sir Isaac Newton, Calculus. Newton, instead of \( dx \) write \( x \) (with a dot over it), for \( dy \), \( y \), &c., which foreigners object against, on account of that confusion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, which they imagine arises when differentials are again differenced; besides, that the printers are more apt to overlook a point than a letter. Stable quantities being always expressed by the first letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> \( d^a = o \), \( d^b = o \), \( d^c = o \); therefore \( d(x+y-a) = dx + dy \), and \( d(x-y+a) = dx - dy \). So that the differencing of quantities is easily performed by the addition or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUBTRACTION">subtraction</a> of their compounds. To difference quantities that multiply each other; the rule is, first, multiply the differential of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a> into the other factor, the sum of the two factors is the differential sought: thus, the quantities being \( x \), \( y \), the differential <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be \( x \cdot dy + y \cdot dx \), i.e. \( d(xy) = xy \cdot dx + y \cdot dx \). Secondly, If there be three quantities mutually multiplying each other, the factum of the two must then be multiplied into the differential of the third; thus suppose \( vxy \), let \( vx = t \), then \( vx \cdot y = ty \); consequently \( d(vxy) = tdxy + y \cdot dt \); but \( dt = 0 \cdot dx + x \cdot dv \). These values, therefore, being substituted in the antecedent differential, \( tdxy + y \cdot dt \), the result is, \( d(vxy) = v \cdot dx + v \cdot dy + x \cdot dv \). Hence it is easy to apprehend how to proceed, where the quantities are more than three. If one variable quantity increase, while the other decreases, it is evident \( y \cdot dx - x \cdot dy \) will be the differential of \( xy \). To difference quantities that mutually divide each other; the rule is, first, multiply the differential of the divisor into the dividend; and on the contrary, the differential of the dividend into the divisor; subtract the last product from the first, and divide the remainder by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of the divisor; the quotient is the differential of the quantities mutually dividing each other. See Fluxions. Calculus Exponentialis, is a method of differencing exponential quantities, or of finding and summing up the differentials or moments of exponential quantities; or at least bringing them to geometrical constructions. By exponential quantity, is here understood a power, whose exponent is variable; e.g. \( x^a \), \( a^x \), \( x^7 \), where the exponent \( x \) does not denote the same in all the points of a curve, but in some stands for 2, in others for 3, in others for 5, &c. To difference an exponential quantity; there is nothing required but to reduce the exponential quantities to logarithmic ones; which done, the differencing is managed as in logarithmic quantities.—Thus, suppose the differential of the exponential quantity \( x^y \) required, let \[ x^y = z \] Then will \( y \cdot dx = dz \) \[ \frac{1}{x} \cdot dy + \frac{y}{x} \cdot dx = \frac{dz}{z} \] That is, \( x^y \cdot dy + y \cdot x^{y-1} \cdot dx = dz \). Calculus Integralis, or Summatorius, is a method of integrating, or summing up moments, or differential quantities; i.e. from a differential quantity given, to find the quantity from whose differencing the given differential results. The integral calculus, therefore, is the inverse of the differential one; whence the English, who usually call the differential method fluxions, give this calculus, which ascends from the fluxions, to the flowing or variable quantities; or as foreigners express it, from the differences to the sums, by the name of the inverse method of fluxions. Hence, the integration is known to be justly performed, if the quantity found, according to the rules of the differential calculus, being differenced, produce that proposed to be summed. Suppose \( f \) the sign of the sum, or integral quantity, then \( f(y \cdot dx) \) will denote the sum, or integral of the differential \( y \cdot dx \). To integrate, or sum up a differential quantity: it is demonstrated, first, that \( f(x) = x \); secondly, \( f(d(x+dy)) = x + y \); thirdly, \( f(x \cdot dy + y \cdot dx) = x \cdot y \); fourthly, \( f(m \cdot x^m \cdot dx) = x^m : \) fifthly, \( f(n \cdot m \cdot x^m \cdot dx) = \frac{x^n}{m} \); Sixthly, \( f(y \cdot dx - x \cdot dy) : y^2 = x \cdot y \). Of these, the fourth and fifth <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> are the most frequent, wherein the differential quantity is integrated, by adding a variable unity to the exponent, and dividing the sum by the new exponent multiplied into the differential of the root; v.g. the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, by \( m - (i + 1) \cdot dx \), i.e. by \( m \cdot dx \). If the differential quantity to be integrated doth not come under any of these formulas, it must either be reduced to an integral finite, or an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, each of whose terms may be summed. It may be here observed, that, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of finites, any quantity may be raised to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of power; but vice versa, the root cannot be extracted out of any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> required; so in the analysis of infinites, any variable or flowing quantity may be differenced; but vice versa, any differential cannot be integrated. And as, in the analysis of finites, we are not yet arrived at a method of extracting the roots of all equations, so neither has the integral calculus arrived at its perfection: and as in the former we are obliged to have recourse to approximation, so in the latter we have recourse to infinite series, where we cannot attain to a perfect integration. Calculus Literalis, or Literal Calculus, is the same with specious arithmetic, or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, so called from its using the letters of the alphabet; in contradistinction to numeral arithmetic, which uses figures. In the literal calculus given quantities are expressed by the first letters, \( a \), \( b \), \( c \), \( d \); and quantities sought by the last \( y \), \( z \), &c. Equal quantities are denoted by the same letters. Calculus, Antecedental, a geometrical method of reasoning invented by Mr Glenie, which, without any consideration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> or velocity, is applicable to all the purposes of fluxions. In this method, says Mr Glenie, "every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> is truly and strictly geometrical, is founded on principles frequently made use of by the ancient geometers, principles admitted into the very first elements of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, and repeatedly used by Euclid himself. As it is a branch of general geometrical proportion, or universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>, and is derived from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the antecedents of ratios, hav- Calculating given consequents and a given standard of comparison in various degrees of augmentation and diminution they undergo by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> and decomposition, I have called it the antecedental calculus. As it is purely geometrical, and perfectly scientific, I have since its first occurrence to me in 1779, always made use of it instead of the fluxionary and differential calculi, which are merely arithmetical. Its principles are totally unconnected with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of motion and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, which, strictly speaking, are foreign to pure geometry and abstract science, though, in mixed mathematics and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy, they are equally applicable to every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, involving the consideration of either with the two numerical methods <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned. And as many such investigations require compositions and decompositions of ratios, extending greatly beyond the triplicate and subtriplicate, this calculus in all of them furnishes every expression in a strictly geometrical form. The standards of comparison in it may be any magnitudes whatever, and are of course indefinite and innumerable; and the consequents of the ratios, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> or decompounded, may be either equal or unequal, homogeneous or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a>. In the fluxionary and differential methods, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, 1, or unit, is not only the standard of comparison, but also the consequent of every ratio compounded or decompounded." See Phil. Trans. Edin. vol. iv. Some mathematicians, however, are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the advantage to be derived from the employment of this calculus is not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> as the author seems to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> from it. **Calculus Minerve**, among the ancient lawyers, denoted the decision of a cause, wherein the judges were equally divided. The expression is taken from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">Oracles</a>, represented by Aeschylus and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>; at whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, before the Areopagites, for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of his mother, the votes being equally divided for and against him, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> interposed, and gave the casting vote or calculus in his behalf. M. Cramer, professor at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARBURG">Marburg</a>, has a discourse exprefs, De Calculo Minerve; wherein he maintains, that all the effect an entire equality of voices can have, is to leave the cause in statu quo. **Calculus Tiburtinus**, a sort of figured stone, formed in great plenty about the catacombs of the Anio, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; of a white colour, and in shape <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, round, or echinated. They are a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the *floria lapidea*, or *flaletites*, and generated like them; and to like fugar plums, that it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> jest at Rome to deceive the unexperienced by serving them up as desserts. **Calculus**, in Medicine, the discale of the stone in the bladder, or kidneys. The term is Latin, and signifies a little pebble. The calculus in the bladder is called lithiasis; and in the kidneys, nephritis. See Medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> calculi are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> formed of different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> or incrustations; sometimes smooth and heavy like mineral <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; but often rough, spongy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and full of inequalities or protuberances: chemically analyzed, or distilled in an open fire, they nearly yield the same principles as urine itself, or at least an empyreumatic volatile urinous matter, together with a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. They never have, nor can have, naturally, any foreign matter for a basis; but they may by accident; an instance of which is related by Dr. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a>, Percival*. A bougie had unfortunately slipped into the bladder, and upon it a stone of considerable size was formed in less than a year. This stone had so much the appearance of chalk, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> was induced to try whether it could be converted into quicklime. His experiment succeeded, both with that and some other calculi; from which he conjectures, that hard waters which contain calcareous earth may contribute towards the formation of these calculi. **Calcutta**, the capital of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, and of all the British possessions in the East Indies, is situated on the river Huguley, a branch of the Ganges, about 100 miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in N. Lat. 23° and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 88° 28' E. from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>. It is but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, built on the site of a village called Gouripur. The English first obtained the Mogul's permission to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the year 1692; and Mr <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> Charnock, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, made choice of the spot on which the city stands, on account of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> shady <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> which grew there; though in other respects it was the worst he could have pitched upon; for three miles to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> lake, which overflows in September, and when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> retires in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, leaves behind such a quantity of fish and other putrefied matter, as renders the air very unhealthy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the Gentoos throwing the dead bodies of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people into the river is also very disagreeable, and undoubtedly contributes to render the place unhealthy, as well as the cause already mentioned. Calcutta is now become a large and populous city, being supposed at present to contain 500,000 inhabitants. It is elegantly built, at least the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> inhabited by the English; but the rest, and that the greatest part, is built after the fashion of the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> in general. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of all these is nearly the same; their streets are exceedingly confined, narrow, and crooked, with a vast number of ponds, reservoirs, and gardens interspersed. A few of the streets are paved with brick. The houses are built, some with brick, others with mud, and a still greater number with bamboos and mats; all which different kinds of fabrics standing intermixed with one another, form a very uncouth appearance. The brick houses are seldom above two stories <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, but those of mud and bamboos are only one, and are covered with thatch. The roofs of the brick houses are flat and terraced. These, however, are much fewer in number than the other two kinds; so that fires, which often happen, do not sometimes meet with a brick <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to obstruct their progress in a whole street. Within these 20 or 25 years Calcutta has been greatly improved both in appearance and in the salubrity of its air: the streets have been properly drained, and the ponds filled; thereby removing a vast surface of stagnant water, the exhalations of which were particularly hurtful. The citadel is named Fort William, and is superior as a fortress to any in India; but is now on too extensive a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> to answer the purpose for which it was intended, viz. the holding a post in case of extremity. It was begun on this extended plan by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Clive immediately after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASSEY">Plassey</a>. The expense attending it was supposed to amount to two millions <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. Calcutta is the emporium of Bengal, and the residence dence of the governor general of India. Its flourishing state may in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> be supposed owing to the unlimited toleration of all religions allowed here; the Pagans being suffered to carry their idols in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, the Mahomedans not being discomfited, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> being allowed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. At about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a>'s distance from the town is a plain where the natives annually undergo a very strange kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> on the 9th of April; some for the sins they have committed, others for those they may commit, and others in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> made by their parents. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> is performed in the following manner: Thirty bamboos, each about the height of 20 feet, are erected in the plain above-mentioned. On the top of these they contrive to fix a swivel, and another bamboo of thirty feet or more crosses it, at each end of which hangs a rope. The people pull <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> one end of this rope, and the devotee placing himself under it, the brahmin pinches up a large piece of skin under both the shoulderblades, sometimes in the breasts, and thrusts a strong <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> hook through each. These hooks have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> garlands hanging to them, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> makes fast to the rope at the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> bamboo, and at the same time puts a fish round the body of the devotee, laying it loyally in the hollow of the hooks, left by the skin's giving way, he should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to the ground. When this is done, the people haul down the other end of the bamboo; by which means the devotee is immediately lifted up 30 feet or more from the ground, and they run round as fast as their legs can carry them. Thus the devotee is thrown out the whole length of the rope, where, as he swings, he plays a thousand antic tricks; being painted and dressed in a very particular manner, on purpose to make him look more ridiculous. Some of them continue swinging half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, others less. The devotees undergo a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of four days for this ceremony. On the first and third they abstain from all kinds of food; but eat fruit on the other two.
