Father Torquemado describes a creature which he calls a species of large bear, something like a buffalo, of the size of a steer, and nearly of the figure of a stag. Its hair is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a yard in length, its neck long and awkward, and on its forehead are horns branched like those of a stag. The tail is a yard in length and half a yard in breadth; and the hoofs cloven like those of an ox. With regard to birds, we have but an imperfect account; only, in general, Father Vinegas tells us that the coast is plentifully stored with peacocks, bustards, geese, cranes, and most of the birds <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in other parts of the world. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fish which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to these coasts is incredible. Salmon, turbot, barbel, skate, mackerel, &c., are caught here with very little trouble; together with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> oysters, common oysters, lobster, and a variety of exquisite shell fish. Plenty of turtle are also caught on the coasts. On the South sea coasts are found shell fish peculiar to it, and perhaps the most beautiful in the world; their luster surpassing that of the finest pearl, and darting their rays through a transparent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> of an elegant vivid blue, like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> lazuli. The fame of California for pearls soon drew forth great numbers of adventurers, who searched every part of the gulf, and are still employed in that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, notwithstanding fashion has greatly diminished the value of this elegant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> production. Father Torquemado observes that the sea of California affords very rich pearl <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>; and that the beds, or beds of oysters, may be seen in three or four fathom water, almost as plain as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were on the surface. The extremity of the peninsula towards Cape St Lucar is more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, temperate, and fertile, than the other parts, and consequently more woody. In the more distant parts, even to the farthest missions on the east coast, no large <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> hath yet been discovered. A species of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANNA">manna</a> is found in this country, which, according to the accounts of the Jesuits, has all the sweetness of refined <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> without its whiteness. The natives firmly believe that this juice drops from heaven. The Californians are well made, and very strong. They are extremely pugnacious, inconstant, stupid, and even intemperate, and seem extremely desirous of the character given to the Indians in general, under the article America. Before the Europeans penetrated into California, the natives had no form of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The missionaries indeed tell us many tales concerning them, but they evidently bear the marks of forgery as not to be worth repeating. Each <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> was then an assemblage of several cottages more or less numerous, that were all mutually confederated by alliances, but without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. They were strangers even to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> obedience. No kind of dress was used by the men; but the women made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of some coverings, and were even fond of ornamenting themselves with California pearls and such other trinkets as the country afforded. What most displayed their ingenuity was the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> nets, which are said by the Jesuits to have even exceeded in goodness those made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. They were made by the women, of a coarse kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> procured from some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which grow there. Their houses were built of branches and leaves of trees; nay, many of them were only enclosures of earth and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, raised half a yard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, without any covering; and even these were so small, that they could not stretch themselves at length in them. In winter, they dwelt underground in caves either natural or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>. In 1526, Ferdinand Cortez having reduced and settled Mexico, attempted the conquest of California; but was obliged to return, without even taking a survey of the country, a report of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> having dispersed the Mexicans to a general insurrection. Some other attempts were made by the officers of Cortez, but these were also unsuccessful; and this valuable coast was long neglected by the Spaniards, who, to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> have but one settlement upon it. In 1595, a galleon was sent to make discoveries on the Californian shore; but the vessel was unfortunately lost. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> years after, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Monteroy, then viceroy of New Spain, sent Sebastian Biscayno on the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> with two ships and a tender; but he made no discovery of importance. In 1684, the marquis de Laguna, also viceroy of New Spain, despatched two ships with a tender to make discoveries on the lake of California. He returned with an indifferent account, but was among the first who asserted that California was not an island; which was afterwards confirmed by Father Cino, as already related. In 1697, the Spaniards being discouraged by their losses and disappointments, the Jesuits solicited and obtained permission to undertake the conquest of California. They arrived among the savages with curiosities that might amuse them, corn for their food, and clothes for which they could not but perceive the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. The hatred these people bore the Spanish name could not support itself against these demonstrations of benevolence. They testified their acknowledgments as much as their want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> and their inconstancy would permit them. These faults were partly overcome by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> instructors, who pursued their project with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of warmth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> peculiar to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. They made themselves carpenters, masons, weavers, and husbandmen; and by these means succeeded in imparting knowledge, and in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for the useful arts, to this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> people, who have been all successively formed into one body. In 1745, they composed 43 villages, separated from each other by the barrenness of the soil and the want of water. The inhabitants of these small villages subsist principally on corn and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, which they cultivate; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and domestic animals of Europe, the breeding of which last is an object of continual <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. The Indians have each their field, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of what they reap, but such is their want of foresight, that they would squander in a day what they had gathered, if the missionary did not take upon himself to distribute it to them as they stand in need of it. They manufacture some coarse stuffs; and the necessaries they are In want of are purchased with pearls, and with wine nearly resembling that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a>, which they sell to the Mexicans and to the galleons, and which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> hath shown the necessity of prohibiting in California. A few laws, which are very simple, are sufficient to regulate this rising state. In order to enforce them, the missionary chooses the most intelligent person of the village; who is empowered to whip and imprison; the only punishments of which they have any knowledge. In all California there are only two garrisons, each consisting of 30 men, and a soldier with every missionary. These troops were chosen by the legislators, though they are paid by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Were the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> to push their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with half the zeal of the Jesuits, California might become one of the most valuable of their acquisitions, an account of the pearls and other valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> which the country contains. At present the little Spanish town near Cape St Lucar is made use of for no other purpose than as a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of refreshment for the Manila ships, and the head residence of the missionaries.

CALIGA

Pages 87-87

in Roman antiquity, was the proper folder's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>, made in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a> fashion, without upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> to cover the superior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the foot, though otherwise reaching to the middle of the leg, and fastened with thongs. The sole of the caliga was of wood, like the sabot of the French peasants, and its bottom stuck full of nails; which clavi are supposed to have been very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the shoes of the scouts and sentinels; whence these were called by way of distinction, caligae speculatoriae; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> by mounting the wearer to a higher pitch, they gave a greater advantage to the fight; though others <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the caligae speculatoriae to have been made soft and woolly, to prevent their making a noise. From these caligae it was that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Caligula took his name, as having been born in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and afterwards bred up in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> folder. According to Du Cange, a sort of caligae was also worn by monks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, when they celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> pontifically.

CALIGATI

Pages 87-87

an appellation given by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> folders in the Roman armies, by reason of the caliga which they wore. The caliga was the badge <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> symbol of a folder; whence to take away the caliga and belt, imported a dismiffing or cashiering.

CALIGO

Pages 87-87
or CALIGATIO, in Medicine, an opacity, or cloudiness of the anterior surface of the crystalline lens of the eye, causing a dimness or fulness of sight.

CALIGULA

Pages 87-87

the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, A.D. 37, began his reign with every promising appearance of becoming the real father of his people; but at the end of eight months he was seized with a fever, which, it is thought, left a frenzy on his mind; for his disposition totally changed, and he committed the most atrocious acts of impiety, cruelty, and folly; such as proclaiming his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, feeding it at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, introducing it to the temple in the vestments of the priests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, &c., and causing sacrifices to be offered to himself, his wife, and the horse. After having murdered many of his subjects with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and caused others to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> cause, he was assassinated by a tribune of the people as he came out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, A.D. 41, in the 29th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and 4th of his reign.

CALIN

Pages 87-87

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> metal, whereof the Chinese make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> canisters, and the like. The ingredients seem to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> and tin.

CALIPH

Pages 87-87
or KHALIF, the supreme ecclesiastical dignity among the Saracens; or, as it is otherwise defined, a sovereign dignity among the Mahometans, vested with absolute authority in all matters relating both to religion and policy. In the Arabic it signifies successor or vicar; the caliphs bearing the same relation to Mahomet that the popes pretend they do to Jesus Christ or St Peter. It is at this day one of the Grand Signor's titles, as successor of Mahomet; and of the Sophi of Persia, as successor of Ali. One of the chief functions of the caliph, in quality of imam or chief priest of Mussulmanism, was to begin the public prayers every Friday in the chief mosque, and to deliver the khutba or sermon. In after times, they had affiliates for this latter office; but the former the caliphs always performed in person. The caliph was also obliged to lead the pilgrims to Mecca in person, and to march at the head of the armies of his empire. He granted investiture to princes; and sent swords, standards, gowns, and the like, as presents to princes of the Mahometan religion; who, though they had thrown off the yoke of the caliphate, nevertheless held of it as vassals. The caliphs usually went to the mosque mounted on mules; and the sultans Seljukides, though masters of Bagdad, held their stirrups, and led their mule by the bridle some distance on foot, till such time as the caliphs gave them the sign to mount on horseback. At one of the windows of the caliph's palace, there always hung a piece of black velvet 20 cubits long, which reached to the ground, and was called the caliph's sleeve; which the grandees of his court never failed to kiss every day, with great respect. After the destruction of the caliphate by Hulaku, the Mahometan princes appointed a particular officer, in their respective dominions, who sustains the sacred authority of caliph. In Turkey, he goes under the denomination of mufti, and in Persia under that of saddeh.

CALIPHATE

Pages 87-87

the office <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of caliph: See the preceding article. The successions of caliphs <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Mahomet till the 655th year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a> was taken by the Tartars. After this, however, there were persons who claimed the caliphate, as pretending to be of the family of the Abbasides, and to whom the fanatics of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> rendered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> honours at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, as the true successors of Mahomet; but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> was merely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITULAR">titular</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> allowed them only in matters relating to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and though they bore the sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of caliphs, they were nevertheless subjects and dependents of the sultans. In the year of the Hegira 361, a kind of caliphate was erected by the Fatimites in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and lasted till it was suppressed by Saladin. Historians also speak of a third caliphate in Yemen or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Felix, erected by some princes of the family of the Jobites. The emperors of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a> assume the title of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> chefri; and pretend to be the true caliphs, or successors of Mahomet, though under another name.

CALIPPIC PERIOD

Pages 87-88

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of seventy-five seventy-six years, perpetually recurring; which clasped, the middle of the new and full moons, as its inventor Calippus, an Athenian, imagined, return to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the solar year. Meton, an hundred years before, had invented the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cycle, of nineteen years; assuming the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the solar year $365\frac{1}{4}$ days, $6b. 18' 56'' 50^2$ $21' 34\frac{3}{4}$; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, $29d. 12b. 45' 47'' 26\frac{1}{4} 48\frac{3}{4} 30\frac{3}{4}$; but Calippus, considering that the Metonic quantity of the solar year was not exact, multiplied Meton's period by 4, and thence arose a period of 76 years, called the Calippic. The Calippic period, therefore, contains 27,759 days: and since the lunar cycle contains 235 lunations, and the Calippic period is quadruple of this, it contains 940 lunations. This period began in the third year of the 112th Olympiad, or the 438th of the Julian period. It is demonstrated, however, that the Calippic period itself is not accurate; that it does not bring the new and full moons precisely to their places: $8b. 5' 52'' 60''$, being the excess of 940 lunations above 76 solar years; but brings them too late, by a whole day in 225 years.

CALISTA

Pages 88-88

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Lycaon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, and one of the nymphs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>. Being beloved by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, that god assumed the form of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of chastity, by which means he debauched her: but her disgrace being revealed, as she was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> with her patroness, the incensed deity turned her and the son with which she was pregnant into bears; when Jupiter, in compassion to her sufferings, took them up into the heavens, and made them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a> Ursa <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> and Ursa <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALIX">CALIX</a>. See CALYX.

CALIXTINS

Pages 88-88

a name given to those, among the Lutherans, who follow the sentiments of George Calixtus, a celebrated divine, and professor at Helmstadt, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, who died in 1656: he opposed the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of St Augustin, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, and free <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and endeavoured to form an union among the various members of the Romish, Lutheran, and reformed churches; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, rather, to join them in the bonds of mutual forbearance and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. Calixtins also denote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, derived from the Hussites, about the middle of the 15th century, who asserted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the cup as essential to the eucharist. And hence their name; which is formed from the Latin calyx, a cup. The Calixtins are not ranked by Romanists in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of heretics, since in the main they still adhered to the doctrine of Rome. The reformation they aimed at terminated in the four following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. 1. In restoring the cup to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>. 2. In subjecting the criminal clerks to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. 3. In stripping the clergy of their lands, lordships, and all temporal jurisdiction. 4. In granting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to all capable priests to preach the word of God.

CALKA

Pages 88-88

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, to the east of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. CALKING. See CAULKING.

CALKINS

Pages 88-88

the prominent parts at the extremities of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>, bent downwards, and forged to a sort of point. Calkins are apt to make horses trip: they also occasion bleymes, and ruin the back finews. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> fashioned in form of a hare's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> of a horse's heel be pared a little low, they do little damage; whereas, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> calkins quite spoil the foot. Calkins are either single <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, that is, at one end of the shoe, or at both: these last are deemed less hurtful, as the horses can <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> more even.

CALL

Pages 88-88

among fowlers, the noise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cry of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> especially to its young, or to its mate in coupling <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. One method of catching partridges is by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> call of a hen trained for the purpose, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the cocks to her, they are entangled in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>. Different birds require different sorts of calls; but they are most of them composed of a pipe or reed, with a little leathern bag or purse, somewhat in form of a bellows; which, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> given thereto, yields a noise like that of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of bird to be taken. The call for partridges is formed like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> bored through, and fitted with a pipe or swan's quill, &c. to be blown with the mouth, to make the noise of the cock <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>, which is very different from the call of the hen. Calls for quails &c. are made of a leathern purse in shape like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, stuffed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and fitted at the end with the bone of a cat's, hare's, or coney's leg, formed like a flageolet. They are played by squeezing the purse in the palm of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, at the same time striking on the flageolet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> with the thumb to counterfeit the call of the hen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-QUAIL">quail</a>. Call of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>. See CALLING.

CALLAO

Pages 88-89

a strong town of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. It is the port of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>, from which it is distant about five miles. The town is built on a low flat point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore. It is fortified; but the fortifications were much damaged by the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> earthquake, and have not since been repaired. The town is not above <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ten feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> mark; but the tide does not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> rise or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> above five feet. The streets are drawn in a line; but are full of dust, which is very troublesome. In a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> near the sea side are the governor's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the vicerey's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of three pieces of cannon. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side are the warehouses for the merchandise brought from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, and other parts of Peru. The other churches are built with reeds, and covered with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> or clay, but they look tolerably neat. There are five monasteries ries and an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, though the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of families does not exceed 400. The trade of Callao is considerable. From Chili they bring cordage, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, tallow, dried fish, and corn; from Chiloé, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> planks, woollen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and carpets; from Peru, sugars, wines, brandy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, cordage, timber for shipping, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CACAO">cacao</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and molasses; from Mexico, pitch, tar, woods for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, sulphur, balsam of Peru both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, as well as commodities from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. At the port of Callao the watering is easy, but the wood is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> or two distant. Earthquakes are very frequent in these parts, which have done vast mischief to Lima and Callao. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 76° 15'. S. Lat. 12° 29'.

CALLE

Pages 89-89

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Hither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, situated on an eminence which hangs over the river Durius; whose port was at the mouth of the river. Now Porto, Oporio, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Port a Port.

CALLEN

Pages 89-89

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILKENNY">Kilkenny</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, about ten miles south-west of Kilkenny. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 22'. N. Lat. 52° 25'. CALLICARPA. See JOHNSONIA.

CALLICO

Pages 89-89

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a sort of cloth resembling linens made of cotton. The name is taken from that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALICUT">Calicut</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar, being the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at which the Portuguese landed when they discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> trade. The Spaniards still call it calicu. Callicoes are of different kinds, plain, printed, painted, stained, dyed, chints, mullins, and the like, all included under the general denomination of callicoes. Some of them are painted with various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of different colours; others are not stained, but have a stripe of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver quite through the piece, and at each end is fixed a tassel of gold, silver, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, intermixed with flowers. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> of callicoes was first set on foot in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> about the year 1676.

CALLICRATES

Pages 89-89

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> sculptor, who engraved some of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s verses on a grain of millet, made an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> chariot that might be concealed under the wing of a fly, and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">ant</a> of ivory in which all the members were distinct; but Ælian justly blames him for exerting his genius and talents in things so useless, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> so difficult. He flourished about the year 472 before Christ. CALLIGONUM. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CALLIGRAPHUS anciently denoted a copyist, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scrivener, who transcribed fair, and at length, what the notaries had taken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in notes or minutes. The word is compounded of καλλις, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and γραφω, I write. The minutes of acts, &c., were always taken in a kind of cypher, or short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; such as the notes of Tyro in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GRUTER">Gruter</a>: by which means the notaries, as the Latins called them, or the επιγραφηται and ταχυγραφοι, as the Greeks called them, were enabled to keep pace with a speaker or person who dictated. These notes, being understood by few, were copied over fair, and at length, by persons who had a good hand, for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, &c. These persons were called calligraphi; a name frequently met with in the ancient writers.

CALLIGRAPHY

Pages 89-89

the art of fair <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. Calligrates is said to have written an elegant distich on a fefanum feed. Junius speaks of a person, as very extraordinary, who wrote the apostles creed, and beginning of St John's Gospel, in the compass of a farthing. What would he have said of our famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>, who in 1575 wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, creed, ten commandments, and two short prayers in Latin, with his own name, motto, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, year of the Lord, and reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, in the compass of a single <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>, enchased in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> and border of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and covered with a crystal, all so accurately wrought as to be very legible?

CALLIMACHUS

Pages 89-89

a celebrated Greek poet, native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, flourished under <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHUS">Philadelphus</a> and Ptolemy Euergetes kings of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, about 280 years before Christ. He palled, according to Quintilian, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the Greek elegiac poets. His style is elegant, delicate, and nervous. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small poems, of which we have only some hymns and epigrams remaining. Catullus has closely imitated him, and translated into Latin <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> his small poem on the locks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERENICE">Berenice</a>. Callimachus was also a good grammarian and a learned critic. There is an edition of his remains, by Meff. le Fevre, quarto; and another in two volumes 8vo, with notes by Spanheim, Gravius, Bentley, &c. CALLING the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, in the British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, is the calling over the members names, every one answering to his own, and going out of the house, in the order in which he is called: this they do in order to discover whether there be any person there not returned by the clerk of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any member be absent without the leave of the house. CALLINICUS of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a>, inventor of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> to burn in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, called the Greek, and since Wild fire. See Grecian Fire. CALLIDONUS of Ephesus, a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek poet, inventor of elegiac verse; some specimens of which are to be found in the collection of Stoebus. He flourished about 776 years before Christ.

CALLIOPE

Pages 89-90

in the Pagan <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, the Muse who presides over eloquence and heroic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. She was thus called from the sweetness of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, and was reckoned the first of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>. Her distinguishing office was to record the worthy actions of the living; and accordingly she is represented with tablets in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. CALLIPÆDIA, the art of getting <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> breeding fine and beautiful children. We find <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> rules and practices, relating to this art, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a>, a sort of medicine called ermeia was administered to pregnant women, as a means of producing a beautiful issue. Of this kind were the kernels of pine nuts ground with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, saffron, plum wine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. The Jews are said to have been so solicitous about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of their children, that care was taken to have some very beautiful child placed at the door of the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, that the women at at going out being struck with his appearance, and retaining the idea, might all have children as fine as he. The Chinese take still greater care of their breeding women, to prevent unclean objects of any kind from striking their imagination. Musicians are employed at night to entertain them with agreeable songs and odes, in which are set forth all the duties and comforts of a conjugal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; that the infant may receive good impressions even before it is born, and not only come forth agreeably formed in body, but well disposed in mind. Callipedia, nevertheless, seems to have been first erected into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> art by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a> Quillet de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINON">Chinon</a>, a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, who, under the fictitious name of Calvédus Latus, has published a fine Latin poem in four books, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Callipedia, seu de pulchrae proelis habenda ratione; wherein are contained all the precepts of that new art. There is a translation of it into English <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> by Mr Rowe.

CALLIPOLIS

Pages 90-90

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the name of several cities of antiquity, particularly one upon the Hellepont, next the Propontis, and opposite to Lampacus in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLIPOLI">Gallipoli</a>. CALLIPIC <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">PERIOD</a>. See Callictic.

CALLIRHOE

Pages 90-90

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, surnamed Enneacrunos, from its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> channels; a fountain not far from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, greatly adorned by Piatiratus, where there were several <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, but this the only running <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. Callirhoe was also the name of a very fine spring of hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> beyond Jordan near the Dead <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, into which it empties itself. CALLISIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CALLISTEA

Pages 90-90

in Grecian antiquity, a Lesbian festival, wherein the women presented themselves in Juno's temple, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> was assigned to the fairest. There was another of these contentions at the festival of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> Eleusina among the Parrhaeans, and another among the Eleans, where the most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was presented with a complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of armour, which he consecrated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, to whose temple he walked in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, being accompanied by his friends who adorned him with ribbons, and crowned him with a garland of myrtle. CALLISTHENES the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> and relation of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, by whose desire he accompanied Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> in his expeditions; but proving too severe a censurer of that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>'s conduct, he was by him put to the torture (on a suspicion of a treasonable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a>), and died under it, 328 years before Christ.

CALLISTRATUS

Pages 90-90

an excellent Athenian orator, was banished for having obtained too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> an authority in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a> was so struck with the force of his eloquence, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> it procured him, that he abandoned <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, and resolved from thenceforward to apply himself to oratory.

CALLITRICE

Pages 90-90
or Star-grass, in Botany: A genus of the digynia order, belonging to the monandra class of plants; and in the natural method ranking under the 12th order, Holaracea. There is no calyx, but two petals, and the capsule is bilocular and tetralpermous.

CALLOO

Pages 90-90

a fortress in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the territory of Waes, on the river Scheld, subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. The Dutch were defeated here by the Spaniards in 1638. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 10'. N. Lat. 51° 15'.

CALLOSUM CORPUS

Pages 90-90

in Anatomy, a whitish hard substance, joining the two hemispheres of the brain, and appearing in view when the two hemispheres are drawn back. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CALLOT

Pages 90-91

JAMES, a celebrated engraver, born at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NANCY">Nancy</a> in 1593. In his youth he travelled to Rome to learn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> and engraving; and from thence went to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> took him into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, Callot returned to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; when he was very favourably received by Henry duke of Lorraine, who settled a considerable pension upon him. His reputation being soon after spread all over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, the infant of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a> drew him to Bruxelles, where he engraved the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII. made him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>, and that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Rhé. The French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, having taken Nancy in 1631, made Callot the proposal of representing that new conquest, as he had already done the taking of Rochelle; but Callot begged to be excused; and some courtiers resolving to oblige him to do it, he answered, that he would sooner cut off his thumb than do anything against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his prince and country. This excuse the king accepted; and said, that the duke of Lorraine was happy in having such faithful and affectionate subjects. Callot followed his business so closely, that, though he died at 43 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he is said to have left of his own execution about 1500 pieces. The following are a few of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of the innocents, a small oval plate, engraved at Florence. Callot engraved the same subject at Nancy, with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the figures on the back ground. The former is the most rare; a fine <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of it is very difficult to be found. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of Cana in Galilee, from Paolo Veronele, a middling sized plate, lengthwise. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of Christ, on 12 very small upright plates: first impressions very scarce. 4. St John in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATMOS">Patmos</a>, a small plate, nearly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. 5. The temptation of St Anthony, a middling sized plate, lengthwise. He also engraved the same subject larger; which, though not the best, is notwithstanding the rarest print. There is a considerable difference in the treatment of the subject in the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>. 6. The punishments, wherein is seen the execution of several criminals. The marks of the best impressions of this plate are, a small square tower which appears above the houses, towards the left, and a very small image of the Virgin placed in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the wall, near the middle of the print. 7. The miseries of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, 18 small plates, lengthwise. There is another set on the same subject, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> plates less than the former. 8. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fair of Florence, so called because it was engraved at Florence. As several parts of this plate were not equally bitten by the aquafortis, it is difficult to meet with a fine impression. Callot, on his return to Nancy, re-engraved this plate without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>. The copy, however, is by no means equal to the original. The first is distinguished from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> by the words in Firenze, which appear below at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> corner of the plate. The second has these words in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, Fe. Florentinis, excudit Nancei. There is also a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> copy of this print, reversed, published by Savery; but the difference is easily distinguished between it and the true print. 9. The little fair, otherwise called the players at bowls; where also some peasants are represented. presented <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>. This is one of the scarcest of Cal- <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>'s prints; and it is very difficult to meet with a fine impression of it, for the distances and other parts of the plate failed in the biting it with the aquafortis. 10. The tilting, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the new street at Nancy, a middling sized plate, lengthwise. 11. The Garden of Nancy, where young men are playing with a balloon, the same. 12. View of the Pont Neuf, a small plate, lengthwise. 13. View of the Louvre, the same. 14. Four landscaper, small plates, lengthwise.

CALLUS

Pages 91-91
or CALLOSITY, in a general sense, any cutaneous, cornous, or osseous hardness, whether na- tural or preternatural; but most frequently it means the callus generated about the edges of a fracture, pro- vided by nature to preserve the fractured bones, or di- vided parts, in the situation in which they are replaced by the surgeon. A callus, in this last sense, is a sort of jelly, or liquid viscid matter, that sweats out from the small arteries and bony fibres of the divided parts, and fills up the chinks or cavities between them. It first appears of a cartilaginous substance; but at length becomes quite bony, and joins the fractured part so firm- ly together, that the limb will often make greater re- sistance to any external violence, with this part than with those which were never broken. Callus is also a hard, dense, inflexible knob, rising on the hands, feet, &c. by much friction and pressure against hard bodies.

CALM

Pages 91-91

the state of rest which appears in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> when there is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> stirring. A calm is more dreaded by a seafaring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> than a storm, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he has a strong ship and sea room enough; for, under the line excessive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> sometimes produces such dead calms, that ships are obliged to lay two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three months without being able to stir one way or other. Two opposite winds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> sometimes make a calm. This is frequently observed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, at no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from the shore, where some gulf or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> wind will so poise the general easterly wind, as to produce a per- fect calm. Calms are never so great on the ocean as on the Mediterranean, because the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> and reflux of the former keep the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in a continual agitation, even where there is no wind; whereas there being no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> in the latter, the calm is sometimes so dead, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the water is as clear as a looking glass; but such calms are almost constant presages of an approach- ing storm. On the coasts about <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> calm is reputed a prognostic of an earthquake. It is not uncommon for the vessels to be calmed, or becalmed, as the sailors express it, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> of the constant Levantine winds, in places where they ride near the land. Thus between the two capes of Car- tocho towards the main, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Antonio in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBA">Cuba</a>, the sea is narrow, and there is often a calm produced by some gust of a land wind, that poises the Levantine wind, and renders the whole perfectly still for two or three days. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the current that runs here is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to the vessels, if it sets <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; when it sets easter- ly, a ship will have a passage in three or four days to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAVANNAH">Havannah</a>; but if otherwise, it is often a fortnight or three weeks sail, the ship being embayed in the gulf of Mexico. When the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> is perfectly calm, no wind at all stirring, the sailors try which way the current lets, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> which they fend out, and which will ride at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, though there is no bottom to be found, as regularly and well as if fastened by the strongest an- chor to the bottom. The method is this: they row the boat to a little distance from the ship, and then throw over their plummet, which is about forty pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; they let this sink to about two hundred fath- oms; and then, though it never reaches the bottom, the boat will turn head against the current, and ride as firmly as can be. Calm Latitudes, in sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, are situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, between the tropic of Cancer and the latitude of 20° N. or they denote the space that lies be- tween the trade and variable winds, because it is fre- quently subject to calms of long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>.

CALMAR

Pages 91-91

a strong <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Smaland, divided into two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, the old and the new; but of the former there remains only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and a few houses. The new town is built a little way from the other, and has <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handsome houses. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. 15. N. Lat. 56. 48.

CALMET

Pages 91-91

Augustine, one of the most learned and laborious writers of the 18th century, was born at Melnil le Horgne, a village in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Toul in France, in the year 1672, and took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a> in 1688. Among the many works he published are, 1. A literal exposition in French, of all the books in the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> volumes folio. 2. An historical, critical, chronological, geographical, and literal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, in four vols., folio, enriched with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of figures of Jewish an- tiquities. 3. A civil and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Lor- <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, three vols., folio. 4. A history of the Old and New Testament, and of the Jews, in two volumes fol- io, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> vols., duodecimo. 5. An universal sacred and profane history, in several volumes quarto. He died in 1757. CALMUCKS. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALMUCKS">Kalmucks</a>.

CALNE

Pages 91-91

a town of Wiltshire in England, seated on a river of the same name. It has a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 59. N. Lat. 51. 30.

CALNEH

Pages 91-91

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Shinar, built by Nimrod, and the last city men- tioned (Gen. x. 10.) as belonging to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It is believed to be the same with Calno, mentioned in Isaiah (x. 9.) and with Cannah in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> (xxvii. 23.) with still greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>. It is observed, that it must have been situated in Mesopotamia, since the prophets join it with Haran, Eden Assyrian, and Chil- mad, which carried on a trade with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>. It is said by the Chaldee interpreters, as also by Eusebius and Jerome, to be the same with Ctesiphon, standing upon the Tigris, about three miles distant from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, and that for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city of the Parthians.

CALOGERI

Pages 91-91

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, monks of the Greek church, divided into three degrees: the novices, called archari; the ordinary professed, called microche- mi; and the more perfect, called megalochemi: they are likewise divided into canonites, anchorets, and recluses. The canonites are employed in reciting their offices from midnight to sunlet, they are obliged to make three genuflexions at the door of the choir, and, return- ing, to bow to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and to the left, to their bre- thren.

CALOMEL

Pages 91-92
or dulcified sublimate of mercury, is a combination of mercury with the muriatic acid, in the present nomenclature called a sub-muriate of mercury. See Pharmacy and Chemistry Index. CALOPHYLLUM. See Botany Index.

CALOTTE

Pages 92-92

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a round cavity <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a>, in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> or cup, lathed and plastered, used to diminish the rise or elevation of a moderate chapel, cabinet, alcove, &c., which without such an expedient would be too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> for other pieces of the apartment.

CALPE

Pages 92-92

a mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; at the foot of which, towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, stands the town of Gibraltar. It is half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> in height towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and so steep that there is no approaching it on that side.

CALPURNIUS

Pages 92-92

Titus, a Latin Sicilian poet, lived under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARUS">Carus</a> and his son. We have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of his elegies remaining.

CALQUING

Pages 92-92
or Calking, a term used in painting, &c., where the back side of any thing is covered over with a black or red colour, and the strokes or lines traced through on a waxed plate, wall, or other matter, by passing lightly over each stroke of the design with a point, which leaves an impression of the colour on the plate or wall. CALTHA. See Botany Index. There is only one species known, which grows naturally in moist boggy lands in many parts of England and Scotland. The flowers gathered before they expand, and preserved in salted vinegar, are a good substitute for capers. The juice of the petals, boiled with a little alum, stains paper yellow. The remarkable yellowness of the butter in spring is supposed to be caused by this plant; but cows will not eat it, unless compelled by extreme hunger; and then, Boerhaave says, it occasions such an inflammation, that they generally die. Upon May-day, the country people strew the flowers upon the pavement before their doors. Goats and sheep eat this plant; horses, cows, and swine, refuse it. CALTROP. See Tribulus, Botany Index. Caltrop, in military affairs, an instrument with four iron points, disposed in a triangular form, so that three of them are always on the ground, and the fourth in the air. They are scattered over the ground where the enemy's cavalry is to pass, in order to embarrass them.

CALUMET

Pages 94-94

a symbolical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance among the American Indians.—It is nothing more than a pipe, whose bowl is generally made of a soft <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> marble: the tube of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> reed, ornamented with the wings and feathers of birds. No affair of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> is transacted without the calumet. It ever appears in meetings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> exchanges; in congregates for determining of peace or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and even in the very fury of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a> of the calumet is a mark of concurrence with the terms proposed; as the refusal is a certain mark of rejection. Even in the rage of a conflict this pipe is sometimes offered; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> accepted, the weapons of destruction instantly drop from their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and a truce ensues. It seems the sacrament of the favours; for no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> is ever violated which is confirmed by a whiff from this holy reed. When they treat of war, the pipe and all its ornaments are usually red, or sometimes red only on one side. The size and decorations of the calumet are for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> proportioned to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the persons to whom they are presented, and to the importance of the occasion. The calumet of peace is different from that of war. They make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the former to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> their alliances and treaties, to travel with safety, and to receive strangers; but of the latter to proclaim war. It consists of a red <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, like marble, formed into a cavity resembling the head of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> pipe, and fixed to a hollow reed. They adorn it with feathers of various colours; and name it the calumet of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, to which luminary they present it, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of thereby obtaining a change of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> as often as they desire. From the winged ornaments of the calumet, and its conciliating uses, writers compare it to the caduceus of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, which was carried by the caduceatores, or messengers of peace, with terms to the hostile states. It is singular, that the most remote nations, and the most opposite in their other customs and manners, should in some things have, as it were, a certain consent of thought. The Greeks and the Americans had the same idea, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the caduceus of the one, and the calumet of the other. Dance of the Calumet, is a solemn rite among the Indians on various occasions. They dare not wash themselves in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, without performing it; and the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> always confirms a peace or precedes a war. It is performed in the winter <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in their cabins, and in summer in the open fields. For this purpose they choose a spot among trees to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> them from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the sun, and lay in the middle a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> mat, as a carpet, setting upon it the monitor, or god, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of this image they <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the calumet, as their great deity, erecting around it a kind of trophy with their arms. Things being thus disposed, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> come, those who are to sing take the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> seats under the shade of the trees. The company is then ranged round, every one, before he sits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, saluting the monitor, which is done by blowing upon the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of their tobacco. Each person next receives the calumet in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>, and holding it with both hands, dances to the cadence of the vocal music, which is accompanied with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> of a sort of drum. During this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, he gives a signal to one of their warriors, who takes a bow, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>, and axe, from the trophies already mentioned, and fights him; the former defending himself with the calumet only, and both of them dancing all the while. This mock engagement being over, he who holds the calumet makes a speech, in which he gives an account of the battles he has fought, and the prisoners he has taken, and then receives a cloak, or some other present, from the chief of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. He then resigns the calumet to another, who, having acted a similar part, delivers it to a third, who afterwards gives it to his neighbour, till at last the instrument returns to the person that began the ceremony, who presents it to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> invited to the feast, as a mark of their friendship, and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>, when this is the occasion of the entertainment.

CALUMNY

Pages 94-94

the crime of accusing another falsely, and knowingly so, of some heinous offence. Oath of Calumny, juramentum (<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather jusjurandum) Calumniae, among civilians and canonists, was an oath which both parties in a cause were obliged to take; the plaintiff that he did not bring his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, and the defendant that he did not deny it, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to abuse each other, but because they believed their cause was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and good; that they would not deny the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, nor create unnecessary delays, nor offer the judge or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> any gifts or bribes. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the plaintiff refused this oath, the complaint or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a> was dismissed; if the defendant, it was taken pro confesso. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was taken from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> athletes; who, before they engaged, were to swear that they had no malice, nor would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> any unfair means for overcoming each other. The juramentum calumniae is much abused, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> occasion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>. Anciently the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> and proctors also took this oath; but of late it is dispensed with, and thought sufficient that they take it once for all at their first admission to practice. See also <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> III. No clxxxiv. 7.

CALVARIA

Pages 92-92

in Anatomy, the hairy scalp <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the head, which, either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> or old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, grows bald first.

CALVART

Pages 92-92

Denis, a celebrated painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1552; and had for his masters Prospero Fontana and Lorenzo Sabbatini. He opened a school at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, which became celebrated; and from which proceeded Guido, Albani, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> masters. Calvart was well skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, and anatomy, which he considered as necessary to a painter, and taught them to his pupils. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are at Bologna, Rome, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGGIO">Reggio</a>. He died at Bologna in 1619.

CALVARY

Pages 92-92

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> so called, because it resembles the cross on which our Saviour suffered. It is always set upon fleurs.

CALVERT

Pages 92-92

George, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALTIMORE">Baltimore</a>, was born at Kipling in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> about the year 1582, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of arts, and afterwards travelled. At his return, he was made secretary to Sir Robert Cecil; he was afterwards knighted, and in 1618 appointed one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> secretaries of state. But after he had enjoyed that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> about five years, he willingly resigned it; freely owning to his majesty that he was become a Roman Catholic, so that he must either be wanting to his trust, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> violate his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> in discharging his office. This ingenuous confession so affected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James, that he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> him privy counsellor all his reign, and the same year created him baron of Baltimore in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. He had before obtained a patent for him and his heirs, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Avalon in Newfoundland; but that being exposed to the insults of the French, he abandoned it, and afterwards obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., who called it <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARYLAND">Maryland</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>: but he died in April 1632 (aged 50), before the patent was made out. It was, however, filled up to his son Cecil Calvert Lord Baltimore; and bears <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 20, 1632. It is held from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> as part of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Windlor, on one very singular condition, viz. to present two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> arrows yearly, on Easter Tuesday, at the castle, where they are kept and shown to visitors.—His lordship wrote, 1. A Latin poem on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Sir Henry Upton. 2. Speeches in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. 3. Various letters of state. 4. The answer of Tom Tell-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. 5. The Practice of Princes. And, 6. The Lamentation of the Kirk.

CALVI

Pages 92-92

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lavoro, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, situated near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, about fifteen miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Naples. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 45. N. Lat. 41. 15. Calvi is also the name of a sea port in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Corsica, situated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, on the west side of the island, about 40 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTIA">Bastia</a>. E. Long. 9. 5. N. Lat. 42. 16.

CALVIN

Pages 92-93

John, the celebrated reformer of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> from Romish superstitions and doctrinal nal errors, and founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> since called Calvinists, was born in 1509. He was the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COOPER">cooper</a> of Noyon in Picardy; and his real name was Chauvin, which he chose to latinize into Calvinus, styling himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> page to his first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> (a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on Seneca de Clementia), "Lucius Calvinus, Civis Romanus;" an early <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, at about 24 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>.
