Camden was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and integrity; profoundly learned in the history and antiquities of this kingdom, and a judicious and conscientious historian. He was reverenced and esteemed by the literati of all nations, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be ever remembered as an honour to the age and country wherein he lived. Besides the works already mentioned, he was author of an excellent Greek <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, and of several tracts in Hearne's collection. But his great and most useful work, the Britannia, is that upon which his fame chiefly built. The edition above mentioned, to which he put his last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, was correctly printed in folio, much augmented, amended where it was necessary, and adorned with maps. It was first translated into English, and published in folio at London, in 1611, by the laborious Dr Philemon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, a physician of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, who is thought to have consulted our author himself; and therefore great respect has been paid to the additions and explanations that occur. (a) The reign of Queen Elizabeth was so recent when the first volume of the Annals was published, that many of the persons concerned, or their dependents, were still living. It is no wonder, therefore, that the honest historian should offend those whose actions would not bear inquiry. Some of his enemies were clamorous and troublesome; which determined him not to publish the second volume during his life; but that poverty might be in no danger of disappointment, he deposited one copy in the Cotton library, and transmitted another to his friend Dupuy at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. It was first printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1625.

CAMEL

Pages 102-102

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, a kind of machine used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> for raising <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lifting ships, in order to bring them over the Pampus, which is at the mouth of the river Y, where the shallowness of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> hinders <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships from passing. It is also used in other places, particularly at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCK">dock</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>, the vessels built here being in their passage to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRONSTADT">Cronstadt</a>; lifted over the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> by means of camels. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> were originally invented by the celebrated De <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">Wit</a>, for the purpose above mentioned; and were introduced into Russia by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, who obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of them when he worked in Holland as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> shipwright. A camel is composed of two separate parts, whose outsides are perpendicular, and whose insides are concave, shaped so as to embrace the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">hull</a> of a ship on both sides. Each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> has a small cabin with fifteen pumps and ten plugs, and contains 20 men. They are braced to a ship underneath by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, and entirely enclose its sides and bottom; being then towed to the bar, the plugs are opened, and the water admitted until the camel sinks with the ship and runs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a>. Then, the water being pumped out, the camel rises, lifts up the vessel, and the whole is towed over the bar. This machine can raise the ship eleven feet, or, in other words, make it draw eleven feet less water.

CAMELFORD

Pages 102-102

a borough town of Cornwall in England, consisting of about 100 houses, badly built; but the streets are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and well paved. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 4'. N. Lat. 50° 40'. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of baron to Thomas Pitt, elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>. CAMELIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CAMELODUM. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMALODUNUM">CAMALODUNUM</a>.

CAMELOPARDALIS

Pages 102-102

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Cervus. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CAMELUS

Pages 102-102
or CAMEL, in Zoology, a genus of quadrupeds belonging to the order of pecora. See MAMMALIA Index. CAMEO. See Camaieu.

CAMERA AEOLIA

Pages 102-102

a contrivance for blowing the fire, for the fusion of ores, without bellows; by means of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> falling through a funnel into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> vessel, which feeds it so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vapour as continually blows the fire: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be the space of another vessel for it to expiate in by the way, it there lets <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> its humidity, which otherwise might hinder the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. This contrivance was named camera AEOLIA by Kircher. CAMERA <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LUCIDA">Lucida</a>, a contrivance of Dr Hook for making the image of any thing appear on a wall in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> room, either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> or night. Opposite to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> or wall where the appearance is to be, make a hole of at least a foot in diameter, or if there be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> window with a crenelation of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a> in it, this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> do much better without such hole or crenelation opened. At a convenient distance, to prevent its being perceived by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> in the room, place the object or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> intended to be represented, but in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> situation. If the picture be transparent, reflect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s rays by means of a looking glass, so as that they may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through it towards the place of representation; and to prevent any rays from passing aside it, let the picture be encompassed with some board or cloth. If the object be a statue, or a living creature, it must be much enlightened by casting the sun's rays on it, either by reflection, refraction, or both. Between this object and the place of representation put a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> convex glass, ground to such a convexity as that it may represent the object distinctly in such place. The nearer this is situated to the object, the more will the image be magnified on the wall, and the further the less: such diversity depending on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the spheres of the glasses. If the object cannot be conveniently inverted, there must be two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> glasses of proper spheres, situated at suitable distances, easily found by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, to make the representations erect. This whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of object, glasses, &c., with the persons employed in the management of them, are to be placed without the window or hole, so that they may not be perceived by the spectators in the room, and the operation itself will be easily performed. Phil. Trans. No. 38. p. 741. seq. CAMERA Obscura, or Dark Chamber, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, a machine, or apparatus, representing an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> eye; whereon the images of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects, received through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> convex glass, are exhibited distinctly, and in their native colours, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> placed within the machine, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of the glass. The first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> is ascribed to Baptista Porta. See his Magia Naturalis, lib. xvii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 6. first published at Frankfort about the year 1589 or 1591; the first four books of this work were published at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1560. The camera obscura affords very diverting <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a>; both by exhibiting images perfectly like their objects, and each clothed in their native colours; and by expressing, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, all their motions; which latter no other art can imitate. By means of this instrument, a person unacquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> will be able to delineate objects with the greatest accuracy and truthfulness, and another well versed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> will find many things herein to perfect his art. See the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> under DROPTICS.

CAMERARIUS

Pages 103-103

Joachim, son of the former, and a learned physician, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> in 1534. After having finished his studies in Germany, he went into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he obtained the esteem of the learned. At his return he was courted by several princes to live with them; but he was too much devoted to books, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, to comply. He wrote a Hortus Medicus, and several other works. He died in 1598.

CAMERET BAY

Pages 103-103

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Brittany in France, forms the harbour of Brest. See BREST.

CAMERINO

Pages 103-103

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> state in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° 7'. N. Lat. 45° 5'.

CAMERLINGO

Pages 103-103

according to Du Cange, signified formerly the pope's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>: at present, camerlingo is nowhere used but at Rome, where it denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> who governs the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> state, and administers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. It is the most eminent office at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome, because he is at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. During a vacation of the papal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, the cardinal camerlingo publishes edicts, coins <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and exerts every other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of a sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; he has under him a treasurer-general, auditor-general, and 12 prelates called clerks of the chamber.

CAMERON

Pages 103-103

John, one of the most famous divines among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> of France in the 17th century, was born at Glasgow in Scotland, where he taught the Greek tongue; and having read lectures upon that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> for about a year, travelled, and became professor at several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and minister at Bordeaux. He published, 1. Theological lectures; 2. Icon Johannis Cameronis; and some miscellaneous pieces. He died in 1625, aged 60.

CAMERONIANS

Pages 103-103
or Cameronites, is also the denomination of a party of Calvinists in France, who asserted that the will of man is only determined by the practical judgment of the mind; that the cause of men's doing good or evil proceeds from the knowledge which God infuses into them; and that God does not move the will physically, but only morally, in virtue of its dependence on the judgment of the mind. They had this name from John Cameron, a famous professor, first at Glasgow, where he was born, in 1580, and afterwards at Bourdeaux, Sedan, and Saumur; at which last place he broached his new doctrine of grace and free will, which was formed by Amyraut, Cappel, Bochart, Daille, and others of the more learned among the reformed ministers, who judged Calvin's doctrines on these points too harshly. The Cameronians are a sort of mitigated Calvinists, and approach to the opinion of the Arminians. They are also called Universalists, as holding the universality of Christ's death; and sometimes Amyraldists. The rigid adherents to the synod of Dort accused them of Pelagianism, and even of Manicheism. The controversy between the parties was carried on with a zeal and subtlety scarce conceivable; yet all the question between them was only, Whether the will of man is determined by the immediate action of God upon it, or by the intervention of a knowledge which God impregnes into the mind? The synod of Dort had defined that God not only illuminates the understanding, but gives motion to the will by making an internal change therein. Cameron only admitted the illumination, whereby the mind is morally moved; and explained the sentiment of the synod of Dort so as to make the two opinions consistent.

CAMES

Pages 103-103

a name given to the small slender rods of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> of which the glaziers make their turned lead. Their lead being cast into slender rods of twelve <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fourteen inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> each, is called the came; sometimes also they call each of these rods a came, which being afterwards drawn through their vice, makes their turned lead.

CAMILLUS

Pages 103-104

Marcus Furius, was the first who rendered the family of Furius illustrious. He triumphed four times, was five times <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>, and was honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> founder of Rome. In a word, he acquired all the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Lucius Apuleius, one of the tribunes, prosecuted him to make him give an account of the spoils taken at <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol20.html#article-VEII">Veii</a>. Camillus anticipated judgment, and banished himself voluntarily. During his banishment, instead of rejoicing at the devastation of Rome by the Gauls, he exerted all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and bravery to drive away the enemy; and yet kept with the utmost strictness the sacred <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of Rome, in refusing to accept the command, which several private persons offered him. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> who were besieged in the capitol, created him dictator in the year 363; in which office he acted with so much bravery and conduct, that he entirely drove the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the Gauls out of the territories of the commonwealth. He died in the 81st year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, 365 years before the Christian era. CAMILLI and CAMILLAE, in Antiquity, boys and girls of ingenuous birth, who ministered in the sacrifices of the gods; and especially those who attended the flamens diales, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. The word seems borrowed. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMINHA">Caminha</a> borrowed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Heturians, where it signified minister, and was changed from *cal- millus*. The Tuscans also gave the appellation *Camil- lus* to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of minister of the gods.

CAMINHA

Pages 104-104

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Entre-Duero-e-Minho, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It is situated at the mouth of the river Minho, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 15'. N. Lat. 41° 44'.

CAMIS

Pages 104-104
or **KAMIS**, in the Japanese theology, denote deified souls of ancient heroes, who are supposed still to intercede themselves in the welfare of the people whom they ancienly commanded. The camis answer to the heroes in the ancient Greek and Roman theology, and are venerated like the saints in the modern Roman church. Besides the heroes or camis beatified by the consent of antiquity, the *mikaddos*, or pontiffs, have deified many others, and continue still to grant the apotheosis to new worthies; so that they swarm with camis: the principal one is *Tenjo Dai Sin*, the common father of Japan, to whom are paid devotions and pilgrimages extraordinary.

CAMISADE

Pages 104-104

in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, an attack by surprise in the night, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, when the enemy is supposed to be asleep. The word is said to have taken its rise from an attack of this kind; wherein, as a badge or signal to know one another by, they bore a shift, in French called *chemise*, or *camise*, over their arms.

CAMISARDS

Pages 104-104

a name given by the French to the Calvinists of the Cevennes, who formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, and took up arms in their own defense, in 1688.

CAMLETINE

Pages 104-104

a slight stuff, made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, in the manner of camlet. It is now out of fashion.

CAMMA

Pages 104-104

and **GOBBI**, two provinces of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Loango in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The inhabitants are continually at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with each other. The weapons they formerly used in their wars were the short pike, bows and arrows, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and dagger; but since the Europeans have become acquainted with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, they have supplied them with fire-arms. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of Gobbi lies about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s journey from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.—Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> abound with a variety of fish; but are infested with sea horses, which do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mischief both by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the natives is in logwood, elephants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> and tails, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of which is highly valued, and used for several curious purposes.

CAMMIN

Pages 104-104

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of Germany, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> Pomerania, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15°. N. Lat. 54°.

CAMPAIGN

Pages 107-107

in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, denotes the space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> keeps the field, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> is encamped.—Campaign The beginning of every campaign is considerably more unhealthy than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the men were to remain in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. After the first fortnight or three weeks encampment, the sickness decreases daily; the most infirm being by that time in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> daily growing warmer. This healthy state continues throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, unless the men get wet clothes or wet beds; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, a greater or less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the dysentery <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear in proportion to the preceding heats. But the most sickly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the campaign begins about the middle or end of August, whilst the days are still hot, but the nights cool and damp, with fogs and dews: then, and not sooner, the dysentery prevails; and though its violence is over by the beginning of October, yet the remitting fever gaining ground, continues throughout the rest of the campaign, and never entirely ceases, even in winter-quarters, till the frosts begin. At the beginning of a campaign the sickness is so uniform, that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> may be nearly predicted; but for the rest of the season, as the diseases are then of a contagious <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and depend so much upon the heats of summer, it is impossible to foresee how many may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> sick from the beginning to the end of autumn. It is also observed, that the last fortnight of a campaign, if protracted till the beginning of winter, is attended with more sickness than the first two months encampment: so that it is better to take the field a fortnight sooner, in order to return into winter-quarters so much the earlier. As to winter expeditions, though severe in appearance, they are attended with little sickness, if the men have strong shoes, quarters, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> marches in summer are not without danger, unless made in the night, or so early in the morning as to be over before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. CAMPANACEÆ, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> in the Fragmenta methodi naturalis of Linnaeus, in which are the following genera, viz. convolvulus, ipomoea, polemonium, campanula, roella, viola, &c. * Sec Be.

CAMPANELLA

Pages 107-107

Thomas, a famous Italian lazy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at Stilo in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, in 1568. He distinguished himself by his early proficiency in learning; for at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 13 he was a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> orators and poets. His peculiar inclination was to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, to which he at last confined his whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. In order to arrive at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, he shook off the yoke of authority: by which means the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of some of his opinions exposed him to many inconveniences; for at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> he was thrown into prison, in which he remained 27 years, and during this confinement wrote his famous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled Atheismus triumphatus. Being at length set at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he was graciously received by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII. and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Richelieu; the latter procured him a pension of 2000 livres, and often consulted him on the affairs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Campanella passed the remainder of his days in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a> at Paris, and died in 1639.

CAMPANI

Pages 107-107

Matthew, of Spoleto, curate at Rome, wrote a curious treatise on the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> glasses for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a>, and made several improvements in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, assisted by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> and pupil <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>. He died after 1678.

CAMPANIA

Pages 107-116

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, Campania: Naples, and in the farther principato, with a bishop's see. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15° 30'. N. Lat. 40° 40'. Campania, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> di Roma, anciently Latiun, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Italy, bounded on the west by the Tiber and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the south-west by the sea, on the south by Terra di Lavoro, on the east by Abruzzo, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Sabina. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is good, it produces little or nothing, on account of the heavy duties on corn; and though the waters are good, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is unwholesome. It is subject to the Pope, and is about 60 miles in length on the Mediterranean sea. It has been generally thought that the air of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> hath something in it peculiarly noxious during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but Mr Condamine is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it is not more unhealthy than any other marshy country. His account follows. "It was after the invasion of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> in the fifth and sixth centuries that this corruption of the air began to manifest itself. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the Tiber being covered by the accumulated ruins of the edifices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Rome, could not but raise itself considerably. But what permits us not to doubt of this fact is, that the ancient and well-preserved pavement of the Pantheon and its portico is overflowed every winter; that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> even rises there sometimes to the height of eight or ten feet: and that it is not possible to suppose that the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> should have built a temple in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> so low as to be covered with the waters of the Tiber on the least inundation. It is evident, then, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the bed of this river is raised several feet; which could not have happened without forming there a kind of dikes or bars. The choking up of its canal necessarily occasioned the overflow and reflux of its waters in such places as till then had not been subject to inundations; to these overflows of the Tiber were added all the waters that escaped out of the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>, the ruins of which are still to be seen, and which were entirely broken and destroyed by Totila. What need, therefore, of anything more to infect the air, in a hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, than the exhalations of such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of stagnating waters deprived of any discharge, and become the receptacle of a thousand impurities, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> of several millions both of men and animals? The evil could not but increase from the same causes while Rome was exposed to the incursions and devastations of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, the Normans, and the Saracens, which lasted for several centuries. The air became so infectious there at the beginning of the 13th century, that Pope Innocent III. wrote, that few people at Rome arrived to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of forty years, and that nothing was more uncommon there than to see a person of sixty. A very short time after, the popes transferred the seat of their residence to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>: during the seventy-two years they remained there, Rome became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>; the monasteries in it were converted into stables; and Gregory XI. on his return to Rome, in 1376, hardly counted there 30,000 inhabitants. At his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> began the troubles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> schism in the west, which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for upwards of 50 years. Martin V., in whom this schism ended in the year 1429, and his first successors, were able to make but feeble efforts against it to extirpate an evil. It was not till the beginning of the 16th century that Leo X., under whom Rome began to resume her wonted splendour, gave himself some trouble about re-establishing the salubrity of the air; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, being shortly after besieged twice successively by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V., <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> itself plunged again into all its old calamities; and from 85,000 inhabitants, which it contained under Leo X., it was reduced under Clement VIII. to 32,000. In short, it is only since the time of Pius V. and Sextus V., at the end of the 16th century, that the popes have constantly employed the necessary methods for purifying the air of Rome and its environs, by procuring proper discharges for the waters, drying up the humid and marshy grounds, and covering the banks of the Tiber and other places reputed uninhabitable with superb edifices. Since that time a person may dwell at Rome, and go in or out of it at all seasons of the year. At the beginning, however, of the present century, they were still afraid to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> out of the city in summer, when they had resided there; as they were also to return to it, when once they had quitted it. They never ventured to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> at Rome, even in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, in any other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> than their own. They are greatly relaxed at present from these ancient scruples: I have seen cardinals, in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and August, go from Rome to lie at Frascati, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIVOLI">Tivoli</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANO">Albano</a>, &c. and return the next or the following days to the city, without any detriment to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>: I have myself tried all these experiments, without suffering the least inconvenience from them: we have even seen, in the last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in Italy, two armies encamped under the walls of Rome at the time when the heats were most violent. Yet notwithstanding all this, the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the country people dare not still venture to lie during that season of the year, nor even as much as sleep in a carriage, in any part of the territory comprehended under the name of the Campagna of Rome." <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPANIFORM">Campaniform</a>, or Campanulated, an appellation given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPANINI">Campanini</a>, a name given to an Italian marble dug out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRARA">Carrara</a>, because, when it is worked, it sounds like a bell. Campanula, or Bell-flower. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Campbell, Archibald, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> and marquis of Argyle, was the son of Archibald earl of Argyle, by the lady <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Douglas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of William earl of Morton. He was born in the year 1558; and educated in the profession of the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, according to the strictest rules of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Scotland, as it was established immediately after the reformation. During the commonwealth he was induced to submit to its authority. Upon the restoration, he was tried for his compliance; a crime <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to him with the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and such a one as the most loyal and affectionate subject might frequently by violence be induced to commit. To make this compliance appear the more voluntary and hearty, there were produced in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> letters which he had wrote to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a>, while that general governed Scotland, and which contained expressions of the most cordial <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the established <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. But, besides the general indignation excited by Albemarle's discovery of this private correspondence, men thought, that even the highest demonstrations of affection might, during jealous times, be exacted as a necessary mark of compliance from a person of such distinction as Argyle; and could not, by any equitable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, imply the crime of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, however, scrupled not to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> upon him, and he suffered with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> and courage. Campbell, Archibald, earl of Argyle, son to the former, had from his youth distinguished himself by his loyalty and his attachment to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family. Though his father was head of the covenanters, he himself refused to concur in any of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>; and when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> was given him by the convention of states, he forbore to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon it till it should be ratified by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. By his respectful behaviour, as well as by his services, he made himself acceptable to Charles when that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was in Scotland, and even after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, all the misfortunes which attended the royal cause could not engage him to desert it. Under Middleton he obstinately persevered to harass and infest the victorious English; and it was not till he received orders from that general, that he would submit to accept of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>. Such jealousy of his loyal attachments was entertained by the commonwealth and protector, that a pretence was soon after fallen upon to commit him to prison; and his confinement was rigorously continued till the restoration. The king, sensible of his services, had remitted to him his father's forfeiture, and created him earl of Argyle; and when a most unjust sentence was passed upon him by the Scots parliament, Charles had anew remitted it. In the subsequent part of this reign Argyle behaved himself dutifully; and though he seemed not disposed to go all lengths with the court, he always appeared, even in his opposition, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of mild dispositions and peaceable deportment. A parliament was summoned at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in summer 1681, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>. Besides granting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to the king, and voting the indefeasible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of succession, this parliament enacted a test, which all persons possessed of offices, civil, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a>, were bound to take. In this test the king's supremacy was asserted, the covenant renounced, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> obedience attested to, and all obligations disclaimed of endeavouring any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in civil or ecclesiastical establishments. This was the state of the test as proposed by the courtiers; but the country party proposed also a clause of adherence to the Protestant religion, which could not with decency be rejected. The whole was of an enormous length, considered as an oath; and, what was worse, a confession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> was there ratified which had been imposed a little after the reformation, and which contained many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> altogether forged by the parliament and nation. Among others, the doctrine of resistance was inculcated; so that the test being voted in a hurry, was found on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> to be a medley of absurdity and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>. Though the courtiers could not reject the clause of adhering to the Protestant religion, they proposed, as a requisite mark of respect, that all princes of the blood should be exempted from taking that oath. This exception was zealously opposed by Argyle; who observed that the sole danger to be dreaded for the Protestant religion must proceed from the perversion of the royal family. By insisting on such topics, he drew on himself the secret indignation of the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, of which he soon felt the fatal consequences. When Argyle took the test as a privy counsellor, he subjoined, in the duke's presence, an explanation which he had beforehand communicated to that prince, and which he believed to have been approved by him. It was in these words. "I have considered the test, and am very desirous of giving obedience as far as I can. I am confident that the parliament never intended to impose contradictory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a>: therefore I think no man can explain it but for himself. Accordingly I take it as far as it is consistent with itself and the Protestant religion. And I do declare that I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> not to bind myself, in my <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, and in a lawful way, from withstanding and endeavouring any alteration, which I think to the advantage of church or state, and not repugnant to the Protestant religion and my loyalty: and thus I understand as a part of my oath." The duke, as was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, heard it with great tranquillity: no one took the least offence: Argyle was admitted to sit that day in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>: and it was impossible to imagine that a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> offence had been committed where occasion seemed not to have been given so much as for a frown or reprimand. Argyle was much surprised a few days after, to find that a warrant was issued for committing him to prison; that he was indicted for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> treason, leasemaking, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>; and that from the innocent words abovementioned an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> was extracted, by which he was to forfeit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, honours, and fortune. It is needless to enter into particulars, where the iniquity of the whole is so evidently apparent. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> was displayed, even her semblance was not put on; and the forms of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> were preserved to sanctify, or rather aggravate, the oppression. Of five judges, three did not scruple to find the guilt of treason and leasemaking to be incurred by the prisoner: a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> of 15 noblemen gave verdict against him; and the king being consulted, ordered the sentence to be pronounced, but the execution of it to be suspended till further orders. Argyle, however, saw no reason to trust to the justice or mercy of such enemies: He made his escape from prison, and till he could find a ship for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> he concealed himself during some time in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The king heard of his lurking place, but would not suffer him to be arrested. All the parts, however, of his sentence, so far as the government in Scotland had power, were rigorously executed; his estate confiscated, his arms reverred and torn. Having got over to Holland, he remained there during the remaining part of the reign of Charles II. But thinking himself at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, before the coronation of James II., to exert himself in order to recover the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> by force of arms, he concerted measures with the duke of Monmouth, and went into Scotland, to assemble his friends: but not meeting with the success he expected, he was taken prisoner; and being carried to Edinburgh, was beheaded upon his former unjust sentence, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 30, 1685. He showed great constancy and courage under his misfortunes: on the day of his death he ate his dinner very cheerfully; and, according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, slept after it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> or more, very soundly. At the place of execution, he made a short, grave, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> speech; and, after solemnly declaring that he forgave all his enemies, submitted to death with great firmness. Campbell, Archibald, first duke of Argyle, son to the preceding, was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> promoter of the revolution. He came over with the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>; was admitted into the convention as earl of Argyle, though his father's attainder was not reversed; and in the claim of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> the sentence against him was declared to be, what most certainly it was, a reproach upon the nation. The establishment of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> upon the prince and princess of Orange being carried by a great majority in the Scottish convention, the earl was sent from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, with Sir James <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERY">Montgomery</a> and Sir John Dalrymple from the barons and boroughs, to offer the crown, in the name of the convention, to their majesties, and tendered them the coronation oath; for which, and many other eminent services, he was admitted a member of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy council</a>, and, in 1692, made one of the lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. He was afterwards made a colonel of the Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> guards; and, in 1694, one of the extraordinary lords of session. He was likewise created duke of Argyle, marquis of Kintyre and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORN">Lorn</a>, earl of Campbell and Cowall, Viscount of Lochow and Glenila, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERARY">Inverary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>, Morvern, and Terrey, by letters-patent, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENSINGTON">Kensington</a> the 23rd of June 1701. He sent over a regiment to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> for King William's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, the officers of which were chiefly of his own name and family, who bravely distinguished themselves through the whole course of the war. He married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, daughter of Sir Lionel Talmath of Helmingham in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, by Elizabeth duchess of Lauderdale his wife, daughter and heiress of William Murray earl of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol8.html#article-DYSART">Dysart</a>, by whom he left three sons and a daughter; namely, John duke of Argyle, the subject of the next article; Archibald, who succeeded his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> as duke of Argyle; and Lady Anne, married to James Stuart, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> earl of Bute, by whom she had a son afterwards earl of Bute. Campbell, John, second duke of Argyle, and also duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> and baron of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>, son to the subject of the preceding article, was born on the 10th of October 1680; and, on the very day when his grandfather suffered at Edinburgh, fell out of a window three <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of stairs high without receiving any hurt. At the age of 15, he had made a considerable progress in classical learning. His father then perceived and encouraged his military disposition, and introduced him to King William, who appointed him to the command of a regiment. In this situation he remained till the death of his father in 1703; when becoming duke of Argyle, he was soon after sworn of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Anne's privy council, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the Scotch horse guards, and appointed one of the extraordinary lords of session. In 1704, her majesty reviving the Scottish order of the thistle, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> was installed one of the knights of that order, and was soon after appointed high-commissioner to the Scotch parliament; where, being of great service in promoting the intended union, he was on his return created a peer of England, by the titles of baron of Chatham and earl of Greenwich, and in 1710 was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>. His grace first distinguished himself in his military capacity at the battle of Oudenarde; where he commanded as brigadier-general, with all the bravery of youth and the conduct of a veteran officer. He was present under the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> at the siege of Ghent, and took possession of the town. He had also a considerable share in the victory obtained over the French at the battle of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALPLAQUET">Malplaquet</a>, by dislodging them from the wood of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SART">Sart</a>, and gaining a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. In this sharp engagement, several musket-balls passed through the duke's clothes, hat, and periwig. Soon after this hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, he was sent to take the command in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Port <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAHON">Mahon</a>, he returned to England. His grace having now a seat in the house of lords, he censured the measures of the ministry with such freedom, that all his places were disputed of to other noblemen: but at the accession of George I. he recovered his influence. At the breaking out of the rebellion in 1715, he was made commander-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of his majesty's forces in North <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; and was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> means and cause of the total extinction, at that time, of the rebellion in Scotland, without much bloodshed. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> opposition to him, or that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> he commanded, at the head of all his Campbells was placed Campbell earl of Braidalbin, of the same family and kindred, by some fatal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> that ever misguided and misled that unhappy family of the Stuarts and all its adherents. The consequence was, that both sets of Campbells, from family affection, refused to strike a stroke, and retired out of the battle. He arrived at London <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 6th 1716, and was in high favour: but, to the surprize of people of all ranks, he was in a few months divested of all his employments; and from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to the year 1718, he signalized himself in a civil capacity, by his uncorrupted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a> and manly eloquence. In the beginning of the year 1719, he was again admitted into favour, appointed lord-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and in April following was created duke of Greenwich. He continued in the administration during all the remaining part of that reign; and, after his late majesty's accession, till April 1740; when he delivered a speech with such warmth, that the ministry being highly offended, he was again dismissed from his employments. To these, however, on the change of the ministry, he was soon restored; but not approving of the measures of the new ministry more than those of the old, he gave up all his posts for the last time, and never after engaged in affairs of state. He now enjoyed privacy and retirement; and died of a paralytic disorder on the 4th of October 1743. To the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his grace a very noble monument was erected in Westminster-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>, executed by the ingenious Roubillac. The duke of Argyle, though never first minister, was a very able statesman and politician, most steadily fixed in those principles he believed to be right, and not to be shaken or changed. His delicacy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> were so great, that it hurt him to be even suspected; witness that application said to be made to him by one of the adherents of the Stuart family before the last rebellion in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, which was considerable both in Scotland and England. He immediately sent the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the secretary of state; and it vexed him much even to have an application made him, lest any person should think him capable of acting a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> part. When he thought measures wrong or corrupt, he cared not who was the author, however great or powerful he might be; witness his boldly attacking the great duke of Marlborough in the house of lords, about his forage and army contracts in Flanders, in the very zenith of his power and popularity. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> popularity, though in all other respects he was the most able general of his time. The duke of Argyle on all occasions spoke well, with a firm, manly, and noble eloquence; and seems to deserve the character given of him by Pope: Argyle the state's whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> born to wield, And thake alike the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and the field. In private life, the duke's conduct was highly exemplary. He was an affectionate husband and an indulgent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. He seldom parted with his servants till age had rendered them incapable of their employments; and then he made provision for their subsistence. He was liberal to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and particularly to persons of merit in distress: but though he was ready to patronize deserving persons, he was extremely cautious not to deceive any by lavish promises or leading them to form vain expectations. He was a strict economist, and paid his tradesmen punctually every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; and though he maintained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, he took care that no part of his income should be wasted in empty pomp or unnecessary expenses. He was twice married; and left five daughters, but no <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> issue. The titles of duke and earl of Greenwich and baron of Chatham became extinct at his death; but in his other titles he was succeeded by his brother Archibald earl of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-ILA">Ila</a>, the subject of the next article. Campbell, Archibald, third duke of Argyle, brother to the subject of the preceding article, was born at Hambrook, in England, in June 1682, and was educated at the university of Glasgow. He afterwards applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the law at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>; but, upon his father's being created a duke, he betook himself to a military life, and served some time under the duke of Marlborough. Upon quitting the army, in which he did not long remain, he applied to the acquisition of that knowledge which would enable him to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> world. In 1705, he was constituted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of Scotland, and made a considerable figure in parliament, though he was not more than 23 years of age. In 1706, he was appointed one of the commissioners for treating of the Union; and the same year was created Lord Orontay, Dunoon, and Arrois, Viscount and Earl of Ila. In 1708, he was made an extraordinary lord of session; and when the Union was effected, he was chosen one of the Sixteen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">Peers</a> for Scotland, in the first parliament of Great-Britain; and was constantly elected to every future parliament till his death, except the fourth. In 1710, he was made justice-general of Scotland. In 1711, he was called to the privy council; and upon the accession of George I, he was nominated lord <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of Scotland. When the rebellion broke out in 1715, he again betook himself to arms, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the house of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, and by his prudent conduct in the West Highlands, he prevented General Gordon at the head of three thousand men, from penetrating into the country and raising levies. He afterwards joined his brother at Stirling, and was wounded at the battle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUMBARTON">Dumbarton</a>. In 1725, he was appointed keeper of the privy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; and from this time, he was entrusted with the management of Scottish affairs. In 1734, upon his resigning the privy seal, he was made keeper of the great seal, which office he enjoyed till his death. Upon the decease of his brother, he became Campbell, duke of Argyle, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> justice-general, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARGYLESHIRE">Argyleshire</a> and the Western Isles, hereditary great master of the household, hereditary keeper of Dunstaffnage, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRICK">Carrick</a>, and several other castles. He was also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the university of Aberdeen; and laboured to promote the interest of that, as well as of the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Scotland. He particularly encouraged the school of physic at Edinburgh, which has now acquired so high a reputation. Having the chief management of Scotch affairs, he was also extremely attentive to promote the trade, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and improvements of his country. It was by his advice that, after the rebellion in 1745, the Highlanders were employed in the royal army. He was a man of great endowments both natural and acquired, well versed in the laws of his country, and possessed considerable parliamentary abilities. He was likewise eminent for his skill in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, had great talents for conversation, and had collected one of the most valuable private <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> in Great Britain. He built himself a very magnificent seat at Inverary. The faculties of his mind continued found and vigorous till his death, which happened suddenly on the 15th of April 1761, in the 90th year of his age. He was married, but had no issue; and was succeeded in his titles and the estates of the family by John Campbell, fourth duke of Argyle, son of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> John Campbell of Mammor, who was the second son of Archibald the ninth earl of Argyle. The family of Argyle was heritable justice generals for Scotland till abolished by the jurisdiction act. They are still heritable masters of the king's household in Scotland, and keepers of Dunstaffnage and Carrick. Campbell, John, an eminent historical, biographical, and political writer, was born at Edinburgh, March 8, 1727-8. His father, Robert Campbell of Glenlyon, Esq.; was captain of horse in a regiment commanded by the then earl of Hyndford; and his mother, Elizabeth, daughter of ——Smith, Esq.; of Windfor in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, had the honour of claiming a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from the poet Waller. Our author, their fourth son, was at the age of five years carried from Scotland to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, where he received the first principles of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; and at a proper age, he was placed out as clerk to an attorney, being intended for the law. This profession, however, he never followed; but by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> application to the acquisition of knowledge of various kinds, became qualified to appear with great advantage in the literary world. In 1736, before he had completed his 30th year, he gave to the public, in two volumes folio, "The Military <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Prince Eugene and the duke of Marlborough," enriched with maps, plans, and cuts. The reputation hence acquired, occasioned him soon after to be solicited to take a part in the "Ancient Universal History." Whilst employed in this capital <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, Mr Campbell found leisure to entertain the world with other productions. In 1739, he published the "Travels and Adventures of Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>, Esq;" 8vo. In the same year appeared his "<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Balhaw Duke de Ripperda," 8vo, reprinted, with improvements, in 1740. These memoirs were followed, Campbell followed, in 1741, by the "Concise History of Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>," 8vo. In 1742, he was the author of "A Letter to a Friend in the Country, on the Publication of Thurlow's State Papers; giving an account of their discovery, importance, and utility." The same year was distinguished by the appearance of the 1st and 2d volumes of his "Lives of the English Admirals, and other eminent British Seamen." The two remaining volumes were completed in 1744; and the whole, not long after, was translated into German. This was the first of Mr Campbell's works to which he prefixed his name; and it is a performance of great and acknowledged merit. In 1743, he published "Herminius revived;" a second edition of which, much improved and enlarged, came out in 1749, under the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>: "Herminius Redivivus: or, the Sage's Triumph over Old Age and the Grave. Wherein a method is laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> for prolonging the life and vigour of man. Including a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> upon an ancient Inscription, in which this great secret is revealed; supported by numerous authorities. The whole interspersed with a great variety of remarkable and well-attested relations." This extraordinary tract had its origin in a foreign publication; but it was wrought up to perfection by the additional ingenuity and learning of Mr Campbell. In 1744 he gave to the public, in two volumes folio, his "Voyages and Travels," on Dr Harris's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, being a very distinguished improvement of that collection which had appeared in 1735. The time and care employed by Mr Campbell in this important undertaking did not prevent his engaging in another great work, the "Biographia Britannica," which began to be published in weekly numbers in 1745, and extended to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> volumes folio; but our author's articles were only in the first four volumes; of which Dr Kippis observes, they constitute the prime merit. When the late Mr Dodfey formed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of "The Preceptor," which appeared in 1748, Mr Campbell was to assist in the undertaking; and the parts written by him were the Introduction to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, and the Discourse on Trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, both of which displayed an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of knowledge upon these subjects. In 1750 he published the first separate edition of his "Present State of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>;" a work which had been originally begun in 1746, in the "<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>," a very valuable periodical performance, printed for Dodfey. There is no production of our author's that hath met with a better reception. It has gone through six editions, and fully deserved this encouragement. The next great undertaking which called for the exertion of our author's abilities and learning, was "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> Universal History." This extensive work was published, from time to time, in detached parts, till it amounted to 16 volumes folio; and a second edition of it, in 8vo, began to make its appearance in 1759. The parts of it written by Mr Campbell were, the histories of the Portuguese, Dutch, Spanish, French, Swedish, Danish, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSTEND">Ostend</a> Settlements in the East-Indies; and the Histories of the Kingdoms of Spain, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, Algarve, Navarre, and that of France, from Clovis to 1656. As our author had thus distinguished himself in the literary world, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of LL.D. was very properly and honourably conferred upon him, June 18, 1754, by the university of Glasgow. His principal and favourite work was, "A political Survey of Great Britain," 2 vol. 4to, published a short time before his death; in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his knowledge, and his patriotic spirit, are equally conspicuous. Dr Campbell's reputation was not confined to his own country, but extended to the remotest parts of Europe. As a striking instance of this, it may be mentioned, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1774, the empress of Russia was pleased to honour him with the present of her <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, drawn in the robes worn in that country in the days of John Basilowicz, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> duke of Muscovy, who was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Queen Elizabeth. To manifest the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of her imperial majesty's goodneds, a set of the "Political Survey of Britain," bound in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, highly ornamented, and accompanied with a letter descriptive of the triumphs and felicities of her reign, was forwarded to St Petersburg, and conveyed into her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> by Prince Orloff, who had resided some months in this kingdom. Dr Campbell in 1736 married Elizabeth, daughter of Benjamin Vobe, of Leominster, in the county of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, with whom he lived nearly 40 years in the greatest conjugal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. So wholly did he dedicate his time to books, that he seldom went abroad: but to relieve himself as much as possible from the inconveniences incident to a sedentary life, it was his custom, when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> would admit, to walk in his garden; or otherwise in some room of his house, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. By this method, united with the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> in eating, and an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> in drinking, he enjoyed a good state of health, though his constitution was delicate. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> manner of living did not preclude him from a very extensive and honourable acquaintance. His house, especially on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> evening, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of the most distinguished persons of all ranks, and particularly of such as had rendered themselves eminent by their knowledge or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of literature. He received foreigners, who were fond of learning, with an affability and kindness which excited in them the highest respect and veneration; and his instructive and cheerful conversation made him the delight of his friends in general. He was, during the latter part of his life, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> for the province of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> in North America; and died at the close of the year 1775, in the 67th year of his age. The doctor's literary knowledge was by no means confined to the subjects on which he more particularly treated as an author; he was well acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and had read much in medicine. It hath been with great reason believed, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had dedicated his studies to this last science, he would have made a very conspicuous figure in the medical profession. He was eminently versed in the different parts of sacred literature; and his acquaintance with the languages extended not only to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Greek and Latin among the ancient, and to the French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, and Dutch, among the modern; but likewise to the Oriental tongues. He was particularly fond of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. His attainment of such a variety of knowledge was exceedingly assisted by a memory surprisingly retentive, and which indeed afforded Campbell, wished every person with whom he was conversant. In communicating his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, he had an uncommon readiness and facility; and the style of his works, which had been formed upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of that of the celebrated Bishop Sprat, was perspicuous, easy, flowing, and harmonious. To all these accomplishments of the understanding, Dr Campbell joined the more important virtues of a moral and pious character. His disposition was gentle and humane, and his manners kind and obliging. He was the tenderest of husbands, a most indulgent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, a kind master, a firm and sincere friend. To his great Creator he paid the constant and ardent tribute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, duty, and reverence; and in his correspondences he showed that a sense of piety was always nearest his heart. Campbell, George, D.D. was born at Aberdeen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1719. He was educated at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school in the same town, and intended for the employment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIGNET">signet</a>-writer, an occupation similar to that of an English attorney, in which he was bound an apprentice. The love of study, however, prevailed over every opposition: in 1741 he attended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> lectures at Edinburgh before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a> was fully completed, and soon after became a regular student in the university of Aberdeen, attending the lectures of Professor Lumiden in King's, and Professor Chalmers in Marischal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. In 1746 he was licensed to preach by the presbytery of Aberdeen. In 1748 he obtained the living of Banchory Ternan, in which situation he became a married man, and was fortunate in possessing a lady "remarkable for the sagacity of her understanding, the integrity of her heart, the general propriety of her conduct, and her skill in the management of domestic economy." Mutual happiness was the consequence of this union, which was not terminated till her death in 1792. In 1757 he was translated to Aberdeen, to be one of the ministers of that town, and in 1759 was presented to the office of principal of Marischal college. Mr Hume's Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a> gave the new principal an opportunity of evincing that he was not unworthy of his office. He opposed it in a sermon preached before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> of Aberdeen, in 1762, which he was requested to publish; but he preferred the form of a dissertation, and in that state sent the manuscript to Dr Blair, to be by him communicated to the metaphysician.
