CANEPHORIA is also the name of a festival in honour of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, celebrated particularly by the Athenians, on which the young maids carried <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> baskets full of fruit, which baskets were covered, to conceal the mystery from the uninformed.

CANES

Pages 144-145

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and other eastern countries, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> sort of buildings for the reception of strangers and travellers. People are accommodated in these with a room at a small price, but with no other necessaries; so that, excepting the room, there are no greater accommodations in these houses than in the deserts, only that there is a market near. CANES Venatici, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the Greyhounds, two new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>, first established by Hevelius, between the tail of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Bear and Bootes's arms, above the Coma Berenices. The first is called asterion, being that next the Bear's tail; the other chara. They comprehend <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANETO">Caneto</a> comprehend 23 stars, of which Tycho only observed two. The longitudes and latitudes of each are given by Hevelius. In the British Catalogue they are:

CANETO

Pages 145-145

a strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, seated on the river Oglio, which was taken by the Imperialists in 1701, by the French in 1702, afterwards by the Imperialists, and then by the French in 1705. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 45'. N. Lat. 40° 55'.

CANGA

Pages 145-145

in the Chinese affairs, a wooden clog borne on the neck, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> offences. The canga is composed of two pieces of wood notched, to receive the criminal's neck; the load lies on his shoulders, and is more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less heavy according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of his offence. Some cangas weigh 200lb; the generality from 50 to 60. The mandarins condemn to the punishment of the canga. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">Sentence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is sometimes changed for this kind of punishment.

CANGE

Pages 145-145
Charles du Fresne, Sieur du, one of the most learned writers of his time, was born at Amiens in 1601, and studied at the Jesuits college in that city. Afterwards he applied himself to the study of the law at Orleans, and gained great reputation by his works; among which are, 1. The history of the empire of Constantinople under the French emperors. 2. John Cinnamus's six books of the history of the affairs of John and Manuel Comnenus, in Greek and Latin, with historical and philological notes. 3. Glos- sarium ad Scriptores medie et infimae Latinitatis.

CANGI

Pages 145-145

Čangi, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cangani, anciently a people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, concerning whose situations antiquaries have been much perplexed. They are all the same people. Camden discovered some traces of them in many different and distant places, as in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, and Cheshire; and he might have found as plain vestiges of them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, Wiltshire, &c. Mr Horley and others are no less perplexed and undetermined in their opinions on this subject. But Mr Baxter seems to have discovered the true cause of all this perplexity, by observing that the Cangi or Ceangi were not a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, seated in one particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but such of the youth of many different nations as were employed in pasturage, in feeding the flocks and herds of their respective tribes. Almost all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> nations of Britain had their ceangi, their patoritia pubes, the keepers of their flocks and herds, who ranged about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers, as they were invited by the season and plenty of pasture for their cattle. This is the reason that vestiges of their name are to be found in so many different parts of Britain; but chiefly in those parts which are most fit for pasturage. These ceangi of the different British nations, naturally brave, and rendered still more hardy by their way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, were constantly armed for the protection of their flocks from wild beasts; and these arms they occasionally employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of their country and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>.

CANGIAGIO

Pages 145-145
or Cambiaso, Ludovico, one of the most eminent of the Genoese painters, was born in 1327. His works at Genoa are very numerous; and he was employed by the king of Spain to adorn part of the Escorial. It is remarked of him, that he was not only a most expeditious and rapid painter, but also that he worked equally well with both hands; and by that unusual power he executed more designs, and finished more grand works with his own pencils, in a much shorter time, than most other artists could do with several assistants. He died in 1685. In the royal collection at Paris there is a Sleeping Cupid, as large as life, and likewise Judith with her attendant, which are painted by Cangiagio, and are an honour to that master. And in the Pembroke collection at Wilton is a picture, reputed the work of Cangiagio, representing Christ bearing his cross.

CANICULA

Pages 145-145

is a name proper to one of the stars of the constellation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANIS">canis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, called also simply the dog <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>; by the Greeks μεγάλος, Sirius, Canicula is the tenth in order in the Britannic catalogue; in Tycho's and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s it is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. It is situated in the mouth of the constellation; and is of the first magnitude, being the largest and brightest of all the stars in the heavens. From the rising of this star not comically, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, but heliacally, that is, its emergence from the sun's rays, which now happens about the 15th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of August, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> reckoned their dies canicularis, or dog days. The Egyptians and Ethiopians began their year at the rising of the Canicula, reckoning to its rise again the next year, which is called the annus canarius, or canicular year. This year consisted ordinarily of 365 days, and every fourth year of 366, by which it was accommodated to the civil year. The reason of their choice of the Canicula before the other stars to compute their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by, was not only the superior brightness of that star, but because its heliacal rising was in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> a time of singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, as falling on the greatest augmentation of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, the reputed father of Egypt. Ephestion adds, that from the aspect and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of Canicula, the Egyptians drew prognostics concerning the rise of the Nile; and, according to Florus, predicted the future state of the year; so that the first rising of this star was annually observed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>.

CANICULUM

Pages 145-145
or CANICULUS, in the Byzantine antiquities, a golden standish or ink vessel, decorated with precious stones, wherein was kept the sacred encylium, or red ink, wherewith the emperors signed their decrees, letters, &c. The word is by some derived from canis, or caniculus; alluding to the figure of a dog which it represented, or rather because it was supported by the figures of dogs. The caniculum was under the care of a particular officer of state.

CANINA

Pages 145-145

the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Epirus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, which now belongs to the Turks, and lies off the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is of the same name, and is seated on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Chimera. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19° 25'. N. Lat. 40° 55'.

CANINANA

Pages 145-145

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and esteemed one of the least poisonous kinds. It grows to about two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and is green on the back, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> on the belly. It feeds on eggs and small birds; the natives cut off the head and tail, and eat the body as a delicate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a>.

CANINE

Pages 145-147

whatever partakes of, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> has any relation to, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, of a dog. Canine Appetite, amounts to much the same with Bulimy. Canine Madness. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Canine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">Teeth</a>, are two sharp-edged teeth in each jaw; one on each side, placed between the incisors and molars. Canini, John Angelo and Marc Anthony, brothers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, celebrated for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of antiquities. John excelled in designs for engraving on <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, particularly heads; Marc engraved them. They were encouraged by Colbert to publish a succession of heads of the heroes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men of antiquity, designed from medals, antique stones, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> remains; but John died at Rome soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was begun: Marc Anthony, however, procured assistance, finished and published it in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in 1666. The cuts of this edition were engraved by Canini, Picard, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALET">Valet</a>; and a curious explanation is given, which discovers the skill of the Caninis in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>. The French edition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, in 1731, is spurious. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANIS">Canis</a>, or dog. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index. Canis <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>, the Great Dog, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the southern hemisphere, below <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORION">Orion</a>'s feet, though somewhat to the westward of him; whose stars <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> makes 29; Tycho observed only 13; Hevelius 21; in the Britannic catalogue they are 31. Canis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, the Little Dog, in Astronomy, a constellation of the northern hemisphere; called also by the Greeks, Procyon, and by the Latins Antecoris and Canicula. The stars in the constellation Canis Minor, are in Ptolemy's catalogue, 2; in Tycho's, 5; in Hevelius's, 13; and in the British catalogue, 14. Canisius, Henry, a native of Nimeguen, and one of the most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was professor of canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> at Ingolstadt; and wrote a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. Summa Juris Canonici. 2. Antiqua Lectiones, a very valuable work. He died in 1609. Canitz, the baron of, a German poet and statesman, was of an ancient and illustrious family in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> in 1654, five months after his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. After his early studies, he travelled to France, Italy, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and England; and upon his return to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with important negotiations by Frederic II. Frederic III. employed him also. Canitz united the statesman with the poet; and was conversant in many languages, dead as well as living. His German poems were published for the tenth time, 1750, in 8vo. He is said to have taken Horace for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, and to have written purely and delicately. But he did not content himself with barely cultivating the fine arts in himself; he gave all the encouragement he could to them in others. He died at Berlin, in 1699, privy counsellor of state, aged 45. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANKER">Canker</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> incident to trees, proceeding chiefly from the nature of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. It makes the bark rot and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the canker be in a bough, cut it off; in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bough, at some distance from the stem; in a small one, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to it: but for over hot strong ground, the ground is to be cooled about the roots with pond mud and cow dung. Canker, among farriers. See Farriery Index. Canna, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> reed. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Cannabis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">Hemp</a>. See Botany Index. From the leaves of hemp pounded and boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the natives of the East Indies prepare an intoxicating liquor of which they are very fond. The plant, when fresh, has a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> narcotic smell; the water in which the stalks are soaked, in order to separate the tough rind for mechanic uses, is said to be violently poisonous, and to produce its effects almost as soon as drunk. The seeds also have some smell of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is unctuous and sweetish; they are recommended, boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, or triturated with water into an emulsion, against coughs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of urine, and the like. They are also said to be useful in inconvenience of urine, and for restraining venereal appetites; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> does not warrant their having any virtues of that kind. Cannae, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Apulia on the Adriatic, at the mouth of the river Aufidus, rendered famous by a terrible overthrow which the Romans here received from the Carthaginians under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>. The Roman consuls Æmilius Paulus and Terentius Varro, being authorized by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> to quit the defensive <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and stake the fortunes of the republic on the chance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, marched from Canium, and encamped a few miles east, in two unequal divisions, with the Aufidus between them. In this position they meant to wait for an opportunity of engaging to advantage; but Hannibal, whose critical situation in a desolated country, without refuge or allies, could admit of no delay, found means to inflame the vanity of Varro by some trivial advantages in skirmishes between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. The Roman, elated with this success, determined to bring matters to a speedy conclusion; but, finding the ground on the south side too confined for the operations of so large an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, crossed the river; and Varro, raising his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> wing upon the Aufidus, drew out his forces in the plain. Hannibal, whose head <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> were at Cannæ, no sooner perceived the enemy in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, than he forded the water below, and marshalled his troops in a line opposite to that of his adversaries. The Romans were vastly superior in number to the Carthaginians; but the latter were superior in cavalry. The army of the former, consisting of 87,000 men, was drawn up in the usual manner; the hastati in the first line, the principes in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and the triarii in the third. The cavalry were posted on the wings. On the right, the Roman knights flanked the legionaries; on the left, the cavalry of the allies covered their own infantry. The two consuls commanded the two wings, Æmilius the right, and Terentius the left; and the two proconsuls, Servilius and Attilius, the main body. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Hannibal, whose army consisted of 40,000 foot and 10,000 horse, placed his Gaulish and Spanish cavalry in his left wing, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> the Roman knights; and the Numidian horse in his right, over against the cavalry of the allies of Rome. As to his infantry, he divided the African battalions into two bodies; one of which he posted near the Gaulish and Spanish horse, the other near the Numidian. Between these two bodies were placed on one side the Gaulish, on the other the Spanish infantry, drawn up in such a manner as to form an obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> projecting a considerable way beyond the two wings. Behind this line he drew up a second which had no projection. Adrûbal commanded the left wing; Maharbal the right; and Hannibal himself, with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGO">Mago</a>, Mago, the main body. He had also taken care to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> himself in such a manner, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> Vulturum, which rises at certain stated times, should blow directly in the faces of the Romans during the fight, and cover them with dust. The onset was begun by the light-armed infantry; the Romans discharging their javelins, and the balistes their stones, with pretty equal success; nevertheless, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> Æmilius was wounded. —Then the Roman cavalry in the right wing advanced against the Gaulish and Spanish in Hannibal's left. As they were thus in by the river Ausidus on one side, and by their infantry on the other, they did not fight, as usual, by charging and wheeling off, and then returning to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> fighting each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> against his adversary, till one of them was killed or retired. After they had made prodigious efforts on both sides to overbear each other, they all on a sudden dismounted, and fought on foot with great fury. In this attack the Gauls and Spaniards soon prevailed; put the Romans to the rout; and, pursuing them along the river, strewed the ground with their dead bodies, Afdubal giving no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> was scarce over, when the infantry on both sides advanced. The Romans first fell upon the Spaniards and Gauls, who, as already observed, formed a kind of triangle projecting beyond the two wings. These gave ground, and, pursuant to Hannibal's directions, sunk into the void space in their rear; by which means they infensibly brought the Romans into the centre of the African infantry, and then the fugitives rallying, attacked them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, while the Africans charged them in both flanks. The Romans being, by this artful retreat drawn into the snare and surrounded, no longer kept their ranks, but formed several platoons in order to face every way. Æmilius, who was on the right wing, seeing the danger of the main body, at the head of his legionaries acted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> both of a folder and general, penetrating into the heart of the enemy's battalions, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> great numbers of them in pieces. All the Roman cavalry that were left, attended the brave consul on foot; and, encouraged by his example, fought like men in despair. But, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, Afdubal, at the head of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of Gaulish and Spanish infantry brought from the centre, attacked Æmilius's legionaries with such fury, that they were forced to give ground and fly: the consul being all covered with wounds, was at last killed by some of the enemy who did not know him. In the main body, the Romans, though invested on all sides, continued to fall their lives dear; fighting in platoons, and making a great slaughter of the enemy. But being at length overpowered, and disheartened by the death of the two proconsuls, Servilius and Attilius, who headed them, they dispersed and fled, some to the right, and others to the left, as they could find opportunity; but the Numidian horse cut most of them in pieces: the whole plain was covered with heaps of dead bodies, in such manner that Hannibal himself, thinking the butchery too terrible, ordered his men to put a stop to it.—There is a great disagreement among authors as to the number of Romans killed and taken at the battle of Cannæ. According to Livy, the republic lost 50,000 men, including the auxiliaries. According to Polybius, of 6000 Roman horse, only 70 escaped to Venaufa with Terentius Varro, and 300 of the auxiliary horse. As to the infantry, that writer tells us, that 70,000 of the Roman foot died on the field of battle fighting like brave men; and that 13,000 were made prisoners. According to Dionysius of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>, of 6000 horse, only 370 escaped the general slaughter, and of 82,000 foot, 3000 only were left. The most moderate computation makes the number of Romans killed to amount to 45,000. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of action is marked out to posterity, by the name of Pezzo di Sangue, "Field of Blood." These plains have more than once, since the Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, afforded room for men to accomplish their mutual destruction. Melo of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, after raising the standard of revolt against the Greek emperors, and defeating their generals in several engagements, was at last routed here in 1019, by the Catapan Bolanus. Out of 250 Norman adventurers, the flower of Melo's army, only ten escaped the slaughter of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. In 1201, the archbishop of Palermo and his rebellious associates, who had taken advantage of the nonage of Frederick of Swabia, were cut to pieces at Cannæ by Walter de Brienne, sent by the Pope to defend the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s dominions. The traces of the town of Cannæ are very faint, consisting of fragments of altars, cornices, gates, walls, vaults, and under-ground granaries. It was destroyed the year before the battle: but being rebuilt, became an episcopal see in the infancy of Christianity. It was again ruined in the fifth century, but seems to have subsisted in a humble state many ages later; for we read of its contending with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARLETTA">Barletta</a> for the territory, which till then had been enjoyed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> by them; and in 1284, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. issued an edict for dividing the lands, to prevent all future litigation. The prosperity of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, which increased in wealth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> by embarkations for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUSADES">crusades</a> and by traffic, proved the annihilation of the great inland cities; and Cannæ was probably abandoned entirely before the end of the thirteenth century. CANNÉQUINS, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> cotton cloths brought from the East Indies. They are a proper commodity for trading on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, particularly about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a>. These linens are folded <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>-wise, and are about eight ells <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. CANNEL COAL. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index.

CANNES

Pages 147-147

a town of France, in Provence, and in the viguerie of Grasse, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, with a harbour and a castle. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 7. N. Lat. 43. 34.

CANNIBAL

Pages 147-147

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> for an anthropophagus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>-eater, more especially in the West Indies. See Anthropophagi.

CANNON

Pages 147-152

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> engine for throwing balls, &c., by the help of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">Gunpowder</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> cannon is by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">Lance</a> ascribed to J. Owen: he says, that they were first known in England in the year 1335; but yet acknowledges, that, in 1346, there were four pieces of cannon in the English <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESSY">Cressy</a>, and that these were the first that were known in France. And Mezeray relates, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward, by five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six pieces of cannon, struck terror into the French army, it being the first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they had seen any of these thundering Cannoning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>; though others affirm that cannon were known also in France at the same time; but that the French king, in his hurry to attack the English, and in confidence of victory, left all his cannon behind him as useless encumbrances (See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">Artillery</a>). The Germans carry the invention farther back, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> it to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBERTUS_MAGNUS">Albertus Magnus</a>, a Dominican monk, about the year 1250. Voetius rejects all these opinions, and finds cannon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> almost 1700 years ago. According to him, they were mounted by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Kitey in the year of Christ 85. For further particulars of their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, &c. see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">Gun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>. For the casting of cannon, see Foundry. For their different parts, proportions, management, operation, and effects, see Gunnery. Cannon, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> founders and printers, the name of the largest size of letters they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Cannonade, the application of artillery to the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of its efforts against some distant object intended to be seized or destroyed, as a ship, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, or fortress. See Gunnery. Since a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ship of war may be considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of floating batteries, it is evident that the efforts of her artillery must be greatly superior to those of a fortress on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; that is to say, in general; because, on some particular occasions, her situation may be extremely dangerous, and her cannonading ineffectual. Her superiority consists in several circumstances, as the power of bringing her different batteries to converge to one point; of shifting the line of her attack so as to do the greatest possible execution against the enemy, or to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> where she <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the least exposed to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>; and chiefly because, by employing a much greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cannon against a fort than it can possibly return, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of her artillery against <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> walls soon becomes decisive and irresistible. Besides these advantages in the attack, she is also greatly superior in point of defense: because the cannon shot, passing with rapidity through her sides seldom do any execution out of the line of their flight, or occasion much mischief by their splinters; whereas they very soon shatter and destroy the faces of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, and produce incredible havoc among the men by the fragments of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, &c. A ship may also retreat when she finds it too dangerous to remain longer exposed to the enemy's fire, or when her own fire cannot produce the desired effect. Finally, the fluctuating situation of a ship, and of the element on which she rests, renders the effects of bombs very uncertain, and altogether destroys the effect of the ricochet, or rolling and bounding shot, which is so pernicious and destructive in a fortress or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> engagement. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> inconvenience to which a ship is exposed, on the contrary, is, that the low-laid cannon in a fort near the brink of the sea, may strike her repeatedly on or under the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, so as to sink her before her cannonade can have any considerable efficacy. Canoe, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in Negroland, with a town of the same name. It is bounded by Zaara on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a> on the south, the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGADES">Agades</a> on the west, and that of Calima on the east. Some of the inhabitants are herdmen, and others till the ground and dwell in villages. It produces corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and cotton. Here are also many deserts, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> covered with woods, in which are wild citrons and lemon trees. The walls and houses of the town are made of clay, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. 18. N. Lat. 21. 5. Canobia, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, seated on the western <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of Lago Maggiore, or the Greater Lake. E. Long. 8. 47. N. Lat. 45. 55. Canoe, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> or vessel, formed of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of a tree hollowed, and sometimes of several pieces of the bark put together. Canoes are of various sizes, according to the uses for which they may be designed, or the countries wherein they are formed. The largest are made of the cotton tree; some of them will carry between 20 and 30 hogheads of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> or molasses. Some are made to carry sail; and for this purpose are steeped in water till they become pliant; after which their sides are extended, and strong beams placed between them, on which a deck is afterwards laid that serves to support their sides. The other sorts very rarely carry sail, unless when going before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>: their sails are made of a sort of short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> gafs or ruffs. They are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> rowed with paddles, which are pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> wood somewhat resembling a corn shovel; and, instead of rowing with it horizontally like an oar, they manage it perpendicularly. The small canoes are very narrow, having only room for one person in breadth, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight lengthwise. The rowers, who are generally American savages, are very expert in managing their paddles uniformly, and in balancing the canoes with their bodies; which would be difficult for a stranger to do, how well accustomed forever to the conducting of European boats, because the canoes are extremely light, and liable to be overturned. The American Indians, when they are under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of landing to avoid a water <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, or of crossing the land from one river to another, carry their canoes on their heads, till they arrive at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where they can launch them again. This is the general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of canoes, and method of managing them: but some nations have vessels going under the name of canoes, which differ considerably from the above; as the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's <a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, Otaheite, &c. Canon, a person who possesses a prebend, or revenue allotted for the performance of divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, or collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Canons are of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity: Pachier observes, that the name canon was not known before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>; at least the first we hear of are in Gregory de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>, who mentions a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of canons instituted by Baldwin XVI. archbishop of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, in the time of Clotharius I. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> attributes the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of this order to Chrodegangus, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a>, about the middle of the eighth century. Originally canons were only priests, or inferior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, who lived in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>; residing by the cathedral church, to assist the bishop; depending entirely on his will; supported by the revenues of the bishopric; and living in the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, as his domestics, or counsellors, &c. They even inherited his moveables, till the year 817, when this was prohibited by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle, and a new rule substituted Canons situated in the place of that which had been appointed by Chrodegangus, and which was observed for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the west till the 12th century. By degrees, these communities of priests, shaking off their dependence, formed separate bodies; whereof the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, however, were still heads. In the tenth century, there were communities or congregations of the same kind, established even in cities where there were no bishops: these were called collegiates, as they used the terms <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> and college indifferently: the name <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, now given to these bodies, being much more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. Under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of the French kings, the canonical, or collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, had spread itself all over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and each cathedral had its chapter, distinct from the rest of the clergy. They had the name canon from the Greek κανών, which signifies three different things; a rule, a pension or fixed revenue to live on, and a catalogue or matricula; all which are applicable to them. In time, the canons freed themselves from their rules, the observance relaxed, and, at length, they ceased to live in community: yet they still formed bodies; pretending to other functions besides the celebration of the common office in the church; yet assuming the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the rest of the clergy: making themselves as a necessary council of the bishop; taking upon them the administration of a fee during a vacancy, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of a bishop to supply it. There are even some chapters exempt from the jurisdiction of the bishop, and owning no head but their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>. After the example of cathedral chapters, collegiate ones also <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to form bodies, after they had abandoned living in community. Canons are of various kinds; as, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Canons, which are those attached, and, as the Latins call it, incardinati to a church, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> is to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>. Domiciliary Canons, were young canons, who not being in orders, had no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> in any particular chapters. Expectative Canons, were such as, without having any revenue or prebend, had the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> and dignities of canons, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the chapter, and a place in the choir; till such time as a prebend should fall. Foreign Canons, were such as did not officiate in the canonries to which they belonged. To these were opposed manorial canons, or canons residentiary. Lay or honorary Canons, are such among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> as have been admitted, out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and respect, into some chapter of canons. Regular Canons, are canons that still live in community; and who, like <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, have, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, to the practice of their rules, added the solemn profession of vows. They are called regulars, to distinguish them from those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> canons who abandon living in community, and at the same time the observance of the canons made as the rule of the clergy, for the maintenance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>. The canons subsisted in their simplicity till the eleventh, some say the twelfth century, when some of them, separating from the community, took with them the name of canons, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACEPHALOUS">acephalous</a> priests, because they declined to live in community with the bishop; and those who were left thenceforth acquired the denomination of canons regular, and adopted most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> of the rule of St Augustine. This order of regular canons of St Augustine was brought into England by Adelwald, confessor to Henry I., who erected a priory at Nottel in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>; and obtained for them the church of Carlisle as an episcopal see, with the privilege of choosing their own bishop. They were singularly protected and encouraged by Henry I., who gave them the priory of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUNSTABLE">Dunstable</a> in 1107; and by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Maud, who, in the following year, gave them the priory of the Holy Trinity in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It appears, that under the reign of Edward I., they had fifty-three priories. Tertiary Canons, those who had only the third part of the revenues of the canonicate. Canon, in an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> or rule, either of doctrine or discipline, enacted especially by a council, and confirmed by the authority of the sovereign. Canons are properly decisions of matters of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; or regulations of the policy and discipline of a church, made by councils, either general, national, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a>. Such are the canons of the council of Nice, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, &c. There have been various collections of the canons of the eastern councils; but four principal ones, each ampler than the preceding. The first, according to Usher, A.D. 380, containing only those of the first ecumenical council, and the first provincial ones: they were but 164 in number. To these, Dionysius Exiguus, in the year 520, added the 50 canons of the apostles, and those of the other general councils. The Greek canons in this second collection end with those of the council of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHALCEDON">Chalcedon</a>; to which are subjoined those of the council of Sardica, and the African councils. The fourth and last collection comes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as low as the second council of Nice; and it is on this that Ballamon and Zonaras have commented. Apostolical Canons, are those which have been usually ascribed to St Clement. Bellarmine, Baronius, &c. will have them to be genuine canons of the apostles: Cotelerius observes, that they cannot be ascribed to the apostles or Clement, because they are not received with other books of Scripture, are not quoted by the writers of the first ages, and contain many things not agreeable to the apostolical times: Hincmar, De Marca, Beveridge, &c. take them to be framed by the bishops who were the apostles disciples in the second or third century; S. Balsagre is of opinion, that they were collected by an anonymous writer in the fifth century; but Daille, &c. maintain them to have been forged by some heretic in the sixth century; and S. Balnage conjectures, that some of them are ancient, and others not older than the seventh century. The Greek church allows only 85 of them, and the Latins only 50; though there are 84 in the edition given of them in the Corpus Juris Canonici. Canon is also used for the authorized catalogue of the sacred writings. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>. The ancient canon, or catalogue of the books of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, was made by the Jews, and is ordinarily attributed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a>; who is said to have distributed them into the law, the prophets, and the hagiographa, to which our Saviour refers, Luke, chap. xxiv. ver. 44. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is also mentioned by Josephus, cont. Appion. This is the canon allowed to have been followed by the primitive church, till the council of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>; and, according to St Jerome, this consisted of no more than 22 books; answering to the number of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>; though at present they are divided into 24 divisions, containing <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEUTERONOMY">Deuteronomy</a>, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Isaiah, Jeremiah, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>, the twelve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> prophets, the Psalms, the Proverbs, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>, Canticles, Ruth, Lamentations, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTES">Ecclesiastes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTHER">Esther</a>, Daniel, Ezra, comprehending the book of Nehemiah and the Chronicles. However, this order is not universally observed either among Jews or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; nor were all the books above enumerated admitted into the canon in Ezra's time. It is most likely, says Dr Prideaux, that the two books of Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACHI">Malachi</a>, were added in the time of Simon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">Just</a>, when the canon was completed. But that council enlarged the canon very considerably, taking into it the books which we call apocryphal: which the council of Trent has further enforced, enjoining all these to be received as books of Holy Scripture, upon pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a>, and being attainted of hereby. The Romanists, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of this canon, say, that it is the same with that of the council of Hippo, held in 393; and with that of the third council of Carthage, in 397, at which were present 46 bishops, and, among the rest, St Augustine; who declared that they received it from their fathers. Their canon of the New Testament perfectly agrees with ours. It consists of books that are well known; some of which have been universally acknowledged; such are the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, thirteen Epistles of St Paul, one Epistle of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, and one Epistle of St John; and others, concerning which doubts were entertained, but which were afterwards received as genuine; such are the epistle to the Hebrews, that of James, the second of Peter, the second and third of John, that of Jude, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a>. These books were written at different times; and they are authenticated, not by the decrees of councils, or infallible authority, but by such kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> as is thought sufficient in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of any other ancient writings. They were very extensively diffused; they were read in every Christian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; they were valued and preserved with care by the first Christians; they were cited by Christian writers of the second, third, and fourth century, as by Irenaeus, Clement the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a>, Tertullian, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, Eusebius, &c., and their genuineness is proved by the testimony of those who were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with the apostles themselves, and by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>. The four Gospels, and most of the other books of the New Testament, were collected either by one of the apostles, or some of their disciples and successors, before the end of the first century. The catalogue of canonical books furnished by the more ancient Christian writers, as Origen about the year 215, Eusebius and Athanasius in 315, Epiphanius in 370, Jerome in 382, Aelfin in 394, and many others, agrees with that which is now received among Christians. For the time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the several books of the New Testament, see the titles of the books themselves; as the Gospel of St Matthew, Mark, &c. Some of the fathers distinguish the inspired writings into three classes; proto-canonical, deutero-canonical, and apocryphal. Pafchal Canon, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the moveable feasts, showing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of Easter, and the other feasts depending on it, for a cycle of 19 years. The pafchal canon is supposed to be the calculation of Eusebius of Caesarea, and to have been done by order of the council of Nice. Canon, in monastic orders, a book wherein the religious of every convent have a fair transcript of the rules of their order, frequently read among them as their local statutes. This is also called regula, as containing the rule and institution of their order. The canon differs from the missale, martyrologium, and necrologium. Canon, again, is used for the catalogue of saints acknowledged and canonized in the Roman church. Canon is also used, by way of excellence, in the Romish church, for the secret words of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the Pater; in the middle of which the priest consecrates the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a>. The common opinion is, that the canon of the mass commences with Te igitur, &c. The people are to be on their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, hearing the canon; and are to rehearse it to themselves, so as not to be heard. Canon, in the ancient music, is a rule or method of determining the intervals of notes. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, rejecting the Aristoxenian way of measuring the intervals in music, by the magnitude of a tone (which was supposed to be formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between a diapente and a diatessaron), thought that musical intervals should be distinguished, according to the ratios or proportions which the sounds terminating those intervals bear to one another, when considered according to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of acuteness or gravity; which, before Aristoxenus, was the old Pythagorean way. He therefore made the diapason consist in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> ratio; the diapente, in a sesquialterate; the diatessaron, in a sesquitertian; and the tone itself, in a sesqui <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a>; and all the other intervals, according to the proportion of the sounds that terminate them; wherefore taking the canon (as it is called) for a determinate line of any length, he shows how this canon is to be cut accordingly, so that it may represent the respective intervals: and this method answers exactly to experiment, in the different lengths of musical chords. From this canon, Ptolemy and his followers have been called Canonici; as those of Aristoxenus were called Musici. Canon, in modern music, is a kind of fugue, which they call a perpetual fugue, because the different parts beginning one after another, repeat incessantly the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Formerly, says Zarlino, they placed, at the head of perpetual fugues, particular directions which showed how this kind of fugues was to be sung; and these directions being properly the rules by which perpetual fugues were composed were called canoni, rules or canons. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, others taking the title for the thing signified, by a metonymy, termed this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> canon. Such canons as are composed with the greatest facility, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> most generally used, begin the fugue either with the octave or the unison; that is to say, that every part repeats in the same tone the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> of the preceding. In order to form form a canon of this kind, it is only necessary for the composer to make an air according to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; to add in score as many parts as he chooses, where the voices in octave or uniform repeat the same melody; then forming a single air from all these parts successively executed, to try whether this succession may form an entire piece which will give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, as well in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> as the melody. In order to execute such a canon, he who sings the first part begins alone, and continues till the air is finished; then recommences immediately, without any suspension of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> or interruption of time; as soon as he has ended the first couplet, which ought to serve for the perpetual subject upon which the whole canon has been composed, the second part begins and repeats the same couplet, whilst the first who had begun pursues the second; others in succession begin, and proceed the same way, as soon as he who precedes has reached the end of the first couplet. Thus, by incessantly recommencing, an universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> can never be found, and the canon may be repeated as long as the fingers please. A perpetual fugue may likewise consist of parts which begin with the intervals of a fourth or fifth; or, in other words, every part may repeat the melody of the first, a fourth or a fifth higher or lower. It is then necessary that the whole canon should be invented di prima intensione, as the Italians say; and that sharps or flats should be added to the notes, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> gradations do not answer exactly, by a fourth or fifth, to the melody of the preceding part, and produce the same intervals with itself. Here the composer cannot pay the least regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>; his only care is, that the melody may be the same, which renders the formation of a canon more difficult; for at every time when any part resumes the fugue, it takes a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>; it changes the tone almost at every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, and what is still worse, no part is at the same time found in the same tone with another; hence it is that this kind of canons, in other respects far from being easy to be performed, never produces a pleasing effect, however good the harmony may be, and however properly it may be sung. There is a third kind of canon, but very scarce, as well because it is extremely difficult, as because it is for the most part incapable of giving pleasure, and can boast no other merit but the pains which have been thrown away in its composition. This may be called a double canon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, as well by the inversions which are practised in it with respect to the melody of the parts, as by those which are found among the parts themselves in fingering. There is such an artifice in this kind of canon, that, whether the parts be sung in their natural order, or whether the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in which they are set be turned the contrary way, to sing them backward from the end to the beginning, in such a manner that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a> becomes the upper part, and the rest undergo a similar change, still you have pretty harmony, and still a regular canon. The reader may consult Rouffleau's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> in this article, where he is referred to Plate D. fig. 11. for two examples of canons of this sort extracted from Bontempi, who likewise gives rules for their composition. But he adds, that the true principle from which this rule is deduced will be found at the word Sylteme, in his account of the system of Tartini, to which we must likewise once more refer the reader; as a quotation of such length must have protracted our article to an enormous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. To form a canon in which the harmony may be a little varied, it is necessary that the parts should not follow each other in a succession too rapid, and that the one should only begin a considerable time after the other. When they follow one another so immediately as at the distance of a semibreve or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIM">minim</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> is not sufficient to admit a great number of chords, and the canon must of necessity exhibit a disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONOTONY">monotony</a>; but it is a method of composing, without much difficulty, a canon in as many parts as the composer chooses. For a canon of four bars only, will consist of eight parts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they follow each other at the distance of half a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>; and by each bar which is added, two parts will constantly be gained. The emperor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VI. who was a great musician, and composed extremely well, took much pleasure in composing and fingering canons. Italy is still replete with most beautiful canons composed for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, by the best masters in that country. To what has been said by Rouffleau, we need only subjoin, that the English catch and the Italian canon are much the same; as any intelligent reader may perceive, from comparing the structure and execution of the English catch with the account of canons which has now been given. Canon, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, a general rule for the solution of all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of a like <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with the present inquiry. Thus every last step of an equation is a canon; and, if turned into words, becomes a rule to solve all questions of the same nature with that proposed. Canon Law, a collection of ecclesiastical laws, serving as the rule and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of church <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. The power of making laws was exercised by the church before the Roman empire became Christian. The canon law that obtained throughout the west, till the 12th century, was the collection of canons made by Dionysius Exiguus in 520, the capitularies of Charlemagne, and the decrees of the popes from Siricius to Anastasius. The canon law, even when papal authority was at its height in England, was of no force when it was found to contradict the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of the king, the laws, statutes and customs of the realm, or the doctrine of the established church. The ecclesiastical jurisdiction of the see of Rome in England was founded on the canon law; and this created quarrels between kings and several archbishops and prelates who adhered to the papal usurpation. Besides the foreign canons, there were several laws and constitutions made here for the government of the church; but all these received their force from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> assent; and if, at any time, the ecclesiastical courts did, by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, endeavour to enforce obedience to such canons, the courts at common law, upon complaints made, would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> prohibition. The authority vested in the church of England of making canons, was ascertained by a statute of Henry VIII., commonly called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the clergy's submission; by which they acknowledged, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> had always been assembled by the king's writ; so that though the power of making canons resided in the clergy met in convocation, their force was derived from the authority of the king's assent to and confirming them. The old canons continued in full force till the reign of James I. when the clergy being assembled in convocation, the king gave them leave to treat and consult upon canons; which they did, and presented them to the king, who gave them the royal assent: these were a collection out of the several preceding canons and injunctions. Some of these canons are now obsolete. In the reign of Charles I. several canons were passed by the clergy in convocation.

CANONESS

Pages 152-152

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a woman who enjoys a prebend, affixed, by the foundation, to maids, without their being obliged to renounce the world <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> make any vows.

CANONICA

Pages 152-152

in philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an appellation given by Epicurus to his doctrine of logic. It was called canonica, as consisting of a few canons <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rules for directing the understanding in the pursuit and knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. Epicurus's canonica is represented as a very slight and insufficient logic by several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, who put a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> value on his ethics and physics. Laertius even affirms us, that the Epicureans rejected logic as a superfluous science; and Plutarch complains that Epicurus made an unskillful and powerless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of syllogisms. But these censures seem too severe. Epicurus was not adverse to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of logic, but even gave better rules in this art than those philosophers who aimed at no <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> but that of logics. He only seems to have rejected the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALECTICS">dialectics</a> of the Stoics, as full of vain subtleties and deceits, and fitted rather for parade and disputation than real use. The stricts of Epicurus's canonica consist in his doctrine of the criteria of truth. All questions in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> are either concerning words or things: concerning things, we seek their truth; concerning words, their signification: things are either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or moral; and the former are either perceived by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> or by the understanding. Hence, according to Epicurus arise three criterions of truth, viz., sense, anticipation or prevision, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. The great canon or principle of Epicurus's logic is, that the senses are never deceived; and therefore, that every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> or perception of an appearance is true.

CANONICAL

Pages 152-152

something that belongs to, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> partakes of, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a rule or canon. CANONICAL Hours, are certain stated times of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, confirmed, more especially by the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, to the offices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. Such are matins, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUDS">lauds</a>, sixth, ninth vespers. In our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> the canonical hours are from eight to twelve in the forenoon, before or after which <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> cannot be legally performed in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church. CANONICAL Obedience, is that submission which, by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> laws, the inferior clergy are to pay to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> to their superiors. CANONICAL Sins, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> church, those which were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> or mortal. Such especially were idolatry, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, and schism. CANONICAL Punishments, are those which the church may inflict; such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> in Roman Catholic countries, also fasting, alms, whipping, &c. CANONICAL <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, the method or rule of living prescribed by the ancient clergy who lived in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. The canonical life was a kind of medium between the monastic and clerical lives. Originally the orders of monks and clerks were entirely distinct; but pious persons, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, instituted colleges of priests and canons, where clerks brought up for the ministry, as well as others already engaged therein, might live under a fixed rule, which, though somewhat more easy than the monastic, was yet more restrained than the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a>. This was called the canonical life, and those who embraced it canons. Authors are divided about the founder of the canonical life. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it to be founded by the apostles; others ascribe it to Pope Urban I. about the year 1250, who is said to have ordered bishops to provide such of their clergy as were willing to live in community, with necessaries out of the revenues of their churches. The generality attributes it to St Augustine; who, having gathered a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of clerks to devote themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, instituted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> within the episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, where he lived in community with them. Onuphrius Paninius brings the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> somewhat lower; according to him, Pope Gelasius I. about the year 495, placed the first regular canons of St Augustine in the Lateran church. CANONICAL Letters, in the ancient church, were a sort of testimonials of the orthodox <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, which the bishops and clergy sent each other to keep up the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, and distinguish orthodox <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a> and other heretics. They were denominated canonical, either as being composed according to a certain rule or form, or because they were given to the canonic, that is, those comprehended in the canon or catalogue of their church. When they had occasion to travel into other dioceses or countries, dimissory and recommendatory letters, also letters of peace, &c. were so many <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of canonical letters. CANONICAL is also an appellation given to those epistles in the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> more frequently called catholic or general epistles.

CANONICUM

Pages 152-152

is more particularly used in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> for a fee paid by the clergy to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, archbishops, and metropolitans, for degrees and promotions.

CANONICUM ALSO

Pages 152-152

M also denotes a due of first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, paid by the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to Du Cange, to their priests. The canonicum is assessed according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of houses or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Comnenus made a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> for regulating the canonicum of bishops, which was confirmed by another made in 1086, by his nephew <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXIS">Alexis</a> Comnenus. A village containing thirty fires, was to pay for its canonicum one piece of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, two of silver, one sheep, six bushels of barley, six of wheat flour, six <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of wine, and thirty hens.

CANONIST

Pages 152-152

a person skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> who makes profession of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and practice of the canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Canonists and civilians are usually combined in the same persons; and hence the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> juris utriusque, or legum doctor, usually expressed in abbreviation, L. L. D. or J. U. D.

CANONIZATION

Pages 152-153

CANONIZATION, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> in the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, by which persons deceased are ranked in the catalogue of the saints. It succeeds beatification. Before a beatified person is canonized, the qualifications of the candidate are strictly examined into, in some consultories held for that purpose; after which, one of the consultory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a>, in the presence of the pope and cardinals, makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> of the person who is to be proclaimed a saint, and gives a particular detail of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>: which done, the holy father decrees his canonization, and appoints the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. On the day of canonization the pope officiates in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and their eminences are drest in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s church is hung with rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, upon which the arms of the pope, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> state requiring the canonization, are embroidered in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver. An infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lights blaze all round the church, which is crowded with pious souls, who wait with devout impatience till the new saint has made his public entry as it were into paradise, that they may offer up their petitions to him without danger of being rejected. The following maxim with regard to canonization is now observed, though it has not been followed above a century, viz. not to enter into the inquiries <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to canonization, till 50 years, at least, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the person to be canonized.
