By the ceremony of canonization, it appears that this rite of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> has something in it very like the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a> or deification of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Romans, and, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, takes its rise from it; at least several ceremonies of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> are conspicuous in both.

CANONRY

Pages 153-153

the benefice filled by a canon. It differs from a prebend, in that the prebend may subsist without the canonicate; whereas the canonicate is inseparable from the prebend: again, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of suffrages, and other privileges, are annexed to the canonicate, and not to the prebend.

CANOPUS

Pages 153-153

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of the first magnitude in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a> of Argo, a constellation of the southern hemisphere. Canopus, in Pagan <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, one of the deities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians, and according to some, the god of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is said, that the Chaldeans, who worshipped fire, carried their fancied deity through other countries to try its powers, in order that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it obtained the victory over the other gods, it might be acknowledged as the true object of worship; and it having easily subdued the gods of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, brafs, silver, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, its priests declared that all gods did it homage. This the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Canopus hearing, and finding that the Chaldeans had brought their god to contend with Canopus, they took a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> earthen vessel, in which they bored several holes, which they afterwards stoppered with wax, and having filled the vessel with water, painted it of several colours, and fitting the head of an idol to it, brought it out, in order to contend with the Chaldean deity. The Chaldeans accordingly kindled their fire all around it; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> having melted the wax, the water gushed out through the holes, and extinguished the fire; and thus Canopus conquered the god of the Chaldeans. Canopus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Canobus, according to Strabo, had been Menelaus's pilot, and had a temple erected to him in a town called Canopus, near one of the mouths of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. Dionysius mentions it: καὶ τοῦτο περιέχει Ἀμυκλαῖον ἐκ Κανοποῦς. There stands Canopus' temple known to fame: The pilot who from fair Amycla came. Vossius remarks on this occasion, the vanity of the Greeks, who, as he conjectures, hearing of an Egyptian deity named Canopus, took from thence an opportunity of deifying the pilot of Menelaus who bore the same name, and giving out that the Egyptian god Canopus had been a Greek. F. Monfaucon gives several representations of this deity. One, in allusion to the victory above-mentioned, throws out water on every side through little holes. Canopus, or Canobus, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, on the Mediterranean, a hundred and twenty stadia, or fifteen miles, to the east of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>; as old as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, Canopus, or Canobus, Menelaus's steersman, being there buried. Canopaei the gentilissimus name; famous for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and debauchery, (Strabo, Juvenal.) See Aboukir.

CANOPY

Pages 153-153

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a>, a magnificent kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a>, serving to cover and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> an altar, throne, tribunal, pulpit, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like. The word is formed from the barbarous Latin canopum, of κανωπία, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> spread over a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> to keep off the gnats, from κανωψ, a gnat. Canopies are also borne over the head in processions of state, after the manner of umbrellas. The canopy of an altar is more peculiarly called ciborium. The Roman grandees had their canopies, or spread veils, called theriza, over their chairs: the like were also in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the gods. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> cardinals still retain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of canopies.

CANOSA

Pages 153-154

a town of Puglia in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, occupying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the site of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANUSIUM">Canusium</a>. The old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> was founded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>, according to Strabo. It afterwards became a Roman colony, and one of the most considerable cities of this part of Italy for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, and magnificence in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. The era of Trajan seems to have been that of its greatest splendour: but this pomp only served to mark it as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> object for the avarice and fury of the Barbarians. Genleric, Totila, and Autharis, treated it with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> cruelty. The deplorable fate to which this Swinburne's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> was reduced in 590 is concisely but strongly Travels in painted by Gregory the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> in these terms: "On <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, every side we hear groans; on every side we behold page 408 crowds of mourners, cities burnt, castles razed to the ground, countries laid waste, provinces become deserts, some citizens led away captives, and others inhumanly massacred." No town in Puglia suffered more than Canosa from the outrages of the Saracens; the contests between the Greeks and Normans increased the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of its woes, which was filled by a conflagration that happened when it was stormed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> Robert. In 1095, it was assigned, by agreement, to Bohemund <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Antioch, who died here in 1117. Under the reign of Ferdinand the Third, this estate belonged to the Grimaldis. On their forfeiture, the Affaiti acquired it, and still retain the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of marquis, though the Capeci are the proprietors of the fief. The ancient city stood in a plain between the hills and the river Ofanto, and covered a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tract of ground. Many brick monuments, though degraded and stripped of their marble casing, still attest its ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. Among them may be traced the fragments of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>, tombs, amphitheaters, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> columns, and two triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, which, by their position, seem to have been two city gates. The present town stands above, on the foundations of the old citadel, and is a most pitiful remnant of so great a city, not containing above three hundred houses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Sabinus, built, as is said, in the fifth century, is now without the enclosure. It is astonishing, that any part of this ancient <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> should have withstood so many calamities. Its altars and pavements are rich in marble; and in a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> adjoining, under an octagonal cupola, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> of Boilemund, adorned in a minute Gothic style.

CANSO

Pages 154-154

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of Acadia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-NOVA_SCOTIA">Nova Scotia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, seated on a narrow strait which separates Nova Scotia from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Breton. Near this town is a fine fishery for cod. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 62° N. Lat. 46°.

CANSTAT

Pages 154-154

a town of Swabia, in Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Würtemberg, situated on the river Neckar, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 9' N. Lat. 48° 51'.

CANT

Pages 154-154

a quaint affected manner of speaking, adapted chiefly to the lower sort. Skinner racks his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> for the origin of this word; which he successively deduces from the German, Flemish, and Saxon tongues. According to the general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, Cant is originally the proper name of a Cameronian preacher in Scotland, who by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> had attained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of talking in the pulpit in such a tone and dialect as was understood by none but his own <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>: since Andrew Cant's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the word has been extended to signify all sudden exclamations, and whining unmusical tones, especially in praying and preaching. But this origin of the word has been disputed by others; and perhaps the true derivation is from the Latin cantare "to sing." Cant is also applied to words and phrases affected by particular persons <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> for low ends, and not authorized by the established <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between cant and technical seems to be this: the former is restrained to words introduced out of folly, affectation, or imposition; the latter is applied to such as are introduced for the sake of clearness, precision, and significance. Cant is also used to denote a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> by auction. The origin of the word in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> is dubious; it may come, according to some, from quantum, how much; according to others, from cantare, to sing or cry aloud; agreeably to which, we sometimes also call it an outcry. Cant Timbers, in ship-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, those timbers which are situated at the two ends of a ship. They derive their name from being canted, or raised obliquely from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> from those whose planes are perpendicular to it. The upper ends of those on the bow, or fore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship, are inclined to the stern; as those in the after or hind part, incline to the stern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> above. See Ship-Building.

CANTABRIA

Pages 154-154

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a district of Tarraconensis, on the Oceanus Cantabricus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>; now Biscay. The inhabitants were famous for their warlike character. In conjunction with the Asturians, they carried on desperate wars with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; but were subdued by them about 25 years before Christ. Being impatient, however, of a foreign yoke, they in a few years revolted. Most of their youth had been already taken prisoners by the Romans, and sold for slaves to the neighbouring nations: but having found means to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> their chains, they cut the throats of their masters; and returning into their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, attacked the Roman garrisons with incredible fury. Agrippa marched against them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> expedition; but on his arrival, met with so vigorous a resistance, that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> began to despair of ever being able to reduce them. As the Cantabrians had waged <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Romans for upwards of 200 years, they were well acquainted with their manner of fighting, no way inferior to them in courage, and were now become desperate; well knowing, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were conquered, after having so often attempted to recover their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, they must expect the most severe usage, and cruel <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. Animated with this reflection, they fell upon the Romans with a fury hardly to be expressed, routed them in several engagements, and defended themselves when attacked by the enemy with such intrepidity, that Agrippa afterwards owned, that he had never, either by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, been engaged in a more dangerous enterprise. That brave commander was obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> entreaties, menaces, and to brand some of his legionaries with ignominy, before he could bring them to enter the lists with such a formidable enemy. But having at last, with much ado, prevailed upon them to try the chance of an engagement in the open field, he so animated them by his example, that, after a most obstinate dispute, he gained a complete victory, which indeed cost him dear, but put an end to that destructive war. All the Cantabrians fit to bear arms were cut in pieces; their castles and strongholds taken and razed; and their women, children, and old men (none else being left alive), were obliged to abandon the mountainous places, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in the plain. Dr Wallis seems to make the Cantabrian the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; which, according to him, like the Gaulish, gave way to a kind of broken Latin called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> or romanía; which by degrees was refined into the Castilian or present Spanish. But we can hardly suppose, that so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a country, inhabited by such a variety of people, spoke all the same language. The ancient Cantabrian, in effect, is still found to subsist in the more barren and mountainous parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Biscay, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a>, and Navarre, as far as Bayonne, much as the British does in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>; but the people only talk it: for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, they use either the Spanish or French, as they happen to live under the one or the other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> this to a jealousy of foreigners learning the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of their language; others to a poverty of words and expressions. The Cantabrian does not appear to have any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with any other known language, abating that some Spanish words have been adopted in it for things whose use the Biscayans were anciently unacquainted with. Its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> is not disagreeable. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, in the Cantabrian tongue, runs thus: Gure aita cerveian aienea, santifica bedi hire icena, etor ledi hire refuna, eguin

CANTABRUM

Pages 155-155

in Antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> used by the Roman emperors, distinguished by its peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> on it some words <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> motto of good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>, to encourage the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>.

CANTACUZENUS

Pages 155-155

Johannes, of Constantinople, a celebrated statesman, general, and historian, was born in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family. He was bred to letters and to arms, and admitted to the highest offices of the state. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Andronicus loaded him with wealth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>; made him <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERALISSIMO">generalissimo</a> of his forces; and was desirous of having him join him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, but this he refused. Andronicus dying in 1341, left to Cantacuzenus the care of the empire, till his son John Paleologus, who was then but <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, should be fit to take it upon himself. This trust he faithfully discharged; till the empress dowager and her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> forming a party against him, declared him a traitor. On this the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> befell him to ascend the throne; and accordingly he was crowned on the 21st of May 1342. This was followed by a civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, which lasted five years; when he admitted John a partner with him in the empire, and their union was confirmed by his giving him his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Suspicions and enmities however, soon arising, the war broke out again, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till John took Constantinople in 1355. A few days after, Cantacuzenus, unwilling to continue the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of blood, abdicated his share of the empire, and retiring to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a monk, and the name of Joasaphos. His wife also retired to a nunnery, and changed her name of Irene for that of Eugenia. In this retirement he lived till the year 1411, when he was upwards of 100 years of age. Here he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his own times, a Latin translation of which, from the Greek manuscript, was published by Pontanus at Ingolstadt, in 1603; and a splendid edition was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1645, in three volumes folio, of the original Greek, and Pontanus's Latin version. He also wrote an apology for the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> against that of Mahomet, under the name of Chriplodulus.

CANTALIVERS

Pages 155-155

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, pieces of wood framed into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sides of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, to suspend the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a> and eyes over it.

CANTAR

Pages 155-155
or Cantaro, an eastern weight, of different value in different places, equal at Acra in Turkey to 603 pounds, at Tunis and Tripoli to 114 pounds. Cantaro is also an Egyptian weight, which is denominated a quintal, and consists of a hundred or of an hundred and fifty rotolos, according to the goods they are to weigh. Cantaro is also an Egyptian weight, which at Naples is equivalent to 25 pounds, at Genoa to 150 pounds. At Leghorn there are three kinds of cantaros, one weighing 150 pounds, another 151, and a third 160 pounds. Cantaro is also a Spanish liquid measure, in use especially at Alicante, containing three gallons. Cantaro is also a measure of capacity, used at Cochinchin, containing four rubis, the rubi 32 rotolos.

CANTARINI

Pages 155-155

Simon, a famous painter, called the Pejarete, from his being born at Pefaro, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Guido; and copied the manner of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> so happily, that it is often difficult to distinguish between their works. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a> in 1648.

CANTATA

Pages 155-155

in Music, a song <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, intermixed with recitatives, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, and different movements, chiefly intended for a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, with a thorough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>, though sometimes for other instruments. The cantata, when performed with judgment, has something in it very agreeable; the variety of the movement not clogging the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, like other compositions. It was first used in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, then in France, whence it passed to us.

CANTAZARO

Pages 155-155

an episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> Ulterior. It is the residence of the governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and is seated near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17°. N. Lat. 38°. 59'.

CANTECROIX

Pages 155-155

a small territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in Brabant, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality; there is a small town of the same name, but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIER">Lier</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>.

CANTEMIR

Pages 155-155

Demetrius, son of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a>. Disappointed by not succeeding his father in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, held under the Ottoman Porte, he went over with his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, against whom he had been sent by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Signior: he signalized himself in the czar's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; and in the republic of letters, by a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the origin and decline of the Ottoman empire, &c. He died in 1723. Cantemir, Antiochus, esteemed the founder of the Ruffian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, was the youngest son of the preceding. Under the most ingenious professors, whom the czar had invited to Petersburgh, he learned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, physic, history, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and polite literature; without neglecting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Holy Scriptures, to which he had a great inclination. Scarce had he finished his academic course, when he printed a Concordance of the Psalms in the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and was elected member of the academy. The affairs of state in which he was soon after engaged, did not make him neglect his literary pursuits. In order to make himself useful to his fellow citizens, he composed his satires, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> certain prejudices which had got footing among them. When but 24 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he was nominated minister at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; and his dexterity in the management of public affairs was as much admired as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for the sciences. He had the same reputation in France, whither he went in 1738, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of minister plenipotentiary, and soon after was invested with the character of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> extraordinary. The wife and prudent manner in which he conducted himself during the different revolutions which happened in Russia during his absence, gained him the confidence and esteem of three successive princes. He died of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in 1744, aged 44. Besides the pieces already mentioned, he wrote, 1. Some Fables and Odes. 2. A translation of Horace's Epistles in Ruffian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. 3. A profe

CANTERBURY

Pages 155-156

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of England, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 15. N. Lat. 51. 16. It had the names of Duravernum and Darvernium given it by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and Durobernia by Bede, which are thought to be derived from Dur-wbem, signifying a rapid stream, such as the Stour, on which it stands, is. The Britons call it Caer Kent, i.e. the city of Kent; and its present English name is of the same import, derived from the Saxon. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> writers in Latin call it Cantuaria. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity appears not only from Antoninus's Itinerary, but from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> way which has been discovered here, and the causeways leading to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> and Lymne, besides the coins and other curiosities found about it. The archiepiscopal and metropolitan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> seems to have been settled here very early; and to prevent its being removed, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a> was decreed against any who should attempt it. After that, the city flourished greatly; though it suffered in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> during the Danish invasions, and at other times by the casualties of fire. The city was given entirely to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> by William Rufus, and was held in the utmost veneration in the Popish times, especially after the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of Becket in the reign of Henry II. to whose shrine so great was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>, and to rich were the offerings, that Erasmus, who was an eye witness of its wealth, says the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and chapel in which he was interred glittered with jewels; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, the plate and jewels filled two great chests, each of which required eight strong men to carry out. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> was granted by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ETHELBERT">Ethelbert</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Kent, upon his conversion, to Austin the monk, together with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and the royalty of the city and its territories. This Austin founded a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> for monks, called from him Augustine. After the cathedral had been several times destroyed by fire and rebuilt, the present was begun about the year 1174, and augmented and embellished by the succeeding archbishops, till it was completed in the reign of Henry V. It is a noble Gothic pile, and before the Reformation had 37 altars. A great many kings, princes, cardinals, and archbishops, are buried in it. At the dissolution, Henry VIII. seized all the revenues both of the church and monastery, except what he allotted for the maintenance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, 12 prebendaries, and fix preachers, whom he established in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the monks. During the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> rebellion, it suffered much; the usurper Cromwell having made a stable of it for his dragoons. After the Restoration, it was repaired, and made what it now appears. Besides the cathedral and other churches, as well as a monastery, the city had anciently a castle on the south side, and strong walls, with towers, a ditch, and rampart; it had also a mint and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. As to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, it seems to have been entirely subject to the archbishop, both in spirituals and temporals; at least from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that William Rufus gave it solely to Bishop Anfelm, till the Reformation. It is now a county of itself: and the corporation consists of a mayor, recorder, 12 aldermen, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, 24 common councilmen, a mace-bearer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-bearer, and four sergeants-at-mace. Every Monday a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> is held at Guildhall Canterbury for civil and criminal causes; and every other Tuesday for the government of the city. Here were formerly 2000 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 3000 French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> manufacture; but this branch is now greatly decayed in the place, since Spitalfields became so flourishing. Besides the cathedral, it contains 15 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> churches, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, a free school, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of correction, a gaol for criminals, and sumptuous conduit for supplying the inhabitants with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It consists of four streets, disposed in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, and divided into six wards, which are about three miles in circumference. It is surrounded on all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> with hop grounds much to its advantage, and is famed for its excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Canterbury contains 257 parishes, besides chapels, in Kent, and about 100 more in other dioceses. These are called Peculiars; it being an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> privilege of this see, that wheresoever the archbishops had either manors or advowsons, the place was exempted from the jurisdiction of the ordinary of the diocese where it was situated, and was deemed in the diocese of Canterbury. This see is valued in the king's books at £216l. 17s. 9½d., but is reckoned to produce a clear revenue of £8000. a year. The clergy's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a> come to £611. 18s. 2½d. This see had many great privileges in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>, some of which it still retains. The archbishop is accounted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> and metropolitan of all England, and is the first peer in the realm; having the precedence of all dukes not of the blood <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, and of all the great officers of state. In common speech he is styled His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>, and he writes himself Divina Providentia; whereas other bishops style themselves Divina Permissione. At coronations, he places the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on the king's head; and, wherever the court may be, the king and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> are the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> parishioners of the archbishop of Canterbury. The bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> is accounted his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> dean, the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a> his subdean, the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, and the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> his chaplain. This see hath yielded to the church 18 saints; to the church of Rome, 9 cardinals; to the civil state of England, 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chancellors, 4 lord treasurers, and 1 lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; and 9 chancellors to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. To this see belongs only one archdeacon, viz. of Canterbury. To the cathedral belongs an archbishop, a dean, a chancellor, an archdeacon, 12 prebends, 6 preachers, 6 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> canons, 6 substitutes, 12 lay clerks, 10 choristers, 2 masters, 50 scholars, and 12 almshouses. CANTERBURY <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">Bell</a>, the English name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of CAMPANULA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CANTERUS

Pages 156-156

WILLIAM, an eminent linguist and philologer, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, in 1541. He studied at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; and gave surprising proofs of his progress in Greek and Latin literature. He afterwards visited the several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Germany and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and died at Louvain, in 1575, aged 33. He understood five languages, besides that of his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and, notwithstanding his dying so young, wrote several philological and critical works, among which are, Notæ, Scholæ, Emendationes, et Explicationes, in Euripidem, Sophoclem, Eschylem, Ciceronem, Propertium, Ausonium, &c. and many translations of Greek authors.

CANTHARIDES

Pages 156-157

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, flies which are employed to produce blisters on the skin.

CANTHARIS

Pages 157-157

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of insecta coleoptera. Linnaeus enumerates 27 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the cantharis, most of them to be found in different parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The cantharis used in making blistering plasters is ranked under the genus Meloe. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CANTHI

Pages 157-157

in Anatomy, cavities at the extremities of the eyelids, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the corners of the eye: the greater of them, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the greater canthus, is next the nose; the lesser of them, or the little canthus, lies towards the temple.

CANTICLES

Pages 157-157

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, otherwise called the Song of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>; by the Jews the Song of Songs, Canticum Canticorum. The book of Canticles is usually supposed to be an epistle written by Solomon, on occasion of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. But those who penetrate further into the mystery, find in it the marriage of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and good men. On this principle the Canticles is held to be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> allegory, wherein under the terms of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> wedding, a divine and spiritual marriage is expressed. This song contains the adventures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days and seven nights; the exact <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> allowed for the celebration of marriage among the Hebrews. The Jews themselves, apprehending the book liable to be understood in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and carnal manner, prohibited the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of it before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 30, and the same usage anciently obtained in the Christian church. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, Theodore Mopstactus rejected the book of Canticles as not divine. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">Divers</a> rabbins have also questioned its being written by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>. It is alleged, that the name of God is not once found in it. Mr Whiston has a discourse expressly to prove that the Canticles is not a sacred book of the Old Testament. He alleges it indeed to have been written by King Solomon the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>; but asserts that it was composed at the time when that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, blinded by his concubines, was sunk in lust and idolatry. This he chiefly infers from the general character of vanity and dissoluteness which reigns through the Canticles: in which there is not, according to Whiston, one thought that leads the mind towards <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, but all is worldly and carnal, to say no worse. For the mystic style, he affects it to be without foundation; and that the book is not cited as canonical by any writer before the destruction of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. Mr Whiston <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it to have been taken into the canon between the years 77 and 128, when allegories came into vogue, and the rabbins began to corrupt the text of Scripture. Grotius, Nierembergus, the Dutch divines who criticized F. Simon, Menetrier, Baphage, and some others, seem also to take the Canticles for a profane <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, on a footing with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> pieces of Catullus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ovid. But this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is refuted by Michaelis, Majus, Witsius, Nat. Alexander, Outrein, Francius, and others. Mr Whiston's arguments have been particularly considered by Itchenor, and also by Dr Gill. R. Akiba finds the book of Canticles more divine than the rest: the whole world, according to this rabbin, is not worth that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> when the Canticles was given to Israel; for, whereas all the hagiographers are holy, the Canticles is the holy of holies.

CANTIMARONS

Pages 157-157
or CATIMARONS, a kind of Cantimaroats or rafts, used by the inhabitants of the coast of Coromandel to go a fishing in, and to trade along the coast. They are made of three or four small canoes, or trunks of trees dug hollow, and tied together with cacao ropes, with a triangular sail in the middle, made of mats. The persons who manage them are almost half in the water, there being only a place in the middle a little raised to hold their merchandise: which last particular is only to be understood of the trading cantimarons, and not of those who go a-fishing.

CANTIN

Pages 157-157
CAPE, a promontory of the coast of Morocco in Africa, situated in W. Long. 10° 2' N. Lat. 33° 9'.

CANTING

Pages 157-157

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> phrase, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> anything about. Canting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Dialect, is a mysterious sort of jargon used by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GYPSIES">gypsies</a>, thieves, and strolling beggars, to express their sentiments to each other, without being understood by the rest of mankind. This dialect is not founded on any rules; yet even out of that irregularity many words seem to retain something of scholarship; as togeman, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, from toga in the Latin; pannam, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, from panis; cafan, cheese, from caseus, &c. It is observable, that, even unknown to ourselves, we have adopted some of their terms into our vulgar language; as bite and billk, to cheat; bounce, to vapour; bowfe, strong drink; fishb, to steal; flog, to whip; rig, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>; roaff, to rally; rhino, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. From the same source proceed the words sham, banter, bubble, bully, sharper, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>, shuffling, palming, &c. An anonymous author has given a canting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, comprehending all the terms used by the several tribes of gypsies, beggars, shoplifters, highwaymen, foot-pads, and other clans of cheats and villains, with a collection of songs in the canting dialect: <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1725, 8vo.

CANTIUM

Pages 157-158

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, literally denoting a headland: giving name to a territory called Cantium, now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>; and to a people called Cantii (Caesar), commended for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>. The promontory now the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Foreland. It is supposed that this was the first district in Britain which received a colony from the continent; and that it had frequently changed its masters, by new colonies coming over from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, and driving the inhabitants further north. In the midst of all these revolutions it still retained its ancient name (which was so agreeable to its shape and situation), and gave the same name to all the successive tribes by which it was inhabited. Those who politicised it at the time of the first Roman invasion were evidently of Belgic origin, and had come over so lately, that they differed in nothing from their countrymen on the continent. "The inhabitants of Kent (says Caesar) are the most civilized of all the Britons, and differ but very little in their manners from the Gauls." This great resemblance between the people of Kent and their neighbours on the continent, might be partly owing to the situation of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which being nearest to the continent, was most frequented by strangers from thence. It was this situation also which exposed them to the first assaults of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. For Caesar, in both his expeditions into this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, landed in Kent; and therefore we may conclude, that the Cantii had a great share in the vigorous opposition that was made to his landing, and in the several battles and skirmishes which were fought against him after his landing; particularly, they made a very bold, but unsuccessful attempt, upon his naval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. The Cantii did not make the same vigorous resistance to the Romans on their next invasion in the reign of Claudius. For Aulus Plautius, the Roman general in that expedition, traversed their country without seeing an enemy; and as they now submitted to the power of Rome without a struggle, so they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in a state of quiet submission to it to the very last. The situation of Cantium occasioned its being much frequented by the Romans, who generally took their way through it in their marches to and from the continent. Few places in Britain are more frequently mentioned by the Roman writers than Rutupium and Portus Rutupensis, most probably Richborough and Stonar. Rutupium was the name in those times that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> is in ours; the usual <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of embarking for, and landing from, the continent. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> departure of the Romans out of Britain, Portus Dubris, now Dover, had become a considerable place, and a well-frequented harbour, where the third iter of Antoninus ends, and from whence they often embarked for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>. Portus Lemanus, supposed to be Lime near West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-HYTHE">Hythe</a>, was also a noted seaport in these times, and the termination of the fourth iter of Antoninus. Du-robriæ and Durovernum, now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, were both Roman <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and stations, and are often mentioned in the Itinerary and other books. Besides these, there were several other Roman stations, towns, and ports in Cantium, which need not be particularly enumerated here. Cantium, in the most perfect state of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> which was called Flavia Caesariensis.

CANTO

Pages 158-158

denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a poem, answering to what is otherwise called a book. The word is Italian, where it properly signifies song. Tasso, Ariosto, and several other Italians, have divided their longer or heroic poems into cantos. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of them, Scarron has also divided his Gigantomachia, and Boileau his Lutrin, into chants or songs. The like usage has been adopted by some English writers, as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">Butler</a>, who divides his Hudibras, and Dr Garth's Dispensary, into cantos. A late translator of part of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s Æneid has even subdivided a book of Virgil into several cantos. Canto, in the Italian music, signifies a song; hence canto semplice is where all the notes or figures are equal, and called also canto <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FERMO">fermo</a>; canto figurato, that where the figures are unequal, and express different motions.

CANTO ALSO

Pages 158-158

o also signifies the treble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a song; hence <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTO">canto</a> concertante, the treble of the little chorus; canto ripieno, the treble of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> chorus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which sings only now and then in particular places. Canto signifies the first treble, unless some other word be added to it, as secondo; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> treble.

CANTON

Pages 158-161

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, denotes a small district <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> constituting a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; such are the cantons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. Canton, Quang-si, or Koanton, one of the southern provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east by Fukien, on the north by Kiang-si, on the west by Quang-si and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Tonking, and everywhere else by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The country is diversified with hills and plains, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general so fertile that it produces two crops annually. Besides many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in other parts of the Indies, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Canton produces some peculiar to itself. Abundance of valuable aromatic woods are also to be met with in this province, as well as eagle wood, ebony, &c., and in the mineral kingdom the province furnishes <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, tin, quicksilver, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">Silk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> are also cultivated here, and pearls are fished up on the coasts; so that everything which can contribute to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or convenience of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is to be met with in Canton. "One begins (says F. Piemare) to have an idea of China, on entering the river Canton. Both sides of it present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fields of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> which resemble green meadows, and extend beyond the reach of sight. They are intersected by an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, in such a manner that the barks which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> and repass in them seem at a distance, while the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which carries them is concealed, to glide along the groves. Farther inland the country appears covered with trees, and cultivated along the valleys; and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> is interspersed with villages, rural seats, and such a variety of delightful prospects, that one is never tired of viewing them, and regrets to be obliged to pass them so quickly. All the coasts of this province abound with fish, and furnish vast numbers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, oysters, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TORTOISES">tortoises</a> of an immense size. The inhabitants keep a prodigious number of tame ducks, which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCH">hatch</a> in ovens or dunghills, though it does not appear that they borrowed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> from the Egyptians. The docility of these creatures exceeds what we should be apt at first to imagine. The inhabitants load a number of small barks with them, and carry them in flocks to feed on the sea shore, where they find shrimps and other animals proper for their nourishment. But though the ducks from the different barks are thus unavoidably mixed together in the daytime, they are easily collected by only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASON">bason</a>, on which they immediately collect themselves into different flocks, and each returns to his proper bark. In this province the Chinese have also a method of preserving not only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of the ducks in such a manner that it loses nothing of its original flavour, but their eggs also. The latter operation is performed by covering the eggs with a coat of clay mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. When mixed in this manner, it seems that the salt has the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of penetrating through the pores of the shell, and thus impregnating the substance in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, which it could not do by simple solution in water. Canton, though it suffered much in the Chinese wars, is at present one of the most flourishing provinces of the empire; and being at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, its government is one of the most important. A great number of fortresses, many of which are cities, provided with numerous garrisons, have been built along the coasts for the suppression of pirates and robbers; for which purpose also a certain number of troops are kept properly posted in different parts of the province. It is divided into ten districts, which contain as many cities of the first class, and 84 of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> in general is warm but healthy, healthy, and the people are very industrious. They possess in an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>; so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are only shown any European <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, they can execute others like it with surprising exactness. The most remarkable cities in the province besides Canton the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> are, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAO_TCHEOU_FOU">Chao-tcheou-fou</a>, chiefly noted for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of bouzes in its neighbourhood, to which the adjacent country belongs, and the origin of which is traced back for 800 or 900 years. It has under its jurisdiction six cities of the third class; near one of these grows a reed of which several instruments are made, which cannot be distinguished from real ebony. The air of Chao-tcheou-fou, however, is unhealthy; and great numbers of the inhabitants are carried off annually by contagious distempers, which prevail from the middle of October to the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. 2. Kao-tcheou-fou, situated in a delightful and plentiful country. In the neighbourhood is found a singular kind of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> much resembling marble, on which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> representations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, landscapes, and trees. These stones are cut into slabs, and made into tables, &c. Crabs are also caught on the coasts here, which very much resemble those of Europe; but, says M. Grosier, they have this singularity, that when taken out of the water, they become petrified without losing any thing of their natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. 3. Kiun-tcheou-fou, the capital of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Hai-nan. See Hai-nan. Canton, a large, populous, and wealthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of China, capital of the province of that name, stands on the banks of the river Taa, or great river, which, near the city, is wide and spacious. The wall of the city is pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and about five or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles in circumference, though not more than one third of the ground is occupied by buildings, the other parts being appropriated to pleasure grounds or to fish ponds. The country is extremely pleasant, and towards the east hilly, so as to command a beautiful prospect of the city and suburbs, the compass of which, together, is about ten miles. The buildings of Canton are in general low, consisting of one story and a ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, which is covered with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> tiles in order to keep it cool; but the houses of the most respectable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and mandarins are comparatively lofty and well built. In different parts of the city and suburbs are joss houses or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, in which are placed the images worshipped by the Chinese; before whom are placed, at particular seasons, a vast variety of sweetmeats, oranges, great plenty of food ready dressed, and also incense, which is kept perpetually <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. The streets of Canton are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and narrow, paved with flat stones, adorned at intervals with triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, which have a pleasing effect, and much crowded with people. On both sides are shops as in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, appropriated to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of different commodities; and a kind of awning is extended from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to house, which prevents the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s rays from incommoding either inhabitants or passengers. At the end of every street is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>, which, with the gates of the city, are shut in the evening. In China street, which is pretty long and considerably wider than the rest, reside merchants; whose trade, so far as respects china, lacquered <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, fans, &c., is wholly confined to Europeans. Most of them speak the foreign languages tolerably well, or at least sufficiently intelligible to transact business. Besides these merchants, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of twelve or thirteen, called the Cohong; who have an exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> by appointment from authority to purchase the cargoes from the different ships, and also to supply them with teas, raw silks, &c., in return. The establishment of the Cohong, though injurious to private trade, is admirably well adapted for the security of the different companies with which they traffic; because each individual becomes a guarantee for the whole; so that if one fail, the others consider themselves as responsible. In Canton there are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>; all burdens are carried by porters across their shoulders on bamsos; as are also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> people in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">sedan</a> chairs, and the ladies always. The streets of Canton may be traversed from morning till evening without seeing a woman, those excepted who are Tartars, and even these but very seldom. On the wharf of the river, which is commodious and pleasant, stand the factories of the different European nations, viz. the Dutch, French, Swedes, Danes, English, &c. In those reside the supercargoes belonging to their respective companies, who are appointed to dispose of the cargoes brought to market; to supply the ships with others from Europe in return; and, during their absence, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> with the merchants for such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> as may be judged necessary for the next fleet. Between the residents of the factories the most perfect cordiality subsists; in each a common and splendid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> is kept at the company's expense, and visits are reciprocally exchanged; so that nothing is wanting to make residence at Canton agreeable to an European, but the pleasure naturally resulting from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of women. The side of the river next the city is covered with boats, which form a kind of town or streets, in which live the poorer sort of the Chinese, or rather the descendants of the Tartars. Some of the men come on shore in the morning to their respective employments, and in those sampans, or boats which are not <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>, the women and also the men carry passengers from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place in the same manner as is done by wherries on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. On this river live many thousand souls who never were permitted to come on shore; whose only habitation is their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>; in which they eat, drink, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, carry on many occupations, keep ducks, &c. and occasionally a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOG">hog</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of Canton are principally carried on in the suburbs; though it has been frequently supposed that they were confined to the city; and this, by some writers, has been given as a reason why Europeans are not permitted to enter within the gates. But this is a mistake; and perhaps the true reason for this very singular restraint is, that the houses in which they keep their women are chiefly within the city. At Wampoa, a large commodious place for anchorage, and which is about 12 or 14 miles from Canton, the European vessels <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> and unload their cargoes, which are transmitted by lighters to the factories; and by the same conveyance receive their respective freights. Between this place and the city are three hoppo, or customhouses, at which the boats passing and repassing are obliged to stop, and undergo with their passengers an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, in order to prevent smuggling. The lighters <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, and also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>'s pinnace, are, however, excepted; the former having proper officers on board for the purpose, and the latter being narrowly watched and examined at the landing. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> at Canton is, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, extremely hot; and in the months of December, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, and February, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>: the country is nevertheless pleasant and healthful, abounding with all the necessaries and delicacies of life, which may be procured on terms much cheaper than in Europe. The number of inhabitants has been estimated at one million; but later calculations have made the number considerably less. N. Lat. 23° 30' E. Long. 113° 20'. Canton, John, an ingenious natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was born at Stroud, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, in 1718; and was placed, when young, under the care of a Mr Davis, of the same place, a very able mathematician, with whom, before he had attained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years, he had gone through both vulgar and decimal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>. He then proceeded to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and particularly to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, wherein he had made a considerable progress, when his father took him from school, and put him to learn his own business, which was that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> cloth weaver. This circumstance was not able to damp his zeal for the acquisition of knowledge. All his leisure <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was devoted to the assiduous cultivation of astronomical science; and, by the help of the Caroline tables annexed to "Wing's Astronomy," he computed eclipses of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> and other phenomena. His acquaintance with that science he applied likewise to the constructing of several kinds of dials. But the studies of our young philosopher being frequently pursued to very late hours, his father, fearing that they would injure his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, forbade him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> in his chamber any longer than for the purpose of going to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and would himself often see that his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a> was obeyed. The son's thirst of knowledge was, however, so great, that it made him attempt to evade the prohibition, and to find means of secreting his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> till the family had retired to rest; when he rose to prosecute undisturbed his favourite pursuits. It was during this prohibition, and at these hours, that he computed, and cut upon stone, with no better an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> than a common <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of a large upright sun <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAL">dial</a>, on which, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, was shown the rising of the sun, his place in the ecliptic, and some other particulars. When this was finished, and made known to his father, he permitted it to be placed before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of his house, where it excited the admiration of several gentlemen in the neighbourhood, and introduced young Mr Canton to their acquaintance, which was followed by the offer of the use of their <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>. In the library of one of these gentlemen, he found "Martin's Philosophical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>," which was the first book that gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In the possession of another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, a few miles from Stroud, he first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of globes; an object that afforded him uncommon pleasure, from the great ease with which he could solve those problems he had hitherto been accustomed to compute. The dial was beautified a few years ago at the expense of the gentlemen at Stroud, several of whom had been his schoolfellows, and who <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> still to regard it as a very distinguished performance. Among other persons with whom he became acquainted in early life, was the late reverend and ingenious Dr Henry Miles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOOTING">Tooting</a>, a learned and respectable member of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> society, and of approved eminence in natural knowledge. This gentleman perceiving that Mr Canton possessed abilities too promising to be confined within the narrow limits of a country town, prevailed on his father to permit him to come to London. Accordingly he arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 4, 1737, and resided with Dr Miles at Tooting till the 6th of May following; when he articled himself for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of five years, as a clerk to Mr Samuel Watkins, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the academy in Spital-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. In this situation, his ingenuity, diligence, and good conduct, were so well displayed, that on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of his clerkship in May 1742, he was taken into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with Mr Watkins for three years; which gentleman afterwards succeeded in Spital-square, and there continued during his whole life. In 1744, he married Penelope, the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Mr Thomas Colbrooke, and niece to James Colbrooke, Esq., banker in London. Towards the end of 1745, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, which seems early to have engaged Mr Canton's notice, received a very capital improvement by the discovery of the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> Phial. This event turned the thoughts of most of the philosophers of Europe to that branch of natural philosophy; and our author, who was one of the first to repeat and to pursue the experiment, found his fidelity and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> rewarded by many capital discoveries. Towards the end of 1749, he was concerned with his friend, the late Mr Benjamin Robins, in making experiments in order to determine what height rockets may be made to ascend, and at what distance their light may be seen. In 1750 was read at the Royal Society Mr Canton's "Method of making <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> magnets, without the use of, and yet far superior to, any natural ones." This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> procured him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being elected a member of the society, and the present of their gold medal. The same year he was complimented with the degree of M.A. by the university of Aberdeen; and, in 1751, was chosen one of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the Royal Society. In 1752, our philosopher was so fortunate as to be the first person in England, who, by attracting the electric fire from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> during a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> storm, verified Dr Franklin's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of the similarity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> and electricity. Next year, his paper entitled, "Electrical Experiments, with an attempt to account for their several Phenomena," was read at the Royal Society. In the same paper Mr Canton mentioned his having discovered, by a great number of experiments, that some clouds were in a positive, and some in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, state of electricity. Dr Franklin, much about the same time, made the like discovery in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. This circumstance, together with our author's constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s hypothesis, induced that excellent philosopher, immediately on his arrival in England, to pay Mr Canton a visit, and gave rise to a friendship which ever after continued without interruption or diminution. In the "Lady's Diary, for 1756," our author answered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> question that had been proposed in the preceding year. The question Canton was, "How can what we call the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> of stars be best accounted for; what is the substance of this phenomenon; and in what state of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> doth it most frequently show itself?"
