The solution, though anonymous, was so satisfactory to his friend, Mr Thomas Simpkin, who then conducted that work, that he sent Mr Canton the prize, accompanied with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, in which he said, he was sure that he was not mistaken in the author of it, as no one besides, that he knew of, could have answered the question. Our philosopher's next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> to the public, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> in the "Gentleman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>," for September 1759, on the electrical properties of the telemalin, in which the laws of that wonderful stone are laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in a very concise and elegant manner. On December 12th, in the same year, was read at the Royal Society, "An attempt to account for the regular diurnal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">Horizontal</a> Magnetic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">Needle</a>; and also for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> variation at the time of an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> Borealis." A complete year's observations of the diurnal variations of the needle are annexed to the paper. On Nov. 5, 1761, our author communicated to the Royal Society an account of the Transit of Venus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 6, 1761, observed in Spital-square. Mr Canton's next communication to the Society, was a letter addressed to Dr Benjamin Franklin, and read Feb. 4, 1762; containing some remarks on Mr Delaval's electrical experiments. On Dec. 16, in the same year, another curious addition was made by him to philosophical knowledge, in a paper entitled, "Experiments to prove that water is not incomprehensible." These experiments are a complete refutation of the famous Florentine experiments, which so many philosophers have mentioned as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the incomprehensibility of water. On St Andrew's day, 1763, our author was the third time elected one of the council of the Royal Society; and on Nov. 8, in the following year, were read before that learned body, his farther "Experiments and observations on the comprehensibility of water, and some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>." The establishment of this fact, in opposition to the received <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, formed on the hasty decision of the Florentine Academy, was thought to be deserving of the society's gold medal. It was accordingly moved for in the council of 1764; and after several invidious delays, which terminated much to the honour of Mr Canton, it was presented to him Nov. 30, 1765. The next communication of our ingenious author to the Royal Society, which we shall take notice of in this place, was on Dec. 22, 1763, being "An easy method of making a Phosphorus that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> imbibe and emit light like the Bolognian stone; with experiments and observations." When he first showed to Dr Franklin the instantaneous light acquired by some of this phosphorus from the near discharge of an electrified bottle, the doctor immediately exclaimed, "And God said, Let there be light, and there was light." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of St Paul's having, in a letter to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, dated March 5, 1769, requested the opinion of the Royal Society relative to the best and most effectual method of fixing electrical conductors to preserve that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> from damage by lightning, Mr Canton was one of the committee appointed to take the letter into consideration, and to report their opinion upon it. The gentlemen joined with him in this Cantoning business were, Dr Watson, Dr Franklin, Mr Delaval, and Mr Willson. Their report was made on the 8th of June following; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> recommended by them has been carried into execution. The last paper of our author's, which was read before the Royal Society, was on Dec. 21, 1769; and contained "Experiments to prove that the Luminousness of the Sea arises from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> of its animal substances." In the account now given of his communications to the public, we have chiefly confined ourselves to such as were the most important, and which threw new and distinguished light on various objects in the philosophical world. Besides these he wrote a number of papers both in earlier and in later life, which appeared in several different publications, and particularly in the Gentleman's Magazine. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and sedentary life of Mr Canton, arising from an unremitting attention to the duties of his profession, and to the prosecution of his philosophical inquiries and experiments, probably contributed to shorten his days. The disorder into which he fell, and which carried him off, was a dropfly. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> happened on March 22, 1772, in the 54th year of his age.

CANTONING

Pages 161-161

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, is the allotting distinct and separate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> to each regiment; the town where they are quartered being divided into as many cantons as there are regiments.

CANTRED

Pages 161-161
or Cantreth, signifies a hundred villages. It is a British word, compounded of the adjective cant, i.e., hundred; and tref, a town or village. In Wales some of the counties are divided into cantreds, as in England into hundreds.

CANTYRE

Pages 161-162

from Cantierre, signifying a "headland," the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the shire of Argyle in Scotland. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, stretching 37 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles in breadth. It is mostly plain, arable, and populous; inhabited promiscuously by Highlanders and Lowlanders, the latter being invited to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by the Argyle family, that the lands might be the better cultivated. It gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of marquis to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, and is by Lochyn divided from Argyle Proper. This loch is an inlet from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, about 60 miles in length and four in breadth, celebrated for its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> fishery. There are many paltry villages in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but no town of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> except Campbelltown. Cantyre was granted to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Argyle after the suppression of a rebellion of the Macdonalds of the Isles (and it is supposed of this peninsula) in the beginning of the last century, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> was afterwards ratified by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants were the Macdonalds, Mac-eachrans, Mac-kays, and Mac-maths. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a> of Cantyre, the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> promontory of the peninsula. There is here a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a> 235 feet above the sea at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, situated on the rocks called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">Merchants</a>. Lat. 55° 22'. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 42'. west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-ILA">Ila</a> from the lighthouse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>, by the compass, N. by E. distant 27 miles; the fourth end of Ila N. N. W. distant 25 miles; the north end of Rathlin <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, N. W. by W. one half W.; the Maiden Rocks, S. by W. one half W. distant 14 miles; Copland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, S. by W. one half W. distant... distant 31 miles. The Ianthorn is seen from N. N. E. 1-4th E. from S. by W. 1-4th W. and intermediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass N. of these two points.

CANTZ

Pages 162-162

a town of Silegia in Germany. L. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16° 36'. N. Lat. 51° 6'.

CANULA

Pages 162-162

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a tube made of different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, principally of silver and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, but sometimes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. They are introduced into hollow ulcers, in order to facilitate a discharge of pus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other substance; or into wounds, either accidental or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cavities, as the thorax or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>: they are used in the operation of bronchotomy; and by some, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, as a drain for urine. Other canulas are used for introducing cauteries, either actual or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIAL">potential</a>, into hollow parts, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the parts adjacent to that to be cauterized, from injury. They are of various figures; some being oval, some round, and others crooked.

CANUSIUM

Pages 162-162

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Apulia, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> south side of the Aufidus, to the west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANNE">Canne</a>, whither the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> fled after the defeat sustained there. It was famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> thinning <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>; whence those who wore clothes made of it were called Canusinati. Now called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANOSA">Canosa</a>; which see.

CANUTE

Pages 162-163

the first Danish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of England after Ironside. He married Emma widow of King <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a>; and put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> several persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> who stood in his way to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Having thus settled his power in England, he made a voyage to his other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, in order to resist the attacks of the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>; and he carried along with him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> body of the English under the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Godwin. This nobleman had here an opportunity of performing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> by which he both reconciled the king's mind to the English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and, gaining to himself the friendship of his sovereign, laid the foundation of that immense fortune which he acquired to his family. He was stationed next the Swedish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; and observing a favourable opportunity which he was obliged suddenly to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a>, he attacked the enemy in the night, drove them suddenly from their trenches, threw them into disorder, pursued his advantage, and obtained a decisive victory over them. Next morning, Canute, seeing the English camp entirely abandoned, imagined that these disaffected troops had deserted to the enemy; and he was agreeably surprised to find that they were at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> engaged in pursuit of the discomfited Swedes. He was so pleased with this success, and the manner of obtaining it, that he bestowed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> upon Godwin, and treated him ever after with the most entire confidence and regard. In another voyage which he afterwards made to Denmark, Canute attacked <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and expelled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> but unwarlike Olaus from his kingdom, of which he kept possession till the death of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. He had now by his conquests and valour attained the utmost height of his ambition; and having leisure from wars and intrigues, he felt the unsatisfactory <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> enjoyments: and equally weary of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and torments of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he began to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> his views towards that future existence, which it is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> for the human mind, whether satiated by prosperity, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disgusted with adversity, to make the object of its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. Unfortunately the spirit which prevailed in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> gave a wrong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>; and, instead of making atonement to those whom he had formerly injured by his acts of violence, he entirely employed himself in those exercises of piety, which the monks represented as most meritorious. He built churches; he endowed monasteries; he enriched <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>; and he bestowed revenues for the support of chantries at Affington and other places, where he appointed prayers to be said for the souls of those who had there fallen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> against him. He even undertook a pilgrimage to Rome, where he performed a considerable time; and, besides obtaining from the pope some privileges for the English school erected there, he engaged all the princes through whose dominions he was obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, to desist from those heavy impositions and tolls which they were accustomed to exact from the English pilgrims. By this spirit of devotion, no less than by his equitable and politic administration, he gained in a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the affections of his subjects. Canute, who was the greatest and most powerful prince of his time, sovereign of Denmark and Norway as well as of England, could not fail to meet with adulation from his courtiers; a tribute which is liberally paid even to the meanest and weakest of princes. Some of his flatterers breaking out one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in admiration of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, exclaimed that every thing was possible for him; upon which the monarch, it is said, ordered a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> to be set on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> shore while the tide was making; and as the waters approached, he commanded them to retire, and obey the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of him who was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the ocean. He feigned to sit some time in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of their submission; but when the sea still advanced towards him, and began to wash him with its billows, he turned to his courtiers, and remarked to them, That every creature in the universe was feeble and impotent, and that power reposed with one Being alone, in whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> were all the elements of nature, who could say to the ocean, "Thus far shalt thou go, and no farther," and who could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with his nod the most towering piles of human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and Canzone and ambition. From that time, it is said, he never would wear a crown. He died in the 20th year of his reign; and was interred at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, in the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>.

CANVAS

Pages 162-162

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a very clear unbleached cloth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, wove regularly in little squares. It is used for working <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, by passing the threads of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, through the intervals or squares. Canvas is also a coarse cloth of hemp, unbleached, somewhat clear, which serves to cover women's stays, also to stiffen men's clothes, and to make some other of their wearing apparel, &c. Canvas is also used among the French for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> or first words whereon an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> or piece of music is composed, and given to a poet to regulate and finish. The canvas of a song contains certain notes of the composer, which show the poet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the verses he is to make. Thus Du <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a> says, he has canvas for ten fonnets against the Mules. Canvas is also the name of a cloth made of hemp, and used for ship sails. Canvas, among painters, is the cloth on which they usually draw their pictures; the canvas being smoothed over with a slick <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, then sized, and afterwards whitened over, makes what the painters called their primed cloth, on which they draw their first sketches with coal or chalk, and afterwards finish with colours.

CANZONE

Pages 163-163

in Music, signifies, in general, a song, where some little fugues are introduced; but it is sometimes used for a sort of Italian poem, usually pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, to which music may be composed in the style of a cantata. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> be added to a piece of instrumental music, it signifies much the same as cantata; if placed in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a sonata, it implies the same meaning as allegro, and only denotes that the part to which it is prefixed is to be played <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sung in a brisk and lively manner.

CANZONETTA

Pages 163-163

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of canzone, denoting a little short song. The canzonette Neapolitan has two strains, each whereof is sung twice over, as the vaudevilles of the French. The canzonette Siciliane is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of jig, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> whereof is usually twelve eighths, and six eighths, and sometimes both, as rondellas.

CAOENS

Pages 104-107
LOUIS DE**, a famous Portuguese poet, the honour of whose birth is claimed by different cities. But according to N. Antonio, and Manuel Correa, his intimate friend, this event happened at Lisbon in 1517. His family was of considerable note, and originally Spanish. In 1572, Vasco Perez de Caamans, disfigured at the court of Castile, fled to that of Lisbon, where King Ferdinand immediately admitted him into his council, and gave him the lordships of Sardoal, Punente, Marano, Amendado, and other considerable lands; a certain proof of the eminence of his rank and abilities. In the war for the succession, which broke out on the death of Ferdinand, Camoens sided with the king of Castile, and was killed in the battle of Aljubarota. But though John I. the victor, feigned a great part of his estate, his widow, the daughter of Gonfalo Tereyro, grand master of the order of Christ, and general of the Portuguese army, was not reduced beneath her rank. She had three sons who took the name of Camoens. The family of the eldest intermarried with the first nobility of Portugal; and even, according to Cafera, with the blood royal. But the family of the second brother, whose fortune was slender, had the superior honour to produce the author of the Lusiad. Early in his life the misfortunes of the poet began. In his infancy, Simon Vaz de Camoens, his father, commander of a vessel, was shipwrecked at Goa, where, with his life, the greatest part of his fortune was lost. His mother, however, Anne de Macedo of Santarene, provided for the education of her son Louis at the university of Coimbra. What he acquired there, his works discover; an intimacy with the classics, equal to that of a Scaliger, but directed by the taste of a Milton or a Pope. When he left the university, he appeared at court. He was handsome; had speaking eyes, it is said; and the finest complexion. Certain it is, however, he was a polished scholar, which, added to the natural ardour and gay vivacity of his disposition, rendered him an accomplished gentleman. Courts are the scenes of intrigue; and intrigue was fashionable at Lisbon. But the particulars of the amours of Camoens rest unknown. This only appears: he had aspired above his rank, for he was banished from the court; and in several of his sonnets he attributes this misfortune to love. He now retired to his mother's friends at Santarene. Here he renewed his studies, and began his poem on the discovery of India. John III. at this time prepared an armament against Africa. Camoens, tired of his inactive obscure life, went to Ceuta in this expedition, and greatly distinguished his valour in several encounters. In a naval engagement with the Moors in the straits of Gibraltar, in the conflict of boarding, he was among the foremost, and lost his right eye. Yet neither hurry of actual service nor the dissipation of the camp could stifle his genius. He continued his *Lusiadas*, and several of his most beautiful sonnets were written in Africa, while, as he expressed it, One hand the pen, and one the sword, employ'd. The fame of his valour had now reached the court, and he obtained permission to return to Lisbon. But, while he solicited an establishment which he had merited in the ranks of battle, the malignity of evil tongues, as he calls it in one of his letters, was injuriously poured upon him. Though the bloom of his early youth was effaced by several years residence under the scorching heavens of Africa, and though altered by the loss of an eye, his presence gave uneasiness to the gentlemen of some families of the first rank where he had formerly visited. Jealousy is the characteristic of the Spaniards and Portuguese; its resentment knows no bounds, and Camoens now found it prudent to banish himself from his native country. Accordingly, in 1553, he sailed for India, with a resolution never to return. As the ship left the Tagus, he exclaimed, in the words of the sepulchral monument of Scipio Africanus, Camoeus canus, Ingrata patria, non possehis affu mea! "Ungrateful country, thou shalt not possess my bones!" But he knew not what evils in the east would awake the remembrance of his native fields. When Camoens arrived in India, an expedition was ready to fail to revenge the king of Cochin on the king of Pimenta. Without any rest on shore after his long voyage, he joined this armament, and in the conquest of the Alagada islands displayed his usual bravery. In the year following, he attended Manuel de Vasconcelos in an expedition to the s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red sea. Here, says Paria, as Camoens had no use for his sword, he employed his pen. Nor was his activity confined to the fleet or camp. He visited Mount Felix and the adjacent inhospitable regions of Africa, which he so strongly pictures in the Lusiad, and in one of his little pieces where he laments the absence of his mistress. When he returned to Goa, he enjoyed a tranquillity which enabled him to bestow his attention on his epic poem. But this serenity was interrupted, perhaps by his own imprudence. He wrote some satires which gave offence; and by order of the viceroy Francisco Barreto, he was banished to China. The accomplishments and manners of Camoens soon found him friends, though under the disgrace of banishment. He was appointed commissary of the defunct in the island of Macao, a Portuguese settlement in the bay of Canton. Here he continued his Lusiad; and here also, after five years residence, he acquired a fortune, though small, yet equal to his wishes. Don Constantine de Braganza was now viceroy of India; and Camoens, desirous to return to Goa, resigned his charge. In a ship, freighted by himself, he set sail; but was shipwrecked in the gulf near the mouth of the river Mehon on the coast of China. All he had acquired was lost in the waves; his poems, which he held in one hand, while he swammed with the other, were all he found himself possessed of when he stood friendless on the unknown shore. But the natives gave him a most humane reception: this he has immortalized in the prophetic song in the tenth Lusiad; and in the seventh, he tells us, that here he lost the wealth which satisfied his wishes. Agora da elparanga ja adquirida, etc. Now blest with all the wealth fond hope could crave, Soon I beheld that wealth beneath the wave For ever lost; My life, like Judah's heaven-doom'd king of yore, By miracle prolong'd— On the banks of the Mehon he wrote his beautiful paraphrase of the psalm, where the Jews, in the finest strain of poetry, are represented as hanging their harps on the willows, by the rivers of Babylon, and weeping their exile from their native country. Here Camoens continued some time, till an opportunity offered to carry him to Goa. When he arrived at that city, Don Constantine de Braganza, the viceroy, whose characteristic was politeness, admitted him into intimate friendship, and Camoens was happy till Count Redondo assumed the government. Those who had formerly procured the banishment of the satirist, were silent while Constantine was in power; but now they exerted all their arts against him. Redondo, when he entered on office, pretended to be the friend of Camoens; yet, with all that unfeeling indifference with which he made his most horrible witticism on the Zamorin, he suffered the innocent man to be thrown into the common prison. After all the delay of bringing witnesses, Camoens, in a public trial, fully refuted every accusation of his conduct while commissary at Macao, and his enemies were loaded with ignominy and reproach. But Camoens had some creditors, and these detained him in prison a considerable time, till the gentlemen of Goa began to be ashamed that a man of his singular merit should experience such treatment among them. He was set at liberty; and again he assumed the profession of arms, and received the allowance of a gentleman volunteer, a character at this time common in Portuguese India. Soon after, Pedro Barreto, appointed governor of the fort at Sofala, by high promises, allured the poet to attend him thither. The governor of a distant fort, in a barbarous country, shares in some measure the fate of an exile. Yet, though the only motive of Barreto was, in this unpleasant situation, to retain the conversation of Camoens at his table, it was his least care to render the life of his guest agreeable. Chagrined with his treatment, and a considerable time having elapsed in vain dependence upon Barreto, Camoens resolved to return to his native country. A ship, on the homeward voyage, at this time touched at Sofala, and several gentlemen who were on board were desirous that Camoens should accompany them. But this the governor ungallantly endeavoured to prevent, and charged him with a debt for board. Anthony de Cabra, however, and Hector de Sylveira, paid the demand; and Camoens, says Farin, and the honour of Barreto, were told together. After an absence of 16 years, Camoens, in 1569, returned to Lisbon, unhappy even in his arrival, for the pestilence then raged in that city, and prevented his publication for three years. At last, in 1572, he printed his Lusiad, which, in the opening of the first book, in a most elegant turn of compliment, he addressed to his prince, King Sebastian, then in his 18th year. The king, says the French translator, was so pleased with his merit, that he gave the author a pension of 4000 reals, on condition that he should reside at court. But this salary, says the same writer, was withdrawn by Cardinal Henry, who succeeded to the crown of Portugal, lost by Sebastian at the battle of Alcazar. Though the great patron of one species of literature, a species the reverence of that of Camoens, certain it is, that the author of the Lusiad was utterly neglected by Henry, under whose inglorious reign he died in all the misery of poverty. By some, it is said, he died in an alms-house. It appears, however, that he had not even the certainty of subsistence which these houses provide. He had a black servant, who had grown old with him, and who had long experienced his master's humanity. This grateful Indian, a native of Java, who, according to some writers, saved his master's life in the unhappy shipwreck where he lost his effects, begged in the streets of Lisbon for the only man in Portugal on whom God had bestowed these talents which have a tendency to erect the spirit of a downward age. To the eye of a careful observer, the fate of Camoens throws Camomile throws great light on that of his country, and will appear strictly connected with it. The same ignorance, the same degenerated spirit, which suffered Camoens to depend on his share of the alms begged in the streets by his old hoary servant, the same spirit which caused this funk the kingdom of Portugal into the most abject vassalage ever experienced by a conquered nation. While the grandees of Portugal were blind to the ruin which impended over them, Camoens beheld it with a pungency of grief which hastened his exit. In one of his letters he has these remarkable words: *Em fim acabarey à vida, e verram todos que fui eficaz contra a minha patria, &c.* "I am ending the course of my life; the world will witness how I have loved my country. I have returned, not only to die in her bosom, but to die with her." In this unhappy situation, in 1579, in his 62d year, the year after the fatal defeat of Don Sebastian, died Louis de Camoens, the greatest literary genius ever produced by Portugal; in martial courage and spirit of honour, nothing inferior to her greatest heroes. And in a manner suitable to the poverty in which he died, was he buried. **CAMOMILE.** See Anthemis, Botany Index. **CAMP,** the ground on which an army pitch their tents. It is marked out by the quartermaster general, who appoints every regiment their ground. The chief advantages to be minded in choosing a camp for an army, are, to have it near the water, in a country of forage, where the soldiers may find wood for dressing their victuals; that it have a free communication with garrisons, and with a country from whence it may be supplied with provisions; and, if possible, that it be situated on a rising ground, in a dry gravelly soil. Besides, the advantages of the ground ought to be considered, as marshes, woods, rivers, and enclosures; and if the camp be near the enemy, with no river or marsh to cover it, the army ought to be intrenched. An army always encamps fronting the enemy; and generally in two lines, running parallel about 500 yards distance; the horse and dragoons, on the wings; and the foot, in the centre: sometimes a body of two, three, or four brigades, is encamped behind the two lines, and is called the body of reserve. The artillery and bread-waggons are generally encamped in the rear of the two lines. A battalion of foot is allowed 80 or 100 paces for its camp; and 30 or 40 for an interval between one battalion and another. A squadron of horse is allowed 30 for its camp, and 30 for an interval, and more if the ground will allow it. Where the grounds are equally dry, those camps are always the most healthful that are pitched on the banks of large rivers; because, in the hot season, situations of this kind have a stream of fresh air from the water, serving to carry off the moist and putrid exhalations. On the other hand, next to marshes, the worst encampments are on low grounds close before trees; for then the air is not only moist and hurtful in itself, but by stagnating becomes more susceptible of corruption. However, let the situation of camps be ever so good, they are frequently rendered infectious by the putrid effluvia of rotten straw, and the privies of the army, more especially if the bloody flux prevails; in which case the best method of preventing a general infection, is to leave the ground with the privies, foul straw, and other filth, of the camp behind. This must be frequently done, if consistent with the military operations: but when these render it improper to change the ground often, the privies should be made deeper than usual, and once a day a thick layer of earth thrown into them till the pits are near full; and then they are to be well covered, and supplied by others. It may also be a proper caution to order the pits to be made either in the front or the rear, as the then stationary winds may best carry off their effluvia from the camp. Moreover, it will be necessary to change the straw frequently; as being not only apt to rot, but to retain the infectious steams of the sick. But if fresh straw cannot be procured, more care must be taken in airing the tents, as well as the old straw. The disposition of the Hebrew encampment was at first laid out by God himself. Their camp was of a quadrangular form, surrounded with an enclosure of the height of 10 hands-breadth. It made a square of 12 miles in compass about the tabernacle; and within this was another called the Levites' camp. The Greeks had also their camps fortified with gates and ditches. The Lacedemonians made their camp of a round figure, looking upon that as the most perfect and defensible of any form: we are not, however, to imagine, that they thought this form so essential to a camp, as never to be dispensed with when the circumstances of the place required it. Of the rest of the Grecian camps, it may be observed, that the most valiant of the soldiers were placed at the extremities, the rest in the middle. Thus we learn from Homer, that Achilles and Ajax were posted at the ends of the camp before Troy, as bulwarks on each side of the rest of the princes. The figure of the Roman camp was a square divided into two principal parts: in the upper part were the general's pavilion, or praetorium, and the tents of the chief officers; in the lower, those of inferior degree were placed. On one side of the praetorium stood the questorium, or apartment of the treasurer of the army; and near this the forum, both for a market place and the assembling of councils. On the other side of the praetorium were lodged the legati; and below it the tribunes had their quarters, opposite to their respective legions. Aside of the tribunes were the praefecti of the foreign troops, over against their respective wings; and behind these were the lodgments of the evocati, then those of the extraordinarii and ablest equites, which concluded the higher part of the camp. Between the two partitions was a spot of ground called principia, for the altars and images of the gods, and probably also for the chief ensigns. The middle of the lower partition was assigned to the Roman horse; next to them were quartered the triarii; then the principes, and close by them the hastati; afterwards the foreign horse, and lastly, the foreign foot. They fortified their camp with a ditch and parapet, which they termed fossa and wallum; in the latter some distinguished two parts, viz. the agger or earthen, and the fossae or wooden stakes driven in to secure it. The camps were sometimes surrounded by walls made of hewn stone; and the tents themselves formed of the same matter. In the front of the Turkish camp are quartered the janizaries and other foot, whose tents encompass their aga; in the rear are the quarters of the spahis and other Camp other horsemen. The body of the camp is possessed by the flatly tents or pavilions of the vizier or general, rais effendi or chancellor, khajia or steward, the teftedar baihaw or lord treasurer, and kapilar kahiafeer or master of the ceremonies. In the middle of these tents is a spacious field, wherein is erected a building for the divan, and a hafna or treasury. When the ground is marked out for a camp, all wait for the pitching of the tent lafiae, the place where the courts of justice are held; it being the disposition of this that is to regulate all the rest. The Arabs still live in camps, as the ancient Scenites did. The camp of the Affyne Emir, or king of the country about Tadmor, is described by a traveller who viewed it, as spread over a very large plain, and possessing so vast a space, that though he had the advantage of a rising ground, he could not see the utmost extent of it. His own tent was near the middle; scarce distinguishable from the rest, except that it was bigger, being made, like the others, of a sort of haircloth. Camp, is also used by the Siamese, and some other nations in the East Indies, as the name of the quarters which they assign to foreigners who come to trade with them. In these camps, every nation forms, as it were, a particular town, where they carry on all their trade, not only keeping all their warehouses and shops there, but also live in these camps with their whole families. The Europeans, however, are so far indulged, that at Siam, and almost everywhere else, they may live either in the cities or suburbs, as they shall judge most convenient. Camp-fight, or Kamp-fight, in law writers, denotes the trial of a cause by duel, or a legal combat of two champions in the field, for decision of some controversy. In the trial by camp fight, the accuser was, with the peril of his own body, to prove the accused guilty; and by offering him his glove, to challenge him to this trial, which the other must either accept of, or acknowledge himself guilty of the crime whereof he was accused. If it were a crime deserving death, the camp-fight was for life and death: if the offence deserved only imprisonment, the camp fight was accomplished when one combatant had subdued the other, so as either to make him yield or take him prisoner. The accused had liberty to choose another to fight in his stead, but the accuser was obliged to perform it in his own person, and with equality of weapons. No women were permitted to be spectators, nor men under the age of thirteen. The priest and the people who looked on, were engaged silently in prayer, that the victory might fall to him who had right. None might cry, shriek, or give the least sign; which in some places was executed with so much strictness, that the executioner stood ready with an axe to cut off the right hand or foot of the party that should offend therein. He that, being wounded, yielded himself, was at the other's mercy either to be killed or suffered to live. But if life were granted him, he was declared infamous by the judge, and disabled from ever bearing arms, or riding on horseback. CAMPAGNA. See CAMPANIA.

CAOUTCHOUC

Pages 163-165
Elastic Resin, or India rubber, a substance produced from the syringe tree of Cayenne and other parts of South America, and possessed of the most singular properties. No substance is yet known which is so pliable, and at the same time so elastic; and it is farther a matter of curiosity, as being capable of resisting the action of very powerful menstrua. From the account of M. de la Condamine, we learn that this substance oozes out, under the form of a vegetable milk, from incisions made in the tree; and that it is gathered chiefly in time of rain, because, though it may be collected at all times, it flows then most abundantly. The means employed to infuse and indurate it, M. de la Borde says, are kept a profound secret. M. Bomare, and others, affirm, that it thickens and hardens gradually by being exposed to the air; and as soon as it acquires a solid confidence it manifests a very extraordinary degree of flexibility and elasticity. Accordingly the Indians make boots of it which water cannot penetrate, and which, when smoked, have the appearance of real leather. Bottles are also made of it, to the necks of which are fastened hollow reeds, so that the liquor contained in them may be squirted through the reeds or pipes by pressure. One of these filled with water is always presented to each of the guests at their entertainments, who never fail to make use of it before eating. This whimsical custom led the Portuguese in that country to call the tree that produces the resin pau da xirringa; and hence the name of seringa is given both to the tree and to its resinous production. Flambeaux, an inch and a half in diameter, and two feet long, are likewise made of this resin, which give a beautiful light, have no bad smell, and burn twelve hours. A kind of cloth is also prepared from it, which the inhabitants of Quito apply to the same purpose as our oil cloth and fail cloth. It is formed, in fine, by means of moulds, into a variety of figures for use and ornament; and the process is said to be thus:—The juice, which is obtained by incision, is spread over pieces of clay formed into the desired shape; and as fast as one layer is dry, another is added, till the vessel be of the proper thickness: the whole is then held over a strong smoke of vegetables on fire, whereby it hardens into the texture and appearance of leather; and before the finishing, while yet soft, is capable of having any impression made on the outside, which remains ever after. When the whole is done, the inside mould is picked out. Since this resin has been known in Europe, its chemical qualities and other interesting properties have been very diligently investigated. In particular, it has been endeavoured to discover some method of dissolving it in such a manner that it would assume different figures, with equal ease as when in its original state fluid. In the memoirs of the Academy of Sciences for 1768, we have an account of several attempts for this purpose, and how it may be effected.—The state of vegetable milk in which the caoutchouc resin is found when it comes from the tree, led M. Macquer to imagine that it was composed of an oil and a watery matter. From its wanting aromatic flavour, from its little volatility, and from its being incapable of solution in spirit of wine, he concluded that the oil which entered its composition was not an essential, but a fatty one. Hence he thought it probable that it passed from a fluid to a solid form by the evaporation of the watery part, and that the oily solvents would reduce it to a soft state. The first trials he made for dissolving it were with linseed oil, essence of turpentine, and several others. But all he could obtain by means of these menstrua was a viscid substance incapable of being hardened, and totally void of elasticity. The rectified essential oil of turpentine was employed seemingly with greater success. To separate from this menstruum the caoutchouc which it had dissolved, M. Macquer added spirit of wine; but the consequence was, that part only of the oil united with the spirit; the rest remaining obstinately attached to the resin which it had dissolved, and thus preventing it from assuming a solid consistence. The author next endeavoured to dissolve it by means of heat in Papin's digester. But neither water, nor spirit of wine, although in this way capable of dissolving the hardest bones, could produce any other effect upon it than to render it more firm than before. After this, he tried what effect the milky juice of other vegetables would have upon it. He used several kinds, particularly that of the fig. But, in this way, he could obtain no solution. From the great volatility of ether, he was next induced to try it as a menstruum; and, for this purpose, he prepared some with great attention. The caoutchouc, cut into little bits, and put into a proper vessel with as much ether as was sufficient to cover it, was perfectly dissolved without any other heat than that of the atmosphere. This solution was transparent and of an amber colour. It still preserved the smell of ether, but mixed with the disagreeable odour of the caoutchouc, and it is a little less fluid than pure ether. Upon its being thrown into water, no milky liquor was produced; but there arose to the surface a solid membrane which possessed the great elasticity and other peculiar properties of the caoutchouc. He observes, however, that two pints of the best ether, obtained by rectifying eight or ten pints of the common ether by a gentle heat, must be used, in order to the success of the operation. The distinguishing properties of this substance, viz. its solidity, flexibility, and elasticity, and its quality of resisting the action of aqueous, spirituous, saline, oily, and other common solvents, render it extremely fit for the construction of tubes, catheters, and other instruments, in which these properties are wanted. In order to form this resin into small tubes, M. Macquer prepared a solid cylindrical mould of wax, of the desired size and shape; and then dipping a pencil into the ethereal solution of the resin, daubed the mould over with it, till he had covered it with a coat of resin of sufficient thickness. The whole piece is then thrown into boiling water; by the heat of which the wax is soon melted, and rises to the surface, leaving the resinous tube completely formed behind. Grosart informs us, that he has succeeded very well in employing the essential oils of turpentine and lavender as a solvent for the elastic gum, and thus forming it into tubes or giving it any shape that is wanted. When the elastic tube is prepared with oil of lavender, the latter may be separated by immersing the tube in alcohol, which charges itself with the oil, and becomes a good lavender water. Alcohol serves another purpose beside taking up the essential oil. It accelerates very much the drying of caoutchouc instruments, which are thus formed. Oil of turpentine appeared always to have a kind of stickiness; and the smell which could not be got rid of, by any means yet discovered, was another inconvenience. Grosart proposes another solvent, which is easily procured, and is not liable to the inconvenience just mentioned. This solvent is water. "I conceive (says he) it will appear strange to mention water as a solvent of elastic gum, that liquid having been always supposed to have no action upon it. I myself resisted the idea; but reflecting that ether, by being saturated with water, is the better enabled to act on caoutchouc, and that this gum when plunged into boiling water becomes more transparent at the edges, I presumed that this effect was not due simply to the dilatation of its volume by the heat. I thought that, at that temperature, some action might take place, and that a long-continued ebullition might produce more sensible effects. I was not disappointed in my expectations, and one of those tubes was prepared without any other solvent than water and heat. I proceeded in the same manner as with ether: the elastic gum dilates but very little in boiling water; it becomes whitish, but recovers its colour again by drying it in the air and light. It is sufficiently prepared for use when it has been a quarter of an hour in boiling water: by this time its edges are sometimes transparent. It is to be turned spirally round the mould, in the manner we described before, and replunged frequently into the boiling water, during the time that is employed in forming the tube, to the end that the edges may be disposed to unite together. When the whole is bound with packthread, it is to be kept some hours in boiling water; after which it is to be dried, still keeping on the binding. "If we wish to be more certain that the connexion is perfect, the spiral may be doubled; but we must always avoid placing the exterior surfaces of the slips one upon the other, as those surfaces are the parts which most resist the action of solvents. This precaution is necessary when ether is employed, on account of its great action upon the caoutchouc. "It might be feared that the action of water upon caoutchouc would deprive us of the advantages which might otherwise be expected; but these fears will be removed, if we consider that the affinities differ according to the temperatures; that it is only at a very high temperature that water exercises any sensible action upon caoutchouc. I can affirm, that at 120° of Reaumur's thermometer (302° of Fahrenheit) this affinity is not such as that the water can give a liquid form to caoutchouc; and it does not appear that we have anything to fear in practice from a combination between these two bodies, which, though it really is a true solution, does not take place in any sensible degree but at a high temperature. It is therefore at present easy to make of caoutchouc whatever instruments it may be advantageous to have of a flexible, supple, and elastic substance, which is impermeable to water at the temperature of our atmosphere, and resists the action of acids as well as that of most other solvents. As to the durability of these instruments, few substances promise more than this, because it may be soldered afresh in a damaged part. Any woven substance may be covered with it; it is only required that the substance should be of a nature not to be acted upon during the preparation, either by ether or by boiling water; for these two agents are those which appear to me to merit the preference. Artists will frequently find an advantage in employing ether, as it requires less time; so that a person may make, in a single day, any tube he may have occasion for. The expense of ether is very little, since it is needful only to dispose the caoutchouc to adhere; and being brought into that state, the caoutchouc may be kept in a vessel perfectly well closed. It would also diminish the expense of the ether, if, instead of washing it with a large quantity of water, there should be added to it only as much water as it can take up." A resin similar to this was some years ago discovered by M. Poivre, in the Isle of France; and there are various milky juices extracted from trees in America and elsewhere, which by previous mixtures and preparations are formed into an elastic resin, but of an inferior quality to that of Cayenne; such, for instance, are the juices obtained from the Cecropia peltata, the Ficus religiosa and Indica, &c. Of the genuine trees, those growing along the banks of the river of the Amazons are described by M. Condamin as attaining a very great height, being at the same time perfectly straight, and having no branches except at top, which is but small, covering no more than a circumference of ten feet. Its leaves bear some resemblance to those of the manioc: they are green on the upper part, and white beneath. The seeds are three in number, and contained in a pod consisting of three cells, not unlike those of the ricinus or palma Christi; and in each of them there is a kernel, which being stripped and boiled in water produces a thick oil or fat, answering the purpose of butter in the cookery of that country. A method of dissolving this elastic gum without ether, for the purposes of a varnish or the like, is as follows: Take one pound of the spirit of turpentine, and C A O Caoutchouc—a pound of the gum cut into very small pieces; pour the turpentine into a long-necked matraf, which must be placed in a sand bath; throw in the gum, not all at once, but by little and little according as it is perceived to dissolve: When it is entirely dissolved, pour into the matrafs a pint of nut or linseed oil, or oil of poppies, rendered deficcative in the usual manner with litharge: Then let the whole boil for a quarter of an hour, and the preparation is finished. This would make an excellent varnish for air balloons, were it not so expensive on account of the price of the gum. —Another method, invented by Mr Baldwin, is as follows. Take any quantity of the caoutchouc, as two ounces avoirdupois: cut it into small bits with a pair of scissors. Put a strong iron ladle (such as plumbers or glaziers melt their lead in) over a common pit-coal or other fire. The fire must be gentle, glowing, and without smoke. When the ladle is hot, much below a red heat, put a single bit into the ladle. If black smoke issues, it will presently flame and disappear; or it will evaporate without flame: the ladle is then too hot. When the ladle is left hot, put in a second bit, which will produce a white smoke. This white smoke will continue during the operation, and evaporate the caoutchouc: therefore no time is to be lost; but little bits are to be put in, a few at a time, till the whole are melted. It should be continually and gently stirred with an iron or brass spoon. Two pounds, or one quart, of the best drying oil (or of raw linseed oil, which, together with a few drops of neats foot oil, has stood a month, or not so long, on a lump of quicklime, to make it more or less drying) is to be put into the melted caoutchouc, and stirred till hot: and the whole poured into a glazed vessel, through a coarse gauze, or fine sieve. When settled and clear, which will be in a few minutes, it is fit for use, either hot or cold. The Abbé Clavigero informs us, that the elastic gum is called by the Mexicans Olin or Olli, and by the Spaniards of that kingdom Ule: That it diffuses from the olivierwood, which is a tree of moderate size; the trunk of which is smooth and yellowish, the leaves pretty large, the flowers white, and the fruit yellow and rather round, but angular; within which there are kernels as large as filberts, and white, but covered with a yellowish pellicle: That the kernel has a bitter taste, and the fruit always grows attached to the bark of the tree: That when the trunk is cut, the juice which diffuses from it is white, liquid, and viscid; afterwards it becomes yellow; and lastly of a leaden colour, though rather blacker, which it always retains. The tree, he adds, is very common in the kingdom of Guatemala. Different trees, it would appear, yield the elastic gum. Aublet, in his Histoire des Plantes de la Guiane (p. 871.), describes the tree, the fruit, and manner of collecting the juice; but never saw the flower: he calls it, however, Hevea Guianensis. In Jacquin's America, it is called Echeites Corymbosa. The younger Linnæus, in his Supplementum Plantarum (p. 422), names it Jatropha Elastica; but acknowledges that he only gives it this name from the structure of the fruit having most resemblance to that genus, his dry species wanting the flowers. Of the above gum, it is said, the Chinese make e- Vol. V. Part I. CAP lactic rings for lascivious purposes.—Among us it is used by surgeons for injecting liquids, and by painters for rubbing out black lead pencil marks, &c.

CAPACITY

Pages 166-167

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> contents of any body; Capacity body; also our hollow <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> for wine, beer, corn, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, &c. are called measures of capacity. Capacity, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the ability of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> body politic, to give or take lands or other things, or sue actions. Our law allows the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> two capacities; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a>: in the first, he may purchase lands to him and his heirs; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, to him and his successors. The clergy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England have the like. Caparison, or Caparison, the covering or clothing laid over a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; especially a sumpter horse, or horse of state. The word is Spanish, being an augmentative of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a>, caput, head. Anciently the caparisons were a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> armour, wherewith horses were covered in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>.

CAPE

Pages 167-167

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> running out with a point into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, as Cape <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NORD">Nord</a>, Cape <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>, the Cape of Good Hope, &c. Cape <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELK">Elk</a>. See Cervus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cape Breton. See Breton. Cape-Cooff Castle. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">Coast</a>. Cape of Good Hope. See Good Hope. Cape Verde. See Verd. Capell, Edward, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> well known by his indefatigable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the works of Shakespeare, was a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, and received his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the school of St Edmund's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">Bury</a>. In the dedication of his edition of Shakespeare, in 1768, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Grafton, he observes; that "his father and the grandfather of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, were friends, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the deceased nobleman he owed the leisure which enabled him to bestow the attention of 20 years on that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>." The office which his grace bestowed on Mr Capell was that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>-instructor of the plays, to which a salary is annexed of £200 a-year. So early as the year 1745, as Mr Capell himself informs us, shocked at the licentiousness of Hanmer's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, he first projected an edition of Shakespeare, of the strictest accuracy, to be collated and published in due <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, ex fide codicum. He immediately proceeded to collect and compare the oldest and rarest copies; noting the original excellencies and defects of the rarest quartos, and distinguishing the improvements <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> variations of the first, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and third folios; and after many years labour produced a very beautiful small octavo, in 10 volumes, with an "Introduction." There is not, the authors of the Monthly Review observe, among the various publications of the present literary era, a more singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> than that "Introduction." In style and manner it is more obsolete and antique than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of which it treats. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Herbert of Cherbury, walking the new pavement in all the trappings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>; but, like Lord Herbert, it displays many valuable qualities accompanying this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of extravagance, much <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and appropriate erudition. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>-page of "Mr William Shakespeare, his Comedies, Histories, and Tragedies," it was also announced and promulgated, "Whereunto <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be added, in some other volumes, notes critical and explanatory, and a body of various readings entire." "The Introduction" likewise declared, that these "notes and various readings" would be accompanied with another work, disclosing the sources from which Shakespeare "drew the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his knowledge in mythological and classical matters, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and even the seeming peculiarities of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>—to which," says Mr Capell, "we have given for title, The School of Shakespeare." Nothing surely could be more properly conceived than such designs; nor have we ever met with any thing better grounded on the subject of "the learning of Shakespeare" than what may be found in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> to this part of Mr Capell's Introduction. It is more <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> than even the popular "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a>" on this topic. Certain quaintnesses of style, and peculiarities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNCTUATION">punctuation</a>, attended the whole of this publication. The outline, however, was correct; and the critic, with unremitting toil, proceeded in his undertaking. But while he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVING">diving</a> into the classics of Caxton (to continue the Reviewers account), and working his way under ground, like the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLE">Mole</a>, in order to emerge with all his glories; while he was looking forward to his triumphs, certain other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> spirits went to work upon his plan; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> out the promised treasures, laid them prematurely before the public, defeating the effect of our critic's discoveries by anticipation. Stevens, Malone, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">Farmer</a>, Percy, Reed, and a whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a> of literary ferrets, burrowed into every hole and corner of the warren of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> antiquity, and overrun all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, whose map had been delineated by Edward Capell. Such a contingency nearly flagged the steady and unshaken perseverance of our critic, at the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a> of the completion of his labours, and as his editor informs us—for, alas! at the end of near 40 years, the publication was posthumous, and the critic himself no more!—he was almost determined to lay the work wholly aside. He persevered, however, by the encouragement of some noble and worthy persons; and to such their encouragement, and his perseverance, the public was, in 1783, indebted for three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> volumes in 4to, under the title of "Notes and various readings of Shakespeare; together with the School of Shakespeare, or Extracts from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> English Books, that were in print in the Author's time; evidently flowing from whence his several Fables were taken, and some parcel of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">Dialogue</a>. Also farther Extracts, which contribute to a due understanding of his Writings, or give a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to the History of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, or to the Dramatic History of his Time. By Edw. Capell." Besides the works already mentioned, Mr Capell was the editor of a volume of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poems called "Prolusions;" and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of "Anthony and Cleopatra," as acted at Drury Lane in 1758. He died <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 24, 1781. Capella, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a bright fixed <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> in the left shoulder of the constellation <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURIGA">Auriga</a>. Capelle, a town of France, in Picardy, and in the Tierache, eight miles from Guise. It was taken by the Spaniards in 1636; but retaken the year after. E. Long. 3° 59'. N. Lat. 49° 58'. Capellets. See Farriery Index. Capellus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, an eminent French Protestant divine, born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a> in Champagne about the year 1579. He was author of some learned works; but is chiefly known from the controversy he engaged in with the younger Buxtorf concerning the antiquity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, which Capellus undertook to disprove. His Critica Sacra was also an elaborate work,

CAPEQUIN

Pages 168-168

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, situated on the river Blackwater. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 50. N. Lat. 52. 5.

CAPEROLANS

Pages 167-168

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, so called from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Caperole their founder, in the 15th century. The Milanese and Venetians being at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the enmity occasioned thereby spread itself to the very cloisters. The superiors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> brothers, which extended itself as far as the territories of the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, carried it so haughtily over the Venetians, that those of the convent of Brescia resolved to shake off a yoke which was grown insupportable to them. The superiors, informed of this, expelled out of the province those whom they considered as the authors of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of whom were Peter Caperole, Matthew de Tharvillo, and Bonaventure of Brescia. Peter Caperole, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of an enterprising genius, found means to separate the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of Brescia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERGAMO">Bergamo</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREMONA">Cremona</a>, from the province of Milan, and subject them to the conventuals. This occasioned a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> general and these convents, which was determined in favour of the latter; and these convents, in 1475, by the authority of Pope Sixtus IV, were erected into a distinct vicariate, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of that of Brescia. This not satisfying the ambition of Caperole, he obtained, by the interposition of the doge of Venice, that this vicariate might be erected into a congregation, which was called from him Caperolans. This congregation still subsists in Italy, and is composed of 24 convents, situated in Brescia, Bergamo, and Cremona.

CAPESTAN

Pages 168-168

a town of France, in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARBONNE">Narbonne</a>, and near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> canal. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 5. N. Lat. 43. 35.

CAPH

Pages 168-168

a Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of capacity for things, estimated by Kimchi at the 30th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the log, by Arbutnott at the 16th part of the hin <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 32d of the seah, amounting to five-eighths of an English pint. The caph does not occur in Scripture as the name of any measure.

CAPHAR

Pages 168-168

a duty which the Turks raised on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> who carry <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> send merchandises from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> and other places in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. This duty of caphar was first imposed by the Christians themselves, when they were in possession of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, for the maintenance of the troops which were planted in difficult passes to observe the Arabs and prevent their incursions. It is still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, and much increased by the Turks, under pretence of defending the Christians against the Arabs; with whom, nevertheless, they keep a secret intelligence, favouring their excursions and plunder.

CAPI-AGA

Pages 168-168
or CAPI-Aga, a Turkish officer who is governor of the gates of the seraglio, or grand master of the seraglio. The capi-aga is the first dignity among the white eunuchs: he is always near the person of the grand signior: he introduces ambassadors to their audience: nobody enters or goes out of the grand signior's apartment but by his means. His office gives him the privilege of wearing the turban in the seraglio, and of going everywhere on horseback. He accompanies the grand signior to the apartment of the sultaness, but stops at the door without entering. His appointment is very moderate; the grand signior bears the expense of his table, and allows him at the rate of about sixty French livres per day; but his office brings him in abundance of presents; no affair of consequence coming to the emperor's knowledge without passing through his hand. The capi-aga cannot be baffled when he quits his post.

CAPIAS

Pages 168-169

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ of two sorts; one before judgment in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and the other after. That before judgment is called capias <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> respondendum, where an original is issued out, to take the defendant, and make him answer the plaintiff. That after judgment is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds; as, Capias ad Satisfaciendum, a writ of execution that issues on a judgment obtained, and lies where any person recovers in a personal action, as for debt, damages, &c. in which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> this writ issues to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, commanding him to take the body of him against whom the debt is recovered, who is to be kept in prison till he makes satisfaction. **Capias pro Fine** is a writ lying where a person is fined to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, for some offence committed against a statute, and he does not discharge the fine according to the judgment; therefore his body shall be taken by this writ, and committed to gaol till the fine is paid. **Capias Ullegatum**, a writ which lies against any one outlawed, upon any action personal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> criminal, by which the sheriff is ordered to apprehend the party outlawed, for not appearing on the exigent, and keep him in safe custody till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of return, when he is ordered to present him to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, to be there farther ordered for his contempt. **Capias in Withernam**, a writ that lies for cattle in withernam: that is, where a distress taken is driven out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, so that the sheriff cannot make deliverance upon a replevin; then this writ issues, commanding the sheriff to take as many beasts of the distrainer, &c. **Capigi**, a porter or doorkeeper of the Turkish feraglio. There are about five hundred capigis or porters in the feraglio, divided into two companies; one consisting of three hundred, under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> called Capigi-Baffa, who has a stipend of three ducats per day; the other consists of two hundred, distinguished by the name of Cucciocapigi, and their chief Cucciocapigi-Baffa, who has two ducats. The capigis have from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> to fifteen alpers per day; some more, others less. Their business is to assist the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">janizaries</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of the first and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> gates of the feraglio; sometimes all together; as when the Turk holds a general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, receives an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, or goes to the mosque; and sometimes only in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; being ranged on either side to prevent people entering with arms, any tumults being made, &c. The word, in its original, signifies, gate. **Capillament**, in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>: whence the word is applied to several things, which on account of their length or their fineness resemble hairs: as, **Capillaments of the Nerves**, in Anatomy, the fine fibres or filaments whereof the nerves are composed. **<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CAPILLARY">Capillary</a>**, in a general sense, an appellation given to things on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> fineness or resembling hair. **Capillary Tuber**, in Physics, are small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> of glass, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> are extremely narrow, their diameter being only a half, a third, or a fourth of a line. The ascent of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, &c., in capillary tubes, is a phenomenon that has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> embarrassed the philosophers; for let one end of a glass tube open at both extremities be immersed in water, the liquor within the tube <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> rise to a considerable height above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> surface: or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> two or more tubes are immersed in the same fluid, one a capillary tube, and the other of a larger bore, the fluid will ascend higher in the former than in the latter; and this will be in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> ratio of the diameters of the tubes.
