In order to account for this phenomenon, it will be necessary first to premise, that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> between the particles of glass and water is greater than the attraction between the particles of water themselves: for if a glass tube be placed in a position <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon, and a drop of water be applied to the under side of the tube, it will adhere to it: nor will it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the glass till its bulk and gravity are so far increased, as to overcome the attraction of the glass. Hence it is easy to conceive how sensibly such a power must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> on the surface of a fluid, not viscid, as water, contained within the small cavity or bore of a glass tube; as also that it will be proportionably stronger as the diameter of the bore is smaller; for it will be evident that the efficacy of the power is in the inverse proportion of the diameter, when it is considered, that such particles only as are in contact with the fluid, and those immediately above the surface, can effect it. Now these particles form a periphery contiguous to the surface, the upper part of which attracts and raises the surface, while the lower part, which is in contact with it, supports it: so that neither the thickness nor length of the tube is of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> here; the periphery of particles only, which is always proportionable to the diameter of the bore, is the only acting power. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the fluid raised will therefore be as the surface of the bore which it fills, that is, as the diameter; for otherwise the effect would not be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the cauld, since the quantities are always as the ratio of the diameters; the heights therefore to which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> will rise, in different tubes, will be inversely as the diameters. Some doubt whether the law holds throughout, of the ascent of the fluid being always higher as the tube is smaller; Dr Hook's experiments, with tubes almost as fine as cobwebs, seem to show the contrary. The water in these, he observes, did not rise so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as one would have expected. The highest he ever found it, was at 21 inches above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the water in the basin; which is much short of what it ought to have been by the law above mentioned. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">Cohesion</a>. **Capillary Vessels.** Many small vessels of animal bodies have been discovered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of injecting the vessels of animals with a coloured fluid, which upon cooling grows hard. But though most anatomists know the manner of filling the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trunks, few are acquainted with the art of filling the capillaries. Dr Monro, in the Medical Essays, has given what after many trials he has found most successful. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJECTION">Injection</a>. **Capillus veneris.** See Adiantum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Capilupi**, or **Capilupus**, Camillus, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> in the 16th century. He wrote a book, entitled, *The Stratagem*; in which he relates not only what was perpetrated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> during the massacre on St Bartholomew's day, but also the artful preparations which preceded that horrid massacre. It is, however, blended with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of falsities. **Capilupi**, Lucius, an Italian poet, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the former, made himself famous by some Centos of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. The manner in which he applied Virgil's expressions to represent things which the poet never dreamt of, is admired. His Cento against women is very ingenious, but too satirical. The poems of Capilupi are inserted in the *Delicia Poetarum Italorum*. **<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPISCOLUS">Capiscolus</a>,**

CAPISCOLUS

Pages 169-170
or Capischolus, in ecclesiastical writers, denotes a dignitary in certain cathedrals, who had the superintendency of the choir, or band of music, answering to what in other churches is called chanter or precentor. The word is also written cabiscolus, and capuscholar, q. d. the head of the school, or band of music. The capiculus is also called scolaisticus, as having the instruction of the young clerks and choristers, how to perform their duty.

CAPITA

Pages 170-170

Succession by, where the claimants are next in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to the ancestor, in their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and not by right of representation.

CAPITAL

Pages 170-171

of the Latin capit "the head," is used, on various occasions, to express the relation of a head, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>: thus, Capital <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">City</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, denotes the principal city of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, state, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. Capital Stock, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, and traders, signifies the sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> which individuals bring to make up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stock of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> when it is first formed. It is also said of the stock which a merchant at first puts into trade for his account. It likewise signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of a trading <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> or corporation, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the word stock is generally added to it. Thus we say, the capital stock of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, &c. The word capital is opposed to that of profit or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>, though the profit often increases the capital, and becomes of itself <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the capital, when joined with the former. Capital Crime, such a one as subjects the criminal to capital <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, that is, to loss of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Capital <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">Picture</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, denotes one of the finest and most excellent pieces of any celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. Capital Letters, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">Printing</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> or initial letters, wherein titles, &c. are composed; with which all periods, verses, &c. commence; and wherewith also all proper names of men, kingdoms, nations, &c. begin. The practice which, for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, obtained among our printers, of beginning every substantive with a capital, is now justly fallen into disrepute; being a manifest perversion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of capitals, as well as an offence against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and distinctness. Capital, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the uppermost part of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> or pilaster, serving as the head or crowning, and placed immediately over the shaft, and under the entablature. See Architecture. Capitana, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Galley, the chief or principal galley of a flote, not dignified with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a kingdom. The capitana was anciently the denomination of the chief galley of France, which the commander went on board of. But since the suppression of the office of captain general of the galleys in 1669, they have no capitana, but the first galley is called reale, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> parone. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITANATA">Capitanata</a>, one of the 12 provinces of the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, on the east by the Terra di <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASILICATA">Basilicata</a> and the Farther Principato, and on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> di Molise and a small part of Hither Abruzzo. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, without trees; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> hot: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, however, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, is fertile in pastures. The capital town is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANFREDONIA">Manfredonia</a>. Capitaneate, in a general sense, the same with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITANIA">capitania</a>. Capitanates, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, are a kind of noble feuds or estates, which, besides their revenue, raise their owners to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. They are otherwise called starofiefs. Capitanei, or Catanei, in Italy, was a denomination given to all the dukes, marquises, and counts, who were called capitanei regis. The same appellation was also given to persons of inferior rank who were invested with fees, formerly distinguished by the appellation valdofres majores. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITANEUS">Capitaneus</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> writers, denotes a tenant in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a>, or chief. Capitaneus Ecclesiae, the same with advocate. Capitania, in Geography, an appellation given to the 12 governments established by the Portuguese in the Brazils. Capitation, a tax or imposition raised on each person, in proportion to his labour, industry, office, rank, &c. It is a very ancient kind of tribute. The Latins call it tributum, by which taxes on persons are distinguished from taxes on merchandise, which were called vexigalia. Capitations are never practised among us but in exigencies of state. In France the capitation was introduced by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in 1695; and is a tax very different from the taille, being levied from all persons, whether they be subject to the taille or not. The clergy pay no capitation, but the princes of the blood are not exempted from it. Capite, in law, (from capit, i.e. rex; whence tenere in capitae, is to hold of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, the head or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> paramount of all the lands in the kingdom): An ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> of land, held immediately of the king, as of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, or by socage. It is now abolished. See Tenure. Capite Censi, in antiquity, the lowest rank of Roman citizens, who in public taxes were rated the least of all, being such as never were worth above 35 s. ales. They were supposed to have been thus called, because they were rather counted and marshalled by their heads than by their estates. The capite censi made part of the sixth class of citizens, being below the proletarii, who formed the other moiety of that class. They were not enrolled in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, as being judged not able to support the expense of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; for in those days the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> maintained themselves. It does not appear that before <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Marius any of the Roman generals lifted the capite censi in their armies. Capitol, Capitolium, in Antiquity, a famous fort or castle, on the Mons Capitolinus at Rome, wherein was a temple dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, thence also denominated Capitolinus, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> anciently assembled; and which still serves as the city <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, or townhouse, for the meeting of the conservators of the Roman people.—It had its name capital, from capit, "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s head," said to have been found fresh, and yet bleeding, upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> the foundation of the temple built in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Jupiter. Arnobius adds, that the man's name was Tolus, whence capit tolium.—The first foundations Capitoline foundations of the capitol were laid by Tarquin the Elder, in the year of Rome 139. His successor Servius raised the walls; and Tarquin the Proud finished it in the year 221. But it was not consecrated till the third year after the expulsion of the kings, and establishment of the consulship. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of the dedication of the temple was performed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> Horatius in 246. The capitol consisted of three parts; a nave sacred to Jupiter, and two wings, the one consecrated to Juno, the other to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>: it was ascended by stairs; the frontispiece and sides were surrounded with galleries, in which those who were honoured with triumphs entertained the senate at a magnificent banquet, after the sacrifice had been offered to the gods. Both the inside and outside were enriched with an infinity of ornaments, the most distinguished of which was the statue of Jupiter with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> thunderbolt, his sceptre, and crown. In the capitol also were a temple to Jupiter the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">Guardian</a>, and another to Juno, with the mint; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the hill was the temple of Concord. This beautiful edifice contained the most sacred deposits of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, such as the ancilia, the books of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIBYLS">Sibyls</a>, &c. The capitol was burnt under Vitellius, and rebuilt under Vespasian. It was burnt a second time by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> under Titus, and restored by Domitian. Anciently the name capitoli was likewise applied to all the principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> in most of the colonies throughout the Roman empire; as at Constantinople, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a>, &c.—That of Thoulouse has given the name of capitouls to the echevins or sheriffs.

CAPITOLINE GAMES

Pages 171-171

annual games instituted by Camillus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Capitolinus, and in commemoration of the capitol's not being taken by the Gauls. Plutarch tells us that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> consisted in the public criers putting up the Hetrurians to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> by auction: they also took an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and tying a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> bulla about his neck, exposed him to the public derision. Festus says they also drested him in a pretexta.—There was another kind of Capitoline games, instituted by Domitian, wherein there were rewards and crowns bestowed on the poets, champions, orators, historians, and musicians. These last Capitoline games were celebrated every five years, and became so famous, that instead of calculating <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by lustra, they began to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> by Capitoline games, as the Greeks did by Olympiads. It appears, however, that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was not of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance.

CAPITOLINUS

Pages 171-171

JULIUS, an historian in the beginning of the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> under Diocletian, to whom he <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> the Lives of Verus, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>, Claudius Balbinus, Macrinus, the Maximins, and the Gordians. He wrote other lives, which are most of them lost.

CAPITOUL

Pages 171-171
or CAPITOL, an appellation given to the chief magistrates of Thoulouse, who have the administration of justice and policy both civil and mercantile in the city. The capitouls at Thoulouse are much the same with the echevins at Paris, and with the consuls, bailiffs, burgomasters, mayors, and aldermen, &c., in other cities. In ancient acts they are called consules, capitarii, or capitolini, and their body capitulums. From this last come the words capitularis and capitouls. The appellative capitolini arose hence, that Capitulate they have the charge and custody of the townhouse, which was anciently called capitoul. The office lasts only one year, and ennobles the bearers. In some ancient acts they are called capitulum novellum Tolosae. Those who have borne it style themselves afterwards burgesses. They are called to all general councils, and have the jus imaginum; that is, when the year of their administration is expired, their pictures are drawn in the townhouse; a custom which they have retained from the ancient Romans, as may be seen in Sigonius.

CAPITULAR

Pages 171-171
or CAPITULARE, denotes an act passed in a chapter, either of knights, canons, or religious. The capitularia or capitulars of Charlemagne, Charles the Bald, &c., are the laws, both ecclesiastical and civil, made by those emperors in the general councils or assemblies of the people; which was the way in which the constitutions of most of the ancient princes were made; each person present, though a plebeian, setting his hand to them. Some distinguish these from laws; and say, they were only supplements to laws. They had their name, capitulars, because divided into capitula, chapters, or sections. In these capitulars did the whole French jurisprudence anciently consist. In process of time, the name was changed for that of ordinances. Some distinguish three kinds of capitulars, according to the difference of their subject matter: those on ecclesiastical affairs are really canons, extracted from councils; those on secular affairs, real laws; those relating to particular persons, or occasions, private regulations.

CAPITULATE

Pages 171-171

an appellation given to the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> districts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Thoulouse, each under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a capitoul; much like the wards of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, under their aldermen. Thoulouse is now divided into eight capitulatures or quarters, which are subdivided into moulants, each of which has its tithingman, whose business is to inform the capitoul of what paffes in his tithing, and to inform the inhabitants of the tithing of the orders of the capitoul.

CAPITULATION

Pages 171-172

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> affairs, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> made between the inhabitants <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> garrison of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> besieged and the besiegers, for the delivering up the place on certain conditions. The most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> and ordinary terms of capitulation are, To <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> out at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> with arms and baggage, drums <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a>, colours <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> lighted at both ends, and some pieces of cannon, waggons and convoys for their baggage, and for their sick and wounded. Capitulation in the German polity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> makes with the electors, in the name of all the princes and states in the empire, before he is declared emperor, and which he ratifies before he is raised to that sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> which the emperor undertakes to observe are, 1. To defend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and empire. 2. To observe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> laws of the empire. 3. To maintain and preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, privileges, and immunities of the electors, princes, and other states of the empire, specified in the capitulation. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> and capitulations are presented to the emperor by the electors only, without the concurrence of the other states. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULUM">Capitulum</a> states, who have complained from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time of such proceedings; and in the time of the Westphalian treaty, in 1648, it was proposed to deliberate in the following diet, upon a way of making a perpetual capitulation; but the electors have always found means of eluding the execution of this article. In order, however, to give some satisfaction to their adversaries, they have inserted in the capitulations of the emperors, and in that of Francis I., in particular, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> all their influence to bring the affair of a perpetual capitulation to a conclusion. Some German authors own, that this capitulation limits the emperor's power; but maintain that it does not weaken his sovereignty: though the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> maintain that he is not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>, because he receives the empire under conditions, which set bound to an absolute authority.

CAPITULUM

Pages 172-172

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, denoted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> read and explained. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they said, *ire <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> capitulum*, "to go to such a lecture." Afterwards the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apartment where such theological exercises were performed was denominated *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOMUS">domus</a> capituli*.

CAPNICON

Pages 172-172

in Antiquity, chimney <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a tax which the Roman emperors levied for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, and which of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was due from all, even the poorest, who kept a fire. This was first invented by Nicephorus.

CAPNOMANCY

Pages 172-172

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a> by means of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> in their sacrifices. The words come from *naevus smoke*, and *pauma divination*. The general rule was, when the smoke was thin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and rose straight up, it was a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the contrary, it was an ill one. There was also another <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of capnomancy, consisting in the observation of the smoke rising from poppy and jasmine seed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon lighted coals.

CAPO FINO

Pages 172-172

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> barren rock in the territory of the Genoese, which has a castle on its eastern peak. Near it is a small harbour of the same name, 13 miles east by south of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>. CAPO d'Iliria, a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in Itria, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIESTE">Trieste</a>, with a bishop's see, and subject to the Venetians. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is wholesome and temperate; its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> revenue consists in wine and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. L. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. o. N. Lat. 45. 48.

CAPON

Pages 172-172

a cock chicken, gelded as soon as left by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as soon as he begins to crow. They are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> either to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> chickens, ducklings, pheasants, &c. and defend them from the kits and buzzards; or to feed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, they being reckoned more delicate than either a cock or a hen.

CAPONIERE

Pages 172-172
or CAPONIERE, in fortification, a covered lodgement sunk four or five feet into the ground encompassed with a little parapet about two feet high, serving to support several planks covered with earth. The caponiere is large enough to contain 15 or 20 soldiers; and is usually placed in the glacis on the extremity of the counterescarp, and in dry moats; having little embrasures for the folders to fire through.

CAPPADOCIA

Pages 174-175

of Christianity, that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> whatever has produced greater champions of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> prelates of more unblemished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. We have now no system of the Cappadocian laws, and scarce wherewithal to form any particular idea of them. As to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, they carried on a considerable trade in horses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of which were produced in their country; and we read of them in Scripture as frequenting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> with this commodity. As Cappadocia abounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, and afforded great store of alabaster, crystal, and jasper, it is probable that they might supply the neighbouring countries with these commodities. The religion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Cappadocians was much the same with that of the Persians. At Comana there was a rich and stately temple dedicated to Bellona; whose battles the priests and their attendants used to represent on stated days, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> and wounding each other as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> seized with an enthusiastic fury. No less famous and magnificent were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> Catanius, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>: the last of which had 3000 sacred servants, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> votaries. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> was next in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> to that of Comana; and, according to Strabo, had a yearly revenue of 15 talents. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> Perica was worshipped in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> called Caflaballa, where women, devoted to the worship of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, were reported to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> barefooted on <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> coals, without receiving any hurt. The temples of Diana at Diofpolis, and of Anias at Zela, were likewise held in great veneration both by the Cappadocians and Armenians, who flocked to them from all parts. In the latter were tendered all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; and the chief among the priests was no way inferior in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, power, and wealth, to any in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; having a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> attendance, and an unlimited authority over all the inferior servants and officers of the temple. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who willingly adopted all the superstitions and superstitious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of the nations they conquered, greatly increased the revenues of this and other temples; conferring the priesthood on such as they thought most fit for carrying on their designs.—We are told that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> sacrifices were offered at Comana; and that this barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was brought by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">Oracles</a> and his sister Iphigenia from Taurica Scythica, where men and women were immolated to Diana. But this custom, if ever it obtained in Cappadocia, was abolished in the times of the Romans.

CAPPARUS

Pages 175-175

a name given by some authors to a worm that adheres to and gnaws the bottoms of ships; to which it is extremely pernicious, especially in the East and West Indies; to prevent this, several ships have lately been sheathed with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; the first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of which was made on his majesty's frigate the Alarm. CAPPARIS. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The buds of this plant pickled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, &c., are brought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> annually from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and the Mediterranean. They are supposed to excite appetite and assist digestion; and to be particularly useful as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETERGENTS">detergents</a> and aperients in obstructions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> and spleen.

CAPRA

Pages 175-175
or Goat. See Mammalia Index. Capra Saltans, in Meteorology, a fiery meteor or exhalation sometimes seen in the atmosphere. It forms an inflected line, resembling in some measure the caperings of a goat; whence it has its name.

CAPRARA

Pages 175-175

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Corsica, on which it depends. It is pretty populous, and has a strong castle for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. It is about 15 miles in circumference. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 5'. N. Lat. 43° 15'. CAPRARIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CAPRAROLA

Pages 175-175

one of the most magnificent palaces in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, seated on a hill, in Ronciglione, whose foot is watered by the river Tircia. It was built by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Farnese; and has five fronts, in the middle of which is a round <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, though all the rooms are <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and well proportioned. It is 27 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Rome. CAPREÆ. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPRI">Capri</a>.

CAPRELUS

Pages 175-175

Elias, an excellent civilian, and learned historian, born at Brescia in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Brescia, and other works: died in 1519.

CAPRI

Pages 175-175

(anciently Caprea), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> at the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 50'. N. Lat. 40° 45'.—The island is only four miles long and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; the city is a bishop's see, and situated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock at the west end of the island. Caprea was anciently famous for the retreat of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Tiberius for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, during which he indulged himself in the most scandalous debaucheries*. Before Tiberius came hither, Capri had attracted the notice of Augustus, as a most eligible retreat, though in sight of populous cities, and almost in the centre of the empire. His successor preferred it to every other residence; and in order to vary his pleasures, and enjoy the advantages as well as avoid the inconveniences of each revolving season, built 12 villas in different situations, dedicated to the 12 greater gods: the ruins of some of them are still to be seen: at Santa <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> are extensive vaults and reservoirs; and on an adjoining brow are the remains of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a>; two broken columns indicate the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. According to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius, this island was wild and barren before the Caesars took it under their immediate protection: at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portion of its surface is uncultivated and impracticable; but every spot that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit the hoe is industriously tilled, and richly laden with the choicest productions of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. The odium attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Tiberius proved fatal to his favourite abode; scarce was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> proclaimed at Rome, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> issued orders for the demolition of every fabric he had raised on the island, which by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> was thenceforward destined to be a state prison. The wife and sister of Commodus were banished to its inhospitable rocks, which were soon stained with their blood. In the middle ages Capri became an appendage of the Amalfitan republic, and after the downfall of that state, belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Naples. There stood a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHAROS">pharos</a> on this island, which, a few days before the death of Tiberius, was overthrown by an earthquake.

CAPRIATA

Pages 175-175
Peter John, a civilian and historian, was born at Genoa. He wrote, in Italian, the history of the wars of Italy; an English translation of which was printed in London in 1663.

CAPRICORN

Pages 175-176

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, one of the 12 signs of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>. See Astronomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> accounted Capricorn the tenth sign; and when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> arrived thereat, it made the winter solstice with regard to our hemisphere: but the stars having advanced a whole sign towards the calf, Capricorn is now rather the 11th sign; and it is at the sun's entry into Sagittary that the solstice happens, though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> manner of speaking is still retained. This sign is represented on ancient monuments, medals, &c., as having the forepart of a goat and the hind-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a fish, which is the form of an Ægipan; sometimes simply under the form of goat. Tropic of Capricorn, a lesser circle of the sphere, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the equinoctial, and at 23° 30' distance from it southwards; passing through the beginning of Capricorn.

CAPRIFICATION

Pages 176-177

a method used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, for ripening the fruit of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> fig tree, by means of insects bred in that of the wild fig tree. The most ample and satisfactory accounts of this curious operation in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a> are those of Tournefort and Pontedera: the former, in his Voyage to the Levant, and in a Memoir delivered to the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1755; the latter, in his Anthologia. The substance of Tournefort's account follows: "Of the thirty <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> varieties of the domestic fig tree which are cultivated in France, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, there are but two cultivated in the Archipelago. The first species is called ornii, from the old Greek erinos, which answers to caprificus in Latin, and signifies a wild fig-tree. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is the domestic or garden fig-tree. The former bears successively, in the same year, three sorts of fruit, called fornites, cratitires, and ornii; which, though not good to eat, are found absolutely necessary towards ripening those of the garden fig. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> have a fleck even skin; are of a deep green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and contain in their dry and mealy inside several <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> placed upon distinct footstalks, the former above the latter. The fornites appear in August, and continue to November without ripening: in these are bred small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, which turn to a sort of gnats nowhere to be seen but about these trees. In October and November, these gnats of themselves make a puncture into the second fruit, which is called cratitires. They do not show themselves till towards the end of September. The fornites gradually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> away after the gnats are gone; the cratitires, on the contrary, remain on the tree till May, and enclose the eggs deposited by the gnats when they pricked them. In May, the third sort of fruit, called ornii, begins to be produced by the wild fig-trees. This is much bigger than the other two; and when it grows to a certain size, and its bud begins to open, it is pricked in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> by the gnats of the cratitires, which are strong enough to go from one fruit to another to deposit their eggs. It sometimes happens that the gnats of the cratitires are slow to come forth in certain parts, while the ornii in those very parts are disposed to receive them. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the husbandman is obliged to look for the cratitires in another part, and fix them at the ends of the branches of those fig-trees whose ornii are in a fit disposition to be pricked by the gnats. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they miss the opportunity, the ornii fall, and the gnats of the cratitires fly away. None but those that are well acquainted with the culture know the critical moment of doing this; and in order to know it, their eye is perpetually fixed on the bud of the fig; for that part not only indicates the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the prickers are to issue forth, but also when the fig is to be successfully pricked; if the bud is too hard and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, the gnat cannot lay its eggs; and the fig drops when the bud is too open. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of all these three sorts of fruit is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> the fruit of the garden fig-tree, in the following manner: During the mouths of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, the peasants take the ornii, at the time their gnats are ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out, and carry them to the garden fig-trees; if they do not nick the moment, the ornii fall; and the fruit of the domestic fig-tree, not ripening, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> in a very little time fall in like manner. The peasants are so well acquainted with these precious moments, that every morning, in making their inspection, they only transfer to their garden fig-trees such ornii as are well conditioned, otherwise they lose their crop. In this case, however, they have one remedy, though an indifferent one; which is, to strew over the garden fig-trees another plant in whose fruit there is also a species of gnats which answer the purpose in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>." The caprification of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, described by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>, Plutarch, Pliny, and other authors of antiquity, corresponds in every circumstance with what is practised at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in the Archipelago and in Italy. These all agree in declaring, that the wild fig-tree, caprificus, never ripened its fruit; but was absolutely necessary for ripening that of the garden or domestic fig, over which the husbandman suspended its branches. The reason of this success has been supposed to be, that by the punctures of these insects the vessels of the fruit are lacerated, and thereby a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of nutritious juice derived thither. Perhaps, too, in depositing their eggs, the gnats leave behind them some sort of liquor proper to ferment gently with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of the figs, and to make their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> tender. The figs in Provence, and even at Paris, ripen much sooner for having their buds pricked with a straw dipped in olive-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. Plums and pears likewise, pricked by some insects, ripen much the faster for it; and the flesh round such puncture is better taffed than the rest. It is not to be disputed, that considerable changes happen to the texture of fruits so pricked, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> the same as to parts of animals pierced with any sharp <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. Others have supposed that these insects penetrated the fruit of the tree to which they were brought, and gave a more free admission to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. Linnaeus explained the operation, by supposing that the insects brought the farina from the wild fig, which contained male flowers only, to the domestic fig, which contained the female ones. Hafelquist, from what he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, seemed to doubt of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of fructification. M. Bernard, in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, opposes it more decidedly. He could never find the insect in the cultivated fig; and, in reality, it appeared to leave the wild fig, after the flamina were mature, and their pollen dissipated: besides, he adds, what they may have brought on their wings must be rubbed away, in the little aperture which they would form for themselves. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, where there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight varieties of the domestic fig, this operation is only performed on those which ripen latest: the former are of a proper size, fine flavour, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance without it; so that he thinks the caprification only hampers the ripening. Caprimul. ripening. He examined the parts of fructification of the fig; and he observes, if this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> be made previous to the ripening, that round the eye of the fig, and in the subfance of its covering, may be seen triangular dentated leaves, prefed one against another; and under these leaves are the flamina, whose pollen is defined for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a> of the grains, which fill the rest of the fruit. These male organs are much more numerous in the wild fig than in the domestic; and the flamina are found to contain a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> dust, which may be collected when it is ripe. The wild figs, when ripe, are not succulent, and have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, though the grains are disposed in the same manner as in the other kind. The pith of the grain of the wild fruit serves as food to a species of the cynips, whose larva is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, till the moment of its transformation; and it is by an opening, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a>, that the insect penetrates the grain. From this account it is thought probable that the insect is only communicated by accident to the domestic fig, and that the flowers of this genus are sometimes hermaphrodites. But the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of hermaphrodite flowers being fewer on the cultivated than on the wild fig, the seeds are fecundated more certainly and quickly by the capricious; and every botanist knows, that when the impregnation is completed, the flower soon withers; while, if by any accident it is delayed, it continues in bloom much longer. This view of the subject, therefore, explains very completely the reason why, in Malta, the capricious is practised on the late kind of figs, because it hastens the formation and maturity of the fruit.

CAPRIOLLES

Pages 177-177

in the Manege, leaps that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> makes in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> without advancing, in such a manner, that, when he is at the height of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>, he jerks out with his hinder legs even and near. It is the most difficult of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> manege. It differs from a croupade, in this, that, in a croupade, a horse does not show his floes; and from a ballotade, because in this he does not jerk out. To make a horse <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> well at caprioles, he must be put between two pillars, and taught to raise first his fore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, and then his hind quarters while his fore ones are yet in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; for which end you must give him the whip and the poinson.

CAPSA

Pages 177-177

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>, situated amidst vast deserts, waste, uncultivated, and full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, where Jugurtha kept his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>. In his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was taken and razed by Marius the Roman general, who put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> all the citizens capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> arms, and sold the rest for slaves. It was, however, afterwards rebuilt by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and strongly fortified; but, on the decline of their empire, was taken and demolished a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time, by Occuba a famous Arab general. The walls of the citadel are still remaining, and are monuments of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and strength of Capfa. They are 24 fathoms in height, and five in thickness, built of large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and have now acquired the solidity and firmness of a rock. The walls of the town were rebuilt by the inhabitants since their first demolition; but were afterwards destroyed by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> Almanzar, who sent a governor and troops into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. In Marmol's time Capfa was very populous, and abounded with Caparius, stately mosques and other structures of superb and elegant workmanship: but at present it is occupied by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and indigent people, fleeced and oppressed by the Tunisian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. In the very centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> stands an enclosed fountain, which both supplies the people with drink, and affords them an agreeable bath. The adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is now cultivated, and produces several kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is unhealthy. The inhabitants are remarkable for their peevishness of temper. Both men and women dress handsomely except their feet, which they cover with coarse shoes of bungling workmanship, and made of the rough skins of wild beasts, equally inconvenient and unbecoming. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 3. N. Lat. 33. 15.

CAPSARIUS

Pages 177-177

among the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, was he who had the care of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coffer.

CAPSICUM

Pages 177-177
or Guinea-pepper. Sec Botany Index. The bell-pepper produces fruit fit for pickling; for which purpose they must be gathered before they arrive at their full size, while their rind is tender. They must be slit down on one side to get out the seeds, after which they should be soaked two or three days in salt and water; when they are taken out of this and drained, boiling vinegar must be poured on them in a sufficient quantity to cover them, and closely stopped down for two months; then they should be boiled in the vinegar to make them green; but they want no addition of any spice, and are the wholesomest and best pickle in the world. Another species is used for making what is called cayen-butter or pepper-pot, by the inhabitants of America, and which they esteem the best of all the spices. The following is a receipt for making of a pepper-pot: "Take of the ripe seeds of this sort of capsicum, and dry them well in the sun; then put them into an earthen or stone pot, mixing flour between every stratum of pods; and put them into an oven after the baking of bread, that they may be thoroughly dried; after which they must be well cleansed from the flour; and if any of the stalks remain adhering to the pods, they should be taken off, and the pods reduced to a fine powder; to every ounce of this add a pound of wheat flour, and as much leaven as is sufficient for the quantity intended. After this has been properly mixed and wrought, it should be made into small cakes, and baked in the same manner as common cakes of the same size: then cut them into small parts, and bake them again, that they may be as dry and hard as biscuit; which being powdered and sifted, is to be kept for use." This is prodigiously hot and acrimonious, setting the mouth as it were on fire. It is by some recommended as a medicine for flatulencies; but it is greatly to be doubted whether all those hot irritating medicines are not productive of more harm than good, in this country at least. If the ripe pods of capsicum are thrown into the fire, they will raise strong and noisome vapours, which occasion vehement sneezing,

CAPSQUARES

Pages 177-178

strong plates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> which come over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNNIONS">trunnions</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, and keep it in the carriage. They are fastened by a hinge to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>-plate, that they may lift up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> in the middle to receive a third part of the thickness of the trunnions: for two-thirds are let into the carriage, and the other end is fastened by two iron wedges called the fore-locks and keys.

CAPSTAN

Pages 178-178
or CAPSTERN, a strong maffy column of timber, formed like a truncated cone, and having its upper extremity pierced with a number of holes to receive the bars or levers. It is let perpendicularly down through the decks of a ship; and is fixed in such a manner, that the men, by turning it horizontally with their bars, may perform any work which requires an extraordinary effort. A capstern is composed of several parts, where A is the barrel, b the whelps, c the drumhead, and d the spindle. The whelps rise out from the main body of the capstern like buttresses, to enlarge the sweep, so that a greater quantity of cable, or whatever rope encircles the barrel, may be wound about it at one turn, without adding much to the weight of the capstern. The whelps reach downwards from the lower part of the drumhead to the deck. The drumhead is a broad cylindrical piece of wood resembling a mill-stone, and fixed immediately above the barrel and whelps. On the outside of this piece are cut a number of square holes parallel to the deck to receive the bars. The spindle or pivot d, which is fitted with iron, is the axis or foot upon which the capstern rests, and turns round in the saucer, which is a sort of iron socket let into a wooden stock or standard called the flop, resting upon and bolted to the beams. Besides the different parts of the capstern above explained, it is furnished with several appurtenances, as the bars, the pins, the pawls, the swifter, and the saucer, already described. The bars are long pieces of wood, or arms, thrust into a number of square holes in the drumhead all round, in which they are as the radius of a circle, or the spokes in the nave of a wheel. They are used to heave the capstern round, which is done by the men setting their breasts against them, and walking about, like the machinery of a horse mill, till the operation is finished.—The pins e, are little bolts of iron thrust perpendicularly through the holes of the drumhead, and through a correspondent hole in the end of the bar, made to receive the pins when the bars are fixed. They are used to confine the bars, and to prevent them from working out as the men heave, or when the ship labours. Every pin is fastened to the drumhead with a small iron chain; and that the bars may exactly fit their respective holes, they are all numbered.—The pawls f, No. 1, are situated on each side the capstern, being two short bars of iron, bolted at one end through the deck to the beams close to the lower part of the whelps; the other end which occasionally turns round on the deck, being placed in the intervals of the whelps, as the capstern turns round, prevents it from recoiling or turning back by any sudden jerk of the cable, as the ship rises on the sea, which might greatly endanger the men who heave. There are also hanging pawls gg, No. 3, used for the same purpose, reaching from the deck above to the drumhead immediately below it. The swifter is a rope passed horizontally through holes in the outer end of the bars, and drawn very tight; the intent of this is to keep the men steady as they walk round when the ship rocks, and to give room for a greater number to assist by pulling upon the swifter itself. The most frequent use of the capstern is to heave in the cable, and thereby remove the ship or draw up the anchor. It is also used to wind up any weighty body, as the masts, artillery, &c. In merchant ships it is likewise frequently employed to discharge or take in the cargo, particularly when consisting of weighty materials that require a great exertion of ref="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical powers to be removed. There are commonly two capsterns in a man of war, the main and the gear capstern; the former of which has two drumheads, and may be called a double one. This is represented in No. 3. The latter is represented in No. 2. Formerly the bars of the capstern went entirely through the head of it, and consequently were more than double the length of the present ones; the holes were therefore formed at different heights, as represented in No. 1. But this machine had several inconveniences, and has long been entirely disused in the navy. Some of these sort of capsterns, however, are still retained in merchant ships, and are usually denominated crabs. The situation of the bars in a crab, as ready for heaving, is represented in No. 4. To rig the CAPSTERN, is to fix the bars in their respective holes, and thrust in the pins, in order to confine them.—Surge the CAPSTERN, is the order to slacken the rope heaved round upon it, of which there are generally two turns and a half about the barrel at once, and sometimes three turns.—To Heave the CAPSTERN, is to go round with it heaving on the bars, and drawing in any rope of which the purchase is created.—To Come-up the CAPSTERN, is to let go the rope upon which they had been heaving.—To Pawl the CAPSTERN, is to fix the pawls to prevent it from recoiling during any pause of heaving.

CAPSULE

Pages 178-180

among botanists, a dry hollow seed-vessel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pericarpium, that cleaves or splits in some determinate manner. See Pericarpium, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of seed-vessel is frequently fleshy and succulent, like a berry, before it has attained maturity; but, in ripening, becomes dry, and often so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> as to dart the seeds from their departments with considerable velocity. This elasticity is remarkably conspicuous in wood <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>; balfan impatiens; African spirea, diosma; fraxinella; justicia; ruellia; barleria; lathra; and many others.—The general aptitude or disposition of this species of seed-vessel to cleave or separate for the purpose of dispersing its seeds, distinguishes it not less remarkably than its texture from the pulpy or succulent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the apple, berry, and cherry kind. This opening of the capsule for discharging ging its seeds when the fruit is ripe, is either at the top, as in most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; at the bottom, as in triglochin; at the side, through a pore or small hole, as in campanula and orchis; horizontally, as in plantain, amaranthus, and anagallis; or longitudinally, as in convolvulus. All fruit that is jointed opens at every one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, each of which contains a single seed. Capsules, in splitting, are divided, externally, into one or more pieces, called by Linnaeus valves. The internal divisions of the capsules are called cells, locula menta: these, in point of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, are exceedingly diversified; some having only one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, as the primrose; and others many, as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> lily. Hence a capsule is termed unilocular, bilocular, trilocular, &c., according as it has one, two, three, &c., cells or cavities. Capsule Atrabiliaria, called also glandula renalis, and renes succenturiatae. See Anatomy Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> officer, whereof there are several kinds, according to their commands. Captain of a Troop or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, an inferior officer who commands a troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or a company of foot, under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a>. The duty of this officer is to be careful to keep his company full of able-bodied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>; to visit their tents and lodgings, to see what is wanting; to pay them well; to cause them to keep themselves neat and clean in their clothes, and their arms bright. He has power in his own company of making sergeants, corporals, and lancepates. In the horse and foot guards, the captains have the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of colonels. Captain General, he who commands in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. Captain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a>, he who with the rank of captain, but the pay of lieutenant, commands a troop or company in the name and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of some other person who is dispensed with, on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, from performing the functions of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>. Thus the colonel being usually captain of the first company of his regiment, that company is commanded by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Captain-lieutenant. So in England, as well as in France, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, dauphin, princes, &c., have usually the title of captain of the guards, gens d'armes, &c., the real duty of which offices is performed by captain-lieutenants. Captain Reformed, one who, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the forces, has his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> and company suppressed; yet is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> captain, either as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> to another, or without any post or command at all. Captain of a Ship of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, the officer who commands a ship of the line of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, or a frigate carrying 22 or more cannon. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of a captain in his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> is very comprehensive, in as much as he is not only answerable for any bad conduct in the military <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and equipment of the ship he commands, but also for any neglect of duty or ill management in his inferior officers, whose several charges he is appointed to superintend and regulate. On his first receiving information of the condition and quality of the ship he is appointed to command, he must attend constantly, and hasten the necessary preparations to fit her for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. So strict, indeed, are the injunctions laid on him by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, or commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, that he is forbidden to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> out of his ship, from his arrival on board to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of his discharge, unless by particular leave from the admiralty or from his commander in chief. He is enjoined to show a laudable example of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and virtue to the officers and men; and to discontinue all dissolute, immoral, and disorderly practices, and such as are contrary to the rules of subordination and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; as well as to correct those who are guilty of such offences as are punishable according to the usage of the sea. He is ordered particularly to survey all the military stores which are sent on board, and to return whatever is deemed unfit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. His diligence and application are required to procure his complement of men; observing carefully to enter only such as are fit for the necessary duty, that the government may not be put to unnecessary expense. When his ship is fully manned, he is expected to keep the established number of men complete, and superintend the muster himself <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there is no clerk of the check at the port. When his ship is employed on a cruising station, he is expected to keep the sea the whole length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> previously appointed; but if he is compelled by some unexpected accident to return to port sooner than the time limited, he ought to be very cautious in the choice of a good situation for anchoring, ordering the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> or other careful officers to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and discover the depths of water and dangers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. Previous to any possibility of an engagement with the enemy, he is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> the officers and men to the necessary stations according to their office and abilities, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> them in the management of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, that they may be more expert in time of battle. His station in the time of an engagement is on the quarter-deck: at which time he is expected to take all opportunities of annoying his enemy, and improving every advantage over him; to exhibit an example of courage and fortitude to his officers and crew; and to place his ship opposite to his adversary in such a position as that every cannon shall do effectual execution. At the time of his arrival in port, after his return from abroad, he is to assemble his officers, and draw up a detail of the observations that have been made during the voyage, of the qualities of the ship as to her <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a>, ballast, stowage, manner of sailing, for the information and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of those who may succeed him in the command: and this account is to be signed by himself and officers, and to be returned to the resident <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the navy at the port where the ship is discharged. Captain of a Merchant-ship, he who has the direction of the ship, her crew, and lading, &c. In small ships and short voyages, he is more ordinarily called the master. In the Mediterranean, he is called the patroon.—The proprietor of the vessel appoints the captain or master; and he is to form the crew, and choose and hire the pilots, mates, and seamen; though, where the proprietor and master reside on the same spot, they generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> together. Captain Bajhaw, or Capoadan Bajhaw, in the policy of the Turks, signifies the Turkish high admiral. He possesses the third office of the empire, and is invested with the same power at sea that the vizier has on shore. Soliman II. instituted this office in favour of the famous Barbarossa, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> authority over the officers of the marine and arsenal, whom he may punish, cashier, or put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, as soon as he is with- out the Dardanelles. He commands in chief in all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> countries, cities, castles, &c., and, at Constantinople, is the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> in the villages on the side of the Porte, and the canal of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> sea. The mark of his authority is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, which he carries in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, both in the arsenal and with the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>.—The captain balmaw enjoys two sorts of revenues; the one fixed, the other casual. The first arises from a capitation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Archipelago, and certain governments in Nato- lia and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GALIPOLI">Galipoli</a>. The latter consists in the pay of the men who die during a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>; in a fifth of all prizes made by the begs; in the profits accruing from the labour of the slaves, whom he hires as rowers to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior; and in the contributions he exacts in all places where he passes.

CAPTION

Pages 180-180

in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ issuing under his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIGNET">signet</a>, in his majesty's name, obtained at the instance of a creditor in a civil debt, commanding messengers at arms and other officers of the law to apprehend and imprison the person of the debtor until he pay the debt.—It is also the name of a writ issued by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of session against the agents of the court, to return papers belonging to processes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> law suits, or otherwise to go to prison.

CAPTIVE

Pages 180-180

a slave <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a person taken from the enemy. Formerly captives in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> became the slaves of those who took them; and though <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, such as obtained among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, is now abolished, some shadow of it still remains in respect of prisoners of war, who are accounted the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of their captors, and have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> but by concession from them. —The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> used their captives with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> severity; their necks were exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to be trampled on, and their persons afterwards sold by public auction. Captives were frequently burnt in the funeral piles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> warriors, as a sacrifice to the infernal gods. Those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> or noble blood had their heads thrown, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> sent to Rome to serve as decorations for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> toys, &c. They were led in triumph loaded with chains through Rome, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s train, at least as far as the foot of the Capitoline mount, for they were not permitted to ascend the sacred hill, but carried thence to prison.
