Those of the prime <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> were honoured with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> chains on their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet, and golden collars on their necks. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they made their escape, or killed themselves, to avoid the ignominy of being carried in triumph, their images or effigies were frequently carried in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

CAPTIVITY

Pages 180-180

in sacred <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> which God inflicted upon his people for their vices and infidelities. The first of these captivities is that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, from which Moses delivered them; after which, are reckoned six during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the judges; but the greatest and most remarkable were those of Judah and Israel, which happened under the kings of each of these kingdoms. It is generally believed, that the ten tribes of Israel never came back again after their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a>; and Josephus and St Jerome are of this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>: nevertheless, when we examine the writings of the prophets, we find the return of Israel from captivity pointed out in a manner almost as clear as that of the tribes of Benjamin and Judah: See Hosea i. 10, 11. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOS">Amos</a> ix. 14. The captivities of Judah are generally reckoned four; the fourth and last of which fell in the year of the world 3416, under Zedekiah: and from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> begins the 70 years captivity foretold by Jeremiah. Since the destruction of the temple by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the Hebrews boast that they have always had their heads <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> particular princes, whom they call princes of the captivity, in the east and west. The princes of the captivity in the east governed the Jews that dwelt in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; and the princes of the captivity in the west governed those who dwelt in Judea, Egypt, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and in other parts of the Roman empire. He who resided in Judea <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> took up his abode at Tiberias, and assumed the name of Rabbi, "head of the fathers or patriarchs." He presided in assemblies, decided in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>, levied taxes for the expenses of his visits, and had officers under him who were despatched through the provinces for the execution of his orders. As to the princes of the captivity at Babylon, or the east, we know neither the original nor succession of them. It only appears that they were not in being before the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century.

CAPTURE

Pages 180-180

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prey; particularly that of a ship taken at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Captures made at sea were formerly held to be the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the captors after a possession of twenty-four hours; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authorities require, before the property can be changed, the goods must have been brought into port, and have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a night intra praedia, in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of safe custody, so that all hope of recovering them was lost.

CAPUA

Pages 180-181

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a very ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in Campania, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of that district. It is famous for the abode of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> the Carthaginian general after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Cannae, and where Livy accuses him, but unjustly, of having enervated himself with pleasures.* It still retains the name, and is the *See Capua of an archbishop. It is seated on the river Volturnus, no, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 5. N. Lat. 41. 7. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Capua is thus shortly deduced by Mr Swinburne. "It was a settlement of the Osci long before the foundation of Rome. As the amazing fertility of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> and a lucrative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> poured immense wealth upon its inhabitants, it became one of the most extensive and magnificent cities in the world. With <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> excessive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> crept in, and the Capuans grew insolent; but by their effeminacy they soon lost the power of repelling those neighbouring nations which their insolence had exasperated. For this reason Capua was continually exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of calling for foreign aid, and endangering its safety by the uncommon temptations it offered to needy auxiliaries. The Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> sent to defend Capua were on the point of making it their prey, and often the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the Roman people was loud for a removal from the barren unwholesome banks of the Tiber to the garden of Italy, near those of the Volturnus. Through well-founded jealousy of the ambition of Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as Livy and other partial writers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> it, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> inconstancy, the Capuans warmly espoused the quarrel of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>: Hannibal made Capua his winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> after the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of Cannae; and there, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we are to believe historians, his rough and hitherto invincible soldiers were enervated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and indolence. "When through a failure of supplies from Carthage Hannibal was under a necessity of remaining in Bruttium, and leaving the Capuans to defend themselves, this city, which had been long invested, was surrendered at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> to the consuls Appius Claudius and Q. Fulvius Flaccus. The senators were put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> imprisoned for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and all the citizens sold and dispersed. Vibius, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of Hannibal's friends, avoided this ignominious fate, and escaped from the cruel vengeance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by a voluntary death. —When the mob inflicted upon the gates being thrown open to the enemy, Vibius assembled his heady associates, and sat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with them to a superb banquet, after which each of the guests swallowed a poisonous draught, and expired in full possession of their freedom. The buildings were spared by the victor; and Capua was left to be merely a harbour for the husbandmen of the plain, a warehouse for goods, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a> for corn; but so advantageous a situation could not long be neglected; colonies were sent to inhabit it, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it regained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of importance. "Genetrix the Vandal was more cruel than the Roman conquerors had been; for he massacred the inhabitants, and burnt the town to the ground. Narves rebuilt it; but in 841 it was totally destroyed by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Saracens, and the inhabitants driven into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Some time after the retreat of these <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> invaders, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a> ventured down again into the plain; but not deeming their force adequate to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a circuit as the old city, they built themselves a smaller one on the river, and called it Capua.—They chose the site of Caflinum, famous in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, for the refinance made by its garrison against Hannibal. Since the foundation of the new city, Old Capua has remained in ruins. "In 856, Landulph formed here an independent earldom dismembered from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENEVENTO">Benevento</a>, and in the course of a few generations Capua acquired the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality. In the 11th century, the Normans of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AVERSA">Aversa</a> expelled the Lombard <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of princes, and Richard their chief became <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Capua; the grandson of Tancred of Hauteville drove out the descendants of Richard, and united this state to the rest of his possessions. "Capua is at present a neat little city, fortified according to the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> art, and may be considered as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; though far removed from the frontier, it is the only fortification that really covers the approach to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>."

CAPUCHINS

Pages 181-181
religious of the order of St Francis in its strictest observance; deriving their name from capucis, or capuchon, a stuff cap, or cowl, wherewith they cover their heads. They are clothed with brown or gray; always barefooted; are never to go in a coach, nor ever shave their beard.—The Capuchins are a reform made from the order of Minors, commonly called Cordeliers, set on foot in the 16th century by Matthew Bachi, a religious observant of the monastery of Montefalcone; who, being at Rome, was advertised several times from heaven, to practise the rule of St Francis to the letter. Upon this he made application to Pope Clement in 1525: who gave him permission to retire into a solitude, with as many others as chose to embrace the strict observance. In 1528, they obtained the pope's bull. In 1529, the order was brought into complete form: Matthew was elected general, and the chapter made constitutions. In 1543, the right of preaching was taken from the Capuchins by the pope: but in 1545 it was restored to them again with honour. In 1578, there were already 17 general chapters in the order of Capuchins.

CAPUT

Pages 181-181

the head. See HEAD. CAPUT baroniae, the head of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> customs, denotes the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> seat or castle of a nobleman, where he made his usual residence, and held his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; sometimes also called caput honoris, or the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. The caput baroniae could not be settled in dowry; nor could it be divided among the daughters, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> there was no son to inherit; but was to descend entire to the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, ceteris filiabus aliounde satisfactis. CAPUT gallinaginis, in Anatomy, is a kind of septum, or spongy border, at the extremities or apertures of each of the vesiculae seminales; serving to prevent the seed coming from one side, from rushing upon, and so stopping, the discharge of the other. CAPUT lupinum. Anciently an outlawed felon was said to have caput lupinum, and might be knocked on the head like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>, by any one that should meet him; because, having renounced all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he was to be dealt with as in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, when every one that should find him might slay him; yet now, to avoid such inhumanity, it is holden that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is entitled to kill him wantonly and wilfully; but in so doing he is guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, unless it is done in the endeavour to apprehend him. CAPUT Mortuum, a Latin name given to fixed and exhausted residuum remaining in retorts after distillations. As these residua are very different, according to the substances distilled, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> employed, they are by the more accurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> chemists particularly specified by adding a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> denoting their qualities; as earthy residuum, cherty residuum, saline residuum, &c.

CARABINE

Pages 181-181

a fire arm shorter than a musket, carrying a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of 24 in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, borne by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, hanging at a belt over the left shoulder. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> is two feet and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and is sometimes furrowed spirally within, which is said to add to the range of the piece.

CARABINEERS

Pages 181-181

regiments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, carrying longer carabines than the rest, and sometimes used on foot. CARABUS. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CARACALLA

Pages 181-182

M. Antoninus Bassianus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> after his father Severus in 211, put the physicians to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> for not despatching his father, as he would have had them. He killed his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Geta; and put Papinius to death, because he would not defend nor excuse his patricide. In short, it is said that 20,000 persons was massacred by his order. He married Julia, his father's widow. Going to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, he slew the inhabitants, and applied to the magicians and astrologers. At last, going from Edessa to Mesopotamia, Caracalla one of his captains slew him, by order of Macrinus, who succeeded him. He died after he had reigned somewhat more than six years. Caracalla, in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> garment, having a sort of capuchin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hood a-top, and reaching to the heels; worn equally among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by the men and the women, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. Spartan and Xiphilian represent the emperor Caracalla as the inventor of this garment, and hence suppose the appellation Caracalla was first given him. Others, with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, make the caracalla originally a Gallic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and only brought to Rome by the emperor above-mentioned, who first enjoined the soldiery to wear it. The people call it antoninian, from the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who had borrowed the name of Antoninus. The caracalla was a sort of caftan, or furtout. Salmasius, Scaliger, and after them Du Cange, even take the name caftaque to have been formed from that of caftaque, for caracalla. This is certain from St Jerome, that the caracalla, with a retrenchment of the capuchin, became an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> garment. It is described as made of several pieces cut and sewed together, and hanging <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the feet; but it is more than probable there were some made shorter, especially out of Rome, otherwise we do not see how it could have fitted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>' purposes.

CARACCAS

Pages 182-182

a district of Terra Firma in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, belonging to the Spaniards. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> is rocky and mountainous, interspersed with small fertile valleys; subjected at certain seasons of the year to dry <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west winds, but blest in general with a clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and wholesome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. A very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> illicit trade is carried on by the English and Dutch with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, notwithstanding all the vigilance of the Spaniards, who have scouts perpetually employed, and breastworks raised in all the valleys. A vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CACAO">cacao</a> trees are cultivated in this province; and it is reckoned that the crop of cacao produced here amounts to more than 100,000 fanegas of 110 pounds each. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SANTA_FE">Santa Fe</a> confumes 20,000; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> a little more; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a> a small cargo; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> from 50 to 60,000. The cultivation of the plant employs 10 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12,000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>. Such of them as have obtained their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> have built a little town called Nirva, into which they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not admit any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> people. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is likewise called Caracas, and is situated in N. Lat. 10° 10'. Dampier says it stands at a considerable distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, wealthy, and populous; and extremely difficult of access, by reason of the steep and craggy hills over which an enemy must take his rout. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of this town, to which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Guaira at two leagues' distance serves for a harbour, was for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> open to all the subjects of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, and is still so to the Americans; but the Europeans are not so well treated. In 1728 a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> was formed at St Sebastian, which obtained an exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of maintaining connexions with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the new world. Four or five ships which they dispatch every year, sail from thence, but they return to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>.

CARACCI

Pages 182-183
Lewis, Augustine, and Hannibal, three celebrated painters of the Lombard school, all of Bologna. Lewis was born in 1555; and was cousin-german to Augustine and Hannibal, who were brothers, the sons of a taylor, who was yet careful to give them a liberal education. They were both disciples of Caracci, their cousin Lewis. Augustine gained a knowledge of mathematics, ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural philosophy, music, poetry, and most of the liberal arts; but, though painting was his principal pursuit, he learned the art of engraving from Cornelius Cort, and surpassed all the masters of his time. Hannibal, again, never deviated from his pencil. These three painters, at length, having reaped all the advantages they could by contemplation and practice, formed a plan of association, continued always together, and laid the foundation of that celebrated school which has ever since been known by the name of Caracci's academy. Hither all the young students, who had a view of becoming masters, resorted to be instructed in the rudiments of painting; and here the Caracci taught freely, and without reserve, all that came. Lewis's charge was to make a collection of antique statues and bas-reliefs. They had designs of the best masters, and a collection of curious books on all subjects relating to their art; and they had a skilful anatomist always ready to teach what belonged to the knitting and motions of the muscles, &c. There were often disputations in the academy; and not only painters, but men of learned professions, proposed questions, which were always decided by Lewis. Every body was well received; and though flattered hours were allotted to treat of different matters, yet improvements might be made at all hours by the antiquities and the designs which were to be seen. The fame of the Caracci reaching Rome, the cardinal Farnese sent for Hannibal thither, to paint the gallery of his palace. Hannibal was the more willing to go, because he had a great desire to see Raphael's works, with the antique statues and bas-reliefs. The gusto which he took there from the ancient sculpture, made him change his Bolognian manner for one more learned but less natural in the design and in the colouring. Augustine followed Hannibal, to assist him in his undertaking of the Farnese gallery; but the brothers not rightly agreeing, Farnese sent Augustine to the court of the duke of Parma, where he died in the year 1602, being only 45 years of age. His most celebrated piece of painting is that of the Communion of St Jerome, in Bologna. In the mean while, Hannibal continued working in the Farnese gallery at Rome; and, after inconceivable pains and care, finished the paintings in the perfection in which they are now to be seen. He hoped that the cardinal would have rewarded him in some proportion to the excellence of his work, and the time it took him up, which was eight years; but he was disappointed. The cardinal, influenced by an ignorant Spaniard, his domestic, gave him but a little above 200l. though it is certain he deserved more than twice as many thousands. When the money was brought him, he was so surprized at the injustice done him, that he could not speak a word to the person who brought it. This confirmed him in a melancholy to which his temper naturally inclined, and made him resolve never more to touch his pencil; which resolution he had undoubtedly kept if his necessities had not compelled him to break it. It is said, that his melancholy gained so much upon him, that at certain times it deprived him of the use of his senses. It did not, however, put a stop to his amours; and his debauches at Naples, whither he had retired for the recovery of his health, brought a distemper upon him, of which he died in 1629, when he was 49 years of age. His veneration for Raphael was so great, that it was his deathbed request to be buried in the same tomb with him; which was accordingly done, in the pantheon or rotunda at Rome. There are extant several prints of the blest Virgin, and some other subjects, etched by the hand of this incomparable artist. He is said to have been a friendly, plain, honest, and open-hearted man; very communicative to his scholars, and so extremely kind to them, that he generally kept his money in the same box with his colours, where they might have recourse to either as they had occasion. While Hannibal Caracci worked at Rome, Lewis was courted from all parts of Lombardy, especially by the clergy, to make pictures in their churches; and we may judge of his capacity and facility, by the great number of pictures he made, and by the preference that was given him to other painters. In the midst of these employments Hannibal solicited him to come and assist him in the Farnese gallery; and so earnestly, that he could not avoid complying with his request. He went to Rome; corrected several things in that gallery; painted a figure or two himself; and then returned to Bologna, where he died in 1619, aged 64.

CARACOL

Pages 183-183

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, denotes a staircase in a helix <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spiral form.

CARACOLI

Pages 183-183

a kind of metal of which the Caribbeans, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> natives of the Lesser Antilles, make a sort of ornament in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, which they also call caracoli.—This metal comes from the main <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is, that it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, something like the Corinthian bras among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> are so perfectly mixed and incorporated together, that the compound which results from them, it is said, has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> that never alters, how <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> soever it remains in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> or under ground. It is somewhat brittle; and they who <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> at it are obliged to mix a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion of gold with it, to make the compound more tough and malleable.

CARACT

Pages 183-183
or CARAT, the name of that weight which expresses the degree of fineness that gold is of. The word is also written carract, carrat, karrat, and karat. Its origin is contested: but the most probable opinion is, that of Kennet, who derives it from careola, a term which anciently denoted any weight, and came not till of later days to be appropriated to that which expresses the fineness of gold and the gravity of diamonds. These carats are not real determinate weights, but only imaginary. The whole mass, be the weight what it will, is conceived to be divided into 24 carats; and as many 24th parts as it contains of pure gold, it is called gold of so many carats or so many carats fine. Thus, gold of 18 carats is a mixture, of which 18 parts are pure gold, and the other fix an inferior metal, &c.—This is the common way of reckoning in Europe, and at the gold mines in the Spanish West Indies, but with some variation in the subdivision of the carat: among us, it is divided into four grains; among the Germans, into 12 parts; and by the French, according to Mr Helot, into 32. The Chinese reckon by a different division called touches, of which the highest number, or that which denotes pure gold, is 100; so that 100 touches correspond to our 24 carats, &c. CARACT is also a certain weight which goldsmiths and jewellers use wherewith to weigh precious stones and pearls.—In this sense, the word is by some supposed to be derived from the Greek καράτων, a fruit which the Latins call filique, and we carob bean; each of which may weigh about four grains of wheat, whence the Latin filique has been used for a weight of four grains. This caract weighs four grains, but they are sometimes lighter than the grains of other weights. Each of these grains is subdivided in 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, &c.

CARACTACUS

Pages 183-183

a renowned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> British people called Silures, inhabiting South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. Having valiantly defended his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, he was at length defeated; and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> to Cartimunda, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the Brigantes (inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>), was by her treacherously delivered up to the Romans, and led in triumph to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius then at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; where his noble behaviour, and heroic but pathetic speech, obtained him not only his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, but the esteem of the emperor, A.D. 52.

CARAGOUTH

Pages 183-183

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of the empire, weighing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> drachms. It goes at Constantinople for 120 aspers. There are four sorts of them, which are all equally current and of the same value.

CARAITES

Pages 183-184

in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Jews, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> among that people, whereof there are still some subsisting in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, Russia, Constantinople, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, and other places of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, whose distinguishing tenet and practice it is, to adhere closely to the words and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the Scripture, exclusive of allegories, traditions, and the like. Leo of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, a rabbin of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, observes, that of all the heresies among that people, before the destruction of the temple, there is none now left but that of the Caraim, a name derived from Micra, which signifies the pure text of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, because of their keeping to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, observing it to the letter, and rejecting all interpretations, paraphrases, and constitutions of the rabbins. Aben <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a>, and some other rabbins, treat the Caraites as Sadducees; but Leo de Juda calls them, more accurately, Sadducees reformed; because they believe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, paradise, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>, &c., which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Sadducees denied. He adds, however, that they were doubtless originally real Sadducees, and sprung from among them. M. Simon, with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, supposes them to have risen hence; that the more knowing among the Jews opposing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> and reveries of the rabbins, and using the pure texts of Scripture to refute their groundless traditions, had the name of Caraim given them; which signifies as much as the barbarous Latin Scripturarius; i.e., people attached to the text of Scripture. The other Jews gave them the odious name Sadducees, from their agreement with those sectaries on the head of traditions. Scaliger, Vossius, and Spanheim, Caraïtes <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> the Caraïtes among the Sabæans, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANICHEES">Manichees</a>, and Mufîlmaus, but by mistake: Wolfgang, Fabricius, &c. say the Sadducees and Esseni were called Caraïtes, in opposition to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a>; others take them for the doctors of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> so often mentioned in the Gospels: but these are all conjectures. Josephus and Philo make no mention of them; which shows them to be more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> than either of those authors. In all probability, this fact was not formed till after the collection of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALMUD">Talmud</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Gemara; perhaps not till after the compiling of the Mishnah in the third century. The Caraïtes themselves pretend to be the remains of the ten tribes led captive by Shalmaneser. Wolfius, from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Mardacheus, a Caraïte, refers their origin to a massacre among the Jewish doctors, under Alexander Janneus, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, about 100 years before Christ: because Simeon, son of Schetach, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, making his escape into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, there forged his pretended traditions; and, at his return to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, published his visions; interpolating the law after his own fancy, and supporting his novelties on the notices which God, he said, had communicated by the mouth of Moses, whose depository he was: he gained many followers; and was opposed by others, who maintained, that all which God had revealed to Moses was written. Hence the Jews became divided into two sects, the Caraïtes and Tradionaries: among the first, Juda, son of Tabbaï, distinguished himself; among the latter, Hillel. Wolfius reckons not only the Sadducees, but also the Scribes, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Caraïtes. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> of the Pharisees prevailed against them all; and the number of Caraïtes decreased: Anan, indeed, in the eighth century, retrieved their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> a little; and Rabbi Schalom in the ninth. They succeeded pretty well till the fourteenth; but since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they have been declining. The Caraïtes are but little known; their works coming only into very few <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, even among the greatest Hebraists. Buxtorf never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> more than one; Selden two; but Mr Trigland says, he has recovered enough to speak of them with assurance. He affirms, that soon after the prophets had ceased, the Jews became divided on the subject of works, and supererogation: some maintaining their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>; whilst others, keeping <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the written law, set them aside; and it was from these last that Caraitism commenced. He adds, that after the return from the Babylonian <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, the observation of the law being to be re-established, there were several practices found proper for that end; and these once introduced, were looked upon as essential, and appointed by Moses; which was the origin of Pharisaism: as a contrary party, continuing to keep close to the letter, founded Caraitism. The modern Caraïtes, Leo of Modena observes, have their synagogues and ceremonies; they pretend to be the sole proper Jews, or observers of the laws of Moses; calling the rest by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> Rabbanim, or followers of the Rabbins: these hate the Caraïtes mortally; refusing to ally or even to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with them, and treating them as mamzeim, bastards; because of their rejecting the constitutions of the rabbins relating to marriages, repudiations, purifications of women, &c. This aversion is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a Caraïte should become a Rabbinist, he would never be received by the other Jews. The Caraïtes, however, do not absolutely reject all kinds of traditions; but only such as do not appear well grounded. Selden, who is very express on this point, in his Uxor Hebraica, observes, that, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> text, they have certain interpretations, which they call <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>, and which are proper traditions. Their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> only seems to differ from that of the other Jews, in that it is purer, and clearer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>: they give no credit to the explications of the Cabalistic, chimerical allegories, nor to any constitutions of the Talmud, but what are conformable to the Scripture, and may be drawn from it by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and necessary consequences. Peringer observes of the Caraïtes in Lithuania, that they are very different, both in aspect, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and manners, from the Rabbinites, whereewith the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounds. Their mother tongue is the Turkifh; and this they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> and synagogues. In visage they resemble the Mahometan Tartars. Their synagogues are placed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and south; and the reason they give for it is, that Shalmaneser brought them northward: so that in praying, to look to Jerusalem, they must turn to the south. He adds, that they admit all the books of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; contrary to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of many of the learned, who hold that they reject all but the Pentateuch. Caleb, a Caraïte, reduces the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them and the Rabbinites to three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>: 1. In that they deny the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORAL">oral</a> law to have come from Moses, and reject the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABALA">Cabala</a>. 2. In that they abhor the Talmud. 3. In that they observe the feasts, as the sabbaths, &c., much more rigorously than the Rabbins do. To this may be added, that they extend the degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a>, wherein <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> is prohibited, almost to infinity.

CARAMANIA

Pages 184-184

a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the south <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>. Bajazet united this province to his empire about the year 1488, and since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it has <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the possession of the Turks. Satalia was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, but is now much decayed.

CARAMANTA

Pages 184-184

a town of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the same name in Terra Firma, and in the audience of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SANTA_FE">Santa Fe</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 72° 35'. N. Lat. 5° 18'. The province of Caramanta is extended on both sides the river Cauca; and is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the district of Cartagena, on the east by New Grenada, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPAYAN">Popayan</a>, and on the west by Popayan and by the audience of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a>. It is a valley surrounded on every side by very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>.

CARANGA

Pages 184-184

an inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> near <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a> in the East Indies. It affords nothing but some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, fowls, and goats, for that market.

CARANNA

Pages 184-184
or Karanna, a very scarce gum which comes from New Spain. It is said to possess many extraordinary medical virtues, but the present practice takes no notice of it.

CARANUS

Pages 184-184

the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon, and the seventh of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of the Heraclidae. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">MACEDONIA</a>.

CARARA

Pages 184-184

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>, and in other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, used in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> and cod fish, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to 60 pounds of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

CARAVAN

Pages 185-185
or KARAVANNE, in the east, signifies a company or assembly of travellers and pilgrims, and more particularly of merchants, who, for their greater security, and in order to assist each other, march in a body through the deserts, and other dangerous places, which are infested with Arabs or robbers. There are four regular caravans which go yearly to Mecca; the first from Damascus, composed of the pilgrims from Europe and Asia; the second from Cairo, for the Mahomedans of Barbary; the third from Zibith, a place near the mouth of the s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red Sea, where those of Arabia and India meet; the fourth from Babylon, where the Persians assemble. Most of the inland commerce of the East is carried on by caravans. The late czar Peter the Great established a trade between Russia and China by means of a caravan. M. Bougnon, geographer to the duke of Lorraine, has given a treatise of the caravans of merchants in Asia; wherein he shows what they are composed of, how many sorts there are; the several uses of the different sorts of animals in them; the prices given for them, the officers and men appointed to conduct them, and the pay of each, with their manner of marching, halting, fighting, retreating, &c. Caravans of this kind are large convoys of armed men, merchants, and travellers, with divers sorts of animals for the carriage of their provisions. There are commonly four chief officers of a caravan, viz., the caravan bachi, or chief; the captain guide; captain of reil; and captain of distribution. The first has absolute command over all the rest; the second is absolute in the march; the office of the third only commences when the caravan stops and makes a stay; to the fourth it belongs to dispose of every part of the corps, in case of an attack or battle; he has also the inspection over the distribution of provisions, which is made under him by several distributors, who give security to the master of the caravan, and have each of them a certain number of persons, elephants, drongedaries, &c. to take care of at their own peril. The treasurer of the caravan makes a fifth officer, who has under him several agents and interpreters, who keep journals of all that passes, for the satisfaction of those concerned in fitting out the caravan. Any dealer is at liberty to form a company, in order to make a caravan. He in whose name it is raised, is considered as the caravan bachi, or chief of the caravan, unless he appoint some other in his place. If there are several merchants equally concerned, they elect a caravan bachi; after which, they appoint officers to conduct the caravan, and decide all controversies that may arise during the journey. There are also sea caravans; established on the same footing, and for the same purpose: such is the caravan of vessels from Constantinople to Alexandria.

CARAVANSERA

Pages 185-185
or KARAVANSERA, a place appointed for receiving and loading the caravans. It is commonly a large square building, in the middle of which there is a very spacious court; and under the arches or piazzas that surround it there runs a bank, raised some feet above the ground, where the merchants, and those who travel with them in any capacity, take up their lodgings as well as they can; the Caravansera beasts of burden being tied to the foot of the bank. Over the gates that lead into the court, there are sometimes little rooms, which the keepers of the caravanseras let out at a very high price to such as have a mind to be private. The caravanseras in the east are something of the nature of the inns in Europe; only that you meet with little accommodation either for man or beast, but are obliged to carry almost everything with you: there is never a caravansera without a well, or spring of water. These buildings are chiefly owing to the charity of the Mahometans: they are esteemed sacred dwellings, where it is not permitted to insult any person, or to pillage any of the effects that are depoited there. There are also caravanseras where most things may be had for money; and as the profits of these are considerable, the magistrates of the cities to whose jurisdiction they belong, take care to store them well. There is an inspector, who, at the departure of each caravan, fixes the price of the night's lodging, from which there is no appeal.

CARAVANSERASKIER

Pages 185-185

the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> keeper of a CARAVANSERA. He keeps an account of all the merchandises that are sold upon trust, and demands the payments of the sums due to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> for what has been sold in the caravansera, on the seller's paying two per cent. CARAVEL; thus they call a small vessel on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of France, which goes to fish for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> on the banks. They are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> from 25 to 30 tons burden. Those which are designed for the same fishery in the British channel are called by the French trinquarts; these are from 12 to 15 tons burden. CARAWAY. See CARUM. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CARBONADE

Pages 185-185
or CARBONADO, in cookery; flesh, fowl, or the like, seasoned and broiled on the coals.

CARCASS

Pages 186-186
or CARCUS, in the art of war, an iron cale, or hollow capacity, about the bigness of a bomb, of an oval figure, made of ribs of iron, filled with combustible matters, as meal powder, saltpetre, sulphur, broken glaifs, shavings of horn, turpentine, tallow, &c. It has two or three apertures out of which the fire is to blaze, and the design of it is to be thrown out of a mortar, to set houses on fire, and do other execution. It has the name carcase, because the circles which pass from one ring or plate to the other seem to represent the ribs of a human carcass.

CARCASSONNE

Pages 186-186

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, with a bishop's see. It is divided into the upper and lower town. They are both surrounded with walls; and though their situations are different, they are both watered by the river Aude. The upper town is seated on a hill, with a castle that commands it, as well as the lower town. It is strong, not only by its situation on a craggy rock, but also by several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> towers which are joined to its walls, and which render it difficult to access. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is remarkable for nothing but its antiquity. The lower town is large, and built after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The streets are very straight, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to a large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> in the middle, from whence may be seen the four gates of the town. There is here a manufacture of cloth. The neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is full of olive-trees; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> there is a fine marble, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called marble of Languedoc. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 25. N. Lat. 43. 11. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> bore a considerable share in that celebrated crusade undertaken against the Albigenses in the beginning of the 13th century, and which forms one of the most astonishing instances of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> and of atrocious barbarity to be found in the annals of the world. When the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> power was nearly annihilated, during the reigns of the last kings of the Carolingian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> in France, most of the cities of Languedoc erected themselves into little independent states, governed by their own princes. Carcassonne was then under the dominion of viceroys. At the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when Pope Innocent III. patronized and commanded the prosecution of hostilities against the Albigenses for the crime of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, Raymond the reigning viceroy was included in that proscription. Simon de <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONTFORT">Montfort</a>, general of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the church, invested the city of Carcassonne in 1209. The inhabitants, terrified at the fate of several other places where the most dreadful massacres had been committed, demanded leave to capitulate; but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of mercy was only extended to them under a condition equally cruel, incredible, and unparalleled in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we were not compelled to believe it by the unanimous testimony of all the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> writers. The people found in the place were all obliged, without distinction of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, to evacuate it in a state of nudity; and Agnes the viceroy was not exempted, though young and beautiful, from this ignominious and shocking <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. "On les fit fortir tout nus de la ville de Carcassonne (says an ancient author) afin qu'ils recueillent de la honte, en montrant ces parties du corps que la pureté de la langue n'exprime point, delquelles ils avoient abusé, et s'en écartent servis dans des crimes excrables." It seems by this imputation that the Albigenses were accused by their enemies of some enormities, probably unjust, and similar to those which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> enmity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> have attributed to the followers of Zinzendorf in the present century.

CARCERES

Pages 186-186

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Circenian games, were inclosures in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>, wherein the horses were restrained till the signal was given for starting, when by an admirable contrivance, they all at once flew open.

CARCHEMISH

Pages 186-186

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town lying upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, and belonging to the Assyrians. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECHO">Necho</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> took it from the king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, 2 Chr. xxxv. 20. Necho left a garrison in it, which was taken and cut to pieces, in the fourth year of Jehoiachin king of Judah, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a> king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, 2 Kings xxiii. 29. Isaiah (xv. 9.) speaks of Carchemish, and seems to say, that Tiglath-pileser made a conquest of it, perhaps from the Egyptians. This is thought to be the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> with that called Circeum by the Greeks and Latins.

CARCINOMA

Pages 186-186

in Medicine; the same with CANCER. See MEDICINE and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">SURGERY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CARD

Pages 186-186

among artificers, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of wood, befit with sharp <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, serving to arrange the hairs of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and the like: there are different kinds of them, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, stock-cards, &c. They are made as follows: A piece of thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, of the size intended for the card, is strained in a frame for that purpose; and then pricked full of holes, into which the teeth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> wire are inserted. After which the leather is nailed by the edges to a flat piece of wood, in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, about a foot in length and half a foot in breadth, with a handle placed in the middle of one of the longer sides. The teeth are made in the following manner. The wire being drawn of the size intended, a skin or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of wires are cut into proper lengths by means of a gauge, and then doubled in a tool contrived for that purpose: after which they are bent into the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> by means of another tool; and then placed in the leather, as mentioned above.

CARDAMINE

Pages 187-187

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>: A genus of the filiquea order, belonging to the tetradynamia clas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 39th order, Siliqueae. The filique parts adnate with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and the valves roll spirally backward; the stigma is entire, and the calyx a little gaping. Of this there are 15 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; but the most remarkable is the praireus, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> purple flower. This grows naturally in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and is also called cuckow flower. There are four varieties, viz. the fingle, with purple and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which are frequently intermixed in the meadows; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, of both colours. The fingle sorts are not admitted into gardens; but the double deserve a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, as making a pretty appearance during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they are in flower. They <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> thrive in a moist shady border; and are propagated by parting their roots, which is best performed in autumn. They delight in a soft loamy <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, not too stiff. By some the plant is reckoned antiscorbutic.

CARDAN

Pages 187-188

Jerom, one of the most extraordinary geniuses of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a> on the 24th of September 1501. As his mother was not married, she tried every method to procure an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABORTION">abortion</a>, but without effect. She was three days in labour, and they were at last obliged to cut the child from her. He was born with his head covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> curled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. When he was four years old, he was carried to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>; his father being an advocate in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. At the age of 20, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at the university of that city; and two years afterwards he explained Euclid. In 1524, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>; and the same year he was admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts: in the end of the following year, he took the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic. He married about the year 1531. For ten years before, his impotency had hindered him from having knowledge of a woman; which was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mortification to him. He attributed it to the evil influences of his planet under which he was born. When he enumerates, as he frequently does, the greatest misfortunes of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, this ten years impotency is always one. At the age of 32, he became professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at Milan. In 1539, he was admitted member of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of physicians at Milan; in 1543, he read public lectures of medicine in that city, and at Pavia the year following; but discontinued them because he could not get payment of his salary, and returned to Milan. In 1552, he went into Scotland, having been sent for by the archbishop of St Andrew's, who had in vain applied to the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s physicians, and afterwards to those of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Germany. This prelate, then 40 years old, had for ten years been afflicted with a shortness of breath, which returned every eight days for the last two years. He began to recover from the moment that Cardan prescribed for him. Cardan took his leave of him at the end of six weeks and Cardan's journey to Scotland gave him an opportunity of visiting several countries. He crossed France in going thither; and returned through Germany, and the Low Countries, along the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>. It was on this occasion, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and calculated King Edward's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>. This tour took up about four months: after which, coming back to Milan, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> there till the beginning of October 1552; and then went to Pavia, from whence he was invited to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> in 1562. He taught in this last city till the year 1570; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was thrown into prison; but some months after he was sent home to his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. He left Bologna in 1573; and went to Rome, where he lived for some time without any public employment. He was however, admitted a member of the college of physicians, and received a pension from the pope. He died at Rome on the 21st of September 1575, according to Thuanus. This account might be sufficient to show the reader that Cardan was of a very fickle temper; but he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have a much better idea of his singular and odd turn of mind by examining what he himself has written concerning his own good and bad qualities. He paid himself congratulatory compliments for not having a friend in this world; but that in requital, he was attended by an aerial spirit, emanated partly from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and partly from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, who was the constant guide of his actions, and teacher of every duty to which he was bound. He declared, too, that he was so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> in his manner of walking the streets, as induced all beholders to point at him as a fool. Sometimes he walked very slowly, like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> absorbed in profound meditation; then all on a sudden quickened his steps, accompanying them with very absurd attitudes. In Bologna his delight was to be drawn about in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> vehicle with three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>. When <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> did not visit him with any pain, he would procure to himself that disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> by biting his lips to wantonly, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pulling his fingers to such a vehement degree, as sometimes to force the tears from his eyes: and the reason he affirmed for so doing, was to moderate certain impetuous fallies of the mind, the violence of which was to him far more insupportable than pain itself; and that the sure <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of such a severe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> was the enjoying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. He says elsewhere, that, in the greatest tortures of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, he used to whip his legs with rods, and bit his left arm; that it was a great relief to him to weep, but that very often he could not; that nothing gave him more pleasure than to talk of things which made the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> uneasy; that he spoke on all subjects, in season and out of season; and he was so fond of games of chance, as to spend whole days in them, to the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of his family and reputation, for he even staked his furniture and his wife's jewels. Cardanus makes no scruple of owning that he was revengeful, envious, treacherous, a dealer in the black-art, a backbiter, a calumniator, and addicted to all the foul and detestable excesses that can be imagined: yet, notwithstanding (as one would think) so humbling a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, there was never perhaps a vainer mortal, or one that with less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> expressed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> he had of himself, than Cardanus was known to do, as will appear by the following proofs. "I have been admired by many nations: an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of panegyrics, both in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, have been composed to celebrate my fame. I was born to relieve the world from the manifold errors under which it groaned. What I have found out could not be discovered either by my predecessors or my contemporaries; and that is the reason why those authors who write anything worthy of being remembered, scruple not to own that they are indebted to me for it. I have composed a book on the dialectic art, in which there is neither one superfluous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> nor one deficient. I finished it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days, which seems a prodigy. Yet where is there a person to be found, that can boast of his having become master of its doctrine in a year? And he that shall have comprehended it in that time, must appear to have been instructed by a familiar daemon." The same capriciousness observable in his outward conduct is to be observed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of his works. We have a multitude of his treatises in which the reader is stopped almost every moment by the obscurity of his text, or his digressions from the point in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. In his arithmetical performances there are several discourses on the motions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, and on the tower of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BABEL">Babel</a>. In his dialectic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, we find his judgment on the historians and the writers of epistles. The only apology which he makes for the frequency of his digressions is, that they were purposely done for the sooner filling up of his sheet, his bargain with the bookseller being at so much per sheet; and that he worked as much for his daily support as for the acquisition of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. The Lyons edition of his works, printed in 1663, consists of ten volumes in folio. It was Cardanus who revived in latter times all the secret <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of the Cabbala or Cabalistics, which filled the world with spirits; a likeness to whom, he affected, we might attain by purifying ourselves with philosophy. He chose for himself, however, notwithstanding such reveries, this fine device, Tempus mea poesia, tempus meus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGER">ager</a>: "Time is my sole possession, and the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> I have to improve." In fact, when we consider the transcendent qualities of Cardan's mind, we cannot deny his having cultivated it with every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of knowledge, and his having made a greater progress in philosophy, in the medical art, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, in mathematics, &c. than the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his contemporaries who had applied their minds but to one of those sciences. Scaliger affirms, that Cardan, having fixed the time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, abstained from food, that this prediction might be fulfilled, and that his continuance to live might not discredit his art. Cardan's father, who was a doctor of medicine, and a professor of civil and canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, died in the same manner in the year 1524, having abstained from all sustenance for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> days. His son tells us, that he had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> eyes, and could see in the night-time.

CARDASS

Pages 188-188

a sort of card proper for carding flocks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, to make cappadocian of it. It is also the name which the French give to those flocks of silk.

CARDASSES

Pages 188-188

is also the name which, in the cloth manufactories of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, they give to a sort of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> card, which is used for carding the dyed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, designed for making cloth of mixed colours.

CARDERS

Pages 188-189

CARDERS, in the woollen manufactory, are persons who prepare <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, &c. for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>, &c. Carders, spinners, weavers, fullers, sheermen, and dyers, not performing their duty in their occupations, shall yield to the party grieved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> damages; to be committed until payment. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to hear and determine complaints. Carders, combers, sorters, spinners, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> weavers, conveying away, embezzling, or detaining any wool or yarn, delivered by the clothier, or any other person, shall give the party grieved such satisfaction, as two justices, mayor, &c. shall think fit: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not able or willing to make satisfaction, for the first offence to be whipped, or set in the stocks in some market-town, or in any other town where the offence is committed: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> offence to incur the like, or such further <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> by whipping, &c. as justices shall think proper. Conviction by one witness on oath, or confession.

CARDIAC

Pages 189-189

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies all medicines beneficial to the heart, whether internally <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> externally applied. The word comes from the Greek word καρδία, cor; the heart being reputed the immediate seat of their operation.

CARDIACS

Pages 189-189

in a more particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denote medicines which raise the spirits and give present strength and cheerfulness; these amount to the same with what are properly called cordials. Cardiacs are medicines anciently supposed to exert themselves immediately in comforting and strengthening the heart: but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> physicians rather suppose them to produce the effect by putting the blood into a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, whereby the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, before decayed, are repaired and invigorated, and the tone and elasticity of the fibres of the vessels restored; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which is a more easy and brisk circulation.

CARDIALGIA

Pages 189-189

in Medicine, a violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> acrimony felt towards the upper or left side of the stomach, though seemingly at the heart; sometimes accompanied with palpitations of the heart, fainting, and a propensity to vomit; better known by the name of cardiac <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, or heart-burn. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CARDIFF

Pages 189-189

a town of Glamorganshire, in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, seated on the river Tawe, in a rich and fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, well built town, having a castle, a wall, and four gates, built by Robert Fitz-Hamon, a Norman, about the year 1100. It is governed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> of the castle, 12 aldermen, 12 burgesses, &c. and sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Here the assizes and sessions are held, besides several courts. There is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river, to which small vessels come to take in their lading. It has now only one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s having been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> since thrown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the undermining of the river. The castle, though much decayed, makes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> appearance even at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and the walls of the town are very strong and thick. The church has a fine tower-steeple, and the town-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> is a good structure. The magistrates are elected every year by the majority of the burgesses. W. Long. 3. 20. N. Lat. 51. 30. Cardiff gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of British Baron to the family of Bute in Scotland.

CARDIGAN

Pages 189-189

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town of Cardiganshire, in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, is seated near the mouth of the river Teivy, on the Irish channel. It is indifferently <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well-built, containing three wards, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>-goal. It is governed by a mayor, 13 aldermen, 13 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> men, &c. Here are the ruins of a castle which was built by Gilbert de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>, about the year 1160. It sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and has two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, held on Tuesdays and Saturdays. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 38. N. Lat. 52. 15.

CARDIGANSHIRE
