Pages 189-189

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERIONETHSHIRE">Merionethshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a>, on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a> and Brecknockshire, on the west by the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAERNARVONSHIRE">Caernarvonshire</a>. Its length from north-west to south-east is about 44 miles, and its breadth near 20. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, as in other parts of Wales, varies with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, which in the southern and western parts is more upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> than this principality generally is, which renders the air mild and temperate. But as the northern and eastern parts are mountainous, they are consequently more barren and bleak. However, there are cattle bred in all parts; but they have neither wood nor coals of their own for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>: they have rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, and fish in plenty, with fowls both tame and wild. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Teivy, the Ridel, and the Iltwth. This county hath five market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, viz. Cardigan, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABERYSTWITH">Aberystwith</a>, Llanbadarnfawr, Llanbedar, and Tregaron, with 77 parishes; and was formerly computed to have upward of 3000 houses, and 520,000 acres of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; one for the county, and one for Cardigan.

CARDINAL

Pages 189-192

an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, being one who has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the conclave at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of a pope. Some say the cardinals were so called from the Latin incardinatio, which signifies the Cardinal. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> in any church made of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of a foreign church, driven thence by misfortune; and add, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the word commenced at Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>; the revenues of the churches of which cities being very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, they became the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> refuge of the unhappy priests of all other churches. The cardinals compose the pope's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>: in the Vatican is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of Pope John, which regulates the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and titles of the cardinals; and which declares, that as the pope represents Moses, so the cardinals represent the seventy elders, who, under the pontifical authority, decide private and particular differences. Cardinals, in their first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, were only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> priests, or incumbents of the parishes of Rome. In the primitive church, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> priest of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, who immediately followed the bishop, was called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESBYTER">presbyter</a> cardinalis, to distinguish him from the other petty priests, who had no church nor preferment; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> was first applied to them in the year 150; others say, under Pope Silvester, in the year 300. These cardinal priests were alone allowed to baptize, and administer the eucharist. When the cardinal priests became <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, their cardinalate became vacant; they being then supposed to be raised to a higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>.—Under Pope Gregory, cardinal priests, and cardinal deacons, were only such priests and deacons as had a church or chapel under their particular care: and this was the original use of the word. Leo IV. in the council of Rome, held in 853, calls them presbyteros sui cardinalis; and their churches, parochias cardinalis. The cardinals <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on this footing till the eleventh century: but as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and state of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> became then exceedingly augmented, he would have his council of cardinals make a better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> priests had done. It is true, they still preserved their ancient <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>; but the thing expressed by it was no more. It was a good while, however, before they had the precedence over bishops, or got the election of the pope into their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>: but when they were once possessed of those privileges, they soon had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hat and purple; and growing still in authority, they became at length superior to the bishops, by the sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of being cardinals. Du Cange observes, that originally there were three kinds of churches: the first or genuine churches were properly called parishes; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> deanories, which were chapels joined to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and served by deacons; the third were simple oratories, where private masses were said, and were discharged by local and resident chaplains. He adds, that to distinguish the principal or parish churches from the chapels and oratories, the name cardinales was given to them. Accordingly, parish churches gave titles to cardinal priests; and some chapels also, at length, gave the title of cardinal deacons. Others observe, that the term cardinal was given not only to priests, but also to bishops and deacons who were attached to certain churches, to distinguish them from those who only served them en paßant, and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITULAR">Titular</a> churches, or benefices, were a kind of parishes, i.e., churches, assigned each to a cardinal priest; with some stated district depending on it, and a font for administering of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where the bishop himself could not administer it. These cardinals were subordinate to the bishops; and according, Cardinally, in councils, particularly that held at Rome in 868, subscribed after them. It was not, however, only at Rome, that priests bore this name; for we find there were cardinal priests in France: thus, the curate of the parish of St John de Vignes is called in old charters the cardinal priest of that parish. The title of cardinal is also given to some bishops, quatenus bishops; e.g., to those of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>; the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a> is also, in ancient writings, called cardinal; and the church of Bourges, a cardinal church. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Vendome calls himself cardinalis natus. The cardinals are divided into three classes or orders; containing six bishops, fifty priests, and fourteen deacons; making in all seventy: which constitute what they call the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. The cardinal bishops, who are, as it were, the pope's vicars, bear the titles of the bishoprics assigned to them; the rest take such titles as are given them: the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cardinal bishops has been fixed; but that of cardinal priests and deacons, and consequently the sacred college itself, is always fluctuating. Till the year 1125, the college only consisted of fifty-two or fifty-three: the council of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a> reduced them to twenty-four; but Sixtus IV. without any regard to that restriction, raised them again to fifty-three, and Leo to sixty-five. Thus, as the number of cardinal priests was anciently fixed to twenty-eight, new titles were to be established, in proportion as new cardinals were created. As for the cardinal deacons, they were originally no more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> for the fourteen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of Rome; but they were afterwards increased to nineteen, and after that were again diminished. Accordingly to Onuphrius, it was Pope Pius IV. who first enacted, in 1562, that of the pope should be chosen only by the senate of cardinals; whereas, till that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the election was by all the clergy of Rome. Some say, the election of the pope reposed in the cardinals, exclusive of the clergy, in the time of Alexander III. in 1160. Others go higher still, and say, that Nicholas II. having been elected at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>, in 1058, by the cardinals alone, occasioned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of election to be taken from the clergy and people of Rome; only leaving them that of confirming him by their consent; which was at length, however, taken from them. See his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> for this purpose, issued in the Roman council of 1059, in Hardouin's Acta Conciliorum, tom. vi. pt. i. p. 1165. Whence it appears, that the cardinals who had the right of suffrage in the election of his successors, were divided by this pontiff into cardinal bishops and cardinal clerks: meaning by the former the seven bishops who belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and territory of Rome; and by the latter, the cardinal presbyters, or ministers of the twenty-eight Roman parishes, or principal churches. To these were added, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, under Alexander III. and other pontiffs, new members, in order to appease the tumults occasioned by the edict of Nicholas II. At the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of a new cardinal, the pope performs the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of opening and shutting his mouth; which is done in a private confessor. The shutting his mouth implies the depriving him of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of giving his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in congregations; and the opening Cardinal his mouth, which is performed 15 days after, signifies the taking off his restraint. However, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the pope happens to die during the time a cardinal's mouth is shut, he can neither give his voice in the election of a new pope, nor be himself advanced to that dignity. The dress of a cardinal is a red fountaine, a rocket, a short purple mantle, and a red hat. The cardinals began to wear the red hat at the council of Lyons, in 1243. The decree of Pope Urban VIII, whereby it is appointed, that the cardinals be addressed under the title of eminence, is of the year 1630; till then, they were called illuftrifimi. When cardinals are sent to the courts of princes, it is in quality of legates à latere; and when they are appointed governors of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is called by the name of legation. Cardinal has also been applied to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> officers. Thus, the prime ministers in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius, are called cardinales. Cassiodorus, lib. vii. formul. 31, makes mention of the cardinal prince of the city of Rome; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bretagne, in 1447, we meet with one Raoul de Thorel, cardinal of Quillart, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of the vicount de Rohan; which shows it to have been an inferior quality. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARDIOID">Cardioid</a>, in the higher <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, an algebraical curve, so called from its resemblance to a heart. Cardiospermum. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cardium, or Cockle, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of vermes terrestres. The shell consists of two equal valves, and the sides are equal. There are 21 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this genus. Common on all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> coasts, lodged a little beneath the sand; their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is marked by a depressed spot. They are wholesome and delicious food. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARDONA">Cardona</a>, a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Catalonia, with a strong castle, and the title of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. Near it is an inexhaustible mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of several colours, as red, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, carnation, and green; but when washed, it becomes white. There are also vineyards which produce excellent wine, and very lofty pines. It is seated on an eminence, near the river Cardenero. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 26. N. Lat. 41. 42. Carduus. See Botany Index. Carduus Benedictus, Blest thistle. See Cnicus, Botany Index. Careening, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, the bringing a ship to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on one side, in order to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> and caulk the other side. A ship is said to be brought to the careen, when, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">mull</a> of her lading being taken out, she is hulled down on one side, by a small vessel, as low as necessary; and there kept by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the ballast, ordnance, &c., as well as by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, lest her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> should be strained too much; in order that her sides and bottom may be trimmed, seams caulked, or anything that is faulty under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> mended. Hence, when a ship lies on one side when the sails, she is said to fail on the careen. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">Career</a>, in the Manege, a place inclosed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>, wherein they run the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>. The word is also used for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> or course of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> itself, provided it do not exceed 200 paces. In the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>, the career was the space the bigae, or quadrigae, were to run at full speed, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>. See Circus. Career, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALCONRY">Falconry</a>, is a flight or tour of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, about 120 yards. If the mount more, it is called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> career; if less, a semi-career. Carelia, the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a> divided into Swedish Carelia, and Mulcovite Carelia. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the latter is Povenza, and of the former Weiburg. Carelscroon, a sea-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, in Blekingia, or Bleking, on the Baltic sea, with a very good harbour defended by two forts. It was built in 1679; and is very populous, with arsenals for the marine: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>-general of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> is in this town, and here the Swedes lay up their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. E. Long. 15. 5. N. Lat. 56. 15. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARENTAN">Carentan</a>, a town of France in Lower Normandy, and in the Contentin, with an ancient castle. W. Long. 1. 14. N. Lat. 49. 20. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARET">Caret</a>, among grammarians, a character marked thus A, signifying that something is added on the margin, or interlined, which ought to come in where the caret stands. Carew, George, born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> in 1557, an eminent commander in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; when, joining his forces with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Thomond, he reduced the Irish insurgents, and brought the earl of Desmond to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James made him governor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUERNSEY">Guernsey</a>, and created him a baron. As he was a valiant commander, he was no less a polite scholar; and wrote Pacata Hibernia, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the late wars in Ireland, printed after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in 1633. He made several collections for a history of Henry V. which are digested into Speed's History of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Besides these, he collected materials of Irish history in four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> MSS. volumes, now in the Bodleian library, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. Carew, Thomas, descended from the family of Carew in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of the privy chamber to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. who always esteemed him one of the most celebrated wits of his court. He was much respected by the poets of his time, particularly by Ben Johnson and Sir William Davenant; and left behind him several poems, and a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASQUE">masque</a> called Calum Britannicum, performed at Whitehall on Shrove Tuesday night, 1633, by the king, and several of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> with their sons. Carew was assisted in the contrivance by Inigo Jones, and the music was set by Mr Henry Lawes of the king's chapel. He died in the prime of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, about the year 1639. Carew, Richard, author of the "Survey of Cornwall," was the eldest son of Thomas Carew of East Anthony, and was born in 1555. When very young, he became a gentleman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> of Christ-church college, Oxford; and at 14 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of disputing, extempore, with the afterwards famous Sir Phillip <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYDNEY">Sydney</a>, in the presence of the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. After spending three years at the university, he removed to the Middle Temple, where he resided the same length of time, and then travelled into foreign parts. Not long after his return to England, he married, in 1577, Juliana <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a>, of Trecice. In 1581, Mr Carew was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, and in 1586 was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cornwall; about which time he was likewise queen's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>. In 1589, he was elected a member of the college of Antiquaries, a distinction to which he was entitled by his literary abilities and pursuits. What particularly engaged his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was his native county, his "Survey" of which was published, in 4to, at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in 1602. It hath been twice reprinted, first in 1723, and next in 1769. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> Camden hath spoken in high terms, and acknowledges his obligations to the author. In the present improved state of topographical knowledge, and since Dr Borlase's excellent publications relative to the county of Cornwall, the value of Carew's "Survey" must have been greatly diminished. Mr Gough remarks, that the history and monuments of this county were faintly touched by Carew; but it is added, that he was a person extremely capable of describing them, if the infancy of those studies at that time had afforded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and materials. Another work of our author was a translation from the Italian, entitled, "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of Men's Wits." In which, by discovering the variety of natures, is showed for what profession each one is apt, and how far he shall profit therein." This was published at London in 1594, and afterwards in 1604; and though Richard Carew's name is prefixed to it, hath been principally ascribed by some persons to his father. According to Wood, Carew wrote also, "The true and ready Way to learn the Latin Tongue," in answer to a query, whether the ordinary method of teaching the Latin by the rules of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> be the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of instructing youths in that language? This tract is involved in Mr Hartlib's book upon the same subject, and with the same title. It is certain that Carew was a gentleman of considerable abilities and literature, and that he was held in great estimation by some of the most eminent scholars of his time. He was particularly intimate with Sir Henry Spelman, who extols him for his ingenuity, virtue, and learning. Carew, George, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the subject of the last article, was educated in the university of Oxford, after which he studied the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> in the inns of court, and then travelled to foreign countries for farther improvement. On his return to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he was called to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, and after some time was appointed secretary to Sir Christopher Hatton, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chancellor of England. This was by the special recommendation of Queen Elizabeth herself, who gave him a prothonotaryship in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, and conferred upon him the honour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. In 1597, Sir George Carew, who was then a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in chancery, was sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. In the next reign, he was one of the commissioners for treating with the Scotch concerning an union between the two kingdoms; after which he was appointed ambassador to the court of France, where he continued from the latter end of the year 1605 till 1609. During his residence in that country, he formed an intimacy with Thuanus, to whom he communicated an account of the transactions in Poland whilst he was employed there, which was of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to that admirable author in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up the 121st book of his history. After Sir George Carew's return from France, he was advanced to the important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of master of the court of wards, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> situation he did not long live to enjoy; for it appears from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> written by Thuanus to Camden in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> 1613, that he was then lately deceased. Sir George Carew married Thomasine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir Francis Godolphin, great grandfather of the lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Godolphin, and had by her two sons and three daughters. When Sir George Carew returned, in 1609, from his French embassy, he drew up, and addressed to James I., "A Relation of the State of France, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of Henry IV. and the principal persons of that Court." The characters are drawn from personal knowledge and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> observation, and might be of service to a general historian of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is perspicuous and manly, and entirely free from the pedantry which prevailed in the reign of James I. but this is the less surprising, as Sir George Carew's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> had been formed in a better era, that of Queen Elizabeth. The valuable tract we are speaking of lay for a long time in MS. till happily falling into the hands of the earl of Hardwicke, it was communicated by him to Dr Birch, who published it, in 1749, at the end of his "Historical View of the Negotiations between the Courts of England, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>, from 1592 to 1617." That intelligent and industrious writer justly observes, that it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> upon which ambassadors may form and digest their motions and representations; and the late celebrated poet Mr Gray hath spoken of it as an excellent performance.

CARDS

Pages 186-187

among gamesters, little pieces of fine thin pasteboard of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, of several sizes; but most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, three inches and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and two and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, on which are painted several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> and figures. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> and blocks for making cards are exactly like those that were used for the first printed books. They lay a sheet of wet <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> moist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, which is very lightly done over with a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> diluted in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and mixed with some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STARCH">starch</a> to give it a body. They afterwards rub it off with a round lift. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-cards are coloured by means of several patterns, styled <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-filers. These consist of papers cut through with a penknife; and in these apertures they apply severally the various colours, as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, black, &c. These patterns are painted with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-colours, that the brushes may not wear them out; and when the pattern is laid on the pasteboard, they slightly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which, leaving it within the openings, forms the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> or figure of the card. Among harpers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> sorts of false and fraudulent cards have been contrived; as, 1. Marked cards, where the aces, kings, queens, knaves, are marked on the corners of the backs with spots of different <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and order, either with clear water or water tinged with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ink, that those in the secret may distinguish them. Aces are marked with single spots on two corners opposite diagonally; kings with two spots at the same corners; knaves with the same number transferred. 2. Breef cards, those which are longer or broader than the rest; chiefly used at whist and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIQUET">piquet</a>. The broad cards are usually for kings, queens, knaves, and aces; the long for the rest. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>, to enable him in the secret to cut the cards disadvantageously to his adversary, and draw the person unacquainted with the fraud to cut them favourably for the sharper. As the pack is placed either endwise or sidewise to him that is to cut, the long or broad cards naturally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> him to cut to them. Breef cards are sometimes made thus by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a>; but, in defect of these, sharpeners pare all but the breefs with a penknife or razor. 3. Corner <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>, denotes four cards turned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> finely at one corner, to serve as a signal to cut by. 4. Middle bend, or Kingstone-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, is where the tricks are bent two different ways, which causes an opening or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> in the middle, to direct likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>. Cards were invented about the year 1390, to divert <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VI. of France, who had fallen into a melancholy disposition. The inventor proposed, by the figures of the four suits or colours, as the French call them, to represent the four classes of men in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. By the coeurs (hearts) are meant the gens de chevau, choir-men, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>; and therefore the Spaniards, who certainly received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of cards from the French, have copas, or chalices, instead of hearts. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, or prime <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the kingdom, are represented by the ends or points of lances or pikes; and our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the meaning or the resemblance of the figure induced us to call them spades: The Spaniards have espadas, swords, in lieu of pikes, which are of similar import. By diamonds are designed the order of citizens, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, or tradesmen, carreaux, (<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, tiles, or the like): The Spaniards have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, dineros, which answers to it; and the Dutch call the French word carreaux "spreuken," stones and diamonds, from the form. Trefle, the trefoil-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, or clover-grafs (corruptly called clubs), alludes to the husbandmen and peasants. But how this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> came to be called clubs is not easily explained; unless borrowing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> from the Spaniards, who have bastos (staves or clubs) instead of the trefoil, we give the Spanish signification to the French figure. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the four kings, which the French, in drudery, sometimes call the cords, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, Alexander, Caesar, and Charles; which names were then, and still are on the French cards. These respectable names represent the four celebrated monarchies of the Jews, Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and Franks under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. By the queens are intended Argine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTHER">Esther</a>, Judith, and Pallas (names retained in the French cards), typical of birth, piety, fortitude, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, the qualifications residing in each person. Argine is an anagram for <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-REGINA">regina</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>. By the knaves were designed the servants to knights (for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNAVE">knave</a> originally meant only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>); but French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> and valets, now indiscriminately used by various orders of persons, were formerly only allowed to persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, esquires (esquires), shield or armour bearers. Others fancy that the knights themselves were designed by those cards; because Hogier and Lahire two names on the French cards, were famous knights at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> cards were supposed to have been invented. Deceptions with Cards. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGERDEMAIN">Legerdemain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. i.

CAREY

Pages 192-193

HARRY, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> distinguished by both <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and music, but perhaps more so by a certain facetiousness, which made him agreeable to everybody. He published in 1720 a little collection of poems; and in 1732, five cantatas, written and composed by himself. He also composed sundry songs for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> comedies, particularly those in the "Provoked Husband:" he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> called "The Contrivances," in which were several little songs to very pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>: he also made two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three little dramas for Goodman's-fields <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, which were very favourably received. In 1729, he published by subscription his poems much enlarged: with the addition of one entitled "Namby Pamby," in which <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> Philips is ridiculed. Carey's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, says his historian, lay in humour and unamiable satire: to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> the rant and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOMBAST">bombast</a> of modern tragedies he wrote one, to which he gave the strange <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "Chrononhotonthologos," acted in 1734. He also wrote a farce called "The Honest Yorkshireman." Carey was a thorough Englishman, and had an unmountable aversion to the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> and the singers in it: he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a> opera on the subject of the "Dragon of Wantley;" and afterwards a sequel to it, entitled, "The Dragoness," both which were esteemed a true burlesque upon the Italian opera. His qualities being of the entertaining kind, he was led into more expenses than his finances could bear, and thus was frequently in distress. His friends, however, were always ready to assist him by their little subscriptions to his works: and encouraged by these, he republished, in 1740, all the songs he had ever composed, in a collection, entitled, "The Musical Century, in 100 English Ballads, &c." and, in 1743, his dramatic works, in a small volume, 4to. With all his mirth and good humour, he seems to have been at times deeply affected with the malevolence of some of his own profession, who, for reasons that no one can guess at, were Cargadors were his enemies; and this, with the pressure of his circumstances, is supposed to have occasioned his untimely end; for, about 1744, in a fit of desperation, he laid violent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on himself, and, at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Warner-street, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">Cold</a>-bath Fields, put an end to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, which, says Sir John Hawkins, had been led without reproach. It is to be noted, and it is somewhat singular in such a character, that in all his songs and poems on wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, and such kind of subjects, he seems to have manifested an inviolable regard for decency and good manners.

CARGADORS

Pages 193-193

a name which the Dutch give to those brokers whose business is to find freight for ships outward bound, and to give notice to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, who have commodities to send by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, of the ships that are ready to sail, and of the places for which they are bound.

CARGAPOL

Pages 193-193
or KARGAPOL, the capital of a territory of the same name, in the province of Dwina, in Muscovy. E. Long. 36°. N. Lat. 63°.

CARGO

Pages 193-193

O denotes all the merchandises and effects which are laden on board a ship. Super-Cargo, a person employed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> to go a voyage, oversee the cargo, and dispose of it to the best advantage.

CARIA

Pages 193-193

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; whose limits are extended by some, while they are contracted by others. Mela and Pliny extend the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> Caria from Japhus and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>, to Calynda, and the borders of Lycia. The inland Caria <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> extends to the Meander and beyond. Car, Cariates, Cariatia, Carifia, and Coris, and Caira, are the gentilis names; Carius and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARICUS">Caricus</a> the epithets. In Carae periculum, was a proverbial saying on a thing exposed to danger, but of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> value. The Carae being the Swils of those days, were hired and placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, (Cicero.) Cum Carae Carifia, denoted the behaviour of clowns. The Carae came originally from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> to the continent, being formerly subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, and called Lelages: this the Cretans affirm, and the Carae deny, making themselves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABORIGINES">aborigines</a>. They are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> origin with the Myli and Lydi, having a common temple, of a very ancient standing, at Melasfa, a town of Caria, called Jovis Carii Delubrum, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>.) <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> calls the Carians, barbarians in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>.

CARIATI

Pages 193-193

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hither <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, with a bishop's see, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality. It is two miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARANTO">Taranto</a>, and 37 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Cofenza. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17. 19. N. Lat. 35. 38.

CARIBBEE ISLANDS

Pages 193-194

a cluster of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a> between 59 and 63 degrees of west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between 11 and 18 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the form of a bow <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>, stretching almost from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a> north, to near the river Oronoque. Those that lie nearest the east have been called the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDWARD">Windward</a> Islands, the others the Leeward, on account of the winds blowing generally from the eastern point in those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. Abbé Raynal conjectures them to be the tops of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> formerly belonging to the continent, which have been changed into islands by some revolution that has laid the flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the Caribbee islands, beginning from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOBAGO">Tobago</a>, is nearly north and N. N. W. This direction is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, forming a line somewhat curved towards the north-west, and ending at Antigua. In this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the line becomes at once curved; and extending itself in a straight direction to the west and north-west, meets in its course with Porto-Rico, St Domingo, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBA">Cuba</a>, known by the name of the Leeward Islands, which are separated from each other by channels of various breadths. Some of these are 6, others 15 or 20 leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; but in all of them the foundings are from 100 to 120 or 150 fathoms. Between Grenada and St Vincent's there is also a small archipelago of 30 leagues, in which the foundings are not above ten fathoms. The mountains in the Caribbee islands run in the same direction as the islands themselves. The direction is regular, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we were to consider the tops of these mountains only, independent of their bases, they might be looked upon as a chain of hills belonging to the continent, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARTINICO">Martinico</a> would be the most northerly promontory. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of water which flow from the mountains in the Windward islands, run all in the western parts of these islands. The whole eastern coast is without any running water. No springs come <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> there from the mountains: and indeed they would have been useless; for after having run over a very short tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rapidity, they would have fallen into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORTO_RICO">Porto Rico</a>, St Domingo, and Cuba, there are a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that discharge themselves on the northern side, and whose sources rise in the mountains running from east to west, that is, through the whole length of these islands. From the other side of the mountains facing the south, where the sea, flowing with great impetuosity, leaves behind it marks of its inundations, several rivers flow down, the mouths of which are capable of receiving the largest ships. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the Caribbees consists mostly of a layer of clay or gravel of different thickness: under which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or rock. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of some of these soils is better adapted to vegetables than others. In those places where the clay is drier and more friable, and mixes with the leaves and remains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, a layer of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is formed of greater depth than where the clay is moister. The sand or gravel has different properties according to its peculiar nature; wherever it is less hard, less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and less porous, small pieces separate themselves from it, which, though dry, preserve a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of coolness useful to vegetation. This soil is called in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> a pumice-stone soil. Whenever the clay and gravel do not go through such modifications, the soil becomes barren, as soon as the layer formed by the decomposition of the original plants is destroyed.—By a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> concluded in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1660, between the French and English, the Caribs were confined to the islands of St Vincent's and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINICA">Dominica</a>, where all the scattered body of this people were united, and at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> did not exceed in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> 6200 men. See St Vincent's and Dominica. As the Caribbee islands are all between the tropics, their inhabitants are exposed, allowing for the varieties resulting from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of situation and soil, to a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, which generally increases from the rising of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> till an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after noon, and then declines in proportion as the sun declines. The variations of the temperature of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> seem to depend rather on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> than on the changes of the seasons. In those places places where the wind does not blow, the air is excessively hot, and none but the easterly winds contribute to temper and refresh it; those that blow from the south and west afford little relief; but they are much less frequent and less regular than that which blows from the east. The branches of the trees exposed to the influence of the latter are forced round towards the west; but their roots are stronger, and more extended under the ground, towards the east than towards the west; and hence they are easily thrown down by strong west winds or hurricanes from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. The easterly wind is scarce felt in the Caribbee islands before <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten o'clock in the morning, increases in proportion as the sun rises above the horizon, and decreases as it declines. Towards the evening it ceases entirely to blow on the coasts, but not on the open sea. It has also been observed, that it blows with more force and more regularity in the dog-days than at any other time of year. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> also contributes to the temperature of the Caribbee islands, though not equally in them all. In those places where the easterly wind meets with nothing to oppose its progress, it dispels the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> as they begin to rise, and causes them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> either in the woods or upon the mountains. But whenever the storms are too violent, or the blowing of the easterly wind is interrupted by the changeable and temporary effect of the southerly or westerly ones, it then begins to rain. In the other Caribbee islands, where this wind does not generally blow, the rains are so frequent and plentiful, especially in the winter season, which lasts from the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> to the middle of October, that, according to the most accurate observations, as much rain falls in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> as in our climates in a year. Instead of those mild refreshing showers which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in the European climates, the rains of the Caribbee islands are torrents, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of which might be mistaken for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, were not that almost totally unknown under so <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> a sky. These showers indeed refresh the air; but they occasion a dampness, the effects of which are not less disagreeable than fatal. The dead must be interred within a few hours after they have expired. Meat <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not keep sweet above 24 hours. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> decay, whether they are gathered ripe or before their maturity. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> must be made up into biscuits, to prevent its growing mouldy. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> wines turn sour, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> turns rusty, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s time. The seeds can only be preserved by constant <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and care, till the proper season returns for sowing them. When the Caribbee islands were first discovered, the corn that was conveyed there for the support of the Europeans, was soon damaged that it became necessary to send it out in the ears. This necessary precaution so much enhanced the price of it, that few were able to purchase it. Flour was then substituted in lieu of corn; which lowered indeed the expenses of transport, but had this inconvenience, that it was sooner damaged. It was imagined by a merchant, that if the flour were entirely separated from the bran, it would have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> advantage of being cheaper and keeping longer. He caused it therefore to be sifted, and put the finest flour into strong casks, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together with iron <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a>, till it became so close a body that the air could scarcely penetrate it. This method was found to answer the purpose; and if, by it, the flour cannot be preserved as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as in our dry and temperate climates, it may be kept for six months, a year, or longer, according to the degree of care taken in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>. However troublesome these effects of the rain may be, it is attended with some others still more formidable; namely, frequent and dreadful earthquakes—these happening generally during the time or towards the end of the rainy season, and when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> are highest, some ingenious naturalists have supposed that there might be a connexion between them. The waters of the sky and of the sea undermine, dig up, and ravage the earth in several different ways. Among the various shocks to which the Caribbee islands are exposed from the fury of the boisterous ocean, there is one distinguished by the name of raz de maree, or whirlpool. It constantly happens once, twice, or thrice, from July to October, and always on the western coasts, because it takes place after the time of the westerly or southerly winds, or while they blow. The waves, which at a distance seem to advance gently within 400 or 500 yards, suddenly swell against the shore, as if acted upon in an oblique direction by some superior force, and break with the greatest impetuosity. The ships which are then upon the coast, or in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> beyond it, unable either to keep their anchors or to put out to sea, are dashed to pieces against the land, and all on board most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> perish. The hurricane is another terrible phenomenon in these islands, by which incredible damage is occasioned; but happily it occurs not often. The produce of the Caribbee islands is exceedingly valuable to the Europeans, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, rum, molasses, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, &c., a particular account of which is given under the names of the respective islands as they occur in the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>.

CARIBBIANA

Pages 194-194
or CARIBIANA, the north-east coast of Terra Firma, in South America, otherwise called New Andalusia.

CARICA

Pages 194-194

the papaw. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The fruit of one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is by the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> eaten with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> as melons, but is much inferior to a melon in its native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but those which have ripened in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> were detestable: the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to which Mr Miller says he has known them put was, when they were about half grown, to soak them in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to get out the acrid juice, and then pickle them for onagos, to which they are a good substitute.

CARICATURA

Pages 194-194

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, denotes the concealment of real beauties, and the exaggeration of blemishes, but still so as to preserve a resemblance of the object. The word is Italian; formed of caricà, a load, burden, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like.

CARICOUS

Pages 194-194

an epithet given to such tumours as resemble the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a fig. They are frequently found in the piles.

CARIES

Pages 194-194

the corruption <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mortification of a bone. See Medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CARIGNAN

Pages 194-194

a fortified town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, situated on the river Po, about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 25'. N. Lat. 44° 30'. It was taken in 1544 by the French; who demolished the fortifications, but spared the cattle. It was also taken, and retaken, in 1691.

CARILLONS

Pages 194-195

CARILLONS, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of chimes frequent in the Low Countries, particularly at Ghent and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, and played on a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of bells in a belfrey, forming a complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of tones and semitones, like those on the harpsichord and organ. There are pedals communicating with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> bells, upon which the carillonner with his feet plays the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a> to sprightly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, performed with the two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> upon the upper species of keys. These keys are projecting sticks, wide enough aflutter to be struck with violence and velocity by either of the hands edgewise, without the danger of hitting the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>. The player is provided with a thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> covering for the little finger of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against the violence of the stroke. These carillons are heard through a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town.

CARINA

Pages 195-195

a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, properly signifying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> of a ship; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> running along the bottom of the ship from head to stern, upon which the whole structure is built or framed. Carina is also frequently used for the whole capacity or bulk of a ship: containing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">hull</a> or all the space below the deck. Hence the word is also sometimes used by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> for the whole ship. Carina is also used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> gave the name carina to all buildings in form of a ship, as we still give the name nave to the middle or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> vault of our Gothic churches; because it has that figure. Carina, among anatomists, is used to denote the spine dorfi; as likewise for the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> or embryo of a chick appearing in an incubated <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>. The carina consists of the entire vertebrae, as they appear after ten or twelve days incubation. It is thus called, because crooked in form of the keel of a ship.—Botanists also, for the like reason, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the word carina, to express the lower petalum of a papilionaceous flower. Carinæ were also weepers or women hired among the ancient Romans to weep at funerals: they were thus called from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> whence most of them came.

CARINOLA

Pages 195-195

an episcopal town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and Terra di Lavoro. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15° 5'. N. Lat. 41° 15'.

CARINTHIA

Pages 195-195

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Germany, in the circle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, bounded by the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a> and the Venetian territories on the south, on the west by Tyrol, and on the east by Styria. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was anciently called Carnia, and the inhabitants Carni; but the former afterwards obtained the name of Carinthia, and the latter Carantani <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Carinthi. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of this country is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general mountainous and barren; but there are some fruitful dales and valleys in it, which produce wheat and other grain. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, brooks, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, which are very numerous, abound with fish; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> yield <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and in many places are covered with woods. The river Drave, which runs across the country, is the most considerable in Carinthia. The inhabitants are partly descendants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Germans, and partly of the Slavonians or Wends. The states are constituted as in Austria, and their assemblies are held at Clagenfurt. The archbishop of Salzburg and the bishop of Bamberg have considerable territories in this country. Christianity was planted here in the 7th century. The only profession tolerated at present is the Roman Catholic. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> are those of Gurk, and Lavant, who are subject to the archbishop of Salzburg. This duchy was formerly a part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>. In the year 1282, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Rudolph I. gave it to Maynard <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Tyrol, on condition that when his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> issue failed, it should revert to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Austria; which happened in 1331. Carinthia has its particular governor or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, as he is called; and contributes annually towards the expense of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> establishment 637,695 florins. Only one regiment of foot is usually quartered in it.

CARIPPI

Pages 195-195

a kind of cavalry in the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The caripi to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of about 1000, are not slaves, nor bred up in the feraglio, like the rest; but are generally Moors <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> renegade <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who having followed adventures, being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and having their fortune to seek by their dexterity and courage, have arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> guards to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Signior. CARISSA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CARITAS.—The poculum caritatis, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> cup, was an extraordinary allowance of wine or other liquors, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> at festivals drank in commemoration of their founders and benefactors.

CARISBROOK CASTLE

Pages 195-195

a castle situated in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. was imprisoned. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 30'. N. Lat. 50° 40'.

CARISTO

Pages 195-195

an episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, in the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGROPONT">Negropont</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Loro. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 24° 15'. N. Lat. 38° 6'.

CARKE

Pages 195-195

denotes the 30th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a sarplar of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. CARLE. See Churl.

CARLETON

Pages 195-195

Sir <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a>, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, 1573, and bred in Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. He went as secretary to Sir Ralph Winwood into the Low Countries, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James resigned the cautionary <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> to the States; and was afterwards employed for 20 years as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, Savoy, and the United Provinces. King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> created him Viscount <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORCHESTER">Dorchester</a>, and appointed him one of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> secretaries of state; in which office he died in 1631. He was esteemed a good statesman, though an honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and published several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> works.

CARLINE

Pages 195-195
or CAROLINE THISTLE. See Carlina. It is said to have been discovered by an angel to Charlemagne, to cure his army of the plague; whence its denomination. CARLINE or Caroline, a silver coin current in the Neapolitan dominions, and worth about 4d. of our money.

CARLINES

Pages 195-195
or CARLINGS, in a ship, two pieces of timber lying fore and aft, along from one beam to another, directly over the keel; serving as a foundation for the whole body of the ship. On these the ledges rest, whereon the planks of the deck and other matters of carpentry are made fast. The carlines have their ends let into the beams called culver-tail-ways. CARLINE Knees, are timbers going athwart the ship, from the sides to the hatchway, serving to sustain the deck on both sides.

CARLINGFORD

Pages 195-196

a port town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, seated on Carlingford <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUTH">Louth</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, 22 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROGHEDA">Drogheda</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 24. N. Lat. 24. 5.

CARLISLE

Pages 196-196

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, seated on the south of the river Eden, and between the Petterel on the east, and the Caude on the west. It is surrounded by a strong <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> wall, and has a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> castle in the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, as also a citadel in the eastern part, built by Henry VIII. It flourished in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, as appears from the antiquities that are to be met with here, and the Roman coins that have been dug up. At the departure of the Romans this city was ruined by the Scots and Piets; and was not rebuilt till the year 680, by Egfrid, who encompassed it with a wall, and repaired the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. In the 8th and 9th centuries, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was again ruined, and the city laid desolate by the incursions of the Norwegians and Danes. In this condition it remained till the time of William Rufus; who repaired the walls and the castle, and caused the houses to be rebuilt. It was fortified by Henry I. as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> against Scotland; he also placed a garrison in it, and made it an episcopal see. It was twice taken by the Scots, and afterwards burnt accidentally in the reign of Richard II. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, the suburbs, and 1300 houses were destroyed at that time. It is at present in a good condition; and has three gates, the English on the south, the Scotch on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and the Irish on the west. It has two parishes, and as many churches, St Cuthbert's and St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s, the last of which is the cathedral, and is separated from the town by a wall of its own. The eastern part, which is the newest, is a curious piece of workmanship. The choir with the aisles is 71 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and has a stately east-window 48 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and 30 broad, adorned with curious pillars. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is elegantly vaulted with wood; and is embellished with the arms of England and France quartered; as also with Piercy's, Ley's, Warren's, Mowbray's and many others. In the choir are the monuments of three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> who are buried there. This see was erected in 1133 by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry I. and made suffragan to the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. The cathedral church here had been founded a short time before by Walter, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> in these parts for King William Rufus, and by him dedicated to the Virgin Mary. He likewise built a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, and filled it with canons regular of St Augustine. This foundation <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of monasteries, when its lands were added to the see, and the maintenance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, &c., placed here in their room. The church was almost ruined by the usurper Cromwell and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>; and has never since recovered its former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, although repaired after the Restoration. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> contains the greatest part of the counties of Cumberland and Westmorland, in which are only 93 parishes; but these (as all the northern are) exceeding large; and of them 18 are impropriations. Here is one archdeacon, viz. of Carlisle. The see is valued in the king's books at £30l. 4s. 11½d., but is computed to be worth annually £200l. The clergy's tenth amounts only to £16l. 13s. 7½d. To this cathedral belong a bishop, a dean, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, an archdeacon, four prebendaries, eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> canons, &c.; and other inferior officers and servants. The Piets wall, which was built across the country from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, terminates near this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Carlisle was a fortified place, and still has its governor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-governor, but no garrison. It was taken by the rebels, Nov. 15, 1745; and was retaken by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Cumberland on the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> following, and deprived of its gates. It is governed by a mayor, twelve aldermen, two bailiffs, &c., and has a considerable market on Saturdays. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of Carlisle are chiefly of printed linens, for which near 3000l. per annum is paid in duties.
