It is also noted for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> manufacture of whips, in which a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of children are employed.—Salmons appear in the Eden in numbers, so early as the months of December and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and even Newcastle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are supplied with early fish from this river; but it is remarkable, that they do not visit the Els in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> till April; notwithstanding the mouths of the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are at a small distance from each other.—Carlisle sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to a branch of the Howard family.

CARLOCK

Pages 196-196

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a sort of inglass, made with the sturgeon's bladder, imported from Archangel. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it is for clarifying wine, but is also used by the dyers. The best carlock comes from Africcan, where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sturgeon is caught.

CARLOSTAD

Pages 196-196
or Carlstad, a town of Hungary, capital of Croatia, and the usual residence of the governors of the province. It is seated on the river Kulph, in E. Long. 16. 5. N. Lat. 45. 34.

CARLOWITZ

Pages 196-196

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, in Sclavonia, remarkable for a peace concluded here between the Turks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in 1669. It is seated on the west side of the Danube, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19. 5. N. Lat. 45. 25.

CARLSCRONA

Pages 196-197
or Carlscroon, a sea port town in the Baltic, belonging to Sweden. It derives its origin and name from Charles XI. who first laid the foundation of a new town in 1680, and removed the fleet from Stockholm to this place, on account of its advantageous situation in the centre of the Swedish seas, and the superior security of its harbour. The greatest part of Carlscrona stands upon a small rocky island, which rises gently in a bay of the Baltic; the suburbs extend over another small rock, and along the mole close to the basin where the fleet is moored. The way into the town from the mainland is carried over a dyke to an island, and from thence along two long wooden bridges joined by a barren rock. The town is spacious, and contains about 18,000 inhabitants. It is adorned with one or two handsome churches, and a few tolerable houses of brick; but the generality of buildings are of wood. The suburbs are fortified towards the land by a stone wall. The entrance into the harbour, which by nature is extremely difficult from a number of shoals and rocky islands, is still further secured from the attack of an enemy's fleet by two strong forts built on two islands, under the batteries of which all vessels must pass. Formerly vessels in this port when careened and repaired, were laid upon their sides in the open harbour, boar, until a dock, according to a plan given by Polheim, was hollowed in the solid rock: it was begun in 1714, and finished in 1724; but as it was too small for the admission of men of war, it has lately been enlarged, and is now capable of receiving a ship of the first rate. But new docks have been begun upon a stupendous plan, worthy of the ancient Romans. According to the original scheme, it was intended to construct 30 docks, for building and laying up the largest ships, at the extremity of the harbour. A large basin, capable of admitting two men of war, is designed to communicate, by sluices, with two smaller basins, from each of which are to extend, like the radii of a circle, five rows of covered docks: each row is to be separated by walls of stone; and each dock to be provided with sluice gates, so as to be filled or emptied by means of pumps. Close to the docks, magazines for naval stores, are to be constructed, and the whole to be enclosed with a stone wall. The project was begun in 1757; but was much neglected until the accession of his present majesty, who warmly patronized the arduous undertaking. At the commencement of the works, 25,000l. were annually expended upon them; which sum has been lessened to about 600l. per annum, and the number of docks reduced to 20. The first dock was finished in 1779, and it was computed that the whole number would be executed in 20 years.

CARLSTADT

Pages 197-197

a town of Germany, in the circle of Franconia, and bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WURZBURG">Wurzburg</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 51' N. Lat. 50° 0'.

CARLTON

Pages 197-197

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> held by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>, that they shall present 1000 herrings baked in 14 pyes to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, wherever he shall be when they first come in season.

CARMAGNIOLA

Pages 197-197

a fortified town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, with a good castle. It was taken by the French in 1694, and retaken by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Eugene the same year. It is seated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding in corn, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, near the river Po, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 32' N. Lat. 44° 43'.

CARMANIA

Pages 197-197

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, to the east of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, Gedrosia to the east, to the south the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, and in part the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a>, called the Carmanian Sea; distinguished into Carmania Deferta, and Carmania Propria, the former lying to the south of Parthia; and to the south of that, the Propria, quite to the sea. Its name is from the Syriac, Carma, signifying a "vine," for which that country was famous, yielding clusters three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. Now Kerman, or Carimania, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Persia.

CARMEL

Pages 197-197

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, standing on the skirts of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and forming the most remarkable headland on all that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. It extends eastward from the sea as far as the plain of Jezreel, and from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of that name quite to Caesarea on the south. It seems to have had the name of Carmel from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fertility; this word, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> import, signifying the vine of God, and is used in Scripture to denote any fruitful spot, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> planted with fruit trees. This mountain, we are assured, was very fertile. Mr Sandys acquaints us, that, when well cultivated, it abounds with olives, vines, and variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and herbs both medicinal and aromatic. Others, however, represent it as rather dry and barren; which perhaps may have happened from the neglect of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in all parts of the Turkish empire, especially where they are exposed to the incursions of the Arabs. Carmel is the name of the mountain, and of a city built on it; as well as of a heathen deity worshipped in it, but without either temple or statue; though anciently there must have been a temple, as we are told that this mountain was a favourite retreat of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, who spent a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the temple, without any person with him. But what hath rendered Mount Carmel most celebrated and revered both by Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, is its having been the residence of the prophet Elijah, who is supposed to have lived there in a cave (which is there shown), before he was taken up into heaven.

CARMELITES

Pages 197-198

an order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, making one of the four tribes of mendicants <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> begging friars; and taking its name from Mount Carmel, formerly inhabited by Elias, Elija, and the children of the prophets; from whom this order pretends to descend in an uninterrupted succession. The manner in which they make out their antiquity has something in it too ridiculous to be rehearsed. Some among them pretend they are descendants of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; others go further, and make <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> a Carmelite, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> regular branches of their order. Phocas, a Greek monk, speaks the most reasonably. He says, that in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, 1185, Elias's cave was still extant on the mountain; near which were the remains of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> which intimated that there had been anciently a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>; that, some years before, an old monk, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>, as he pretended, from the prophet Elias, fixed there, and assembled ten brothers. In 1209, Albert, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, gave the solitaries a rigid rule, which Papebroch has since printed. In 1217, or, according to others, 1226, Pope Honorius III. approved and confirmed it. This rule contained 16 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>; one of which confined them to their cells, and enjoined them to continue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> and night in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>; another prohibited the brethren having any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>; another enjoined fasting from the feast of the holy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> till Easter, except on Sundays; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> at all times from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> was enjoined by another article; one obliged them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> labour; another imposed a strict silence on them from vespers till the third the next day. The peace concluded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Frederic II. with the Saracens, in the year 1229, so disadvantageous to Christendom, and so beneficial to the infidels, occasioned the Carmelites to quit the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, under Alan the fifth general of the order. He first sent some of the religious to Cyprus, who landed there in the year 1328, and founded a monastery in the forest of Fortania. Some Sicilians, at the same time, leaving Mount Carmel, returned to their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where they founded a monastery in the suburbs of Messina. Some English departed out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, in the year 1240, to found others in England. Others of Provence, in the year 1244, founded a monastery in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of Aigualates, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from Marseille; and thus, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of their monasteries increasing, they held their European general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> in the year 1245, at their monastery of Aylesford in England.—This order is so much increased, that it has, at present, provinces, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, in which are 54 monasteries, under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>-general; and the congregations of Barefooted Carmelites in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, which have their peculiar generals. After the establishment of the Carmelites in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, their rule was in some respects altered; the first time, by Pope Innocent IV. who added to the first article a precept of chastity, and relaxed the 11th which enjoins abstinence at all times from flesh, permitting them, when they travelled, to eat boiled flesh; this pope likewise gave them leave to eat in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> refectory, and to keep asses or mules for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Their rule was again mitigated by the popes Eugenius IV. and Pius II. Hence the order is divided into two branches, viz. the Carmelites of the ancient observance, called the moderate, or mitigated; and those of the strict observance, who are the barefooted Carmelites; a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> set on foot in 1549, by St. Theresa, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">nun</a> of the convent of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVILA">Avila</a>, in Castile; these last are divided into two congregations, that of Spain and that of Italy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of the Carmelites was at first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and the cloak laced at the bottom with several huts. But Pope Honorius IV. commanded them to change it for that of the Minims. Their scapulary is a small woollen habit of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, thrown over their shoulders. They wear no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> shirts; but instead of them linen-woolsey, which they change twice a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and once a week in the winter. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a monk of this order lies with a woman, he is prohibited fasting meat for three or four years, is declared infamous, and obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> himself publicly once a week. If he is again guilty of the same fault, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> is doubled; and if a third time, he is expelled the order.

CARMEN

Pages 198-198

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> among the Latins, used in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> to signify a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; but more particularly to signify a spell, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>, form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> exorcism, couched in a few words placed in a mystic order, on which its efficacy depended. Pezron derives the word *carmen* from the Celtic *carm*, the shout of joy, or the verses which the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARDS">bards</a> sung to encourage the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>.—*Carmen* was anciently a denomination given also to precepts, laws, prayers, imprecations, and all solemn formulae couched in a few words placed in a certain order, though written in prose. In which sense it was that the elder Cato wrote a *Carmen de moribus*, which was not in verse but in prose. CARMENTALIA; a feast among the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, celebrated annually upon the 11th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Carmenta, or Carmentis, a prophetess of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, mother of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVANDER">Evander</a>, with whom she came into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> 60 years before the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The solemnity was also repeated on the 15th of January, which is marked in the old <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> by *Carmentalia relata*. This feast was established on occasion of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fecundity among the Roman dames, after a general reconciliation with their husbands, with whom they had been at variance, in regard of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of coaches being prohibited them by an edict of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. This feast was celebrated by the women: he who offered the sacrifices was called *faecordos carmentalis*.

CARMINATIVES

Pages 198-198

medicines used in colics, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other flatulent disorders, to dispel the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. The word comes from the Latin *carminare*, to card or teaze <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and figuratively to attenuate and diffuse wind or vapours, and promote their discharge by perspiration. Though Dr. Quincy makes it more mysterious: He says it comes from the word *carmen*, taking it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of an invocation or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>; and makes it to have been a general name for all medicines which operated like charms, i.e., in an extraordinary manner. Hence, as the most violent pains were frequently those arising from pent-up wind, which immediately cease upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> *carminative* became in a peculiar sense applied to medicines which gave relief in windy <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they cured by enchantment; but this interpretation seems a little too far strained.

CARMINE

Pages 198-198

a powder of a very beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, bordering upon purple; and used by painters in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a>, though rarely, on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> price. The manner of preparing it is kept a secret by the colour-makers; neither do any of those receipts which have for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> been published concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of this and other colours at all answer the purpose. See Colour-making.

CARMONA

Pages 198-198

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>. The gate towards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> is one of the most extraordinary pieces of antiquity in all Spain. It is seated in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, 15 miles east of Seville. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 37'. N. Lat. 37° 34'. CARNATION. See Dianthus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Carnation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a>, among painters, is understood of all the parts of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, in general, which represent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> which are naked and without drapery. Titian and Corregio in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and Rubens and Van Dyke in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, excelled in carnations.—In colouring for flesh, there is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a variety, that it is hard to lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> any general rules for instruction therein; neither are there any regarded by those who have acquired a skill this way; the various colouring for carnations may be easily produced, by taking more or less <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, blue, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISTRE">bistre</a>, whether for the first colouring, or for the finishing; the colour for women should be bluish, for children a little red, both fresh and gay; and for men it should incline to yellow, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are old. Carnation, among dyers. To dye a carnation, or red rose colour, it is directed to take liquor of wheat bran a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> three pounds, tartar two ounces; boil them, and enter 20 yards of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> cloth; after it has boiled three hours, cool and wash it: take fresh clear bran liquor a sufficient quantity, madder five pounds; boil and foddern according to art.—The Bow dyers know that the solution of tin, being put in a kettle to the alum and tartar, in another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, makes the cloth, &c., attract the colour into it, so that none of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a> is left, but the whole is absorbed by the cloth.

CARNEADES

Pages 198-199

a celebrated Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and founder of the third academy. He was so fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, that he not only avoided all entertainments, but forgot even to eat at his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; his maid-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> Melilla was obli- Carnades was put to put the victuals into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. He was an antagonist of the Stoics; and applied himself with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eagerness to refute the works of Chrysippus, one of the most celebrated philosophers of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. The power of his eloquence was dreaded even by a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. The Athenians being condemned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to pay a fine of 500 talents for plundering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Oropus, sent ambassadors to Rome, who got the fine mitigated to 100 talents. Carnades the Academic, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> the Stoic, and Critolaus the Peripatetic, were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with this embassy. Before they had an audience of the senate, they harangued to great multitudes in different parts of the city. Carnades's eloquence was distinguished from that of the others by its strength and rapidity. Cato the Elder made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> in the senate that these ambassadors should be immediately sent back, because it was very difficult to discern the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> through the arguments of Carnades. The Athenian ambassadors (said many of the senators) were sent rather to force us to comply with their demands, than to solicit them by persuasion; meaning, that it was impossible to resist the power of that eloquence with which Carnades addressed himself to them. According to Plutarch, the youth at Rome were so charmed by the orations of this philosopher, that they forsook their exercises and other diversions, and were carried with a kind of madness to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; the humour of philosophizing spreading like enthusiasm. This grieved Cato, who was particularly afraid of the subtilty of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and strength of argument with which Carnades maintained either side of a question. Carnades harangued in favour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and the next day against it, to the admiration of all who heard him, among whom were Galba and Cato, the greatest orators of Rome. This was his element; he delighted in demolishing his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; because it served in the end to confirm his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> principle, that there are only probabilities <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> resemblances of truth in the mind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; so that of two things directly opposite, either may be chosen indifferently. Quintilian remarks, that though Carnades argued in favour of injustice, yet he himself acted according to the strict rules of justice. The following was a maxim of Carnades: "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a man privately knew that his enemy, or any other person whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> might be of advantage to him, would come to sit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on grass in which there lurked an asp, he ought to give him notice of it, though it were in the power of no person whatever to blame him for being silent." Carnades, according to some, lived to be 85 years old; others make him to be 90: his death is placed in the 4th year of the 162nd Olympiad.

CARNEDDE

Pages 199-199

in British antiquity, denote heaps of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, supposed to be druidical remains, and thrown together on occasion of confirming and commemorating a covenant, Gen. xxxi. 46. They are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLESEY">Anglesey</a>, and were also used as sepulchral monuments, in the manner of tumuli; for Mr Rowland found a curious urn in one of these carnedd. Whence it may be inferred, that the Britons had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of throwing stones on the deceased. From this custom is derived the Welsh proverb, Karn ardyben, "I'll betide thee."

CARNEIA

Pages 199-199

in antiquity, a festival in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, named Carneus, held in most cities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, but especially at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, where it was first instituted. The reason of the name, as well as the occasion of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, is controverted. It lasted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> days, beginning on the 13th of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> Carneus. The ceremonies were an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the method of living and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>. CARNEL.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of ships first with their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and beams, and after bringing on their planks, is called carnel <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, to distinguish it from clinch work. Vessels also which go with mizen sails instead of main sails are by some called carnels.

CARNELIAN

Pages 199-199

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of which there are three kinds, distinguished by three colours, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. The red is very well known among us; is found in roundish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> oval masses, much like our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pebbles; and is generally met with between an inch and two or three inches in diameter; it is of a fine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> texture; of a glossy surface; and, in the several specimens, is of all the degrees of red, from the palest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to the deepest blood-red. It is generally free from spots, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, or variegations: but sometimes it is veined very beautifully with an extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> red, or with white; the veins forming concentric circles, or other less regular figures, about a nucleus, in the manner of those of agates. The pieces of carnelian which are all of one colour, and perfectly free from veins, are those which our jewellers generally make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for seals, though the variegated ones are much more beautiful. The carnelian is tolerably hard, and capable of a very good polish: it is not at all affected by acid menstruums: the fire divests it of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of its colour, and leaves it of a pale red; and a strong and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> reduce it to a pale dirty gray. The finest carnelians are those of the East Indies; but there are very beautiful ones found in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of Silesea and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>; and we have some not despicable ones in England. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> have recommended the carnelian as alluring, and attributed a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fanciful virtues to it, we know of no other use of the stone than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> seals on it; to which purpose it is excellently adapted, as being not too hard for cutting, and yet hard enough not to be liable to accidents, to take a good polish, and to separate easily from the wax.

CARNERO

Pages 199-199

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a name given to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> which extends from the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Iltria to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Grofia and the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORLACHIA">Morlachia</a>. CARNERO is likewise the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> to the west of the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Gibraltar.

CARNIFEX

Pages 199-199

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> executioner. By reason of the odiousness of his office, the carnicex was expressly prohibited by the laws from having his dwelling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. In middle-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers carnicex also denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>. Under the Anglo-Danish kings, the carnicex was an officer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; being ranked with the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Goodwin, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>. Flor. Wigorn. ann. 1040, Rex Hardecanutus Africum Ebor. Archiep. Goodwinum comitem, Edricum dispensaorem.

CARNIOLA

Pages 199-200

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Germany, bounded on the south by the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Illyria possessed by the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by Carinthia and Styria; on the east, by Slavonia and Croatia; on the west, by Friuli, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Gorz <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Goritz, and a part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Venice; extending in length about 110 miles, and in breadth about 50. It had its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name Carnia, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> one Carniola, from its ancient inhabitants the Carni, a tribe of Scythians, otherwise called Japoders, whence this and the adjacent countries were also called Japodia. Carniola is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, some of which are cultivated and inhabited, some covered with wood, others naked and barren, and others continually buried in snow. The valleys are very fruitful. Here are likewise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> must be had from the sovereign's magazines. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, besides many medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and inland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people are very hardy, going barefooted in winter through the snow, with open breasts, and sleeping on a hard <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> or bolster. Their food is also very coarse and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>. In winter, when the snow lies deep on the ground, the mountaineers bind either small baskets, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> thin narrow boards, like the Laplanders, to their feet, on which, with the help of a stout <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> or pole, they descend with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> velocity from the mountains. When the snow is frozen, they make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a sort of irons or skis. In different parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> the inhabitants, especially the common sort, differ greatly in their dress, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and manner of living. In Upper and Lower Carniola, they wear long beards. The languages chiefly in use are the Slavonian or Wendish, and German; the first by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a>, and the latter by people of fashion. The duchy is divided into the Upper, Lower, Middle, and Inner Carniola. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> commodities exported hence are, iron, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, lead, quicksilver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of olives, cattle, sheep, cheese, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and a kind of woollen stuff called mabalan, Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, walnuts, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; together with all manner of woodwork, as boxes, dishes, &c. Christianity was first planted here in the eighth century. Lutheranism made a considerable progress in it; but, excepting the Walachians or Ukokes, who are of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and style themselves Staroverzi, i.e., old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a>, all the inhabitants at present are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. Carniola was long a marquise or margravate; but in the year 1231 was erected into a duchy. As its proportion towards the maintenance of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, it pays annually 363,171 florins; but only two regiments of foot are quartered in it.

CARNIVAL

Pages 200-200
or CARNAVAL, a time of rejoicing, a season of mirth, observed with great solemnity by the Italians, particularly at Venice, holding from the twelfth day till Lent. The word is formed from the Italian Carnaval; which M. Du Cange derives from Carn-a-va-l, by reason the flesh then goes to pot, to make amends for the season of abstinence then ensuing. Accordingly, in the corrupt Latin, he observes, it was called Carnale- wamen, and Carniprivium; as the Spaniards still denominate it carnes tollendas. Feasts, balls, operas, concerts of music, intrigues, marriages, &c. are chiefly held in carnival time. The carnival begins at Venice the second holiday in Christmas: Then it is they begin to wear masks, and open their playhouses and gaming houses; the place of St Mark is filled with mountebanks, jack puddings, pedlars, whores, and such like mob, who flock thither from all parts. There have been no less than seven foreign princes and 30,000 foreigners here to partake of these diversions.

CARNIVOROUS

Pages 200-201

an epithet applied to those animals which naturally feed and feed on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. It has been a dispute among naturalists, whether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is naturally carnivorous. Those who take the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> side of the question, insist chiefly on the structure of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, which are mostly incisors <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> molars; not such as carnivorous animals are furnished with, and which are proper to tear flesh in pieces: to which it may be added, that, even when we do feed on flesh, it is not without a preparatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, roasting, &c. and even then that it is the hardest of digestion of all foods. To these arguments Dr Wallis subjoins another, which is, that all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> which feed on herbs or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> colon, with a cæcum at the upper end of it, or somewhat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a>, which conveys the food by a long and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> progress, from the stomach downwards, in order to its slower passage and longer stay in the intestines: but that, in carnivorous animals, such cæcum is wanting, and instead thereof there is a more short and slender gut, and a quicker passage through the intestines. Now, in man, the cæcum is very visible: a strong presumption that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, who is still consistent with herself, did not intend him for a carnivorous animal.—It is true, the cæcum is but small in adults, and seems of little or no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; but in a fetus it is much larger in proportion: And it is probable, our customary change of diet, as we grow up, may occasion this shrinking. But to these arguments Dr Tyton replies, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> man had been by nature designed not to be carnivorous, there would doubtless have been found, somewhere on the globe, people who do not feed on flesh; which is not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. Neither are carnivorous animals always without a colon and cæcum; nor are all animals carnivorous which have these parts: the opossum for instance, hath both a colon and cæcum, and yet feeds on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> and other flesh; whereas the hedgehog, which has neither colon nor cæcum, and so ought to be carnivorous, feeds only on vegetables. Add to this, that hogs which have both, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> feed upon flesh when they can get it; and rats and mice, which have large cæcums, will feed on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">bacon</a> as well as <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and cheese. Lastly, The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> are furnished with teeth necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of all kinds of foods; from whence it would seem, that nature intended we should live on all. And as the alimentary duct in the human body is fitted for digesting all kinds of foods, ought we not rather to conclude, that nature did not intend to deny us any? It is no less disputed whether mankind were carnivorous before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>. St Jerome, Chrysostome, Theodore, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, maintain, that all animal food CARNOSITY food was then forbidden; which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is also strenuously supported among the moderns by Carcella, and refuted by Heidegger, Danzius, Bochart, &c. CARNOSITY is used by some authors for a little fleshly excrecence, tubercle, or wen, formed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a>, the neck of the bladder, or yard, which stops the passage of the urine. Carnosities are very difficult of cure: they are not easily known but by introducing a probe into the passage, which there meets with resistance. They usually arise from some venereal malady ill managed.

CARO

Pages 201-201

ANNIBAL, a celebrated Italian poet, was born at Civita Nuovo in 1507. He became secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Parma, and afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Farnese. He was also made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>. He translated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s Aeneid into his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, with such propriety and elegance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, that he was allowed by the best judges to have equalled the original. He also translated <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, two oratories of Gregory Nazianzen, with a discourse of Cyprian. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>; and a miscellany of his poems was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1584. He died at Rome in 1566.

CAROLINA

Pages 201-202

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, comprehending the most westerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>, and lying between 29 and 35 degrees of N. Lat. It is bounded on the east by the Atlantic, and on the west by the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>, on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, and to the south of Georgia by the Floridas. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is seated between the extremities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, though the heat is more troublesome in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> than the cold in winter; their winters being very short, and the frosty mornings frequently succeeded by warm days. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is generally serene and clear the greatest part of the year; but in February and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> the inhabitants have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the woods, which causes such a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, as to strangers would seem to proceed from a fog <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thickens in the air. The smoke of the tar-kilns likewise deceives strangers, and gives them an ill <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the air of Carolina; to which also conduces a custom of the Indians of setting fire to the woods in their huntings, for many miles round. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rains are in winter, though they are not without heavy showers at midsummer; add to these the constant dews that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in the night, which refresh the ground and supply the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> with moisture. In North Carolina, the northwest winds in the winter occasion very pinching <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; but they are not of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance. Westerly winds bring very pleasant weather; but the southerly are hot and unwholesome, occasioning fevers and other disorders. But this must be understood of summer, for in winter they are very comfortable. The depth of winter is towards the latter end of February, and then the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> is not strong enough to bear a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. In August and September there are sometimes great storms and squalls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, which are so violent as to make lanes of 100 feet wide, more or less, through the woods, tearing up the trees by the roots. These storms generally happen once in about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years; and are attended with dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, and heavy rains. They <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> happen about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the hurricanes which rage so fatally among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> between the tropics; and seem to be occasioned by them, or to proceed from the same cause; but by the time they reach Carolina, their force is much abated; and the farther north they proceed, so much the more do they decrease in fury. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>; but farther up, the country is so fruitful that they have not yet been at the trouble to manure their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The grains most cultivated are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, though any sort <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> thrive well enough; they have also <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> of several sorts, little known in England. All kinds of garden stuff usual in England are cultivated here, and may be had in great plenty. They export <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities yearly of rice, pitch, tar, turpentine, deer-skins, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; cypresses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, sassafras, oak, walnut, and pine. Besides these, they also send out beef, pork, tallow, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, furs, wheat, peas, potatoes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, beeswax, myrtle-wax, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, snake-root, cotton, several sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> and medicinal drugs. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">Indigo</a> is also cultivated in this province, but of an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to that which comes from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee islands</a>. It hath been attempted in vain to cultivate vines, and produce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, in this country; for though the frosts here do not continue long without intervals of warmer weather, they are sufficient to check the growth of the vine, as well as olives, dates, oranges, &c. The furs are bought of the Indians with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, coarse cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and spirituous liquors. As yet they have not a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of handicraftsmen; which renders labour very dear, and a supply of clothes from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> necessary. The aspect of the country is very fine, being adorned with beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and creeks, and the woods with lofty timber, which afford delightful and pleasant seats for the planters, and render the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FENCING">fencing</a> their lands very easy. And as they have plenty of fish, wild-fowl, and venison, besides other necessaries which this country produces naturally, they live easy and luxuriously. Their rivers are large, and navigable a great many miles upon the country. They rise near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and abound with delicate fish, besides <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-fowl of different kinds. In some there are islands which yield good pasture, without the annoyance of wild beasts. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> mountains are the Cherokee or Allegany mountains, which are situated north and northwest, five or six hundred miles distant from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. They are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and abound with trees, plants, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and minerals, of different kinds. This country is divided into North and South Carolina, and Georgia; each of which, before the late revolution, was under a particular governor. The North is subdivided into four counties, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANVILLE">Granville</a>, Colliton, Berkley, and Craven; and South Carolina into two, Clarendon and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a>. This last is also divided into 14 parishes or townships, each of which has a brick or timber <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The former likewise has the same number of parishes. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARLESTOWN">Charlestown</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the whole country. Carolina was discovered by Sebastian Cabot about the year 1520, in the reign of Henry VII., but the settling of it being neglected by the English, a colony of French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, by the encouragement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Coligni, were transported thither; and named the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their first settlement Arc Carolina, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IX., of France; but in a short time that colony was destroyed by the Spaniards; and no other attempt was made by any European power to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> there till the year 1664, when 800 English landed at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Fear in North Carolina, and took possession of the country. In 1670 Cha. II. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> granted Carolina to the lords Berkeley, Clarendon, Albemarle, Craven, and Ashly, Sir George Carteret, Sir William Berkeley, and Sir John Colliton. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> for this new colony was drawn up by the famous Mr Locke, who very wisely proposed an universal toleration in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> matters. The only restriction in this respect was, that every person claiming the protection of that settlement, should, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 17, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> himself in some particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. To civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, however, our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> was not so favourable; the code of Carolina gave to the eight proprietors who founded the colony, and to their heirs, not only all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of a monarch, but all the powers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">legislation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, which was composed of this sovereign body, and called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a> Court, was invested with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of nominating to all employments and dignities, and even of conferring <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; but with new and unprecedented titles. They were, for instance, to create in each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> two caciques, each of whom was to be possessed of 24,000 acres of land; and a landgrave, who was to have 80,000. The persons on whom these honours should be bestowed were to compose the upper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and their possessions were made unalienable. They had only the right of farming or letting out a third part of them at the most for three lives. The lower house was composed of the deputies from the several counties and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. The number of this representative body was to be increased as the colony grew more populous. No tenant was to pay more than about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, and even this rent was redeemable. All the inhabitants, however, both slaves and freemen, were under an obligation to take up arms upon the first order from the Palatine court. It was not long before the defects of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> became apparent. The proprietary lords used every endeavour to establish an arbitrary government; and, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the colonists exerted themselves with great zeal to avoid servitude. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this struggle, the whole province, distracted with tumults and dissensions, became incapable of making any progress, though great things had been expected from its particular advantages of situation. Though a toleration in religious matters was a part of the original constitution, dissensions arose likewise on that account. In 1705, Carteret, now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Granville, who, as the oldest of the proprietors, was sole governor of the colony, formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of obliging all the non-conformists to embrace the ceremonies of the Church of England; and this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of violence, though disapproved and rejected by the mother-country, inflamed the minds of the people. In 1720, while this animosity was still subsisting, the province was attacked by several bands of savages, driven to despair by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> course of the most atrocious violence and injustice. These unfortunate wretches were all put to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; but, in 1728, the lords proprietors having refused to contribute towards the expenses of an expedition, of which they were to share the immediate benefits, were deprived of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, except Lord Granville, who still retained his eighth part. The rest received a recompense of about 24,000l. The colony was taken under the immediate protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and from that time began to flourish. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> into North and South Carolina now took place, and the settlement of Georgia commenced in 1732. See GEORGIA. CAROLINE. See CARLINE. CAROLINE Books, the name of four books, composed by order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, to refute the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice. These books are couched in very harsh and severe terms, containing 120 heads of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> against the council of Nice, and condemning the worship of images.

CAROLOSTADIANS

Pages 202-202
or CAROLOSTADIANS, an ancient sect or branch of Lutherans, who denied the real presence of Christ in the eucharist. They were thus denominated from their leader Andrew Carolostadius, who having originally been archdeacon of Wittenberg, was converted by Luther, and was the first of all the reformed clergy who took a wife; but disagreeing afterwards with Luther, chiefly in the point of the sacrament, founded a sect apart. The Carolostadians are the same with what are otherwise denominated Sacramentarians, and agree in most things with the Zuinglians.

CAROLUS

Pages 202-202

a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, with a little silver mixed with it, struck under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VIII. of France. The carolus was worth 12 deniers when it ceased to be current. Those which are still current in trade in Lorraine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in some neighbouring provinces, go under the name of French fols.

CAROTIDS

Pages 202-202

in Anatomy, two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> of the neck, which convey the blood from the aorta to the brain; one called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and the other the left, carotid.

CARP

Pages 202-203

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, the English name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cyprinus. See CYPRINUS, ICHTHYOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The carp is the most valuable of all kinds of fish for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a> of ponds. It is very quick in its growth, and brings forth the spawn three times a-year, so that the increase is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> does not begin to breed till eight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years old; so that in breeding-ponds a supply must be kept of carp of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The best judges allow, that, in stocking a breeding-pond, four males should be allowed to twelve females. The usual growth of a carp is two or three inches in length in a year; but, in ponds which receive the fattening of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> feeders, they have been known to grow from five inches to 18 in one year. A feeding-pond of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> very well feed 300 carp of three years old, 300 of two years, and 400 of one year old. Carp delight greatly in ponds that have marley sides; they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> also clay-ponds well sheltered from the winds and grown with weeds and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> grass at the edges, which they feed on in the hot months. Carp and tench thrive very fast in ponds and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is a little brackish; but they are not so well tasted as those which live in fresh water. Grains, blood, chicken-guts, and the like, may at times CARPATES times be thrown into carp-ponds, to help to fatten the fish. To make them grow <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and fat, the growth of grass under the water should by all means possible be encouraged. For this purpose, as the water decreases in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the sides of the pond left naked and dry should be well raked with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a>, to destroy all the weeds, and cut up the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; hay-feed should then be sown plentifully in these places; and more ground prepared in the same manner, as the water falls more and more away. By this means there will be a fine and plentiful growth of young grass along the sides of the pond to the water's edge; and when the rains fill up the pond again, this will be all buried under the water, and will make a feeding-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for the fish where they will come early in the morning, and will fatten greatly upon what they find there.

CARPATHUS

Pages 203-203

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, two hundred stadia in compass, and an hundred in length. Its name is said to be from its situation on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>. It lies between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> which, from this island, is called the Carpathian sea, and has to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> the Ionian, to the south the Egyptian, to the west the Cretan and African seas. It is two hundred furlongs in compass, and a hundred in length. It had anciently, according to Strabo, four cities; according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYLAX">Scylax</a>, only three. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> mentions but one, which he calls Pofidium. This island is now called Scarpano. CARPÆA, a kind of dance anciently in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the Athenians and Magnesians, performed by two persons, the one acting a labourer, the other a robber. The labourer, laying his arms, goes to ploughing and sowing, still looking warily about him as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> afraid of being surprised: the robber at length appears; and the labourer quitting his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, betakes himself to his arms, and fights in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his oxen. The whole was performed to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of flutes, and in cadence. Sometimes the robber was overcome and sometimes the labourer; the victor's reward being the oxen and plough. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> was to teach and accustom the peasants to defend themselves against the attacks of ruffians.

CARPENTER

Pages 203-203

a person who practises <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARPENTRY">Carpentry</a>. The word is formed from the French charpentier, which signifies the same, formed of charpente, which denotes <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather from the Latin carpentarius, a maker of carpena, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. Carpenter of a Ship, an officer appointed to examine and keep in order the frame of a ship, together with her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, yards, boats, and all other wooden machinery. It is his duty in particular to keep the ship tight; for which purpose he ought frequently to review the decks and sides, and to caulk them when it is necessary. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, he is to examine up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, with all possible <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, in the lower apartments of the ship, to stop any holes that may have been made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, with wooden plugs provided of several sizes.

CARPENTRAS

Pages 203-203

an episcopal town of France, in the department of Vaucluse, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Venafin. It is subject to the pope; and is seated on the river Aufon, at the foot of a mountain. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 6. N. Lat. 44. 4.

CARPENTRY

Pages 203-203

the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>, framing, and joining <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pieces of wood, for the uses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. It is one of the arts subservient to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, and is divided into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-carpentry and ship-carpentry: the first is employed in raising, roofing, flooring of houses, &c. and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in the building of ships, barges, &c. The rules in carpentry are much the same as those of Joinery; the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is, that carpentry is used in the larger and coarser <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and joinery in the smaller and curious. See Centre, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">Roof</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRENGTH_OF_MATERIALS">Strength of Materials</a>.

CARPENTUM

Pages 203-203

in Antiquity, a name <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> sorts of vehicles, answering to coaches as well as waggons, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even carts, among us. The carpentum was originally a kind of car or vehicle in which the Roman ladies were carried; though in after times it was also used in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Some derive the word from carro; others from Carmenta the mother of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVANDER">Evander</a>, by a conversion of the m into p.

CARPET

Pages 203-203

a sort of covering of stuff, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other materials, wrought with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> or on a loom, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the furniture of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> spread over tables, or laid upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>. Persian and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> carpets are those most esteemed; though at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> there is a manufactory after the manner of Peria, where they make them little inferior, not to say finer, than the true Persian carpets. They are velvety, and perfectly imitate the carpets which come from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. There are also carpets of Germany, some of which are made of woollen stuffs, as serges, &c. and called <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> carpets: others are made of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> also, but wrought with the needle, and pretty often embellished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; and, lastly, there are some made of dogs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. We have likewise carpets made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, which are used either as floor-carpets, or to cover chairs, &c. It is true, we are not arrived at the like perfection in this manufacture with our neighbours the French; but may not this be owing to the want of a like public encouragement? Carpet-Knights, a denomination given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>-men and others, of peaceable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>, who, on account of their birth, office, or merits to the public, or the like, are, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. They take the appellation carpet, because they usually receive their honours from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, kneeling on a carpet. By which they are distinguished from knights created in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, or field of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> prowess. Carpet-knights possess a medium between those called truck, or dungehill-knights, who only purchase or merit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> by their wealth, and knights-bachelors, who are created for their services in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>.

CARPI

Pages 203-204

a principality of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, lying about four leagues from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. It formerly belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Pio; the elder sons of which bore the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Princes of St Gregory. In the beginning of the 14th century, Manfray was the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Carpi; but in the 16th, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V gave the principality to Alfonso <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>. This nobleman, in recompense, gave to Albert Pio, to whom the principality of Carpi belonged by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, the town of Saffuolo and some other lands. Albert was, however, at last obliged to retire to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; where, being stripped of all his estates, he died in 1538, with the reputation of being one of the best and bravest men of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The family of Pio is yet in being, and continues attached to the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Some of them have even been raised to the purple, and still make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Carpi, a town of Italy in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Modena, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the last mentioned principality. It has a strong castle, and is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 12. N. Lat. 44. 45. Carpi, a town of the Veronese in Italy, memorable for a victory gained by the Imperialists over the French in 1701. It is subject to the Venetians; and is situated on the river Adige, in E. Long. 11. 39. N. Lat. 45. 10. Carpi, Ugo da, an Italian painter, of no very considerable talents in that art, but remarkable for being the inventor of that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of engraving on wood, distinguished by the name of chiaro-uro, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>.
