This is performed by using more blocks than one; and Ugo da Carpi usually had three; the first for the outline and dark shadows, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> shadows, and the third for the half tint. In that manner he struck off <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> after several designs, and cartons of Raphael; particularly one of the Sibyl, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from the Crofs, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Simon the Sorcerer. He died in 1500. This art was brought to a still higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection by Baltafar Peruzzi of Siena, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARMIGIANO">Parmigiano</a>, who published several excellent designs in that manner. Carpi, Girolamo da, history and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> painter, was born at Ferrara in 1501, and became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Garofalo. When he quitted that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, he devoted his whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, thoughts, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the works of Correggio, and to copy them with a most critical care and observation; in which labour he spent several years at Parma, Modena, and other cities of Italy, where the best works of that exquisite painter were preserved. He acquired such an excellence in the imitation of Correggio's style, and copying his pictures, that many paintings finished by him were taken for originals, and not only admired, but were eagerly purchased by the connoisseurs of that time. Nor is it improbable that several of the paintings of Girolamo de Carpi <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> for the genuine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Correggio himself. He died in 1556. Carpinus, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>-beam. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Carposalum, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, the fruit of the tree which yields the true oriental balsam. The carposalum is used in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, according to Proper Alpinus, in all the intentions in which the balsam itself is applied: but the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the Europeans make of it is in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> treacle and mithridate; and in these not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, for cubeb and juniper-berries are generally substituted in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Carpoctatians, a branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Gnostics, so called from Carpoctates, who in the second century revived and improved upon the errors of Simon Magus, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a>, Saturninus, and other Gnostics. He owned, with them, one sole principle and father of all things, whose name as well as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> was unknown. The word, he taught, was created by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, vastly inferior to the first principle. He opposed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; making him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, begotten carnally on the body of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, though possessed of uncommon gifts which set him above other creatures. He inculcated a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of women; and taught, that the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> could not be purified, till it had committed all kinds of abominations, making that a necessary condition of perfection. Carpolithi, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Fruit-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> Rocks of the Germans, are composed of a kind of jasper, of the nature of the amygdaloides, or almond-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Bertrand affirms that the latter are those which appear to be composed of elliptical pieces like petrified almonds, though, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, they are only small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> pieces of calcareous stone rounded by attrition, and sometimes small mussel-shells connected by a flinty concretion. The name of Carpolithi, however, is given in general by writers on fossils to all sorts of stony concretions that have any resemblance to fruit of whatever kind. Carpus, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>. See Anatomy Index. Carr, a kind of rolling throne, used in triumphs, and at the splendid entries of princes. See Chariot. The word is from the ancient Gaulish, or Celtic, Carr; mentioned by Cæsar, in his Commentaries, under the name Carrus. Plutarch relates, that Camillus having entered Rome in triumph, mounted on a carr drawn by four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> horses, it was looked on as too haughty an innovation. Carr is also used for a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> open chariot. The carr, on medals, drawn either by horses, lions, or elephants, usually signifies either a triumph or an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a>: sometimes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> of the images of the gods at a solemn supplication, and sometimes of those of some illustrious family at a funeral. The carr covered, and drawn by mules, only signifies a confection, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> done any one of having his image carried at the gates of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>. See Consecration, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRAC">Carrac</a>, or Carraca, a name given by the Portuguese to the vessels they send to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> and the East Indies; being very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, round built, and fitted for flight as well as burden. Their capacity lies in their depth, which is very extraordinary. They are narrower above than underneath, and have sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight floors; they carry about 2000 tons, and are capable of lodging 2000 men; but of late they are little used. Formerly they were also in use among the knights of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, as well as among the Genoese, and other Italians. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> among the Portuguese, when the carracs returned from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, not to bring any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> or sloop for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the ship beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Helena; at which place they sink them on purpose; in order to take from the crew all hopes or possibility of saving themselves, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of shipwreck. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRARA">Carrara</a> marble, among our artists, the name of a species of white marble, which is called marmor lunensis, and ligustrium by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>: it is distinguished from the Parian, now called the statuary marble, by being harder and less bright. Carraveira a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in Europe, with

CARRIAGE

Pages 204-205

a vehicle serving to convey persons, goods, merchandises, and other things, from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another. For the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> principles of wheel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>. Carriage of a cannon, the frame <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on which it is mounted, serving to point it for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a>, or to carry it from one place to another. It is made of two planks of wood, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of one-half the length of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, and joined by three wooden transoms, strengthened with three bolts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. It is mounted on two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, but on a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> has two fore-wheels with limbers added. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> parts of a carriage are the cheeks, transom, bolts, plates, trainbands, bridges, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, hooks, trunion holes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">Block</a>-Carriage, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a> made on purpose for carrying mortars and their beds from place to place. Truck-Carriage, two short planks of wood, supported on two axletrees, having four trucks of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> wood for carrying mortars or guns upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, where their own carriages cannot go. They are drawn by men.

CARRICK

Pages 205-205

the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the shire of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYR">Ayr</a> in Scotland. It borders on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>; stretches 32 miles in length; and is a hilly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> fit for pasture. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Stinchar and Girvan, both abounding with salmon. Here are also several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and forests; and the people on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> employ themselves in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>-fishery, though they have no harbour of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. The only <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of this district are Girvan and Ballantrae; the former at the mouth of the river of the same name, and the latter at the mouth of the Stinchar; and Maybole, an inland town. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, as prince of Scotland, is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Carrick. Carrick on the Sore, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIPPERARY">Tipperary</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 14. N. Lat. 52. 16. Carrick-Fergus, a town of Ireland, in the county of Antrim and province of Ulster. It is a town and county in itself, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It is very rich and populous, with a good harbour; and is governed by a mayor, recorder, and sheriffs.—It has, however, been of far greater consequence than at present, as appears from the mayor having been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of coast in the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> and Antrim, and the corporation enjoying the customs paid by all vessels within these bounds, the creeks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELFAST">Belfast</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a> excepted. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> was repurchased, and the customhouse transferred to Belfast.—Here is the skeleton of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> built by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a> in the reign of James I. an old Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> with many family monuments, and a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> old castle. The town was formerly walled round, and some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the walls is still remaining entire.—Carrick-fergus is seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name in the Irish channel; and is noted for being the landing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William in 1692. Here also Thurrot made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> in 1759, took possession of the castle, and carried away hostages for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> of the town; but being soon after pursued by Commodore Elliot, his three ships were taken, and he himself was killed. Vol. V. Part I.

CARRIER

Pages 205-206

is a person that carries goods for others for hire. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> carrier, having the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> and carriage of goods, is to answer for the same, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the value, to the owner. And where goods are delivered to a carrier, and he is robbed of them, he shall be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> and answer for them, because of the hire. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a common carrier who is offered his hire, and who has convenience, refuses to carry goods, he is liable to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, in the same manner as an innkeeper who refuses to entertain a guest. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSUMPSIT">Assumpsit</a>. One brought a box to a carrier, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and the carrier demanded of the owner what <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. Diff. was in it; he answered, that it was filled with silks, and such like goods; upon which the carrier took it, and was robbed, and adjudged to make it good; but a special <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a>, as, provided there is no charge of money, would have excused the carrier.—A person delivered to a carrier's book-keeper two bags of money sealed up, to be carried from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, and told him that it was 200l. and took his receipt for the same, with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of delivery for 10s. per cent. carriage and risk: though it be proved that there was 400l. in the bags, if the carriage be robbed, he shall answer only for 200l. because there was a particular undertaking for that sum and no more; and his regard, which makes him answerable, extends no farther. If a common carrier loses goods which he is intrusted to carry, a special action on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> lies against him, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the realm, and not trover; and so of a common carrier by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>. An action <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> against a porter, carrier, or barge-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, upon his bare receipt of the goods, if they are lost through negligence. Also a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>-man spoiling goods he is to carry, by letting <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> come to them, action of the case lies against him, on the common custom. Carrier-Pigeon, or courier-pigeon, a sort of pigeon used, when properly trained, to be sent with letters from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another. See Columba. Though you carry these birds hood-winked, 20, 30, nay, 60 or 100 miles, they will find their way in a very little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the place where they were bred. They are trained to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>: and are carried first, while young, short flights of half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, afterwards more, till at length they will return from the farthest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Every bailiwick has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of these pigeons bred in the feraglio, which, upon any emergent occasion, as in insurrection, or the like, he dispatches, with letters braced under their wings, to the feraglio; which proves a more speedy method, as well as a more safe one, than any other; he sends out more than one pigeon, however, for fear of accidents. Lithgow assures us, that one of these birds will carry a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>, which is 30 days journey, in 48 hours. This is also a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> practice: Hirtius and Brutus, at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, held a correspondence with one another by means of pigeons. And Ovid tells us, that Taurophenes, by a pigeon stained with purple, gave notice to his father of his victory at the Olympic Games, sending it to him at Aegina. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, the most noted were the pigeons of Aleppo, which served as couriers at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRETTA">Alexandretta</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>. But this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them has been laid aside for the last 30 or 40 years, because the Kurd robbers kill... ed the pigeons. The manner of sending advice by them was this: they took pairs which had young ones, and carried them on horseback to the place from whence they wished them to return, taking care to let them have a full view. When the news arrived, the correspondent tied a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILLET">billet</a> to the pigeon's foot, and let her loose. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, impatient to see its young, flew off like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, and arrived at Aleppo in ten hours from Alexandretta, and in two days from Bagdad. It was not difficult for them to find their way back, since Aleppo may be discovered at an immense distance. This pigeon has nothing peculiar in its form, except its nostrils, which, instead of being smooth and even, are swelled and rough.

CARRON

Pages 206-208

a small but remarkable river in Scotland, rising about the middle of the isthmus between the firths of Forth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>. Both its source, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it empties itself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, are within the shire of Stirling, which it divides into two nearly equal parts. The whole length of its course, which is from west to east, is not above 14 miles. It falls into the firth of Forth about three miles to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALKIRK">Falkirk</a>. The stream thereof is but small, and scarce deserves the notice of a traveller; yet there is no river in Scotland, and few in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, whose banks have been the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of so many memorable transactions. When the Roman empire was in all its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, and had its eastern frontiers upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, the banks of Carron were its boundaries upon the north-west; for the wall of Antoninus*, which was raised to mark the limits of that mighty empire, stood in the neighbourhood of this river, and ran <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to it for several miles. Near the middle of its course, in a pleasant valley, stand two beautiful mounts, called the Hills of Dunipace, which are taken notice of by most of the Scottish historians as monuments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. The whole structure of these mounts is of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; but they are not both of the same form and dimensions. The more easterly one is perfectly round, resembling an oven, and about fifty feet in height: And that this is an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> does not admit of the least doubt; but we cannot affirm the same, with equal certainty, of the other, though it has been generally supposed to be so too. It bears no resemblance to the eastern one either in shape <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> size. At the foundation it is nearly of a triangular form; but the superstructure is quite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; nor does the height thereof bear any proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of its base. These mounts are now planted with firs, which, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Dunipace standing in the middle between them, and the river running hard by, give this valley a very romantic appearance. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> account given of these mounts is, that they were erected as monuments of a peace concluded in that place between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> and the Caledonians, and that their name partakes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of both people; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUN">Dun</a> signifying a hill in the old language of this island, and Pax "peace" in the language of Rome. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> word, Dunipace, signifies "the hills of peace." And we find in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that no less than three treaties of peace were at different periods entered into between the Romans and Caledonians; the first by Severus about the year 210; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> soon after, by his son <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARACALLA">Caracalla</a>; and the third, by the usurper Carausius, Carron, about the year 280; but of which of these treaties Dunipace is a monument, we do not pretend to determine. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the concurring testimony of historians and antiquaries did not agree in giving this original to these mounts, we would be tempted to conjecture that they are sepulchral monuments. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and urns have been discovered in earthen fabrics of this kind in many parts of this island, and the little mounts or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROWS">barrows</a> which are scattered in great numbers about <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONEHENGE">Stonehenge</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a> plain are generally supposed to have been the sepulchres of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Britons. See BARROWS. From the valley of Dunipace, the river runs for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in a deep and hollow channel, with steep banks on both sides; here it passes by the foundations of the ancient Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>; not far from which, as is generally thought, was the scene of the memorable conference betwixt the Scotch patriot William Wallace and Robert Bruce, father to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of that name, which first opened the eyes of the latter to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> view, both of his own true <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and that of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. After the river has left the village and bridge of Larbert, it soon comes up to another small valley, through the midst of which it has now worn out to itself a straight channel, whereas, in former ages, it had taken a considerable compass, as appears by the track of the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> which is still visible. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and circling banks upon the south side give to this valley the appearance of a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>; and, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the country, there was once an harbour here: nor does the tradition seem altogether groundless, pieces of broken anchors having been found here, and some of them within the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of people yet alive. The stream <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> would still flow near the place, if they were not kept back by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>-head built across the river at Stenhoule; and there is reason to believe, that the stream flowed considerably higher in former ages than it does at present. In the near neighbourhood of this valley, upon the south, stand the ruins of ancient Camelon: which, after it was abandoned by the Romans, was probably inhabited, for some ages, by the natives of the country. Another ancient monument, called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>'s Oven, once stood upon the banks of the Carron; but was, with a spirit truly Gothic, entirely demolished about 40 years ago. The corner of a small inclosure between Stenhoule and the Carron <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-works, is pointed out as the place of its situation. This is generally supposed to have been a Roman work; though it is not easy to conceive what could be their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> for erecting such a fabric, at so great a distance from any other of their works, and in a spot which at that time must have been very remote and unfrequented. The form of it is said to have been perfectly round, and rising perpendicular for some yards at first, but afterwards gradually contracted, till it terminated in a narrow orifice at the top. Antiquaries are not agreed whether it had been a temple, or a trophy, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a>; but the most common <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is, that it had been a temple, and Buchanan thinks, a temple of Terminus. Hector Boetius says, that there were benches of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> all around it upon the inside; and that there had been a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> stone As the Carron extends over the half of the isthmus, and runs so near the ancient boundaries of the Roman empire, the adjacent country fell naturally to be the scene of many battles and encounters. Historians mention a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought near the river between the Romans and the confederate <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the Scots and Picts in the beginning of the 5th century. The scenes of some of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a>'s poems were, in the opinion of the translator, upon the banks of this river. Here Fingal fought with Caracal, the son of the king of the world, supposed to have been the same with Caracalla, the son of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Severus. Here also young Oscar, the son of Ossian, performed some of his heroic exploits. Hereabout was the stream of Crona, celebrated in the ancient compositions of the Gaelic bard; possibly that now called the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of Bonny, which runs in the neighbourhood of the Roman wall, and discharges itself into the Carron at Dunipace. In those poems, mention is made of a green vale upon the banks of this river, with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> standing in the middle of it, where young Oscar's party and the warriors of Caros met. We only take notice of this as it strengthens the conjecture hazarded above, that the mounts of Dunipace, especially the more easterly of them, were sepulchral monuments.—About the distance of half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the river, and near the town of Falkirk, lies the field of that battle which was fought by William Wallace and the English in the beginning of the 14th century. It goes by the name of Graham's muir, from the valiant John Graham, who fell there, and whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>-stone is still to be seen in the church-yard of Falkirk. The river Carron, though it has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> since ceased to roll its stream amidst the din of arms, still preserves its fame, by lending its aid to trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> (see the next article).—The river is navigable for some miles near its mouth, and a considerable trade is carried on upon it by small craft; for the convenience of which, its channel has of late years been straightened and much shortened, and the great Canal has its entrance from it. Carron-Works, a large iron-foundery, two miles north from Falkirk in Scotland. They are conveniently situated on the banks of the Carron, three miles above its entry into the frith of Forth. Above 100 acres of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> have been converted into reservoirs and pools, for water diverted from the river, by magnificent dams built above two miles above the works, which, after <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> 18 large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> for the several purposes of the manufacture, falls into a tide-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> that conveys their castings to the sea. These works are the greatest of the kind in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and were established in 1760. At present, the buildings are of vast extent; and the machinery, constructed by Mr Smeaton, is the first in Britain, both in elegance and correctness: there are 1600 men employed, to whom is paid weekly above £600 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; which has greatly enriched the adjoining country; 650 tons of iron are smelted annually from the mineral with pit-coal, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into cannon, cylinders, &c.—In the founding of cannon, these works have lately arrived at such perfection, that they make above 5000 pieces a-year, many of which are exported to foreign states; and their guns of new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> are the lightest and neatest now in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, not excepting <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> guns; the 32 pounder ship-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> weighing 42 hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, the 6 pounder 8 hundred-weight and one-half, and the other calibers in proportion. The present proprietors are a chartered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of £150,000 sterling, a common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, &c., but their stock is confined to a very few individuals. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRONADE">Carronade</a>, a short kind of ordnance, capable of carrying a large <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, and useful in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> engagements at sea. It takes its name from Carron, the place where this sort of ordnance was first made, or the principle applied to an improved construction. See the article Gunner. CARROT. See Daucus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Deadly Carrrot. See Thapsia, Botany Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARROUSAL">Carrousal</a>, a course of horses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, or a magnificent entertainment exhibited by princes on some public rejoicing. It consists in a cavalcade of several gentlemen, richly dressed and equipped after the manner of ancient cavaliers, divided into squadrons meeting in some public place, and practising jousts, tournaments, &c.—The last carrousals were in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV.—The word comes from the Italian word coro/fello, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of carro, "chariot." Tertullian attributes the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of carrousals to Circe; and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have then instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, her father; whence some derive the word from carrus, or carrus solis. The Moors introduced ciphers, liveries, and other ornaments of their arms, with trappings, &c., for their horses. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> added <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>, plumes, &c. Carruca, in Antiquity, a splendid kind of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a>, or chariot, mounted on four wheels, richly decorated with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, &c., in which the emperors, senators and people of condition, were carried. The word comes from the Latin carrus, or British carr, which is still the Irish name for any wheel-carriage. Carruca, or Caruca, is also used in middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers for a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>. Carruca, or Caruca, also was sometimes used for carrucata. See Carrucate. Carrucage (carucagium), a kind of tax anciently imposed on every plough, for the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. See Carrucate and Hide. Carrucage, Carucage, or Carucage, in husbandry, denotes the ploughing of ground, either ordinary, as for grain, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>; or extraordinary, as for wood, dyers weed, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a>, and the like. Carrucate, (carucato), in our ancient laws and history, denotes a plough land, or as much arable ground as can be tilled in one year with one plough. In Doomsday <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">Inquisition</a>, the arable land is estimated in carrucates, the pasture in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> in acres. Skene makes the carrucata the same with hidda, or bida terra; Littleton the same with soc. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of a carrucate appears to have differed in respect of place as well as time. In the reign of Richard I. it was estimated at 60 acres, and in another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of the same reign at 100 acres; in the time of Edward I. at 180 acres; and in the 23rd of Edward III. a carrucate of land in Burcester contained 112 acres, and in Middleton 150 acres. By a statute under William III. for charging per... Carrying sons to the repair of the highways, a plough-land is rated at fifty pounds per annum, and may contain houset, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, wood, pasture, &c.

CARRYING

Pages 208-208

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALCONRY">Falconry</a>, signifies a hawk's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> away with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>. Carrying is one of the ill qualities of a hawk, which she acquires either by a dislike of the falconer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not being sufficiently broke to the lure. Carrying among huntmen. When a hare runs on rotten ground (or even sometimes in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a>), and it sticks to her feet, they lay the carries. Carrying among riding-masters. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> is said to carry low, when having naturally an ill-shaped neck, he lowers his head too much. All horses that arm themselves carry low, but a horse may carry low without arming. A French branch or gigot is preferred as a remedy against carrying low. A horse is said to carry well, when his neck is raised or arched, and he holds his head <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and firm, without constraint. Carrying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">Wind</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by our dealers in horses to express such a one as frequently tosses his nose as high as his ears, and does not carry handsomely. This is called carrying wind; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between carrying in the wind, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, is this: that the horse who beats upon the hand, shakes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a> and resists it, while he shakes his head; but the horse that carries in the wind puts up his head without shaking, and sometimes beats upon the hand. The opposite to carrying in the wind, is arming and carrying low; and even between these two there is a difference in wind.

CARSE

Pages 208-208
or Carse of Gowry, a district of Perthshire in Scotland. It lies on the north side of the Tay, and extends 14 miles in length from Dundee to Perth, and is from two to four in breadth. It is a rich plain country, cultivated like a garden, and producing as good harvests of wheat as any in Great Britain. It abounds with all the necessaries of life: but from its low damp situation, the inhabitants are subject to agues, and the commonalty are in great want of firing. In this district, not far from the Tay, stands the house of Errol, which formerly belonged to the earls of that name, the chiefs of the ancient family of Hay, hereditary constables of Scotland.

CARSTAIRS

Pages 208-208

William, an eminent Scots divine, whose merit and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> called him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> scenes, and to associate with men to whose <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> and intercourse his birth gave him few pretensions to aspire. A small village in the neighbourhood of Glasgow was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>. His father, of whom little is known, exercised the functions of a clergyman. Young Carstairs turned his thoughts to the profession of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>; and the persecutions and oppressions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, both in regard to civil and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, having excited his strongest indignation, it became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> that he should prosecute his studies in a foreign university. He went accordingly to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>; and his industry and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> being directed with skill, opened up and unfolded those faculties which he was about to employ with equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and himself. During his residence abroad, he became acquainted with Penfiony Fagel, and entered with warmth into the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>. On his return to Scotland to procure a licence to teach doctrines which he had studied with the greatest care, he became disgusted with the proud and insolent conduct of Archbishop Sharp, and prepared to revisit <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; where he knew that religious liberty was respected, and where he hoped he might better his condition by the connections he had formed. His expectations were not vain. His prudence, his reserve, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, were strong recommendations of him to the prince of Orange; and he was employed in personal negotiations in Holland, England, and Scotland. Upon the elevation of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to the English throne, he was appointed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s chaplain for Scotland, and employed in settling the affairs of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. William, who carried politics into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, was solicitous that episcopacy should prevail there as universally as in England. Carstairs, more versed in the affairs of his native country, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> all the impropriety of this project, and the danger that would arise from the enforcing of it. His reasonings, his remonstrances, his intreates, overcame the firmness of King William. He yielded to considerations founded alike in policy and in prudence; and to Carstairs Scotland is indebted for the full establishment of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in the Presbyterian form of government. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of King William was a severe affliction to him; and it happened before that prince had provided for him with the liberality he deserved. He was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, however, in the office of chaplain for Scotland by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>; and he was invited to accept the principality of the University of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. He was one of the ministers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and four times moderator of the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. Placed at the head of the church, he prosecuted its interest with zeal and with integrity. Nor were his influence and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> confined to matters of religion. They were exerted with success in promoting the culture of the arts and sciences. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Scotland owe him obligations of the highest kind. He procured, in particular, an augmentation of the salaries of their professors; a circumstance to which may be ascribed their reputation, as it enabled them to cultivate with spirit the different branches of knowledge. A zeal for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of moderation and order, prudence, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">Principal</a> Carstairs in an uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. His religion had no mixture of austerity; his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> transactions were attended with no imputation of artifice; and the versatility of his talents made him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> with ease from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. He was among the last who suffered torture before the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, in order to make him divulge the secrets intrusted to him, which he firmly refused; and after the revolution, that inhuman <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> the thumb screw was given to him in a present by the council.—This excellent person died in 1715; and in 1774 his State papers and Letters, with an account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, were published in one vol. 4to, by the Rev. Dr M'Cormick.

CARSUCAI

Pages 208-209

RAINIER, a Jesuit, born at Citerna in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, in 1647, was the author of a Latin poem, entitled, Ars bene scribendi, which is esteemed both for the elegance of the style and for the excellent precepts it contains. He also wrote some good epigrams. He died in 1709.

CART

Pages 209-209

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> carriage with two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, drawn <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> by horses, to carry heavy goods, &c. from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another. The word seems formed from the French charrette, which signifies the same, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather the Latin carreta, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of carrus. See CARR. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and Westminster carts shall not carry more than twelve packs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hundred and fifty bricks, one chaldron of coals, &c. on pain of forfeiting one of the horses, (6 Geo. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 6.) By the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, cart-men are forbidden to ride either on their carts or horses. They are to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> or drive them on foot through the streets, on the forfeiture of ten shillings. (Stat. 1 Geo. I. cap. 57.) Criminals used to be drawn to execution on a cart. Bawds and other malefactors are whipped at the cart's tail. Scripture makes mention of a sort of carts or drags used by the Jews to do the office of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THRESHING">threshing</a>. They were supported on low thick wheels, bound with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, which were rolled up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the heaves, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> them, and force out the corn. Something of the like kind also obtained among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, under the denomination of plaustra, of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> makes mention, (Georg. I.) Tardaque Eleusinae matris volventia plaustra, Tribulaque, trabeaque. On which Servius observes, that trabea denotes a cart without wheels, and tribula a sort of cart armed on all sides with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, used chiefly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> for threshing corn. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> and St Jerome represent these carts as furnished with faws, inasmuch that their surface was beset with teeth. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> having taken Rabbah, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONITES">Ammonites</a>, ordered all the inhabitants to be crushed to pieces under such carts, moving on wheels set with iron teeth; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Damascus is said to have treated the Israelites of the land of Gilead in the same manner.

CART-BOTE

Pages 209-209

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies wood to be employed in making and repairing instruments of husbandry.

CARTAMA

Pages 209-209

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Grenada, formerly very considerable. It is seated at the foot of a mountain, near the river Guadala-Medina, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 28'. N. Lat. 36° 40'.

CARTE

Pages 209-209

THOMAS, the historian, was the son of Mr Samuel Carte prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a>, and born in 1686. When he was reader in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at Bath, he took occasion in a 30th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, 1714, to vindicate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., with respect to the Irish massacre, which drew him into a controversy with Mr Chandler the dissenting minister; and on the accession of the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family he refused to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and put on a lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. He is said to have acted as a kind of secretary to Bishop Atterbury before his troubles: and in the year 1722, being accused of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, a reward of 100l. was offered for apprehending him: but <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Caroline, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> patroness of learned men, obtained leave for him to return home in security. He published, 1. An edition of Thuanus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> volumes, folio. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>, three volumes, folio. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of England, four volumes, folio. 4. A Collection of original Letters and Papers concerning the affairs of England, two volumes octavo; and some other works. He died in April 1754. His History of England ends in 1654. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was to have brought it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the Revolution; for which purpose he had taken great pains in copying every thing valuable that could be met with in England, Scotland, France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, &c.—He had (as he himself says, p. 43. of his Vindication of a full answer to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from a bystander), "read abundance of collections relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Charles II. and had in his power a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> from the beginning to the end of that reign; in which all those intrigues and turns at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, at the latter end of that king's life, which Bishop Burnet, with all his gout for tales of secret history, and all his genius for conjectures, does not pretend to account for, are laid open in the clearest and most convincing manner by the person who was most affected by them, and had the best reason to know them."—At his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, all his papers came into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of his widow, who afterwards married Mr Jernegan, a member of the church of Rome. They are now deposited in the Bodleian library, having been delivered by Mr Jernegan to the university, 1778, for a valuable consideration. Whilst they were in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s possession, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Hardwick paid 200l. for the perusal of them. For a consideration of 300l. Mr Macpherson had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them; and from these and other materials compiled his history and state-papers. Mr Carte was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of a strong <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and indefatigable application. When the studies of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> were over, he would eat heartily; and in conversation was cheerful and entertaining. CARTE-Blanche, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, signed at the bottom with a person's name, and sometimes also sealed with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, giving another person power to superscribe what conditions he pleases. Much like this is the French blanc signé, a paper without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, except a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> at the bottom, given by contending parties to arbitrators <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> friends, to fill up with the conditions they judge reasonable, in order to end the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>.

CARTEL

Pages 209-210

L signifies also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of defiance <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a challenge to decide a controversy either in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOURNAMENT">tournament</a> or in a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUEL">Duel</a>. CARTEL Ship, a ship commissioned in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> the prisoners of any two hostile powers; also to carry any particular request or proposal from one to another: Cartes another: for this reason, the officer who commands her is particularly ordered to carry no cargo, ammunition, or implements of war, except a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> for the purpose of firing signals.

CARTES

Pages 210-210

RENE DES, descended of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in Touraine in France, was one of the most eminent philosophers and mathematicians in the 17th century. At the Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> at La Fleche, he made a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in the learned languages and polite literature, and became acquainted with Father Marseenne. His father designed him for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; but his tender <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> then not permitting him to expose himself to such fatigues, he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he launched into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>, in which he had prodigious success. Here Marlenne persuaded him to return to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; which he pursued till he went to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, in May 1616, where he engaged as a volunteer among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>'s troops. While he lay in garrison at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a>, he wrote a treatise on music, and laid the foundation of several of his works. He was at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a> in 1628; returned to Paris; and, a few days after his return, at an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of men of learning in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Monfignor Bagni, the Pope's nuncio, was prevailed upon to explain his sentiments with regard to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, when the nuncio urged him to publish his system. Upon this he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, and from thence to Franeker, where he began his metaphysical meditations, and drew up his discourse on meteors. He made a short tour to England; and not far from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, made some observations concerning the declination of the magnet. He returned to Holland, where he finished his treatise on the world. His books made a great noise in France; and Holland thought of nothing but discarding the old philosophy, and following his. Voetius being chosen rector of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, procured his philosophy to be prohibited, and wrote against him; but he immediately published a vindication of himself. In 1647, he took a journey into France, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> settled a pension of 3000 livres upon him. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, having invited him into that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, he went thither, where he was received with the greatest civility by her majesty, who engaged him to attend her every morning at five o'clock, to instruct her in philosophy, and desired him to revise and digest all his writings which were unpublished, and to form a complete body of philosophy from them. She likewise proposed to allow him a revenue, and to form an academy, of which he was to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>. But these designs were broken off by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1650. His body was interred at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>, and 17 years afterwards removed to Paris, where a magnificent monument was erected to him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Genevive du Mont. The great Dr Halley, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> concerning <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, observes, that though some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> mention refraction as an effect of transparent mediums, Des Cartes was the first who discovered the laws of refraction, and reduced dioptries to a science. As to his philosophy, Dr Keill, in his introduction to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of Dr Burnet's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, says, that Des Cartes was so far from applying <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy, that his whole system is one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> blunder on account of his negligence in that point; the laws observed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> in their revolutions round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> not agreeing with his theory of vortices. His philosophy has accordingly given way to the more accurate discoveries and demonstrations of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, the Newtonian system.

CARTESIANS

Pages 210-210

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of philosophers, who adhered to the system of Des Cartes, founded on the two following principles, the one metaphysical, the other physical. The metaphysical one is, I think, therefore I am; the physical principle is, that nothing exists but substance. Substance he makes of two kinds; the one a substance that thinks, the other a substance extended; whence actual thought, and actual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>, are the essence of substance. The essence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> being thus fixed in extension, the Cartesians conclude that there is no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a> nor any possibility thereof in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; but that the universe is absolutely full: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> space is excluded by this principle; because extension being implied in the idea of space, matter is so too. Upon these principles the Cartesians explained mechanically how the world was formed, and how the present celestial phenomena came to take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CARTHAGE

Pages 210-239

a famed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of antiquity, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> Propria; and which, for many years, founded, disputed with Rome the sovereignty of the world. According to Velleius Paterculus, this city was built 65, according to Justin and Trogus 72, according to others 100 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 140 years before the foundations of Rome were laid. It is on all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> agreed that the Phoenicians were the founders. The beginning of the Carthaginian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, like that of all other nations, is obscure and uncertain. In the 7th year of Pygmalion <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>, his sister Elissa, or Dido, is said to have fled, with some of her Dido, companions and vassals, from the cruelty and avarice of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, who had put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> her husband Sirachus in order to get possession of his wealth. She first touched at the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus, where she met with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, who was desirous of attending her; to which she readily consented, and fixed the priesthood in his family. At that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> in the island of Cyprus, for the young women to go on certain stated days, before <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> side, there to look for strangers, that might possibly arrive on their coasts, in order to prostitute themselves for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>, that they might thereby acquire a dowry. Out of these the Tyrians selected 80, whom they carried along with them. From Cyprus they sailed directly for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Africa; and at last safely landed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> called Africa Propria, not far from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTICA">Utica</a>, a Phoenician city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. The inhabitants received their countrymen with great demonstrations of joy, and invited them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> among them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> is, that the Phoenicians imposed upon the Africans in the following manner: They desired, for their intended settlement, only as much ground as an ox's hide would encompass. This request the Africans laughed at; but were surprised, when, upon their granting it, they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Elissa cut the hide into the smallest threads, by which means it surrounded a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> territory; in which she built the citadel called Lyra. The learned, however, are now unanimous in exploding this fable; and it is certain that the Carthaginians for many years paid an annual tribute to the Africans for the ground they possessed. The new city soon became populous and flourishing, Carthage by the accession of the neighbouring Africans, who came thither at first with a view of traffic. In a short time it became so considerable, that Jarbas, a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, thought of making himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it without any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of blood. In order to this, he desired that an embassy of ten of the most noble Carthaginians might be sent him; and, upon their arrival, proposed to them a marriage with Dido, threatening <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a refusal. The ambassadors, being afraid to deliver this message, told the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> that Jarbas desired some person might be sent him who was capable of civilizing his Africans; but that there was no possibility of finding any of her subjects who would leave his relations for the conversion of such barbarians. For this they were reprimanded by the queen; who told them that they ought to be ashamed of refusing to live in any manner for the benefit of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Upon this, they informed her of the true <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of their message from Jarbas; and that, according to her own decision, she ought to sacrifice herself for the good of her country. The unhappy queen, rather than submit to be the wife of such a barbarian, caused a funeral pile to be erected, and put an end to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> with a dagger. This is Justin's account of the death of Queen Dido, and is the most probable; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s story of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a> with Æneas being looked upon as fabulous, even in the days of Macrobius, as we are informed by that historian. How <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> monarchical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in Carthage, or what happened to this state in its infancy, we are altogether ignorant, by reason of the Punic archives being destroyed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; so that there is a chain in the Carthaginian history for above 300 years. It, however, appears, that from the very beginning, the Carthaginians applied themselves to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs, and were formidable by sea in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> and Cambyses. From Diodorus Siculus and Justin, it appears that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> support of the Carthaginians were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in which country they seem to have established themselves very early. By means of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> drawn from these mines, they were enabled to equip such formidable fleets as we are told they fitted out in the time of Cyrus or Cambyses. Justin intimates, that the first Carthaginian settlement in Spain happened when the city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GADES">Gades</a>, now <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, was but of late standing, or even in its infancy. The Spaniards finding this new colony begin to flourish, attacked it with a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, infomuch that the inhabitants were obliged to call in the Carthaginians to their aid. The latter very readily granted their request, and not only repulsed the Spaniards, but made themselves masters of almost the whole province in which their new city stood. By this success, they were encouraged to attempt the conquest of the whole country; but having to do with very warlike nations, they could not push their conquests to any great length at first; and it appears from the accounts of Livy and Polybius, that the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Spain remained unsubdued till the time of Hamilcar, AIdrubar, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>. About 503 years before the birth of Christ, the Carthaginians entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with the Romans. It related chiefly to matters of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. From it we learn, that the whole island of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, and part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, were then subject to Carthage; that they were very well acquainted with Carthage, the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and had made some attempts upon them before this time: and that, even at this early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, a spirit of jealousy had taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the two republics. Some time near this period, the Carthaginians had a mind to discontinue the tribute they had hitherto paid the Africans for the ground on which their city stood. But, notwithstanding all their power, they were at present unsuccessful; and at last were obliged to conclude a peace, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of which was, that the tribute should be continued. By degrees the Carthaginians extended their power over all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Mediterranean, Sicily excepted; and for the entire conquest of this, they made vast preparations, about 480 years before Christ. Their army consisted of 300,000 men; their fleet was composed of upwards of 2000 men of war, and 3000 transports; and with such an immense armament, they made no doubt of conquering the whole island in a single <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>. In this, however, they found themselves miserably deceived. Hamilcar their general having landed his numerous forces, invested Himera, a city of considerable importance. He carried on his attacks with the greatest avidity; but was at last attacked in his trenches by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GELON">Gelon</a> and Theron, the tyrants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRIGENTUM">Agrigentum</a>, who gave the Carthaginians one of the greatest overthrow mentioned in history. An hundred and fifty thousand were killed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> and pursuit, and all the rest taken prisoners; so that of so mighty an army not a single person escaped. Of the 2000 ships of war and 3000 transports, of which the Carthaginian fleet consisted, eight ships only, which then happened to be out at sea, made their escape: these immediately set sail for Carthage; but were all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> away, and every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> perished, except a few who were saved in a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, and at last reached Carthage with the dismal news of the total loss of the fleet and army. No words can express the consternation of the Carthaginians upon receiving the news of so terrible a disaster. Ambassadors were immediately dispatched to Sicily, with orders to conclude a peace upon any terms. They put to sea without delay; and landing at Syracuse, threw themselves at the conqueror's feet. They begged Gelon, with many tears, to receive their city into favour, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them a peace on whatever terms he should choose to prefer. He granted their request, upon condition that Carthage should pay him 2000 talents of silver to defray the expenses of the war; that they should build two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, where the articles of the treaty should be lodged and kept as sacred; and that for the future they should abstain from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> sacrifices. This was not thought a dear purchase of a peace for which there was such occasion; and to show their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for Gelon's moderation, the Carthaginians complimented his wife Demarata with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> worth 100 talents. From this time we find little mention of the Carthaginians for 70 years. Some time during this period, however, they had greatly extended their dominions in Africa, and likewise shaken off the tribute which gave them so much uneasiness. They had disputes with the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a> the capital of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRENAICA">Cyrenaica</a>, about a regulation of the limits of Carthage of their respective territories. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of these disputes was a war, which reduced both nations so low, that they agreed first to a cessation of arms, and then to a peace. At last it was agreed, that each state should appoint two commissioners, who should set out from their respective cities on the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and that the spot on which they met should be the boundary of both states.
