He wrote, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">Vacuum</a> praescriptum. 2. Terra machinis mota. 3. Mechanicorum, libri octo. 4. De Igne Dissertationes; which is much esteemed. 5. De Angelis Disputatione Theologica. 6. Hydrostaticae Dissertationes. 7. Optica Disputationes. It is remarkable that he wrote this treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a> at 88 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and after he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>. He also wrote several books in Italian.

CASAUBON

Pages 243-244

MERIC, a son of the preceding, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> in 1599. He was bred at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts in 1621. The same year he published a book in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his father against the calumnies of certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>; which gained him the favour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. and a considerable reputation abroad. He was made prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> by Archbishop Laud. In the beginning of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> he lost all his spiritual promotions, but still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to publish excellent works. Oliver Cromwell, then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>'s forces, would have employed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the late war; but he declined it, owning that this subject would oblige him to make such reflections as would be ungrateful, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not injurious, to his lordship. Notwithstanding this answer, Cromwell, sensible of his worth, ordered three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four hundred pounds to be paid him by a bookseller in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, whose name was Cromwell, on demand, without requiring from him any acknowledgement of his benefactor. But this offer he rejected, though his circumstances were then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>. At the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was propounded by his friend Mr Greaves, Cafurina Greaves, who belonged to the library at St James's, that, if Cafaubon would gratify Cromwell in the request above mentioned, all his father's books, which were then in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> library, having been purchased by King James, should be restored to him, and a pension of 300l. a-year paid to the family as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the youngest son of Dr Cafaubon should live; but this also was refused. He likewise refused handsome offers from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, being determined to spend the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in England. At the Restoration he recovered all his preferments, and continued writing till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1671. He was the author of an English translation of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus's Meditations, and of Lucius Florus; editions of several of the classics, with notes; a treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>; a treatise of enthusiasm; with many other works; and he left a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of MSS. to the university of Oxford. CASURINA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CASCADE

Pages 244-244

a steep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from a higher into a lower <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The word is French, formed of the Italian cascata, which signified the same; of cascaro, "to fall," and that from the Latin cadere. Calades are either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, as that at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIVOLI">Tivoli</a>, &c., <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, as those of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, &c., and either falling with a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, as those of Sceaux; or in form of a buffet, as at Trianon; or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> steps, in form of a perron, as at St Cloud; or from bafon to bafon, &c.

CASCAIS

Pages 244-244

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, situated at the mouth of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>, 17 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 15'. N. Lat. 38° 40'. CASCARILLA. See Clutia and Croton.

CASE ALSO

Pages 244-244

e also denotes a receptacle for various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>; as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of knives, of lancets, of pistols, &c. Case, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> frame placed slopewise, divided into several compartments <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> cells; in each of which are lodged a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of types or letters of the same kind, whence the compositor takes them out, each as he needs it, to compose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. See Printing. Case is also used for a certain numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> things. Thus a case of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> glass contains usually 24 tables, each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> being nearly circular, and about three feet six inches diameter; of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> glass, 35 tables; of Normandy glass, 25. Case Hardening of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">Iron</a>, is a superficial conversion of that metal into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, by the ordinary method of conversion, namely, by cementation with vegetable or mineral coals. This operation is generally practised upon small pieces of iron wrought into tools and instruments to which a superficial conversion is sufficient; and it may be performed conveniently by putting the pieces of iron to be case-hardened, together with the cement, into an iron box, which is to be closely shut and exposed to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> during some hours. By this cementation a certain thickness from the surface of the iron <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be converted into steel, and a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> may be afterwards given by sudden extinction of the heated pieces of converted iron in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> fluid. See Steel. Case <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">Shot</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, musket balls, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, old iron, &c. put into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and shot out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> guns.

CASEMENT

Pages 244-244
or Casemate, in Architecture, a hollow moulding, which some architects make one-fifth of a circle, and others one fourth. Casement is also used in building, for a little moveable window, usually within a larger, being made to open or turn on hinges.

CASERN

Pages 244-244

in fortification, lodgings built in garrison <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, generally near the rampart, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the waste places of the town, for lodging <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of the garrison. There are usually two beds in each casern for six soldiers to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a>, who mount the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> alternately; the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> being always on duty.

CASERTA

Pages 244-244

an episcopal town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the Terra de Lavoro, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, seated at the foot of a mountain of the same name, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15° 5'. N. Lat. 41° 5'.

CASES

Pages 244-244
Peter James, of Paris, the most eminent painter of the French school. The churches of Paris and of Versailles abound with his works. He died in 1754, aged 79.

CASH

Pages 244-244

in a commercial style, signifies the stock <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ready <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> which a merchant or other person has in his present disposal to negotiate; so called from the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> caisse, i.e. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>," for the keeping of money. M. Savary shows that the management of the cash of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> is the most considerable article, and that wherein its good or ill success depends. Cash-Book. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOOK_KEEPING">Book-Keeping</a>.

CASHEL

Pages 244-245
or Cashel, a town of Ireland in the county of Tipperary, and province of Munster, with an archbishop's see. The ruins of the old cathedral testify its having been an extensive as well as handsome Gothic structure, boldly towering on the celebrated rock of Cashel, which taken together form a magnificent object, and bear honourable testimony to the labour and ingenuity, as well as the piety and zeal, of its former inhabitants. It is seen at a great distance, and in many directions. Adjoining it are the ruins of the chapel of Cormac McCullin, at once king and archbishop of Cashel, supposed to have been the first stone building in Ireland; and seems, by its rude imitation of pillars and capitals, to have been copied after the Grecian architecture, and long to have preceded that which is usually called Gothic. Cormac McCullin was a prince greatly celebrated by the Irish historians for his learning, piety, and valour. He wrote, in his native language, a history of Ireland, commonly called the Psalter of Cashel, which is still extant, and contains the most authentic account we have of the annals of the country to that period, about the year 600. On the top of the rock of Cashel, and adjoining the cathedral, is a lofty round tower, which proudly defied the too successful attempts of Archbishop Price, who in this century unroofed and thereby demolished the ancient cathedral founded by St Patrick. In the choir are the monuments of Myler Magrath, archbishop of this see, in the reign of Queen Elizabeth, and some other curious remains of antiquity. Cashel was formerly the royal seat and metropolis of the kings of Munster; and on the ascent to the cathedral is a large stone on which which every new king of Munster was, as the inhabitants report from tradition, formerly proclaimed. Cashel is at present but small to what we may suppose it to have been in ancient days. The archbishop's palace is a fine building. Here is a very handsome market house, a sessions house, the county infirmary, a charter school for twenty boys and the same number of girls, and a very good barrack for two companies of foot. Dr Agar finished a very elegant church which was begun by his predecessor. W. Long. 7. 36. N. Lat. 52. 16. CASHEW nut. See Anacardium, Botany Index.

CASHIER

Pages 245-245

the cash-keeper; he who is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with the receiving and paying the debts of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>.—In the generality of foundations, the cashier is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>. Cashiers of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">Bank</a>, are officers who sign the notes that are issued out, examine and mark them when returned for payment, &c.

CASHMIRE

Pages 245-245

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> in the dominions of the Mogul. It is situated at the extremity of Hindoostan, northward of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAHORE">Lahore</a>, and is bounded on the one side by a ridge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, and on the other by the little Tartarian Thibet and Moutian. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of it is not very considerable; but being girt in by a zone of hills, and elevated very considerably above an arid plain, which stretches many miles around it, the scenes which it exhibits are wild and picturesque. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">Rivers</a>, hills, and valleys, charmingly diversify the landscape. Here, Mr Sullivan informs us, a cascade rushes from a foaming precipice; there a tranquil stream glides placidly along; the tinkling rill, too, sounds amidst the groves; and the feathered choristers sing the song of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> sheltered in the glade. At what <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Cashmire came under the dominion of the Mogul <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and how <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and in what manner it was independent, before it was annexed to the territories of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Timur, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> that are beyond our present purpose. Though inconsiderable as to its revenues, it was uniformly held in the highest estimation by the emperors of Hindoostan. Thither they repaired in the plenitude of their greatness, when the affairs of state would admit of their absence; and there they divested themselves of form and all the oppressive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of state. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> manner of travelling to Cashmire was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>, though tedious and unwieldy, and showed, in an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, the splendour and magnificence of an eastern potentate. Aurangzebe, we are told, seldom began his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, for a march certainly it was to be called, without an escort of 80,000 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 100,000 fighting men, besides the gentlemen of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, the attendants of his retaglio, and most of his officers of state. These all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with him during the time he was on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, which generally was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; but no sooner was he arrived at the entrance of those aerial regions, than, with a select party of friends, he separated from the rest of his retinue, and with them ascended the defiles which led him to his Eden. The temperature of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of Cashmire, elevated as it is so much above the adjoining country, together with the streams which continually pour from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, enables the husbandman to cultivate with success the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> he appropriates to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>; whilst the gardener's labour is amply repaid in the abundant produce of his fruit. In short, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> wears her gayest clothing in this enchanting spot. The rivers supply the inhabitants with almost every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fish; the hills yield sweet herbage for the cattle; the plains are covered with grain of different denominations; and the woods are stored with variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>. The Cashmirans, according to our author, seem a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> distinct from all others in the east: Their persons are more elegant, and their complexions more delicate and more tinged with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. On the decadence of the Mogul power in Hindoostan, Cashmire felt some of the ravages of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. It is now however in peace; and the inhabitants are deafuous of keeping it so. They are sprightly and ingenious, and have several curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> much valued in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. They are all Mahometans or idolaters. Cashmire is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

CASIMIR

Pages 245-245

the name of several kings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Poland. Casimir, Matthias Sorbiewski, a Polish Jesuit, born in 1597. He was a most excellent poet; and is, says M. Baillet, an exception to the general rule of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, which teaches us to expect nothing ingenious and delicate from northern climates. His odes, epodes, and epigrams, have been thought not inferior to those of the finest wits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and Rome. Dr Watts has translated one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two of his small pieces, which are added to his Lyric Poems. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARSAW">Warsaw</a> in 1640, aged 43. There have been many editions of his poems, the best of which is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1759.

CASING OF TIMBER WORK

Pages 245-245

among builders, is the plastering the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> all over the outside with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and then striking it while wet, by a ruler, with the corner of a trowel, to make it resemble the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of freestone. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> it to be done upon heart-laths, because the mortar would, in a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, decay the lap laths; and to lay on the mortar in two thicknesses, viz. a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> before the first is dry.

CASK

Pages 245-245
or Casque, a piece of defensive armour wherewith to cover the head and neck; otherwise called the head-piece and helmet. The word is French casque, from casticum or casticus, a diminutive of cassis met. "a helmet." Le Gendre observes, that anciently, in France, the gens d'armes all wore casks. The king wore a cask gilt; the dukes and counts silvered; gentlemen of extraction polished steel; and the rest plain iron. The cask is frequently seen on ancient medals, where we may observe great varieties in the form and fashion thereof; as the Greek fashion, the Roman fashion, &c. F. Joubert makes it the most ancient of all the coverings of the head, as well as the most universal. Kings, emperors, and even gods themselves, are seen therewith. That which covers the head of Rome has usually two wings like those of Mercury: and that of some kings is furnished with horns like those of Jupiter Ammon; and sometimes barely bulls or rams horns, to express uncommon force. Cask, in Heraldry, the same with helmet. See Heraldry, No. 45. Cask, a vessel of capacity, for preserving liquors of divers kinds; and sometimes also dry goods, as sugar, almonds,

CASKET

Pages 245-246

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, a little coffer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cabinet. See CABINET.

CASLON

Pages 246-246

William, eminent in an art of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to literature, the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>-founding, was born in 1692, in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town of Hales Owen which is situated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>. Though he justly attained the character of being the Coryphaeus in that employment, he was not brought up to the business; and it is observed by Mr Mores, that this handiwork is so concealed among the artificers of it, that he could not discover that any one had taught it to another, but every person who had used it had learned it of his own genuine inclination. Mr Caslon served a regular <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a> to an engraver of ornaments on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> barrels; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, carried on this trade in Vine-street, near the Minories. He did not, however, solely confine his ingenuity to that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, but employed himself likewise in making tools for the bookbinders, and for the chiselling of silver-plate. Whilst he was engaged in this business, the elder Mr Bowyer accidentally <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, in a bookbinder's shop, the lettering of a book uncommonly neat; and inquiring who the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> was by whom the letters were made, was hence induced to seek an acquaintance with Mr Caslon. Not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after, Mr Bowyer took Mr Caslon to Mr James's foundery, in Bartholomew-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. Caslon had never before that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> seen any part of the business; and being asked by his friend, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he thought he could undertake to cut types, he requested a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to consider the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; and then replied that he had no doubt but he could. Upon this answer, Mr Bowyer, Mr Bettenham, and Mr Watts, had such a confidence in his abilities, that they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> him £500 to begin the undertaking, and he applied himself to it with equal assiduity and success. In 1720, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> for promoting Christian knowledge, in consequence of a representation from Mr <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> Negri, a native of Damascus in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, who was well skilled in the Oriental tongues, and had been professor of Arabic in places of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, deemed it expedient to print, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the Eastern churches, the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> and Psalter, in the Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. These were intended for the benefit of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, Syria, Mesopotamia, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of which countries did not permit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>. Upon this occasion Mr Caslon was pitched upon to cut the font; in his specimens of which he distinguished it by the name of English Arabic. Under the farther encouragement of Mr Bowyer, Mr Bettenham, and Mr Watts, he proceeded with vigour in his employment; and he arrived at length to such perfection, that he not only freed us from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of importing types from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, but in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and elegance of those made by him he so far exceeded the productions of the best artificers, that his workmanship was frequently exported to the continent. In short, his foundery became, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, the most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> one that existed in this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in foreign countries. Having acquired opulence in the course of his employment, he was put into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of the peace for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>. Towards the latter end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, his eldest son being in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with him, he retired in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> execution of business. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> happened in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1766.

CASNETS

Pages 246-246

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, are small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and fastened to grommets, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> little rings upon the yards; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to make fast the sail to the yard when it is to be furled.

CASPIAN SEA

Pages 246-248

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Astrakhan on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> on the south, east, and west. It is upwards of 400 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> from south to north, and 300 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> from east to west. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> forms several gulfs, and embraces between Astrakhan and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASTRABAD">Astrabad</a> an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. Its bottom is mud, but sometimes mixed with shells. At the distance of some German miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> it is 50 fathoms deep; but on approaching the shore it is everywhere so shallow, that the smallest vessels, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> loaded, are obliged to remain at a distance. When we consider that the Caspian is enclosed on all sides by land, and that its banks are in the neighbourhood of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, we easily see why the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> in it should be perfectly different from that in every other sea. There are certain winds that dominate over it with such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> sway, that vessels are often deprived of every resource; and in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of it there is not a port that can truly be called safe. The north, north-east, and east winds, blow most frequently, and occasion the most violent tempests. Along the eastern shore the east winds prevail; for which reason vessels bound from Persia to Astrakhan always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> their course along this shore. The surface of the Caspian sea is lower than the ocean. Although its extent is immense, the variety of its productions is exceedingly small. This undoubtedly proceeds from its want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the ocean, which cannot impart to it any portion of its inexhaustible stores. But the animals which this lake nourishes multiply to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that the Russians, who alone are in condition to make them turn to account, justly consider them as a never-failing source of profit and wealth. It <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be understood that we speak of the fish of the Caspian, and of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, which make the sole occupation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> trade of the people inhabiting the banks of the Wolga and of the Jaik. This business is distinguished into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and lesser fisheries. The fish comprehended under the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, such as the sturgeon and others, abound in all parts of the Caspian as well as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that communicate with it, and which they ascend at spawning <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The small fishes, such as the salmon and many others, observe the general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of quitting the salt waters for the fresh; nor is there an instance of one of them remaining constantly in the sea. Seals are the only <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> that inhabit the Caspian; but they are there in such numbers as to afford the means of subsistence to many people in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> as well as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>. The varieties of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are numerous, diversified, however, only by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Some are quite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, others quite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; there are some whitish, some yellowish, some of a mouse colour, and some streaked like a tiger. They crawl by means of their fore feet upon the islands, where they become the prey of the fishermen, who kill them. Caspian sea. As soon as one is despatched, he is succeeded by several who come to the assistance of their unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, but come only to share his fate. They are exceedingly tenacious of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and endure more than thirty hard blows before they die. They will even live for several days after having received many mortal wounds. They are most terrified by fire and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>; and as soon as they perceive them, retreat with the utmost expedition to the sea. These animals grow so very fat, that they look rather like <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> bags than animals. At Astrakhan is made a sort of gray <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> with their fat mixed with pot-ashes, which is much valued for its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of cleansing and taking grease from woollen stuffs. The greatest numbers of them are killed in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and autumn. Many small vessels go from Astrakhan merely to catch seals. If the Caspian has few quadrupeds, it has in proportion still fewer of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions which are looked upon as proper only to the sea. There have never been found in it any zoophytes, nor any animal of the order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLLUSCA">mollusca</a>. The same may almost be said of shells; the only ones found being three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four species of cockle, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> mussels, some species of snails, and one or two others. But to compensate this sterility, it abounds in birds of different kinds. Of those that frequent the shores there are many species of the goose and duck kind, of the stork and heron, and many others of the wader tribe. Of birds properly aquatic, it contains the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GREBE">grebe</a>, the crested diver, the pelican, the cormorant, and almost every species of gull. Crows are so fond of fish, that they haunt the shores of the Caspian in prodigious multitudes. The waters of this lake are very impure, the great number of rivers that run into it, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of its bottom, affecting it greatly. It is true, that in general the waters are salt; but though the whole western shore extends from the 46th to the 35th degree of north latitude; and though one might conclude from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> that these waters would contain a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of salt, yet experiments prove the contrary: and it is certain that the saltness of this sea is diminished by the north, north-east, and north-west winds; although we may with equal reason conclude, that it owes its saltness to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of salt which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> along its two banks, and which are either already known or will be known to posterity. The depth of these waters also diminishes gradually as you approach the shores, and their saltness in the same way grows less in proportion to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> to the land; the north winds not unfrequently causing the rivers to discharge into it vast quantities of troubled water impregnated with clay. These variations which the sea is exposed to are more or less considerable according to the nature of the winds; they affect the colour of the river waters to a certain distance from the shore, till these mixing with those of the sea, which then resume the alendency, the fine green colour appears, which is natural to the ocean, and to all those bodies of water that communicate with it. It is well known, that besides its salt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, all sea water has a sensible bitterness, which must be attributed not only to the salt itself, but to the mixture of different substances that unite with it, particularly to different sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, the ordinary effect of different <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. Besides this, the waters of the Caspian have another taste, bitter too, but quite distinct, which affects the tongue with an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> similar to that made by the bile of animals; a property which is peculiar to this sea, though not equally sensible at all seasons. When the north and north-west winds have raged for a considerable time, this bitter taste is sensibly felt; but when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> has been south, very imperfectly. We shall endeavour to account for this phenomenon. The Caspian is surrounded on its western side by the mountains of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, which extend from Derbent to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA">Black sea</a>. These mountains make a curve near Astrakhan, and directing their course towards the eastern shore of the Caspian, lose themselves near the mouth of the Jaik, where they become secondary mountains, being disposed in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a>. As Caucasus is an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of combustible substances, it consequently lodges an affluing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> in its bowels. Accordingly, along the foot of this immense chain of mountains, we sometimes meet with warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, sometimes springs of naphtha of different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; sometimes we find native sulphur, mines of vitriol, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> heated by internal fires. Now the foot of Mount Caucasus forming the immediate western shore of the Caspian sea, it is very easy to imagine that a great quantity of the constituent parts of the former must be communicated to the latter; but it is chiefly to the naphtha, which abounds so much in the countries which surround this sea, that we must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the true cause of the bitterness peculiar to its waters; for it is certain that this bitumen flows from the mountains, sometimes in all its purity, and sometimes mixed with other substances which it acquires in its passage through subterranean channels, from the most interior parts of these mountains to the sea, where it falls to the bottom by its specific gravity. It is certain too, that the north and north-west winds detach the greatest quantities of this naphtha; whence it is evident that the bitter taste must be most sensible when these winds prevail. We may also comprehend why this taste is not so strong at the surface or in the neighbourhood of the shore, the waters there being less impregnated with salt, and the naphtha, which is united with the water by the salt, being then either carried to a distance by the winds, or precipitated to the bottom. But it is not a bitter taste alone that the naphtha communicates to the waters of the Caspian: these waters were analyzed by M. Gmelin, and found to contain, besides the common sea salt, a considerable proportion of Glauber salt, intimately united with the former, and which is evidently a production of the naphtha. As the waters of the Caspian have no outlet, they are discharged by subterranean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> through the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, where they deposit beds of salt; the surface of which corresponds with that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the sea. The two great deserts which extend from it to the east and west are chiefly composed of a saline earth, in which the salt is formed by efflorescence into regular crystals; for which reason salt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and dews are exceedingly common in that neighbourhood. The salt of the marshes at Astrakhan, and that found in efflorescence in the deserts, is by no means pure sea salt, but but much debased by the bitter Glauber salt we mentioned above. In many places indeed it is found with crystals of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOZENGE">lozenge</a> shape, which is peculiar to it, without any cubical appearance, the form peculiar to crystals of sea salt. A great deal has been written on the successive augmentation and decrease of the Caspian sea, but with little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. There is indeed to be perceived in it a certain rise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of its waters; in which, however, no observation has ever discovered any regularity. Many suppose (and there are strong presumptions in favour of the supposition), that the shores of the Caspian were much more extensive in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times than they are at present, and that it once communicated with the Black sea. It is probable too, that the level of this last sea was once much higher than it is at present. If then it be allowed, that the waters of the Black sea, before it procured an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXIT">exit</a> by the straits of Constantinople, rose several fathoms above their present level, which from many concurring circumstances may easily be admitted, it will follow, that all the plains of the Crimea, of the Kuman, of the Wolga, and of the Jax, and those of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a> beyond the lake of Aral, in ancient times formed but one sea, which embraced the northern extremity of Caucasus by a narrow strait of little depth; the vestiges of which are still obvious in the river Mantyfch.

CASSANA

Pages 248-248

Giovanni Agostino, called L'Abate Cassana, was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the preceding, and born in 1664. He was educated along with him by their father Francesco Caffana, and he finished his studies at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, where his brother Nicolo resided for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Although he composed and designed historical subjects with expertness, and with a correctness of outline equal to his brother; yet from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and fraternal affection, he declined to interfere with him, and chose therefore to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> and paint all sorts of animals and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. In that style he arrived at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of excellence, imitating <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with exactness, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>: expressing the various plumage of his birds, and the hairs of the different animals, with such tenderness and delicacy as rendered them estimable to all judges and lovers of the art. His works were admitted into the collections of those of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and accounted ornaments of those repositories of what is curious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> valuable. He also painted fruits of those kinds which were the most uncommon, or naturally of odd and singular colours; and such fishes as seemed worthy to excite admiration by their unusual form, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, or appearance. But besides those subjects, he sometimes painted the portraits of particular persons of distinction, which he designed, coloured and touched, with the same degree of merit that was visible in all his other performances. At last he determined to visit <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, where his family had lived in esteem; and took with him several pictures which he had already finished. His intention was to display his generosity, and to appear as a person of more wealth and of greater <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> than he really was; and to support that character, he bestowed his pictures on several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. But, unhappily, he experienced no grateful return for all that prodigal munificence: he reduced himself by that vain liberality to the most necessitous circumstances; was deprived of the means to procure for himself even the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and waited away the remainder of his days in the bitterness of poverty, misery, and neglect.

CASSANDER

Pages 248-248
king of Macedon after Alexander the Great, was the son of Antipater. He made several conquests in Greece, abolished democracy at Athens, and gave the government of that state to the orator Demetrius. Olympias, the mother of Alexander, having caused Aridaeus and his wife Eurydice, with others of Cassander's party, to be put to death; he besieged Pydna, whither the queen had retired, took it by a stratagem, and caused her to be put to death. He married Theffalonica the sister of Alexander the Great; and killed Roxana and Alexander, the wife and son of that conqueror. At length he entered into an alliance with Seleucus and Lysimachus, against Antigonus and Demetrius; over whom he obtained a great victory near Ipsus in Phrygia, 301 years before the Christian era, and died three years after, in the 19th year of his reign.

CASSANDRA

Pages 248-251

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Priam and Hecuba, was beloved of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, who promised to bestow on her the spirit of prophecy, provided <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASSANO">Cassano</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, rendered remarkable by an obstinate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought there between the Germans and French in 1705. It is subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and is seated on the river Adda, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10°. N. Lat. 45°. 20'. Cassano, a town of Italy in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> citerior, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, with a bishop's see. E. Long. 16°. N. Lat. 39°. 55'. Cassavì, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cassada. See Jatropha, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cassel, a town of French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a chatelainy of the same name: It is seated on a mountain, where the terrace of the castle is still to be seen; and from whence there is one of the finest prospects in the world; for one may see no less than 32 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, from whence it is distant 15 miles. E. Long. 2°. 27'. N. Lat. 50°. 48'. Cassel, the capital <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the landgraviate of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>-Cassel, in the circle of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> in Germany; (see Hesse-Cassel). It is divided into the Old, New, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Towns. The New Town is best built, the houses being of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and the streets <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The houses of the Old Town, which is within the walls, are mostly of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; but the streets are broad, and the market places spacious. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is strongly fortified, but the fortifications are not regular. It contains about 32,000 inhabitants, of whom a great proportion are French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. These have established several manufactories in the place, particularly in the woollen branch. It is seated on the declivity of a hill near the river Fulva, in E. Long. 9°. 28'. N. Lat. 51°. 20'. Cassia. See Botany Index. Cassia Lignea. See Laurus. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASSIDA">Cassida</a>. See Scutellaria, Botany Index. Cassida, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of coleoptera. See Entomology Index. Cassimer, or Casimer, the name of a thin tweedled woollen cloth, much in fashion for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Cassimire, or Cashmire. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASHMERE">Cashmere</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASSINE">Cassine</a>. See Botany Index. The Spaniards who live near the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, are frequently obliged to drink an infusion of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> in order to moisten their breaths; without which they are liable to a sort of suffocation, from the strong metallic exhalations that are continually proceeding from the mines. In Paraguay, the Jesuits make a great revenue by importing the leaves of this plant into many countries, under the name of Paraguay or South sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, which is there drank in the same manner as that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> is with us. It is with difficulty preserved in England. Cassini, Johannes Dominicus, a most excellent astronomer, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a> in 1635. His early proficiency in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> procured him an invitation to be mathematical professor at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> when he was no more than 15 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and a comet appearing in 1652, he discovered that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a> were not accidental meteors, but of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and probably governed by the same laws, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>. In the same year he solved a problem given up by Kepler and Bullialdus as insolvable, which was, to determine geometrically the apogee and eccentricity of a planet from its true and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> place. In 1663, he was appointed inspector general of the fortifications of the castle of Urbino, and had afterwards the care of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> state; he still however prosecuted his astronomical studies, by discovering the revolution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> round its own axis; and, in 1666, published his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s satellites. Cassini was invited into France by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in 1669, where he settled as the first professor in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>. In 1677 he demonstrated the line of Jupiter's diurnal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>; and in 1684 discovered four more satellites belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, Huygens having found one before. He inhabited the royal observatory at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> more than forty years; and when he died in 1712, was succeeded by his only son James Cassini. Cassini, James, another celebrated astronomer, was the younger son of the former. He was born at Paris 18th February 1677. It would appear that his early studies were conducted in his father's house, where, from the pursuits and studies of his father, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and their application to astronomy, it is probable, were not neglected. He became a student afterwards at the Mazarine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the celebrated Vivignon was professor of mathematics. With the affluence of this eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> young Cassini made such progress, that at 15 years of age he supported a mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESIS">thesis</a> with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. At the age of 17 he was admitted a member of the Academy of Sciences; and the same year he accompanied his father in a journey to Italy, where he assisted him in the verification of the meridian at Bologna and other measurements. After his return he performed similar operations in a journey into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and he discovered some errors in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> by Snell, the result of which was communicated to the Academy in 1702. In 1696 he made also a visit to England, where he was made a member of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. In 1712 he succeeded his father as astronomer royal at the observatory of Paris. In 1717 he gave to the Academy his researches on the distance of the fixed stars; in which he showed that the whole annual orbit, of near 200 millions of miles diameter, is but as a point in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of that distance. The same year he communicated also his discoveries concerning the inclination of the orbits of the satellites in general, and especially of those of Saturn's satellites and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>. In 1725 he undertook to determine the cause of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>'s libration, by which she shows sometimes a little towards one side, and sometimes a little on the other, of that half which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> behind or hid from our view. In 1732 an important question in astronomy enga- Cassini, ged the ingenuity of our author. His father had determined, by his observations, that the planet Venus revolved about her axis in the space of 23 hours; and M. Bianchini had published a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in 1729, in which he settled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the same revolution at 24 days 8 hours. From an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of Bianchini's observations which were upon the spots in Venus, he discovered that he had intermitted his observations for the space of three hours, from which cause he had probably mistaken new spots for the old ones, and so had been led into the mistake. He also determined the nature and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCELERATION">acceleration</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of Jupiter at half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> per year, and of that of the retardation of Saturn at two minutes per year; that these quantities would go on increasing for 2000 years, and then would decrease again. In 1740 he published his Astronomical Tables, and his Elements of Astronomy; very extensive and accurate works. Astronomy was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object of our author's consideration, but he did not confine himself absolutely to that pursuit, but made occasional excursions into other fields. We owe to him Experiments on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>, Experiments on the Recoil of Fire-arms; Researches on the Rise of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAROMETER">Barometer</a> at different Heights; Reflections on the perfecting of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">Burning</a>-glasses; and some other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>. One of the most important objects of the French academy was the measurement of the earth. In 1669 Picard measured a little more than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Paris; but as that extent appeared too small from which to conclude the whole circumference with sufficient accuracy, it was resolved to continue that measurement on the meridian of Paris to the north and the south, through the whole extent of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Accordingly, in 1683, the late M. de la Hire <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> that on the north side of Paris, and the older Cassini that on the south side. The latter was assisted in 1700 in the continuation of this operation by his son our author. The same work was farther continued by the same academicians; and, finally, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> left unfinished by De la Hire in the north was finished in 1718 by our author, with the late Maraldi, and De la Hire the younger. These operations produced a considerable degree of precision. From this measured extent of five degrees, it appeared also, that the degrees were of different lengths in different parts of the meridian; and our author concluded, in the volume published for 1718, that they decreased more and more towards the pole, and that therefore the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the earth was that of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> spheroid, or having its axis longer than the equatorial diameter. He also measured the perpendicular to the same meridian, and compared the measured distance with the differences of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> as before determined by the eclipses of Jupiter's satellites: from which he concluded that the length of the degrees of longitude was smaller than it would be on a sphere, and that therefore again the figure of the earth was an oblong spheroid, contrary to the determination of Newton by the theory of gravity. Newton was indeed of all men the most adverse to controversy; but the other mathematicians in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> did not tamely submit to conclusions in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> opposition to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> doctrine of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, that the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> sent two different sets of measurers, the one to measure Cassini's degree at the equator, the other at the polar circle; and the comparison of the whole determined the figure to be an oblate spheroid, contrary to Cassini's determination. After a long and laborious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, James Cassini died in April 1756, and was succeeded in the Academy and Observatory by his second son. He published, A Treatise on the Magnitude and Figure of the Earth; as also, The Elements or Theory of the Planets, with Tables; beside a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of papers in the Memoirs of the Academy, from the year 1699 to 1755. Cassini de Thury, César François, a celebrated French astronomer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the observatory, and member of most of the learned <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, was born at Paris <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 17, 1714. He was the second son of James Cassini, whose occupations and talents he inherited and supported with great honour. He received his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> in astronomy and mathematics from MM. Maraldi and Camus; and made such a rapid progress, that when he was not more than ten years of age he calculated the phases of a total eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. At the age of eighteen he accompanied his father in his two journeys undertaken for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the perpendicular to the observatory meridian from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a> to Brest. A general chart of France was from that time devised; for which purpose it was necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> the country by several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> and perpendicular to the meridian of Paris. Our author was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with the conduct of this business; in which he was so scrupulous as to measure again what had been measured by his father. This great work was published in 1740, with a chart shewing the new meridian of Paris, by two different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of triangles, passing along the sea coasts to Bayonne, traversing the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> to the Mediterranean and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIBES">Antibes</a>, and thence along the eastern limits of France to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a>, with parallel and perpendicular lines described at the distance of 6000 toises from one another, from side to side of the country. Our author made a tour in 1741, in Flanders, in the train of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. This gave rise, at his majesty's instance, to the chart of France; relative to which Cassini published different works, as well as a great number of the sheets of the chart itself. He undertook, in 1761, an expedition into Germany, for the purpose of continuing to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> the perpendicular of the Paris meridian; to unite the triangles of the chart of France with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> taken in Germany; to prepare the means of extending into that country the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> as in France; and thus to establish successively for all Europe a most useful uniformity.—Our author was at Vienna the 6th of June 1761, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the transit of the planet Venus over the sun, of which he observed as much as the state of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> would permit him to do, and published the account of it in his Voyage en Allemagne. Cassini, always meditating the perfection of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, profited of the peace of 1783 to propose the joining of certain points taken upon the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> with those which had been determined on the coast of France, and thus to connect the general chart of the latter with that of the British isles, as he had before united it with those of Flanders and Germany. The proposal was favourably received by the English government, Between the years 1735 and 1770, M. Cassini published, in the volumes of Memoirs of the French Academy, a great number of pieces, consisting chiefly of astronomical observations and questions; among which are researches concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLAX">parallax</a> of the sun, the moon, Mars, and Venus; on astronomical refractions, and the effect caused in their quantity and laws by the weather; numerous observations on the obliquity of the ecliptic, and on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of its variations. He cultivated astronomy for 50 years, the most important for that science that ever elapsed for the magnitude and variety of objects; and in which he commonly sustained a principal share. M. Cassini was of a very strong and vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, which carried him through the many laborious operations in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a> and astronomy which he conducted. An habitual retention of urine, however, rendered the last twelve years of his life very painful and distressing, till it was at length terminated by the smallpox the 4th of September 1784, in the 71st year of his age. He was succeeded in the academy, and as director of the observatory, by his only son John-Dominic Cassini, the fourth in order of direct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> who has filled that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> station. Hutton's Math. Dict. Cassiodorus, Marcus Aurelius, secretary of state to Theodoric king of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, was born at Squillace, in the kingdom of Naples, about the year 470. He was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> in 514, and was in great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> under the reigns of Athalaric and Vitiges; but at 70 years of age retired into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> in Calabria, where he amused himself in making sun dials, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> glasses, and perpetual lamps. He also formed a library; and composed several works, the best edition of which is that of Father Garet, printed at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a> in 1679. Those most esteemed are his Divine Institutions, and his Treatise on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">Soul</a>. He died about the year 562. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASSIOPEIA">Cassiopeia</a>, in fabulous history, wife to Cepheus king of Ethiopia, and mother of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROMEDA">Andromeda</a>. She thought herself more beautiful than the Nereides, who desired <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the affront; so that he sent a sea monster into the country, which did much harm. To appease the god, her daughter Andromeda was exposed to the monster, but was rescued by Perseus; who obtained of Jupiter, that Cassiopeia might be placed after her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> among the stars: hence the constellation of that name. Cassiopeia, in Astronomy, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a> of the northern hemisphere, situated next to Cepheus. In 1572, there appeared a new <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> in this constellation, which at first surpassed in magnitude and brightness Jupiter himself; but it diminished by degrees, and at last disappeared, at the end of eighteen months. It alarmed all the astronomers of that age, many of whom wrote dissertations on it; among the rest Tycho Brahe, Kepler, Maurolycus, Lycetus, Gramineus, &c. Beza, the landgrave of Hesse, Rosa, &c. wrote to prove it a comet, and the same which appeared to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a> at the birth of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, and that it came to declare his second coming; they were answered on this subject by Tycho. The stars in the constellation Cassiopeia, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, are 13; in Hevelius's, 37; in Tycho's, 46; but in the Britannic catalogue Mr. Flamsteed makes them 55. Cassius, in antiquity, a plated or metallic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>; different from the galea, which was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. Cassiteria, in the history of fossils, a genus of crystals, the figures of which are influenced by an admixture of some particles of tin. The caffiteria are of two kinds; the whitish pellucid caffiterion, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> caffiterion. The first is a tolerably bright and pellucid crystal, and seldom subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> blemishes of crystal: it is of a perfect and regular form, in the figure of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRILATERAL">quadrilateral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>: and is found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> and Cornwall principally. The brown caffiterion is like the former in figure: it is of a very smooth and glossy surface, and is also found in great plenty in Devonshire and Cornwall. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASSITERIDES">Cassiterides</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Geography, a clutter of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> to the west of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a>'s End; opposite to Celtiberia, (Pliny); famous for their tin, which he calls candidum plumbum, formerly open to none but the Phoenicians; who alone carried on this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GADES">Gades</a>, concealing the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> from the rest of the world, (Strabo). The appellation is from Cafliteros, the name for tin in Greek. Now thought to be the Scilly islands, or Sorlings, (Camden). Cassius, Spurius, a renowned Roman general and consul, whose enemies accusing him of aspiring to royalty, he was thrown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the Tarpeian rock 485 years before Christ; after having thrice enjoyed the consular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, been once general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> under the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a> that was created at Rome, and twice received the honour of a triumph. Cassius, Longinus, a celebrated Roman lawyer, flourished 113 years before Christ. He was so inflexible a judge, that his tribunal was called the Rock of the impeached. It is from the judicial severity of this Cassius, that very severe judges have been called Cafliani. Cassius, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a> of Julius Caesar: after his defeat by Mark Antony at the battle of Philippi, he ordered one of his freed men to put him to death with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, 41 years before Christ. See Rome. Cassock, or Cassula, a kind of robe or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, worn over the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, particularly by the clergy. The word cassock comes from the French caflaque, a horseman's coat. Cassonade, in commerce, cask-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, or sugar put into casks or chelts, after the first purification, but which has not been refined. It is sold either in powder or in lumps; the whitest, and that of which the lumps are largest, is the best. Many imagine it to sweeten more than loaf sugar; but it is certain that it yields a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> more foam. Cassowary. See Struthio, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index. Cassumar, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, a root resembling that of zedoary. It is cardiac and sudorific, and famous in nervous <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>; it is also an ingredient in many compositions, and is prescribed in powders, boluses, and infusions. Its dose is from five to fifteen grains. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASSUMBAZAR">Cassumbazar</a>,

CASSUMBAZAR

Pages 251-252

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, situated on the river Ganges, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 37. and N. Lat. 24. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">CAST</a> is peculiarly used to denote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> small statue of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>. See BRONZE.

CAST

Pages 252-252
or Caste, in speaking of the eastern affairs, denotes a tribe, or number of families, of the same rank and profession. The division of a nation into casts chiefly obtains in the dominions of the Great Mogul, kingdom of Bengal, island of Ceylon, and the great peninsula opposite thereto. In each of these there are, according to Father Martin, four principal casts, viz. the cast of the bramins, which is the first and most noble; the cast of the rajas, or princes, who pretend to be descended from divers royal families; the cast of the choutries, which comprehends all the artificers; and that of the parias, the lowest and most contemptible of all: though Henry Lord, it must be observed, divides the Indians about Surat into four casts, somewhat differently from Martin, viz. into bramins, or priests; cutters, or soldiers; fluddery, which we call banians, or merchants; and wyfe, the mechanics or artificers. Every art and trade is confined to its proper caste, nor is allowed to be exercised by any but those whose fathers professed the same. So that a tailor's son can never rise to be a painter, nor a painter's son fall to be a tailor; though there are some employments that are proper to all the casts, e.g., everybody may be a folder or a merchant. There are also divers casts which are allowed to till the ground, but not all. The cast of parias is held infamous, inasmuch that it is a disgrace to have any dealings or conversation with them; and there are some trades in the cast of choutries, which debase their professors almost to the same rank. Thus shoemakers, and all artificers in leather, as also fishermen, and even shepherds, are reputed no better than parias.

CASTAGNO

Pages 252-252
