Andrea Dal, historical painter, was born at a small village called Caflagno, belonging to the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, in 1499: and being deprived of his parents, was employed by his uncle to attend the herds of cattle in the fields; but, having accidentally seen an ordinary painter at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he observed him for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with surprize and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and afterwards made such efforts to imitate him, as astonished all who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> his productions. The extraordinary genius of Andrea became at last a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> topic of discourse in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>; and so far excited the curiosity of Bernadetto de Medici, that he sent for Andrea: and perceiving that he had promising talents, he placed him under the care of the best masters who were at that time in Florence. Andrea diligently pursued his studies, devoted himself entirely to practice under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of his instructors, became particularly eminent in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and in a few years made so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a progress, that he found as much employment as he could possibly execute. He painted only in tempera, and fresco, with a manner of colouring that was not very agreeable, being rather dry and hard, till he learned the secret of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> from Domenico Venetiano, who had derived his knowledge of that new discovery from Antonello da Messina. Andrea was the first of the Florentine artists who painted in oil; but although he was in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> indebted to Domenico for disclosing the secret, yet he secretly envied the merit of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who taught him the art; and because his own works seemed to be much less admired than those of Domenico, he determined to affront his friend and benefactor. He executed his design with the utmost ingratitude and treachery (for Domenico at that time lived with him, and painted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with him), and he stabbed him at a corner of a street so secretly, that he escaped, unobserved and unsuspected, to his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where he composedly sat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to work; and thither Domenico was soon after conveyed, to die in the arms of his murderer. The real author of so inhuman a transaction was never discovered, till Andrea, through remorse of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>, disclosed it on his deathbed, in 1480. He finished several considerable works at Florence, by which he gained great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and as great a reputation; but when his villainous misconduct became public, his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> was ever after held in the utmost detestation. The most noted work of this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> at Florence, representing the execution of the conspirators against the house of Medicis. CASTALIAN <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">SPRING</a>. See CASTALIUS.

CASTALIO

Pages 252-253

Sebastian, was born at Chatillon, on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, in the year 1515. Calvin conceived such an esteem and friendship for him, during the stay he made at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a> in 1540 and 1541, that he lodged him some days at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and procured him a regent's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>. Castalio, after continuing in this office near three years, was forced to quit it in the year 1544, on account of some particular opinions which he held concerning <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s Song, and Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. He retired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, where he was made Greek professor, and died in that place in 1564, aged 48. He incurred the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> displeasure of Calvin and Theodore Beza, for differing with them concerning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of heretics. His works are very considerable both on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. In 1545, he printed at Basil four books of dialogues, containing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> histories of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> in elegant Latin: so that youth might thereby make a proficiency in piety and in the Latin tongue at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. But his principal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is a Latin and French translation of the Scripture. He began the Latin translation at Geneva in 1542, and finished it at Basil in 1550. It was printed at Basil in 1551, and dedicated by the author to Edward VI. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of England. The French version was dedicated to Henry II. of France. CASTALIUS FONS (Strabo, Pausanias); Caffalia, (<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>); A fountain at the foot of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>, near the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>; sacred to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, thence called Caffalides. Its murmurs were thought prophetic, (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NONIUS">Nonius</a>, Lucian.) See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> DELPHI and PARNASSUS. CASTANEA. See FAGUS. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>.

CASTANETS

Pages 253-253

CASTAGNETTES, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> CASTANETAS, a kind of musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, wherewith the Moors, Spaniards, and Bohemians, accompany their dances, farabands, and guitars. It consists of two little round pieces of wood dried, and hollowed in manner of a spoon, the concavities whereof are placed on one another, fastened to the thumb, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time with the middle finger, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> and cadences. The castanets may be beat eight or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> times in the space of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of a minute.

CASTANOVITZ

Pages 253-253

a town of Croatia, situated on the river Unna, which divides Christendom from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17. 20. N. Lat. 45. 40. It is subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>.

CASTEL

Pages 253-253
LEWIS BERTRAND, a learned Jesuit, was born at Montpelier in 1688, and entered among the Jesuits in 1703. He studied polite literature in his youth; and at length applied himself entirely to the study of mathematics and ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural philosophy. He distinguished himself by writing on gravity; the mathematics; and on the music of colours, a very whimsical idea, which he took great pains to reduce to practice. His piece on gravity, entitled Traité de la Penfateur universelle, was printed at Paris, in 1724. He afterwards published his Mathematique universelle; which occasioned his being unanimously chosen a fellow of the Royal Society of London, without the least solicitation. He was also a member of the academies of Bordeaux and Rouen; but his Clavecin vocabulaire made the most noise; and he spent much time and expense in making an harpsichord for the eye, but without success. He also wrote for and against Sir Isaac Newton, and published several other works; the principal of which are, Le Plan du Mathématique abrégée, and a treatise entitled Optique des Couleurs. He led a very exemplary life, and died in 1757.

CASTELAMARA

Pages 253-253

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and the Hither Principato, with a bishop's see and a good harbour. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 15. N. Lat. 41. 40. CASTEL-ARAGONÈSE, a strong town of Italy, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, with a bishop's see, and a good harbour. It is seated on the N.W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the island, in E. Long. 8. 57. N. Lat. 40. 56. CASTEL-Branco, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEIRA">Beira</a>; seated on the river Lyra, 35 miles N.W. of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCANTARA">Alcantara</a>. W. Long. 8. 0. N. Lat. 39. 35. CASTEL-Franco, a very small, but well fortified frontier town of the Bolognese, in Italy, belonging to the Pope. CASTEL-de-Vide, a small strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALENTEJO">Alentejo</a>. It was taken by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> V. W. Long. 6. 25. N. Lat. 39. 15. CASTEL-Foït, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Catalonia, seated on an inaccessible eminence, between Gironne and Campredon, about 15 miles from each, and near the river Fulva. CASTEL-Gandolfo, a town of Italy, in the territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, with a castle, to which the pope retires in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season; 10 miles S. by E. of Rome. E. Long. 12. 46. N. Lat. 41. 44. CASTEL-Novo, a strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, subject to the Venetians; seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Cattalo, in E. Long. 18. 45. N. Lat. 42. 25. CASTEL-Rodrigo, a town of Portugal, in the province of Tra-os-Montes, in W. Long. 7. 1. N. Lat. 41. 0. CASTEL-Novo-de-Carfagnana, a town of Italy, in the Modenesi, with a strong fortress. It is the capital of the valley of Carfagnana, and seated on the river Serchio, 17 miles above <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>. CASTEL-del-Ovo, a small island in the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in the gulf of Naples, near a town of that name, to which it is joined by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. The fortress is called Caffel del Ovo, in which there is always a good garrison.

CASTELBAR

Pages 253-253

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Mayo, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Connaught, 35 miles N. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALWAY">Galway</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 25. N. Lat. 53. 45.

CASTELL

Pages 253-253

EDMUND, D.D. A learned English divine of the 17th century, distinguished by his skill in the eastern languages. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; where he was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Catharine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, and Arabic professor; and was at length canon of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. He had the greatest share in the Polyglott <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and wrote the Heptaglottion pro septem Orientibus, &c. On this excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which occupied a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he bestowed incredible pains and expense, even to the breaking of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and exhausting of his fortune, having expended no less than 12,000l. upon that work. At length, when it was printed, the copies remained uncollected upon his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. He died in 1685; and lies buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of Higham Gobyon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>, of which he was rector. It appears from the inscription on his monument, which he erected in his lifetime, that he was chaplain to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. He bequeathed all his oriental <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> to the university of Cambridge, on condition that his name should be written on every copy in the collection.

CASTELLA

Pages 253-253

a town of the Mantuan, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, about five miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 15. N. Lat. 45. 30.

CASTELLAN

Pages 253-253

the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>: the castellans are senators of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, but senators only of the lower class, who, in diets, sit on low seats, behind the palatines, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> senators. They are a kind of lieutenants of provinces, and command a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> under the palatine.

CASTELLANY

Pages 253-253

the territory belonging to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> town, chiefly used in France, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>: Thus we say, the castellany of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LILLE">Lille</a>, Ypres, &c.

CASTELLARIUS

Pages 253-253

the keeper, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> curator, of a castellum. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GRUTER">Gruter</a> gives an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> sepulchral inscription in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of a castellarius. Hh CASTELLATIO,

CASTELLATIO

Pages 253-254

in middle-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a castle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of fortifying a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and rendering it a castle.—By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> English laws, cattellation was prohibited without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s special licence.

CASTELLI

Pages 254-254

Bernard, an Italian painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> in 1577; and excelled in colouring and in portraits. He was the intimate friend of Tasso, and took upon himself the task of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETCHING">etching</a> the figures of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> Delivered. He died at Genoa in 1629. Valerio Caffelli, one of his sons, was born at Genoa in 1625, and surpassed his father. He particularly excelled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> battles; which he composed with spirit, and executed them with so pleasing a variety, and so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> freedom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, as gained him universal applause. His horses are admirably drawn, thrown into attitudes that are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and becoming, full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In that style of painting he showed all the fire of Tintoretto, united with the fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of Paolo Veronese. He died in 1639. The works of this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> are not very frequent; but they are deservedly held in very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem. It is believed that a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his easel pictures are in the collections of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry of England, than in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

CASTELLORUM OPERATIO

Pages 254-254

castle <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and labour done by inferior tenants for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and upholding of castles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; towards which some gave personal affluence, and others paid their contributions. This was one of the three necessary charges to which all lands among the Anglo-Saxons were expressly subject.

CASTELVETRO

Pages 254-254
Lewis, a native of Modena, of the 16th century, famous for his Comment on Aristotle's Poetics. He was prosecuted by the inquisition for a certain book of Melanchthon, which he had translated into Italian. He retired to Basil, where he died.

CASTIGATION

Pages 254-254

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of an offender by blows, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> with a wand or switch. Cafligation was chiefly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> punishment; the power of inflicting of which on the soldiery was given to the tribunes. Some make it of two kinds; one with a stick or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, called flagellatio; the other with rods, called flagellatio; the latter was the most dishonourable. CASTIGATORY for SCOLDS. A woman indicted for being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> scold, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> convicted, shall be placed in a certain engine of correction, called the trebucket cafligatory, or cucking stool; which, in the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifies the scolding stool; though now it is frequently corrupted into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCKING">ducking</a> stool; because the residue of the judgment is, that when she is placed therein, she shall be plunged in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> for her punishment.

CASTIGLIONE

Pages 254-254

a small but strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, with a castle. It was taken by the Germans in 1701, and the French defeated the Imperialists near it in 1706. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 1° 29'. N. Lat. 43° 23'.

CASTIGLIONI

Pages 254-254

Balthazar, an eminent Italian nobleman, descended from an illustrious and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, and born at his own villa at Cafalico in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> in 1478. He studied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, as appears from a book he wrote in favour of these arts; and excelled so much in them, that Raphael Urbino, and Buonarotti, though incomparable artists, never thought their works complete without the approbation of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Caffiglioni. When he was 26 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, Guido Ubaldo, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Urbino, sent him <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to Pope Julius II. He was sent upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> embassy to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII. of France, and upon a third to Henry VII. of England. After he had dispatched his business here, he returned, and began his celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled the Courrier; which he completed at Rome in 1516. This work is full of moral and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> instruction; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we seek for the Italian tongue in perfection, it is said to be nowhere better found than in this performance. A version of this work, together with the original Italian, was published at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1727, by A. P. Caffiglioni, a gentlemen of the same family, who resided there under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of Dr Gibbon bishop of London. Count Caffiglioni was sent by Clement VII. to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of legate, and died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a> in 1529.

CASTILE

Pages 254-255

Old, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It is about 192 miles in length, and 115 in breadth; bounded on the south by New Castile, on the east by Arragon and Navarre, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>. CASTILE Biscay and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a>, and on the west by the kingdom of Leon. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGOS">Burgos</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town. CASTILLO-de-Oro, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, lying to the west of the Oroonoko. It comprehends eight governments; viz. Terra Firme, Proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>, St Martha, Rio de la Hacha, Venezuela, New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPAYAN">Popayan</a>, and the kingdom of New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>.

CASTILLAN

Pages 255-255

is also a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> for weighing <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. It is a hundredth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> Spanish weight. What they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> call a weight of gold in Spain is always understood of the castillian.

CASTILLARA

Pages 255-255

a town of the Mantuan in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated six miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 25'. N. Lat. 45° 20'.

CASTILLON

Pages 255-255

a town of France, in the department of Gironde, situated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORDOGNE">Dordogne</a>, 16 miles east of Bordeaux. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 40'. N. Lat. 44° 50'.

CASTING

Pages 255-258

in foundry, the running of metal into a mould, prepared for that purpose. Casting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">Metals</a>, of Letters, Bells, &c. See the article FOUNDRY. Casting in Sand <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>, is the running of metals between two frames, or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>, filled with sand or earth, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> that the metal is to take has been impressed en creux, by means of the pattern. Casting, among sculptors, implies the taking of casts and impressions of figures, busts, medals, leaves, &c. The method of taking of casts of figures and busts is most generally by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, i.e. alabaster calcined by a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. The advantage of using this substance preferably to others is, that notwithstanding a slight calcination reduces it to a pulverine state, it becomes again a tenacious and cohering body, by being moistened with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and afterwards suffered to dry; by which means either a concave or a convex figure may be given by a proper mould or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> to it when wet, and retained by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> it acquires when dry: and from these qualities, it is fitted for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> purpose of making both casts, and moulds for forming those casts. The particular manner of making casts depends on the form of the subject to be taken. Where there are no projecting parts, it is very simple and easy; as likewise where there are such as form only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or any greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> surface of the body; but where parts project in lesser <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, or form a curve inclined towards the principal surface of the body, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is more difficult. The first step to be taken is the forming the mould. In order to this, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the original or model be a bas-relief, or any other piece of a flat form, having its surface first well greased, it must be placed on a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and surrounded by a frame, the sides of which must be at such a distance from it as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> allow a proper thickness for the sides of the mould. As much plaster as will be sufficient to cover and rise to such a thickness as may give sufficient strength to the mould, as also to fill the hollow betwixt the frame and the model, must be moistened with water, till it be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> of such consistence as will allow it to be poured upon the model. This must be done as soon as possible; or the plaster would concrete or set, so as to become more troublesome in the working, or unfit to be used. The whole must then be suffered to remain in this condition, till the plaster has attained its hardness; and then the frame being taken away, the preparatory <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> or mould thus formed may be taken off from the subject entire. Where the model or original subject is of a round or erect form, a different method must be pursued; and the mould must be divided into several pieces; or if the subject consists of detached and projecting parts, it is frequently most expedient to cast such parts separately, and afterwards join them together. Where the original subject or mould forms a round, or spheroid, or any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of such round or spheroid, more than one half the plaster must be used without any frame to keep it round the model; and must be tempered with water to such a consistence, that it may be wrought with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> like very soft paste; but though it must not be so fluid as when prepared for flat-figured models, it must yet be as moist as is compatible with its cohering sufficiently to hold together; and being thus prepared, it must be put upon the model, and comprimbed with the hand, or any flat <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, that the parts of it may adapt themselves, in the most perfect manner, to those of the subject, as well as to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> with respect to themselves. When the model is so covered to a convenient thickness, the whole must be left at rest till the plaster be set and firm, so as to bear dividing without falling to pieces, or being liable to be put out of its form by flight violence; and it must then be divided into pieces, in order to its being taken off from the model, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> it with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> with a very thin blade; and being divided, must be cautiously taken off, and kept till dry; but it must be always carefully observed, before the separation of the parts be made, to notch them across the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, at proper distances, that they may with ease and certainty be properly joined again; which would be much more precarious and troublesome without such directive marks. The art of properly dividing the moulds, in order to make them separate from the model, requires more dexterity and skill than any other thing in the art of casting; and does not admit of rules for the most advantageous conduct of it in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. Where the subject is of a round or spheroidal form, it is best to divide the mould into three parts, which will then easily come off from the model; and the same will hold good of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> or any regular curved figure. The mould being thus formed, and dry, and the parts put together, it must be first greased, and placed in such a position that the hollow may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> upwards, and then filled with plaster mixed with water, in the same proportion and manner as was directed for the casting the mould; and when the cast is perfectly set and dry, it must be taken out of the mould, and repaired where it is necessary; which finishes the operation. This is all that is required with respect to subjects where the surfaces have the regularity above-mentioned; but where they form curves which intersect each other, the conduct of the operation must be varied with respect to the manner of taking the cast of the mould from off the subject or model; and where there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> projecting parts, such as legs or arms, they should be wrought in separate casts. The operator may easily judge, from the original subjects, what parts will come off together, and what require to be separated: the principle of the whole consists only in this, that where under-workings, as they are called, occur, that is, wherever a straight line drawn from the basis or insertion of any projection, would be cut or crossed by any part of such projection, such part cannot be taken off without a division; which must be made either in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the projection would <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the straight line; or, as that is frequently difficult, the whole projection must be separated from the main body, and divided also lengthwise into two parts; and where there are no projections from the principal surfaces, but the body is so formed as to render the surface a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of such curves, that a straight line being drawn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the surface of one part would be cut by the outline, in one or more places, of another part, a division of the whole should be made, so as to reduce the parts of it into regular curves, which must then be treated as such. In larger masses, where there would otherwise be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> thickness of the plaster, a core or body may be put within the mould, in order to produce a hollow in the cast; which both saves the expense of the plaster, and renders the cast <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>. This core may be of wood, where the forming a hollow of a straight figure, or a conical one with the basis outward, will answer the end: but if the cavity require to be round, or of any curve figure, the core cannot be then drawn while entire; and consequently should be of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> as may be taken out piecemeal. In this case, the core is best formed of clay; which must be worked upon wires to give it a tenacity, and suspended in the hollow of the mould by cross wires lying over the mouth; and when the plaster is sufficiently set to bear handling, the clay must be picked out by a proper instrument. Where it is desired to render the plaster harder, the water with which it is tempered should be mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> size properly prepared, which will make it very firm and tenacious. In the same manner, figures, busts, &c., may be cast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, or any other metal, in the moulds of plaster; only the expense of plaster, and the tediousness of its becoming sufficiently dry, when in a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, to bear the heat of melted metal, render the use of clay, compounded with some other proper materials, preferable where large subjects are in question. The clay, in this case, should be washed over till it be perfectly free from gravel or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; and then mixed with a third or more of fine sand to prevent it cracking; or, instead of sand, coal ashes sifted fine may be used. Whether plaster or clay be employed for the casting in metal, it is extremely necessary to have the mould perfectly dry: otherwise the moisture, being rarefied, will make an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> that will blow the metal out of the mould, and endanger the operator, or at least crack the mould in such a manner as to frustrate the operation. Where the parts of a mould are larger, or project much, and consequently require a greater tenacity of the matter they are formed of to keep them together, flocks of cloth, prepared like those designed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> hangings, or fine cotton plucked or cut till it is very short, should be mixed with the ashes or sand before they are added to the clay to make the composition for the mould. The proportion should be according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> required; but a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> will answer the end, if the other ingredient of the composition be good, and the parts of the mould properly linked together by means of the wires above directed. There is a method of taking casts in metals from small animals, and the parts of vegetables, which may be practised for some purposes with advantage: particularly for the decorating grottoes or rock work, where <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is imitated. The proper kinds of animals are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIZARDS">lizards</a>, snakes, frogs, birds, or insects; the casts of which, if properly coloured, will be exact representations of the originals. This is to be performed by the following method. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> or proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> for forming the mould being prepared of clay, or four pieces of boards fixed together, the animal or parts of vegetables must be suspended in it by a string; and the leaves, tendrils or other detached parts of the vegetables, or the legs, wings, &c., of the animals, properly separated and adjusted, in their right position by a small <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of pincers: a due quantity of plaster of Paris and calcined tallow, in equal quantities, with some <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> arabic, must then be tempered with water to the proper consistence for casting; and the subject from whence the cast is to be taken, also the sides of the coffin, moistened with spirit of wine. The coffin or chest must then be filled with the tempered composition of the plaster and tallow, putting at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a piece of straight stick or wood to the principal part of the body of the subject, and pieces of thick wire to the extremities of the other parts, in order that they may form, when drawn out after the matter of the mould is properly set and firm, a channel for pouring in the melted metal, and vents for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; which otherwise by the rarefaction it would undergo from the heat of the metal would blow it out or burst the mould. In a short time the plaster and tallow will set and become hard, when the stick and wires may be drawn out, and the frame or coffin in which the mould was cast taken away; and the mould must then be put first into a moderate heat, and afterwards, when it is as dry as it can be rendered by that degree, removed into a greater; which may be gradually increased till the whole be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot. The animal or part of any vegetable, which was included in the mould, will then be burnt to a coal; and may be totally calcined to ashes, by blowing for some time gently into the channel and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> made for pouring in the metal, and giving vent to the air, which will, at the same time that it destroys the remainder of the animal or vegetable matter, blow out the ashes. The mould must then be suffered to cool gently; and will be perfect; the destruction of the substance of the animal or vegetable having produced a hollow of a figure correspondent to it; but it may be nevertheless proper to shake the mould, and turn it upside <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, as also to blow with the bellows into each of the air vents, in order to free it wholly from any remainder of the ashes; or where there may be an opportunity of filling the hollow with quicksilver without expense, it will be found a very effectual method of clearing the cavity, as all dust, ashes, or small detached bodies, will necessarily Casting necessarily rise to the surface of the quicksilver, and be poured out with it. The mould being thus prepared, it must be heated very hot when used, if the cast be made with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>; but a less degree will serve for lead or tin; and the matter being poured in, the mould must be gently struck; and then suffered to rest till it be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; at which time it must be carefully taken from the cast, but without the least force; for such parts of the matter as appear to adhere more strongly, must be softened by soaking in water till they be entirely loosened, that none of the more delicate parts of the cast may be broken off or bent. Where the alumen plumbosum, or talk, cannot easily be procured, the plaster may be used alone; but it is apt to be calcined by the heat used in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the animal or vegetable from whence the cast is taken, and to become too incohering and crumbly texture; or, for cheapness, Sturbridge or any other good clay, washed over, till it be perfectly fine, and mixed with an equal part of sand, and some flours cut small, may be employed. Pounded pumice <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and plaster of Paris, taken in equal quantities, and mixed with washed clay in the same proportion, is said to make excellent moulds for this and parallel uses. Casts of medals, or such small pieces as are of a similar form, may be made in plaster by the method directed for bas relieves. Indeed there is nothing more required than to form a mould by laying them on a proper board, and having surrounded them by a rim made by the piece of a card or any other pastebone, to fill the rim with soft tempered plaster of Paris; which mould, when dry, will serve for several casts. It is nevertheless a better method to form the mould of melted sulphur; which will produce a sharper <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> in the cast, and be more durable than those made of plaster. The casts are likewise frequently made of sulphur, which being melted must be treated exactly in the same manner as the plaster. For taking casts from medals, Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> recommends a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of brimstone and red lead: equal parts of these are to be put over the fire in a ladle, till they soften to the consistence of pap; then they are kindled with a piece of paper, and stirred for some time. The vessel being afterwards covered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on the fire, the mixture grows fluid in a few minutes. It is then to be poured on the metal, previously oiled and wiped clean. The casts are very neat; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> sometimes a pretty deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, sometimes a dark grey; they are very durable; and when soiled, may be washed clean in spirits of wine. Dr Lettfrom recommends tin foil for taking off casts from medals. The thinnest kind is to be used. It should be laid over the subject from which the impression is to be taken, and then rubbed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, the point of a skewer, or a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>, till it has perfectly received the impression. The tin foil should now be prepared close to the edge of the medal, till it is brought to the same circumference: the medal must then be reversed, and the tin foil will drop off into a chip box or mould placed ready to receive it. Thus the concave side of the foil will be uppermost, and upon this plaster of Paris, prepared in the usual manner, may be poured. When dry, the whole is to be taken out, and the tin foil sticking on the plaster will give a perfect representation of the medal, almost equal in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> to silver. If the box or mould is a little larger than the medal, the plaster running round the tin foil will give the appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> frame or circular border; whence the new made medal will appear more neat and beautiful. Casts may be made likewise with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, prepared in the following manner: "Take any iron <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, or piece of a similar form; and having heated it red-hot, hold it over a vessel containing water, and touch it very slightly with a roll of sulphur, which will immediately dissolve it, and make it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in drops into the water. As much iron as may be wanted being thus dissolved, pour the water out of the vessel; and pick out the drops formed by the melted iron from those of the sulphur, which contain little or no iron, and will be distinguishable from the other by their colour and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>." The iron will, by this means, be rendered so fusible, that it will run with less heat than is required to melt lead; and may be employed for making casts of medals, and many other such purposes, with great convenience and advantage. Impressions of medals, having the same effect as casts, may be made also of isinglass <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>, by the following means. Melt the isinglass, beaten, as when <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used, in an earthen pipkin, with the addition of as much water as will cover it, stirring it gently till the whole is dissolved; then with a brush of camel's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, cover the medal, which should be previously well cleaned and warmed, and then laid horizontally on a board or table, greased in the part around the medal. Let them rest afterwards till the glue be properly hardened; and then, with a pin, raise the edge of it; and separate it carefully from the medal: the cast will be thus formed by the glue as hard as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>; and so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, that a thousand will scarcely weigh an ounce. In order to render the relief of the medal more apparent, a small quantity of carmine may be mixed with the melted isinglass; or the medal may be previously coated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> by breathing on it, and then laying it on the leaf, which will by that means adhere to it; but the use of leaf gold is apt to impair a little the sharpness of the impression. Impressions of medals may be likewise taken in putty; but it should be the true kind made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> of tin, and drying <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. These may be formed in the moulds, previously taken in plaster or sulphur; or moulds may be made in its own substance, in the manner directed for those of the plaster. These impressions will be very sharp and hard; but the greatest disadvantage that attends them, is their drying very slowly, and being liable in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time to be damaged. Impressions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>, or other engravings, may be taken from copperplates, by cleansing them thoroughly, and pouring plaster upon them; but the effect in this way is not strong enough for the eyes; and therefore the following method is preferable, where such impressions on plaster are desired. Take <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a>, or any other coloured pigment, finely powdered, and rub it over the plate; then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> a folded piece of paper, or the flat part of the hand, over the the plate, to take off the colour from the lights or parts where there is no engraving; the proceeding must then be the same as where no colour is used. This last method is also applicable to the making of impressions of copperplates on paper with dry colours; for the plate being prepared as here directed, and laid on the paper properly moistened, and either passed under the rolling press, or any other way strongly forced down on the paper, an impression of the engraving will be obtained. Impressions may be likewise taken from copperplates, either on plaster or paper, by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>; if, instead of rubbing them with any colour, the plate be held over the candle or lamp till the whole surface become black, and then wiped off by the flat of the hand, or paper. These methods are not, however, of great use in the case of copperplates, except where impressions may be desired on occasions where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> cannot be procured; but as they may be applied likewise to the taking impressions from snuff boxes, or other engraved subjects, by which means designs may be instantly borrowed by artists or curious persons, they may in such instances be very useful. The expedient of taking impressions by the smoke of a candle or lamp may be employed also for botanical purposes in the case of leaves, as a perfect and durable representation of not only the general figure, but the contexture and disposition of the larger fibres, may be contemporaneously obtained at any time. The same may be nevertheless done in a more perfect manner, by the use of linseed oil, either alone, or mixed with a small proportion of colour, where the oil can be conveniently procured: but the other method is valuable on account of its being applicable at almost all seasons, and in all places, within the time that the leaves will keep fresh and plump. In taking these impressions it is proper to bruise the leaves, so as to take off the projections of the large ribs, which might prevent the other parts from plying to the paper. Leaves, as also the petals, or flower leaves, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, may themselves be preserved on paper, with their original appearance, for a considerable length of time, by the following means.—Take a piece of paper, and rub it over with shellac glue treated as above directed for taking impressions from medals; and then lay the leaves in a proper position on the paper. The glue laid on the paper being let, brush over the leaves with more of the same; and that being dry likewise, the operation will be finished, and the leaves so secured from the air and moisture, that they will retain their figure and colour much longer than by any other treatment. Butterflies, or other small animals of a flat figure, may also be preserved in the same manner. Casting is also sometimes used for the quitting, laying, or throwing aside any thing; thus deer cast their horns, snakes their skins, lobsters their shells, hawks their feathers, &c. annually. Casting of feathers is more properly called moulting or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEWING">mewing</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> casts his hair, or coat, at least once a year, viz. in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, when he casts his winter coat; and sometimes, at the close of autumn, he casts his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> coat, in case he has been ill kept. Horses also sometimes cast their hoofs, which happens frequently to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">coach</a> horses brought from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; these being bred in a moist marshy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, have their hoofs too flabby; so that coming into a drier <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and less juicy provender, their hoofs fall off, and others that are firmer succeed. Casting a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLT">Colt</a>, denotes a mare's proving abortive. Casting <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">Net</a>, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> net, so called, because it is to be cast or thrown out; which when exactly done, nothing escapes it, but weeds and every thing within its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> are brought away.

CASTLE

Pages 261-262

Edmund.** See CASTEL. **CASTLE-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">BAR</a>,** a borough and market town, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Mayo in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, is a well-inhabited <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and carries on a brisk trade: it has a barrack for a troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; and there is here a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> school capable of receiving 50 children, and endowed with two acres of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, rent free, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Lucan, who has also granted a lease of 20 acres more at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a> corn yearly. **CASTLE-CARY,** a remarkable Roman station about four miles west from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALKIRK">Falkirk</a> on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STIRLINGSHIRE">Stirlingshire</a> in Scotland. It comprehends several acres of ground, is of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> form, and is surrounded with a wall of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>: all the space within the walls has been occupied by buildings, the ruins of which have raised the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> eight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ten feet above its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> surface; so that the fort now seems like a hill top surrounded with a funk <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a>. In 1770, some workmen employed in searching for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> canal, which passes very near it, discovered several apartments of stone; and in one of them a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of stones about two feet in length, and standing erect, with marks of fire upon them, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been employed in supporting some vessel under which fire was put. In a hollow of the rock near this place, in 1771, a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wheat quite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> was found, with some wedges and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a> supposed to be Roman. **CASTLE-RISING,** a borough town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> in England, which sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 40'. N. Lat. 52° 46'. **CASTLE-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">WORK</a>,** <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> or labour done by inferior tenants, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and upholding castles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, toward which some gave their personal affluence, and others paid their contributions. This was one of the three necessary charges to which the Anglo-Saxons were expressly subject. **CASTLETOWN,** the capital of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, seated on the south-west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. It has a strong castle; but of no great importance, on account of its distance from the rocky and shallow harbour. W. Long. 4° 39'. N. Lat. 53° 30'. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">CASTOR</a>,** the Beaver, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> belonging to the order of glires. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **CASTOR,** in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a moiety of the constellation Gemini; called also <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">APOLLO</a>. Its latitude northwards, for the year 1700, according to Hevelius, was 10° 4′ 23″; and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, of Cancer, 17° 4′ 14″. Is also called Rafalgenze, Apollo, Aphellan, Avellar, Anelar. **CASTOR and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">POLLUX</a>,** in Pagan <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> having an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a> with Leda, the wife of Tyndarus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, in the form of a swan, he brought forth two eggs, each containing twins. From that impregnated by Jupiter proceeded Pollux and Helena, who were both immortal: from the other Castor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLYTEMNESTRA">Clytemnestra</a>, who being begot by Tyndarus were both mortal. They were all, however, called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name of Tyndaridae. These two brothers entered into an inviolable friendship; they went with the other noble youths of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> in the expedition to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a>, and, on several occasions, signalized themselves by their courage; but Castor being at length killed, Pollux obtained leave to share his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> with him; so that they are said to live and die alternately every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>: for, being translated into the skies, they form the constellation of Gemini, one of which stars rises as the other sets. A martial dance, called the Pyrrhic or Caistorian dance, was invented in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of those deities, whom the Cephelenes placed among the Dii Magni, and offered to them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> also paid them particular honours on account of the affluence they are said to have given them in an engagement against the Latins; in which, appearing mounted on white horses, they turned the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of victory in their favour, for which a temple was erected to them in the forum. **CASTOR and POLLUX,** a fiery <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a>, which at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> appears sometimes sticking to a part of the ship, in form of one, two, or even three or four fire balls; when one is seen alone, it is more properly called HELENA; two are denominated Castor and Pollux, and sometimes Tyndaridae. Castor and Pollux are called by the Spaniards, San Elmo; by the French St. Elme, St Nicholas, St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>, St Helene; by the Italians, Heremo; by the Dutch, Tree Vuuren. Castor and Pollux are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> judged to portend a cessation of the storm, and a future calm; being rarely seen till the tempest is nigh spent. Helena alone portends ill, and witnesse the severest part of the storm yet behind. When the meteor sticks to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, yards, &c., they conclude, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>'s not having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> enough to dissipate this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, that a profound calm is at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; if it flutter about, it indicates a storm. **CASTOREUM,** in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, castor; the inguinal glands of the beaver. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had a notion that it was lodged in the testicles; and that the animal, when hard pressed, would bite them off, and leave them to its pursuers, as if conscious of what they wanted to destroy him for. The best sort of castor is what comes from Ruffia. So much is Rufian castor superior to the American, that two guineas per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> are paid for the former, and only 8s. 6d. for the latter. The Ruffian castor is in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> hard round cods, which appear, when cut, full of a brittle, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> coloured substance, interperforated with membranes and fibres exquisitely interwoven. An inferior sort is brought from Dantzig, and is generally fat and moist. The American calior, which is the worst of all, is in longish thin cods. Ruffia castor has a strong disagreeable smell; and an acrid, bitterish, and nauseous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a> extracts the nauseous part, with little of the finer bitter; rectified spirit extracts this last without much of the nauseous; <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> spirit both: water elevates the whole of its flavour in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>; rectified spirit brings over nothing. Castor is looked upon as one of the capital nerve and antithyric medicines: some celebrated practitioners, nevertheless, have doubted its virtues; and Newmann and Stahl de- <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASTRATION">Castration</a>, clare it insignificant. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a>, however, has shown that the virtues of castrators are considerable, though less than they have been generally supposed.

CASTRATION

Pages 262-262

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, the operation of gelding, i.e., of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the testicles, and putting a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> animal out of the capacity of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. Castration is much in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, especially among the Turks, who practise it on their slaves, to prevent any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with their women. The Turks often make a general amputation. Castration also obtains in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where it is used with a view to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> for singing. See EUNUCH. The Persians, and other eastern nations, have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> methods of making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>, different from those which obtain in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>: we say, of making eunuchs, for it is not always done among them by cutting, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even collission. Cicuta and other poisonous herbs do the same office, as is shown by Paulus Aegineta. Those eunuched in this manner are called thlibia. Besides which there is another sort called thlofia, in whom the genitals are left entire, and only the veins which should feed them are cut; by which means the parts do indeed remain, but so lax and weak, as to be of no use. Castration was for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>. By the laws of the Visigoths, Sodomites underwent the same punishment. By the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, it is made penal in physicians and surgeons to castrate, even with consent of the party, who is himself included in the same penalty, and his effects forfeited. The offence of Mayhem by castration is, according to all our old writers, felony; though committed upon the highest provocation. See a record to this purpose of Henry III. transcribed by Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, 3 Inst. 62. or Blackstone's Commentaries, vol. iv. p. 266. Castration is sometimes found necessary on medicinal considerations, as in mortifications, and some other diseases of the testicles, especially the farcocele and varicocele. Some have also used it in maniac <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. Castration is also in some fort practised on women. Athenaeus mentions that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Andromytes was the first who castrated women. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HESYCHIUS">Hesychius</a> and Suidas say Gygges did the same thing. Galen observes, that women cannot be castrated without danger of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and Dalechampius, on the fore-mentioned passage of Athenaeus, holds, that it is only to be understood of simple padding. Castration, in respect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, is called gelding and spaying.

CASTRATION ALSO

Pages 262-262

n also denotes the art of retrenching, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> away any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a thing from its whole.—Castrating a book, among bookellers, is the taking out some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, sheet, or the like, which renders it imperfect and unfit for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is also applied to the taking away particular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, on account of their obscenity, too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> freedom with respect to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASTRATION">Castration</a>, among botanists, a term derived from the fancied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and animals. The castration of plants consists in cutting off the antherae, or tops of the stamens, before they have attained maturity, and dispersed the pollen or fine dust contained within their substance. This operation has been frequently practised by the moderns, with a view to establish or confute the doctrine of the sexes of plants; the antherae or tops being considered by the sexualists as the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. The experiment of castration succeeds principally on plants which, like the melon, have their male <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> detached from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>. In such as have both male and female flowers contained within the same covers, this operation cannot be easily performed without endangering the neighbouring organs. The result of experiments on this subject by Linnæus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTON">Alton</a>, and other eminent botanists, may be seen under the article <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>.

CASTREL

Pages 262-262

a kind of hawk resembling the lanner in shape, but the hobby in size. The castril is also called keffrel, and is of a slow and cowardly kind; her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> is the grouse, though she <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> kill a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>.

CASTRES

Pages 262-262

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a> in France, about 35 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2°. N. Lat. 43. 40. It is a bishop's see.

CASTRO

Pages 262-262

Pietro de', a celebrated painter, who flourished about the middle of the 17th century. The subjects which this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> chose to paint, were what are distinguished by the name of still <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; vases, shells, musical instruments, gems, vessels of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and crystal, books, and rich bracelets: and in those subjects his choice and disposition were elegant, and his execution admirable.

CASTRUCCIO

Pages 262-263

Castracani, a celebrated Italian general, was born (no body knows of whom) at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> in 1284, and left in a vineyard covered with leaves, where he was found by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, a widow lady, the sister of Antonio, a canon of St Michael in Lucca, who was descended from the illustrious family of the Castracani. The lady having no children, she resolved to bring him up, and educated him as carefully as he had been her own. She intended him for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>; but he was scarcely 14 years old when he began to devote himself to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> sports, and those violent exercises which suited his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength of body. The factions named the Guelfs and Gibelines then shared all <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> between them; divided the popes and the emperors; and engaged in their different interests not only the members of the same town, but even those of the same family. Francisco, a considerable person on the side of the Gibelines, observing Castruccio's uncommon spirit and great qualities, prevailed with Antonio to let him turn soldier; on which Castruccio soon became acquainted with everything belonging to that profession, and was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of foot by Francisco Guinigi. In his first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> he gave such proofs of his courage and conduct as spread his fame all over <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>; and Guinigi, dying soon after, committed to him the care of his son and the management of his estate. Still distinguishing himself by his exploits, he filled his commander in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> with such jealousy and envy, that he was imprisoned by stratagem in order to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. But the people of Lucca soon released him, and afterwards chose him for their sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>.—The Gibelines considered him as the chief of their party; Castruccio, party; and those who had been banished from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> fled to him for protection, and unanimously promised, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he could restore them to their estates, they would serve him so effectually that the sovereignty of their country should be his reward. Flattered by these promises, he entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>. He kept his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> constantly on foot, employing it as best suited his own designs. For services he had done the pope, he was made senator of Rome with more than ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>; but while there, received news which obliged him to hasten back to Lucca. The Florentines entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with him, but Castruccio fought his way through them; and the supreme authority of Tuscany was ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> was put to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In May 1328, he gained a complete victory over his enemies, who amounted to 30,000 foot and 10,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; in which 22,000 of them were slain, with the loss of not quite 1600 of his own men; but as he was returning from the field of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, tired with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and covered with sweat, he halted a little, in order to thank and care for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> as they passed; when, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blowing upon him, he was immediately seized with an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGUE">ague</a>, which he at first neglected, but it carried him off in a few days, in the 44th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Machiavel, who has written the life of Castruccio, says, that he was not only an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in his own age, but would have been so in any other. He was of a noble aspect, and of the most winning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>. He had all the qualities that make a man great; was grateful to his friends, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> to his subjects, terrible to his enemies. No man was more forward to encounter dangers; no man more careful to escape them. He had an uncommon presence of mind, and often made repartees with great smartness.
