Some of them are recorded, which discover a singular turn of humour; and, for a specimen, we shall mention three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four of them.—Passing one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> through a street where there was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of bad fame, he surprised a young man, who was just coming out, and, who, upon seeing him, was all over blushes and confusion: “Friend, you should not be ashamed when you come out, but when you go in.”—One asking a favour of him with a thousand impertinent and superfluous words: “Hark you, friend; when you would have anything with me for the future, send another man to ask it.”—Another great talker having tired him with a tedious discourse, excused himself at last, by saying, he was afraid he had been troublesome. “No indeed,” (replied he), “for I did not mind one word you said.”—He was forced to put a citizen of Lucca to death, who had formerly been a great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of his advancement; and being reproached by somebody for having dealt so severely with an old friend, replied, “No, you are mistaken, it was with a new foe.”—One of his courtiers, dextrous to regale him, made a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> and invited him to it. Castruccio came, entertained himself among the ladies, danced, and did other things which did not seem to comport with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. One of his friends intimating that such freedoms might diminish the reverence that ought to be paid him; “I thank you for your caution; but he who is reckoned wise all the day, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never be reckoned a fool at night.” CASTRUM doloris, in middle age writers, denotes a catafalque, or a lofty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of state, erected in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of some person of eminence, usually in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> where his body is interred; and decorated with arms, emblems, lights, and the like. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> writers speak of a ceremony of consecrating a castrum doloris; the edifice was to be made to represent the body of the deceased, and the priest and deacon were to take their posts, and say the prayers after the same manner as if the corpse were actually present. CASTS. See Casting. CASU consimilis, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ of entry granted where a tenant, by courtesy or for life, aliens either in fee, in tail, or for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of another’s life. It is brought by him in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> against the person to whom such tenant does so alien to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of the reversioner in the tenant’s lifetime. Casu Provisio, in Law, a writ of entry founded on the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, where a tenant in dower aliens the lands the fo holds in fee, or for life; and lies for the party in reversion against the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>.

CASUAL

Pages 263-263

something that happens fortuitously, without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> taken to bring it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. Casual Revenues, are those which arise from forfeitures, confiscations, deaths, attainders, &c. Casual <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, a denomination given to what is more frequently called Casuistry.

CASUALTY

Pages 263-263

in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. Casualties of a superior, are those duties and emoluments which a superior has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to demand out of his vassal’s estate, over and besides the constant yearly duties established by the redendo of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> upon certain casual events.

CASUIST

Pages 263-263

a person who proposes to resolve <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. Elcobar has made a collection of the opinions of all the casuists before him. M. le Fevre, preceptor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII., called the books of the casuists the art of quibbling with God; which does not seem far from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, by reason of the multitude of distinctions and subtleties they abound withal. Mayer has published a bibliotheca of casuists, containing an account of all the writers on cases of conscience, ranged under three heads, the first comprehending the Lutheran, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> the Calvinist, and the third the Romanist casuists.

CASUISTRY

Pages 263-263

the doctrine and science of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> and its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, with the rules and principles of resolving the same; drawn partly from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> reason <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>; partly from authority of Scripture, the canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, councils, fathers, &c. To casuistry belongs the decision of all difficulties arising about what a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may lawfully do or not do; what is sin or not sin; what things a man is obliged to do in order to discharge his duty, and what he may let alone without <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of it.

CASUS AMMISSIONIS

Pages 263-264

in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. In actions proving the tenor of obligations inextinguishable by the debtor’s retiring <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cancelling them, it is necessary for the pursuer, before he is allowed a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the tenor, to condescend upon such a castrum ammissionis, or accident by which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> was destroyed, as shows it was lost while in the writer's possession.

CAT'S EYE

Pages 264-264
or Sun-stone of the Turks, a kind of gem found chiefly in Siberia. Cat's eye is by the Latins called oculus cati, and sometimes onycopalus, as having white zones or rings like the onyx, and its colours variable like opal, from which last it differs chiefly by its superior hardness. It is very hard, and semitransparent, and has different points, from whence the light is reflected with a kind of yellowish radiation somewhat similar to the eyes of cats, from whence it had its name. The best of them are very scarce, and jewellers cut them round to the greatest advantage. One of these stones, an inch in diameter, was in the possession of the duke of Tuscany.

CAT-GUT

Pages 264-264

a denomination given to small strings for fiddles, and other instruments, made of the intestines of sheep <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a>, dried and twisted together, either singly, or several together. These are sometimes coloured <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, sometimes blue, but are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> left whitish or brownish, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the gut. They are also used by watchmakers, cutlers, turners, and other artificers. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> quantities are imported into England, and other northern countries, from Lyons and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>.

CAT-HARPSING

Pages 264-264

a purchase of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> employed to brace in the throats of the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> behind their yards, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> purpose of making the throats more tight, and of affording room to draw in the yards more obliquely, to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> the sails for a side-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, when they are said to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> hauled.

CAT-HEADS

Pages 264-264

two strong short beams of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, which project almost horizontally over the ship's bows on each side of the bowsprit; being like two radii which extend from a centre taken in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the bowsprit. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the cat-head which rests upon the forecastle, is securely bolted to the beams; the other part projects like a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRANE">crane</a>, as above described, and carries in its extremity two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> or sheaves of braids or strong wood, about which a rope called the cat-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, passes and communicates with the cat-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, which also contains three sheaves. The machine formed by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of pulleys is called the cat, which serves to pull the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> up to the cat-head, without tearing the ship's sides with its flukes. The cat-head also serves to suspend the anchor clear of the bow, when it is necessary to let it go: it is supported by a foot of knee, which is generally ornamented with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>. See Plate CXXXVI. The cat-block is filled with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and strong hood, which catches the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of the anchor when it is to be drawn up. CAT-MINT. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTHA">Mentha</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CAT-SALT

Pages 264-264

a name given by our <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> workers to a very beautifully <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANULATED">granulated</a> kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> salt. It is formed out of the bittern, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> leach <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRINE">brine</a>, which runs from the salt when taken out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a>. When they draw out the common salt from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> pans, they put it into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> wooden troughs, with holes bored at the bottom for the brine to drain out; under these troughs are placed vessels to receive this brine, and across them small sticks to which the cat-salt affixes itself in very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and beautiful crystals. This salt contains some portion of the bitter purging salt, is very sharp and pungent, and is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> when powdered, though pellucid in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. It is used by some for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, but the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of what is made of it is used by the makers of hard <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>. CAT-SILVER. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICA">Mica</a>.

CATACHRESIS

Pages 264-264

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a trope which borrows the name of one thing to express another. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, describing Raphael's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from the empyreal heaven to paradise, says, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> thither prone in flight, "He speeds, and through the vast ethereal sky "Sails between worlds and worlds."

CATACOMB

Pages 264-265

a grotto, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> subterraneous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> of the dead. Some derive the word catacomb from the place where ships are laid up, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Latins and Greeks called cumba. Others say, that cata was used for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> and catacombos, for adumbas; accordingly, Dadin says, they anciently wrote cataumbas. Others fetch the word from the Greek, κατα, and κομβης, a hollow, cavity, or the like. Anciently the word catacomb was only understood of the tombs of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul; and M. Chatelet observes, that, among the more knowing of the people of Rome, the word catacomb is never applied to the subterraneous burying-places hereafter mentioned, but only to a chapel in St Sebastian, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> national churches; where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman calendars say the body of St Peter was deposited, under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFUTATION">confutation</a> of Tufcus and Baffus, in 258. CATACOMBS of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; a vast assemblage of subterraneous sepulchres about Rome, chiefly at about three miles from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, in the Via Appia; supposed to be the sepulchre of the martyrs; and which are visited accordingly out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, and relics thence taken and dispersed throughout the catholic countries, after having been first baptized by the pope under the name of some saint. These catacombs are said by many to be caves or cells wherein the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> hid and assembled themselves together, and where they interred such among them as were martyred. Each catacomb is three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and eight or ten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; running in form of an alley or gallery, and communicating with others: in many places they extend within a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> of Rome. There is no masonry or vaulting therein, but each supports itself: the two sides, Catacombs, which we may look on as the *parietes* or walls, were the places where the dead were deposited; which were laid lengthwise, three or four rows over one another, in the same catacomb, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the alley. They were <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> cloathed with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> thick tiles, and sometimes pieces of marble, cemented in a manner imitable by the moderns. Sometimes, though very rarely, the name of the deceased is found on the tile: frequently a palm is seen, painted or engraven, or the cypher Xp, which is commonly read pro Christo. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> held by many Protestant authors is, that the catacombs are heathen sepulchres, and the same with the puticuli mentioned by Feftus Pompeius; maintaining, that whereas it was the practice of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to burn their dead, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was, to avoid expense, to throw the bodies of their slaves to rot in holes of the ground; and that the Roman Christians, observing at length, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration paid to relics, resolved to have a stock of their own: entering therefore the catacombs, they added what cyphers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> they pleased; and then shut them up again, to be opened on a favourable occasion. Those in the secret, add they, dying or removing, the contrivance was forgot, till chance opened them at last. But this opinion has even less of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> than the former. Mr Monro, in the Philosophical Transactions, supposes the catacombs to have been originally the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sepulchres of the first Romans, and dug in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of these two opinions, viz. that shades hate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; and that they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to hover about the places where the bodies are laid. Though the catacombs of Rome have made the greatest noise of any in the world, there are such belonging to many other cities. Those of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, according to Bishop Burnet, are much more noble and spacious than the catacombs of Rome. Catacombs have also been discovered at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> and Catanea in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>. The Roman catacombs take particular names from the churches in their neighbourhood, and seem to divide the circumference of the city without the walls between them, extending their galleries everywhere under, and a vast way from it; so that all the ground under Rome, and for many miles about it, some say 20, is hollow. The largest, and those commonly shown to strangers, are the catacombs of San <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEBASTIANO">Sebastiano</a>, those of Saint Agnese, and the others in the fields a little off Saint Agnese. Women are only allowed to go into the catacombs in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of the Vatican on WhitSunday Monday, under pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a>. There are men kept constantly at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in the catacombs. As soon as the labourers discover a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> with any of the supposed marks of a saint upon it, intimation is given to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> camerlingo, who immediately sends men of reputation to the place, where finding the palm, the monogram, the coloured glass, &c., the remains of the body are taken up with great respect, and translated to Rome. After the labourers have examined a gallery, they stop up the entry that leads to it; so that most of them remain thus closed up; only a few being left open to keep up the trade of showing them to strangers. This, they say, is done to prevent people from losing themselves in these subterraneous labyrinths, which indeed has often happened; but more probably to deprive the public of the means of knowing whither Catacombs, and how far the catacombs are carried. The method of preserving the dead in catacombs seems to have been common to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the ancient nations. The catacombs of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> are still extant about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> leagues from the city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, and two miles from the city of Zaccara. They extend from thence to the pyramids of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a>, which are about eight miles distant. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in a field covered with a fine running sand, of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is dry and hilly; the entrance of the tombs is choked up with sand; there are many open, but more that are still concealed. The bodies found in catacombs, especially those of Egypt, are called mummies; and as their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> was formerly reckoned an efficacious medicine, they were much sought after. In this work the labourers were often obliged to clear away the sand for weeks together, without finding what they wanted. Upon coming to a little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> opening of about 18 feet in depth, they descend into it by holes for the feet placed at proper intervals; and there they are sure of finding a mummy. These caves, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> as they call them there, are hollowed out of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> free <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which is found in all this country a few feet below the covering of sand. When one gets to the bottom of these, which are sometimes 40 feet below the surface, there are several square openings on each side into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of 10 or 15 feet wide; and these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to chambers of 15 or 20 feet square. These are all hewn out in the rock; and in each of the catacombs are to be found several of these apartments communicating with one another. They extend a great way underground, so as to be under the city of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMPHIS">Memphis</a>, and in a manner to undermine its environs. In some of the chambers the walls are adorned with figures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>; in others the mummies are found in tombs, round the apartment, hollowed out in the rock. The Egyptians seem to have excelled in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a> and preserving their dead bodies; as the mummies found in the Egyptian catacombs are in a better state than the bodies found either in the Italian catacombs or those of any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world. See Embalming and Mummy. Laying up the bodies in caves, is certainly the original way of disposing of the dead; and appears to have been propagated by the Phoenicians throughout the countries to which they sent colonies; the interring as we now do in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> was first introduced by the Christians. When an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> died, or was killed in a foreign expedition, as his body was liable to corruption, and for that reason unfit to be transported entire, they fell on the expedient of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, in order to bring home the ashes, to oblige the *manes* to follow; that so his country might not be destitute of the benefit of his tutelage. It was thus burning seems to have had its original; and by degrees it became common to all who could bear the expenses of it, and took place of the ancient burying; thus catacombs became diffused among the Romans, after they had borrowed the manner of burning from the Greeks, and then none but slaves were laid in the ground. See Burial, &c.

CATACOUSTIC CURVES

Pages 264-264

in the higher <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of caustic curves which are formed by reflection. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">FLUXIONS</a>.

CATADROMUS

Pages 265-266

from κατά and ῥόμος, I run, in antiquity, a stretched sloping rope in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> which the funambuli walked to show their skill. Some have taken the word to signify the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPODROME">hippodrome</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> decuriorium, wherein the Roman knights used to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> themselves in running and fighting on horseback. But the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> meaning is that of a rope fastened at one end to the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, and at the other to the bottom, to walk or run down, which was the highest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> acrobates, or funambuli. Elephants were also taught to run down the catadromus. Suetonius speaks of the exploit of a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, who passed down the catadromus mounted on an elephant's back.

CATAGOGION

Pages 266-266

a heathen festival at Ephesus, celebrated on the 22d of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, in which the devotees run about the streets, dressed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> antic and unseemly manners, with huge cudgels in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and carrying with them the images of their gods; in which guise they ravished the women they met with, abused and often killed the men, and committed many other disorders, to which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> gave sanction.

CATAGRAPHIA

Pages 266-266

in antiquity, denote oblique figures <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> views of men's faces; answering to what the moderns call profiles. Catagraphia are said to be the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of Simon Cleonaeus, who first taught painters to vary the looks of their figures, and sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> them upwards, sometimes downwards, and sometimes sidewise or backwards.

CATALEPSIS

Pages 266-266
or CATALEPSY, in Medicine, a kind of apoplexy, or a drowsy disease, wherein the patient is taken speechless, senseless, and fixed in the same posture wherein the disease first seized him; his eyes open, without seeing or understanding. See Medicine Index.

CATALOGUE

Pages 266-266

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enumeration of the names of several books, men, or other things, disposed according to a certain order. Catalogues of books are digested in different manners, some according to the order of the times when the books were printed, as that of Mattaire; others according to their form and size, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> book-sellers catalogues; others according to the alphabetical order of the authors' names, as Hyde's catalogue of the Bodleian library; others according to the alphabetical order of matters or subjects, which are called real or classical catalogues, as those of Lipenius and Draudius; lastly, others are digested in a mixed method, partaking of several of the former, as De <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>'s catalogue of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Slufius's library, which is first divided according to the subjects or sciences, and afterwards the books in each are recited alphabetically. The most applauded of all catalogues is that of Thuanus's library, in which are united the advantages of all the rest. It was first drawn up by the two Puteani in the alphabetical order, then digested according to the sciences and subjects by Ilm. Bullifeldus, and published by F. Quinel at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1679; and reprinted, though incorrectly, at Hamburgh, in 1704. The Catalogue books are here ranged with judicious under their several sciences and subjects, regard being still had to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, &c., of every writer. Add, that only the best and choicest books on every subject are found here, and the most valuable editions. Yet the catalogue of M. le Telliers archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>' library, made by M. Clement, is not inferior to any published in our age, either on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and choice of the books, or the method of its disposition. One advantage peculiar to this catalogue is, the multitude of anonymous and pseudonymous authors detected in it, scarce to be met with elsewhere. Some even prefer it to Thuanus's catalogue, as containing a greater variety of classes and books on particular subjects. The conditions required in a catalogue are, that it indicate at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the order of the authors and of the matters, the form of the book, the number of volumes, the chronological order of the editions, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> it is written in, and its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the library; so as that all these circumstances may appear at once in the shortest, clearest, and easiest manner possible. In this view all the catalogues yet made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found to be defective. An anonymous French writer has laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a new <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of a catalogue, which shall unite all the advantages and avoid all the inconveniences of the rest. The Jesuits of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> have given us a catalogue of the popes; which makes what they call their Propileum.

CATALOGUE OF THE STARS

Pages 266-269

is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the fixed stars, disposed in their several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>; with the longitudes, latitudes, &c., of each; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> according to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> ascensions, that is, the order of their passing over the meridian. The first who undertook to reduce the fixed stars into a catalogue was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIPPARCHUS">Hipparchus</a> Rhodius, about 120 years before Christ; in which he made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the observations of Timocharis and Arityllus for about 180 years before him. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> retained Hipparchus's catalogue containing 1026 fixed stars; though he himself made abundance of observations, with a view to a new catalogue, A.D. 140. About the year of Christ 880, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBATEGNI">Albategni</a>, a Syrian, brought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the same to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Anno 1437, Ulugh Beigh, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, made a new catalogue of 1022 fixed stars, since translated out of Persian into Latin by Dr. Hyde. The third who made a catalogue from his own observations was Tycho Brahe, who determined the places of 777 stars for the year 1600, which Kepler from other observations of Tycho afterwards increased to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 1000 in the Rudolphine tables; adding those of Ptolemy omitted by Tycho, and of other authors; so that his catalogue amounts to above 1160. At the same time, William landgrave of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>, with his mathematicians Christopher Rothmannus and Julius Byrgius, determined the places of 400 fixed stars by his own observations, with their places rectified for the year 1593; which Havelius prefers to those of Tycho's. Ricciolus, in his Astronomia Reformata, determined the places of 101 stars for the year 1700, from his own observations; for the rest he followed Tycho's catalogue, altering it where he thought fit. Anno 1667, Dr. Halley, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St. Helena, observed Catalogue observed 350 southern stars not visible in our horizon. The same labour was repeated by F. Noel in 1710, who published a new catalogue of the same stars constructed for the year 1687. Bayer, in his Uranometria, published a catalogue of 1160 stars, compiled chiefly from Ptolemy and Tycho, in which every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> is marked with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>; the biggest star in any constellation being denoted by the first letter, the next by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, &c., and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the number exceeds the Greek alphabet, the remaining stars are marked by letters of the Roman alphabet, which letters are preferred by Flamsteed, and by Senex on his globes. The celebrated Hevelius composed a catalogue of 1888 stars, 1553 of which were observed by himself; and their places were computed for the year 1660. The last and greatest is the Britannic catalogue, compiled from the observations of the accurate Mr. Flamsteed; who for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of years devoted himself wholly thereto. As there was nothing wanting either in the observer or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, we may look on this as a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> so far as it goes. It is to be regretted the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> had not passed through his own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>: that now extant was published by authority, but without the author's consent: it contains 2734 stars. There was another published in 1725, pursuant to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>; containing no less than 3000 stars, with their places rectified for the year 1689: to which is added Mr Sharp's catalogue of the southern stars not visible in our hemisphere, adapted to the year 1726. The first catalogue, we believe, that was printed in the new or second form, according to the order of the right ascensions, is that of De la Caille, given in his Ephemerides for the ten years between 1755 and 1765, and printed in 1755. It contains the right ascensions and declinations of 307 stars, adapted to the beginning of the year 1750. In 1757 De la Caille published his Astronomiae Fundamenta, containing a catalogue of the right ascensions and declinations of 398 stars, likewise adapted to the beginning of 1750. And in 1763, the year after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, was published the Catalogus Astrale Stelliferum of the same author; containing a catalogue of the places of 1042 stars, all situated to the southward of the tropic of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPRICORN">Capricorn</a>, and observed by him while he was at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope in 1751 and 1752; their places being also adapted to the beginning of 1750. In the same year was published his Ephemerides for the ten years between 1765 and 1775; in the introduction to which are given the places of 515 zodiacal stars, all deduced from the observations of the same author; the places adapted to the beginning of the year 1765. In the Nautical Almanac for 1773, is given a catalogue of 387 stars, in right ascension, declination, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> and latitude, derived from the observations of the late celebrated Dr Bradley, and adjusted to the beginning of the year 1760. This small catalogue, and the results of about 1200 observations of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, are all that the public have yet seen of the multiplied labours of this most accurate and indefatigable observer, although he has now (1798) been dead upwards of 36 years. In 1775 was published a thin volume, entitled, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">Opera</a> Medita, containing several papers of the late Tobias Mayer, and among them a catalogue of the right ascensions and declinations of 998 stars, which may be occulted by the moon and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>; the places being adapted to the beginning of the year 1756. At the end of the first volume of "Astronomical Observations made at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">Observatory</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>," published in 1776, Dr Maskelyne, the present astronomer royal, has given a catalogue of the places of 34 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> stars, in right ascension and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> polar distance, adapted to the beginning of the year 1770. These being the result of several years repeated observations, made with the utmost care, and the best instruments, it may be presumed are exceedingly accurate. In 1782, M. Bode of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> published a very extensive catalogue of 1058 of the fixed stars, collected from the observations of Flamsteed, Bradley, Hevelius, Mayer, De la Caille, Messier, Monnier, D'Arquier, and other astronomers; all adapted to the beginning of the year 1780; and accompanied with a celestial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">atlas</a> or set of maps of the constellations, engraved in a most delicate and beautiful manner. To these may be added Dr Herschel's catalogue of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> stars, printed in the Phil. Trans. for 1782 and 1783; Messier's nebulae and clusters of stars, published in the Connaissance des Temps for 1784; and Herschel's catalogue of the same kind, given in the Phil. Trans. for 1786. In 1789 Mr Francis Wollaston published "A Specimen of a General Astronomical Catalogue, in Zones of North-polar Distance, and adapted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1, 1790." These stars are collected from all the catalogues before-mentioned, from that of Hevelius downwards. This work contains five distinct catalogues; viz.: Dr Maskelyne's new catalogue of 36 principal stars; a general catalogue of all the stars, in zones of north polar distance; an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> to the general catalogue; a catalogue of all the stars in the order in which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the meridian; and a catalogue of zodiacal stars, in longitude and latitude. Finally, in 1792, Dr Zach published at Gotha, Tabula Motuum Solis; to which is annexed a new catalogue of the principal fixed stars, from his own observations made in the years 1787, 1788, 1789, 1790. This catalogue contains the right ascensions and declinations of 381 principal stars, adapted to the beginning of the year 1800. Hutton's Math. Dict. Besides these two methods of forming catalogues of the stars, Dr Herschel has proposed a new one, in which the comparative brightness of the stars is accurately expressed. It is long since astronomers were first led to arrange the stars in classes of different magnitudes by their various degrees of brilliancy or lustre. Brightness and size have at all times been considered as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> terms; so that the brightest stars have been referred to the class comprehending those of the first magnitude; and as the subsequent orders of stars have been supposed to decrease in lustre, their magnitude has been determined in the same decreasing progression: but the want of some fixed and satisfactory standard of lustre has been the source of considerable confusion and uncertainty in settling the relative magnitudes of the stars. A star marked 1. 2m. is supposed to be between the first and second magnitude; but 2. 1m. intimates, that the star is nearly of the second magnitude, Catalogue magnitude, and that it partakes somewhat of the lustre of the Stars, of a star of the first order. Such subdivisions may be of some use in ascertaining stars of the first, second, and third classes; but the expressions 5m, 6m, 7m, 8m, must be very vague and indefinite. Dr Herchel observes that he has found them so in fact; and he therefore considers this method of pointing out the different lustre of stars as a reference to an imaginary standard. If any dependence could be placed on this method of magnitudes, "it would follow, that no less than 11 stars in the constellation of the Lion, namely β, σ, π, ξ, A, b, c, d, 54, 48, 72, had all undergone a change in their lustre since Flamsteed's time: For if the idea of magnitudes had been a clear one, our author, who marked β 1.2m. and γ 2m. ought to be understood to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> that β is larger than γ; but we now find that actually γ is larger than β. Every one of the eleven stars (says Dr Herchel) which I have pointed out may be reduced to the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>." The author has pointed out the insufficiency of the insufficiency of this method, and of the uncertain conclusions that are deduced from it, in determining the comparative brightness of stars found not only in Mr Flamsteed's catalogue, but also in the catalogues of other astronomers. It is sufficiently apparent that the present method of expressing the brightness of the stars is very defective. Dr Herchel therefore proposes a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, that is more precise and satisfactory. "I <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> each star (he says), instead of giving its magnitude, into a short series, constructed upon the order of brightness of the nearest proper stars. For instance, to express the lustre of D, I say CDE. By this short notation, instead of referring the star D to an imaginary uncertain standard, I refer it to a precise and determined existing one. C is a star that has a greater lustre than D, and E is another of less brightness than D. Both C and E are neighbouring stars, chosen in such a manner that I may see them at the same time with D, and therefore may be able to compare them properly. The lustre of C is in the same manner ascertained by BCD; that of B by ABC; and also the brightness of E by DEF; and that of F by EFG. "That this is the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, as well as the most effectual way to express the brightness of a star, and by that means to detect any change that may happen in its lustre, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear, when we consider what is requisite to ascertain such a change. We can certainly not wish for a more decisive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, than to be assured, by actual inspection, that a certain star is now no longer more or less bright than such other stars to which it has been formerly compared; provided we are at the same time assured that those other stars remain still in their former unaltered lustre. But if the star D will no longer stand in its former order CDE, it must have undergone a change; and if that order is now to be expressed by CED, the star has lost some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of its lustre; if, on the contrary, it ought now to be denoted by DCE, its brightness must have had some addition. Then, if we should doubt the stability of C and E, we have recourse to the orders BCD and DEF, which express their lustre; or even to ABC and EFG, which continue the series both ways. Now having before us the series BCDEF, or if necessary even the more extended one ABCDEFG, it will be impossible to mistake a change of brightness in D, when every member of the series is found in its proper order except D." In the author's journal or catalogue, in which the order of the lustre of the stars is fixed, each star bears its own proper name or number, e.g., "the brightness of the star δ Leonis may be expressed by δ & Leonis, or better by 94—68—17 Leonis; these being the numbers which the three above stars bear in the British catalogue of fixed stars." This method of arrangement occurred to Dr Herchel so early as the year 1782; but he was diverted from the regular pursuit of it by a variety of other astronomical engagements. After many trials, he proposed, in the Transactions of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> for 1796, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> which appeared to him the most eligible. It is as follows:—Instead of denoting particular stars by letters, he makes use of numbers; and in his choice of the stars which are to express the lustre of any particular one, he directs his first view to perfect equality. When two stars seem to be similar both in brightness and magnitude, he puts down their numbers together, separated merely by a point, as 30.24 Leonis; but if two stars, which at first seemed alike in their lustre, appeared on a longer inspection to be different, and the preference should be always decidedly in favour of the same star, he separates these stars by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMA">comma</a>, thus, 41.94 Leonis. This order must not be varied; nor can three such stars, as 20, 40, 39 Librae, admit of a different arrangement. If the state of the heavens should be such as to require a different order in these numbers, we may certainly infer that a change has taken place in the lustre of one or more of them. When two stars differ very little in brightness, but so that the preference of the one to the other is indisputable, the numbers that express them are separated by a short line, as—17—70 Leonis, or 68—17—70 Leonis. When two stars differ so much in brightness, that one or two other stars might be interposed between them, and still leave sufficient room for distinction, they are distinguished by a line and comma, thus,—, or by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, as 32—41 Leonis. A greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> than this is denoted by a broken line, thus——29 Bootis. On the whole, the author observes the marks and distinctions which he has adopted cannot possibly be mistaken; "a point denoting equality of lustre; a comma indicating the least perceptible difference; a short line to mark a decided but small superiority; a line and comma, or double line, to express a considerable and striking excess of brightness; and a broken line to mark any other superiority which is to be looked upon as of no use in estimations that are intended for the purpose of directing changes." The difficulties that attend this arrangement are not disguised; but the importance and utility of it more than compensate for the labour which it must necessarily require. By a method of this kind, many discoveries of changeable and periodical stars might probably have been made, which have escaped the most diligent and accurate observers. We might then, as the author suggests, be enabled to resolve a problem in which we are all immediately concerned. "Who, for instance, would not wish to know what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of permanency we ought to ascribe to the lustre of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>? Not only the stability of our climates, but..." Catalogue the very existence of the whole animal and vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> itself, is involved in the question. Where can we hope to receive information upon this subject but from astronomical observations? If it be allowed to admit the similarity of stars with our own as a point established, how necessary will it be to take notice of the fate of our neighbouring suns, in order to guess at that of our own? That star, which among the multitude we have dignified by the name of sun, to-morrow may slowly begin to undergo a gradual decay of brightness, like α Leonis, α Ceti, α Draconis, α Ursae majoris, and many other diminishing stars that will be mentioned in my catalogues. It may suddenly increase, like the wonderful star in the back of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASSIOPEIA">Cassiopeia</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, and the no less remarkable one in the foot of Serpentarius; or gradually come on, like β Geminorum, β Ceti, γ Sagittarii, and many other increasing stars, for which I also refer to my catalogues; and, lastly, it may turn into a periodical one of 25 days <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, as Algol is one of three days, δ Cephei of five, β Lyrae of six, α Antiohi of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days, and as many others as are of various periods. Having thus explained the general principle on which this catalogue is formed, as we find it in the author's first memoir on the subject, we must refer the reader to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s own account for its particular arrangement, observing only that the catalogue subjoined comprehends <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> constellations, which are arranged in alphabetical order, with the comparative brightness of the stars accurately stated. In a subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, published in the same volume, he has completely verified the utility of his method by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, and shown that there is no permanent change of lustre in the stars. In the notes to his first catalogue he mentioned α Herculis as a periodical star. By a series of observations on this star, compared with α Ophiuchi, which was most conveniently situated for his purpose, he has been able not only to confirm this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, but to ascertain its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. His observations are arranged in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, by means of which he determines that this star had gone through four successive changes in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of 241 days; and therefore the duration of its period must be about 60 days and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. This fact concurs with other circumstances in evincing the rotatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the stars on their axes. "Dark spots, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portions of the surface less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> than the rest, turned alternately in certain directions, either towards or from us, will account for the phenomena of periodical changes in the lustre of the stars, so satisfactorily, that we certainly need not look out for any other cause." If it be alleged that the periods in the change of lustre of some stars, such as Algol, β Lyrae, δ Cephei, and α Antiohi, are short, being only 3, 5, 6, and 7 days respectively; while those of α Ceti, and of the changeable star in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRA">Hydra</a>, and that in the neck of the Swan, are long, amounting to 331, 394, and 497 days; and that we cannot ascribe phenomena so different in their duration to the same cause—it may be answered to this objection, that the force of it is founded on our limited acquaintance with the state of the heavens. To the 7 stars, the periodical changes of which were before known, we may now add α Herculis, which performs a revolution of its changes in 60 days. "The step from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of α Herculis to that of α Ceti is far less considerable than that from the period of Algol to the rotation of α Herculis; and thus a link in the chain is now supplied, which removes the objection that arose from the vacancy." The rotation of the fifth satellite of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> is proved by the change observable in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; and "this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of light, owing to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> exposition of a more or less bright hemisphere of this periodical satellite, plainly indicates, that the similar phenomenon of a changeable star arises from the various lustre of the different parts of its surface, successively turned to us by its rotatory motion." Besides, we perceive a greater similarity between the sun and the stars, by means of the spots that must be admitted to exist on their surfaces, as well as on that of the sun. Dr Herschel farther observes, that the stars, besides a rotatory motion on their axes, may have other movements; "such as nutations or changes in the inclination of their axes; which, added to bodies much flattened by quick rotatory motions, or surrounded by rings like Saturn, will easily account for many new phenomena that then offer themselves to our extended views."

CATALONIA

Pages 269-269

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Pyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which divide it from France; by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Arragon and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a> on the west; and by the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the south and east. It is 155 miles in length, and 100 in breadth. It is watered by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are the Llobregat, the Ter, and the Segra. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate and healthy; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is mountainous, except in a few places. It produces, however, corn, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, sufficient for the inhabitants. The mountains are covered with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> forests of tall trees, such as the oak, the ever-green oak, the beech, the pine, the fir, the chestnut, and many others; with cork trees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, and medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are several quarries of marble of all colours, crystal, alabaster, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMETHYST">amethyst</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> lazuli. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> dust has been found among the sands of one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two of the rivers; and there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of tin, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, vitriol, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. They likewise fish for coral on the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. The inhabitants are hardy, courageous, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, vigorous, and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, but apt to be discontented. The miquelets are a sort of soldiers which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the passes over the mountains, and ought to protect travellers; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are not paid to their minds, they seldom fail to pay themselves. The river Llobregat divides Catalonia into two parts, the east and west, according to their situation. This province comprehends 17 vigueries or territories; two of which are in Roussillon, and belong to the French. The rest are subject to the Spaniards. The principal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARRAGONA">Tarragona</a>, Tortosa, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LERIDA">Lerida</a>, Solsona, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARDONA">Cardona</a> Vich, Girona, Seu d'Urgell, Pui Cerda, and Cervera. Catalonia was the last province in Spain which submitted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> in the Succession <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>.

CATANA

Pages 269-269
or Catina, in Ancient Geography, a town of Sicily, situated opposite to Acina, to the south-east; one of the five Roman colonies; anciently built by the people of Naxus seven years after the building of Syracuse, 728 years before Christ. It was the country of

CATANEA

Pages 270-270
or CATANIA, a city of Sicily, seated on a gulf of the same name, near the foot of Mount Aetna, or Gibel. It was founded by the Chalcidians soon after the settlement of Syracuse, and enjoyed great tranquillity till Hiero I. expelled the whole body of citizens; and after replenishing the town with a new stock of inhabitants, gave it the name of Aetna: immediately after his decease, it regained its ancient name, and its citizens returned to their abodes. Catania fell into the hands of the Romans, among their earliest acquisitions in Sicily, and became the residence of a praetor. To make it worthy of such an honour, it was adorned with sumptuous buildings of all kinds, and every convenience was procured to supply the natural and artificial wants of life. It was destroyed by Pompey's son, but restored with superior magnificence by Augustus. The reign of Decius is famous in the history of this city, for the martyrdom of its patroness St Agatha. On every emergency her intercession is implored. She is piously believed to have preserved Catania from being overwhelmed by torrents of lava, or shaken to pieces by earthquakes; yet its ancient edifices are covered by repeated streams of volcanic matter; and almost every house, even her own church, has been thrown to the ground. In the reign of William the Good, 20,000 Catanians, with their palaces at their head, were destroyed before the sacred veil could be properly placed to check the flames. In the last century the eruptions and earthquakes raged with redoubled violence, and Catania was twice demolished. See AETNA. The present prince of Biscari has been at infinite pains, and spent a large sum of money, in working down to the ancient town, which, on account of the numerous torrents of lava that have flowed out of Mount Aetna for these last thousand years, is now to be sought for in dark caverns many feet below the present surface of the earth. Mr Swinburne informs us that he descended into baths, sepulchres, an amphitheatre, and a theatre, all very much injured by the various catastrophes that have befallen them. They were erected upon old beds of lava, and even built with square pieces of the same substance, which in no instance appears to have been fused by the contact of new lavas. The scoria or stones of cold lava, have constantly proved as strong a barrier against the flowing torrent of fire as any other stone could have been, though some authors were of opinion that the hot matter would melt the old masts and incorporate with it. This city has been frequently defended from the burning streams by the solid walls of its own ramparts, and by the air compressed between them and the lava; as appears by the torrent having floated within a small distance of the walls, and taken another direction. But when the walls were broken or low, the lava collected itself till it rose to a great height, and then poured over in a curve. A similar instance is seen at the Torre del Greco near Naples, where the stream of liquid fire from Vesuvius divided itself into two branches, and left a church untouched in the middle. There is a well at the foot of the old walls of Catania, where the lava, after running along the parapet, and then falling forwards, has produced a very complete lofty arch over the spring. The church here is a noble fabric. It is accounted the largest in Sicily, though neither a porch nor cupola has been erected, from a doubt of the solidity of the foundations, which are no other than the bed of lava that ran out of Aetna in 1669, and is supposed to be full of cavities. The organ is much esteemed by connoisseurs in musical instruments. Catania, according to Mr Swinburne's account, is reviving with great splendour. "It has already (he says) much more the features of a metropolis and royal residence than Palermo: the principal streets are wide, straight, and well paved with lava. An obelisk of red granite, placed on the back of an antique elephant of touchstone, stands in the centre of the great square, which is formed by the townhall, seminary, and cathedral. The cathedral erected by the abbot Angerius in the year 1094, was endowed by Earl Roger with the territories of Catania and Aetna, for the small acknowledgement of a glass of wine and a loaf of bread offered once a-year. It has suffered so much by earthquakes, that little of the original structure remains, and the modern parts have hardly anything except their materials to recommend them. The other religious edifices of the city are profusely ornamented, but in a bad taste. The spirit of building seems to have seized upon the people, and the prince of Biscari's example adds fresh vigour. It were natural to suppose men would be backward in erecting new habitations, especially with any degree of luxury, on ground so often shaken to its centre, and so often buried under the ashes of a volcano; but such is their attachment to their native soil, and their contempt of dangers they are habituated to, that they rebuild their houses on the warm cinders of Vesuvius, the quaking plains of Calabria, and the black mountains of Etna at Catania; it is however surprising to see such embellishments lavish'd in so dangerous a situation. There is a great deal of activity in the disposition of this people: they know by tradition that their ancestors carried on a flourishing commerce; and that before the fiery river filled it up, they had a spacious convenient harbour, where they now have scarce a creek for a felucca: they therefore wish to restore those advantages to Catania, and have often applied to government for assistance towards forming a mole and port, an undertaking their strength alone is unequal to; but whether the refusal originates in the deficiencies of the public treasury or the jealousy of the other cities, all the projects have ended in fruitless applications. The number of inhabitants dwelling in Catania amounts to 30,000; the Catanians make it double: A considerable portion of this number pertains to the university, the only one in the island, and the nursery of all the lawyers." E. Long, 15° 10' N. Lat. 37° 30'

CATANZARO

Pages 270-270

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> Ulterior, with a bishop's see. It is the usual residence of the governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and is seated on a mountain, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18° 20' N. Lat. 28° 58'

CATAPHONICS

Pages 270-270

the science which considers the properties of reflected sounds. See Acoustics.

CATAPHRACTA

Pages 270-271

CATAPHRACTA, (from κατάφραξις, and φράξω, I. fortify <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> arm), in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, a piece of heavy defensive armour, formed of cloth or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, fortified with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> scales, or links wherewith sometimes only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, sometimes the whole body, and sometimes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> too, was covered. It was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the Sarmatians, Persians, and other barbarians. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> also adopted it early for their foot; and, according to Vegetius, kept to it till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Gratian, when the military <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> growing remiss, and field exercises and labour discontinued, the Roman foot thought the cataphracta as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a load to bear; and therefore threw both by, choosing rather to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> against the enemy bare-breasted; by which, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, multitudes were destroyed.

CATAPHRACTAE NAVES

Pages 271-271

ships armed and covered in fight, so that they could not be easily damaged by the enemy. They were covered over with boards <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> planks, on which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were placed to defend them; the rowers sitting underneath, thus screened from the enemy's weapons.

CATAPHRACTUS

Pages 271-271
or Cataphractarius, more particularly denotes a horseman, or even horse, armed with a cataphracta. The cataphracti equites were a sort of cuirassiers, not only fortified with armour themselves, but having their horses guarded with solid plates of brass or other metals, usually lined with skins, and wrought into plumes or other forms. Their use was to bear down all before them, to break in upon the enemy's ranks, and spread terror and havoc wherever they came, as being themselves invulnerable and secure from danger. But their disadvantage was their unwieldiness, by which, if once unhorsed or on the ground, they were unable to rise, and thus fell a prey to the enemy.

CATAPHRYCIANS

Pages 271-271

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, so called as being of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>. They were orthodox in every thing, letting aside this, that they took Montanus for a prophet, and Priscilla and Maximilla for true prophetesses, to be consulted in every thing relating to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; as supposing the Holy Spirit had abandoned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. See MONASTIAN.

CATAPLASMA

Pages 271-271

a poultice; from καταπλάσσω, illino, to spread like a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>. Cataplasm take their name sometimes from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> to which they are applied, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> effects they produce; so are called anacoloma, frontale, epicranium, epiphalicum, sphenactorium; and when mustard is an ingredient, they are called fennaplasma. These kinds of applications are softer and more easy than plasters or ointments. They are formed of some vegetable substances, and applied of such a consistence as neither to adhere nor run: they are also more useful when the intention is effected by the perpetuity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> which they contain, for they retain them longer than any other kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. When designed to relax, or to promote suppuration, they should be applied warm. Their warmth, moisture, and the obstruction they give to perspiration, is the method of their answering that end. The proper heat, when applied warm, is no more than to promote a kindly pleasant fenestration; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> heat prevents the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> for which they are used. They Catapulta should be renewed as often as they cool. For relaxing and suppurring, none excel the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> poultice, made with the crumb of an old loaf, a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> to boil the bread in until it is soft, and a little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; which last ingredient, besides preventing the poultice from drying and sticking to the skin, also retains the heat longer than the bread and milk alone would do. To preserve the heat longer, the poultice, when applied, may be covered with a strong ox's bladder. When designed to repel, they should be applied cold, and ought to be renewed as oft as they become warm. A proper composition for this end is a mixture of oatmeal and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>.

CATAPULTA

Pages 271-272

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> engine contrived for the throwing of arrows, darts, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> upon the enemy.—Some of these engines were of such force that they would throw stones of an hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Josephus takes notice of the surprising effects of these engines, and says, that the stones thrown out of them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, knocked off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of the towers, and would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> a whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a> of men from one end to the other, was the phalanx ever so deep. This was called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERING">Battering</a> CATAPULTA, and is represented on Plate CXXXV. This catapulta is supposed to carry a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, &c. of an hundred weight; and therefore a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be sufficient to explain the doctrine of all the rest; for such as threw stones of 500 and upwards were constructed, on the same principles. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">bale</a> is composed of two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> beams 2, 3. The length of these beams is fifteen diameters of the bore of the capitals 9. At the two extremities of each beam, two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> mortises are cut to receive the eight tenons of two crofs beams, each of them four of the diameters in length. In the centre of each of the beams of the bale, and near two-thirds of their length, a hole, perfectly round, and 16 inches in diameter, should be bored; these holes must be exactly opposite to each other, and should increase gradually to the inside of the beams, so that each of them, being 16 inches on the outside towards the capitals 9, should be 17½ at the opening on the inside, and the edges carefully rounded off. The capitals 9 are, in a manner, the foul of the machine, and serve to twist and strain the cordage, which forms its principle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. The capitals are either of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; each consisting of a wheel with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, C 10, of 2½ inches thick. The hollow or bore of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> should be 11½ inches in diameter, perfectly round, and the edges smoothed down. As the friction would be too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the capitals rubbed against the beams by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> straining of the cordage, which draws them towards these beams, that inconvenience is remedied by the means of eight friction wheels, or cylinders of brass, about the 1/12th of an inch in diameter, and an inch and one sixth in length, placed circularly, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> upon axes, as represented at D 13, B 12. One of these friction wheels at large with its screw, by which it is fastened into the beam, is represented at A. Upon this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cylindrical wheels the capitals 9 must be placed in the beams 2, 3, so that the cylinders Catapults do not extend to the teeth of the wheels, which must receive a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">pinion</a> 14. By means of this pinion the wheel of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is made to turn for straining the cordage with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> 15. The capital wheel has a strong catch 16, and another of the same kind may be added, to prevent anything from giving way through the extreme and violent force of the strained cordage. The capital piece of the machine is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> of iron, 17, seen at C, and hammered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> into its form. It divides the bore of the capitals exactly in two equal parts, and fixed in grooves about an inch deep. This piece, or nut, ought to be about two inches and one third thick at the top 18, as represented in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTION">section</a> at B; and rounded off and polished as much as possible, that the cords folded over it may not be hurt or cut by the roughness or edges of the iron. Its height ought to be eight inches, decreasing gradually in thickness to the bottom, where it ought to be only one inch. It must be very exactly inserted in the capitals. After placing the two capitals in the holes of the two beams in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line with each other, and fixing the two cross diametrical nuts or pieces over which the cordage is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, one end of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> is reeved through a hole in one of the capitals in the base, and made fast to a nail withinside of the beam. The other side of the cord is then carried through the hole in the opposite beam and capital, and so wound over the cross pieces of iron in the centre of the two capitals, till they are full, the cordage forming a large skein. The tension or straining of the cordage ought to be exactly equal, that is, the several foldings of the cord over the capital pieces should be equally strained, and so near each other as not to leave the least space between them. As soon as the first folding or skein of cord has filled up one whole space or breadth of the capital pieces, another must be carried over it; and so on, always equally straining the end till no more will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the capitals, and the skein of cordage entirely fills them, observing to rub it from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>. At three or four inches behind the cordage, thus wound over the capital pieces, two very strong upright beams 21 are raised: these are posts of oak 14 inches thick, crossed over at top by another of the same solidity.
