in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a hollow member, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> round concave moulding, containing a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> of a circle, and having a quite contrary effect to that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> round: it is used as an ornament in cornices.

CAVEZON

Pages 304-304

in the manege, a sort of nose band, either of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wood, sometimes flat, and at other times hollow or twisted, clapt upon the nose of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> to wring it, and so forward the suppling and breaking of the horse.

CAVIARE

Pages 304-305

a kind of food lately introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It is made of the hard roes of sturgeon*, *See Acipenseridae., formed into small cakes, about an inch thick and three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The method of making it is, by taking out of the spawn all the nerves <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> strings, then washing it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wine or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and spreading ing it on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. It is then salted and packed in a fine bag; after which it is cased up in a vessel with a hole at the bottom, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any moisture is left it may run out. This kind of food is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> request among the Muscovites, on account of their three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a>, which they keep with a superstitious exactness; wherefore the Italians settled at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a> drive a very great trade in this commodity throughout that empire, there being a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sturgeon taken at the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. A pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of the commodity is also consumed in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and France. They get the caviare from Archangel, but <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> buy it at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the English and Dutch.—According to Savary, the best caviare brought from Muscovy is prepared from the beluga, a fish eight or ten feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, caught in the Caspian sea, which is much preferable to that made of the spawn of sturgeon. A kind of caviare, or rather sauce, is also made from the spawn of some other fishes; particularly a sort of mullet caught in the Mediterranean. See MUGIL and BOTARGO. CAVIDOS. See CABIDOS.

CAXAMALCA

Pages 308-308

the name of a town and district of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, where there was a most sumptuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> belonging to the Incas, and a magnificent temple dedicated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>.

CAXTON

Pages 308-308

William, a mercer of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, eminent by the works he published, and for being reputed the first who introduced and practised the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> in England; as to which, see (the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) PRINTING.

CAYENNE

Pages 308-309

a rich town and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the French settlements there, is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Dutch colonies of Surinam, and situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 53. 10. N. Lat. 50. This settlement was begun in 1643. A report had prevailed for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before, that in the interior parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUIANA">Guiana</a>, there was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> known by the name of El Dorado, which contained immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; more than ever Cortez and Pizarro had found in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>; and this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> had fired the imagination of every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It is supposed that this was the country in quest of which Sir Walter Raleigh went on his last voyage; and as the French were not behind their neighbours in their endeavours to find out so desirable a country, some attempts for this purpose were likewise made by that nation much about the same time; which at last coming to nothing, the adventurers took up their residence on the island of Cayenne. In 1643, some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a> united their flock, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to support the new colony; but, committing their affairs to one Poncet de Bretigny, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of a ferocious disposition, he declared <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> both against the colonists and savages, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he was soon massacred. This catastrophe entirely extinguished the ardour of these associates; and in 1651 a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> was established. This promised to be much more considerable than the former; and they set out with such a capital as enabled them to collect 700 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 800 colonists in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> itself. These embarked on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, in order to sail <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAVRE">Havre</a> de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>; but unfortunately the Abbé de Marivaux, a man of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> virtue, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> promoter of the undertaking, was drowned as he was stepping into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>. Another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, who was to have acted as general, was assassinated on his passage, and 12 of the principal adventurers who had promised to put the colony into a flourishing situation, not only were the principal perpetrators of this fact, but uniformly behaved in the same atrocious manner. At last they hanged one of their own <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; two died; three were banished to- Cayenne, Caylus. a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> island; and the rest abandoned themselves to every kind of excess. The commandant of the citadel deserted to the Dutch with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his garrison. The savages, roused by numberless provocations, fell upon the remainder: so that the few who were left thought themselves happy in escaping to the Leeward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a> in a boat and two canoes, abandoning the fort, ammunition, arms and merchandise, fifteen months after they had landed on the island. In 1663, a new company was formed, whose capital amounted only to £750l. By the assistance of the ministry they expelled the Dutch who had taken possession of the island, and settled themselves much more comfortably than their predecessors. In 1667 the island was taken by the English, and in 1676 by the Dutch, but afterwards restored to the French: and since that time it has never been attacked. Soon after some pirates, laden with the spoils they had gathered in the South seas, came and fixed their residence at Cayenne; resolving to employ the treasures they had acquired in the cultivation of the lands. In 1688, Ducaffe, an able seaman, arrived with some ships from France, and proposed to them the plundering of Surinam. This proposal exciting their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> turn for plunder, the pirates betook themselves to their old trade, and almost all the rest followed their example. The expedition, however, proved unfortunate. Many of the assailants were killed, and all the rest taken prisoners and sent to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee islands</a>. This loss the colony has never yet recovered. The island of Cayenne is about 16 leagues in circumference, and is only parted from the continent by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. By a particular formation, uncommon in islands, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is highest near the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> side, and low in the middle. Hence the land is so full of morasses, that all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the different parts of it is impossible, without taking a great circuit. There are some small tracts of an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> to be found here and there; but the generality is dry, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, and soon exhausted. The only town in the colony is defended by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> way, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ditch, a very good mud rampart, and five bastions. In the middle of the town is a pretty considerable eminence, of which a redoubt has been made that is called the fort. The entrance into the harbour is through a narrow channel; and ships can only get in at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> water, through the rocks and reefs that are scattered about this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. The first produce of Cayenne was the arnotto; from the culture of which the colonists proceeded to that of cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, and lastly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. It was the first of all the French colonies that attempted to cultivate coffee. The coffee tree was brought from Surinam in 1721 by some deserters from Cayenne, who purchased their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> by so doing. Ten or twelve years after they planted cocoa. In the year 1752 there were exported from Cayenne 260,541 pounds of arnotto, 80,263 pounds of sugar, 17,919 pounds of cotton, 26,881 pounds of coffee, 91,916 pounds of cocoa, 618 trees for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, and 104 planks.

CAYLUS

Pages 309-310
Count de, Marquis de Sternay, Baron de Bronfoc, was born at Paris in 1692. He was the eldest of the two sons of John Count de Caylus, lieutenant general of the armies of the king of France, and of the marchioness de Villette. The count and countess his father and mother were very careful of the education of their son. The former instructed him in the profession of arms, and in bodily exercises; the latter watched over and fostered the virtues of his mind, and this delicate task she discharged with singular success. The countess was the niece of Madame de Maintenon, and was remarkable both for the solidity of her understanding and the charms of her wit. She was the author of that agreeable book entitled "The Recollections of Madame de Caylus," of which Voltaire lately published an elegant edition. The amiable qualities of the mother appeared in the son; but they appeared with a bold and military air. In his natural temper he was gay and sprightly, had a taste for pleasure, a strong passion for independence, and an invincible aversion to the ferocity of a court. Such were the instructors of the Count de Caylus. He was only twelve years of age when his father died at Brussels in 1704. After finishing his exercises, he entered into the corps of the Musqueteers; and in his first campaign in the year 1709, he distinguished himself by his valour in such a manner, that Louis XIV. commended him before all the court, and rewarded him with an ensigncy in the Gendarmerie. In 1711 he commanded a regiment of dragoons, which was called by his own name; and he signalized himself at the head of it in Catalonia. In 1713, he was at the siege of Fribourg, where he was exposed to imminent danger in the bloody attack of the covered way. The peace of Raftadt having left him in a state of inactivity ill suited to his natural temper, his vivacity soon carried him to travel into Italy; and his curiosity was greatly excited by the wonders of that country, where antiquity is still fruitful, and produces so many objects to improve taste and to excite admiration. The eyes of the count were not yet learned; but he was struck with the sight of so many beauties, and soon became acquainted with them. After a year's absence, he returned to Paris with so strong a passion for travelling and for antiquities, as induced him to quit the army. He had no sooner quitted the service of Louis, than he sought for an opportunity to set out for the Levant. When he arrived at Smyrna, he visited the ruins of Ephesus. From the Levant he was recalled in February 1717 by the tenderness of his mother. From that time he left not France, but to make two excursions to London. The Academy of Painting and Sculpture adopted him an honorary member in the year 1731; and the count, who loved to realize titles, spared neither his labour, nor his credit, nor his fortune, to instruct, assist, and animate the artists. He wrote, the lives of the most celebrated painters and engravers that have done honour to this illustrious academy; and, in order to extend the limits of the art, which seemed to him to move in too narrow a circle, he collected, in three different works, new subjects for the painter, which he had met with in the works of the ancients. Such was his passion for antiquity, that he wished to have had it in his power, to bring the whole of it to life again. He saw with regret, that the works of the ancient painters, which have been discovered in our times, are effaced and destroyed almost as soon as they are drawn from the subterraneous mansions where they were buried. A fortunate accident fur- Caylus, nished him with the means of showing us the composition and the colouring of the pictures of ancient Rome. The coloured drawings which the famous Pietro Sante Bartoli had taken there from antique pictures, fell into his hands. He had them engraved; and, before he enriched the king of France's cabinet with them, he gave an edition of them at his own expense. It is perhaps the most extraordinary book of antiquities that ever will appear. The whole is painted with a purity and a precision that are inimitable; we see the liveliness and the freshness of the colouring that charmed the Caesars. There were only 30 copies published; and there is no reason to expect that there will hereafter be any more. Count de Caylus was engaged at the same time in an enterprise still more favourable to Roman grandeur, and more interesting to the French nation. Colbert had framed the design of engraving the Roman antiquities that are still to be seen in the southern provinces of France. By his orders Mignard the architect had made drawings of them, which Count de Caylus had the good fortune to recover. He resolved to finish the work begun by Colbert, and to dedicate it to that great minister; and so much had he this enterprise at heart, that he was employed in it during his last illness, and warmly recommended it to M. Mariette. In 1742, Count Caylus was admitted honorary member of the Academy of Belles Lettres; and then it was that he seemed to have found the place for which nature designed him. The study of literature now became his ruling passion; he consecrated to it his time and his fortune; he even renounced his pleasures to give himself wholly up to that of making some discovery in the field of antiquity. But amidst the fruits of his research and invention, nothing seemed more flattering to him than his discovery of encaustic painting. A description of Pliny's, but too concise a one to give him a clear view of the matter, suggested the idea of it. He availed himself of the friendship and skill of M. Magault, a physician in Paris, and an excellent chemist; and by repeated experiments found out the secret of incorporating wax with divers tints and colours, and of making it obedient to the pencil. Pliny has made mention of two kinds of encaustic painting practised by the ancients; one of which was performed with wax, and the other upon ivory, with hot punches of iron. It was the former that Count Caylus had the merit of reviving; and M. Muntz afterwards made many experiments to carry it to perfection. In the hands of Count Caylus, literature and the arts lent each other a mutual aid. But it would be endless to give an account of all his works. He published above 40 dissertations in the Memoirs of the Academy of Belles Lettres. The artists he was particularly attentive to; and to prevent their falling into mistakes from an ignorance of costume, which the ablest of them have sometimes done, he founded a prize of 500 livres, the object of which is to explain, by means of authors and monuments, the usages of ancient nations. In order that he might enjoy with the whole world the treasures he had collected, he caused them to be engraved, and gave a learned description of them in a work which he embellished with 800 copper plates. The strength of his constitution seemed to give him hopes of a long life; but a humour settling in one of his legs, which entirely destroyed his health, he expired on the 5th of September 1765, and by his death his family is extinct. The tomb erected to the honour of Count Caylus is to be seen in the chapel of St Germain l'Auxerrois, and deserves to be remarked. It is perfectly the tomb of an antiquary. This monument was an ancient sepulchral antique, of the most beautiful porphyry, with ornaments in the Egyptian taste. From the moment he procured it, he had destined it to grace the place of his interment. While he awaited the fatal hour, he placed it in his garden, where he used to look upon it with a tranquil but thoughtful eye, and pointed it out to the inspection of his friends. The character of Count Caylus is to be traced in the different occupations which divided his cares and his life. In society, he had all the frankness of a soldier, and a politeness which had nothing in it of deceit or circumvention. Born independent, he applied to studies which suited his taste. His heart was yet better than his abilities. In his walks he used frequently to try the honesty of the poor, by sending them with a piece of money to get change for him. In these cases he enjoyed their confusion at not finding him; and then presenting himself, used to commend their honesty, and give them double the sum. He said frequently to his friends, "I have this day lost a crown; but I was sorry that I had not an opportunity of giving a second. The beggar ought not to want integrity."

CAYSTER

Pages 310-310
or CAYSTRUS, in Ancient Geography, a river of Ionia, whose mouth Ptolemy places between Colophon and Ephesus; commended by the poets for its swans, which it had in great numbers. Its source was in the Montes Cilbiani, (Pliny). Caystrus Campus was a part of the territory of Ephesus. Campi Cazibiani of Lydia were plains lying in the middle between the inland parts and Mount Tmolus.

CAZEROM

Pages 310-310
or CAZERON, a city of Asia, in Persia, situated in E. Long. 70. N. Lat. 29. 15.

CAZIC

Pages 310-310
or CAZIQUE, a title given by the Spaniards to the petty kings, princes, and chiefs, of the several countries of America, excepting those of Peru, which are called curatos. The French call them caziques, a denomination which they always give to the Tartarian hordes.—The cazics, in some places, do the office of physicians, and in others of priests, as well as of captains. The dignity of cazic among the Chittas, a people of South America, does not descend to children, but must be acquired by valour and merit. One of the prerogatives attached to it is, that the cazic may have three wives, while the other people are allowed only one. Mexico comprehended a great number of provinces and islands, which were governed by lords called caziques, dependent on and tributary to the emperor. Thirty of these vassals are said to have been so powerful, that they were able, each of them, to bring an army of 100,000 men into the field.

CAZIMIR

Pages 310-310

a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUBLIN">Lublin</a>, situated on a hill covered with trees, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 10. N. Lat. 51. 5. CEA. See CEOS.

CEBES

Pages 310-312

CEBES, of Thebes, a Socratic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, author of the admired *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of Cebes*; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "Dialogues on the Birth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">Death</a> of Mankind." He flourished about 405 years before Christ.—The above piece is mentioned by some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, by Lucian, D. Laertius, Tertullian, and Suidas: but of Cebes himself we have no account, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> that he is once mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, and once by Xenophon. The former says of him, in his "Phaedo," that he was a sagacious investigator of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and never assented without the most convincing reasons: the latter, in this "Memorabilia," ranks him among the few intimates of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, who excelled the rest in the innocency of their lives. Cebes's *Tabula* is usually printed with Epictetus's *Manuals*. Cecil, William, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Burleigh, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of England in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, was the son of Richard Cecil, Esq.; <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the robes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. He was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of his grandfather, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Cecil, Esq., at Bourn in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, in the year 1520; and received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANTHAM">Grantham</a>. From thence he was removed to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAMFORD">Stamford</a>; and about the year 1535, was entered of St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. Here he began his studies with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of enthusiastic application very uncommon in young gentlemen of family. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16 he read a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> lecture, and at 19 a voluntary Greek lecture, which was the more extraordinary as being at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> was by no means universally understood. In 1541 he went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and became a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Gray's Inn, with an intention to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but he had not been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in that situation before an accident introduced him to King Henry, and gave a new bias to his pursuits. O'Neil, a famous Irish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, coming to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, had brought with him two Irish chaplains, violent bigots to the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; with these Mr Cecil, visiting his father, happened to have a warm dispute in Latin, in which he displayed uncommon abilities. The king, being informed of it, ordered the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> into his presence, and was so pleased with his conversation, that he commanded his father to find a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for him. He accordingly requested the reverence of the *cujus brevium*, which Mr Cecil afterwards persisted. About this time he married the sister of Sir John Cheke, by whom he was recommended to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol10.html#article-HERTFORD">Hertford</a>, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Somerset and protector. Soon after King Edward's accession, Mr Cecil came into the possession of the office of *cujus brevium*, worth about £400 a-year. His first lady dying in 1543, he married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir Anthony Cook, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the king's studies. In 1547, he was appointed by the protector, master of requests; and soon after attended his noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> on his expedition against the Scots, and was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MUSSELBURGH">Musselburgh</a>. In this battle, which was fought on the 10th of September 1547, Mr Cecil's life was miraculously preserved by a friend, who on pushing him out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of a cannon, had his arm shattered to pieces. The fight and judgment of his friend must have been as extraordinary as his friendship, to perceive the precise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a cannon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>; unless we suppose, that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> was almost quite spent; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the thing is not impossible. The story is told in his life by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>. In the year 1548, Mr Cecil was made secretary of state; but in the following year, the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> prevailing, he suffered in the disgrace of the protector Somerset, and was sent prisoner to the tower. After three months confinement he was released; in 1551 restored to his office; and soon after knighted, and sworn of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. In 1553 he was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a>, with an annual fee of 100 marks. On the death of Edward VI. Mr Cecil prudently refused to have any concern in Northumberland's attempt in favour of the unfortunate Lady Jane Gray; and when Queen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> acceded to the throne, he was graciously received at court; but not choosing to change his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, was dismissed from his employments. During this reign, he was twice elected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the shire for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>; and often spoke in the house of commons, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> freedom and firmness, in opposition to the ministry. Nevertheless, though a Protestant and a patriot (that is, a courtier out of place), he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to steer through a very dangerous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> without shipwreck. Queen Elizabeth's accession in the year 1558 immediately dispelled the cloud which had obscured his fortunes and ministerial capacity. During the horrid reign of her father, he had constantly corresponded with the princess Elizabeth. On the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of her accession, he presented her with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> containing twelve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> necessary for her immediate dispatch; and, in a few days after, was sworn of the privy council, and made secretary of state. His first advice to the queen was, to call a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and the first business he proposed after it was assembled, was the establishment of a national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of reformation was accordingly drawn up under his immediate inspection, and the legal establishment of the church of England was the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. Sir William Cecil's next important concern, was to restore the value of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, which had in the preceding reigns been considerably debased. In 1561, he was appointed master of the wards; and, in 1571, created baron of Burleigh, as a reward for his services, particularly in having lately stifled a formidable rebellion in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. The following year he was honoured with the garter, and raised to the office of lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> treasurer of England. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> we find him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMUM_MOBILE">primum <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOBILE">mobile</a> of every material transaction during the glorious reign of Queen Elizabeth. Notwithstanding the temporary influence of other favourites, Lord Burleigh was, in fact, her prime minister, and the person on whom she chiefly confided in matters of real importance. Having filled the highest and most important offices of the state for 40 years, and guided the helm of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> during the most glorious period of English <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, he departed this life on the 4th of August 1598, in the 78th year of his age. His body was removed to Stamford, and there deposited in the family vault, where a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> was erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>.—Notwithstanding his long enjoyment of such lucrative employments, he left only an estate of £4000 per annum, £11,000 in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and effects worth about £14,000. He lived, indeed, in a manner suitable to his high <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and importance, portance. He had four places of residence, viz., his lodgings at court, his house in the Strand, his seat at Burleigh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">Park</a> near Stamford, and his seat at Theobald's. The last of these was his favourite place of retirement, where he frequently entertained the queen at vast expense. Lord Burleigh was doubtless a man of singular abilities and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, amiable in his private character, and one of the most able, upright, and indefatigable ministers ever recorded in the annals of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. La Complainte de l'ame pechereffe, or the Complaint of a sinful <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">Soul</a>, in French <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, in the king's library. 2. Materials for Patten's Diarium expedit. Scotiae, London 1541, 12mo. 3. Slanders and lies maliciously, grossly, and impudently vomited out, in certain traitorous books and pamphlets, against two counsellors, Sir Francis <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> and Sir William Cecil. 4. A speech in parliament, 1562, Strype's Memoir iv. p. 107. 5. Precepts or directions for the well ordering of a man's life, 1637, Harl. Cat. vol. ii. p. 755. 6. Meditations on the death of his lady, Ballard's Mem. p. 184. 7. Meditations on the state of England during the reign of Queen Elizabeth, manuscript. 8. The execution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in England for the maintenance of public and Christian peace, &c. Lond. 1581, 1583, Somer's tracts, 4th Collect. vol. i. p. 5. 9. Advice to Queen Elizabeth in matters of religion and state, ib. p. 101, 106. 10. A great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of letters. See Peck's Defiderata Curiosa, Howard's collections, &c. 11. Several pedigrees, some of which are preserved in the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>'s library at Lambeth, No. 299, 747.

CECENA

Pages 348-349
CESENA, a town of Romagna in Italy, with a bishop's see, subject to the pope, and seated on the river Savio, in E. Long. 12° 46'. N. Lat. 44° 8'. CESPITOSÆ PLANTÆ (from cespites, turf or sod), are those plants which produce many stems from one root, and thence form a close thick carpet on the surface of the earth. CESPITOSÆ Paludes, turf-bogs.

CECILIA

Pages 312-312

Sr., the patroness of music, has been honoured as a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> ever since the fifth century. Her story, as delivered by the notaries of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and from them transcribed into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGEND">Legend</a> and other books of the like kind, says, that she was a Roman lady, born of noble parents about the year 225. That, notwithstanding she had been converted to Christianity, her parents married her to a young pagan nobleman named Valerianus; who going to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> to her on the wedding night, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is, says the book, was given to understand by his spouse, that she was nightly visited by an angel, and that he must forbear to approach her, otherwise the angel would destroy him. Valerianus, somewhat troubled at these words, desired that he might see his rival the angel; but his spouse told him that was impossible, unless he would consent to be baptized and become a Christian. This he consented to; after which, returning to his wife, he found her in her closet at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, and by her side, in the shape of a beautiful young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, an angel clothed with brightness. After some conversation with the angel, Valerianus told him that he had a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> named Tiburtius, whom he greatly wished to see a partaker of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> which he himself had received. The angel told him that his desire was granted, and that they should be both crowned with martyrdom in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Upon this the angel vanished, and was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in showing himself as good as his word; Tiburtius was converted, and both he and his brother Valerianus were beheaded. Cecilia was offered her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> upon condition that she would sacrifice to the deities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; but she refused; upon which she was thrown into a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALDRON">caldron</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and scalded to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; others say, that she was stifled in a dry bath, i.e., an enclosure from whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> was excluded, having a slow fire underneath it; which kind of death was sometimes inflicted by the Romans upon women of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> who were criminals. Upon the spot where her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> stood, is a church, said to have been built by Pope Urban I. who administered <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> to her husband and his brother: it is the church of St. Cecilia at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRALEE">Tralee</a>; within is a most curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> of the saint, as also a flatly monument with a cumbent statue of her with her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> downwards. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of St. Cecilia, that she excelled in music; and that the angel who was thus enamoured of her, was drawn from the celestial regions by the charms of her <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>: this has been deemed authority sufficient to making her the patroness of music and musicians. The legend of St. Cecilia has given frequent occasion to painters and sculptors to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> their genius in representations of her, playing on the organ, and sometimes on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>. Raphael has painted her fingering with a regal in her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; and Domenichino and Mignard, fingering and playing on the harp.

CECROPS

Pages 312-312

the founder and first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Moses the lawgiver of the Hebrews. He was the first who established civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> among the Greeks; and died after a reign of 50 years. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, No. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">CEDAR</a>. See Juniperus and Pinus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cedar famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, is that popularly called the cedar of Lebanon (Pinus cedrus), by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> cedrus magna, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cedar; also cedrelate, kideksharn. See Pinus, Botany Index.

CEDRENUS

Pages 312-312

GEORGE, a Grecian monk, lived in the 11th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and wrote "Annals, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an abridged <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, from the beginning of the World to the Reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Comnenus <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Constantinople, who succeeded Michael IV. in 1057." This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is no more than an extract from several historians. There is an edition of it, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1647, with the Latin version of Xylander, and the notes of Father Goar a Dominican.

CEDRUS

Pages 312-312

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> tree, mahogany, &c. See Juniperus, Pinus, and Swietenia, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CEILING

Pages 312-312

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the top <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a lower room; or a covering of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, over laths nailed on the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOISTS">joists</a> that bear the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of the upper room; or where there is no upper room, on joists for the purpose; hence called ceiling joists. The word ceiling answers pretty accurately to the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACUNAR">lacunar</a>, "every thing over head." Plastered ceilings are much used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, more than any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; nor are they without their advantages, as they make the room lightsome; are good in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of fire; stop the passage of the dust; lessen the noise over head; and, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> cooler. Ceiling, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, denotes the inside planks of a ship.

CEIMELIA

Pages 312-312

from εἰμιλία, "to be laid up," in antiquity, denotes choice <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> precious pieces of furniture or ornaments, referred or laid up for extraordinary

CEIMELIOPHYLAX

Pages 313-313

(from κειμελίαν and φυλάσσω I keep), the keeper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> curator of a collection of ceimelia; sometimes also denominated ceimelarcha. The ceimelarcha, or ceimeliophylax, was an officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> churches or monasteries, answering to what was otherwise denominated chartophylax, and cullos archivorum. CELÆNE, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> Magna, situated on a cognominal mountain, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sources of the Meander and Marlyas. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> had a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> beneath the citadel, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the Marlyas, which rose in the market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, not less in size than the Meander, and flowed through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> the younger had also a palace there, but by the springs of the Meander, which river passed likewise through the city. He had moreover, an extensive paradise or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a>, full of wild beasts, which he hunted on horseback for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> or amusement; and watered by the Meander, which ran through the middle. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> was said to have built these palaces and the citadel after his return from his expedition into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Antiochus Soter removed the inhabitants of Celæne into a city, which he named from his mother, Apamea; and which became afterwards a mart inferior only to Ephesus. See APAMEA. CELANDINE. See CHELIDONIUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CELANO

Pages 313-313

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in Farther Abruzzo. It is seated a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the lake Celano, anciently called FUCINUS. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 13. 39. N. Lat. 41. 56.

CELARENT

Pages 313-313

among logicians, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of syllogism, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> and conclusion are universal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> an universal affirmative. E.gr. cE None whose understanding is limited can be omniscient. IA Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s understanding is limited. rEnt Therefore no man is omniscient. CELASTRUS. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the powder of the root of this plant as a specific against gonorrhoeas, which it is said to cure in eight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sometimes in three days. An infusion of the bark of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> tree, which grows in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of France, is said to possess the same virtues.

CELEBES

Pages 313-313

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, situated under the equator, and called by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACASSAR">Macassar</a>. The length and breadth have not been accurately computed; but the circumference, at a medium, is about 800 miles. It had formerly five kingdoms, which are reduced to one. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is hot and moist; and subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rains during the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west winds, which blow from November to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is overflowed, and for this reason they build their housetops on piles of wood ten feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The most healthful time is during the northern monsoons, which seldom fail blowing regularly in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the year. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> vegetables are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and cocoes; but they have ebony, sanders, &c. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are much the same as in the neighbouring parts of the Indies. They have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BETEL">betel</a>, areca, the finest cotton, and opium. The natives have bright olive complexions, and the women have shining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. They are thought to be very handsome by the Dutch and Chinese, who often purchase them for bedfellows. The men are industrious, robust, and make excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. Their arms are sabres, and trunks, from whence they blow poisoned darts, which are pointed with the tooth of a sea fish. Some likewise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> poisoned daggers. They were the last of the Indian nations that were enslaved by the Dutch, which could not be effected till after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. They teach their children to read and write, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> have some resemblance of the Arabic. Their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> being Mahometan, the men indulge themselves in many wives and concubines. The employment of the women is <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>, cookery, and making their own and their husbands clothes. The men wear jewels in their ears, and the women <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> chains about their necks. The inhabitants in general go half naked, without anything on their head, legs, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> feet, and some have nothing but a cloth about their middle. The streets of the town Macasar are spacious, and planted with trees on every side. It stands by the side of the only <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river they have in the island. The Dutch have a fort here, mounted with 40 guns, and garrisoned with 700 men. There is only one other town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, called Jampanam, where they also have a fort. The island is not near so populous, as when the Dutch conquered it; the men being hired for soldiers in most of the neighbouring countries. The religion of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> was formerly idolatry. They worshipped the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. They sacrificed to them in the public squares, having no materials which they thought valuable enough to be employed in raising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>. About two centuries ago, some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> and Mahometans having brought their opinions to Celebes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the country took a dislike to the national worship. Having convened a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, he ascended an eminence, when, spreading out his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> towards heaven, he told the Deity, that he would acknowledge for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> that doctrine whose ministers should first arrive in his dominions, and, as the winds and waves were at his command, the Almighty would have himself to blame <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he embraced a falsehood. The assembly broke up, determined to wait the orders of heaven, and to obey the first missionaries that should arrive. The Mahometans were the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and their religion accordingly prevailed.

CELERES

Pages 313-314

in Roman antiquity, a regiment of body-guards belonging to the Roman kings, established by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, and composed of 300 young men, chosen out of the most illustrious Roman families, and approved by the suffrages of the curiae of the people, each of which furnished ten. The name comes from celere, "quick, ready;" and was given them because of their promptness to obey the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. The celeres always attended near the king's person, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> him, to be ready to carry his orders, and to execute execute them. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> they made the van-guard in the engagement, which they always began first; in retreats, they made the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REAR_GUARD">rear-guard</a>. Though the celers were a body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, yet they usually dismounted, and fought on foot; their commander was called tribune, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prefect of the celers. They were divided into three troops of 100 each, commanded by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> called centurio: their tribune was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> person in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Plutarch says, Numa broke the celers; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this be true, they were soon re-established; for we find them under most of the succeeding kings: witness the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Brutus, who expelled the Tarquins, and who was the tribune of the celers.

CELERI

Pages 314-314

Wild**, (*Apium antarticum*), was found in considerable quantities by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks and Dr Solander, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Terra del <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEGO">Fuego</a>. It is like the garden celeri in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and disposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, but the leaves are of a deeper green. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is between that of celeri and parsley. It is a very useful ingredient in the soup for lepers, because of its antiscorbutic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>.

CELERITY

Pages 314-314

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, the swiftness of any body in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. It is also defined to be an affection of motion, by which any moveable body runs through a given space in a given <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

CELESTES

Pages 315-315
or CELESTAE, (from κέλευσις, a race-horse), in antiquity, denote single or saddle horses, by way of contradiction from those yoked or harnessed together, called bigarii, quadrigarii, &c. The same denomination is also given to the cavaliers or riders on horseback; and hence some deduce celeres, the name of Romulus's guard.

CELESTINS

Pages 314-315

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order so called from their founder <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> de Meuron, afterwards raised to the pontificate under the name of Celestin V. This Peter, who was born at Ifernia, a little town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in the year 1245, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> parents, retired, while very young, to a solitary mountain, in order to dedicate himself wholly to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and mortification. The fame of his piety brought several, out of curiosity, to see him; some of whom, charmed with his virtues, renounced the world to accompany him in his solitude. With these he formed a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> in the year 1254: which was approved by Pope Urban IV. in 1264, and erected into a distinct order, called the hermits of St Damien. Peter de Meuron governed this order till 1286, when his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of solitude and retirement induced him to quit the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1294, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation of his sanctity raised him, though much against his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, to the pontificate. He then took the name of Celestin V. and his order that of Celestins from him. By his bull he approved their constitutions, and confirmed all their monasteries to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 20. But he sat too short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of St Peter to do many great things for his order; for having governed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> five months months and a few days, and considering the great burden he had taken upon him, to which he thought himself unequal, he solemnly renounced the pontificate in a consistory held at Naples. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1296, his order made great progress not only in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, but in France likewise; whether the then general Peter of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIVOLI">Tivoli</a> sent 12 religious, at the request of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> the Fair, who gave them two monasteries; one in the forest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, and the other in the forest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPEIGNE">Compeigne</a> at Mount Chartres. This order likewise passed into several provinces of Germany. They have about 96 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> in Italy, and 21 in France, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of priories. The Celestins rise two hours after midnight to say matins. They eat no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> at any time, except when they are sick. They fast every Wednesday and Friday, from Easter to the feast of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXALTATION">exaltation</a> of the holy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>; and, from that feast to Easter, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. As to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, it consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, a capuche, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCAPULAR">scapular</a>. In the choir, and when they go out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, they wear a black <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COWL">cowl</a> with the capuche; their thirts are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERGE">serge</a>.

CELEUSMA

Pages 315-315
or Celeuma, in antiquity, the shout or cry of the seamen, whereby they animated each other in their work of rowing. The word is formed from καλεῖν, to call, to give the signal. Celeusma, was also a kind of song or formula, rehearsed or played by the master, or others, to direct the strokes and movements of the mariners, as well as to encourage them to labour. See Celeustes.

CELEUSTES

Pages 315-315

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, the boatswain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> officer appointed to give the rowers the signal, when they were to pull, and when to stop. He is also denominated epopeus, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, portifexus; sometimes simply bortator.

CELIBACY

Pages 315-315

the state of unmarried persons. Scaliger derives the word from the Greek καρπος, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>," and λύκων, linquo, "I leave;" others say it is formed from cali beatitudine, q.d. the blessedness of heaven.

CELIBATE

Pages 315-316

the same with celibacy; but it is chiefly used in speaking of the single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the Popish clergy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the obligation they are under to abstain from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we say the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of celibate. Monks and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> take a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> of celibate; and what is more, of chastity. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome imposes an universal celibacy on all its clergy, from the pope to the lowest deacon and subdeacon. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for this usage pretend that a vow of perpetual celibacy was required in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> church as a condition of ordination, even from the earliest apostolic ages. But the contrary is evident from numerous examples of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and archbishops, who lived in a state of matrimony, without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> to their ordination or their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>. It is generally agreed that most of the apostles were married. Some say all of them, except St Paul and St John. Others say St Paul himself was married, because he writes to his yoke-fellow, whom they interpret his wife. Be this as it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, in the next ages after the apostles, we have accounts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> married bishops, presbyters, and deacons, without any reproach or mark of dishonour set on them; e.g., <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENS">Valens</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESBYTER">presbyter</a> of Philippi, mentioned by Polycarp; and Cheremon, bishop of Nitus. Novatus was a married presbyter of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, as we learn from Cyprian; who himself was also a married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, as Pagri confesses; and so was Cæcilius the presbyter who converted him; and Numidius, another presbyter of Carthage. The reply which the Romanists give to this is, that all married persons, when they came to be ordained, promised to live separate from their wives by consent, which answered the vow of celibacy in other persons. But this is not only said without <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, but against it. For Novatus presbyter of Carthage was certainly allowed to cohabit with his wife after ordination; as appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> that Cyprian brings against him, that he had struck and abused his wife, and thereby caused her to miscarry. There seems indeed to have been, in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, a tendency towards the introduction of such a law by one or two zealots; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> was no sooner made than it was quashed by the authority of wiser men. Thus Eusebius observes, that Pinytus, bishop of Gnoffus in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, was for laying the law of celibacy upon his brethren; but Dionysius bishop of Corinth wrote to him, that he should consider the weakness of men, and not impose that heavy burden on them. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice, anno 325, the motion was renewed for a law to oblige the clergy to abstain from all conjugal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> with their wives, whom they had married before their ordination; but Paphnutius, a famous Egyptian bishop, and one who himself never was married, vigorously declaimed against it, upon which it was unanimously rejected. So <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> and Sozomen tell the story; to which all that Valesius, after Bellarmine, has to say, is, that he supports the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of it. The council in Trullo, held in 692, made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in this respect between bishops and presbyters; allowing presbyters, deacons, and all the inferior orders, to cohabit with their wives after ordination; and giving the Roman church a smart rebuke for the contrary prohibition, but at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> laying an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a> upon bishops to live separate from their wives, and appointing the wives to betake themselves to a monastic life, or become deaconesses in the church. And thus was a total celibate established in the Greek church as to bishops, but not In the Latin church, the like establishment was also made, but by slow steps in many places. For in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, even bishops themselves cohabited with their wives at the time of the council of Trullo. The celibacy of the clergy, however, appears of an ancient standing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not of command and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>; yet as of counsel and choice. But as it is clearly neither of divine nor apostolical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, it is at first hard to conceive from what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome persisted so very obstinately to impose this institution on the clergy. But we are to observe that this was a leading step to the execution of the project formed of making the clergy independent of princes, and rendering them a separate body to be governed by their own laws. In effect, while priests had children, it was very difficult to prevent their dependence on princes, whose favours have such an influence on private men; but having no family, they were more at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to adhere to the pope.

CELIDOGRAPHIA

Pages 316-316

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the spots which appear on the surfaces of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>. See **<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a>**.

CELL

Pages 316-316

(*Cella*) in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apartment usually under ground, and vaulted, in which were stored up some sort of necessaries, as wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and the like; and according to which it was called *Cella Vinaria*, *Olearia*, *Mellaria*, &c. The word is formed from the Latin *celare*, to conceal. *Cella* was also used for the lodge or habitation of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> prostitute, as being anciently under ground, hence also denominated *fornix*. *Intravit calidum veteri centone lupanar*, *Et cellam vacuam*. Juv. Sat. vi. ver. 121. On which place an ancient scholiast remarks, that the names of the whores were written on the doors of their several cells; by which we learn the meaning of *inscripta cella* in Martial, lib. xi. Ep. 46. *Cella* was also applied to the bedchambers of domestics and servants; probably as being low and narrow.—Cicero, inveighing against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> of Antony, says the beds in the very cells of his servants were spread with pompous purple coverlets. *Cella* is also applied to the members or apartments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. Of these there were three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, called *frigidaria*, *tepidaria*, and *caldaria*; to which may be added a fourth, called *cella affa*, and sometimes *sudatoria*. *Cella* likewise signified the *adyta*, or inmost and most retired parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, wherein the images of the gods to whom the edifices were consecrated were preserved. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we meet with *cella jovi*, *cella Concordiae*. *Cella* is also used for a lesser or subordinate sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> dependent on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> one, by which it was erected, and continues still to be governed. The great abbeys in England had most of them cells in places distant from the mother <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, to which they were accountable, and from which they received their superiors. The alien priories in England were cells to abbeys in Normandy, France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, &c. The name *cell* was also given to rich and considerable monasteries not dependent on any other. *Cell* signifies also a little apartment or chamber, such as those wherein the ancient monks, solitaries, and hermits, lived in retirement. Some derive the word from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> נֶסֶר, i.e., "a prison, or place where any thing is shut up." The same name is still retained in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> monasteries. The dormitory is frequently divided into many cells or lodges. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHUSIANS">Carthusians</a> have each a separate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which serves them as a cell. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> wherein the Roman conclave is held, is divided, by partitions, into divers cells, for the several cardinals to lodge in. *Cell* is also a name given to the little divisions in honeycombs, which are always regular hexagons. See **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEE">BEE</a>**.

CELLAR

Pages 316-316

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, denotes the same with *cella*, viz. a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSERVATORY">conservatory</a> of eatables, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> drinkables. Cellar differs from vault, as the latter is supposed to be deeper, the former being frequently little below the surface of the ground. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, *cellarium* also differed from *penus*, as the former was only a storehouse for several days, the latter for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Thus it is the *bastroperatae*, a sort of ancient Cynics, are said by St Jerome to carry their cellar about with them. *Cellarium* also denoted an allowance of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, or other provision, furnished out of the cella, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> and his officers, &c. In which sense, the word amounts to much the same with *annona*.

CELLARER

Pages 316-317
or **CELLERER**, (*Cellerarius* or *Cellarius*), an officer in monasteries, to whom belong the care and procurement of provisions for the convent. The denomination is said to be borrowed from the Roman law, where *cellarius* denotes an examiner of accounts and expenses. Ulpian defines it thus: "Cellarius, id est, ideo praepotitus ut rationes salvae sint." The *cellarius* was one of the four *obedientiarii*, or great officers of monasteries: under his ordering was the *pilfrium* or bakehouse, and the *bracinum*, or brewhouse. In the richer houses there were particular lands set apart for the maintenance of his office, called in ancient writings *ad cibum monachorum*. The *cellarius* was a great man in the convent. His whole office in ancient times had a respect to that origin: he was to see his lord's corn got in, and laid up in granaries; and his appointment consisted in a certain proportion thereof, usually fixed at a thirteenth part of of the whole, together with a furred gown. The office of cellarer then only differed in name from those of bailiff and minstrel; excepting that the cellarer had the receipt of his lord's rents throughout the whole extent of his jurisdiction. Cellarer was also an officer in chapters, to whom belonged the care of the temporals, and particularly the distributing of bread, wine, and money, to canons, on account of their attendance in the choir. In some places he was called cellarer, in others burser, and in others currier.

CELLARIUS

Pages 317-317

CHRISTOPHER, was born in 1638, at Smalcade in Franconia, of which town his father was minister. He was successively rector of the colleges at Weymar, Zeits, and Merlbourgh; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> having founded an university at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALLE">Halle</a> in 1693, he was prevailed on to be professor of eloquence and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> there, where he composed the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his works. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> application to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> hastened the infirmities of old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; for it is said, he would spend whole days and nights together at his books, without any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even the calls of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. His works relate to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, history, and the oriental languages; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them is amazing. He died in 1707.

CELLARS

Pages 316-316

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, are the lowest rooms in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the ceilings of which usually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the surface of the ground on which the house is built; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> they are situated under the pavement before the house, especially in streets and squares. Cellars, and other places vaulted under ground, were called by the Greeks *hypogeae*: the Italians still call them *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDI">fundi</a> deli*.

CELLINI

Pages 317-317

BENVENUTO, an eminent statuary, who was bred a jeweller and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDSMITH">goldsmith</a>, but seems to have had an extraordinary genius for the fine arts in general. He was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Michael Angelo and Julio Romano, and was employed by popes, kings, and other princely patrons of sciences and arts, so highly cultivated in the days of Leo X. and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V., some of his productions being esteemed most exquisite.
