Centuries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a>, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> history, ranged into 13 centuries, carried <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the year 1298, compiled by several hundred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">protestants</a> of Magdeburg, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of whom was Flacius Illyricus. CENTUSSIS in Roman antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> containing 100 asses.

CENTZONTLI

Pages 343-343

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, the Mexican name of the Turdus polyglottus. See Turdus, Ornithology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CEODIES

Pages 343-343

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>: A genus of the dioica order, belonging to the polygamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is no calyx; the corolla is monopetalous, with a short turbinated tube; the stamens are ten filiform filaments; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTHER">anther</a> roundish.

CEORLES

Pages 343-343

the name of one of the classes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> orders into which the people were distinguished among the Anglo-Saxons. The ceorles, who were persons completely free, and descended from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of freemen, constituted a middle class between the labourers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> (who were generally slaves, or descended from slaves), on the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> on the other. They might go where they pleased, and pursue any way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> that was most agreeable to their humour; but so many of them applied to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, and farming the lands of the nobility, that a ceorl was the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name for a husbandman or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> in the Anglo-Saxon times. These ceorls, however, seem in general to have been a kind of gentlemen farmers; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any one of them prospered so well as to acquire the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, upon which he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> gate, and obtained a seat and office in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, he was esteemed a nobleman or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THANE">thane</a>. If a ceorl applied to learning, and attained to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>'s orders, he was also considered as a thane; his weregild, or price of his life, was the same, and his testimony had the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in a court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. When he applied to trade, and made three voyages beyond <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in a ship of his own, and with a cargo belonging to himself, he was also advanced to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a thane. But if a ceorl had a greater propensity to arms than to learning, trade, or agriculture, he then became the fithcuman, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> retainer, to some potent and warlike <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a>, and was called the hufcarle of such an earl. If one of these hufcarles acquitted himself so well as to obtain from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> either five hides of land, or a gilt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREASTPLATE">breastplate</a>, as a reward of his valour, he was likewise considered as a thane. Thus the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> stood open to these ceorls, whether they applied themselves to agriculture, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, letters, or arms, which were then the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> esteemed worthy of a freeman.

CEOS

Pages 343-344

Cea, Cia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cos, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the Cyclades, lies opposite to the promontory of Achaia called Sunium, and is 50 miles in compass. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is commended by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> for its fertility and the richness of its pastures. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stuffs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Pliny and Solinus are to be credited, were wrought here. Ceos was particularly famous for the excellent figs it produced. It was first peopled by Ariadne, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, who being grieved for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his son Agion, retired from Thebes, at the persuasion of his mother, and went over with some Thebans to Ceos, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> uninhabited. Diodorus Siculus tells us, that he retired to the island of Cos; but the ancients, as Servius observes, called both these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> by the name of Cos. Be that as it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, the island of Ceos became so populous, that a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> prevailed there, commanding all persons upwards of sixty to be poisoned, that others might be able to subsist; so that none above sixty were to be seen in the island, being obliged, after they arrived at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, either to submit to the law, or abandon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, together with their effects. Ceos had, in former times, four famous cities, viz. Julis, Carthaea, Corellus, and Prae-ella. The two latter were, according to Pliny, swallowed up by an earthquake. The other two flourished in Strabo's time. Carthaea stood on a rising ground, at the end of a valley, about three miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The situation of it agrees with that of the present town of Zena, which gives name to the whole island. The ruins both of Carthaea and Julis are still remaining; those of the latter take up the whole mountain, and are called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> inhabitants Polis, that is, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Near this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> are the ruins of a flatly temple, with many pieces of broken pillars, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of most exquisite workmanship. The walls of the city were of marble, and some pieces are still remaining above 12 feet in length. Julis was, according to Strabo, the birth-place of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIMONIDES">Simonides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHYLIDES">Bacchylides</a>, Eratosthenes, and Aristo. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> marbles tell us, that Simonides, the son of Leopepis, invented a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, the principles of which he explained at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; and add, that he was defended by another Simonides, who was a poet no less renowned than himself. One of these two poets invented those melancholy verses which were sung at funerals, and are called by the Latins nanie. Strabo says, that the Athenians, having besieged the city of Julis, raised the siege, upon advice that the inhabitants had resolved to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> all the children under a certain age, that useless persons might not be employed in looking after them. Ceos was, with the other Greek islands, subdued by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and bestowed upon the Athenians by Mark Antony the triumvir, together with Eginia, Tinos, and some other adjoining islands, which were all reduced to one Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> by Vespasian. The island is now called Zea.

CEPHALENIA

Pages 344-344
or CEPHALLENIA, an island of the Ionian sea, between Ithaca and Zacynthus, known in Homer's time by the names of Samos and Epirus Melena, is about eighty miles in length, forty in breadth, and a hundred and thirty in compass. It had anciently four cities, one of which bore the name of the island. Strabo tells us, that in his time there were only two cities remaining; but Pliny speaks of three; adding, that the ruins of Same, which had been destroyed by the Romans, were still in being. Same was the metropolis of the island, and is supposed to have stood in the place which the Italians call Porto Guiccardo. The names of the four cities were, according to Thucydides, Same, Prone, Cranii, and Palae. This island was subdued by the Thebans, under the conduct of Amphitryon, who is said to have killed Pterelas, who then reigned here. While Amphitryon was carrying on the war in Cephalenia, then called Samos, one Cephalus, a man of great distinction at Athens, having accidentally killed his wife Procris in shooting at a deer, fled to Amphitryon, who, pitying his case, not only received him kindly, but made him governor of the island, which henceforth was called Cephalenia. After it had been long in subjection to the Thebans, it fell under the power of the Macedonians, and was taken from them by the Aetolians, who held it till it was reduced by M. Fulvius Nobilior, who having gained the metropolis after a four months siege, sold all the citizens for slaves, adding the whole island to the dominions of the republic. Now called CEPHALONIA.

CEPHALIC

Pages 344-344

in a general meaning, signifies anything belonging to the head. CEPHALIC Medicines, are remedies for disorders of the head. Cordials are comprehended herein, as are also whatever promotes a free circulation of the blood through the brain. Except when the disorder arises from excess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an inflammatory disposition in the head, moist topicals should never be used, but always dry ones. To rub the head after it is shaved proves an instantaneous cure for a cephalalgia, a stuffing of the head, and a weakness of the eyes, arising from a weak and relaxed state of the fibres. And as by every fresh evacuation of the humours their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is not only lessened, but also their recrementitious parts derived thither, the more frequently the head is shaved, the larger quantity of humour is discharged; so that the frequent shaving of the head and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> is likewise a perpetual blifter; and in as much as it is useful, it is a cephalic. CEPHALIC Vein, in Anatomy, creeps along the arm between the skin and the muscles, and divides it into two branches; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> goes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>, where it joins the basilica, and turns up to the back of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; the internal branch, together with a small one of the basilica, makes the mediana. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> used to open this vein for disorders of the head, for which reason it bears this name; but a better acquaintance with the circulation of the blood informs us that there is no foundation for such a notion.

CEPHALONIA

Pages 344-344

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the same name, situated in the Mediterranean, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Epirus, and subject to the Venetians. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 21. N. Lat. 30° 30'.

CEPHEUS

Pages 344-344

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the northern hemisphere. See Astronomy, No 406.

CERAM

Pages 344-344

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, between the Molucca <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and those of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBOYNA">Amboyna</a> and Banda on the south, lying between E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 126. and 129. in S. Lat. 3. It is about 150 miles long, and 60 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and here the Dutch have

CERAMBYX

Pages 344-345

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a genus of insects of the beetle kind, belonging to the order of insects coleoptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CERASTES

Pages 345-345

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Anguis and Coluber. See Ophiology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CERATE

Pages 345-345

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a thickish kind of ointment, applied to ulcerations, excoriations, &c. See Pharmacy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CERATION

Pages 345-345

the name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to the small seeds of ceratonia, used by the Arabian physicians as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> to adjust the doses of medicines; as the grain weight with us took its rise from a grain of barley. Ceration, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ceratium, was also a silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, equal to one-third of an obolus. CERATOCARPUS. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CERATONIA

Pages 345-345

the Carob Tree, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> St John's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The pods of this plant are called St John's bread, from an ill-founded assertion of some writers on Scripture, that these were the locusts which St John ate with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> in the wilderness. CERATOPHYLLUM. See Botany Index.

CERAUNIA

Pages 345-345

Ceraunias, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ceraunius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">Lapis</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a sort of flinty <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of no certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, but of a pyramidal or wedge-like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; popularly supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of thunderstorms, and to be possessed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> notable virtues, as promoting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, preserving from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, &c. The word is from the Greek ξεραυνις, thunderbolt. The ceraunia is the same with what is otherwise called the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>-stone, or thunder-bolt; and also sometimes sagitta, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>'s-head, on account of its shape. The ceraunia are frequently confounded with the ombrice and brontite, as being all supposed to have the same origin. The generality of naturalists take the ceraunia for a native stone, formed among the pyrites, of a saline, concrete, mineral juice. Mercatus and Dr Woodward assert it to be <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, and to have been fashioned thus by tools. The ceraunia, according to these authors, are the heads of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> weapons of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; which, upon the introduction of that metal, growing into disuse, were dispersed in the fields through this and the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Some of them had possibly served in the early ages for axes, others for wedges, others for chisels; but the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> for arrow-heads, darts, and lances. The ceraunia is also held by Pliny for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or crystal-coloured gem, that attracted lightning to itself. What this was, is hard to say. Prudentius also speaks of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> ceraunia; by which he supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARBUNCLE">carbuncle</a> or pyropus. CERBERA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CERBERUS

Pages 345-345

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a dreadful three-headed mastiff, born of Typhon and Echidna, and placed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the gates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. He fawned upon those who entered, but devoured all who attempted to get back. He was, however, mastered by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, who dragged him up to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, when, in struggling, a foam dropped from his mouth, which produced the poisonous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> called aconite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>'s-bane. Some have supposed that Cerberus is the symbol of the earth, or of all-devouring <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and that its three mouths represent the present, past, and future. The victory obtained by Hercules over this monster denotes the conquest which this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> acquired over his passions. Dr Bryant supposes that Cerberus was the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and that it signified the temple of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>; deriving it from Kir Abor, the place of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. This temple was also called Tor-Capp El, which was changed to ἐγκαππας; and hence Cerberus was supposed to have had three heads. It was likewise called Tor-Keren, Turris Regia; whence τρις κεφαλαι, from τρις, three, and κεφαλαι, head.

CERCLE

Pages 345-345

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>: a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> cercle is a cross which, opening at the ends, turns round both ways like a ram's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>. See Cross.

CERCOPITHECI

Pages 345-345

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the name given by Mr Ray to monkeys, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the clasps of apes with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> tails. See Simia, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CERDA

Pages 345-345

John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> de la, a learned Jesuit of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, wrote <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> commentaries on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, which have been much esteemed; also several other works. He died in 1643, aged 80.

CERDONIANS

Pages 345-345
ancient heretics, who maintained most of the errors of Simon Magus, Saturninus, and the Manichees. They took their name from their leader Cerdon, a Syrian, who came to Rome in the time of Pope Hyginus, and there abjured his errors; but in appearance only; for he was afterwards convicted of perfuming in them, and accordingly cast out of the church again. Cerdon asserted two principles, the one good and the other evil: this last, according to him, was the creator of the world, and the god that appeared under the old law. The first, whom he called unknown, was the father of Jesus Christ; who, he taught, was incarnate only in appearance, and was not born of a virgin; nor did he suffer death but in appearance. He denied the resurrection, and rejected all the books of the Old Testament, as coming from an evil principle. Marcion, his disciple, succeeded him in his errors.

CEREALIA

Pages 345-347

in Antiquity, feasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, instituted by Triptolemus, son of Celeus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Eleusine in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for his having been instructed by Ceres, who was supposed to have been his nurse, in the art of cultivating corn and making <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. There were two feasts of this kind at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; the one called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEUSINIA">Eleusinia</a>, the other Thesmophoria. See the article Eleusinia. What both agreed in, and was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all the cerealia, was, that they were celebrated with a world of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and purity; so that it was esteemed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pollution to meddle, on those days, in conjugal matters. It was not Ceres alone that was honoured here, but also <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. The victims offered were hogs, by reason of the waste they make in the products of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>: whether there was any wine offered <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of much debate among the critics. Plautus and Macrobius seem to countenance the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> side; Cato and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> the positive. Macrobius says, indeed, they did not offer wine to Ceres, but mulsum, which was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of wine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> boiled up together: that the sacrifice... CER Cerealia made on the 21st of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, was a pregnant sow, together with cakes and mulsum; and that this is what Virgil means by Mili Baccho. The cerealia passed from the Greeks to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who held them for eight days successively; commencing, as generally held, on the fifth of the ides of April. It was the women alone who were concerned in the celebration, all dressed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; the men, likewise in white, were only spectators. They ate nothing till after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>-set; in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Ceres, who in her search after her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> took no repast but in the evening. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Cannae, the desolation was so great at Rome, that there were no women to celebrate the feast, by reason they were all in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>; so that it was omitted that year. Cerealia, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, from Ceres, the goddess of corn; Linnaeus's name for the larger eculent seeds of the grasses; these are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, wheat, rye, barley, oats, millet, panic grass, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> millet, holcus, zizania, and maize. To this head may be likewise referred dandelion, (Taraxacum); which, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, is rendered eculent. Cerebellum, the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the head. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cerebrum, the brain. Its structure and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> are not so fully known as some other parts of the body; and different authors confide it in various manners. However, according to the observations of those most famed for their accuracy and dexterity in anatomical inquiries, its general structure is as given in Anatomy Index. Dr Hunter observes, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> parts of the medullary substance of the brain in idiots and madmen, such as the thalami nervorum opticorum, and medulla oblongata, are found entirely changed from a medullary to a hard, tough, dark-coloured substance, sometimes resembling white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONIAL">Ceremonial</a> (ceremoniale), a book in which is prescribed the order of the ceremonies to be observed in certain actions and occasions of solemnity and pomp. The ceremonial of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is called ordo Romanus. It was published in 1516 by the bishop of Coreyra; at which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of cardinals were so scandalized, that some of them voted to have the author as well as book burnt, for his temerity in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> the sacred ceremonies to the eyes of profane people. Ceremonial, is also used for the set or system of rules and ceremonies which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> has introduced for regulating our behaviour, and which persons practice towards each other, either out of duty, decency, or civility. Ceremonial, in a more particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes the manner in which princes and ambassadors use to receive and to treat one another. There are endless disputes among sovereigns about the ceremonial; some endeavouring to be on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, and others to be superior; inasmuch that numerous schemes have been proposed for settling them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> are, 1. To accommodate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> by compromise or alternation; so that one shall precede now, the other the next <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; or one in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the other in another; 2. By seniority; so that an elder <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in years shall precede a younger, without any other distinction. These expedients, however, have not yet been accepted by any, except some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> princes, as they are called, in Germany. Ceremonial is more particularly used in speaking of the laws and regulations given by Moses relating to the worship of God among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Jews. In this sense it amounts to much the same with what is called the Levitical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and stands contradistinguished from the moral as well as judicial law. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">Ceremony</a>, an assemblage of several actions, forms, and circumstances, serving to render a thing more magnificent and solemn. In 1646, M. Ponce published a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of ancient ceremonies, tracing the rise, growth, and introduction of each rite into the church, and its gradual advancement to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> therein. Many of them were borrowed from Judaism; but more seemingly from Paganism. Dr Middleton has given a fine discourse on the conformity between the Pagan and Popish ceremonies, which he exemplifies in the use of incense, holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, lamps, and candles, before the shrines of saints, votive gifts or offerings round the shrines of the deceased, &c. In effect, the altars, images, crosses, processions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, and legends; nay, even the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a>, pontificate, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> orders, &c. of the present Romans, he shows, are all copied from their heathen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>.—We have an ample and magnificent account of the religious ceremonies and customs of all nations in the world, represented in figures designed by Picart, with historical explanations, and many curious dissertations. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of the Ceremonies, an officer instituted by King James I. for the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> reception of ambassadors and strangers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. He wears about his neck a chain of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, with a medal under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, having on one side an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of peace, with this motto, Beati pacifici; and on the other, an emblem of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, with Dieu et mon droit; his salary is £300 per annum. Assistant Master of the Ceremonies, is to execute the employment in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, whenever the master of the ceremonies is absent. His salary is £141l. 13s. 4d. per annum. Marshall of the Ceremonies is their officer, being subordinate to them both. His salary is £100 per annum. Cerenza, town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, with a bishop's see. It is seated on a rock, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 5'. N. Lat. 39° 23'. Ceres, a pagan deity, the inventor or goddess of corn; in like manner as Bacchus was of wine. According to the poets, she was the daughter of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and Ops, and the mother of Proserpine, whom she had by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. Pluto having stolen away Proserpine, Ceres travelled all over the world in quest of her daughter, by the help of a torch, which she had lighted in Mount Aetna. As Ceres was thus travelling in search of her daughter, she came to Celeus king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a>, and undertook to bring up his infant son Triptolemus. Being desirous to render her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> immortal, she fed him in the daytime with divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and in the night covered him with fire. Celeus observing an unusual improvement in his son, resolved to watch his nurse, to which end he hid himself in that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> where she used to cover the child with fire; but when he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> her put the infant under the embers, he cried out and discovered himself. Ceres punished the curiosity and indiscretion of the father with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Afterwards she taught the youth the art of sowing corn and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and mounted him in a chariot drawn by winged dragons, that he might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> the world, and teach mankind the use of corn and fruits. After this, having discovered, by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> Arethusa, that Proserpine was in the infernal regions, she applied to Jupiter, and obtained from him that Proserpine should be restored, on condition that she had tasted nothing during her stay in that place; but it being discovered, by the information of Ascalaphus, that, as she was walking in Pluto's orchard, she had gathered an apple, and had tasted of some of the seeds, she was forbidden to return. Ceres, out of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, turned Ascalaphus into an owl. At length, Jupiter, to mitigate her grief, permitted that Proserpine should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> one half of the year in the infernal regions with Pluto, and the other half with her mother on earth. Cicero speaks of a temple of Ceres at Catanae in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, where there was a very ancient statue of that goddess, but entirely concealed from the sight of men, everything being performed by matrons and virgins.

CERET

Pages 347-347

a town of France in Roussillon, with a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of a single <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>. It is situated near the river Tec, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 46. N. Lat. 42. 23.

CERIGO

Pages 347-347

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, anciently called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYTHERA">Cythera</a>; noted for being the birth-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Helen, and, as the poets say, of Venus. At present there is nothing very delightful in the place; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is mountainous, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> dry. It abounds in hares, quails, turtle, and excellent falcons. It is about 50 miles in circumference, and had formerly good <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; but there is now none remaining but that which gives name to the island. This is strong both by art and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, it being seated on a craggy rock. The inhabitants are Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and subject to the Venetians, who keep a governor there, whom they change every two years.

CERINES

Pages 347-347

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus, with a good cattle, a harbour, and a bishop's see. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 33. 35. N. Lat. 35. 22. CERINTHE HONEYWORT. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CERINTHIANS

Pages 347-347
ancient heretics, who denied the deity of Jesus Christ.—They took their name from Cerinthus, one of the first heresarchs in the church, being contemporary with St John. See Cerinthus. They believed that Jesus Christ was a mere man, born of Joseph and Mary; but that, in his baptism, a celestial virtue descended upon him in form of a dove; by means whereof he was consecrated by the Holy Spirit, and made Christ. It was by means of this celestial virtue, therefore, that he wrought so many miracles; which, as he received it from heaven, quitted him after his passion, and returned to the place whence it came; so that Jesus, whom they called a pure man, really died and rose again; but that Christ, who was distinguished from Jesus, did not suffer at all. It was partly to refute this fact that St John wrote his gospel. They received the gospel of St Matthew, to countenance their doctrine of circumcision, form Christ's being circumcised; but they omitted the genealogy. They discarded the epistles of St Paul, because that apostle held circumcision abolished.

CERINTHUS

Pages 347-347

a heresarch, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with the apostles, ascribed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> not to God, but to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. He taught that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, and that circumcision ought to be retained under the gospel. He is looked upon as the head of the converted Jews, who raised in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Antioch the tumult of which St Luke has given the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in the 15th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the Acts. Some authors ascribe the book of the Apocalypse to Cerinthus; adding, that he put it off under the name of St John, the better to authorize his reveries touching Christ's reign upon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>: and it is even certain that he published some works of this kind under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Apocalypse. See Apocalypse. CEROPEGIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CERTHIA

Pages 347-347

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, the creeper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ox-eye, a genus belonging to the order of picas. See Ornithology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CERTIFICATE

Pages 347-347
Trial by, in the law of England, a species of trial allowed in such cases where the evidence of the person certifying is the only proper criterion of the point in dispute*. For when the fact in question lies out of the cognizance of the court, the judges must rely on the solemn averment or information of persons in such a station as affords them the most clear and competent knowledge of the truth. As Blackfriars therefore such evidence, if given to a jury, must have been conclusive, the law, to save trouble and circuitry, permits the fact to be determined upon such certificate merely. Thus, 1. If the issue be whether A was absent with the king in his army out of the realm in time of war, this shall be tried by the certificate of the marshal of the king's host in writing under his seal, which shall be sent to the justices. 2. If, in order to avoid an outlawry, or the like, it was alleged that the defendant was in prison, ultra mare, at Bordeaux, or in the service of the mayor of Bordeaux, this should have been tried by the certificate of the mayor, and the like of the captain of Calais. But when this was law, those towns were under the dominion of the crown of England. And therefore, by a parity of reason, it should now hold, that in similar cases arising at Jamaica or Minorca, the trial should be by certificate from the governor of those islands. We also find that the certificate of the queen's messengers, sent to summon home a peerage of the realm, was formerly held a sufficient trial of the contempt in refusing to obey such summons. 3. For matters within the realm; the customs of the city of London shall be tried by the certificate of the mayor and aldermen, certified by the mouth of their recorder, upon a summons from the party alleging it, that the custom ought to be thus tried; else it must be tried by the country: As, the custom of distributing the effects of freemen deceased; of enrolling apprentices, or that he who is free of one trade may use another; if any of these, or other similar points come in issue. 4. The trial of all customs and practice of the courts shall be by certificate from the proper officers of those courts respectively;

CERTIORARI

Pages 347-348

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ which issues out of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, directed to an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, to call up the records of a cause there depending, in order that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> may be done. And this writ is obtained upon complaint, that the party who seeks it has received hard usage, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> is not like to have an impartial <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> in the inferior court. A certiorari is made returnable either in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas, or in chancery. It is not only used out of the court of chancery, but likewise out of the king's bench; in which last mentioned court it lies where the king would be certified of a record. Indictments from inferior courts, and proceedings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> sessions of the peace, may also be removed into the king's bench by a certiorari: and here the very record must be returned, and not a transcript of it; though usually in chancery, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a certiorari be returnable there, it removes only the tenor of the record.

CERTITUDE

Pages 348-348

considered in the things <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> which are the objects of our understandings, is a necessary agreement or disagreement of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of our knowledge with another: as applied to the mind, it is the perception of such agreement or disagreement; or such a firm well-grounded assent, as excludes not only all manner of doubt, but all conceivable possibility of a mistake. There are three sorts of certitude, or assurance, according to the different natures and circumstances of things. 1. A physical or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> certitude, which depends upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; so that I see such or such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, or hear such or such a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>; nobody questions the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this, where the organs, the medium, and the object, are rightly disposed. 2. Mathematical certitude, is that arising from mathematical evidence; such as, that the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of a triangle are equal to two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> ones. 3. Moral certitude is that founded on moral evidence, and is frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a mathematical one; as that there was formerly such an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> as Julius Caesar, and that he wrote the commentaries which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> under his name; because the historians of these times have recorded it, and no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> has ever disproved it since; this affords a moral certitude, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sense so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that one would be thought a fool or a madman for denying it.

CERTOSA

Pages 348-348

a celebrated Carthusian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>; in the territory of the Pavefe, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, four miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>: its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a> is surrounded with a wall 20 miles in circumference; but there are several small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages therein. CERVANTES. See SAAVEDRA.

CERUMEN

Pages 348-348

a thick, viscid, bitter, excrementitious humour, separated from the blood by proper glands placed in the meatus auditorius, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> outer passage of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>.

CERUS

Pages 348-348
WHITE LEAD, a sort of calx of lead, made by exposing plates of that metal to the vapour of vinegar. See Chemistry Index. Cerfs, as a medicine, is used externally either mixed in ointments, or by sprinkling it on old gleeting and watery ulcers, and in many diseases of the skin. If, when it is reduced into a fine powder, it is received in with the breath in inspiration, and carried down into the lungs, it causes incurable asthmas. Instances of the very pernicious effects of this metal are too often seen among those persons who work lead in any form, but particularly among the workers in white lead. The painters use it in great quantities; and that it may be afforded cheap to them, it is generally adulterated with common whiting.

CERVERA

Pages 348-348

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in Catalonia, seated on a small river of the same name, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 9. N. Lat. 41. 28.

CERVIA

Pages 348-348

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in Romagna, with a bishop's see, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 5. N. Lat. 44. 16.

CERVICAL NERVES

Pages 348-348

are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of nerves, so called, as having their origin in the cervix, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> neck.

CERVICAL VESSELS

Pages 348-348

among anatomists, denote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a>, veins, &c., which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the vertebrae and muscles of the neck up to the skull.

CERVIX

Pages 348-348

in Anatomy, properly denotes the hind <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the neck; as contradistinguished from the fore part, which is called jugulum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the throat. Cervix of the Scapula, denotes the head of the shoulder blade, or that upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> whose sinus receives the head of the humerus. Cervix of the Uterus, the neck of the uterus, or that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> canal or passage between the internal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> orifices, which receives and encloses the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a> like a sheath, whence it is also called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VAGINA">Vagina</a>.

CERVUS

Pages 348-348
or DEER, in Zoology, a genus of quadrupeds belonging to the order of Pecora. See Mammalia Index. CERVUS Volans, in href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History, a name given by authors to the flag-fly, or horned beetle, a very large species of beetle with horns sloped, and something like those of the stag.

CERYX

Pages 348-348

in antiquity. The ceryces were a sort of public criers appointed to proclaim <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> publish things aloud in assemblies. The ceryx among the Greeks answered to the praeco among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Our criers have only a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their office and authority. There were two kinds of ceryces, civil and sacred. The former were those appointed to call assemblies, and make silence therein; also to go on messages, and do the office of our heralds, &c. The sacred ceryces were a sort of priests, whose office was to proclaim silence in the public games and sacrifices, publish the names of the conquerors, proclaim feasts, and the like. The priesthood of the ceryces was annexed to a particular family, the descendants of Ceryx, son of Eumolpus. To them it also belonged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> solemn victims to slaughter. Before the ceremonies began, they called silence in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, by the formula, Εὐρημένεις σιγή παρ' ἐκεῖ λαοῦ; answering to the favete linguis of the Romans. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> was over, they dismissed the people with this formula, Δαιμόνιον ἀφείσθω, Ἰεροῦ ἀπολύσις.

CESARE

Pages 348-348

among logicians, one of the modes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of syllogisms; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> proposition of which is an universal affirmative, and the other two universal negatives: thus, CE No immoral books ought to be read; SA But every obscene book is immoral; RE Therefore no obscene books ought to be read.

CESSATION

Pages 349-349

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of intermitting, discontinuing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> interrupting, the course of any thing, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, or the like. CESSATION of Arms, an armistice or occasional truce. See TRUCE. When the commander of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> finds things reduced to an extremity, so that he must either surrender, or sacrifice the garrison and inhabitants to the mercy of the enemy, he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a>, or beats the chamade; on which a cessation of arms and hostilities commences, to give room for a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>.

CESSIO BONORUM

Pages 349-349

in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the name of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> by which an insolvent debtor may apply for liberation from prison, upon making over his whole real and personal estate to his creditors.

CESSION

Pages 349-349

in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is when an ecclesiastical person is created a bishop, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> when a parson of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> takes another benefice, without dispensation, or being otherwise qualified. In both these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> their first benefices became void by cession, without any resignation; and to those livings that the person had, who was created bishop, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> may present for that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, whoever is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of them; and in the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the patron may present: but by dispensation of remainder, a bishop may retain some or all the preferments he was entitled to before he was made bishop.

CESTUI

Pages 349-349

a French word, signifying he <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> him, frequently used in the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> writings. Thus, Cestui qui trust, a person who has lands, &c., committed to him for the benefit of another; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> such person does not perform his trust, he is compellable to it in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>. Cestui qui vie, one for whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> any lands, &c., are granted. Cestui qui ufe, a person to whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> any one is inclosed of lands or tenements. Formerly the feoffees to uses were deemed owners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, but now the possession is adjudged in cestui qui ufe.

CESTUS

Pages 349-349

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets, a fine embroidered girdle said to be worn by Venus, to which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> ascribes the power of charming and conciliating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. The word is also written cestium and cestum: it comes from xéos, a girdle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other thing embroidered or wrought with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>; derived, according to Servius, from xéos, pungere; whence also incestus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used at first for any indecency by undoing the girdle, &c., but now restrained to that between persons near akin. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INCEST">INCEST</a>.

CETACEOUS

Pages 349-349

an appellation given to the fishes of the whale kind. See CETOLOGY.

CETERACH

Pages 349-349

the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Asplenium. See ASPLENIUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CETOLOGY

Pages 377-380

Whale-Fishery. Soon apparent. At that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> (1786) the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ships employed from England in the whale-fishery amounted to 139, besides 15 from Scotland. The proposed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the following year (1787); and notwithstanding the diminution of the bounty, the trade increased; the number of ships employed the same year from England amounting to 217, and the next year (1788) to 222. Their cargoes consisted of 5989 tons of clean <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; 7054 tons of whalebone, beside 13,386 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> skins. For some years British <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> has been employed in a southern whale-fishery; and this has also been a very lucrative branch of trade. This fishery was first prosecuted with vigour about the commencement of the American <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. In the year 1785, 18 ships which produced 29,000l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> were employed in it. Two years afterwards the number of ships was doubled, and the returns increased in a much greater proportion, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the flourishing state of the trade. The number of ships in 1787 was 38, and the produce amounted to 107,000l. sterling. Some American families, when the war broke out in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, emigrated to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-NOVA_SCOTIA">Nova Scotia</a>, where they proposed to carry on the whale-fishery; but being discouraged from particular circumstances, on the invitation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Mr Greville, they settled at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILFORD">Milford</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILFORD_HAVEN">Milford Haven</a>, and fitted out a ship, which had a very successful voyage. The number of ships soon increased to four, and at present (1803), that number is doubled, so that 18 ships are now employed in the southern whale-fishery from this port, with a capital afloat of not less than 80,000l. sterling. This fact is stated by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a> in his travels in southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; and "I mention it," says he, "as a striking instance to show the importance of the south-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> fishery, and as a proof that, contrary to the generally received <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, it may be carried on by skill and management, and without the adventitious aid of trading, so as fully to answer the purpose of those who are properly qualified to embark in the undertaking. For where men, by industry in their profession, rise from small beginnings into affluence, such profession may be followed with a greater certainty of success than many others which appear to hold out more seducing prospects. The American fishermen never set out with a capital, but invariably <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> themselves into one; and the south-sea fishery from England may succeed on the same principle, as the above example clearly shows, under every disadvantage, when properly conducted." "It is difficult to point out the grounds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> policy in giving tonnage bounties to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> fishery, and only premiums to successful adventurers in the southern fishery. A voyage to Greenland is four months, the outfit of which is covered by the tonnage bounty, and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> wholly unsuccessful, the same ship can make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> voyage the same year to some of the ports of the Baltic. A voyage to the South sea is from 12 to 18 months, and must depend solely on the success in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>. A Greenland ship sets out on a small capital, and builds on a quick return; but a south-sea whaler must expend a very considerable capital in making his outfit, for which he can reckon on no returns for at least 18 months. Hence the usual practice of lending them out in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> capacity of fishers and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRABAND">contraband</a> traders, in order that the losses they may sustain by ill success in fishing may be made good by smuggling. "If by extending the fishery we should be enabled to supply the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, two objects should never be out of the view of the legislature—the exemption from duty of all the produce of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, and particularly spermaceti, which, if manufactured into candles, and subject only to the same duty as tallow candles, would produce much more to the revenue than when taxed as it now is, as wax. I have heard it asserted that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the premium system, by doubling its present amount, which never could exceed 30,000l. a-year, would be adequate encouragement to supply the home market with spermaceti and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> whale oil, and that the bonding of foreign oil in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> would throw the whole agency of American fishery on England with greater advantage to both countries than by any other system. "But when we consider that the home market is necessarily secured to British subjects by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> duties on foreign oil, we should also consider that every means to lessen the charges of outfit should strengthen our adventure in this lucrative branch of trade. Among others that would seem to have this tendency, are the facilities that might be afforded by the happy position of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope. If at this station was established a kind of central depot for the southern whale-fishery, it might, in time, be the means of throwing into our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> exclusively the supply of Europe with spermaceti oil. To the protection of the fisheries on the east and west coasts of southern Africa, the Cape is fully competent, and the fisheries on these coasts would be equally undisturbed in war as in peace. From hence they would, at all times, have an opportunity of acquiring a supply of refreshments for their crews, and of laying in a stock of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> at one-fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the expense of carrying them out from England." The Dutch were very early engaged in the Greenland whale-fishery, which soon became one of the most important objects of their trade. In 1611 a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> in the was established in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> for carrying on the whale-fishery on the coasts of Spitzbergen and <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol16.html#article-NOVA_ZEMBLA">Nova Zembla</a>. This branch of trade has in general succeeded better with the Dutch than with any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> reason which has been assigned for this success is the greater economy and frugality of this people, in this as in all their concerns, by which they are able to undersell others in oil and whalebone. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of fitting out all their ships is also mentioned as a cause of their prosperity in this fishery. The ship-builder, the rope-maker, the baker, the brewer, and other tradesmen employed in fitting out these ships, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> take a share in the voyage. When it proves fortunate, they are double gainers; but when it is unsuccessful, the loss which they sustain is probably not greater than if they had merely furnished the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> without having a chance of the profit; and in this respect have the advantage of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. It is observed by De Witt that this fishery since it fell into the hands of individuals has seldom failed to be profitable; but while it was monopolized by the Dutch Greenland company, the profit was inconsiderable. Some idea may be formed of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> to which the Dutch have carried this trade by stating their fishery. that for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of 46 years preceding the year 1722, 5886 ships were employed in it, and in this period they took 32,907 whales. Each whale at an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, valued at £500, makes the total amount above 16 millions sterling. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> affords at one view a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> record of the Dutch whale-fishery from 1661 to 1788. The number of ships employed for each year and the number of whales taken are stated in separate columns. | Year | Ships | Fish | |------|-------|------| | 1661 | 133 | 452½ | | 1662 | 149 | 862 | | 1663 | 202 | 932½ | | 1664 | 193 | 782 | | 1665 | War with England, no ships out. | 1712 | | 1666 | | | | 1667 | | | | 1668 | 155 | 573 | | 1669 | 133 | 1013½ | | 1670 | 148 | 792 | | 1671 | 138 | 1088½ | | 1672 | War with England, no ships out. | 1719 | | 1673 | | | | 1674 | | | | 1675 | 147 | 900½ | | 1676 | 145 | 812½ | | 1677 | 145 | 785½ | | 1678 | 120 | 1118½ | | 1679 | 126 | 792 | | 1680 | 151 | 1373 | | 1681 | 175 | 876 | | 1682 | 195 | 1444 | | 1683 | 242 | 1338½ | | 1684 | 233 | 1153½ | | 1685 | 209 | 1283½ | | 1686 | 189 | 664½ | | 1687 | 194 | 621½ | | 1688 | 214 | 340½ | | 1689 | 160 | 241½ | | 1690 | 117 | 785 | | 1691 | war with France. | 1738 | | 1692 | 32 | 56½ | | 1693 | 90 | 175 | | 1694 | 63 | 161½ | | 1695 | 97 | 187½ | | 1696 | 122 | 428 | | 1697 | 131 | 1279 | | 1698 | 139 | 1483½ | | 1699 | 151 | 77½ | | 1700 | 173 | 913½ | | 1701 | 208 | 207½ | | 1702 | 224 | 687½ | | 1703 | 207 | 644 | | 1704 | 130 | 632½ | | 1705 | 157 | 1678 | | 1706 | 151 | 966 | | 1707 | 131 | 126 | This table is interesting, as it shows us the precarious <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of this fishery. But it would have been still more valuable, if some other circumstances had been stated, such as the nature of the seasons when the fishery was less successful; whether the preceding winter was unusually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> or severe; whether the short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of these regions was not remarkable for extremes or sudden changes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, sudden changes and variations of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, the prevalence of particular winds; or other facts which might enable us to trace the causes of the extraordinary failure and success of the fishery. The French made an attempt to revive this branch of trade in 1784. Six ships fitted out at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a> at the French expense of the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, made some successful voyages both in the northern and southern whale-fishery. The advantages of the trade were obvious, and the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> were eager to improve them. In the year 1786, some of the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Nantucket, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, were invited to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> at Dunkirk to carry on the fishery. Several families accepted the invitation, and to encourage them to prosecute the trade, they were permitted to enjoy peculiar privileges and immunities. Ships were sent out to different seas, and had prosperous voyages. But this trade, as well as every other branch of French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, has probably been completely interrupted by the late revolution, and the particular circumstances in which that nation has been with regard to foreign powers. Besides the nations which we have mentioned, who have been most deeply concerned in this fishery, the inhabitants of other countries have also embarked in it. Some ships were equipped at Embden in 1768 by order of the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; the Swedish government in 1774 granted to a company established at Gottenburgh the exclusive privilege of the Davis straits and Greenland fishery for 20 years; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> in 1775 attempted to take a share in the benefits of that fishery, which many of the nations of Europe, more enterprising or more industrious, had long successfully enjoyed on the shores of the Danish dominions. The whale-fishery commences in May. It is about this time that the whales are seen in great numbers the fishery between. between the 76th and 79th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of north latitude; and at a distance they exhibit the appearance of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> rising from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a> of a great town by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which is thrown into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> by their spouting or blowing. The fishery continues for the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, when it must be abandoned whether it has been successful or unprofitable; because it is necessary to be clear of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> by the end of August. The ships return home at the earliest in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of September. But if the fishery happen to begin early in May, and prove abundant, they sometimes return in June or July. We shall now conclude this article with a short account of the different modes that are practised in taking the whale. The following is employed in the Greenland fishery by Europeans. Every ship is provided with six boats, to each of which belong six men for rowing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, and a harpooner, whose business it is to strike the whale with his harpoon. Two of these boats are kept constantly on the watch at some distance from the ship, fastened to pieces of ice, and are relieved by others every four hours. As soon as a whale is perceived, both the boats set out in pursuit of it, and if either of them can come up before the whale finally descends, which is known by his throwing up his tail, the harpooner discharges his harpoon at him. There is no difficulty in choosing the place where the whale is to be struck, as some have asserted; for these animals only come up to the surface in order to breathe, or blow, as the fishermen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> it, and therefore always keep the soft and vulnerable part of their bodies above water. A late improvement was made in the method of discharging the harpoon; namely, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> it out of a kind of swivel or musketoon; but it does not appear, that since this improvement was made, the whale-fishing ships have had better success than before.—As soon as the whale is struck, the men set up one of their oars in the middle of the boat as a signal to those in the ship. On perceiving this, the watchman alarms all the rest with the cry of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>! fall! upon which all the other boats are immediately sent out to the assistance of the first. The whale finding himself wounded, swims off with prodigious velocity. Sometimes he descends perpendicularly; and sometimes goes off horizontally, at a small depth below the surface. The rope which is fastened to the harpoon is about 200 fathoms long, and properly coiled up, that it may freely be given out as there is a demand for it. At first, the velocity with which this line runs over the side of the boat is so great, that it is wetted to prevent its taking fire: but in a short time the strength of the whale begins to fail, and the fishermen, instead of letting out more rope, strive as much as possible to pull back what is given out already, though they always find themselves necessitated to yield at last to the efforts of the animal, to prevent his sinking their boat. If he runs out the 200 fathoms of line contained in one boat, that belonging to another is immediately fastened to the end of the first, and so on; and there have been instances, where all the rope belonging to the six boats has been necessary, though half that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is seldom required. The whale cannot stay long below water, but again comes up to blow; and being now much fatigued and wounded, stays longer above water than usual. This gives another boat time to come up with him, and he is again struck with a harpoon. He again descends, but with less force than before; and when he comes up again, is generally incapable of descending, but suffers himself to be wounded and killed with long lances which the men are provided with for that purpose. He is known to be near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> when he spouts up the water deeply tinged with blood. The whale being dead, is lashed alongside the ship. They then lay it on one side, and put two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, one at the head, and the other in the place of the tail, which, together with the fins, is struck off as soon as he is taken, to keep these extremities above water. On the off-side of the whale are two boats, to receive the pieces of fat, utensils, and men, that might otherwise fall into the water on that side. These precautions being taken, three or four men with irons at their feet to prevent slipping, get on the whale, and begin to cut out pieces of about three feet thick and eight long, which are hauled up at the capstan or windlass. When the fat is all got off, they cut off the whalebone of the upper jaw with an axe. Before they cut, they are all lashed to keep them firm; which also facilitates the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>, and prevents them from falling into the sea; when on board, five or six of them are bundled together, and properly flowed; and after all is got off, the carcass is turned adrift, and devoured by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> bears, who are very fond of it. In proportion as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pieces of fat are cut off, the rest of the crew are employed in slicing them smaller, and picking out all the lean. When this is prepared, they throw it under the deck, where it lies till the fat of all the whales taken during the fishery is on board; then cutting it still smaller, they put it up in tubs in the hold, cramming them full and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. At the end of the season they return home, where the fat is boiled and pressed to give out the oil. But a different method is practised by the rude inhabitants of the different nations on the coasts of the frozen ocean. On some parts of the sea coasts of Kamtchatka, the return of the fishing season is celebrated with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> festival and great rejoicings in their subterranean winter habitations, in which many superstitious ceremonies are performed. In one part of the ceremonies dogs are sacrificed, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> of drums and other rude musical instruments. The priests who attend and conduct the festival, transport with great solemnity and pomp a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a whale, made of wood, from the summer habitation to the winter cottage. As the ceremonies proceed, the whole company assembled shout with a great noise, that the whale has made its escape from the cottage to the sea; and they pretend even to throw the traces of the whale in its course, as if it had really made its way through the opening in the cottage. These ceremonies being ended, the men prepare their nets, and embark in their canoes. The nets are set at the openings of bays, where fish, which are the food of the whale, are abundant, and in the pursuit of which entering the bays he is taken.
