Schwenterus, in his Practical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, tells us, he has observed a rope fifteen feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> reduced to fifteen in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> falling of a hoar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a>. To obviate these inconveniences, Wolfius directs, that the little strands whereof the rope consists be twisted contrariwise, and the rope dipped in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> hot <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and when dry, drawn through melted wax. A rope thus prepared will not get or lose anything in length, even though kept under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. **Chain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">Pump</a>.** See **Pump.** **Chain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">Shot</a>,** two bullets with a chain between them. They are used at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to shoot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> yards or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, and to cut the shrouds or rigging of a ship. **Top Chain,** on board a ship, a chain to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLING">sling</a> the sail yards in time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, in order to prevent them from falling down when the ropes by which they are hung happen to be shot away or rendered incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. **Chain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>,** or **Channels,** of a ship, (porteboissoirs), are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and thick planks projecting horizontally from the ship's outside, abreast of and somewhat behind the masts. They are formed to extend the shrouds from each other, and from the axis or middle line of the ship, so as to give a greater security and support to the masts, as well as to prevent the shrouds from damaging the gunwale, or being hurt by rubbing against it. Every mast has its chain wales, which are either built above or below the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> deck ports in a ship of the line; they are strongly connected to the side by <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, bolts, and standards, besides being confined thereto by the chains, whose upper ends pass through notches on the outer edge of the chain wales, so as to unite with the shrouds above. **Chains,** in Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a>, are strong links or plates of iron, the lower ends of which are bolted through the ship's side to the timbers. **Hanging in Chains,** a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a>. By stat. 25 Geo. II. c. 37, the judge shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> such to be executed on the next day but one, unless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> intervene; and their bodies to be delivered to the surgeons to be dissected and anatomized; and he may direct them afterwards to be hung in chains. During the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> and execution, the prisoner shall be kept alone, and sustained only with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and water. The judge, however, hath power to reprieve the execution, and relax the other restraints of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>. **Chain <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>,** an island lately discovered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Wallis in the South sea. It seemed to be about five miles long and as much broad, lying in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west and south-east. It appeared to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> range of woody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> joined together by reefs, so as to compose one island of an oval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, with a lake in the middle. The trees are large, and from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> that issued from the woods, it appeared to be inhabited. W. Long. 145° 54'. S. Lat. 17° 23'. **Chajotli,** or **Chayori,** a Mexican fruit of a round shape, and similar in the husk with which it is covered to the chestnut, but four or five times larger, and of a much deeper green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Its kernel is of a greenish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and has a large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in the middle, which is white, and like it in substance. It is boiled, and the stone eaten with it. This fruit is produced by a twining perennial plant, the root of which is also good to eat. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">Chair</a>,** (Cathedra), was anciently used for the pulpit, or suggestum, whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> spoke to the people. It is still applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where professors and regents in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> deliver their lectures, and teach the sciences to their pupils; thus, we say, the professor's chair, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s chair, &c. **Curule Chair,** was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> seat placed on a car, wherein were seated the prime magistrates of Rome, and those to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a triumph had been granted. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a> Chair,** a vehicle supported by poles, wherein persons are carried; borne by two men. There are 200 chairs allowed by act of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and no person is obliged to pay for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HACKNEY">hackney</a> chair more than the rate allowed by the act for a hackney <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">coach</a> driven two-thirds parts of the said distance. 9 Ann. c. 23. § 8. Their number is since increased by 10 Ann. c. 19. and 12 Geo. I. c. 12. to 400. See **Hackney Coaches.** Chair is also applied by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to certain feasts, held anciently in commemoration of the translation of the see, or seat of the vicarage of Christ, by St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>. The perforated chair, wherein the new elected pope is placed, F. Mabillon observes, is to be seen at Rome: but the origin thereof he does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a>, as is commonly done, to the adventure of Pope Joan; but says there is a mystery in it; and it is intended,

CHAIRMAN

Pages 394-395

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> speaker of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, &c. We say, the chairman of a committee, &c.

CHALAZA

Pages 395-395

among naturalists, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> knotty sort of a string at each end of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, formed of a plexus of the fibres of the membranes, whereby the yolk and white are connected together. See EGG. CHALCAS. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CHALCEDON

Pages 395-395
or CALCEDON, anciently known by the names of Proceraphis and Colchuca; a city of Bithynia, situated at the mouth of the Euxine, on the north extremity of the Thracian Bosphorus, over against Byzantium. Pliny, Strabo, and Tacitus, call it, The City of the Blind; alluding to the answer which the Pythian Apollo gave to the founders of Byzantium, who, consulting the oracle relative to a place where to build a city, were directed to choose that spot, which lay opposite "to the habitation of the blind;" that is, as was then understood, to Chalcedon: the Chalcedonians well deserving that epithet for having built their city in a barren and sandy foil, without seeing that advantageous and pleasant spot on the opposite shore, which the Byzantines afterwards chose.—Chalcedon, in the Christian times became famous on account of the council which was held there against Eutyches. The emperor Valens caused the walls of this city to be levelled with the ground for hiding with Procopius, and the materials to be conveyed to Constantinople, where they were employed in building the famous Valentinian aqueduct. Chalcedon is at present a poor place, known to the Greeks by its ancient name, and to the Turks by that of Gadiaci, or, "the judges town."

CHALCEDONY

Pages 395-395

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a genus of the fempellucid gems. They are of an even and regular not tabulated structure; of a semi-opaque crystalline basis, and variegated with different colours; but those ever disposed in form of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> nicely examined, found to be owing to an admixture of various coloured earths, but imperfectly blended in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, and often visible in distinct molecule.—It has been doubted by some whether the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were at all acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> we call Chalcedony; they having described a Chalcedonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARBUNCLE">carbuncle</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERALD">emerald</a>, neither of which can at all agree with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of our stone; but we are to consider that they have also described a Chalcedonian jasper which seems to have been the very same stone as they describe by the word turbida, which extremely well agrees with our chalcedony. There are four known <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the chalcedony. 1. A bluish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> one. This is the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> of all, and is found in the shape of our flints and pebbles, in masses of two or three inches or more in diameter. It is of a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with a faint cloud of blue diffused all over it, but always in the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> near the surface. This is a little less hard than the oriental onyx. The oriental chalcedonies are the only ones of any value; they are found in vast abundance on the shores of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in all parts of the East Indies, and frequently come over among the ballast of the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> ships. They are common in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> also; but with us are less hard, more opaque, and of very little value. 2. The dull milky-veined chalcedony. This is a stone of little value; and is sometimes met with among our lapidaries, who mistake it for a kind of nephritic stone. It is of a somewhat yellowish white or cream colour, with a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>-white veins. This is principally found in New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. 3. The third is a brownish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, dull, and cloudy one, known to the ancients by the name of smoky jasper, or jaspis capnitis. This is the least beautiful stone of all the clasps; it is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> brownish white, clouded all over with a blackish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIST">mist</a>, as the common chalcedony is with a blue. It is common both in the East and West Indies, and in Germany; but is very little valued, and is seldom worked into anything better than the handles of knives. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> chalcedony is greatly superior to all the rest in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; and is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> repute in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, though very little known among us. It is naturally composed of an admixture of red and yellow only, on a clouded crystalline basis; but is sometimes found blended with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of common chalcedony, and then is mixed with blue. It is all over of the milky hue of the common chalcedony. This is found only in the East Indies, and there not plentifully. The Italians make it into beads, and call them cagliarones; but they are not determinate in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the word, but call beads of several of the agates by the same name.—All the chalcedonies readily give fire with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, and make no effervescence with aquafortis.

CHALCIDENE

Pages 395-396
or CHALCIDICE, in Ancient Geography, an inland country of Syria, having Antioch or Seleucia to the west, Cyrheftica to the north, to the south Apamene and Caelofyria, and to the east Chalybonites; being so called from its principal city Chalcis. This province, one of the most fruitful in Syria, was seized by Ptolemy the son of Menæus during the troubles of Syria, and by him made a separate kingdom. Ptolemy himself is styled by Josephus and Hegesippus only prince of Chalcis, but his son Lyfanias is honoured both by Josephus and Dio with the title of king. Upon the death of Antiochus Dionysius king of Syria, Ptolemy attempted to make himself master of Damascus and all Caelofyria; but the inhabitants having an utter aversion to him on account of his cruelty and wickedness, chose rather to submit to Aretas king of Arabia, by whom Antiochus and his whole army had been cut off. He opposed Pompey on his entering Syria; but was by him defeated, taken prisoner, and sentenced to death; which, however, he escaped by paying a thousand talents, and was left also in possession of his kingdom. After Arisphobulus king of Judea had been poisoned by the friends of Pompey, and Alexander his son beheaded at Antioch, he sent Philippion his son to Acalon, whither the widow of Arisphobulus had retired with her other children, to bring them all to Chalcis; proposing, as he was in love with one of the daughters named Alexandra, to maintain them in his own kingdom in a manner suitable to their rank: but Philippion like Chalcedonias being in love with Alexandra, married her on the way; for which presumption Ptolemy put him to death on his return, and then took her to wife. On account of this affinity, he supported to the utmost of his power Antigonus the younger son of Ariotibulus, who took the field at the head of a considerable army, but on his entering Judæa was entirely defeated by Herod. Ptolemy soon after died, and was succeeded by his son Lysimachus, who espousing the cause of the Amonoean family with great warmth, promised to Barzapharnes who commanded the Parthian troops in Syria, and to Pacorus the king's son, a thousand talents and five hundred women, provided they should put Antigonus in possession of the kingdom of Judæa, and depose Hyrcanus. He was not long after put to death by Mark Antony, at the instigation of Cleopatra; who, in order to have his dominions, accused him falsely of having entered into an alliance with the Parthians.

CHALCIDIC

Pages 396-396

CHALCIDICUM, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> CHALCEDONIUM, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> belonging to a tribunal or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Petrus says, it took its name from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> Chalcis; but he does not give the reason. Philander <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it to be the court or tribunal where affairs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COINAGE">coinage</a> were regulated; so called from ἐκκατάστημα, brafis, and δικαίωμα, justice. Others say, the money was struck in it; and derive the word from ἐκκατάστημα, and ὀξύς, boye. In Vitruvius, it is used for the auditory of a basilica; in others of the ancient writers for a hall or apartment where the heathens imagined their gods to eat.

CHALCIDICE

Pages 396-396

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an eastern district of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, stretching northwards between the Sinus Toronaeus and Singiticus. Formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Thrace, but invaded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon. Named from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> Chalcis near Olynthus.

CHALCIDIUS

Pages 396-396

a famous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> in the third century, who wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a>, which is esteemed, on the Timæus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> has been translated from the Greek into Latin.

CHALCIS

Pages 396-396

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Chalcidice. See Chalcidice. Another of Ætolia, near the mouth of the river Evenus, on the Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, at the foot of a cognominal mountain; and therefore called by some Hypocalcis.—Another of Eubœa (Strabo), on the Euripus, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Lycophron the poet, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> which formed the constellation Pleiades. Now Negroponite. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 24. 30. Lat. 38. 30.—A fourth, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Chalcidene in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> Belem, a fountain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a river; and ad Libanon, from its situation (Pliny.)

CHALCITIS

Pages 396-396

one of the divisions <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> districts of Mæopotamia, to the south of Anthemusia, the most northern district, next to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, and situated between Edessa and Caræ. Chalcitis (Pliny), an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHALCEDON">Chalcedon</a>.

CHALCONDYLAS

Pages 396-396

Lucius, a famous Greek historian of the 15th century, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; and wrote an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Turks, from Ottomans, who reigned about the year 1300, to Mahomet II. in 1453.

CHALDEA

Pages 396-396

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, taken in a larger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, included <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>; as in the prophecies of Jeremiah and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>. In a restricted sense, it denoted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Babylonia, towards <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Deferta; called in Scripture, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of the Chaldeans. Named from Chaled the fourth son of Nahor. See BABYLONIA.

CHALDEE LANGUAGE

Pages 396-396

that spoken by the Chaldeans <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> people of Chaldea. It is a dialect of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>.

CHALDEE PARAPHRASES

Pages 396-396

in the rabbinical style, is called TARGUM. There are three Chaldee paraphrases in Walton's Polyglot; viz. that of Onkelos, that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a> son of Uzziel, and that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>.

CHALDRON

Pages 396-396

a dry English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, consisting of thirty-five bushels, heaped up according to the sealed bushel kept at Guildhall, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>: but on shipboard, twenty-one chaldrons of coals are allowed to the score. The chaldron should weigh two thousand pounds.

CHALICE

Pages 396-396

the cup <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vessel used to administer the wine in the sacrament, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the chalice, or communicating in both kinds, is by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome denied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>, who communicate only in one kind, the clergy alone being allowed the privilege of communicating in both kinds.

CHALIS

Pages 395-395

a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> open chariot, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> calash. Aurelius Victor relates, that Trajan first introduced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> chaises; but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> is generally ascribed to Augustus; and was probably only improved by Trajan and succeeding emperors.

CHALK

Pages 396-399

(Creta), is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> found plentifully in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, France, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, said to have been anciently dug chiefly in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, and thence to have received its name of Creta. They have a very easy way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> chalk in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> in England. It is there found on the sides of hills; and the workmen undermine it so far as appears proper; then digging a trench at the top, as far distant from the edge as the undermining goes at bottom, they fill this with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which foaks through in the space of a night, upon which the whole flake falls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> at once. In other parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, chalk generally lies deeper, and they are forced to dig for it at considerable depths, and draw it up in buckets. Chalk is of two kinds; hard, dry, and firm, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> soft and unctuous; both of which are adapted to various purposes. The hard and dry kind is much the poorest for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> into lime; but the soft and unctuous chalk is the best for using as a manure for lands. Chalk, whether burnt into lime or not, is in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> an excellent manure. Pure chalk melts easily with alkali and flint into a transparent colourless glass. With alkaline felspar it melts somewhat more difficulty, and with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a> somewhat more easily, than with flint or sand. It requires about half its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of borax and its whole weight of alkali to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUSE">fuse</a> it. Sal mirabilis, and sandiver, which do not vitrify at all with the crystalline earths, form, with half their weight of chalk, the first a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, the latter a greenish glass. Nitre, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> fluxes for flint, does not perfectly vitrify with chalk. This earth notably promotes the vitrification of flint; a mixture of the two requiring less alkali than either of them separately. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> glass made from flint and alkali is further saturated with the flint, so as to be incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> bearing any further addition of that earth without becoming opaque and milky, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> fill in a strong fire take up a considerable proportion, one-third or one-fourth of its weight, of chalk, without injury to its transparency: hence chalk is sometimes made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in compositions for glaas, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> may then be spared. Chalk likewise has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> effect in melting the stony matters intermixed with metallic ores, and hence might be of use in smelting ores; as indeed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> is used for that purpose. But it is remarkable, that chalk, when deprived of its fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and converted into limestone, loses much of its disposition to vitrify. It is then found to melt very difficultly and imperfectly, and to render the glass opaque and milky. Chalk readily imbibes water; and hence masses of it are employed for drying precipitates, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, earthy powders that have been levigated with water, and other moist preparations. Its economical uses in cleaning and polishing metallic or glass utensils are well known. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is powdered and washed from any gritty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> it may contain, and is then called whiting.—In medicine it is one of the most useful absorbents, and is to be looked upon simply as such. The astringent virtues which some have attributed to it have no foundation, unless in so far as the earth is saturated with an acid, with which it composes a saline concrete manifestly astringent. For the further properties of chalk, see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Black Chalk, a name given by painters to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of earth with which they draw on blue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, &c. It is found in pieces from two to ten feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and from four inches to twenty in breadth, generally flat, but somewhat rising in the middle, and thinner towards the edges, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> lying in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities together. While in the earth, it is moist and flaky; but being dried, it becomes considerably hard and very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>: but always breaks in some particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; and if attentively examined when first broken, appears of a striated texture. To the touch it is soft and smooth, stains very freely, and by virtue of its smoothness makes very neat marks. It is easily reduced into an impalpable soft powder without any diminution of its blackness. In this state it mixes easily with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> into a smooth paste; and being diffused through water it slowly settles in a black flaky or muddy form; properties which make its use very convenient to the painters, both in oil and water colours. It appears to be an earth quite different from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> chalk, and rather of the flaky bituminous kind. In the fire it becomes white with a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, and very friable, retaining its flaky structure, and looking much like the white flaky masses which some sorts of pit-coal leave in burning. Neither the chalk nor these ashes are at all affected by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> shops are supplied with this earth from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> or Germany; though some parts of England afford substances nearly, if not entirely, of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and which are found to be equally serviceable both for marking and as black paints. Such particularly is the black earth called kilow, said by Dr Merret in his Pinax Rerum Britannicarum to be found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, and by Mr DaCosta, in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Foffils, to be plentiful near the top of Cay-Avon, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hill in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERIONETHSHIRE">Merionethshire</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Chalk, an earth much used by painters and artificers, and common in the colour shops. It is properly an indurated clayey ochre, and is dug in Germany, Italy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and France, but in greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. It is of a fine, even, and firm texture; very heavy, and very hard; of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> red on the outside, but of a deep dusky chocolate colour within. It adheres firmly to the tongue, is perfectly insipid to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and makes no effervescence with acids. Chalk <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a>. Barley and wheat will succeed very well on the better sort of chalky land, and oats generally do well on any kind of it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> produce of this sort of land in weeds, is that sort of small vetch called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TINE">tine</a>-tare, with poppies, may-weed, &c. Sainfoin and hop clover will generally succeed tolerably well on these lands; and where they are of a better sort, the great clover will do. The best manure is dung, old rags, and the sheep dung left after folding them. Chalk-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">Stones</a>, in Medicine, signify the concretions of calcareous matter in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet of people violently afflicted with the gout. Leeuwenhoek has been at the pains of examining these by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. He divides them into three parts. The first is composed of various small parcels of matter looking like white grains of sand; this is harder and drier, and also whiter, than the rest. When examined with large magnifiers, those are found to be composed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> particles laid closely and evenly together; though the whole small stones are opaque, their components parts of them are pellucid, and resemble pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> cut short, only that they are somewhat pointed at both ends. These are so extremely thin, that Mr Leeuwenhoek computes, that 1000 of them placed together would not amount to the size of one hair of our heads. The whole stones in this harder part of the chalk are not composed of these particles, but there are confusedly thrown in among them some broken parts of other substances, and in a few places some globules of blood and small remains of other juices. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> kind of chalky matter is less hard and less white than the former, and is composed of fragments or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> parts of those oblong bodies which compose the first or hardest kind, and these are mixed among tough and clear matter, and interspersed with the small broken globules of blood discoverable in the former, but in much greater quantity. The third kind appears red to the naked eye; and, when examined with glaases, is found to be a more tough and clammy white matter, in which a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of globules of blood are interspersed; these give it the red appearance it has. Challenge, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTEL">cartel</a> or invitation to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUEL">duel</a> or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>*. A challenge either by word or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, or to be the bearer of such a challenge, is punishable by fine and imprisonment on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> or information. Challenge, among hunters. When hounds or beagles, at first finding the scent of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, preferently open and cry, they are said to challenge. Challenge, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a> of England, is an exception made to jurors†; and is either in civil or criminal cases. I. In civil cases challenges are of two sorts; challenges to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>, and challenges of the poll. 3 A 2 1. Challenges Challenges to the array are at once an exception to the whole panel, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> are arrayed, or fet in order by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> in his return; and they may be made upon account of partiality or some default in the sheriff or his under officer who arrayed the panel. Also, though there be no personal objection against the sheriff, if yet he arrays the panel at the nomination, or under the direction of either party, this is good cause of challenge to the array. Formerly, if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> had a cause to be tried, and no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> was returned upon the jury, it was a cause of challenge to the array: also by the policy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> law, the jury was to come de vicineto, from the neighbourhood of the vill or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> was laid in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>: and therefore some of the jury were obliged to be returned from the hundred in which such vill lay; and, if none were returned, the array might be challenged from defect of hundreders. For, living in the neighbourhood, these were supposed to know beforehand the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the parties and witnesses; and therefore they better knew what <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to give to the facts alleged in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>. But this convenience was overbalanced by another very natural and almost unavoidable inconvenience; that jurors, coming out of the immediate neighbourhood, would be apt to intermix their prejudices and partialities in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. And this the law was so sensible of, that it for a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> has been gradually relinquishing this practice; the number of necessary hundreders in the whole panel, which in the reign of Edward III. was constantly six, being in the time of Fortescue reduced to four; afterwards by statute 26 Eliz. c. 6. to two; and at length, by statute 4 and 5 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, c. 16. it was entirely abolished upon all civil actions, except upon penal statutes; and upon those also by the 24 Geo. II. c. 18. the jury being now only to come de corpore comitatus, from the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> at large, and not de vicineto, or from the particular neighbourhood. The array by the ancient law may also be challenged, if an alien be party to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, and upon a rule obtained by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> for a jury de mediate lingua, such a one be not returned by the sheriff pursuant to the statute 28 Edward III. c. 13. enforced by 8 Hen. VI. c. 29. which enacts, that where either party is an alien born, the jury shall be one half denizens and the other aliens (if so many be forthcoming in the place), for the more impartial trial; a privilege indulged to strangers in no other country in the world; but which is as ancient in England as the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a>, in whose statute de monticolis Wallie (then aliens to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England), c. 3. it is ordained, that "duodenii legales homines, quorum <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> Walli et lex Angli erunt, Anglis et Wallis jus dicunto." 2. Challenges to the polls, in capitae, are exceptions to particular jurors; and seem to answer the recusatio judicis in the civil and canon laws; by the constitutions of which a judge might be refused upon any suspicion of partiality. By the laws of England also, in the times of Bracton and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLETA">Fleta</a>, a judge might be refused for good cause; but now the law is otherwise, and it is held that judges or justices cannot be challenged. For the law will not suppose a possibility of bias or favour in a judge who is already sworn to administer impartial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and whose authority greatly depends on that presumption and idea. And, should the fact at any time prove flagrantly such, as the delicacy of the law will not presume beforehand, there is no doubt but that such misbehaviour would draw down a heavy censure from those to whom the judge is accountable for his conduct. But challenges to the polls of the jury (who are judges of fact) are reduced to four heads by Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>: propter honoris respectum; propter defectum; propter affectum; and propter delictum. 1. Propter honoris respectum; as, if a lord of parliament be impannelled on a jury, he may be challenged by either party, or he may challenge himself. 2. Propter defectum; as, if a jurymen be an alien born, this is defect of birth; if he be a slave or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDMAN">bondman</a>, it is defect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and he cannot be a liber et legalis homo. Under the word homo also, though a name common to both sexes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> is however excluded, propter defectum sexus: except when a widow feigns herself with child in order to exclude the next heir, and a supposititious birth is suspected to be intended; then upon the writ de ventre inspiciendo, a jury of women is to be impannelled to try the question whether with child or not. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> deficiency is defect of estate sufficient to qualify him to be a juror, which depends upon a variety of statutes*. 3. Jurors* see may be challenged propter affectum, for suspicion of bias Blackstone's or partiality. This may be either a principal challenge, or the favour. A principal challenge is such, where the cause assigned carries with it, prima facie, evident marks of suspicion either of malice or favour; as, that a juror is of kin to either party within the ninth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; that he has an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the cause; that there is an action depending between him and the party; that he has taken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for his verdict, &c., which if true, cannot be overruled; for jurors must be omni exceptione majoris. Challenges to the favour are where the party hath no principal challenge; but objects only some probable circumstances of suspicion, as acquaintance, and the like; the validity of which must be left to the determination of triers, whose office is to decide whether the juror be favourable or unfavourable. 4. Challenges propter delictum, are for some crime or misdemeanor that affects the juror's credit, and renders him infamous: As for a conviction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, felony, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a>; or if for some infamous offence, he hath received judgment of the pillory or the like. II. In criminal cases, challenges may be made either on the part of the king, or on that of the prisoner; and either to the whole array, or to the separate polls, for the very same reasons that they may be in civil causes. For it is here at least as necessary as there, that the sheriff or returning officer be totally indifferent; that, where an alien is indicted, the jury should be de mediate, or half foreigners, if so many are found in the place (which does not indeed hold in treasons; aliens being very improper judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>; nor yet in the case of Egyptians under the statute 22 Hen. VIII. c. 10.) that on every panel there should be a competent number of hundreders; and that the particular jurors should be omni exceptione majoris, not liable to objections either propter honoris respectum, propter defectum, propter affectum, or propter delictum. Challenges Challenges on any of the foregoing accounts are fly-led challenges for cause; which may be without flint in both civil and criminal trials. But in criminal cases, or at least in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> ones, there is, in favorem vitae, allowed to the prisoner an arbitrary and capricious species of challenge to a certain number of jurors, without showing any cause at all; which is called a peremptory challenge: a provision full of tenderness and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> to prisoners for which our laws are justly famous. This is grounded on two reasons: 1. As every one must be sensible what sudden impressions and unaccountable prejudices we are apt to conceive upon the bare looks and gestures of another; and how necessary it is that a prisoner, when put to defend his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, should have a good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his jury, the want of which might totally disconcert him; the law wills not that he should be tried by any one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> against whom he has conceived a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> even without being able to assign a reason for such his dislike. 2. Because upon challenges for cause shown, if the reason assigned prove insufficient to set aside the juror, perhaps the bare questioning his indifference may sometimes provoke a resentment; to prevent all ill consequences from which, the prisoner is still at liberty, if he pleases, peremptorily to set him aside. This privilege of peremptory challenges, though granted to the prisoner, is denied to the king by the statute 33 Edward I. stat. 4, which enacts, that the king shall challenge no jurors without assigning a cause certain to be tried and approved by the court. However, it is held that the king need not assign his cause of challenge till all the panel is gone through, and unless there cannot be a full jury without the persons so challenged. And then, and not sooner, the king's counsel must show the cause, otherwise the juror shall be sworn. The peremptory challenges of the prisoner must, however, have some reasonable boundary, otherwise he might never be tried. This reasonable boundary is settled by the common law to the number of 35; that is, one under the number of three full juries. For the law judges, that 35 are fully sufficient to allow the most timorous man to challenge through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> caprice; and that he who peremptorily challenges a greater number, or three full juries, has no intention to be tried at all. And therefore it deals with one who peremptorily challenges above 35, and will not retract his challenge, as with one who stands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a> or refuses his trial; by sentencing him to the pein forte et dure in felony, and by attainting him in treason. And so the law stands at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> with regard to treason of any kind. But by statute 22 Hen. VIII. c. 14. (which, with regard to felonies, stands unrepealed), no person arraigned for felony can be admitted to make more than 20 peremptory challenges. CHALONS-SUR-SAÔNE, an ancient town of France, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, and capital of the Chalonnois, with a citadel and bishop's see. It is seated on the river Saône, in E. Long. 5° 7'. N. Lat. 46° 47'.

CHALONER

Pages 399-400

Sir Thomas, the younger, though inconsiderable as an author, deserves to be recorded as a skilful naturalist, in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> wherein <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> was very little undertook in this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and particularly as the founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> works in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, which have since proved so exceedingly advantageous. CHALYBEAT tageous to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. He was the only son of Sir Thomas Chaloner mentioned in the last article, and was born in the year 1559. Being very young at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Burleigh, taking <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, sent him to St Paul's school, and afterwards to Magdalen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where, like his father, he discovered extraordinary talents for Latin and English <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. About the year 1580, he made the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and returned to England before 1584; for in that year, we find him a frequent attendant in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. About this time he married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir William Fleetwood, recorder of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. In 1601 he was knighted; and, some time after, discovered the alum <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> on his estate at Gibborough, near the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEES">Tees</a> in Yorkshire (a). Towards the latter end of the queen's reign, Sir Thomas visited Scotland; and returning to England in the retinue of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. found such favour in the sight of his majesty, that he was immediately appointed governor to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry, whom he constantly attended, and, when his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> pupil visited Oxford, was honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts. How he was employed after the death of the prince is not known. Some years before that event, he married a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife, the daughter of Mr William Blount of London, by whom he had some children. He died in the year 1615, and was buried at Chiswick in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>. His eldest son William was created a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARONET">baronet</a> in the 18th of James, anno 1620. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> was extinct in 1681. He wrote, 1. Dedication to Lord Burleigh of his father's poetical works, dated 1579. 2. The virtue of nitre, wherein is declared the sundry cures by the same effect. Lond. 1684, 4to.

CHALONS-SUR-MARNE

Pages 399-399

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> episcopal town of France, in Champagne. It carries on a considerable trade in falloons and other woollen stuffs. It is seated between two fine meadows on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a>, Mau, and Nau, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 37'. N. Lat. 48° 57'.

CHALYBEAT

Pages 400-400

in Medicine, an appellation given to any liquid, as wine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, impregnated with particles of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>. See MINERAL WATERS.

CHALYBES

Pages 400-400

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an ancient people of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Their situation is differently assigned; Strabo placing them in Paphlagonia, to the east of Synope; Apollonius Rhodius and Stephanus, on the east of the Thermodon, in Pontus; called Haliones, by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. They either gave their name to, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> took it from, their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> (Xenophon, Val. Flaccus), their only support, their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> being barren and ungrateful, (Dionysius Periegetes).

CHAM

Pages 400-400
or KHAN, the title given to the sovereign princes of Tartary. The word, in the Persian, signifies mighty lord; in the Slavonic, emperor. Sperlingius, in his dissertation on the Danish term of majesty, koning, king, thinks the Tartarian cham may be well derived from it; adding, that in the north they say kan, konnen, konge, kon- (a) Sir Thomas during his residence in Italy, being particularly fond of href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural history, spent some time at Puzzoli, where he was very attentive to the art of producing alum. This attention proved infinitely serviceable to his country, though of no great benefit to himself or his family, his attempt being attended with much difficulty and expense. It was begun about the year 1600, in the reign of Queen Elizabeth; but was not brought to any degree of perfection till some time in the reign of Charles I., by the assistance of one Ruffel a Walloon, and two other workmen brought from the alum works at Rochelle. By one of the arbitrary acts of Charles, it was then deemed a mine royal, and granted to Sir Paul Findar. The long parliament adjudged it a monopoly, and justly restored it to the original proprietors.

CHAMARIN

Pages 400-401

a word which occurs in several places of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, and is generally translated the priests of the idols, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the priests clothed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, because chamar signifies "black," or "blackness." St Jerome, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book of Kings, renders it arufijer. In Hosea and Zephaniah, he translates it adinai or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> wardens. But the best commentators are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that by this word we are to understand the priests of the false gods, and in particular the worshippers of fire; because they were, as they say, drest in black; or perhaps the Hebrews gave them this name in derision, because, as they were continually employed in taking care about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and keeping up the fire, they were always as black as smiths or colliers. We find priests, among those of Isis, called melanephoroi, that is to say, that wear black; but whether this may be by reason of their dresting in black, or whether it were because they wore a certain shining black veil in the processions of this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, is not certain. Camar, in Arabic, signifies the "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>." Isis is the same deity. Grotius thinks the Roman priests, called camilli, came from the Hebrew chamarim. Those among the heathens who sacrificed to the infernal gods were drest in black.

CHAMBER

Pages 401-402

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, a member of a lodging, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> piece of an apartment, ordinarily intended for sleeping in; and called by the Latins cubiculum. The word comes from the Latin camera; and that, according to Nicod, from the Greek xauwev, vault or curve; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> chamber being originally confined to places arched over. A complete apartment is to consist of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, anti-chamber, chamber, and cabinet. Privy Chamber. Gentlemen of the privy chamber, are servants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, who are to wait and attend on him and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, in their diversions, &c. Their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> is forty-eight, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chamberlain, twelve of whom are in quarterly waiting, and two of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the privy chamber. In the absence of the lord chamberlain, or vice chamberlain, they execute the king's orders; at coronations, two of them personate the dukes of Aquitain and Normandy; and fix of them, appointed by the lord chamberlain, attend ambassadors from crowned heads to their audiences, and in public entries. The gentlemen of the privy chamber were instituted by Henry VII. Chamber, in Policy, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where certain assemblies are held, also the assemblies themselves. Of these some are established for the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, others for commercial affairs. Of the first kind are, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">Star</a> chamber, so called because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> was painted with stars; the authority, power, and jurisdiction of which, are absolutely abolished by the statute 17 Car. I. 2. Imperial chamber of Spire; the supreme court of judicatory in the empire, erected by Maximilian I. This chamber has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of judging by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>; and is the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of all civil affairs of the states and subjects of the empire, in the same manner as the aulic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. Chamber. Nevertheless it is restrained in several <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>: it takes no notice of matrimonial causes, these being left to the pope; nor of criminal causes, which either belong to particular princes or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in their respective territories, or are cognizable by all the states of the empire in a diet. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Olmberg, in 1648, fifty assessors were appointed for this chamber, whereof 24 were to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and 26 Catholics; besides five presidents, two of them Protestants, and the rest Catholics. 3. Chamber of accounts, a sovereign court in France, where accounts are rendered of all the king's revenues, inventories, and avowals thereof registered; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of fidelity taken, and other things relating to the finances transacted. There are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in France: that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>; it registers proclamations, treaties of peace, naturalizations, titles of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, &c. All the members wear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> gowns of velvet, of satin, or damask, according to their places. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> chambers in France, which judge by appeal of differences about collecting the tythes. 5. Chamber of audience, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> chamber, a jurisdiction in each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of France, the counsellors of which are called jugeurs, or judges, as those of the chamber of inquests are called raporteurs, reporters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. 6. Chamber of the edict, or miaparty, a court established by virtue of the edict of pacification in favour of those of the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. This chamber is now suppressed. 7. Apostolical chamber of Rome, that wherein affairs relating to the revenues of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and the pope are transacted. This council consists of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> camerlenga, the governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTA">rota</a>, a treasurier, an auditor, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, one advocate-general, a solicitor-general, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> and twelve clerks. 8. Chamber of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, an apartment in Guildhall, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is deposited. Of the last sort are, the chambers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>: the chambers of assurance; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> or syndical chamber of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a> in France. 1. The chamber of commerce is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and traders, where the affairs relating to trade are treated of. There are several established in most of the chief cities of France; and in our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> we have lately seen chambers of this kind erected, particularly in London, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and Glasgow. 2. Chamber of assurance in France, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of merchants and others for carrying one the business of insuring; but in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> it signifies a court of justice, where causes relating to insurances are tried. 3. Chamber of booksellers in Paris, an assembly consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNDIC">syndic</a> and assistants, elected by four delegates from the printers, and twelve from the booksellers, to visit the books imported from abroad, and to search the houses of sellers of marbled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, print-sellers, and dealers in printed paper for hangings, who are prohibited from keeping any letters proper for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> books. In the visitation of books, which ought to be performed by three persons at least from among the syndic and assistants, all libels against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of God, and the welfare of the state, and all books printed either within or without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of their regulations and privileges, are kept, even with the merchandises that may happen to be in the bales with such libels or other prohibited books. Chamber, The days appointed for this chamber to meet are Tuesdays and Fridays, at two o'clock in the afternoon. Chamber, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs. 1. Powder chamber, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a> chamber; a place sunk under ground for holding the powder, or bombs, where they may be out of danger, and secured from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. 2. Chamber of a mine; the place, most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of a cubical form, where the powder is confined. 3. Chamber of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>; that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the chafe, much narrower than the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, where the powder lies. It is of different forms; sometimes like a reversed cone; sometimes globular, with a neck for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the cylinder, whence it is called a bot-tled chamber; but most commonly cylindrical, that being the form which is found by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to carry the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> to the greatest distance.

CHAMBERLAIN

Pages 402-402

an officer <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with the management and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a chamber. See CHAMBER, in policy. There are almost as many kinds of chamberlains as chambers; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> whereof are as follows: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Chamberlain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; the fifth great officer of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; to whom belong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> and lodging in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and there are certain fees due to him from each archbishop <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bishop when they perform their homage to the king, and from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> at their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> or doing their homage. At the coronation of every king, he is to have forty ells of crimson velvet for his own robes. This officer, on the coronation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, is to bring the king his shirt, coif, and wearing clothes; and after the king is drest, he claims his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and all the furniture of his chamber, for his fees: he also carries, at the coronation, the coif, gloves, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, to be used by the king on that occasion; also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and scabbard; the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> to be offered by the king, and the robes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> and crown: he drestes and undrestes the king on that day, waits on him before and after dinner, &c. To this officer belongs the care of providing all things in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; to him also belongs the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Westminster; he dispenses likewise of the sword of state, to be carried before the king, to what lord he pleases. The great chamberlain of Scotland was ranked by King Malcolm, as the third great officer of the crown, and was called Camerarius Domini Regis. Before a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> was appointed, it was his duty to collect the revenue of the crown; and he disbursed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> necessary for the king's expenses, and the maintenance of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>. From the time that a treasurer was appointed, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> was limited to the boroughs throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, where he was a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> general, as he had a power for judging of all crimes committed within the borough, and of the crime of foretelling. He was to hold chamberlain ayres every year. He was supreme judge; nor could any of his decrees be questioned by any inferior judicatory. His sentences were put in execution by the magistrates of the boroughs. He also regulated the prices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> within the borough, and the fees of the workmen in the mint house. His salary was only £200. a-year. The finalness of his salary, and his great powers, had no doubt been the causes of much oppreßion in this officer, and the chamberlain ayres was called rather a legal robbery than a court of justice; and when the combined lords feigned King James VI. August 24. 1582, and carried him to Ruthven Castle, they issued a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> in the king's name, discharging the chamberlain ayres to be kept. The chamberlain had great fees arising from the profits of elecheats, fines, tolls, and customs. This office was granted heritably to the family of Stuart <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lenox: and when their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> line failed, King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. conferred it in like manner upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son, whom he created duke of Monmouth, and on his forfeiture it went to the duke of Lenox; but that family surrendered the office to the crown in 1793. Lord Chamberlain of the Household, an officer who has the oversight and direction of all officers belonging to the king's chambers, except the precinct of the king's bedchamber. He has the oversight of the officers of the wardrobe at all his majesty's houses, and of the removing wardrobes, or of beds, tents, revels, music, comedians, hunting, messengers, &c. retained in the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. He moreover has the oversight and direction of the serjeants at arms, of all physicians, apothecaries, surgeons, barbers, the king's chaplains, &c., and administers the oath to all officers above stairs. Other chamberlains are those of the king's court of exchequer, of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, &c. in which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> this officer is generally the receiver of all rents and revenues belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> whereof he is chamberlain. In the exchequer there are two chamberlains, who keep a controlment of the pells of receipts and exitus, and have certain keys of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, records, &c. Chamberlain of London keeps the city money, which is laid up in the chamber of London: he also presides over the affairs of masters and apprentices, and makes free of the city, &c. His office lasts only a year; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> usually obtains to re-choose the same person, unless charged with any misdemeanor in his office.

CHAMBERLAYNE

Pages 402-403

JOHN, son to the author of "The Present State of England," and continuator of that useful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, was admitted into Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, 1685; but it doth not appear that he took any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. Beside the Continuation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, he was author of "Dissertations historical, critical, theological, and moral, on the most memorable events of the Old and New Testaments, with Chronological Tables;" one vol. Chambery, vol. folio; and translated a variety of works from the French, Dutch, and other languages. He likewise was F. R. S. and communicated some pieces, inserted in the Philosophical Transactions. It was said of him that he understood fifteen languages; but it is certain that he was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the Greek, Latin, French, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> and Low Dutch, Portuguese, and Italian. Though he was qualified for employment, he had none but that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> usher to George <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. After a useful and well-spent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he died in the year 1724. He was a very pious and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> in promoting the advancement of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of true Christianity; for which purpose he kept a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> correspondence abroad.

CHAMBERS

Pages 403-403

Ephraim, author of the Scientific <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> which goes under his name, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Westmorland. His parents were dissenters of the Presbyterian persuasion; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> no other than that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> one which is intended to qualify a youth for trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. When he became of a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he was put apprentice to Mr Senex the globe-maker, a business which is connected with literature, and especially with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>. It was during Mr Chambers's residence with this skilful mechanic, that he contracted that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for science and learning which accompanied him through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and directed all his pursuits. It was even at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that he formed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the "Cyclopedia;" and some of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of it were written behind the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>. Having conceived the idea of so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> an undertaking, he justly concluded that the execution of it would not confit with the avocations of trade; and therefore he quitted Mr Senex, and took chambers at Gray's Inn, where he chiefly resided during the rest of his days. The first edition of the Cyclopaedia, which was the result of many years intense application, appeared in 1728, in two vols. folio. It was published by subscription, the price being 4l. 4s.; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of subscribers was very respectable. The dedication, which was to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, is dated October 15, 1727. The reputation that Mr Chambers acquired by his execution of this undertaking, procured him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being elected F. R. S. November 6, 1729. In less than ten years time a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition became necessary; which accordingly was printed, with corrections and additions, in 1738; and was followed by a third the very next year. Although the Cyclopaedia was the grand business of Mr Chambers's life, and may be regarded as almost the sole foundation of his fame, his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was not wholly confined to this undertaking. He was concerned in a periodical publication, entitled, "The Literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>," which was begun in 1735. In this work he wrote a variety of articles, and particularly a review of Morgan's "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">Moral <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>."
