There is another fish not unlike this, called cannadella, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather channadella, which at Marfeilles is known by the name of charina.

CHANNEL

Pages 412-412

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a narrow sea between two continents; or between a continent and an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Such are the British channel, St George's channel, the channel of Constantinople, &c. CHANNEL of a ship. See Chain-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. CHAN-si, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and one of the smallest in the empire, is bounded on the east by Petcheli, on the south by Honan, on the west by Chen-fu, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> wall. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is healthful.

CHANTILLY

Pages 412-413

a village in France, about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where there is a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> and fine forest formerly belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a>.

CHANTOR

Pages 413-413

a finger of a choir in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. The word is almost grown obsolete, chorister <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> singing-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> being <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used instead of it. All <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> chapters have chantors and chaplains to assist the canons, and officiate in their absence. CHANTOR is used by way of excellence for the precentor or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the choir, which is one of the first dignities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>. At St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, where there is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, he is next in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> to the bishop. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> called the chantor primicerius cantorum. To him belonged the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the deacons and other inferior officers. Chantors, in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, were a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Levites employed in singing the praises of God, and playing upon instruments before his altar. They had no habits distinct from the rest of the people; yet in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of removing the ark to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s temple, the chantors appeared drested in tunics of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BYSSUS">byssus</a> or fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. 2 Chron. v. 12.

CHANTRY

Pages 413-413
or CHAUNTRY, was anciently a church or chapel endowed with lands, or other yearly revenue, for the maintenance of one or more priests, daily saying or singing mass for the souls of the donors, and such others as they appointed. Hence chauntry-rents are rents paid to the crown by the tenants or purchasers of chauntry-lands.

CHAOLGY

Pages 413-413

the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>. See Chaos. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, in his chaology, sets forth the different alterations, secretions, and diverse forms, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> went through till it became inhabitable, which amounts to the same with what we otherwise call cosmogony. Dr Burnet, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, represents the chaos as it was at first, entire, undivided, and universally rude and deformed; or the tohu bohu; then shows how it came to be divided into its respective regions; how the homogeneous matter gathered itself apart from all of a contrary principle; and lastly, how it hardened and became a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> habitable globe. See Earth.

CHAOS

Pages 413-414

that confusion in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> lay when newly produced out of nothing at the beginning of the world, before God, by his almighty word, had put it into the order and condition wherein it was after the six days <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>. Chaos is represented by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> as the first principle, ovum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seed of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and the world. All the sophists, fages, naturalists, philosophers, theologues, and poets, held that chaos was the eldest and first principle, το αρχαιον και. The Barbarians, Phoenicians, Egyptians, Persians, &c. all refer the origin of the world to a rude, mixed, confused <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of matter. The Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a>, Aridophanes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>, and the writers of the Cyclic Poems, all speak of the first chaos; the Ionic and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> philosophers build the world out of it. The Stoics hold, that as the world was first made of a chaos, it shall at last be reduced to a chaos; and that its periods and revolutions in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> are only transitions from one chaos to another. Lastly, The Latins, as Ennius, Varro, Ovid, Lucretius, Statius, &c. are all of the same Nor is there any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> whatever that does not derive their *diaorunias*, the structure of the world, from a chaos. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> first arose among the Barbarians, whence it spread to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> and other nations. Dr Burnet observes, that besides <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and a few other Pseudo-Pythagoreans, nobody ever asserted that our world was always from eternity of the same nature, form, and structure, as at present; but that it had been the standing opinion of the wise men of all ages, that what we now call the terrestrial globe, was originally an unformed, indigested mass of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> matter, called *chaos*; and no more than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> and materials of the present world. It does not appear who first broached the notion of a chaos. Moses, the eldest of all writers, derives the origin of this world from a confusion of matter, dark, void, deep, without form, which he calls *tobu bohu*; which is precisely the chaos of the Greek and Barbarian philosophers. Moses goes no further than the chaos, nor tells us whence it took its origin, or whence its confused state; and where Moses stops, there precisely do all the rest. Dr Burnet endeavours to show that as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, &c., who wrote of the cosmogony, acknowledged a chaos for the principle of their world; so the divines, or writers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOGONY">theogony</a>, derive the origin or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of their fabled gods from the same principle. Mr Whiston supposed the ancient chaos, the origin of our earth, to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> of a comet; which, though new, yet, all things considered, is not the most improbable assertion. He endeavours to make it out by many arguments, drawn from the agreement which appears to be between them. So that, according to him, every planet is a comet, formed into a regular and lasting <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and placed at a proper distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, revolving in a nearly circular orbit; and a comet is a planet either beginning to be destroyed or re-made; that is, a chaos or planet uniformed or in its primeval state, and placed as yet in an orbit very eccentric. *Chaos*, in the phrase of Paracelcus, imports the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. It has also some other significations amongst the alchemists. *Chaos*, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of vermes zoophyta. The body has no shell or covering, and is capable of reviving after being dead to appearance for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time: it has no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> organs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>. There are five <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, mostly obtained by infusions of different vegetables in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and only discoverable by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. See *Ani-malcule*.

CHAPEAU

Pages 414-414

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> worn by dukes, being scarlet-coloured velvet on the outside, and lined with a fur. It is frequently borne above a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> instead of a wreath, under gentlemen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>.

CHAPEL

Pages 414-414

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of divine worship, so called. The word is derived from the Latin *capella*. In former times, when the kings of France were engaged in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, they always carried St Martin's hat into the field, which was kept in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a> as a precious relic; from whence the place was called *capella*; and the priests, who had the custody of the tent, *capellani*. Afterwards the word *capella* became applied to private Chapels. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> there are several sorts of chapels. 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">Parish</a> chapels: these differ from parish churches only in name; they are generally small, and the inhabitants within the district few. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> there be a presentation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> ecclesiam instead of *capellam*, and an admission and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> upon it, it is no longer a chapel, but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. 2. Chapels, which adjoin to, and are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the church: such were formerly built by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> persons, as burying places for themselves and their families. 3. Chapels of ease: these are usually built in very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> parishes, where all the people cannot conveniently repair to the mother church. 4. Free chapels; such as were founded by kings of England. They are free from all episcopal jurisdiction, and only to be visited by the founder and his successors; which is done by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>: yet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> may license any subject to build and endow a chapel, and by letters patent exempt it from the visitation of the ordinary. 5. Chapels in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, belonging to particular colleges. 6. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">Domestic</a> chapels, built by noblemen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gentlemen for the private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of God in their families. See CHAPLAIN. CHAPLAIN is also a name given to a printer's workhouse; because, according to some authors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> was first actually performed in chapels or churches; or, according to others, because Caxton, an early printer, exercised the art in one of the chapels in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they say, the orders or laws of the chapel, the secrets of the chapel, &c. Knights of the Chapel, called also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">Poor</a> knights of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, were instituted by Henry VIII. in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>. Their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> was at first thirteen, but has been since augmented to 26. They assist in the funeral services of the kings of England: they are subject to the office of the canons of Windsor, and live on pensions assigned them by the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a>. They bear a blue or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> cloak, with the arms of St George on the left shoulder.

CHAPELAIN

Pages 414-414

JAMES, an eminent French poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1595, and often mentioned in the works of Balzac, Menage, and other learned men. He wrote several works, and at length distinguished himself by a heroic poem called *La Pucelle, ou France Deliverée*, which employed him several years; and which raising the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of the public, was as much decried by some as extolled by others. He was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s counsellors; and died in 1647, very rich, but was very covetous and fordid.

CHAPELET

Pages 414-414

in the manege, a couple of stirrup-leathers, mounted each of them with a stirrup, and joined at top in a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> buckle, called the head of the chapelet, by which they are made fast to the pommel of the saddle, after being adjusted to the rider's length and bore. They are used both to avoid the trouble of taking up <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> letting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the stirrups every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> mounts on a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and saddle, and to supply the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the academy saddles, which have no stirrups to them.

CHAPELLE

Pages 414-415

CLAUDIUS EMANUEL LUILIER, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of Francis Luillier, took the name of Chapelle from a village between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> and St Denys, where he was born. He distinguished himself by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> small pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, in which he discovered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> delicacy. Chaperon delicacy, an easy turn, and an admirable felicity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. He was the friend of Gaffendi and Moliere; and died in 1686.

CHAPERON

Pages 415-415

CHAPERONNE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> CHAPEROON, properly signifies a sort of hood or covering for the head, anciently worn both by men and women, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> and the populace, and afterwards appropriated to the doctors and licentiates in colleges, &c. Hence the name passed to certain little shields, and other funeral devices, placed on the foreheads of the horses that drew the hearse in pompous funerals, and which are still called chaperoons or hofferoons; because such devices were originally fastened on the chaperonner, or hoods, worn by those horses with their other coverings of state. CHAPERON of a bit-mouth, in the manege, is only used for fatch-mouths, and all others that are not cannon-mouths, signifying the end of the bit that joins to the branch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> by the banquet. In fatch-mouths the chaperon is round, but in others it is oval: and the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> that in fatch and other mouths is called chaperon, is in cannon-mouths called frongeau.

CHAPITERS

Pages 415-415

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, formerly signified a summary of such matters as were inquired of, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> presented before justices in eyre, justices of assize, or of the peace, in their sessions. Chapiters, at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, denotes such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> as are delivered by the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> to the inquest.

CHAPLAIN PROPERLY

Pages 415-415

N properly signifies a person provided with a chapel, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> who discharges the duty thereof. CHAPLAIN is also used for an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> person, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, or a person of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, who officiates in their chapels, &c. In England there are 48 chaplains to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, who wait four each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, preach in the chapel, read the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the family, and to the king in his private oratory, and say <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> in the absence of the clerk of the closet. While in waiting they have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> and attendance, but no salary. In Scotland the king has six chaplains, with a salary of 50l. each, three of them having in addition the deanery of the chapel <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> divided between them, making up above 100l. to each. The only duty at present is to say prayers at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> for Scotland to fit in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>.—According to a statute of Henry VIII., the persons vested with a power of retaining chaplains, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> each is allowed to qualify, is as follows: An archbishop, eight; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> or bishop, six; marquis or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a>, five; viscount, four; baron, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, three; a duke, marchioness, countess, baroness, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> and comptroller of the king's house, clerk of the closet, the king's secretary, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of the chapel, almoner, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the rolls, each of them two; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the king's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, and warden of the cinque-ports, each one. All these chaplains may purchase a licence or dispensation, and take two benefices in cure of souls. A chaplain must be retained by letters testimonial under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; for it is not sufficient that he serve as chaplain in the family. The first chaplains are said to have been those instituted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kings of France, for preserving the chape, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a>, with the other relics of St Martin, which the kings kept in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and carried out with them to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The first chaplain is said to have been Gul. de Mesmes, chaplain to St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>. CHAPLAIN in the order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, is used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> or class in that order; otherwise called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANO">diano</a>. The knights make the first class, and the chaplains the second. CHAPLAINS of the Pope, are the auditors, or judges of cause in the sacred palace; so called, because the pope anciently gave audience in his chapel, for the decision of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> sent from the several parts of Christendom. He hither summoned as affilors the most learned lawyers of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and they hence acquired the appellation of capellani, chaplains. It is from the decrees formerly given by these that the body of decrets is composed: their number Pope Sixtus IV. reduced to twelve. Some say, the shrines of relics were covered with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a> cape, or capella, i.e. little cape; and that hence the priests, who had the care of them, were called chaplains. In time these relics were repolished in a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, either contiguous to a larger or separate from it; and the same name, capella, which was given to the cover, was also given to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it was lodged: and hence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> who superintended it came to be called chaplain.

CHAPLET

Pages 415-415

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ornament for the head, like a garland <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wreath: but this word is frequently used to signify the circle of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. There are instances of its being borne in a coat of arms, as well as for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>; the paternal arms for Lafulles are argent, three chaplets, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULES">gules</a>.

CHAPLET ALSO

Pages 415-421

T also denotes a string of beads used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of their prayers. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of it is ascribed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the hermit, who probably learned it of the Turks, as they owe it to the East Indians. Chaplets are sometimes called pater-nothers; and are made of coral, of diamonds, of wood, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAPLET">chaplet</a> contains 50 ave-marias, and five pater-nothers. There is also a chaplet of our Saviour, consisting of 33 beads, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his 33 years living on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, instituted by Father Michael the Camaldulian. The Orientals have a kind of chaplets which they call chains, and which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in their prayers, rehearsing one of the perfections of God on each link <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> head. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul is said to have 18 of these chains, all precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; some diamonds, others rubies, pearls, &c. The Turks have likewise chaplets, which they bear in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, or hang at the girdle; but Father Dandini observes, they differ from those used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, in that they are all of the same bignefs, and have not that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> into decades, though they consist of six decades, or 60 heads. He adds, that the Musselmans run over the chaplet almost in an instant, the prayers being extremely short, as containing only these words, "praise to God," or "<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> to God," for each bead. Besides the common chaplet they have likewise a larger one consisting of 100 beads, where there is some distinction, as being being divided by little threads into three parts; on one of which they repeat 30 times "souhban Allah," i.e., "God is worthy to be praised;" on another, "ellamb Allah," "glory be to God;" and on the third, "Allah echer," "God is great." These thrice thirty times making only 90; to complete the number 100, they add other prayers for the beginning of the chaplet.—He adds, that the Mahometan chaplet appears to have had its rise from the mea beracoth, or "hundred benedictions," which the Jews are obliged to repeat daily, and which we find in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> books; the Jews and Mahometans having this in common, that they scarce do any thing without pronouncing some laud or benediction. Menage derives the word chaplet from chapeau, "hat." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Latins call it chappellina, the Italians more frequently corona. Chaplet, or Chapelet, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a little moulding, cut or carved into round beads, pearls, olives, or the like. Chapman, George, born in 1557, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> highly esteemed in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for his dramatic and poetical works. He wrote 17 plays; translated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> and some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets; and was thought no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> genius. He died in 1634; and was buried in St Giles's in the Fields, where his friend Inigo Jones erected a monument to him. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPPE">Chappe</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the dividing an escutcheon by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> drawn from the centre of the upper edge to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> below, into three parts, the sections on the sides being of different metal or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> from the rest. Chappel in Frith, a market town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, about 26 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 50' N. Lat. 53° 22'. Chapel, William, a learned and pious bishop of Cork, Cloyne, and Rofs in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, born in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a> in 1582. When the troubles began under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. he was persecuted by the puritan party in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and retired to Derby, where he devoted himself to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1649. He wrote Methodus Concionandi, i.e. "the Method of Preaching," and he is one of those to whom the Whole Duty of Man has been attributed. He left behind him also his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> written by himself in Latin, which has been twice printed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">Chapter</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> polity, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of clergymen belonging to the cathedrals and collegiate churches. It was in the eighth century that the body of canons began to be called a chapter. The chapter of the canons of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> were a standing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> to the bishop, and, during the vacancy of the see, had the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. In the earlier ages, the bishop was head of the chapter; afterwards abbots and other dignitaries, as deans, provosts, treasurers, &c. were preferred to this distinction. The deans and chapters had the privilege of choosing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> in England; but Henry VIII. got this power vested in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and as the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> expelled the monks from the cathedrals, and placed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> canons in their room, those he thus regulated were called deans and chapters of the new foundation; such are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, Carlisle, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a>. Chapter, in matters in literature, a division in a book for keeping the subject treated of more clear and distinct. Char, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Salmo. Chara. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Charabon, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town on the northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a> in the East Indies. E. Long. 10° 8'. S. Lat. 6°. Characene, the most southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Susiana, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, lying on the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, between the Tigris and the Eulaeus. It was so named from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Chorax, called first <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, from its founder Alexander the Great; afterwards Antiochia, from Antiochus V. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, who repaired and beautified it; and lastly, Chorax Spafine, or Pafine, that is, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLE">Mole</a> of the Spafines, an Arabian king of that name having secured it against the overflowing of the Tigris, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> or mole, extending three miles, which served as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> to all that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Dionysius Periegetes, and Hidorus, author of the Parthae Manfones, were both natives of this city. The small district of Characene was seized by Pafines, the son of Sogdonacus, king of the neighbouring Arabs, during the troubles of Syria, and erected into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Lucian calls him Hylpafines, and adds, that he ruled over the Characeni and the neighbouring people: he died in the 85th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The other kings of this country we find mentioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> are, Teræus, who died in the 92d year of his age, and after him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTABAZUS">Artabazus</a> the seventh, as Lucian informs us, who was driven from the throne by his own subjects, but restored by the Parthians. And this is all we find in the ancients relating to the kings of Characene. Character, in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies a mark or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, drawn on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, metal, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, graver, chisel, or other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, to signify or denote any thing. The word is Greek, χαρακτηρισμος, formed from the verb, χαρακτηριζω, inculpere, "to engrave, impress," &c. The various kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> may be reduced to three heads, viz. Literal Characters, Numerical Characters, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">Abbreviations</a>. I. Literal Character, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>, serving to indicate some articulate <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, expressive of some idea or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of the mind. See Alphabet. 1. They may be divided, with regard to their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and use, into Nominal Characters, or those we properly call letters; which serve to express the names of things: See Letter. Real Characters; those that instead of names express things and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>: See Idea, &c. Emblematical or Symbolical Characters: which have this in common with real ones, that they express the things themselves; but have thus further, that they in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> personate them, and exhibit their form: such are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a> of the ancient Egyptians. See Hieroglyphic, Symbol, &c. 2. Literal Characters may be again divided, with regard to their invention and use, into particular and general or universal. Particular Characters, are those peculiar to this or that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Such are the Roman, Italic, Greek, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Arabic, Gothic, Chinese, &c. characters.—See Hebrew, Gothic, Chinese, &c. Universal Characters, are also real characters, and make what some authors call a Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a>. That diversity of characters used by the several nations to express the same idea, is found the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> obstacle to the advancement of learning: to remove this, several authors have taken occasion to propose plans of characters that should be universal, and which each people should read in their own language. The character here is to be real, not nominal; to express things and notions; not, as the common ones, letters or sounds: yet to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>, like letters, and arbitrary; not emblematical, like hieroglyphics. Thus, every nation should retain its own language, yet every one understand that of each other, without learning it; only by seeing a real or universal character, which should signify the same things to all people, by what sounds forever each expresses it in their particular idiom. For instance, by seeing the character defined to signify to drink, an Englishman should read to drink; a Frenchman, boire; a Latin, bibere; a Greek, πίνω; a Jew, יין; a German, trinken; and so of the rest: in the same manner as seeing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, each people expresses it after their own manner; but all mean the same animal. This real character is no chimera; the Chinese and Japanese have already something like it. They have a common character which each of those nations understand alike in their several languages; though they pronounce them with such different sounds, that they do not understand one another in speaking. The first and most considerable attempts for a real character, or philosophical language, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, are those of Bishop Wilkins and Dalgarno: but these, with how much art forever they were contrived, have yet proved ineffectual. M. Leibnitz had some thoughts the same way; he thinks those great men did not <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> method. It was probable, indeed, that by their means, people, who do not understand one another might easily have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> together; but they have not hit on true real characters. According to him, the characters should resemble those used in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>: which, in effect, are very simple, yet very expressive; without anything superfluous or equivocal; and contain all the varieties required. The real character of Bishop Wilkins has its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> applause: Dr. Hook recommends it on his own knowledge and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, as a most excellent scheme; and to engage the world to the study thereof, publishes some fine inventions of his own therein. M. Leibnitz tells us, he had under consideration an alphabet of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> thoughts; in order to a new philosophical language, on his own scheme: but his death prevented its being brought to maturity. M. Lodwig, in the Philosophical Transactions, gives us a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of an universal alphabet or character of another kind: this was to contain an enumeration of all such single sounds, or letters, as are used in any language; by means whereof, people should be enabled to pronounce truly and readily any language; to describe the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> of any language that shall be pronounced in their hearing, so as others accustomed to this language, though they had never heard the language pronounced, shall at first be able truly to pronounce it: and, lastly, this character to serve as a standard to perpetuate the sounds of any language. In the Journal Litteraire, an. 1720, we have a very ingenious project for an universal character. The author, after obviating the objections that might be made against the feasibility of such schemes in the general, proposes his own: his characters are to be the common Arabic, or numeral figures. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of these <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> are sufficient to express distinctly an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of numbers, much more than we shall need terms to signify our actions, goods, evils, duties, passions, &c. Thus is all the trouble of framing and learning any new character at once saved; the Arabic figures having already all the universality required. The advantages are immense. For, too, we have here a stable, faithful interpreter; never to be corrupted or changed, as the popular languages continually are. Whereas the difficulty of pronouncing a foreign language is such as usually gives the learner the greatest trouble, and there are even some sounds which foreigners never attain to: in the character here proposed, this difficulty has no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: every nation is to pronounce them according to the particular pronunciation that already obtains among them. All the difficulty is, the accustoming the pen and the eye to affix certain notions to characters that do not, at first sight, exhibit them. But this trouble is no more than we find in the study of any language whatever. The inflections of words are here to be expressed by the common letters. For instance, the same character shall express a filly or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLT">colt</a>, a horse or a mare, an old horse or an old mare, as accompanied with this or that distinctive letter, which shall show the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, youth, maturity, or old age: a letter also to express the bigness or size of things; thus e.g., a man with this or that letter, to signify a great man, or a little man, &c. The use of those letters belongs to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>; which, once well understood, would abridge the vocabulary exceedingly. An advantage of this grammar is, that it would only have one declension and one conjugation: those numerous anomalies of grammarians are exceeding troublesome; and arise hence, that the common languages are governed by the populace, who never reason on what is best: but in the character here proposed, men of sense having the introduction of it, would have a new ground, whereon to build regularly. A new universal character has been proposed by Mr Northmore of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, by which different nations may communicate their sentiments to each other. His original plan was, to make the same numerical figure represent the same word in all languages. But he found afterwards that it might be improved, by using a figure not for every word, but every useful word. And even these he thinks might be abbreviated by adopting certain uniform fixed signs, the number of which would not exceed 20, for the various parts of speech. Words of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATION">negation</a>, he proposed, to be expressed by a prefixed sign. A few instances <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> explain the author's meaning. Suppose the number 5 to represent the word see, | Number | Meaning | |--------|---------| | 6 | a man | | 7 | happy | | 8 | never | | 9 | I | "I..." I would then (says he) express the tenses, genders, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, &c., in all languages, in some such uniform manner as following: 1. \( \text{present tense} \) 2. \( \text{perfect tense} \) 3. \( \text{perfect participle} \) 4. \( \text{present participle} \) 5. \( \text{future} \) 6. \( \text{substantive} \) 7. \( \text{personal substantive} \) 8. \( \text{nominative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>} \) 9. \( \text{genitive} \) 10. \( \text{dative} \) 11. \( \text{<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMININE">feminine</a>} \) 12. \( +\text{plural} \) 13. \( \text{positive} \) 14. \( \text{comparative} \) 15. \( \text{superlative} \) 16. \( -\text{negation} \) Thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> \( \text{plu} \) be the appellation or the sign of characters, the plural number, six, nine, four, three, plu will be horse. Thus (says our author), I hope, it is evident that about 30 or 40 distinct syllables are sufficient for the above purpose; but I am much mistaken if eleven only will not answer the same end. This is to be done by substituting the first 20 or 30 numerals for the signs, and saying, as in algebra, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is in the power of such a number, which may be expressed by the simple word under. Ex. gr. Let 6943 represent the word horse; and suppose 4 to be the sign of the plural number, I would write the word thus, \( \text{6943}^4 \); and pronounce it, fix, nine, four, three, in the power of or under four. By these means eleven distinct appellations would be sufficient, and time and use would much abbreviate the pronunciation. But the difficulty is not in inventing the most simple, easy, and commodious character, but in engaging the several nations to use it; there being nothing they agree less in, than the understanding and pursuing their common <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. 3. Literal characters may again be divided, with respect to the nations among whom they have been invented, into Greek characters, Roman characters, Hebrew characters, &c. The Latin character now used through all Europe, was formed from the Greek, as the Greek was from the Phoenician; and the Phoenician, as well as the Chaldee, Syriac, and Arabic characters, were formed from the ancient Hebrew, which subsisted till the Babylonish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>; for after that event the character of the Assyrians, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> Hebrew now in use, prevailed, the ancient being only found on some Hebrew medals, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Samaritan medals. It was in 1091 that the Gothic characters, invented by Ulfila, were abolished, and the Latin ones established in their room. Medallists observe, that the Greek character, consisting only of majuscule letters, has preserved its uniformity on all medals, as low as the time of Gallienus, from which time it appears somewhat weaker and rounder: from the time of Constantine to Michael we find only Latin characters: after Michael, the Greek characters recommence; but from that time they began to alter with the language, which was a mixture of Greek and Latin. The Latin medals preserved both their characters and language as low as the translation of the seat of the empire to Constantinople: towards the time of Decius the character began to lose its roundness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; some time after, it retrieved and subsisted tolerably till the time of Justin, when it degenerated gradually into the Gothic. The rounder, then, and better formed a character is upon a medal, the fairer pretence it has to antiquity. II. Numerical Characters, or characters used to express numbers, are either letters or figures. The Arabic character, called also the common one, because it is used almost throughout Europe in all sorts of calculations, consists of these ten digits, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0. The Roman numeral character consists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> majuscule letters of the Roman alphabet, viz. I, V, X, L, C, D, M. The I denotes one, V five, X ten, L fifty, C a hundred, D five hundred, and M a thousand. The I repeated twice makes two, II; thrice, three, Characters, three, III. Four is expressed thus, IV. as I before V or X takes an unit from the number expressed by these letters. To express six, an I is added to a V, VI.; for seven, two, VII.; and for eight, three, VIII. Nine is expressed by an I before X, thus, IX. The same remark may be made of the X before L or C, except that the diminution is by tens; thus, XL denotes forty, XC ninety, and LX sixty. The C before D or M diminishes each by a hundred. The number five hundred is sometimes expressed by an I before a C <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, thus, IO; and instead of M, which signifies a thousand, an I is sometimes used between two C's, the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, and the other inverted, thus, CID. The addition of C and O before or after raises CID by tens; thus, CCIDO expresses ten thousand, CCCIDO a hundred thousand. The Romans also expressed any number of thousands by a line drawn over any numeral less than a thousand; thus, V denotes five thousand, LX sixty thousand; so likewise MM is one million, MMM is two millions, &c. The Greeks had three ways of expressing numbers: 1. Every letter, according to its place in the alphabet, denoted a number, from α, one, to ω, twenty-four. 2. The alphabet was divided into eight units, α one, β two, γ three, &c.; into eight tens, ι ten, κ twenty, λ thirty, &c.; and eight <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, ο one hundred, π two hundred, ρ three hundred, &c. 3. I stood for one, Π five, Δ ten, Η a hundred, Χ a thousand, Μ ten thousand; and when the letter Π enclosed any of these, except I, it showed the enclosed letter to be five times its value; as, [α] fifty, [ι] five hundred, [κ] five thousand, [λ] fifty thousand. The French Characters used in the chamber of accounts, and by persons concerned in the management of the revenue, is properly speaking, nothing else than the Roman numerals, in letters that are not majuscule: thus, instead of expressing fifty-six by LVI, they denote it by smaller characters, lvj. III. Characters of Abbreviations, &c. In several of the arts, are symbols contrived for the more concise and immediate conveyance of the knowledge of things. For the Characters used in Algebra, see Algebra, Introduction.
