CC characters that distinguish the movements of common time, the first implying slow, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> quick, and the third very quick. ⅓, ⅓, ⅓, ⅓, ⅓, ⅓, characters of simple triple time, the measure of which is equal to three semibreves, or to three minims. ⅔, ⅔, or ⅔, characters of a mixed triple time, where the measure is equal to six crotchets, or six quavers. ⅔, ⅔, or ⅔, or ⅔, or ⅔, or ⅔, characters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> triple time. ⅔, ⅔, ⅔, or ⅔, or ⅔, or ⅔, characters of that species of triple time called the measure of twelve times. Character, in human life, that which is peculiar in the manners of any person, and distinguishes him from all others. Good Character is particularly applied to that conduct which is regulated by virtue and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; in an inferior but very common sense, it is understood of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> honesty of dealing between man and man. The importance of a good character in the commerce of life seems to be universally acknowledged.—To those who are to make their own way either to wealth or honours, a good character is usually no less necessary than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and abilities. To transcribe the observation of an elegant moralist: though human nature is degenerate, and corrupts itself still more by its own inventions; yet it usually retains to the last an esteem for excellence. But even if we are arrived at such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> degree of depravity as to have lost our native reverence for virtue; yet a regard to our own interest and safety, which we seldom lose, will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to apply for aid, in all important transactions, to men whose character integrity is unimpeached. When we choose an assistant, a partner, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, our first inquiry is concerning his character. When we have occasion for a counsellor or attorney, a physician or apothecary, whatever we may be ourselves, we always choose to trust our <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> and persons to men of the best character. When we fix on the tradesmen who are to supply us with necessaries, we are not determined by the sign of the lamb, or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>, or the fox; nor by a shop fitted up in the most elegant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; but by the fairest reputation. Look into a daily newspaper, and you will see, from the highest to the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, how important the characters of the employed appear to the employers. After the advertisement has enumerated the qualities required in the person wanted, there constantly follows, that none need apply who cannot bring an undeniable character. Offer yourself as a candidate for a seat in parliament, be promoted to honour and emolument, or in any respect attract the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of mankind upon yourself, and if you are vulnerable in your character, you will be deeply wounded. This is a general testimony in favour of honesty, which no writings and no practices can possibly refute. Young men, therefore, whose characters are yet unfixed, and who consequently may render them just such as they wish, ought to pay great attention to the first steps which they take on entrance into life. They are usually careless and inattentive to this object. They pursue their own plans with ardour, and neglect the opinions which others entertain of them. By some thoughtless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, they suffer a mark to be impressed upon them, which scarcely any subsequent merit can entirely erase. Every man will find some persons, who, though they are not professed enemies, yet view him with an envious or a jealous eye, and who will gladly revive any tale to which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> has given the slightest foundation. In this turbulent and confused <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, where our words and actions are often misunderstood, and oftener misrepresented, it is indeed difficult even for innocence and integrity to avoid reproach, abuse, contempt, and hatred. These not only hurt our interest and impede our advancement in life, but forcibly afflict the feelings of a tender and delicate mind. It is then the part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> first to do every thing in our power to preserve an irreproachable character, and then to let our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> depend chiefly on the approbation of our own consciences, and on the advancement of our interest in a world where liars shall not be believed, and where slanderers shall receive countenance from none but him who, in Greek, is called, by way of eminence, Diabolus, or the calumniator. Character, in Poetry, particularly the epopee and drama, is the result of the manners or peculiarities by which each person is distinguished from others. The poetical character, says M. Boffu, is not properly any particular virtue or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of several which are mixed together, in a different degree, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> and the unity of the action; there must be one, however, to reign over all the rest; and this must be found, in some degree, in every part. The first quality in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>, is wrath; in Ulysses, dissimulation; and in Aeneas, Character, Æneas, mildness: but as these characters cannot be alone, they must be accompanied with others to embellish them, as far as they are capable, either by hiding their defects, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> of Achilles, which is palliated by extraordinary valour; or by making them centre in some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> virtue, as in Ulysses, whose dissimulation makes a part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>; and in Æneas, whose mildness is employed in a submission to the will of the gods. In the making up of which union, it is to be observed, the poets have joined together such qualities as are by nature the most compatible; valour with anger, piety with mildness, and prudence with dissimulation. The fable required prudence in Ulysses, and piety in Æneas; in this, therefore, the poets were not left to their choice: but Homer might have made Achilles a coward without abating any thing from the justness of this fable; so that it was the necessity of adorning his character, that obliged him to make him valiant: the character, then of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> in the epic poem, is compounded of three sorts of qualities; the first essential to the fable; the second, embellishments of the first; and valour, which sustains the other two, makes the third. Unity of character is as necessary as the unity of the fable. For this purpose a person should be the same from the beginning to the end: not that he is always to betray the same sentiments, or one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; but that he should never speak nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> inconsistently with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> character. For instance, the weak may sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into a warmth, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> of the passionate be calm, a change which often introduces in the drama a very affecting variety: but if the natural disposition of the former was to be represented as boisterous, and that of the latter mild and soft, they would both act out of character, and contradict their persons. True characters are such as we truly and really see in men, or may exist without any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to nature: no man questions but there have been men as generous and as good as Æneas, as passionate and as violent as Achilles, as prudent and wise as Ulysses, as impious and atheistical as Mezentius, and as amorous and passionate as Dido; all these characters, therefore, are true, and nothing but just imitations of nature. On the contrary, a character is false when an author foists it, that one can see nothing like it in the order of nature wherein he designs it shall stand: these characters should be wholly excluded from a poem, because transgressing the bounds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> and reason, they meet with no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> from the readers; they are fictions of the poet's brain, not imitations of nature; and yet all poetry consists of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of nature. Character is also used for certain visible qualities, which claim respect or reverence to those vested therein.—The majesty of kings gives them a character which procures respect from the people. A bishop should sustain his character by learning and solid piety, rather than by worldly lustre, &c. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW_OF_NATIONS">law of nations</a> secures the character of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from all insults. Character, among naturalists, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of the genera of animals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, &c. Characteristic, in general, is that which characterizes a thing or person, i.e. constitutes its character, whereby it is distinguished. See Characteristic, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARADE">Charade</a>. Characteristic, is peculiarly used in grammar, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> letter of a word: which is preserved in most of its tenors and moods, its derivatives and compounds. Characteristic of a Logarithm, is its index or exponent. See Logarithm. Characteristic Triangle of a Curve, in the higher geometry, is a rectilinear right-angled triangle, whose hypotenuse makes a part of the curve, not sensibly different from a right line. It is so called, because curve lines are used to be distinguished hereby. See Curve. Charade, the name of a new species of composition or literary amusement. It owes its name to the idler who invented it. Its subject must be a word of two syllables, each forming a distinct word: and these two syllables are to be concealed in an enigmatical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, first separately, and then together. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of charades, if not greatly instructive, is at least innocent and amusing. At all events, as it has made its way into every fashionable circle, and has employed even Garrick, it will scarcely be deemed unworthy of attention. The fillipines indeed of most that have appeared in the papers under this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, are not only destitute of all pleasantry in the stating, but are formed in general of words utterly unfit for the purpose. They have therefore been treated with the contempt they deserved. In trifles of this nature, inaccuracy is without excuse. The following examples therefore are at least free from this blemish. I. My first, however here abused, Designs the sex alone; In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIA">Cambria</a>, such is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>'s pow'r, 'Tis Jenkin, John, or Joan. My second oft is loudly call'd, When men prepare to fist it: Its name delights the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>; Its force, may none resist it! It binds the weak, it binds the strong, The wealthy and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; Still 'tis to joy a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSPORT">passport</a> deem'd, For sullied fame a cure. It may endure an age of bliss, Yet miseries oft attend it; To fingers, ears, and noses too, Its various lords commend it. My whole may chance to make one drink, Though vended in a fish shop; 'Tis now the monarch of the seas, And has been an archbishop. Her-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>. II. My first, when a Frenchman is learning English, Serves him to swear by. My second, is either hay or corn. My whole, is the delight of the present age; and will be the admiration of posterity. Gar-rick.

CHARAG

Pages 422-422

the tribute which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> and Jews pay to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior. It consists of ten, twelve, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fifteen francs per annum, according to the estate of the party. Men begin to pay it at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or at sixteen years old; women are dispensed with, as also priests, rabbins, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>.

CHARAIMS

Pages 422-422

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Jews in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. They live by themselves, and have a separate synagogue; and as the other Jews are remarkable for their eyes, so are those for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> noses, which run through all the families of this sect. These are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Essenes. They strictly observe the five books of Moses, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>; and receive no written traditions. It is said that the other Jews would join the Charaims; but those not having observed the exact rules of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> with regard to divorces, these think they live in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>. CHARANTIA. See MOMORDICA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CHARBON

Pages 422-422

in the manege, that little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> spot <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mark which remains after a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> spot in the cavity of the corner <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>: about the seventh, or eighth year, when the cavity fills up, the tooth being smooth and equal, it is said to be raised.

CHARCAS

Pages 422-422

the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, remarkable for the silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of Potosi.

CHARCOAL

Pages 422-424

a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> coal, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, consisting of wood half burnt; chiefly used where a clear strong fire, without <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, is required; the humidity of the wood being here mostly dissipated, and exhaled in the fire wherein it is prepared. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> discovers a surprising <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Charcoal pores in charcoal: they are disposed in order, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> it lengthwise; so that there is no piece of charcoal, how <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> soever, but may be easily blown through. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a piece be broken pretty short, it may be seen through with a microscope. In a range the 18th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an inch long, Dr Hook reckoned 150 pores; whence he concludes, that in a charcoal of an inch diameter, there are not less than 5,724,000 pores. It is to this prodigious number of pores, that the blackness of charcoal is owing: for the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> striking on the charcoal, are received and absorbed in its pores, instead of being reflected; whence the body must of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> appear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, blackness in a body being no more than a want of reflection. Charcoal was anciently used to distinguish the bounds of estates and inheritances; as being incorruptible, when let very deep within ground. In effect, it preserves itself so long, that there are many pieces found entire in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tombs of the northern nations. M. Dodart says, there is charcoal made of corn, probably as old as the days of Caesar: he adds, that it has kept so well, that the wheat may be still distinguished from the rye; which he looks on as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of its incorruptibility. The operation of charring wood, is performed in the following manner: The wood intended for this purpose is cut into proper lengths, and piled up in heaps near the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the charcoal is intended to be made: when a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wood is thus prepared, they begin constructing their stacks, for which there are three methods. The first is this: They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> a proper spot of ground, of about 12 or 15 feet in diameter, near the piles of wood; in the centre of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILLET">billet</a> of wood, split across at one end and pointed at the other, is fixed with its pointed extremity in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and two pieces of wood inserted through the clefts of the other end, forming four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>; against these <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> pieces four other billets of wood are placed, one end on the ground, and the other leaning against the angles. This being finished, a number of large and straight billets are laid on the ground to form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, each being as it were the radius of the circular area: on this floor a proper quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> or small wood is strewed, in order to fill up the interstices, when the floor <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be complete; and in order to keep the billets in the same order and position in which they were first arranged, pegs or stumps are driven into the ground in the circumference of the circle, about a foot distant from one another: upon this floor a flage is built with billets set upon one end, but something inclining towards the central billet; and on the tops of these another floor is laid in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, but of shorter billets, as the whole is, when finished, to form a cone. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the stacks for making charcoal is performed in this manner: A long pole is erected in the centre of the area above described, and several small billets ranged round the pole on their ends: the interstices between these billets and the pole is filled with dry brushwood, then a floor is laid, on that a stage in a reclining position, and on that a second floor, &c. in the same manner as described above; but in the lower floor there is a billet larger and longer than the rest, extending from the central Charcoal, central pole to some distance beyond the circumference of the circle. The third method is this: A chimney, or aperture of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> form, is built with billets in the centre, from the bottom to the top; and round these, floors and inclined stages are erected, in the same manner as in the stacks above described, except that the base of this, instead of being circular like the others, is square; and the whole stack, when completed, forms a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>. The stack of either form being thus finished, is coated over with turf, and the surface plastered with a mixture of earth and charcoal dust well tempered together. The next operation is the setting the stack on fire. In order to this, if it be formed according to the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, the central billet in the upper stage is drawn out, and some pieces of very dry and combustible wood are placed in the void space, called, by workmen, the chimney, and fire set to these pieces. If the stack be built according to the second construction, the central pole is drawn out, together with the large horizontal billet above described; and the void space occupied by the latter being filled with pieces of very dry combustible wood, the fire is applied to it at the base of the stack. With regard to the third construction, the square aperture or chimney is filled with small pieces of very dry wood, and the fire applied to it at the top or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">apex</a> of the pyramidal stack. When the stack is set on fire, either at the top or bottom, the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is necessary in the workman; for in the proper management of the fire the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> difficulty attending the art of making good charcoal consists. In order to this, care is taken, as soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> begins to issue some height above the chimney, that the aperture be covered with a piece of turf, but not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> as to hinder the smoke from puffing out; and whenever the smoke appears to issue very thick from any part of the pile, the aperture must be covered with a mixture of earth and charcoal dust. At the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as it is necessary that every part of the stack should be equally burnt, it will be requisite for the workman to open vents in one part and shut them in another. In this manner the fire must be kept up till the charcoal be sufficiently burnt, which will happen in about two days and a half if the wood be dry; but if green, the operation will not be finished in less than three days. When the charcoal is thought to be sufficiently burnt, which is easily known from the appearance of the smoke, and the flames no longer issuing with impetuosity through the vents; all the apertures are to be closed up very carefully with a mixture of earth and charcoal dust, which, by excluding all access of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, prevents the coals from being any further consumed, and the fire goes out of itself. In this condition it is suffered to remain, till the whole is sufficiently cooled; when the cover is removed, and the charcoal is taken away. If the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is skilfully managed, the coals will exactly retain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the pieces of wood: some are said to have been so dexterous as to char an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> without altering even the figure of the feather. There are considerable differences in the coals of different vegetables, in regard to their habitu to fire: the very light coals of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, cotton, some fungi, &c., readily catch fire from a spark, and soon burn out; the more dense ones of woods and roots are set on fire more difficulty, and burn more slowly: the coals of the black berry-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> alder, of the hazel, the willow, and the lime tree, are said to answer best for the making of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> and other pyrotechnical compositions, perhaps from their being easily inflammable: for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of metallic calces those of the heavier woods, as the oak and the beech, are preferable, these seeming to contain a larger proportion of the phlogistic principle, and that, perhaps, in a more fixed state; considered as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fuel, those of the heavy woods give the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and require the most plentiful supply of air to keep them <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>; those of the light woods prefer a glowing heat, without much draught of air, till the coals themselves are consumed; the bark <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> crackles and flies about in burning, which the coal of the wood itself very seldom does. Mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> makers, engravers, &c., find charcoal of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to polish their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> plates after they have been rubbed clean with powdered pumice <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Plates of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> are polishable in the same way, and a glost may be afterwards given with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">tripoli</a>. The coals of different substances are also used as pigments; hence the bone-black, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>-black, &c., of the shops. Most of the paints of this kind, besides their incorruptibility, have the advantage of a full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> freely in all the forms in which powdery pigments are applied; provided they have been carefully prepared, by thoroughly burning the subject in a close vessel, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> the coal into a powder of due fineness. Pieces of charcoal are used also in their entire state for tracing the outlines of drawings, &c.; in which intention they have an excellence, that their mark is easily wiped out. For these purposes, either the finer pieces of common charcoal are picked out and cut to a proper shape; or the pencils are formed of wood, and afterwards burnt into charcoal in a proper vessel well covered. The artists commonly make choice of the smaller branches of the tree freed from the bark and pith; and the willow and vine are preferred to all others. This choice is confirmed by the experiments of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, who has found that the wood of the trunks of trees produces charcoal of a harder <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> than their small twigs or branches; and the hard woods, such as box and guaiacum, produced coals very sensibly harder than the softer woods. Willow he prefers to all others. The shells and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> yielded coals so hard that they would scarce mark on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> at all; while the coals of the kernels of fruits were quite soft and mellow. The several coals produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s experiments were levigated into fine powder, mixed both with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and applied as paints both thin and thick, and diluted with different degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. All of them, when laid on thick, appeared of a strong full black, nor could it be judged that one was of a finer colour than another; diluted with white, or when spread thin, they had all somewhat of a bluish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. Horns and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> both of fishes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> animals, gave coals rather glossier and deeper coloured than vegetables; and which, in general, were very hard, so as difficultly, or not at all, to stain paper. Here also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of the coal seemed to depend on that of the subject from whence it was prepared; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, woollen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, blood, and the fleecy parts of animals, yielded soft coals. Some of these differed from others very sensibly in colour; that of ivory is superior to all the rest, and indisputably the finest of all the charcoal blacks. The animal coals had much less of the bluish cast in them than the vegetable, many of them inclining rather to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. Charred pit coal, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, seemed to have this blueness in a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. For the chemical properties of charcoal see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CHARDIN

Pages 424-424

Sir John, a celebrated traveller, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1643. His father, who was a jeweller, had him educated in the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; after which he travelled into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. He traded in jewels, and died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1713. The account he wrote of his travels is much esteemed.

CHARENTON

Pages 424-424

the name of two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of France, the one upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a> in the Bourbonnais; the other in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, near the confluence of the Marne with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">CHARLES</a> the Lydian, a celebrated statuary, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Lydius; and made the famous Colossus of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>. Flourished 288 years before Christ.

CHARGE

Pages 424-424
or rather Overcharge, in painting, is an exaggerated representation of any person; wherein the likeness is preserved, but at the same time ridiculed. Few painters have the genius necessary to succeed in these charges: the method is, to select and heighten something already amiss in the face, whether by way of defect, or redundancy: thus v.g. if Nature hath given a man a nose a little larger than ordinary, the painter falls in with her, and makes the nose extravagantly long: or if the nose be naturally too short, in the painting it will be a mere stump; and thus of the other parts.

CHARGED

Pages 424-424

in electrical experiments, is when a phial, pane of glass, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other electric substance, properly coated on both sides, has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a> communicated to it; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the one side is always electrified positively, and the other negatively.

CHARIOT

Pages 424-426

a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">coach</a>, having only a seat behind, with a stool before. See Coach. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, were called by the several names of biga, triga, &c., according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of horses applied to draw them. Every chariot carried two men, who were probably the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> and the charioteer; and we read of several men of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> and valour employed in driving the chariot. When the warriors came to encounter in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> fight, they alighted out of the chariot, and fought on foot; but when they were weary, which often happened by reason of their armour, they retired into their chariot, and thence annoyed their enemies with darts and missile weapons. These chariots were made so strong, that they lasted for several generations. Besides this sort, we find frequent mention of the currus falcati, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> those chariots armed with hooks or scythes, with which whole ranks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were cut off together, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had not the art of avoiding the danger; these were not only used by the Persians, Syrians, Egyptians, &c., but we find them among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> cient Britons; and notwithstanding the imperfect state of some of the most necessary arts among that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> before the invasion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, it is certain that they had war chariots in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance. By the Greek and Roman historians, these chariots are described by the six following names: viz. Benna, Petoritum, Currus or Carrus, Covinus, Efedum, and Rheda. The benna seems to have been a chariot designed rather for travelling than war. It contained two persons, who were called combennones, from their fitting together in the same machine. The petoritum seems to have been a larger kind of chariot than the benna; and is thought to have derived its name from the British word ped-war, signifying four; this kind of carriage having four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>. The currus or currus was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a> or waggon. This kind of chariot was used by the ancient Britons, in times of peace, for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and merchandise, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of war, for carrying their baggage, and wives and children, who <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> followed the armies of all the Celtic nations. The covinus was a war chariot, and a very terrible <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of destruction; being armed with sharp scythes and hooks for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> and tearing all who were so unhappy as to come within its reach. This kind of chariot was made very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and had few or no men in it besides the charioteer; being designed to drive with great force and rapidity, and to do execution chiefly with its hooks and scythes. The efedum and rheda were also war chariots, probably of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> size, and stronger made than the covinus, designed for containing a charioteer for driving it, and one or two warriors for fighting. The far greatest number of the British war chariots seem to have been of this kind. These chariots, as already observed, were to be found in great numbers among the Britons; insomuch that Caesar relates, that Cassibelanus, after dismissing all his other forces, retained no fewer than 4000 of these war chariots about his person. The same author relates, that, by continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, they had at last arrived at such perfection in the management of their chariots, that "in the most steep and difficult places they could stop their horses upon full stretch, turn them which way they pleased, run along the pole, rest on the harness, and throw themselves back into their chariots, with incredible dexterity." Chariots, in the heathen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, were sometimes consecrated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; and the Scripture observes, that Josiah burnt those which had been offered to the sun by the kings his predecessors. This superstitious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the heathens, and principally of the Persians, who had horses and chariots consecrated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the sun. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Xenophon, and Quintus Curtius, speak of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> chariots crowned, which were consecrated to the sun, among the Persians, which in their ceremonies were drawn by white horses consecrated to the same luminary. Triumphal Chariot, was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ornaments of the Roman celebration of a victory. The Roman triumphal chariot was generally made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, round like a tower, or rather of a cylindrical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; it was sometimes gilt at the top, and ornamented with crowns; and to represent a victory more naturally, they used to slay it with blood. It was usually drawn by four white horses; but oftentimes by lions, elephants, tygers, bears, leopards, dogs, &c. Charisia, in the heathen <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, a wake, or night festival, instituted in honour of the Graces. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the whole night, most of which time was spent in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>; after which, cakes made of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> flour mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and other sweetmeats, were distributed among the assistants.—Charisia is also sometimes used to signify the sweetmeats used on such occasions. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARISIUS">Charisius</a>, in the heathen theology, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. The word is derived from ἔχειν, gratia, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>" or "favour;" he being the god by whose influence men obtain the favour and affection of one another. On which account the Greeks used at their meals to make a libation of a cup to Jupiter Charisius. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARISTIA">Charistia</a>, a festival of the ancient Romans, celebrated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of February, wherein the relations by blood and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> met, in order to preserve a good correspondence; and that if there happened to be any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> among them, it might be the more easily accommodated by the good humour and mirth of the entertainment. Ovid. Fast. i. 617. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARISTICARY">Charisticary</a>, commendatory, or donatory, a person to whom is given the enjoyment of the revenues of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, or benefice. The Charisticaries among the Greeks, were a kind of donatories, or commendatories, who enjoyed all the revenues of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> and monasteries without giving an account thereof to any person.—The original of this abuse is referred to the Iconoclasts, particularly Constantine Copronymus, the avowed enemy of the monks, whose monasteries he gave away to strangers. In after times, the emperors and patriarchs gave many to people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, not by way of gift to reap any temporal advantage from them, but to repair, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and patronize them. At length avarice crept in, and those in good condition were given away, especially such as were rich; and at last they were all given away, rich and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, those of men and of women, and that to laymen and to married men. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">Charity</a>, among divines, one of the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> theological virtues, consisting in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of God and of our neighbour, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and disposition of loving God with all our heart, and our neighbour as ourselves. Charity is also used for the effect of a moral virtue, which consists in supplying the necessities of others, whether with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, counsel, assistance, or the like. As pecuniary relief is generally the most efficacious, and at the same time that from which we are most apt to excuse ourselves, this branch of the duty merits particular illustration; and a better cannot be offered than what is contained in the following extracts (if we may be permitted to make them) from the elegant Moral System of Archdeacon Paley. Whether pity be an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> or a habit, it is in fact a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which God appointed; and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> cause for which it was appointed, is to afford to the miserable, in the compassion of their fellow-creatures, a remedy for those inequalities and distresses which God foretold that many must be exposed to, under Charity. under every general rule for the distribution of property. The Christian Scriptures are more copious and explicit upon this duty than almost any other. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> which Christ hath left us of the proceedings of the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, establishes the obligation of bounty beyond controversy. "When the Son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a> shall come in his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, and all the holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory, and before him shall be gathered all nations; and he shall separate them one from another. Then shall the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> say unto them on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Come ye blest of my father, inherit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> prepared for you from the foundation of the world: For I was an hungered, and ye gave me meat; I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink; I was a stranger, and ye took me in; naked, and ye clothed me; I was sick, and ye visited me; I was in prison, and ye came unto me. And inasmuch as ye have done it to one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." It is not necessary to understand this passage as a literal account of what <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> actually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> on that day. Supposing it only a scathing description of the rules and principles by which the Supreme Arbiter of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> will regulate his decisions, it conveys the same lesson to us; it equally demonstrates of how great value and importance these duties in the fight of God are, and what stress will be laid upon them. The apostles also describe this virtue as propitiating the divine favour in an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. And these recommendations have produced their effect. It does not appear that, before the times of Christianity, an infirmary, hospital, or public charity of any kind, existed in the world; whereas most countries in Christendom have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> abounded with these institutions. To which may be added, that a spirit of private liberality seems to flourish amidst the decay of many other virtues; not to mention the legal provision for the poor, which obtains in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and which was unknown and unthought of by the most polished nations of antiquity. St Paul adds upon the subject an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; and which is practicable by all who have anything to give. "Upon the first day of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> (or any other stated time) let every one of you lay by in store, as God hath prospered him." By which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> may be understood to recommend what is the very thing wanting with most men, the being charitable upon a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; that is, from a deliberate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of our fortunes with the reasonable expenses and expectations of our families, to compute what we can spare, and to lay by so much for charitable purposes, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> or other. The mode will be a consideration afterwards. The effect which Christianity produced upon some of its converts, was such as might be looked for from a divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> coming with full force and miraculous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> upon the consciences of mankind. It overwhelmed all worldly considerations in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of a more important existence. "And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; neither said any of them that aught of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things in common.—Neither was there any among them that lacked; for as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold, and laid them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> at the apostles feet; and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need." Acts iv. 32. Nevertheless, this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of goods, however it manifested the sincere zeal of the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, is no precedent for our imitation. It was confined to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; continued not long there; was never enjoined upon any (Acts v. 4); and, although it might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> with the particular circumstances of a small and select <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, is altogether impracticable in a large and mixed community. The conduct of the apostles upon the occasion deserves to be noticed. Their followers laid down their fortunes at their feet; but so far were they from taking advantage of this unlimited confidence to enrich themselves or establish their authority, that they soon after got rid of this business as inconsistent with the main object of their mission, and transferred the custody and management of the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> to deacons elected to that office by the people at large (Acts vi.) There are three kinds of charity, our author observes, which prefer a claim to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. 1. The first, and apparently one of the best, is to give stated and considerable sums, by way of pension or annuity to individuals or families, with whose behaviour and distresses we ourselves are acquainted. In speaking of considerable sums, it is meant only, that five pounds, or any other sum, given at once or divided amongst five or fewer families, will do more good than the same sum distributed amongst a greater number in shillings or half crowns; and that, because it is more likely to be properly applied by the persons who receive it. A poor fellow who can find no better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> than to drink his benefactor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and purchase half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>'s recreation for himself, would hardly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a> for any such purpose, or be so improvident as not to lay it by for an occasion of importance, for his rent, his clothing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, or stock of winter's provision. It is a still greater recommendation of this kind of charity, that pensions and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a>, which are paid regularly, and can be expected at the time, are the only way by which we can prevent one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a poor man's sufferings, the dread of want. 2. But as this kind of charity supposes that proper objects of such expensive benefactions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> within our private knowledge and observation, which does not happen to all, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> method of doing good, which is in every one's power who has the money to spare, is by subscription to public charities. Public charities admit of this argument in their favour, that your money goes farther towards attaining the end for which it is given, than it can do by any private and separate beneficence. A guinea, for example, contributed to an infirmary, becomes the means of providing one patient, at least, with a physician, surgeon, apothecary, with medicine, diet, lodging, and suitable attendance; which is not the tenth part of what the same affluence, if it could be procured at all, would cost to a sick person or family in any other situation. 3. The last, and, compared with the former, the lowest exertion of benevolence, is in the relief of beggars. Nevertheless, the indiscriminate rejection of all who implore our alms, in this way, is by no means approved.

is defined by some a fallacious kind of reason, carrying some resemblance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, which a person, knowing its falsehood, advances in dispute for the sake of victory. The art of framing fictions <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fallacies is called by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a> cavillatoria.

CXXXVI

Pages 292-293
CATOPTRICS. 1.) The spherical convex mirror, GHI, (fig. 2); and the spherical concave mirror, GHI, (fig. 3.) 2.) The point K, (fig. 2, 3,) round which the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror is described, is called its centre. The line KH, drawn from its centre perpendicular to its two surfaces, is the axis of the mirror; and the point H, to which that line is drawn, is its vertex. 3.) The distance between the lines AG and BG, (fig. 1,) is called the angle of incidence, and the distance between BG and CG is the angle of reflection. Sect. II. Aphorisms. I. In a plane mirror. 1.) The image DF, (fig. 1,) will appear as far behind the mirror as the object AC is before it. 2.) The image will appear of the same size, and in the same position as the object. 3.) Every such mirror will reflect the image of an object of twice its own length and breadth. 4.) If the object be an opaque body, and its rays fall on the mirror nearly in direct lines, there will be only one image visible, which will be reflected by the inner surface of the glass. But, 5.) If the object be a luminous body, and its rays fall very obliquely on the mirror, there will appear to an eye placed in a proper position, several images; the first of which reflected from the outer surface of the glass, will not be so bright as the second, reflected from the inner surface. The following images, that are produced by the repeated reflections of the rays between the two surfaces of the glass, will be in proportion less vivid, to the eighth or tenth, which will be scarce visible. II. In a spherical convex mirror. 1.) The image DF, (fig. 2,), will always appear behind it. 2.) The image will be in the same position as the object. 3.) It will be less than the object. 4.) It will be curved, but not, as the mirror, spherical. 5.) Parallel rays falling on this mirror will have the focus or image at half the distance of the centre K from the mirror. 6.) In converging rays, the distance of the object must be equal to half the distance of the centre, to make the image appear behind the mirror. 7.) Diverging rays will have their image at less than half the distance of the centre. If the object be placed in the centre of the mirror, its image will appear at one eighth of that distance behind it. III. In a spherical concave mirror. 1.) That point where the image appears of the same dimensions as the object, is the centre of that mirror. 2.) Parallel rays will have their focus at one half the distance of the centre. 3.) Converging rays will form an image before the mirror. 4.) In diverging rays, if the object be at less than one-half the distance of the centre, the image will be behind the mirror, erect, curved, and magnified, as DEF, (fig. 3,) but if the distance of the object be greater, the image will be before the mirror, inverted and diminished, as DEF, (fig. 4.) 5.) The sun's rays falling on a concave mirror, and being parallel, will be collected in a focus at half the distance of its centre, where their heat will be augmented in proportion of the surface of the mirror to that of the focal spot. 6.) If a luminous body be placed in the focus of a concave mirror, its rays being reflected in parallel lines, will strongly enlighten a space of the same dimension with the mirror, at a great distance. If the luminous object be placed nearer than the focus, its rays will diverge, and consequently enlighten a larger space. It is on this principle that reverberators are constructed. IV. In all plane and spherical mirrors the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. Sect. III. Entertaining Experiments. I. Of all our senses the sight is certainly subject to the greatest illusion. The various writers on optics have described a great number of instances in which illusions deceives us, and have constantly endeavoured to investigate the causes, to explain their effects, and to reconcile appearance with reality. We every day discover new phenomena, and doubtless many more are reserved for posterity. It frequently happens, moreover, that a discovery which at first seemed of little consequence has led to matters of the highest importance. Take a glass bottle A (fig. 14,) and fill it with water to the point B; leave the upper part BC empty, and cork it in the common manner. Place this bottle opposite a concave mirror, and beyond its focus, that it may appear reversed, and before the mirror (see Sect. II. aph. 3, 4, of a spher. concave mirror,) place yourself still further distant from the bottle, and it will appear to you in the situation, a b c, (fig. 15.) Now it is remarkable in this apparent bottle, that the water, which, according to all the laws of catoptrics, and all the experiments made on other objects, should appear at a b, appears on the contrary at b c, and consequently the part a b appears empty. If the bottle be inverted and placed before the mirror (as in fig. 16.), its image will appear in its natural erect position; and the water, which is in reality at BC, will appear at a b. If while the bottle is inverted it be uncorked, and the water run gently out, it will appear, that while the part BC, is emptying, that of a b in the image is filling; and what is likewise very remarkable, as soon as the bottle is empty the illusion ceases, the image also appearing entirely empty. If the bottle likewise be quite full there is no illusion. If while the bottle is held inverted, and partly empty, some drops of water fall from the bottom A towards BC, it seems in the image as if there were formed at the bottom of that part a b, bubbles of air that rose from a to b; which is the part that seems full of water. All these phenomena constantly appear. The remarkable circumstances in this experiment are, first, not only to see an object where it is not, but also where the image is not; and secondly, that of two objects which are really in its same place, as the surface at one place, and the other at another; and to see the bottle in the place of its image, and the water where neither it nor its image are. II. Construct a box AB, of about a foot long, eight inches

in the other the tube MF, and observe that in each of these is to be inserted another tube, as H and I (a). Furnish the first of these tubes with an object-glass at G, and a concave eye-glass at F. You are to observe, that in regulating the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of these glasses, with regard to the length of the tube, you are to suppose it equal to the line G, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> visual pointed ray, which entering at the aperture G, is reflected by the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>, and goes out at the other aperture F, where the ocular glass is placed. Put any glass you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> into the two ends of the moveable tubes H and I; and lastly, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the machine on a stand E, moveable at the point S, that it may be elevated or depressed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. When the eye is placed at F, and you look through the tube, the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> that proceed from the object T, passing through the glass G, are successively reflected by the mirrors O, P, Q, and R, to the eye at F, and there paint the object T, in its proper situation, and these rays appear to proceed directly from that object. The two moveable tubes H and I, at the extremities of each of which a glass is placed, serve only the more to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> the illusion, for they have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the interior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the machine. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> being moveable on the stand E, may be directed to any object; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> furnished with proper glasses will answer the purpose of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>. The two moveable tubes H and I being brought together, the machine is directed toward any object, and desiring a person to look at the end F, you ask him if he sees distinctly that object. You then separate the two moveable tubes, and leaving a space between them sufficient to place your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, or any other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body; you tell him that the machine has the power of making objects visible through the most opaque body; and as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> you desire him then to look at the same object, when to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> surprise, he will see it as distinct as when there was no solid body placed between the tubes. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>, This experiment is the more extraordinary, as it is very difficult to conceive how the effect is produced. The two arms of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> appearing to be made to support the perspective glass; and to whatever object it is directed, the effect is still the same. VI. In the partition <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>, make two apertures, CD, and EF, of a foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and ten inches wide, and about a foot distant from each other. Let them be at the common height of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s head; and in each of them place a transparent glass, surrounded with a frame, like a common mirror. Behind this partition place two mirrors H and I, inclined to it in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of forty-five degrees; that is, half way between a line drawn perpendicular to the ground and its surface; let them be both 18 inches <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>: let all the space between them be enclosed, by boards or pasteboard painted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and well closed, that no light may enter: let there be also two curtains to cover them, which may be drawn aside at pleasure. When a person looks into one of these supposed mirrors, instead of seeing his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, he will perceive the object that is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the other; so that if two persons present themselves at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before these mirrors, instead of each one seeing himself, they will reciprocally see each other. Note, There should be a sconce with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> placed on each side of the two glasses in the wainscot, to enlighten the faces of the persons who look in them, otherwise this experiment will have no remarkable effect. This experiment may be considerably improved by placing the two glasses in the partition in adjoining rooms, and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons being previously placed in one room, when a stranger enters the other, you may tell him his face is dirty; and desire him to look in the glass, which he will naturally do; and on seeing a strange face he will draw back; but returning to it, and seeing another, another, and another, like the phantom kings in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a>, what his surprise will be is more easy to conceive than express. After this, a real mirror may be privately let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the back of the glass; and if he can be prevailed to look in it once more, he will then, to his further astonishment, see his own face; and may be told, perhaps persuaded, that all he thought he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> before was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> effect of imagination. How many tricks, less artful than this, have passed in former times for sorcery; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> at this time, in some countries, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a>! Note, When a man looks in a mirror that is placed perpendicular to another, his face will appear entirely deformed. If the mirror be a little inclined, so as to make an angle of 80 degrees (that is, one-ninth part from the perpendicular), he will then see all the parts of his face, except the nose and forehead. If it be inclined to 60 degrees (that is, one-third part), he will appear with three noses and six eyes: in short, the apparent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> will vary at each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of inclination; and when the glass comes to 45 degrees (that is, half-way down), the face will vanish. Instead of placing the two mirrors in this situation, they are so disposed that their junction may be vertical, their different inclinations will produce other effects; as the situation of the object relative to these mirrors is quite different. The effects of these mirrors, though remarkable enough, occasions but little surprise, as there is no method of concealing the cause by which they are produced. VII. Make a box of wood, of a cubical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, Fig. 13, ABCD, of about 15 inches every way. Let it be fixed to the pedestal P, at the usual height of a man's head. In each side of this box, let there be an opening. (a) These four tubes must terminate in the substance of the case, and not enter the inside, that they may not hinder the effect of the mirrors. The fourfold reflection of the rays of light from the mirrors, darkens in some degree the brightness of the object; some light is also lost by the magnifying power of the perspective: If, therefore, instead of the object-glass at G, and concave eye-glass at F, plain glasses were substituted; the magnifying power of the perspective will be taken away, and the object appear brighter. ing of an oval form, of ten inches high, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> wide. In this box place two mirrors A, D, with their backs against each other; let them <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the box in a diagonal line, and in a vertical position. Decorate the openings in the sides of this box with four oval frames and transparent glases, and cover each of them with a curtain, so contrived that they may all draw up together. Place four persons in front of the four sides, and at equal distances from the box, and then draw up the curtains that they may see themselves in the mirrors; when each of them, instead of his own figure, will see that of the person who is next him, and who, at the same time, will seem to him to be placed on the opposite side. Their confusion will be the greater, as it will be very difficult for them to discover the mirrors concealed in the box. The reason of this phenomenon is evident; for though the rays of light may be turned aside by a mirror, yet, as we have before said, they always appear to proceed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. VIII. Provide a box ABCD of about two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, 15 inches wide, and 12 inches high. At the end AC place a concave mirror, the focus of whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> rays is at 18 inches from the reflecting surface. At IL place a pasteboard blacked, in which a hole is cut sufficiently <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> to see on the mirror H the object placed at BEFD. Cover the top of the box, from A to I, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, that the mirror H may be entirely darkened. The other part IB must be covered with a glass, under which is placed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>. Make an aperture at G, near the top of the side EB; beneath which, on the inside, place, in succession, paintings of different subjects, as vistas, landscapes, &c., so that they may be in front of the mirror H. Let the box be so placed that the object may be strongly illuminated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, or by wax lights placed under the enclosed part of the box AI. By this simple <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> the objects placed at GD will be thrown into their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> perspective; and if the subjects be properly chosen, the appearance will be altogether as pleasing as in optical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> of a much more complicated form. Note, A glass mirror should be always here used, as those of metal do not represent the objects with equal vivacity, and are beside subject to tarnish. It is also necessary that the box be sufficiently large, that you may not be obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a mirror whose focus is too short; for in that case, the right lines near the border of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> will appear bent in the mirror, which will have a disagreeable effect, and cannot be avoided. IX. To set fire to a combustible body by the reflection of two concave mirrors, fig. 18. Place two concave mirrors, A and B, at about 12 or 15 feet distance from each other, and let the axis of each of them be in the same line. In the focus C of one of them, place a live coal, and in the focus D of the other some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>. With a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> bellows, which make a continual blast, keep constantly blowing the coal, and notwithstanding the distance between them, the powder will presently take fire. It is not necessary that these mirrors be of metal or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, those made of wood or pasteboard gilded, will produce the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a>, which has sometimes taken effect at the distance of 50 feet, when mirrors of 18 inches, or two feet diameter, have been used. This experiment succeeds with more difficulty at great distances; which may proceed from the moisture in a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. It would doubtless take effect more readily, if a tin tube, of an equal diameter with the mirrors, were to be placed between them. X. Behind the partition AB, place, in a position something oblique, the concave mirror EF, which must appear, be at least ten inches in diameter, and its distance from the partition equal to three-fourths of the distance of its centre. In the partition make an opening of seven or eight inches, either square or circular: it must face the mirror, and be of the same height with it. Behind this partition place a strong light, so disposed that it may not be seen at the opening, and may illumine an object placed at C, without throwing any light on the mirror. Beneath the aperture in the partition place the object C, that you intend shall appear on the outside of the partition, in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> position; and which we will suppose to be a flower. Before the partition, and beneath the aperture, place a little flowerpot D, the top of which should be even with the bottom of the aperture, that the eye, placed at G, may see the flower in the same position as if its stalk came out of the pot. Take care to paint the space between the back part of the partition and the mirror black, to prevent any reflections of light from being thrown on the mirror; in a word, so dispose the whole that it may be as little enlightened as possible. When a person is placed at the point G, he will perceive the flower that is behind the partition, at the top of the pot at D; but on putting out his hand to pluck it, he will find that he attempts to grasp a shadow. If in the opening of the partition a large double convex <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENS">lens</a> of a short focus be placed, or, which is not quite so well, a bottle of clear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the image of the flower reflected thereon will appear much more vivid and distinct.
